meta.title_en: The Revival of the Religious Sciences

chapters.title_en: The Revival of the Religious Sciences — Introduction and Overview of the Four Quarters
chapters.arabic_text:
### |

بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم
أحمد الله أولا حمدا كثيرا متواليا وإن كان يتضاءل دون حق جلاله حمد
الحامدين وأصلي واسلم على رسله ثانيا صلاة تستغرق مع سيد البشر سائر
المرسلين وأستخيره تعالى ثالثا فيما انبعث عزمي من تحرير كتاب في إحياء
علوم الدين وأنتدب لقطع تعجبك رابعا أيها العاذل المتغالي في العذل من بين
زمرة الجاحدين المسرف في التقريع (1) PageV01P001
والإنكار من بين طبقات المنكرين الغافلين فلقد حل عن لساني عقدة الصمت
وطوقني عهدة الكلام وقلادة النطق ما أنت مثابر عليه من العمى عن جلية الحق
مع اللجاج في نصرة الباطل وتحسين الجهل والتشغيب على من آثر النزوع قليلا
عن مراسم الخلق ومال ميلا يسيرا عن ملازمة الرسم إلى العمل بمقتضى العلم
طمعا في نيل ما تعبده الله تعالى به من تزكية النفس وإصلاح القلب وتداركا
لبعض ما فرط من إضاعة العمر يائسا عن تمام حاجتك في الحيرة وانحيازا عن
غمار من قال فيهم صاحب الشرع صلوات الله عليه وسلامه أشد الناس عذابا يوم
القيامة عالم لم ينفعه الله سبحانه بعلمه (1) ولعمري إنه لا سبب لإصرارك
على التكبر إلا الداء الذي عم الجم الغفير بل شمل الجماهير من القصور عن
ملاحظة ذروة هذا الأمر والجهل بأن الأمر إد والخطب جد والآخرة مقبلة
والدنيا مدبرة والأجل قريب والسفر بعيد والزاد طفيف والخطر عظيم والطريق سد
وما سوى الخالص لوجه الله من العلم والعمل عند الناقد البصير رد وسلوك طريق
الآخرة مع كثرة الغوائل من غير دليل ولا رفيق متعب ومكد فأدله الطريق هم
العلماء الذين هم ورثة الأنبياء وقد شغر منهم الزمان ولم يبق إلا المترسمون
وقد استحوذ على أكثرهم الشيطان واستغواهم الطغيان وأصبح كل واحد بعاجل حظه
مشغوفا فصار يرى المعروف منكرا والمنكر معروفا حتى ظل علم الدين مندرسا
ومنار الهدى في أقطار الأرض منطمسا ولقد خيلوا إلى الخلق أن لا علم إلا
فتوى حكومة تستعين به القضاة على فصل الخصام عند تهاوش الطغام أو جدل يتدرع
به طالب المباهاة إلى  الغلبة والإفحام أو سجع مزخرف يتوسل به الواعظ إلى
استدراج العوام إذ لم يروا ما سوى هذه الثلاثة مصيدة للحرام وشبكة للحطام
فأما علم طريق الآخرة وما درج عليه السلف الصالح مما سماه الله سبحانه في
كتابه فقها وحكمة وعلما وضياء ونورا وهداية ورشدا فقد أصبح من بين الخلق
مطويا وصار نسيا منسيا
ولما كان هذا ثلما في الدين ملما وخطبا مدلهما رأيت الاشتغال بتحرير هذا
الكتاب مهما إحياء لعلوم الدين وكشفا عن مناهج الأئمة المتقدمين وإيضاحا
لمباهي العلوم النافعة عند التبيين والسلف الصالحين
وقد أسسته على أربعة أرباع وهي ربع العبادات وربع العادات وربع المهلكات
وربع المنجيات
وصدرت الجملة بكتاب العلم لأنه غاية المهم لأكشف أولا عن العلم الذي تعبد
الله على لسان رسوله صلى الله عليه وسلم الأعيان بطلبه إذ قال رسول الله
صلى الله عليه وسلم طلب العلم فريضة على كل مسلم (2) وأميز فيه العلم
النافع من الضار إذ قال صلى الله عليه وسلم نعوذ بالله من علم لا ينفع (3)
وأحقق ميل أهل العصر عن شاكلة الصواب وانخداعهم بلامع السراب واقتناعهم من
العلوم بالقشر عن اللباب
ويشتمل ربع العبادات على عشرة كتب كتاب العلم وكتاب قواعد العقائد وكتاب
أسرار الطهارة وكتاب أسرار الصلاة وكتاب أسرار الزكاة وكتاب أسرار الصيام
وكتاب أسرار الحج وكتاب آداب تلاوة القرآن وكتاب الأذكار والدعوات وكتاب
ترتيب الأوراد في الأوقات PageV01P002
وأما ربع العادات فيشتمل على عشرة كتب كتاب آداب الأكل وكتاب آداب النكاح
وكتاب أحكام الكسب وكتاب الحلال والحرام وكتاب آداب الصحبة والمعاشرة مع
أصناف الخلق وكتاب العزلة وكتاب آداب السفر وكتاب السماع والوجد وكتاب
الأمر بالمعروف والنهي عن المنكر وكتاب آداب المعيشة وأخلاق النبوة
وأما ربع المهلكات فيشتمل على عشرة كتب كتاب شرح عجائب القلب وكتاب رياضة
النفس وكتاب آفات الشهوتين شهوة البطن وشهوة الفرج وكتاب آفات اللسان وكتاب
آفات الغضب والحقد والحسد وكتاب ذم الدنيا وكتاب ذم المال والبخل وكتاب ذم
الجاه والرياء وكتاب ذم الكبر والعجب وكتاب ذم الغرور
وأما  ربع المنجيات فيشتمل على عشرة كتب كتاب التوبة وكتاب الصبر والشكر
وكتاب الخوف والرجاء وكتاب الفقر والزهد وكتاب التوحيد والتوكل وكتاب
المحبة والشوق والأنس والرضا وكتاب النية والصدق والإخلاص وكتاب المراقبة
والمحاسبة وكتاب التفكر وكتاب ذكر الموت
فأما ربع العبادات فأذكر فيه خفايا آدابها ودقائق سننها وأسرار معانيها
ما يضطر العالم العامل إليه بل لا يكون من علماء الآخرة من لا يطلع عليه
وأكثر ذلك مما أهمل في فن الفقهيات
وأما ربع العادات فأذكر فيه أسرار المعاملات الجارية بين الخلق وأغوارها
ودقائق سننها وخفايا الورع في مجاريها وهي مما لا يستغني عنها متدين
وأما ربع المهلكات فأذكر فيه كل خلق مذموم ورد القرآن بإماطته وتزكية
النفس عنه وتطهير القلب منه وأذكر من كل واحد من تلك الأخلاق حده وحقيقته
ثم أذكر سببه الذي منه يتولد ثم الآفات التي عليها تترتب ثم العلامات التي
بها تتعرف ثم طرق المعالجة التي بها منها يتخلص كل ذلك مقرونا بشواهد
الآيات والأخبار والآثار
وأما ربع المنجيات فأذكر فيه كل خلق محمود وخصلة مرغوب فيها من خصال
المقربين والصديقين التي بها يتقرب العبد من رب العالمين وأذكر في كل خصلة
حدها وحقيقتها وسببها الذي به تجتلب وثمرتها التي منها تستفاد وعلامتها
التي بها تتعرف وفضيلتها التي لأجلها فيها يرغب مع ما ورد فيها من شواهد
الشرع والعقل ولقد صنف الناس في بعض هذه المعاني كتبا ولكن يتميز هذا
الكتاب عنها بخمسة أمور
الأول حل ما عقدوه وكشف ما أجملوه
الثاني ترتيب ما بددوه ونظم ما فرقوه
الثالث إيجاز ما طولوه وضبط ما قرروه
الرابع حذف ما كرروه وإثبات ما حرروه
الخامس تحقيق أمور غامضة اعتاصت على الأفهام لم يتعرض لها في الكتب أصلا
إذ الكل وإن تواردوا على منهج واحد فلا مستنكر أن يتفرد كل واحد من
السالكين بالتنبيه لأمر يخصه ويغفل عنه رفقاؤه أو لا يغفل عن التنبيه ولكن
يسهو عن إيراده في الكتب أو لا يسهو ولكن يصرفه عن كشف الغطاء عنه صارف
فهذه خواص هذا الكتاب مع كونه حاويا لمجامع هذه العلوم
وإنما حملني على تأسيس هذا الكتاب على أربعة أرباع أمران أحدهما وهو
الباعث الأصلي أن هذا الترتيب في التحقيق والتفهيم كالضرورة لأن العلم الذي
يتوجه به إلى الآخرة ينقسم إلى علم المعاملة وعلم المكاشفة وأعني
PageV01P003
بعلم المكاشفة ما يطلب منه كشف المعلوم فقط وأعني بعلم المعاملة ما يطلب
منه مع الكشف العمل به والمقصود من هذا الكتاب علم المعاملة فقط دون علم
المكاشفة التي لا رخصة في إيداعها الكتب وإن كانت هي غاية مقصد الطالبين
ومطمع نظر الصديقين وعلم المعاملة طريق إليه ولكن لم يتكلم الأنبياء صلوات
الله عليهم مع الخلق إلا في علم الطريق والإرشاد إليه
وأما علم المكاشفة فلم يتكلموا فيه إلا بالرمز والإيماء على سبيل التمثيل
والإجمال علما منهم بقصور أفهام الخلق عن الاحتمال والعلماء ورثة الأنبياء
فما لهم سبيل إلى العدول عن نهج التأسي والاقتداء ثم إن علم المعاملة ينقسم
إلى علم ظاهر أعني العلم بأعمال الجوارح وإلى علم باطن أعني العلم بأعمال
القلوب والجاري على الجوارح إما عادة وإما عبادة والوارد على القلوب التي
هي بحكم الاحتجاب عن الحواس من عالم الملكوت إما محمود وإما مذموم فبالواجب
انقسم هذا العلم إلى شطرين ظاهر وباطن والشطر الظاهر المتعلق بالجوارح
انقسم إلى عادة وعبادة والشطر الباطن المتعلق بأحوال القلب وأخلاق النفس
انقسم إلى مذموم ومحمود فكان المجموع أربعة أقسام ولا يشذ نظر في علم
المعاملة عن هذه الأقسام
الباعث الثاني
أني رأيت الرغبة من طلبة العلم صادقة في الفقه الذي صلح عند من لا يخاف
الله سبحانه وتعالى المتدرع به إلى المباهاة والاستظهار بجاهه ومنزلته في
المنافسات وهو مرتب على أربعة أرباع والمتزيي بزي المحبوب محبوب فلم أبعد
أن يكون تصوير الكتاب بصورة الفقه تلطفا في استدراج القلوب ولهذا تلطف بعض
من رام استمالة قلوب الرؤساء إلى الطب فوضعه على هيئة تقويم النجوم موضوعا
في الجداول والرقوم وسماه تقويم الصحة ليكون أنسهم بذلك الجنس جاذبا لهم
إلى  المطالعة والتلطف في اجتذاب القلوب إلى العلم الذي يفيد حياة الأبد أهم
من التلطف في اجتذابها إلى الطب الذي لا يفيد إلا صحة الجسد فثمرة هذا
العلم طب القلوب والأرواح المتوصل به إلى حياة تدوم أبد الآباد فأين منه
الطب الذي يعالج به الأجساد وهي معرضة بالضرورة للفساد في أقرب الآماد
فنسأل الله سبحانه التوفيق للرشاد والسداد إنه كريم جواد
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ح-م-د (ḥ-m-d)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To praise, to commend; praise rendered for beneficence received; the core sense is the acknowledgment of excellence and favor.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Praise (ḥamd) is the acknowledgment of the Beneficent (al-Munʿim) with veneration; it is the verbal counterpart to gratitude (shukr) which is the acknowledgment of favor through action.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal usage (ḥaqīqah) is praise directed to God for His essential attributes; metaphorical usage (majāz) is praise of creatures for contingent qualities.
- Sībawayh Rule: Inceptive Clause (al-ibtidāʾ) — The opening "I praise God" (aḥmadu Allāha) is a nominal sentence with an implied subject, establishing the authorial voice and the foundational act of worship before all discourse.

- Root: ع-ل-م (ʿ-l-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Knowledge, cognition, perception of a thing as it is; the opposite of ignorance (jahl).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Knowledge (ʿilm) is the apprehension of the reality of a thing; in the Qur'an it is distinguished from mere opinion (ẓann) and is the means by which the servant draws near to God.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal knowledge is certain apprehension; metaphorical usage extends to the means of knowledge (e.g., the known object, the act of teaching).
- Sībawayh Rule: ʿAṭf al-Bayān (Appositional Clarification) — The sequence "knowledge, wisdom, light, guidance, right-mindedness" (ʿilman wa ḥikmatan wa ḍiyāʾan wa nūran wa hidāyatan wa rushdan) functions as explanatory apposition, each term clarifying the nature of the true religious science.

- Root: ق-ل-ب (q-l-b)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The heart; the physical organ and, by extension, the seat of intellect and spiritual perception; the root conveys the idea of turning and alternating.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The heart (qalb) is the locus of understanding (fahm) and discernment (tamyīz); its rectification (iṣlāḥ) is the very purpose of religious devotion.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal usage is the physical organ; metaphorical usage is the spiritual faculty that perceives divine realities.
- Sībawayh Rule: Taʿlīq (Suspension) — The clause "the rectification of the heart" (iṣlāḥ al-qalb) is governed by the preceding verbal noun "attainment" (nayl), showing the teleological structure of the author's purpose.
chapters.translation:
In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

I praise God, firstly, with abundant and continuous praise—even though the praise of all praisers falls short of the due measure of His majestic glory. And I send blessings and peace, secondly, upon His messengers—a blessing that encompasses, along with the master of mankind, all the other messengers. And I seek His guidance, thirdly, in what my resolve has arisen to accomplish: the composition of a book on the Revival of the Religious Sciences. And I undertake, fourthly, to silence your reproach, O you who exceed all bounds in blame among the ranks of the deniers, and who are immoderate in censure and rejection among the classes of the heedless objectors!

For the knot of silence has been loosened from my tongue, and the covenant of speech and the necklace of utterance have been bound upon me—[speech] concerning what you persist in: blindness to the clear truth, obstinacy in defending falsehood, beautifying ignorance, and railing against one who has chosen to withdraw somewhat from the conventions of the people, and who has inclined slightly away from clinging to mere custom toward acting in accordance with knowledge—hoping thereby to attain what God, exalted is He, has made obligatory upon him: the purification of the soul and the rectification of the heart—and seeking to make up for some of what has been squandered of his life in heedlessness, despairing of your complete need being fulfilled in your perplexity, and withdrawing from the throng of those of whom the Master of the Law—God's blessings and peace be upon him—said: {«The most severely punished of people on the Day of Resurrection is a scholar whom God, glorified is He, did not benefit with his knowledge»}.

By my life! There is no cause for your persistence in arrogance except the malady that has afflicted the great multitude—nay, that has encompassed the masses—namely, the failure to observe the summit of this matter, and ignorance of the fact that the affair is grave, the matter is serious, the Hereafter is approaching, this world is receding, the term is near, the journey is long, the provision is meager, the peril is great, and the road is blocked. And nothing other than what is purely for the face of God—of knowledge and action—is, in the sight of the discerning critic, rejected. And traversing the path of the Hereafter, amid its many perils, without a guide or a companion, is wearisome and toilsome.

The guides of the path are the scholars, who are the heirs of the prophets. Yet the age has become empty of them, and none remain but those who merely imitate the outward forms. Satan has gained mastery over most of them, and tyranny has led them astray. Each one has become infatuated with his immediate share, so that he now sees the known good as evil and evil as the known good—until the science of religion has become obliterated, and the beacon of guidance in the regions of the earth has been extinguished.

They have made it appear to the people that there is no knowledge except the legal opinion (fatwā) of governance by which judges aid themselves in settling disputes when the rabble clash, or disputation by which the seeker of vainglory arms himself to achieve victory and silencing of opponents, or embellished rhymed prose by which the preacher seeks to entice the common folk. For they have seen nothing beyond these three as a snare for the forbidden and a net for ruin.

As for the science of the path of the Hereafter—that upon which the righteous predecessors (al-salaf al-ṣāliḥūn) proceeded, which God, glorified is He, named in His Book "jurisprudence" (fiqh), "wisdom" (ḥikmah), "knowledge" (ʿilm), "illumination" (ḍiyāʾ), "light" (nūr), "guidance" (hidāyah), and "right-mindedness" (rushd)—it has become folded away among the people and rendered utterly forgotten.

Since this was a breach in religion of grave import and a calamity of immense magnitude, I saw that occupying myself with the composition of this book would be a revival of the religious sciences, an unveiling of the methodologies of the earlier imams, and a clarification of the splendors of the beneficial sciences upon examination—and [a revival] of the righteous predecessors.

I have founded it upon four quarters (rubāʿ): the Quarter of Acts of Worship (rubʿ al-ʿibādāt), the Quarter of Customs and Daily Practices (rubʿ al-ʿādāt), the Quarter of Destructive Matters (rubʿ al-muhlikāt), and the Quarter of Saving Matters (rubʿ al-munjiyāt).

I have prefaced the whole with the Book of Knowledge, for it is the most important of all. For I wish first to make clear the knowledge whose pursuit God, on the tongue of His Messenger—peace be upon him—has made obligatory upon individuals, for he said: {«The pursuit of knowledge is an obligation upon every Muslim»}. And I wish to distinguish therein the beneficial knowledge from the harmful, for he said—peace be upon him: {«We seek refuge in God from knowledge that does not benefit»}. And I wish to make manifest the deviation of the people of this age from the path of correctness, their being deceived by the glittering mirage, and their contentment with the husks of the sciences instead of their kernels.

The Quarter of Acts of Worship comprises ten books: the Book of Knowledge; the Book of the Foundations of Beliefs; the Book of the Secrets of Purification; the Book of the Secrets of Prayer; the Book of the Secrets of Almsgiving (zakāh); the Book of the Secrets of Fasting; the Book of the Secrets of Pilgrimage (ḥajj); the Book of the Etiquettes of Qur'anic Recitation; the Book of Remembrances (adhkār) and Supplications; and the Book of the Ordering of Liturgical Wirds (awrād) in their Times.

As for the Quarter of Customs and Daily Practices, it comprises ten books: the Book of the Etiquettes of Eating; the Book of the Etiquettes of Marriage; the Book of the Rulings on Earning a Livelihood; the Book of the Lawful and the Unlawful; the Book of the Etiquettes of Companionship and Social Intercourse with the Various Classes of People; the Book of Seclusion (ʿuzlah); the Book of the Etiquettes of Travel; the Book of Auditory Experience (samāʿ) and Ecstatic Rapture (wajd); the Book of Enjoining the Good and Forbidding the Evil; and the Book of the Etiquettes of Daily Living and the Moral Traits of Prophethood.

As for the Quarter of Destructive Matters, it comprises ten books: the Book of the Explanation of the Wonders of the Heart; the Book of the Discipline of the Soul; the Book of the Harms of the Two Appetites—the appetite of the belly and the appetite of the loins; the Book of the Harms of the Tongue; the Book of the Harms of Anger, Resentment, and Envy; the Book of the Censure of This World; the Book of the Censure of Wealth and Miserliness; the Book of the Censure of Status and Ostentation (riyāʾ); the Book of the Censure of Pride and Self-Admiration; and the Book of the Censure of Delusion (ghurūr).

As for the Quarter of Saving Matters, it comprises ten books: the Book of Repentance (tawbah); the Book of Patience (ṣabr) and Gratitude (shukr); the Book of Fear (khawf) and Hope (rajāʾ); the Book of Poverty (faqr) and Asceticism (zuhd); the Book of Divine Unity (tawḥīd) and Trust in God (tawakkul); the Book of Love (maḥabbah), Longing (shawq), Intimacy (uns), and Contentment (riḍā); the Book of Intention (niyyah), Truthfulness (ṣidq), and Sincerity (ikhlāṣ); the Book of Self-Watchfulness (murāqabah) and Self-Reckoning (muḥāsabah); the Book of Reflection (tafakkur); and the Book of the Remembrance of Death (dhikr al-mawt).

In the Quarter of Acts of Worship, I shall mention the hidden etiquettes thereof, the subtleties of its practices (sunan), and the secrets of its meanings—such things as the practicing scholar is compelled to know; nay, no one is among the scholars of the Hereafter who does not come to know them. And most of this is what has been neglected in the art of jurisprudence (fiqh).

In the Quarter of Customs and Daily Practices, I shall mention the secrets of the transactions that occur among people, their depths, the subtleties of their practices, and the hidden aspects of scrupulous piety (waraʿ) in their conduct—matters from which no religious person can dispense.

In the Quarter of Destructive Matters, I shall mention every blameworthy trait that the Qur'an has commanded to be removed, and the purification of the soul from it, and the cleansing of the heart from it. And I shall mention, for each of these traits, its definition (ḥadd) and its reality (ḥaqīqah); then its cause from which it is generated; then the harms that are consequent upon it; then the signs by which it is recognized; then the methods of treatment by which one is delivered from it—all of this accompanied by evidences from the verses [of the Qur'an], the reports [of the Prophet], and the traditions [of the Companions].

In the Quarter of Saving Matters, I shall mention every praiseworthy trait and desirable quality among the characteristics of those brought near (al-muqarrabūn) and the veracious (al-ṣiddīqūn), by which the servant draws near to the Lord of the Worlds. And I shall mention, for each quality, its definition, its reality, its cause by which it is attracted, its fruit from which benefit is derived, its sign by which it is recognized, and its excellence on account of which it is desired—along with what has been reported concerning it from the evidences of the Sacred Law and reason.

People have indeed composed books on some of these meanings, but this book is distinguished from them by five things:

First: the resolution of what they have left unresolved, and the unveiling of what they have summarized.
Second: the ordering of what they have scattered, and the systematizing of what they have dispersed.
Third: the abridgment of what they have lengthened, and the consolidation of what they have established.
Fourth: the deletion of what they have repeated, and the affirmation of what they have verified.
Fifth: the elucidation of obscure matters that have defied comprehension and that have not been addressed in the books at all.

For although all [authors] have converged upon a single path, there is nothing objectionable in each of the wayfarers being uniquely granted the indication of a matter particular to him, which his companions have neglected—or not neglected the indication, but forgotten to include it in their books—or not forgotten, but a hindrance has turned them away from unveiling it.

These, then, are the distinctive properties of this book, along with its being comprehensive of the sum total of these sciences.

What impelled me to found this book upon four quarters are two matters. The first—and it is the original motive—is that this arrangement is, in truth and for the purpose of understanding, virtually necessary. For the knowledge by which one is directed toward the Hereafter divides into the science of practical conduct (ʿilm al-muʿāmalah) and the science of unveiling (ʿilm al-mukāshafah). By "the science of unveiling" I mean that from which only the unveiling of the known object is sought. By "the science of practical conduct" I mean that from which, along with unveiling, action in accordance with it is sought. The purpose of this book is only the science of practical conduct, not the science of unveiling—for there is no license to deposit the latter in books, even though it is the ultimate goal of the seekers and the aspiration of the vision of the veracious. The science of practical conduct is the path to it. But the prophets—God's blessings be upon them—did not speak to the people except concerning the science of the path and guidance toward it.

As for the science of unveiling, they did not speak of it except by allusion and indication, by way of metaphor and summary—knowing, as they did, the inadequacy of people's intellects to bear it. And the scholars are the heirs of the prophets; what path have they to deviate from the course of emulation and following?

Then the science of practical conduct divides into an outward science—namely, knowledge of the acts of the bodily members—and an inward science—namely, knowledge of the acts of the hearts. What proceeds from the bodily members is either custom (ʿādah) or worship (ʿibādah). What enters upon the hearts—which, by virtue of their being veiled from the senses, belong to the realm of the Kingdom (malakūt)—is either praiseworthy or blameworthy. Necessarily, therefore, this science divides into two halves: outward and inward. The outward half, pertaining to the bodily members, divides into custom and worship. The inward half, pertaining to the states of the heart and the traits of the soul, divides into the blameworthy and the praiseworthy. Thus the total becomes four divisions, and no consideration within the science of practical conduct falls outside these divisions.

The second motive: I have observed that the desire of the students of knowledge is sincere concerning jurisprudence (fiqh)—that [jurisprudence] which has become serviceable for those who do not fear God, glorified and exalted is He, arming themselves with it for vainglory and seeking support through its prestige and standing in competitions. And it is arranged upon four quarters. And one who is adorned with the adornment of the beloved is beloved. So I did not deem it far-fetched that the fashioning of this book in the form of jurisprudence would be a subtle means of enticing hearts [toward the truth]. For this reason, one of those who sought to win the hearts of the powerful to medicine subtly composed it in the form of an astrological almanac, arranged in tables and figures, and called it "The Almanac of Health" (taqwīm al-ṣiḥḥah)—so that their familiarity with that genre would draw them to perusal. And the subtlety in drawing hearts to the knowledge that yields the life of eternity is more important than the subtlety in drawing them to medicine, which yields only the health of the body. For the fruit of this knowledge is the healing of hearts and spirits, by which one attains to a life that endures for all eternity. Where is medicine—which treats bodies that are necessarily subject to corruption in the nearest of times—compared to it?

So we ask God, glorified is He, for success in right guidance and soundness of action. Verily, He is Generous, Bountiful.

chapters.title_en: The Book of Knowledge, Containing Seven Chapters
chapters.arabic_text:
### |

### || كتاب العلم وفيه سبعة أبواب

الباب الأول في فضل العلم والتعليم والتعلم
الباب الثاني في فرض العين وفرض الكفاية من العلوم وبيان حد الفقه
والكلام من علم الدين وبيان علم الآخرة وعلم الدنيا
الباب الثالث فيما تعده العامة من علوم الدين وليس منه وفيه بيان جنس
العلم المذموم وقدره
الباب الرابع في آفات المناظرة وسبب اشتغال الناس بالخلاف والجدل
الباب الخامس في آداب المعلم والمتعلم
الباب السادس في آفات العلم والعلماء والعلامات الفارقة بين علماء الدنيا
والآخرة
الباب السابع في العقل وفضله وأقسامه وما جاء فيه من الأخبار

### ||| الباب الأول في فضل العلم والتعليم والتعلم وشواهده من النقل والعقل
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ع ل م (ʿ-l-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Knowledge, perception, and the mark or sign by which a thing is known; the act of knowing as distinct from mere opinion (ẓann).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): ʿIlm as the firm comprehension of a thing as it truly is (idrāk al-shayʾ ʿalā mā huwa bihi), encompassing both divine and human knowledge; its opposite is jahl (ignorance).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) usage denotes certain cognition; metaphorical (majāz) usage extends to the known object itself (al-maʿlūm) or to the act of teaching (taʿlīm).
- Root: ف ر ض (f-r-ḍ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To make obligatory, to determine, to cut or notch; a prescribed duty with a fixed limit.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Farḍ as that which God has decisively required, divided into farḍ al-ʿayn (individual obligation) and farḍ al-kifāyah (communal sufficiency obligation).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense is the cutting of a thing; metaphorically, the divine decree that cuts through human discretion, fixing what must be done.
- Root: ف ق ه (f-q-h)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Deep understanding and discernment; in the ʿAyn, the penetration into the inner meaning of speech.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Fiqh as the comprehensive comprehension of religious rulings and their underlying wisdoms, not mere memorization of legal branches.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal usage is the understanding of intent; technical usage restricts it to knowledge of the sharīʿah's practical rulings.
- Root: ك ل م (k-l-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Speech, utterance, and wounding; the act of speaking that affects the hearer.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Kalām as the science of theological discourse (ʿilm al-kalām) concerning divine unity and attributes, defending creed through rational argument.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense is articulate speech; metaphorical sense denotes the discipline of rational theology that "wounds" falsehood through argument.
- Root: ج د ل (j-d-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To twist, to braid tightly; disputation that interweaves arguments.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Jadāl as argumentation aimed at victory, often blameworthy when it departs from truth-seeking.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense is the twisting of ropes; metaphorical sense is the twisting of speech in debate, whether praiseworthy (against falsehood) or blameworthy (for vanity).
- Sībawayh Rule: Al-ʿAṭf bi-al-Bāb (Coordination of Chapter Headings) — The repeated use of "الباب" with ordinal numerals (الأول، الثاني...) establishes a coordinated series governed by the genitive construction (al-iḍāfah) with "كتاب العلم," each heading functioning as a nominal sentence with an implied predicate (al-mubtadaʾ wa-al-khabar).
chapters.translation:
I say: This is the Book of Knowledge, and it contains seven chapters.

Chapter One: On the excellence of knowledge, of teaching, and of learning.
Chapter Two: On the individual obligation (farḍ al-ʿayn) and the communal sufficiency obligation (farḍ al-kifāyah) with respect to the sciences; and on the clarification of the limit of jurisprudence (fiqh) and of theology (kalām) as belonging to the science of religion; and on the science of the Hereafter and the science of this world.
Chapter Three: On those things which the common people count among the religious sciences but which are not of them; and in it is the clarification of the genus of blameworthy knowledge and its measure.
Chapter Four: On the afflictions of disputation (munāẓarah) and the cause of people's occupation with contention (khilāf) and argumentation (jadāl).
Chapter Five: On the etiquette of the teacher and the student.
Chapter Six: On the afflictions of knowledge and of the scholars, and the distinguishing marks between the scholars of this world and the scholars of the Hereafter.
Chapter Seven: On the intellect (ʿaql), its excellence, its divisions, and what has come down concerning it from the transmitted reports (akhbār).

Then follows: Chapter One: On the excellence of knowledge, of teaching, and of learning, and its evidences from transmission (naql) and reason (ʿaql).

chapters.title_en: The First Chapter on the Excellence of Knowledge, Teaching, and Learning, with Its Evidences from Transmission and Reason
chapters.arabic_text: || الباب الأول في فضل العلم والتعليم والتعلم وشواهده من النقل والعقل
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ف ض ل (faḍl)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Increase, surplus, excellence; that which exceeds necessity or equality.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Merit (faḍīlah) as a moral and intellectual virtue; in theological usage, divine grace (faḍl) as unmerited bounty.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense is "excess" (ziyādah); metaphorical sense is "superiority in rank or virtue" — here used in the latter, established as ḥaqīqah ʿurfiyyah (customary literal).
- Root: ع ل م (ʿilm)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Firm comprehension, cognition, knowledge; opposite of ignorance (jahl).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Knowledge as the apprehension of a thing as it is (idrāk al-shayʾ ʿalā mā huwa bihi); in Kalām, distinguished from mere opinion (ẓann) and conjecture.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — certainty (yaqīn); metaphorical — any cognitive state, but here strictly literal as certain knowledge.
- Root: ع ل م (ʿallama) / ت ع ل م (taʿallama)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Teaching (taʿlīm) is the act of causing another to know; learning (taʿallum) is the receptive acquisition of knowledge.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Teaching is a divine attribute (al-Muʿallim) and a prophetic function; learning is the human counterpart, an act of worship when pursued for God.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Both are literal actions, but rhetorically paired to emphasize the reciprocal relation (musāwāt) between giver and receiver.
- Root: ش ه د (shahida)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To witness, testify, be present; evidence (shāhid) as that which makes something manifest.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In proof (istidlāl), shawāhid are the empirical or transmitted evidences that corroborate a rational claim.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — presence at an event; metaphorical — any proof or indication (dalīl) that "attests" to a truth.
- Root: ن ق ل (naql) / ع ق ل (ʿaql)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Naql — transmission, conveyance (of reports); ʿaql — intellect, reason, that which binds and restrains.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Naql refers to revealed texts (naql sharʿī) — Qurʾān and Ḥadīth; ʿaql is the God-given faculty of discernment (nūr fī al-qalb).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Naql is literal "carrying over" (of words); ʿaql is metaphorical "binding" (of the soul from error) — here paired as complementary sources of proof.
- Sībawayh Rule: Al-ʿAṭf bi-al-Wāw (Coordination with "and") — The wāw in "التعليم والتعلم" coordinates two masdars of the same root, indicating inseparable duality; the genitive construction "فضل العلم" (iḍāfah) establishes the topic as a single conceptual domain, with "شواهده" (its evidences) as an appositional expansion (badal) specifying the two-fold proof structure.
chapters.translation: I say: The First Chapter concerns the excellence of knowledge, of teaching, and of learning, together with its evidences drawn from both transmitted revelation (naql) and rational inquiry (ʿaql).

chapters.title_en: The Virtue of Knowledge (Faḍīlat al-ʿIlm)
chapters.arabic_text:
||| فضيلة العلم

شواهدها من القرآن قوله عز وجل شهد الله أنه لا إله إلا هو والملائكة
وأولو العلم قائما بالقسط فانظر
PageV01P004
كيف بدأ سبحانه وتعالى بنفسه وثنى بالملائكة وثلث بأهل العلم وناهيك بهذا
شرفا وفضلا وجلاء ونبلا وقال الله تعالى {يرفع الله الذين آمنوا منكم
والذين أوتوا العلم درجات} قال ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما للعلماء درجات فوق
المؤمنين بسبعمائة درجة ما بين الدرجتين مسيرة خمسمائة عام
وقال عز وجل {قل هل يستوي الذين يعلمون والذين لا يعلمون} وقال تعالى
{إنما يخشى الله من عباده العلماء} وقال تعالى {قل كفى بالله شهيدا بيني
وبينكم ومن عنده علم الكتاب} وقال تعالى {قال الذي عنده علم من الكتاب أنا
آتيك به} تنبيها على أنه اقتدر بقوة العلم
وقال عز وجل {وقال الذين أوتوا العلم ويلكم ثواب الله خير لمن آمن وعمل
صالحا} بين أن عظم قدر الآخرة يعلم بالعلم
وقال تعالى {وتلك الأمثال  نضربها للناس وما يعقلها إلا العالمون} وقال
تعالى {ولو ردوه إلى الرسول وإلى أولي الأمر منهم لعلمه الذين يستنبطونه
منهم} رد حكمه في الوقائع إلى استنباطهم وألحق رتبتهم برتبة الأنبياء في
كشف حكم الله
وقيل في قوله تعالى يا بني آدم قد أنزلنا عليكم لباسا يواري سوءاتكم يعني
العلم وريشا يعني اليقين ولباس التقوى يعني الحياء
وقال عز وجل {ولقد جئناهم بكتاب فصلناه على علم} وقال تعالى {فلنقصن
عليهم بعلم} وقال عز وجل {بل هو آيات بينات في صدور الذين أوتوا العلم}
وقال تعالى {خلق الإنسان علمه البيان} وإنما ذكر ذلك في معرض الامتنان
وأما الأخبار فقال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم من يرد الله به خيرا
يفقهه في الدين ويلهمه رشده (1) وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم العلماء ورثة
الأنبياء (2) ومعلوم أنه لا رتبة فوق النبوة ولا شرف فوق شرف الوراثة لتلك
الرتبة
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم يستغفر للعالم ما في السموات والأرض (3) وأي
منصب يزيد على منصب من تشتغل ملائكة السموات والأرض بالاستغفار له
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم إن الحكمة تزيد الشريف شرفا وترفع المملوك حتى
يدرك مدارك الملوك (4) وقد نبه بهذا على ثمراته في الدنيا ومعلوم أن الآخرة
خير وأبقى
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم خصلتان لا يكونان في منافق حسن سمت وفقه في
الدين (5) ولا تشكن في الحديث لنفاق بعض فقهاء الزمان فإنه ما أراد به
الفقه الذي ظننته وسيأتي معنى الفقه
وأدنى درجات الفقيه أن يعلم أن الآخرة خير من الدنيا وهذه المعرفة إذا
صدقت وغلبت عليه برىء بها من النفاق والرياء
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم أفضل الناس المؤمن العالم الذي إن احتيج إليه
نفع وإن استغني عنه أغنى نفسه (6) وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم الإيمان عريان
ولباسه التقوى وزينته الحياء وثمرته العلم (7) وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم
أقرب الناس من درجة النبوة أهل العلم والجهاد أما أهل العلم فدلوا الناس
على ما جاءت به الرسل وأما أهل الجهاد فجاهدوا بأسيافهم PageV01P005
على  ما جاءت به الرسل (1)
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم لموت قبيلة أيسر من موت عالم (2) وقال عليه
الصلاة والسلام الناس معادن كمعادن الذهب والفضة فخيارهم في الجاهلية
خيارهم في الإسلام إذا فقهوا (3) وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم يوزن يوم القيامة
مداد العلماء بدم الشهداء (4) وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم من حفظ على أمتي
أربعين حديثا من السنة حتى يؤديها إليهم كنت له شفيعا وشهيدا يوم القيامة
(5) وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم من حمل من أمتي أربعين حديثا لقي الله عز وجل
يوم القيامة فقيها عالما (6) وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم من تفقه في دين الله
عز وجل كفاه الله تعالى ما أهمه ورزقه من حيث لا يحتسب (7) وقال صلى الله
عليه وسلم أوحى الله عز وجل إلى إبراهيم عليه السلام يا إبراهيم إني عليم
أحب كل عليم (8) وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم العالم أمين الله سبحانه في الأرض
(9) وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم صنفان من أمتي إذا صلحوا صلح الناس وإذا فسدوا
فسد الناس الأمراء والفقهاء (10) وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم إذا أتى علي يوم
لا أزداد فيه علما يقربني إلى الله عز وجل فلا بورك لي في طلوع شمس ذلك
اليوم (11) وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم في تفضيل العلم على العبادة والشهادة
فضل العالم على العابد كفضلي على أدنى رجل من أصحابي (12) فانظر كيف جعل
العلم مقارنا لدرجة النبوة وكيف حط رتبة العمل المجرد عن العلم وإن كان
العابد لا يخلو عن علم بالعبادة التي يواظب عليها ولولاه لم تكن عبادة وقال
صلى الله عليه وسلم فضل العالم على العابد كفضل القمر ليلة البدر على سائر
الكواكب (13) وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم يشفع يوم القيامة ثلاثة الأنبياء ثم
العلماء ثم الشهداء (14) فأعظم بمرتبة هي تلو النبوة وفوق الشهادة مع ما
ورد في فضل الشهادة
وقال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم ما عبد الله تعالى بشيء أفضل من فقه
في الدين ولفقيه واحد أشد على الشيطان من ألف عابد
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ع-ل-م (ʿ-l-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is "a mark, sign, or trace by which something is known"; knowledge as the impression of reality upon the mind, distinguishing truth from falsehood.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, ʿilm denotes certain cognition (yaqīn) of things as they are, culminating in maʿrifah of God; it is the noblest human attribute, the very purpose of creation.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) — knowledge as direct apprehension; metaphorical (majāz) — knowledge as "light" (nūr) or "life" (ḥayāh) for the heart, as in the ḥadīth "the scholars are heirs of the prophets."
- Root: ف-ق-ه (f-q-h)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Deep understanding and discernment, penetrating into the inner meaning of things beyond surface appearance.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In the Qur'an, fiqh is the comprehension of divine rulings and wisdom; the faqīh is one who grasps the underlying intent (maqṣūd) of revelation.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — understanding; metaphorical — the "opening of the breast" (sharḥ al-ṣadr) by God for Islam, as in the verse {«فمن يرد الله أن يهديه يشرح صدره للإسلام»}.
- Root: د-ر-ج (d-r-j)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Steps, degrees, or ranks of ascent; gradual elevation from one station to a higher one.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In eschatological and spiritual contexts, darajāt are the hierarchical stations of nearness to God, granted according to knowledge and action.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — physical steps; metaphorical — degrees of honor and proximity to the Divine, as in {«يرفع الله الذين آمنوا منكم والذين أوتوا العلم درجات»}.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Taqdīm wa Taʾkhīr (Fronting and Delaying) — In the verse {«شهد الله أنه لا إله إلا هو والملائكة وأولو العلم»}, the fronting of "Allah" and the sequential ordering (nafs, then angels, then scholars) establishes a gradation of honor (tashrīf bi-l-tartīb), a rhetorical device known as tadhīj (sequential elevation).
chapters.translation:
I say: The evidences of the virtue of knowledge from the Qur'an include His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: {«Allah bears witness that there is no god but He, and the angels, and those endowed with knowledge, standing firm in justice»} — so observe how He, Glorified and Exalted, began with Himself, then seconded with the angels, and thirded with the people of knowledge. Sufficient for you is this as honor, virtue, eminence, and nobility. And Allah, Exalted is He, said: {«Allah will raise up those who have believed among you and those who have been given knowledge, in degrees»}. Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "For the scholars there are degrees above the believers, seven hundred degrees, the distance between each two degrees being a journey of five hundred years."

And He, Mighty and Majestic, said: {«Say: Are those who know equal to those who do not know?»} And He, Exalted, said: {«Only those among His servants who possess knowledge fear Allah»}. And He, Exalted, said: {«Say: Allah suffices as a witness between me and you, and whoever has knowledge of the Book»}. And He, Exalted, said: {«He who had knowledge from the Book said: I will bring it to you»} — as an indication that he was empowered by the strength of knowledge.

And He, Mighty and Majestic, said: {«And those who were given knowledge said: Woe to you! The reward of Allah is better for those who believe and work righteousness»} — making clear that the immense magnitude of the Hereafter is known through knowledge. And He, Exalted, said: {«And such are the parables We strike for mankind, but none comprehend them except the learned»}. And He, Exalted, said: {«And if they had referred it to the Messenger and to those in authority among them, those among them who draw out conclusions would have known it»} — He referred the judgment of events to their deduction and elevated their rank to the rank of the prophets in disclosing the judgment of Allah.

And it was said regarding His saying, Exalted is He: {«O children of Adam, We have sent down upon you a garment to conceal your private parts»} — meaning knowledge; {«and feathers»} — meaning certainty (yaqīn); {«and the garment of piety»} — meaning modesty (ḥayāʾ).

And He, Mighty and Majestic, said: {«And We have brought them a Book which We detailed with knowledge»}. And He, Exalted, said: {«Then We will surely relate to them with knowledge»}. And He, Mighty and Majestic, said: {«Rather, it is clear signs in the breasts of those who have been given knowledge»}. And He, Exalted, said: {«He created man; He taught him eloquence»} — and He mentioned this only in the context of bestowing favor.

As for the reports (akhbār), the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: "Whomsoever Allah desires good for, He grants him deep understanding (fiqh) in the religion and inspires him with his right guidance." And he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "The scholars are the heirs of the prophets." And it is known that there is no rank above prophethood, nor any honor above the honor of inheriting that rank.

And he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "The inhabitants of the heavens and the earth seek forgiveness for the scholar." And what station exceeds a station whose occupant is occupied with seeking forgiveness by the angels of the heavens and the earth? And he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Indeed, wisdom increases the noble in nobility and raises the slave until he attains the stations of kings." — thereby pointing to its fruits in this world; and it is known that the Hereafter is better and more enduring.

And he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "There are two traits that are never found in a hypocrite: good bearing and deep understanding (fiqh) in the religion." Do not doubt this report because of the hypocrisy of some jurists of this age, for he did not mean the fiqh you have assumed; the meaning of fiqh will come later. And the lowest degree of the faqīh is that he knows the Hereafter is better than this world; and this knowledge, when it is sincere and prevails over him, acquits him of hypocrisy and ostentation.

And he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "The best of people is the believing scholar who, if needed, benefits others, and if dispensed with, suffices himself." And he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Faith is naked; its garment is piety, its adornment is modesty, and its fruit is knowledge." And he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "The people closest to the degree of prophethood are the people of knowledge and the people of jihad. As for the people of knowledge, they guide the people to what the messengers brought; and as for the people of jihad, they strive with their swords for what the messengers brought."

And he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "The death of a tribe is easier than the death of a scholar." And he, upon him be peace and blessings, said: "People are mines like mines of gold and silver; their best in the pre-Islamic era are their best in Islam, when they acquire understanding (fiqh)." And he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "On the Day of Resurrection, the ink of the scholars will be weighed against the blood of the martyrs." And he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Whoever preserves for my community forty hadiths from the Sunnah, conveying them to them, I will be an intercessor and witness for him on the Day of Resurrection." And he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Whoever carries from my community forty hadiths will meet Allah, Mighty and Majestic, on the Day of Resurrection as a learned jurist (faqīhan ʿāliman)." And he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Whoever acquires deep understanding (tafaqqaha) in the religion of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, Allah will suffice him in what concerns him and provide for him from whence he does not reckon." And he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed to Abraham, upon him be peace: O Abraham, I am the Knowing, and I love every knower." And he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "The scholar is the trustee (amīn) of Allah, Glorified is He, upon His earth." And he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Two classes of my community, if they are righteous, the people are righteous; and if they are corrupt, the people are corrupt: the rulers and the jurists." And he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "If a day comes upon me in which I do not increase in knowledge that draws me nearer to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, then let there be no blessing for me in the rising of the sun of that day." And he, peace and blessings be upon him, said, in preferring knowledge over worship and martyrdom: "The superiority of the scholar over the worshipper is like my superiority over the lowest man among my companions." So observe how he made knowledge commensurate with the degree of prophethood, and how he lowered the rank of mere action devoid of knowledge — although the worshipper is not devoid of knowledge of the worship he persistently performs, for without it there would be no worship. And he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "The superiority of the scholar over the worshipper is like the superiority of the full moon on the night of Badr over the rest of the stars." And he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Three will intercede on the Day of Resurrection: the prophets, then the scholars, then the martyrs." How great is a rank that follows prophethood and surpasses martyrdom, despite what has been reported concerning the virtue of martyrdom!

And the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: "Allah, Exalted is He, has not been worshipped with anything better than deep understanding (fiqh) in the religion; and a single jurist is more severe against Satan than a thousand worshippers. And everything has a pillar, and the pillar of this religion is fiqh." And he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "The best of your religion is its easiest, and the best of worship is fiqh." And he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "The superiority of the believing scholar over the believing worshipper is seventy degrees." And he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "You have entered a time in which its jurists are many, its reciters few, its preachers few, its questioners few, its givers many — in it, action is better than knowledge. And there will come upon the people a time in which its jurists are few, its preachers many, its givers few, its questioners many — in it, knowledge is better than action." And he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Between the scholar and the worshipper are one hundred degrees, between each two degrees is the distance traversed by a swift, well-fed horse in seventy years." And it was said: "O Messenger of Allah, which deeds are best?" He said: "Knowledge of Allah, Mighty and Majestic." It was said: "Which knowledge do you mean?" He, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Knowledge of Allah, Glorified is He." It was said to him: "We ask about action and you answer about knowledge." He, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Indeed, a little action benefits with knowledge of Allah, while much action does not benefit with ignorance of Allah." And he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Allah, Glorified is He, will raise the servants on the Day of Resurrection, then raise the scholars, then say: O company of scholars, I did not place My knowledge in you except out of My knowledge of you; and I did not place My knowledge in you to torment you. Go, for I have forgiven you." We ask Allah for a good end.

As for the traditions of the Companions and Successors (āthār), ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, may Allah be pleased with him, said to Kumayl: "O Kumayl, knowledge is better than wealth. Knowledge guards you while you guard wealth. Knowledge is a judge and wealth is judged upon. Wealth is diminished by expenditure, while knowledge increases through spending."

And ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him, also said: "The scholar is better than the fasting, praying, striving worshipper. And when the scholar dies, a breach is made in Islam that none can fill except a successor from him." And he, may Allah be pleased with him, said in verse:

"There is no pride except for the people of knowledge, for they are guides upon guidance for whoever seeks guidance.
And the worth of every man is what he excels in, and the ignorant are enemies of the people of knowledge.
So seize knowledge and live by it forever; people are dead, and the people of knowledge are alive."

And Abū al-Aswad said: "Nothing is more precious than knowledge. Kings are rulers over the people, and scholars are rulers over the kings." And Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "Solomon, son of David, upon them both be peace, was given the choice between knowledge, wealth, and kingship; he chose knowledge, and was given wealth and kingship along with it." And Ibn al-Mubārak was asked: "Who are the people?" He said: "The scholars." It was said: "Then who are the kings?" He said: "The ascetics (zuhhād)." It was said: "Then who are the base?" He said: "Those who consume this world through religion." And he did not count anyone other than the scholar among the people, because the specific property by which humans are distinguished from all other beasts is knowledge. For a human is human by virtue of that which is noble in him — and that is not the strength of his body, for the camel is stronger than him; nor his size, for the elephant is greater than him; nor his courage, for the beast of prey is braver than him; nor his eating, for the ox has a vaster belly than him; nor his copulation, for the meanest of sparrows is more potent in mating than him. Rather, he was created only for knowledge.

And one of the scholars said: "Would that I knew — what has he attained who has missed knowledge, and what has he missed who has attained knowledge?"

And he, upon him be peace and blessings, said: "Whoever is given the Qur'an and then sees that someone else has been given something better than him has belittled what Allah has magnified." And Fatḥ al-Mawṣilī, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "Is it not the case that a sick person, if deprived of food, drink, and medicine, dies?" They said: "Yes." He said: "Likewise, the heart, if deprived of wisdom and knowledge for three days, dies."

And indeed he spoke truly, for the nourishment of the heart is knowledge and wisdom, and by them is its life, just as the nourishment of the body is food. And whoever loses knowledge, his heart is sick and his death is inevitable — but he does not perceive it, for love of this world and occupation with it have nullified his sensation, just as the dominance of fear may nullify the pain of wounds at the moment, even though it is real. Then when death removes from him the burdens of this world, he perceives his ruin and grieves with great grief, and then it does not avail him. This is like the perception of the secure one of his fear, and the one waking from his intoxication of what befell him of wounds in the state of drunkenness or fear. So we seek refuge in Allah from the Day of the Unveiling of the Cover, for "people are asleep, and when they die, they awaken." And al-Ḥasan, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "The ink of the scholars will be weighed against the blood of the martyrs, and the ink of the scholars will outweigh the blood of the martyrs."

And Ibn Masʿūd, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Upon you is knowledge before it is lifted up, and its being lifted up is the death of its transmitters. For by Him in Whose hand is my soul, men who were killed in the path of Allah as martyrs will wish that Allah would raise them as scholars, because of what they see of their honor. For no one was born a scholar; rather, knowledge is only through learning."

And Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "Discussing knowledge for part of a night is more beloved to me than reviving the whole night in prayer." And likewise it is reported from Abū Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, and Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal, may Allah have mercy on him.

And al-Ḥasan said regarding His saying, Exalted is He: {«Our Lord, give us in this world good, and in the Hereafter good»}: "The good in this world is knowledge and worship, and the good in the Hereafter is Paradise."

And it was said to one of the sages: "Which things are worth acquiring?" He said: "The things that, when your ship sinks, swim with you" — meaning knowledge. And it was said that he meant by the sinking of the ship the destruction of his body by death.

And one of them said: "Whoever takes wisdom as a bridle, the people take him as an imam; and whoever is known for wisdom, eyes observe him with dignity."

And al-Shāfiʿī, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "From the honor of knowledge is that whoever is attributed to it — even in a trivial matter — rejoices, and whoever is stripped of it grieves."

And ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "O people, upon you is knowledge, for Allah, Glorified is He, has a cloak that He loves. Whoever seeks a door of knowledge, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, clothes him with His cloak. Then if he commits a sin, He calls him to repentance three times, lest he strip him of that cloak. And even if that sin prolongs until he dies..."

And al-Aḥnaf, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "The scholars almost become lords. And every glory not founded upon knowledge ends in humiliation."

And Sālim ibn Abī al-Jaʿd said: "My master bought me for three hundred dirhams and freed me. I said: 'With what shall I earn a living?' So I earned my living with knowledge. Not a full year had passed before the governor of Medina came to visit me, and I did not permit him."

And al-Zubayr ibn Abī Bakr said: "My father wrote to me in Iraq: 'Upon you is knowledge, for if you become poor, it will be wealth for you; and if you become rich, it will be beauty for you.'" And this is related in the counsels of Luqmān to his son: "O my son, sit with the scholars and press your knees against theirs, for Allah, Glorified is He, revives the hearts with the light of wisdom just as He revives the earth with the downpour of the sky."

And one of the sages said: "When the scholar dies, the fish in the water and the birds in the air weep for him; his face is lost, but his remembrance is not forgotten."

And al-Zuhrī, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "Knowledge is remembrance, and none love it except the manly among men."

أما الآيات فقوله تعالى {فلولا نفر من كل فرقة منهم طائفة ليتفقهوا في
الدين} وقوله عز وجل {فاسألوا أهل الذكر إن كنتم لا تعلمون}  وأما الأخبار
فقوله صلى الله عليه وسلم من سلك طريقا يطلب فيه علما سلك الله به طريقا
إلى الجنة (1) وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم إن الملائكة لتضع أجنحتها لطالب
العلم رضاء بما يصنع (2) وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم لأن تغدو فتتعلم بابا من
العلم خير من أن تصلي مائة ركعة (3) وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم باب من العلم
يتعلمه الرجل خير له من الدنيا وما فيها (4) وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم
اطلبوا العلم PageV01P008
ولو بالصين (1) وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم طلب العلم فريضة على كل مسلم
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم العلم خزائن مفاتيحها السؤال ألا فاسألوا فإنه
يؤجر فيه أربعة السائل والعالم والمستمع والمحب لهم (2) وقال صلى الله عليه
وسلم لا ينبغي للجاهل أن يسكت على جهله ولا للعالم أن يسكت على علمه (3)
وفي حديث أبي ذر رضي الله عنه حضور مجلس عالم أفضل من صلاة ألف ركعة وعيادة
ألف مريض وشهود ألف جنازة فقيل يا رسول الله ومن قراءة القرآن فقال صلى
الله عليه وسلم وهل ينفع القرآن إلا بالعلم (4) وقال عليه الصلاة والسلام
من جاءه الموت وهو يطلب العلم ليحيي به الإسلام فبينه وبين الأنبياء في
الجنة درجة واحدة (5) وأما الآثار فقال ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما ذللت طالبا
فعززت مطلوبا
وكذلك قال ابن أبي مليكة رحمه الله ما رأيت مثل ابن عباس إذا رأيته رايت
أحسن الناس وجها وإذا تكلم فأعرب الناس لسانا وإذا أفتى فأكثر الناس علما
وقال ابن المبارك رحمه الله عجبت لمن لم يطلب العلم كيف تدعوه نفسه إلى
مكرمة وقال بعض الحكماء إني لا أرحم رجالا كرحمتي لأحد رجلين رجل يطلب
العلم ولا يفهم ورجل يفهم العلم ولا يطلبه
وقال أبو الدرداء رضي الله عنه لأن أتعلم مسألة أحب إلي من قيام ليلة
وقال أيضا كن عالما أو متعلما أو مستمعا ولا تكن الرابع فتهلك
وقال عطاء مجلس علم يكفر سبعين مجلسا من مجالس اللهو
وقال عمر رضي الله عنه موت ألف  عابد قائم الليل صائم النهار أهون من موت
عالم بصير بحلال الله وحرامه
وقال الشافعي رضي الله عنه طلب العلم أفضل من النافلة
وقال ابن عبد الحكم رحمه الله كنت عند مالك أقرأ عليه العلم فدخل الظهر
فجمعت الكتب لأصلي فقال يا هذا ما الذي قمت إليه بأفضل مما كنت فيه إذا صحت
النية
وقال أبو الدرداء رضي الله عنه من رأى أن الغدو إلى طلب العلم ليس بجهاد
فقد نقص في رأيه وعقله
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ع ل م (ʿ-l-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is "knowledge, cognition, perception of a thing as it truly is" — encompassing both sensory and rational apprehension; also "a mark or sign" by which something is known.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, ʿilm is the attribute by which the intellect grasps universals and particulars; it is the noblest human perfection and the means to maʿrifah (gnosis) of God. It is contrasted with jahl (ignorance) as darkness is to light.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) usage denotes actual knowledge in the heart; metaphorical (majāz) usage extends to the means of knowledge (e.g., books, teachers) and to the act of seeking (ṭalab al-ʿilm).
- Root: ف ق ه (f-q-h)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is "deep understanding, comprehension of the inner meaning of speech" — originally broader than jurisprudence, denoting penetration into the subtle intent of a matter.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In the Quranic verse {«لِيَتَفَقَّهُوا فِي الدِّينِ»}, it signifies the acquisition of profound religious understanding that enables one to act correctly and guide others — a communal obligation (farḍ kifāyah).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal usage is intellectual penetration; metaphorical usage in later tradition narrows it to fiqh as legal science, but Ghazālī here restores the broader sense.
- Root: س ل ك (s-l-k)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is "to enter, to traverse a path, to thread" — as one threads a needle or follows a road.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In the ḥadīth, "one who traverses a path seeking knowledge" — the path is both physical (travel to scholars) and spiritual (the method of study and practice).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal usage is physical traversal; metaphorical usage is the pursuit of any means leading to knowledge, including inner discipline.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Clause with Inna (الشّرط مع إنّ) — In the ḥadīth "man salaka ṭarīqan...", the relative clause (ṣilah) functions as a conditional protasis, with the apodosis marked by the emphatic particle "sallaka Allāhu bihi" — the repetition of the verb in the apodosis with the preposition "bi" indicates the instrumental causality of the path itself.
chapters.translation:
I say — may God grant us and you success — let us now expound the virtue of seeking knowledge, drawing upon the Book of God, the Sunnah of His Messenger (peace be upon him), and the sayings of the early scholars (āthār).

As for the Quranic verses: God Most High says {«فَلَوْلَا نَفَرَ مِن كُلِّ فِرْقَةٍ مِّنْهُمْ طَائِفَةٌ لِّيَتَفَقَّهُوا فِي الدِّينِ»} — "Why should not a group from every division of them go forth to gain deep understanding in the religion?" And He, Glorified and Exalted, says {«فَاسْأَلُوا أَهْلَ الذِّكْرِ إِن كُنتُمْ لَا تَعْلَمُونَ»} — "Ask the people of remembrance if you do not know."

As for the prophetic reports (akhbār): He (peace be upon him) said: "Whoever traverses a path seeking therein knowledge, God will cause him to traverse a path to Paradise." (1) And he (peace be upon him) said: "Verily the angels lower their wings for the seeker of knowledge, out of satisfaction with what he does." (2) And he (peace be upon him) said: "That you should go forth in the morning and learn a chapter of knowledge is better than praying one hundred units (rakʿah)." (3) And he (peace be upon him) said: "A chapter of knowledge that a man learns is better for him than the world and all that is in it." (4) And he (peace be upon him) said: "Seek knowledge, even unto China." (1) And he (peace be upon him) said: "Seeking knowledge is an obligation upon every Muslim." And he (peace be upon him) said: "Knowledge is treasuries, and their keys are questioning. So ask, for in it four are rewarded: the questioner, the scholar, the listener, and the one who loves them." (2) And he (peace be upon him) said: "It is not fitting for the ignorant to remain silent upon his ignorance, nor for the scholar to remain silent upon his knowledge." (3)

In the ḥadīth of Abū Dharr (may God be pleased with him): "Attending a gathering of a scholar is better than one thousand units of prayer, visiting one thousand sick persons, and attending one thousand funeral processions." It was said: "O Messenger of God, even better than reciting the Quran?" He (peace be upon him) said: "And does the Quran benefit except through knowledge?" (4) And he (upon him be peace and prayer) said: "Whoever is overtaken by death while he is seeking knowledge to revive Islam thereby, between him and the Prophets in Paradise is but a single degree." (5)

As for the sayings of the early scholars (āthār): Ibn ʿAbbās (may God be pleased with them both) said: "I humbled myself as a seeker, and I was honored as one sought after." Similarly, Ibn Abī Mulaykah (may God have mercy on him) said: "I have never seen the like of Ibn ʿAbbās — when I saw him, I saw the most beautiful of people in countenance; when he spoke, the most eloquent of people in tongue; and when he gave a legal ruling, the most knowledgeable of people in learning."

Ibn al-Mubārak (may God have mercy on him) said: "I marvel at the one who does not seek knowledge — how does his soul call him to nobility?" And one of the sages said: "I do not pity any men as I pity one of two: a man who seeks knowledge but does not understand, and a man who understands knowledge but does not seek it."

Abū al-Dardāʾ (may God be pleased with him) said: "That I should learn a single question is more beloved to me than standing in prayer for a night." And he also said: "Be a scholar, or a learner, or a listener — and do not be the fourth, for you will perish."

ʿAṭāʾ said: "A single gathering of knowledge expiates seventy gatherings of idle amusement."

ʿUmar (may God be pleased with him) said: "The death of one thousand worshippers who stand in prayer by night and fast by day is lighter than the death of a single scholar who is discerning of God's lawful and unlawful."

Al-Shāfiʿī (may God be pleased with him) said: "Seeking knowledge is better than supererogatory worship (nāfilah)."

Ibn ʿAbd al-Ḥakam (may God have mercy on him) said: "I was with Mālik, reading knowledge to him, and the time of noon prayer (ẓuhr) entered. I gathered my books to pray, and he said: 'O man, what you have risen to do is not better than what you were in, if your intention is sound.'"

Abū al-Dardāʾ (may God be pleased with him) said: "Whoever considers that going forth in the morning to seek knowledge is not a form of striving (jihād) has diminished in his opinion and his intellect."
