Rather, He remains in the attributes of His majesty, purified from passing away, and in the qualities of His perfection, independent of any increase in completion.

And that He, in His Essence, is known to exist by the intellects, and His Essence will be seen by the eyes — a grace and kindness from Him to the righteous in the Abode of Permanence, and a completion of bliss through the vision of His noble Face.

[The attribute of life and power:] And that He, exalted, is Living, Powerful, Compelling, Dominant; no deficiency or incapacity befalls Him, nor slumber nor sleep overtakes Him, nor annihilation or death opposes Him. And He is Possessor of sovereignty and dominion, of might and omnipotence. His are authority and subjugation, creation and command. The heavens are folded in His right hand, and all creatures are subdued within His grasp.

And that He alone is unique in creation and origination, singular in bringing into being and innovation. He created creation and their deeds, decreed their provisions and their terms. No thing measured escapes His grasp, nor do the vicissitudes of affairs elude His power. His determined things are beyond count, and His knowledges are beyond enumeration.

[The attribute of knowledge:] And that He is Knower of all known things, encompassing all that transpires from the depths of the earths to the heights of the heavens. He is Knowing — not an atom's weight escapes His knowledge in the earth or in the heaven. Rather, He knows the crawling of the black ant upon the solid rock in the pitch-dark night, and He perceives the movement of the mote in the air. He knows the secret and what is more hidden, and He is aware of the whisperings of consciences, the movements of thoughts, and the hidden things of inner secrets — with an eternal, beginningless knowledge with which He has never ceased to be described in the eternity of eternities, not with a renewed knowledge that inheres in His Essence by indwelling or transition.

[The attribute of will:] And that He, exalted, is Willing for all that comes to be, Directing all that occurs. Nothing transpires in the kingdom and the dominion — little or much, small or great, good or evil, benefit or harm, faith or unbelief, knowledge or denial, success or loss, increase or decrease, obedience or disobedience — except by His decree, His determination, His wisdom, and His will.

So whatsoever He wills comes to be, and whatsoever He does not will does not come to be. The glance of a beholder and the flash of a thought do not escape His will. Rather, He is the Originator, the Restorer, the Doer of whatsoever He wills. There is no repeller of His command, no deferrer of His decree, and no escape for a servant from his disobedience except through His granting of success and His mercy; nor has he any power over his obedience except through His will and His intention. Were all of humankind and jinn, angels and devils to unite in order to move a single atom in the world or to still it without His will and intention, they would be incapable of that.

And that His will is subsisting in His Essence, among the totality of His attributes. He has never ceased to be described thereby, willing in His eternity the existence of things at the times He determined for them; so they came to be at their times exactly as He willed in His eternity, without advance or delay. Rather, they occurred in accordance with His knowledge and His will, without alteration or change.

He directs affairs not through the arrangement of thoughts nor the waiting of time; therefore, no matter occupies Him from another matter.

[The attributes of hearing and sight:] And that He, exalted, is Hearing and Seeing. He hears and sees; no heard thing escapes His hearing, even if hidden, and no seen thing is absent from His vision, even if minute. No distance veils His hearing, and no darkness repels His sight. He sees without pupil or eyelids, and hears without ears or auditory canals — just as He knows without a heart, seizes without a limb, and creates without an instrument. For His attributes do not resemble the attributes of creation, even as His Essence does not resemble the essences of creation.

[The attribute of speech:] And that He, exalted, is Speaking — commanding, forbidding, promising, threatening — with an eternal, beginningless speech subsisting in His Essence, which does not resemble the speech of creation. It is not a sound that arises from the passage of air or the striking of bodies, nor a letter that is cut off by the closing of a lip or the movement of a tongue.

And that the Qurʾān, the Torah, the Gospel, and the Psalms are His books revealed to His messengers, peace be upon them.

And that the Qurʾān is recited by tongues, written in codices, and preserved in hearts — yet with all that, it is eternal, subsisting in the Essence of God, exalted; it does not admit of separation or division by being transferred to hearts and pages. And that Moses, peace be upon him, heard the speech of God without sound or letter, just as the righteous will see the Essence of God, exalted, in the Hereafter without substance or accident.

And since He possesses these attributes, He is Living, Knowing, Powerful, Willing, Hearing, Seeing, and Speaking — through life, power, knowledge, will, hearing, sight, and speech, not through mere essence.

[The doctrine of acts:] And that He, glorified and exalted, — there is no existent other than Him except that it is originated by His act and flows from His justice in the most excellent, most complete, most perfect, and most equitable of ways. And He is Wise in His acts, Just in His decrees. His justice is not measured by the justice of servants, for the servant may be conceived to commit injustice by disposing of another's property; but injustice cannot be conceived from God, exalted, for He encounters no other's property such that His disposal of it would be injustice. So everything other than Him — human, jinn, angel, devil, heaven, earth, animal, plant, inanimate object, substance, accident, perceived, or sensed — is an originated thing He invented by His power after non-existence, an invention; and He brought it into being after it was nothing. For He alone existed, and there was none with Him; then He originated creation afterward as a manifestation of His power and a realization of what had preceded in His will and what was established in eternity from His word — not due to any need or want of Him for it.

And that He is gracious in creation, origination, and obligation (taklīf), not out of necessity; and He is bountiful in beneficence and reform, not out of compulsion. His are grace, goodness, favor, and benefaction — for He is able to pour upon His servants every kind of torment and to afflict them with varieties of pains and maladies; and were He to do so, it would be justice from Him, not ugliness nor injustice.

And that He, mighty and majestic, establishes His believing servants upon acts of obedience by the dictate of generosity and promise, not by the dictate of desert and obligation — for no act is incumbent upon Him toward anyone, nor can injustice be conceived from Him, nor does any right against Him become obligatory for anyone.

And that His right over acts of obedience became obligatory upon creation through His own imposition upon the tongues of His prophets, peace be upon them — not through mere reason. Rather, He sent the messengers and manifested their truthfulness through evident miracles; so they conveyed His command, His prohibition, His promise, and His threat. Thus it became obligatory upon creation to affirm them in all that they brought.

[The meaning of the second testimony — the attestation of the messengers' prophethood:] And that He sent the unlettered Prophet, the Qurayshī, Muḥammad, peace and blessings be upon him, with His message to all Arabs and non-Arabs, jinn and humans. He abrogated by his law (sharīʿa) the previous laws, except what He confirmed thereof; and He favored him above all other prophets and made him the master of humankind.

And He prevented the perfection of faith through the testimony of divine unity — which is your saying "There is no god but God" — unless it is joined by the testimony of the Messenger, which is your saying "Muḥammad is the Messenger of God." And He made it obligatory upon creation to affirm him in all that he reported concerning the matters of this world and the Hereafter.

And that no servant's faith is accepted until he believes in what he (the Prophet) reported concerning what comes after death. Its beginning is the questioning of Munkar and Nakīr — two awesome, terrifying figures who seat the servant in his grave, whole in body and soul, and ask him about divine unity and prophethood, saying to him: "Who is your Lord? What is your religion? Who is your Prophet?" They are the two examiners of the grave, and their questioning is the first trial after death.

And that he believe in the punishment of the grave — that it is true, and its judgment is just, upon body and soul, as God wills.

And that he believe in the Balance (al-mīzān) with its two pans and its tongue, and that its description in magnitude is like the layers of the heavens and the earth. Deeds are weighed by the power of God, exalted; and the weights on that day are the atoms and mustard seeds — a realization of the perfection of justice. The scrolls of good deeds appear in a beautiful form upon the pan of light, and the Balance is weighed down by them according to their degrees with God, by God's grace; and the scrolls of evil deeds are cast in an ugly form upon the pan of darkness, and the Balance is lightened by them, by God's justice.

And that he believe that the Path (al-ṣirāṭ) is true — a bridge stretched over the back of Hell, sharper than a sword and finer than a hair. The feet of the disbelievers slip upon it by the decree of God, glorified, and they plummet with it into the Fire; while the feet of the believers are made firm upon it by God's grace, and they are driven to the Abode of Permanence.

And that he believe in the Pond (al-ḥawḍ) that is approached — the Pond of Muḥammad, peace and blessings be upon him, from which the believers drink before entering Paradise and after crossing the Path. Whoever drinks from it a single draught will never thirst thereafter. Its width is a month's journey; its water is whiter than milk and sweeter than honey; around it are vessels whose number equals the stars of the sky. A hadith mentions that it has two spouts pouring from al-Kawthar — reported by Muslim from the hadith of Thawbān: "In it are two spouts that pour from Paradise, one of gold and the other of silver."

And that he believe in the Reckoning (al-ḥisāb) and the disparity of people therein — some are scrutinized in the reckoning, some are treated with leniency, and some enter Paradise without any reckoning, and they are the near ones (al-muqarrabūn). God, exalted, asks whom He wills of the prophets about the delivery of the message, and whom He wills of the disbelievers about their denial of the messengers; He asks the innovators about the Sunnah, and He asks the Muslims about their deeds.

And that he believe in the extraction of the monotheists from the Fire after retribution, so that no monotheist remains in Hell, by God's grace — for no monotheist will abide eternally in the Fire.

And that he believe in the intercession (shafāʿa) of the prophets, then the scholars, then the martyrs, then the rest of the believers, each according to his standing and rank with God, exalted. And whoever remains of the believers with no intercessor is brought out by God's grace, mighty and majestic — for no believer abides eternally in the Fire. Rather, whoever has in his heart an atom's weight of faith is brought out of it.

And that he hold the conviction of the excellence of the Companions, may God be pleased with them, and their ranking — that the most excellent of people after the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, is Abū Bakr, then ʿUmar, then ʿUthmān, then ʿAlī, may God be pleased with them all.

And that he think well of all the Companions and praise them as God, mighty and majestic, and His Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, praised them all. For all of this is what the reports (akhbār) have conveyed and the traditions (āthār) have attested. Whoever believes all of this with certainty is among the people of truth and the company of the Sunnah, and has parted from the band of error and the party of innovation.

So we ask God for perfection of certainty and good steadfastness in religion, for ourselves and for all Muslims, by His mercy — for He is the Most Merciful of the merciful. And may God send blessings upon our master Muḥammad and upon every chosen servant.

chapters.title_en: Section 25 — On the Method of Gradual Progression toward Guidance and the Ordering of the Degrees of Belief
chapters.arabic_text:
|| الفصل الثاني في وجه التدريج إلى الإرشاد وترتيب درجات الاعتقاد

اعلم أن ما ذكرناه في ترجمة العقيدة ينبغي أن يقدم إلى الصبي في أول نشوه
ليحفظه حفظا ثم لا يزال ينكشف له معناه في كبره شيئا فشيئا فابتداؤه الحفظ
ثم الفهم ثم الاعتقاد والإيقان والتصديق به وذلك مما يحصل في الصبي بغير
برهان
فمن فضل الله سبحانه على قلب الإنسان أن شرحه في أول نشوه للإيمان من غير
حاجة إلى حجة وبرهان وكيف ينكر ذلك وجميع عقائد العوام مباديها التلقين
المجرد والتقليد المحض نعم يكون الاعتقاد الحاصل بمجرد التقليد غير خال عن
نوع من الضعف في الابتداء على معنى أنه يقبل الإزالة بنقيضه لو ألقى إليه
فلا بد من تقويته وإثباته في نفس الصبي والعامي حتى يترسخ ولا يتزلزل
وليس الطريق في تقويته وإثباته إن يعلم صنعة الجدل والكلام بل يشتغل
بتلاوة  القرآن وتفسيره وقراءة الحديث ومعانيه
ويشتغل بوظائف العبادات فلا يزال اعتقاده يزداد رسوخا بما يقرع سمعه من
أدلة القرآن وحججه وبما يرد عليه من شواهد الأحاديث وفوائدها وبما يسطع
عليه من أنوار العبادات ووظائفها وبما يسري إليه من مشاهدة الصالحين
ومجالستهم وسيماهم وسماعهم وهيآتهم في الخضوع لله عز وجل والخوف منه
والاستكانة له فيكون أول التلقين كإلقاء بذر في الصدر وتكون هذه الأسباب
كالسقي والتربية له حتى ينمو ذلك البذر يقوى ويرتفع شجرة طيبة راسخة أصلها
ثابت وفرعها في السماء
وينبغي أن يحرس سمعه من الجدل والكلام غاية الحراسة فإن ما يشوشه الجدل
أكثر مما يمهده وما يفسده أكثر مما يصلحه بل تقويته بالجدل تضاهي ضرب
الشجرة بالمدقة من الحديد رجاء تقويتها بأن تكثر أجزاؤها وربما يفتتها ذلك
ويفسدها وهو الأغلب
والمشاهدة تكفيك في هذا بيانا فناهيك بالعيان برهانا
فقس عقيدة أهل الصلاح والتقى من عوام الناس بعقيدة المتكلمين والمجادلين
فترى اعتقاد العامي في الثبات كالطود الشامخ لا تحركه الدواهي والصواعق
وعقيدة المتكلم الحارس اعتقاده بتقسيمات الجدل كخيط مرسل في الهواء تفيئه
الرياح مرة هكذا ومرة هكذا إلا من سمع منهم دليل الاعتقاد فتلقفه تقليدا
كما تلقف نفس الاعتقاد تقليدا إذ لا فرق في التقليد بين تعليم الدليل أو
تعلم المدلول فتلقين الدليل شيء والاستدلال بالنظر شيء آخر بعيد عنه
ثم الصبي إذا وقع نشوه على هذه العقيدة إن اشتغل بكسب الدنيا لم ينفتح له
غيرها ولكنه يسلم في الآخرة باعتقاد أهل الحق إذ لم يكلف الشرع أجلاف العرب
أكثر من التصديق الجازم بظاهر هذه العقائد فأما البحث والتفتيش وتكلف نظم
الأدلة فلم يكلفوه أصلا
وإن أراد أن يكون من سالكي طريق الآخرة وساعده التوفيق حتى اشتغل بالعمل

chapters.translation:
**Chapter Two: On the Method of Gradual Progression toward Guidance and the Ordering of the Degrees of Belief**

Know that what we have mentioned in the translation of the creed ought to be presented to the child at the very beginning of his upbringing, so that he memorizes it first. Then its meaning continues to unfold for him gradually as he grows older. Thus, his beginning is memorization, then understanding, then belief, certainty, and affirmation of it. This is something that occurs in the child without any proof.

It is among the favors of God—Glory be to Him—upon the human heart that He expanded it at the outset of its formation for faith without need of argument or demonstration. How could this be denied, given that all the beliefs of the common folk have as their starting point mere inculcation and pure imitation? Indeed, the belief acquired through mere imitation is not devoid of a certain weakness at the beginning, in the sense that it is susceptible to removal by its opposite if that were cast upon it. Therefore, it must be strengthened and established in the soul of the child and the commoner until it becomes firmly rooted and does not waver.

The way to strengthen and establish it is not by teaching the craft of dialectical theology (jadl) and scholastic kalām. Rather, one occupies oneself with the recitation of the Qurʾān and its interpretation, and with reading the ḥadīth and their meanings. One also occupies oneself with the duties of worship. Thus, one's belief continues to increase in firmness through what strikes the ear of the Qurʾān's evidences and proofs, through what arrives of the testimonies of the ḥadīth and their benefits, through what shines upon one of the lights of worship and its obligations, and through what permeates one from observing the righteous and sitting in their company—their appearance, their speech, and their demeanor in humility before God—Mighty and Majestic—in fear of Him and in submission to Him. So the initial inculcation is like casting a seed into the breast, and these means are like the watering and nurturing of it, until that seed grows, strengthens, and rises as a goodly tree, firmly rooted, its branches reaching into the sky.

One should guard one's hearing from dialectic and kalām with the utmost vigilance, for what dialectic disturbs is more than what it prepares, and what it corrupts is more than what it rectifies. Rather, strengthening belief through dialectic resembles striking a tree with an iron mallet hoping to strengthen it by increasing the density of its parts—but perhaps that will shatter it and ruin it, and that is the more likely outcome.

Observation suffices you as an explanation of this; the evidence of direct sight is proof enough. Compare the belief of the pious and God-fearing among the common folk with the belief of the scholastic theologians and disputants. You will see the commoner's belief in its firmness like a towering mountain that calamities and thunderbolts do not move. But the belief of the theologian who guards his creed with the divisions of dialectic is like a loose thread in the air that the winds blow this way and that—except for one who heard from them the proof of belief and snatched it up by imitation, just as he snatched up the belief itself by imitation. For there is no difference in imitation between being taught the proof and learning the thing proven. Thus, the inculcation of the proof is one thing, and reasoning by reflection is another thing altogether, far removed from it.

Then, if the child, upon reaching maturity with this creed, occupies himself with earning a livelihood, nothing else opens up for him. But he is saved in the Hereafter by the belief of the people of truth, since the Law did not charge the coarse Arabs with more than firm affirmation of the apparent meanings of these beliefs. As for investigation, scrutiny, and the laborious arrangement of proofs, they were never charged with that at all.

But if he wishes to be among the travelers of the path of the Hereafter, and divine success aids him so that he occupies himself with works, adheres to piety, restrains his soul from caprice, and occupies himself with spiritual discipline and striving (mujāhada), then the gates of guidance open for him, unveiling the realities of this creed through a divine light cast into his heart by virtue of that striving—fulfilling His promise—Mighty and Majestic—when He said: {«And those who strive in Us, We shall surely guide them to Our paths, and indeed God is with the doers of good»}. This is the precious jewel that is the ultimate goal of the faith of the veracious (ṣiddīqīn) and the near ones (muqarrabīn). To this points the secret that was lodged in the breast of Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq—may God be pleased with him—by which he was preferred over all creation.

The unveiling of that secret—rather, of those secrets—has degrees corresponding to the degrees of striving and the degrees of the inner self in its purity and cleanliness from all other than God—Exalted is He—and in its illumination by the light of certainty. This is like the variation among people in the secrets of medicine, jurisprudence, and all other sciences, for these vary according to the variation of effort and the variation of natural disposition in intelligence and acumen. And just as those degrees are not limited, so too are these.

**Question:** If you say: Is learning dialectic and kalām blameworthy, like learning astrology, or is it permissible, or recommended? Know that people have gone to extremes and excess in this matter. Some say it is an innovation (bidʿa) or forbidden (ḥarām), and that if a servant meets God—Mighty and Majestic—with every sin except polytheism, that is better for him than meeting Him with kalām. Others say it is obligatory and a duty—either as a collective obligation (farḍ kifāya) or an individual one (farḍ ʿayn)—and that it is the most virtuous of deeds and the highest of acts of drawing near, for it is the realization of the science of divine unity (tawḥīd) and the defense of the religion of God—Exalted is He.

Al-Shāfiʿī, Mālik, Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal, Sufyān, and all the people of ḥadīth among the Salaf held the view of prohibition.

Ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿlā said: I heard al-Shāfiʿī—may God be pleased with him—on the day he debated Ḥafṣ al-Fard, who was among the Muʿtazilī theologians, say: "That a servant should meet God—Mighty and Majestic—with every sin except polytheism is better than that he should meet Him with anything of the science of kalām. And I heard from Ḥafṣ something I am unable to relate." He also said: "I have come to know of the people of kalām something I never would have imagined. That a servant should be afflicted with everything God has forbidden, except polytheism, is better for him than that he should look into kalām."

Al-Karābīsī related that al-Shāfiʿī—may God be pleased with him—was asked about something of kalām and became angry, saying: "Ask about this Ḥafṣ al-Fard and his companions—may God disgrace them." And when al-Shāfiʿī fell ill—may God be pleased with him—Ḥafṣ al-Fard entered upon him and said to him: "Who am I?" He replied: "Ḥafṣ al-Fard—may God neither preserve nor protect you—until you repent of what you are upon."

He also said: "If people knew what is in kalām of caprices, they would flee from it as they flee from a lion." He also said: "When you hear a man say 'the name is the named' or 'other than the named,' bear witness that he is among the people of kalām and has no religion."

Al-Zaʿfarānī said: Al-Shāfiʿī said: "My judgment concerning the people of kalām is that they should be beaten with palm branches and paraded among the tribes and clans, and it should be said: 'This is the recompense of one who abandoned the Book and the Sunnah and took up kalām.'"

Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal said: "The practitioner of kalām never prospers. You scarcely see anyone who looks into kalām without there being corruption in his heart." He went to great lengths in condemning it, to the point that he abandoned al-Ḥārith al-Muḥāsibī—despite his asceticism and piety—because he authored a book refuting the innovators. He said to him: "Woe to you! Do you not first quote their innovation and then refute them? Do you not, by your authorship, lead people to examine innovation and ponder those doubts, which then invites them to opinion and inquiry?" Aḥmad—may God have mercy on him—said: "The scholars of kalām are heretics (zanādiqa)."

Mālik—may God have mercy on him—said: "What do you think? If one comes to him who is more skilled in disputation than he, will he abandon his religion every day for a new religion?"—meaning that the statements of disputants vary.

Mālik—may God have mercy on him—also said: "The testimony of the people of innovation and caprice is not permissible." Some of his companions said in interpretation of this that he meant by "people of caprice" the people of kalām, whatever school they followed.

Abū Yūsuf said: "Whoever seeks knowledge through kalām becomes a heretic."

Al-Ḥasan said: "Do not dispute with the people of caprice, do not sit with them, and do not listen to them." The people of ḥadīth among the Salaf agreed upon this.

The severities transmitted from them on this matter are not limited. They said: The Companions were silent about it, even though they knew the realities best and were most eloquent in arranging words—only because they knew the evil that would be generated from it. For this reason, the Prophet—peace be upon him—said: "Perished are the nit-pickers, perished are the nit-pickers, perished are the nit-pickers"—that is, those who go deep into inquiry and exhaustive investigation.

They also argued that if this were part of the religion, it would be the most important thing the Messenger of God—peace be upon him—would command, teach its method, and praise it and its practitioners. Yet he taught them the rules of cleansing after relieving oneself, urged them to the knowledge of inheritance shares, and praised them for it—but he forbade them from speaking about divine decree and said: "Restrain yourselves from [speaking of] the decree."

Upon this the Companions—may God be pleased with them—continued. To add beyond the teacher is transgression and injustice. They are the teachers and the models; we are the followers and the students.

As for the other faction, they argued by saying: If the harm of kalām is the term "substance" (jawhar) and "accident" (ʿaraḍ) and these strange technical terms that the Companions—may God be pleased with them—did not know, then the matter is easy. For there is no science in which technical terms have not been introduced for the sake of clarification—like ḥadīth, exegesis, and jurisprudence. If the terms of refutation, breaking, composition, transitivity, and invalidity of position—all the questions raised against analogical reasoning—were presented to them, they would not have understood them. So introducing a term to indicate a sound purpose is like introducing a vessel in a new form for use in what is permissible.

If the harm is the meaning, then we mean by it nothing but knowledge of the proof for the origination of the world (ḥudūth al-ʿālam), the oneness of the Creator, and His attributes, as they came in the Law. From where would knowledge of God—Exalted is He—through proof be forbidden?

If the harm is the branching out, partisanship, enmity, hatred, and what kalām leads to, then that is forbidden and must be guarded against—just as pride, vanity, ostentation, and seeking leadership are things that the sciences of ḥadīth, exegesis, and jurisprudence lead to, and they are forbidden and must be guarded against. But that does not prevent the science itself because of what it leads to.

How could the mention of proof, the demand for it, and the search for it be prohibited, when God—Exalted is He—said: {«Say: Bring your proof»} and said—Mighty and Majestic—{«That he who perished might perish upon clear evidence, and he who lived might live upon clear evidence»} and said—Exalted is He—{«Do you have any authority for this?»}—that is, proof and demonstration—and said—Exalted is He—{«Say: To God belongs the conclusive argument»} and said—Exalted is He—{«Have you not seen him who disputed with Abraham about his Lord...»} to His saying {«So the disbeliever was confounded»}—for He mentioned Abraham's argumentation, his disputation, and his silencing of his opponent in the context of praising him. And He said—Mighty and Majestic—{«And that is Our argument which We gave to Abraham against his people»} and said—Exalted is He—{«They said: O Noah, you have disputed with us and multiplied your disputation»} and said—Exalted is He—in the story of Pharaoh {«...the Lord of the worlds»} to His saying {«...I have come to you with something clear»}. In sum, the Qurʾān from its beginning to its end is an argumentation against the disbelievers. The chief proof of the theologians in divine unity is His saying—Exalted is He—{«Had there been in them gods other than God, they would have been corrupted»}; in prophethood, {«And if you are in doubt about what We have sent down upon Our servant, then bring a chapter like it»}; and in the resurrection, {«Say: He will revive it who brought it forth the first time»}—along with other verses and proofs.

The messengers—peace be upon them—never ceased arguing with the deniers and disputing with them. He said—Exalted is He—{«And dispute with them in the way that is best»}. The Companions—may God be pleased with them—also argued with the deniers and disputed, but only when needed.

The need for it was slight in their time. The first to establish the practice of calling the innovators to truth through disputation was ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib—may God be pleased with him—when he sent Ibn ʿAbbās—may God be pleased with them both—to the Khawārij. He spoke with them and said: "What do you hold against your leader?" They said: "He fought but did not take captives or spoils." He said: "That was in fighting the disbelievers. What do you think—if you had insulted ʿĀʾisha—may God be pleased with her—in the share of one of your arrows, would you deem it lawful to take from her what you take from your slave-girls, when she is your mother by the explicit text of the Book?" They said: "No." And by his disputation, two thousand of them returned to obedience.

It is related that al-Ḥasan disputed with a Qadarī and he recanted his view on divine decree.

ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib—may God honor his face—disputed with a man from the Qadariyya.

ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd—may God be pleased with him—disputed with Yazīd ibn ʿUmayra concerning faith. ʿAbd Allāh said: "If I said I am a believer, I would be saying I am in Paradise." Yazīd ibn ʿUmayra said to him: "O companion of the Messenger of God, this is a slip from you. Is faith anything but believing in God, His angels, His books, His messengers, the resurrection, and the scale, and performing prayer, fasting, and alms? We have sins—if we knew they were forgiven us, we would know we are among the people of Paradise. For that reason we say we are believers, but we do not say we are among the people of Paradise." Ibn Masʿūd said: "You have spoken truly, by God—it was a slip from me."

Thus it should be said: Their engagement in it was little, not much; short, not long; and at the time of need—not by way of authoring books, teaching, or making it a profession.

As for the paucity of their engagement in it, that was due to the paucity of need, since innovation did not appear in that age. As for the brevity, the goal was merely to silence the opponent, secure his admission, unveil the truth, and remove the doubt. Had the opponent's confusion or obstinacy been prolonged, their imposition would inevitably have been prolonged as well. They did not measure the need with a scale or a bushel once they had begun.

As for their not undertaking to teach and author books in it—this was their practice in jurisprudence, exegesis, and ḥadīth as well. If it is permissible to author works of jurisprudence and set down rare cases that occur only on rare occasions—either to store them for the day they occur, even if rare, or to sharpen the minds—then we too may arrange the methods of disputation in anticipation of the need arising from the eruption of a doubt or the stirring of an innovator, or to sharpen the mind, or to store up the argument so as not to be at a loss for it at the moment of need, spontaneously and extemporaneously—like one who prepares weapons before battle for the day of battle. This is what can be mentioned for the two factions.

**Question:** If you say: What is your chosen position on this matter? Know that the truth is that declaring it blameworthy absolutely in every case, or praising it absolutely in every case, is an error. Rather, it must be detailed.

Know first that a thing may be forbidden in itself (li-dhātihi), like wine and carrion. By "in itself" I mean that the cause of its prohibition is a quality in its very essence—namely, intoxication and death. When asked about this, we declare it forbidden absolutely, without regard to the permissibility of carrion in cases of necessity, or the permissibility of swallowing wine when one is choking on a morsel and finds nothing to wash it down with but wine.

There is also what is forbidden for the sake of something else (li-ghayrihi), like selling over the sale of your Muslim brother during the period of option, or selling at the time of the call to prayer, or like eating clay—for it is forbidden because of the harm it contains. This divides into what harms in small and large quantities, about which one declares it absolutely forbidden—like poison, of which a little and a lot kills—and what harms only in excess, about which one declares it permissible—like honey, for much of it harms the feverish—and like eating clay.

It is as if declaring prohibition absolutely on clay and wine, and permissibility on honey, is a consideration of the predominant cases. But when something presents itself in which the cases are balanced, the better course—and the furthest from confusion—is to make the distinction.

So we return to the science of kalām and say: In it there is benefit and there is harm. In consideration of its benefit, at the time of benefiting from it, it is lawful, recommended, or obligatory, as the situation requires. In consideration of its harm, at the time and place of harm, it is forbidden.

As for its harm: it stirs up doubts, agitates beliefs, and removes them from certainty and firm resolve. This occurs at the beginning, and their return through proof is doubtful and varies among individuals. This is its harm to true belief. It has another harm: it reinforces the innovator's belief in his innovation and fixes it in his breast, so that his motives are stirred and his eagerness to persist in it intensifies. But this harm is mediated by the fatigue that arises from disputation. For this reason, you see the common innovator whose belief can be removed by gentleness in the shortest time—unless he was raised in a land where disputation and partisanship appear. For then, even if the first and the last gathered together, they could not pluck the innovation from his breast. Rather, caprice, partisanship, hatred of the disputants' opponents, and division from the dissenters overcome his heart and prevent him from perceiving the truth—to the point that if one said to him: "Would you like God—Exalted is He—to remove the veil for you and make you know by direct sight that the truth is with your opponent?" he would hate that, fearing that his opponent would rejoice in it. This is the chronic disease that has spread through the lands and the people. It is a kind of corruption that the disputants have stirred up through partisanship. This is its harm.

As for its benefit: one might suppose that its benefit is the unveiling of realities and knowing them as they are. Far from it! Kalām does not fulfill this noble demand. Perhaps the confusion and misguidance in it are more than the unveiling and clarification. If you hear this from a traditionist or a ḥashwī, it might cross your mind that people are enemies of what they do not know. So hear this from one who has experienced kalām and then loathed it after true experience—after penetrating into it to the furthest degree of the theologians and beyond that into deep immersion in other sciences akin to the type of kalām—and who ascertained that the path to the realities of knowledge from this direction is blocked.

By my life, kalām is not free of some unveiling, clarification, and elucidation of certain matters—but only rarely, in obvious matters that one almost understands before delving into the craft of kalām. Rather, its benefit is one single thing: guarding the creed that we have translated for the common folk, and preserving it from the disturbances of the innovators through various kinds of disputation. For the commoner is weak; the innovator's argument, even if corrupt, agitates him—and opposing the corrupt with the corrupt repels it.

The people are bound by this creed that we have presented, for the Law came with it because of what it contains of the rectification of their religion and their worldly affairs. The pious Salaf agreed upon it. The scholars are bound to preserve it for the common folk from the obfuscations of the innovators, just as the sultans are bound to preserve their wealth from the incursions of oppressors and usurpers.

Once one has encompassed its harm and its benefit, one should be like the skilled physician in using a dangerous medicine: he does not place it except in its proper place—at the time of need and in the measure of need.

The detail of this is that the common folk occupied with trades and crafts should be left upon the soundness of their beliefs, whatever creed they have received through inculcation of the true belief we have mentioned. For teaching them kalām is pure harm in their case, since it may stir up a doubt for them and shake their belief, and after that one cannot undertake the repair.

As for the commoner who holds an innovation, he should be called to the truth with gentleness, not partisanship—with gentle speech that persuades the soul and affects the heart, close in style to the evidences of the Qurʾān and ḥadīth, mixed with a kind of exhortation and warning. For that is more beneficial than disputation constructed on the conditions of the theologians. When the commoner hears that, he thinks it is a kind of craft of disputation that the theologian learned in order to entice people to his belief. If he is unable to answer, he supposes that the disputants of his own school are also able to repel it. So disputation with this one—and with the first—is forbidden.

Likewise with one who has fallen into doubt: it must be removed with gentleness, exhortation, and evidences that are near, acceptable, and far from the profundities of kalām.

Exhaustive disputation is beneficial only in one place: that a commoner is supposed to have adopted an innovation through a kind of disputation he heard, and one counters that disputation with its like, so that he returns to the true belief. This applies to one for whom familiarity with disputation has become apparent, such that it prevents him from being satisfied with exhortations and common warnings. He has reached a state that only the medicine of disputation can cure, so it is permissible to cast it to him.

As for lands where innovation is rare and schools do not differ, one limits oneself to the translation of the creed we have mentioned, without touching upon proofs, and one waits for a doubt to occur. If one occurs, it is mentioned in the measure of need.

If innovation is widespread and one fears that children may be deceived, then there is no harm in teaching them the amount we have deposited in the book *al-Risāla al-Qudsiyya*, so that it may be a means of repelling the influence of the innovators' disputations should they reach them. This is a brief amount, and we have deposited it in this book for its brevity.

If one has intelligence and by his intelligence perceives the place of a question, or a doubt stirs in his soul, then the feared cause has appeared and the disease has become manifest. There is no harm in elevating him to the amount we have mentioned in the book *al-Iqtiṣād fī al-Iʿtiqād*—about fifty folios—and in it there is no departure from examining the foundations of belief into other matters of the theologians' investigations.

If that convinces him, one stops with him. If it does not convince him, then the cause has become chronic, the disease dominant, and the illness spreading. Let the physician treat him gently as much as he can, and await the decree of God—Exalted is He—concerning him, until the truth is unveiled to him by an awakening from God—Glory be to Him—or he continues in doubt and uncertainty until what is decreed for him. The amount contained in that book, and its genre among authored works, is what one hopes will be beneficial.

As for what lies beyond it, there are two divisions. The first is inquiry into other than the foundations of belief—like investigating the "reliance" (iʿtimādāt), the "modes" (akwān), the "perceptions" (idrākāt), and delving into the vision [of God]: whether it has an opposite called "prevention" (manʿ) or "blindness" (ʿamā); and if so, whether it is one thing preventing all that is unseen, or whether for every visible thing that can be seen there is a prevention corresponding to its number—along with other such misleading nonsense.

The second division is the excessive elaboration of those proofs beyond those foundations, and the multiplication of questions and answers. This too is an over-exhaustiveness that only increases in misguidance and ignorance for one whom that amount did not convince. For there is many a discourse whose prolixity and elaboration only increase its obscurity.

If someone said: "Inquiry into the ruling on perceptions and reliance has the benefit of sharpening the mind, and the mind is the instrument of religion just as the sword is the instrument of jihad—so there is no harm in sharpening it"—this would be like one saying: "Playing chess sharpens the mind, so it is part of religion." That is madness. For the mind is sharpened by all the other sciences of the Law, in which no harm is feared.

By this amount you have come to know the blameworthy portion and the praiseworthy portion of kalām, the situation in which it is blamed, the situation in which it is praised, the person who benefits from it, and the person who does not benefit from it.

**Question:** If you say: Since you acknowledge the need for it in repelling the innovators, and now innovations have erupted, the affliction has become general, and necessity presses—then it must become among the collective obligations (furūḍ al-kifāyāt), like the preservation of wealth and other rights, such as judgeship, governance, and the like. Unless the scholars occupy themselves with spreading it, teaching it, and researching it, it will not endure. If it is abandoned entirely, it will be effaced. There is not in mere natural disposition a sufficiency for resolving the doubts of the innovators unless one learns it. Therefore, teaching it and researching it should also be among the collective obligations—unlike the time of the Companions—may God be pleased with them—when the need was not pressing.

Know that the truth is that in every land there must be one who stands for this science independently, repelling the doubts of the innovators that have arisen in that land. This endures through teaching. But it is not right to teach it publicly like jurisprudence and exegesis are taught. For this is like medicine, and jurisprudence is like food. The harm of food is not feared, but the harm of medicine is feared—because of the kinds of harm we have mentioned in it.

The scholar who should be singled out for teaching this science is one who possesses three qualities. First: devotion to knowledge and eagerness for it—for the one occupied with a craft is prevented by his work from completing it and removing doubts when they arise. Second: intelligence, acumen, and eloquence—for the dull-witted does not benefit from his understanding, and the heavy-tongued does not benefit from his argumentation; one fears for him the harm of kalām and does not hope for his benefit. Third: that his nature be one of righteousness, religiosity, and piety, and that desires not be dominant over him—for the immoral one, at the slightest doubt, is stripped of religion. For that dissolves the restraint upon him and lifts the barrier between him and pleasures, so he does not eagerly seek to remove the doubt but rather seizes upon it to free himself from the burdens of obligation. Thus, what such a learner corrupts is more than what he rectifies.

When you know these divisions, it becomes clear to you that this praiseworthy argument in kalām is only of the genre of the Qurʾān's arguments—gentle words that affect hearts and persuade souls—not the penetration into divisions and subtleties that most people do not understand. And when they do understand them, they think they are sophistry and a craft its practitioner learned for obfuscation. So when one like him in craft confronts him, he resists him.

You have also come to know that al-Shāfiʿī and all the Salaf only forbade engaging in it and devoting oneself to it because of the harm in it that we have pointed out. And that what is transmitted of Ibn ʿAbbās—may God be pleased with them both—disputing with the Khawārij, and what is transmitted of ʿAlī—may God be pleased with him—disputing concerning divine decree and other matters, was of the clear and manifest kind of speech, in a place of need—and that is praiseworthy in every case.

Indeed, the ages may differ in the abundance or scarcity of need, and it is not far-fetched that the ruling should differ accordingly.

This is the ruling on the creed by which creation is bound, and the ruling on the method of defending it and preserving it.

As for removing doubt, unveiling realities, knowing things as they are, and grasping the secrets that the apparent words of this creed translate—there is no key to that except striving (mujāhada), suppressing desires, turning wholly to God—Exalted is He—and adhering to reflection pure of the impurities of disputations. It is a mercy from God—Mighty and Majestic—that flows upon whoever exposes himself to its breezes, in the measure of his provision, in the measure of his exposure, and in the measure of the acceptance of the place and the purity of the heart. That is the sea whose depth cannot be reached and whose shore cannot be attained.

**Question:** If you say: This speech indicates that these sciences have apparent aspects (ẓawāhir) and secrets (asrār), some of which are clear and appear first, and some of which are hidden and become clear through striving, discipline, earnest seeking, pure reflection, and a heart empty of everything of the world's occupations except the sought object. This almost contradicts the Law, for the Law has no apparent and hidden, no secret and public—rather, the apparent, the hidden, the secret, and the public are one in it.

Know that the division of these sciences into hidden and clear is not denied by anyone of insight. Only the deficient deny it—those who snatched up something in early childhood and froze upon it, having no ascent to the heights of excellence and the stations of the scholars and saints. This is evident from the proofs of the Law. The Prophet—peace be upon him—said: "Indeed, the Qurʾān has an apparent and a hidden, a limit and an ascent." ʿAlī—may God be pleased with him—said, pointing to his breast: "Here are abundant sciences, if only I could find carriers for them."

He—peace be upon him—said: "We, the company of prophets, have been commanded to speak to people according to the measure of their intellects." And he—peace be upon him—said: "No one relates to a people a ḥadīth that their intellects do not reach, except that it is a trial for them." And God—Exalted is He—said: {«And those parables—We strike them for the people, but none understand them except the learned»}. And he—peace be upon him—said: "Indeed, among knowledge there is something like the hidden treasure, known only to those who know God—Exalted is He"—the ḥadīth to its end, as we have related in the Book of Knowledge.

And he—peace be upon him—said: "If you knew what I know, you would laugh little and weep much." Would that I knew—if that was not a secret withheld from disclosure because of the deficiency of intellects to grasp it, or for another meaning—why did he not mention it to them? There is no doubt they would have believed him had he mentioned it.

Ibn ʿAbbās—may God be pleased with them both—said concerning His saying—Mighty and Majestic—{«God is He who created seven heavens

- Root: ع-ص-ب (ʿ-ṣ-b)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: A band, party, or company bound together by a common tie; a distinct group united in purpose.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A divinely favored faction distinguished by illumination (anwār al-yaqīn), set apart from deviation.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: a tightly bound group; metaphorical: the elect community of truth.
- Root: ر-ه-ط (r-h-ṭ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: A small company or clan of men; a select band.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The party of truth (ḥaqq) singled out for guidance to the pillars of religion.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: a kin-group; metaphorical: the righteous cohort adhering to divine guidance.
- Root: ق-ط-ب (q-ṭ-b)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: A pivot, axis, or pole around which something revolves.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The foundational principles (uṣūl) upon which the testimony of faith turns.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: an axle; metaphorical: the central pillars of creed.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Coordination (al-ʿAṭf) — The conjunction "wa" links parallel substantives (e.g., "existence, eternity, permanence") maintaining syntactic parity, and the conditional clause "in lam tataḥaqqaq" governs the apodosis "laysa lahu ṭāʾil" with precise modal dependency.
chapters.translation:
I say, in the name of God, the Merciful, the Compassionate.

Praise be to God, who distinguished the band of the Sunnah with the lights of certainty, and favored the party of truth with guidance to the pillars of religion; who preserved them from the aberrations of the deviant and the misguidance of the heretics; who granted them success in following the master of the messengers; who steadied them in emulating the companionship of the most noble; and who facilitated for them the pursuit of the traces of the righteous predecessors — until they clung, against the exigencies of intellects, to the firm cord, and to the clear path through the conduct and creeds of the ancients. Thus they combined, in their discourse, the conclusions of reason with the rulings of transmitted law, and they realized that the utterance by which they are bound to worship — the saying "There is no god but God; Muhammad is the Messenger of God" — has no substance nor fruit unless one attains comprehensive grasp of the poles and principles upon which this testimony revolves. They knew that the two words of testimony, despite their brevity, entail the affirmation of the divine essence, the affirmation of His attributes, the affirmation of His acts, and the affirmation of the veracity of the Messenger. And they understood that the edifice of faith rests upon these pillars, which are four, and that each pillar turns upon ten principles.

The first pillar concerns knowledge of the essence of God, exalted be He, and its orbit comprises ten principles: knowledge of God's existence, His eternity, His permanence; that He is neither substance, nor body, nor accident; that He, glorified be He, is not confined to a direction nor settled upon a place; that He is visible; and that He is one.

The second pillar concerns His attributes, and it comprises ten principles: knowledge that He is living, knowing, powerful, willing, hearing, seeing, speaking; that He is exalted above the inherence of contingent events; and that His speech, knowledge, and will are eternal.

The third pillar concerns His acts, exalted be He, and its orbit comprises ten principles: that the acts of servants are created by God, exalted be He; that they are acquired by the servants; that they are willed by God; that He is gracious in creation and origination; that He may impose obligation beyond capacity; that He may inflict pain upon the innocent; that He is not obligated to observe the most beneficial; that nothing is obligatory except by the Law; that the sending of prophets is permissible; and that the prophethood of our Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, is established and confirmed by miracle.

The fourth pillar concerns the audibles (samʿiyyāt), and its orbit comprises ten principles: the affirmation of the gathering and the resurrection; the questioning of Munkar and Nakīr; the punishment of the grave; the balance; the path (ṣirāṭ); the creation of paradise and hellfire; the rulings of the imamate; that the merit of the Companions follows their order; and the conditions of the imamate.

الأصل الأول معرفة وجوده تعالى وأول ما يستضاء به من الأنوار ويسلك من
طريق الاعتبار ما أرشد إليه القرآن فليس بعد بيان الله سبحانه بيان وقد قال
تعالى ألم نجعل الأرض مهادا والجبال أوتادا وخلقناكم أزواجا وجعلنا نومكم
سباتا وجعلنا الليل لباسا وجعلنا النهار معاشا وبنينا فوقكم سبعا شدادا
وجعلنا سراجا وهاجا وأنزلنا من المعصرات ماء ثجاجا لنخرج به حبا ونباتا
وجنات ألفافا وقال تعالى إن في خلق السموات والأرض واختلاف الليل والنهار
والفلك التي تجري في البحر بما ينفع الناس وما أنزل الله من السماء من ماء
فأحيا به الأرض بعد موتها وبث فيها من كل دابة وتصريف الرياح والسحاب
المسخر بين السماء والأرض لآيات لقوم يعقلون وقال تعالى ألم تروا كيف خلق
الله سبع سموات طباقا وجعل القمر فيهن نورا وجعل الشمس سراجا والله أنبتكم
من الأرض نباتا ثم يعيدكم فيها ويخرجكم إخراجا وقال تعالى أفرأيتم ما تمنون
أأنتم تخلقونه أم نحن الخالقون إلى قوله للمقوين فليس يخفي على من معه أدنى
مسكة من عقل إذا تأمل بأدنى فكرة مضمون هذه الآيات وأدار نظره على عجائب
خلق الله في الأرض والسموات وبدائع فطرة الحيوان والنبات أن هذا الأمر
العجيب والترتيب المحكم لا يستغني عن صانع يدبره وفاعل يحكمه ويقدره بل
تكاد فطرة النفوس تشهد بكونها مقهورة تحت تسخيره ومصرفة بمقتضى تدبيره

الأنبياء صلوات الله عليهم لدعوة الخلق إلى التوحيد ليقولوا لا إله إلا
الله وما أمروا أن يقولوا لنا إله وللعالم إله

بواحد فكيف يعوزها واحد مع أنه لا نهاية لأعدادها

وإذا ثبت حدوثه كان افتقاره إلى المحدث من المدركات بالضرورة
الأصل الثاني العلم بأن الله تعالى قديم لم يزل أزلي ليس لوجوده أول بل
هو أول كل شيء وقبل كل ميت وحي
وبرهانه أنه لو كان حادثا ولم يكن قديما لافتقر هو أيضا إلى محدث وافتقر
محدثه إلى محدث وتسلسل ذلك إلى ما لا نهاية وما تسلسل لم يتحصل أو ينتهي
إلى محدث قديم هو الأول وذلك هو المطلوب الذي سميناه صانع العالم ومبدئه
وبارئه ومحدثه ومبدعه الأصل الثالث العلم بأنه تعالى مع كونه أزليا أبديا
ليس لوجوده آخر فهو الأول والآخر والظاهر والباطن لأن ما ثبت قدمه استحال

chapters.anchors:
- Root: و-ح-د (w-ḥ-d)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Singularity, oneness; that which is alone without second.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Divine unity (tawḥīd) as exclusive uniqueness in essence, attributes, and acts — negating any peer or partner.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Ḥaqīqah: numerical oneness; Majāz: absolute incomparability in divinity.
- Root: ح-د-ث (ḥ-d-th)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Origination, coming-to-be after non-existence; novelty.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Ḥudūth as the contingent mark of all created entities — the cornerstone of the cosmological proof.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: temporal occurrence; metaphorical: ontological dependence on a cause.
- Root: ق-د-م (q-d-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Precedence, anteriority; that which has no beginning.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Qidam as essential eternity — the negation of origination in the Divine essence.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: priority in time; metaphorical: priority in essence and causal necessity.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Constructions (al-sharṭ wa al-istithnāʾ) — for parsing the apodosis in "if it were not thus... then..." arguments, and the disjunctive syllogisms (taqsīm) in the proofs of finitude.
chapters.translation:
I say: As for the first pillar of the pillars of faith — namely, knowledge of the essence of God, Glorified and Exalted be He, and that God, Exalted is He, is One — its compass revolves upon ten principles.

**The First Principle: Knowledge of His Existence, Exalted is He.**

The first thing by which one is illumined from among the lights, and the path of reflection (iʿtibār) that one traverses, is that to which the Qurʾān guides. For after the exposition of God, Glorified be He, there is no exposition. He, Exalted is He, has said: {«أَلَمْ نَجْعَلِ الْأَرْضَ مِهَادًا وَالْجِبَالَ أَوْتَادًا وَخَلَقْنَاكُمْ أَزْوَاجًا وَجَعَلْنَا نَوْمَكُمْ سُبَاتًا وَجَعَلْنَا اللَّيْلَ لِبَاسًا وَجَعَلْنَا النَّهَارَ مَعَاشًا وَبَنَيْنَا فَوْقَكُمْ سَبْعًا شِدَادًا وَجَعَلْنَا سِرَاجًا وَهَّاجًا وَأَنزَلْنَا مِنَ الْمُعْصِرَاتِ مَاءً ثَجَّاجًا لِّنُخْرِجَ بِهِ حَبًّا وَنَبَاتًا وَجَنَّاتٍ أَلْفَافًا»} — "Have We not made the earth a resting-place, and the mountains as pegs, and created you in pairs, and made your sleep a repose, and made the night a covering, and made the day a livelihood, and built above you seven mighty heavens, and made a blazing lamp, and sent down from the rain-clouds pouring water, that We may bring forth thereby grain and vegetation and gardens dense with foliage?" And He, Exalted is He, said: {«إِنَّ فِي خَلْقِ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ وَاخْتِلَافِ اللَّيْلِ وَالنَّهَارِ وَالْفُلْكِ الَّتِي تَجْرِي فِي الْبَحْرِ بِمَا يَنفَعُ النَّاسَ وَمَا أَنزَلَ اللَّهُ مِنَ السَّمَاءِ مِن مَّاءٍ فَأَحْيَا بِهِ الْأَرْضَ بَعْدَ مَوْتِهَا وَبَثَّ فِيهَا مِن كُلِّ دَابَّةٍ وَتَصْرِيفِ الرِّيَاحِ وَالسَّحَابِ الْمُسَخَّرِ بَيْنَ السَّمَاءِ وَالْأَرْضِ لَآيَاتٍ لِّقَوْمٍ يَعْقِلُونَ»} — "Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the alternation of the night and the day, and the ships that sail upon the sea with what benefits mankind, and what God sends down from the sky of water, then revives thereby the earth after its death, and disperses therein every kind of creature, and the directing of the winds and the clouds subservient between the heaven and the earth — are signs for a people who reason." And He, Exalted is He, said: {«أَلَمْ تَرَوْا كَيْفَ خَلَقَ اللَّهُ سَبْعَ سَمَاوَاتٍ طِبَاقًا وَجَعَلَ الْقَمَرَ فِيهِنَّ نُورًا وَجَعَلَ الشَّمْسَ سِرَاجًا وَاللَّهُ أَنبَتَكُم مِّنَ الْأَرْضِ نَبَاتًا ثُمَّ يُعِيدُكُمْ فِيهَا وَيُخْرِجُكُمْ إِخْرَاجًا»} — "Have you not seen how God created seven heavens in layers, and made the moon therein a light, and made the sun a lamp? And God caused you to grow from the earth a growth; then He returns you into it and brings you forth a bringing forth." And He, Exalted is He, said: {«أَفَرَأَيْتُم مَّا تُمْنُونَ أَأَنتُمْ تَخْلُقُونَهُ أَمْ نَحْنُ الْخَالِقُونَ»} — up to His saying {«لِلْمُقْوِينَ»} — "Have you considered what you emit? Do you create it, or are We the Creator?" — up to His saying "for the destitute."

It is not hidden from anyone who possesses the least grasp of intellect, if he reflects with the slightest thought upon the purport of these verses and casts his gaze upon the wonders of God's creation in the earth and the heavens, and the marvels of the constitution (fiṭrah) of animals and plants, that this wondrous affair and this well-ordered arrangement (al-tartīb al-muḥkam) cannot dispense with a Maker (ṣāniʿ) who directs it, and an Agent (fāʿil) who governs it and determines it. Rather, the very innate disposition of souls (fiṭrat al-nufūs) almost bears witness to their being subdued under His subjugation (taskhīr) and disposed according to the requirement of His governance (tadbīr). For this reason, God, Exalted is He, said: {«أَفِي اللَّهِ شَكٌّ فَاطِرِ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ»} — "Is there any doubt about God, the Originator of the heavens and the earth?" And for this reason, the prophets — the blessings of God be upon them — were sent to call creation to monotheism (tawḥīd), that they might say: "There is no god but God" (lā ilāha illā Allāh). They were not commanded to say: "We have a god, and the world has a god" — for that was ingrained in the innate disposition of their intellects from the beginning of their formation and in the prime of their youth. For this reason, He, Mighty and Majestic is He, said: {«وَلَئِن سَأَلْتَهُم مَّنْ خَلَقَ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضَ لَيَقُولُنَّ اللَّهُ»} — "And if you asked them who created the heavens and the earth, they would surely say: God." And He, Exalted is He, said: {«فَأَقِمْ وَجْهَكَ لِلدِّينِ حَنِيفًا فِطْرَةَ اللَّهِ الَّتِي فَطَرَ النَّاسَ عَلَيْهَا لَا تَبْدِيلَ لِخَلْقِ اللَّهِ ذَلِكَ الدِّينُ الْقَيِّمُ»} — "So set your face to the religion, as a ḥanīf — the fiṭrah of God upon which He originated mankind; there is no alteration in the creation of God; that is the upright religion."

Thus, in the innate disposition of man and the evidences of the Qurʾān, there is that which suffices from erecting a demonstrative proof (burhān). Nevertheless, by way of corroboration (istiẓhār) and following the example of the speculative scholars (al-ʿulamāʾ al-nuẓẓār), we say: It is among the primary dictates of intellects (badāʾih al-ʿuqūl) that the originated (al-ḥādith) does not dispense, in its origination (ḥudūth), with a cause (sabab) that originates it. And the world (al-ʿālam) is originated. Therefore, it does not dispense, in its origination, with a cause.

As for our statement that the originated does not dispense, in its origination, with a cause — this is evident. For every originated thing is specified (mukhtaṣṣ) to a time, while the intellect deems it permissible to suppose its advancement or postponement. So its specification to its own time, rather than what precedes it or what follows it, necessarily requires a specifier (mukhassiṣ). As for our statement that the world is originated, its proof is that the bodies (ajsām) of the world are never devoid of motion (ḥarakah) or rest (sukūn), and both of these are originated. And that which is not devoid of originated things is itself originated.

In this proof there are three claims. The first is our statement that bodies are not devoid of motion or rest — and this is apprehended by intuition (badīhah) and necessity (iḍṭirār), requiring no reflection or deliberation. For whoever conceives of a body that is neither at rest nor in motion has mounted the back of ignorance and deviated from the path of intellect.

The second is our statement that both of them are originated. What indicates this is their mutual succession (taʿāqub) and the existence of some of them after others — and this is witnessed in all bodies, both those that have been witnessed and those that have not. For there is no thing at rest except that the intellect judges the permissibility of its motion, and no thing in motion except that the intellect judges the permissibility of its rest. So the one of them that supervenes (al-ṭāriʾ) is originated by virtue of its supervention, and the one that precedes is originated by virtue of its non-existence (ʿadam) — for if its eternity (qidam) were established, its non-existence would be impossible, as will come in the exposition and proof of the subsistence (baqāʾ) of the Maker, Exalted and Sanctified is He.

The third is our statement that that which is not devoid of originated things is itself originated. Its proof is that if it were not so, then before every originated thing there would be originated things with no first — and if those originated things did not all pass away in their entirety, the turn would never reach the existence of the present originated thing in the current moment. And the passing away of that which has no end (mā lā nihāyah lahu) is impossible. And because if the celestial sphere (falak) had rotations (dawrāt) with no end, then their number would not be devoid of being even (shafʿ) or odd (watr), or both even and odd together, or neither even nor odd. And it is impossible for it to be both even and odd together, or neither even nor odd — for that would be a combination of negation and affirmation, since in affirming one of them there is a negation of the other, and in negating one of them there is an affirmation of the other. And it is impossible for it to be even, because the even becomes odd by the addition of one — and how could that which has no end lack one? And it is impossible for it to be odd, because the odd becomes even by one — so how could it lack one, given that its numbers have no end? And it is impossible for it to be neither even nor odd, for then it would have an end.

It is thus established from this that the world is not devoid of originated things, and that which is not devoid of originated things is therefore originated. And when its origination is established, its need for an Originator (muḥdith) becomes among the things apprehended by necessity.

**The Second Principle: Knowledge that God, Exalted is He, is Eternal (qadīm), having never ceased to be, without beginning (azalī) — His existence has no first, but rather He is the First of everything and before every dead and living thing.**

Its proof is that if He were originated and not eternal, He too would need an originator, and His originator would need an originator, and this would regress (tasalsul) to infinity. And that which regresses is never completed — or it terminates at an eternal originator who is the First, and that is the very object sought, which we have named the Maker of the world, its Originator (mubdiʾ), its Creator (bāriʾ), its Originator (muḥdith), and its Inventor (mubdiʿ).

**The Third Principle: Knowledge that He, Exalted is He, while being eternal without beginning, is also eternal without end (abadī) — His existence has no last. He is the First and the Last, the Outward and the Inward.**

For that whose eternity (qidam) is established, its non-existence is impossible. Its proof is that if He were to become non-existent, He would not be devoid of either becoming non-existent by Himself or by a non-existent-maker (muʿdim) that opposes Him. For if it were permissible for something whose continuance is conceivable to become non-existent by itself, then it would be permissible for something whose non-existence is conceivable to come into existence by itself. For just as the supervention of existence requires a cause, so too the supervention of non-existence requires a cause. And it is false that He becomes non-existent by an opposing non-existent-maker, because if that non-existent-maker were eternal, existence would not be conceivable alongside it — and the existence and eternity of Him have already been established by the two preceding principles. So how could His existence be in eternity while His opposite is with Him? And if the opposing non-existent-maker were originated, that would be impossible — for the originated is not more entitled to oppose the eternal so as to cut off its existence, than the eternal is to oppose the originated so as to repel its existence. Rather, repulsion (dafʿ) is easier than cutting off (qaṭʿ), and the eternal is stronger and more entitled than the originated.

**The Fourth Principle: Knowledge that He, Exalted is He, is not a substance (jawhar) occupying space (mutḥayyiz), but rather is exalted and sanctified above any relation to spatial location (ḥayyiz).**

Its proof is that every substance occupying space is specified to its spatial location, and is not devoid of being at rest therein or in motion therefrom — thus it is not devoid of motion or rest. And both of these are originated, and that which is not devoid of originated things is originated. And if a spatial substance that is eternal were conceivable, then the eternity of the substances of the world would be conceivable. If someone calls Him a "substance" but does not mean thereby the spatial entity, he errs in the wording (lafẓ) but not in the meaning (maʿnā).

**The Fifth Principle: Knowledge that He, Exalted is He, is not a body (jism) composed of substances.**

For the body is nothing but that which is composed of substances. And when His being a substance specified to a spatial location is refuted, His being a body is refuted — because every body is specified to a spatial location and composed of substances. For the substance is impossible to be devoid of separation (iftirāq) and conjunction (ijtimāʿ), motion and rest, shape (hayʾah) and magnitude (miqdār) — and these are the marks of origination (simāt al-ḥudūth). And if it were permissible to believe that the Maker of the world is a body, it would be permissible to believe in the divinity of the sun and the moon, or of some other thing among the categories of bodies. And if some audacious one dares to call Him, Exalted is He, a "body" without intending composition from substances, that is an error in the name while being correct in negating the meaning of body.

**The Sixth Principle: Knowledge that He, Exalted is He, is not an accident (ʿaraḍ) subsisting in a body, nor an attribute (ḥāl) indwelling in a locus (maḥall).**

For the accident is that which inheres in a body. Every body is originated, necessarily, and its originator exists before it. So how could He be indwelling in a body, when He existed in eternity alone with nothing else alongside Him, and then originated the bodies and accidents after? And because He is Knowing, Powerful, Willing, Creating — as will come in its exposition — and these attributes are impossible for accidents; rather, they are not intelligible except for an existent that subsists by itself (qāʾim bi-nafsihi) and is independent in its essence (mustaqill bi-dhātihi).

It is thus established from these principles that He is an existent subsisting by Himself, neither a substance, nor a body, nor an accident — and that the entire world is substances, accidents, and bodies. Therefore, He resembles nothing, and nothing resembles Him. Rather, He is the Living, the Self-Subsistent (al-Qayyūm), of whom {«لَيْسَ كَمِثْلِهِ شَيْءٌ»} — "there is nothing like unto Him." And how could the created resemble its Creator, the determined (maqdūr) its Determiner (muqaddir), and the formed (muṣawwar) its Formator (muṣawwir)? The bodies and accidents are all of His creation and handiwork — so it is impossible to judge upon them any likeness or similarity to Him.

**The Seventh Principle: Knowledge that God, Exalted is He, is sanctified in His essence above specification to directions (jihāt).**

For the direction is either above (fawq) or below (taḥt), right (yamīn) or left (shimāl), front (quddām) or back (khalaf). And these directions — He it is who created them and originated them by means of the creation of man. For He created for him two extremities: one upon which he leans upon the earth, called the foot (rijl), and the other opposite to it, called the head (raʾs). Thus arose the name "above" for what faces the direction of the head, and the name "below" for what faces the direction of the foot — so much so that the ant that crawls inverted under the ceiling has its direction of "above" turned into "below" in its regard, even though it is "above" in our regard. And He created for man two hands, one of which is stronger than the other in most cases — thus arose the name "right" (yamīn) for the stronger, and the name "left" (shimāl) for what faces it; and the direction facing the right is called "right" and the other "left." And He created for him two sides, from one of which he sees and toward which he moves — thus arose the name "front" (quddām) for the direction toward which he advances in movement, and the name "back" (khalaf) for what faces it. So the directions are originated with the origination of man. And if man had not been created with this constitution, but rather created round like a sphere, these directions would have no existence whatsoever.

So how could He have been, in eternity, specified to a direction when the direction is originated? And how did He become specified to a direction after not being so? Is it that He created the world above Him? But He is exalted above having anything above Him, for He is exalted above having a head — and "above" is an expression for what is the direction of the head. Or did He create the world beneath Him? But He is exalted above having anything beneath Him, for He is exalted above having a foot — and "below" is an expression for what faces the direction of the foot. And all of this is impossible in the intellect. And because what is intelligible of His being specified to a direction is either that He is specified to a spatial location with the specification of substances, or specified to substances with the specification of accidents — and the impossibility of His being a substance or an accident has already been shown — so His being specified to a direction is impossible. And if by "direction" something other than these two meanings is intended, that is an error in the name while agreeing on the meaning. And because if He were above the world, He would be facing it (muḥādhī), and everything facing a body is either like it, smaller than it, or larger than it — and all of that is a magnitude (taqdīr) that necessarily requires a Determiner (muqaddir), and the One Creator, the Manager, is exalted above it.

As for the raising of hands in supplication toward the direction of the sky — that is because it is the qiblah of prayer (qiblat al-duʿāʾ). And in it there is also an indication of what is an attribute of the One invoked — of majesty (jalāl) and grandeur (kibriyāʾ) — alerting, by intending the direction of height, to the attribute of glory (majd) and elevation (ʿalāʾ). For He, Exalted is He, is above every existent by way of subjugation (qahr) and domination (istīlāʾ).

**The Eighth Principle: Knowledge that He, Exalted is He, is established upon His Throne (istawā ʿalā ʿarshihi) in the sense that God, Exalted is He, intended by "establishment" (istiwāʾ) — which is that which does not contradict the attribute of grandeur, and to which the marks of origination and passing away do not penetrate.**

And it is that which is intended by His saying in the Qurʾān: {«ثُمَّ اسْتَوَىٰ إِلَى السَّمَاءِ وَهِيَ دُخَانٌ»} — "Then He established Himself to the heaven, and it was smoke" — and that is only by way of subjugation and domination, as the poet said:

"Indeed Bishr has established himself (istawā) over Iraq — without sword and without spilled blood."

The people of truth (ahl al-ḥaqq) were compelled to this interpretation (taʾwīl), just as the people of falsehood (ahl al-bāṭil) were compelled to the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He: {«وَهُوَ مَعَكُمْ أَيْنَ مَا كُنتُمْ»} — "And He is with you wherever you are" — since it is carried, by agreement, upon encompassment (iḥāṭah) and knowledge (ʿilm). And His saying, peace and blessings be upon him: "The heart of the believer is between two fingers of the fingers of the Merciful" is carried upon power (qudrah) and strength (quwwah). And His saying, peace and blessings be upon him: "The Black Stone is the right hand of God in His earth" is carried upon honor (tashrīf) and veneration (ikrām). For if it were left upon its literal sense (ẓāhir), the impossible would follow from it. Likewise, if "establishment" (istiwāʾ) were left upon settling (istiqrār) and indwelling (tamakkun), there would follow from it that the one so settled is a body touching the Throne — either like it, larger than it, or smaller than it — and that is impossible. And that which leads to the impossible is itself impossible.

**The Ninth Principle: Knowledge that He, Exalted is He, while being sanctified above form (ṣūrah) and magnitude (miqdār), and hallowed above directions and regions (aqṭār), is yet visible (marʾī) to the eyes and sights (abṣār) in the Abode of the Hereafter, the Abode of Permanence (dār al-qarār).**

This is due to His saying, Exalted is He: {«وُجُوهٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ نَّاضِرَةٌ إِلَىٰ رَبِّهَا نَاظِرَةٌ»} — "Faces on that day are radiant, looking upon their Lord." And He is not seen in this world, in confirmation of His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: {«لَا تُدْرِكُهُ الْأَبْصَارُ وَهُوَ يُدْرِكُ الْأَبْصَارَ»} — "Sights do not comprehend Him, and He comprehends the sights." And His saying, Exalted is He, in the address to Moses, peace be upon him: {«لَن تَرَانِي»} — "You shall not see Me." Would that I knew — how did the Muʿtazilī know, from the attributes of the Lord of Lords, that which Moses, peace be upon him, did not know? And how did Moses, peace be upon him, ask for the vision (ruʾyah) if it were impossible? Perhaps ignorance of the people of innovation (ahl al-bidaʿ) and caprice (ahwāʾ) — who are among the ignorant fools — is more fitting than ignorance of the prophets, the blessings of God be upon them.

As for the manner of carrying the verse of vision upon its literal sense — it is because it does not lead to the impossible. For vision (ruʾyah) is a kind of unveiling (kashf) and knowledge (ʿilm), except that it is more complete (atamm) and more manifest (awḍaḥ) than knowledge. So if knowledge of Him is permissible while He is not in a direction, then vision of Him is permissible while He is not in a direction. And just as it is permissible that God, Exalted is He, sees creation without being in their facing (muqābalah), so it is permissible that creation sees Him without facing. And just as it is permissible that He is known without modality (kayfiyyah) and form (ṣūrah), so it is permissible that He is seen in that manner.

**The Tenth Principle: Knowledge that God, Mighty and Majestic is He, is One (wāḥid) with no partner (sharīk), Single (fard) with no equal (nidd).**

He is unique in creation (khalq) and origination (ibdāʿ), and independent in bringing into existence (ījād) and invention (ikhtirāʿ). He has no like (mithl) to share with Him or equal Him, and no opposite (ḍidd) to contend with Him or oppose Him. Its proof is His saying, Exalted is He: {«لَوْ كَانَ فِيهِمَا آلِهَةٌ إِلَّا اللَّهُ لَفَسَدَتَا»} — "If there were in them gods other than God, they would both be corrupted." Its exposition is that if there were two gods, and one of them willed a matter, then the second — if he were compelled to assist him, this second would be subdued (maqhūr) and impotent (ʿājiz), and would not be a powerful god; and if he were able to oppose him and repel him, then the second would be strong and overpowering, and the first would be weak and deficient, and would not be a powerful god.
