||| الركن الثاني العلم بصفات الله تعالى ومداره على عشرة أصول

الأصل الأول العلم بأن صانع العالم قادر وأنه تعالى في قوله وهو على كل
شيء قدير صادق لأن العالم محكم في صنعته مرتب في خلقته ومن رأى ثوبا من
ديباج حسن النسج والتأليف متناسب التطريز والتطريف ثم توهم صدور نسجه عن
ميت لا استطاعة له أو عن إنسان لا قدرة له كان منخلعا عن غريزة العقل
ومنخرطا في سلك أهل الغباوة والجهل
الأصل الثاني العلم بأنه تعالى عالم بجميع الموجودات ومحيط بكل المخلوقات
لا يعزب عن علمه مثقال ذرة في الأرض ولا في السماء صادق في قوله وهو بكل
شيء عليم ومرشد إلى صدقه بقوله تعالى ألا يعلم من خلق وهو اللطيف الخبير
أرشدك إلى الاستدلال بالخلق على العلم بأنك لا تستريب في دلالة الخلق
اللطيف والصنع المزين بالترتيب ولو في الشيء الحقير الضعيف على علم الصانع
بكيفية الترتيب والترصيف فما ذكره الله سبحانه هو المنتهى في الهداية
والتعريف
الأصل الثالث العلم بكونه عز وجل حيا فإن من ثبت
PageV01P108
علمه وقدرته ثبت بالضرورة حياته ولو تصور قادر وعالم فاعل مدبر دون أن
يكون حيا لجاز أن يشك في حياة الحيوانات عند ترددها في الحركات والسكنات بل
في حياة أرباب  الحرف والصناعات وذلك انغماس في غمرة الجهالات والضلالات
الأصل الرابع العلم بكونه تعالى مريدا لأفعاله فلا موجود إلا وهو مستند
إلى مشيئته وصادر عن إرادته فهو المبدىء المعيد والفعال لما يريد وكيف لا
يكون مريدا وكل فعل صدر منه أمكن أن يصدر منه ضده وما لا ضد له أمكن أن
يصدر منه ذلك بعينه قبله أو بعده
والقدرة تناسب الضدين والوقتين مناسبة واحدة فلا بد من إرادة صارفة
للقدرة إلى أحد المقدورين
ولو أغنى العلم عن الإرادة في تخصيص المعلوم حتى يقال إنما وجد في الوقت
الذي سبق بوجوده لجاز أن يغني عن القدرة حتى يقال وجد بغير قدرة لأنه سبق
العلم بوجوده فيه
الأصل الخامس العلم بأنه تعالى سميع بصير لا يعزب عن رؤيته هواجس الضمير
وخفايا الوهم والتفكير ولا يشذ عن سمعه صوت دبيب النملة السوداء في الليلة
الظلماء على الصخرة الصماء وكيف لا يكون سميعا بصيرا والسمع والبصر كمال لا
محالة وليس بنقص فكيف يكون المخلوق أكمل من الخالق والمصنوع أسنى وأتم من
الصانع وكيف تعتدل القسمة مهما وقع النقص في جهته والكمال في خلقه وصنعته
أو كيف تستقيم حجة إبراهيم صلى الله عليه وسلم على أبيه إذ كان يعبد
الأصنام جهلا وغيا فقال له لم تعبد ما لا يسمع ولا يبصر ولا يغني عنك شيئا
ولو انقلب ذلك عليه في معبوده لأضحت حجته داحضة ودلالته ساقطة ولم يصدق
قوله تعالى وتلك حجتنا آتيناها إبراهيم على قومه وكما عقل كونه فاعلا بلا
جارحة وعالما بلا قلب ودماغ فليعقل كونه بصيرا بلا حدقة وسميعا بلا اذن إذ
لا فرق بينهما
الأصل السادس أنه سبحانه وتعالى متكلم بكلام وهو وصف قائم بذاته ليس بصوت
ولا حرف بل لا يشبه كلامه كلام غيره كما لا يشبه وجوده وجود غيره
والكلام بالحقيقة كلام النفس وإنما الأصوات قطعت حروفا للدلالات كما يدل
عليها تارة بالحركات والإشارات وكيف التبس هذا على طائفة من الأغبياء ولم
يلتبس على جهلة الشعراء حيث قال قائلهم
إن  الكلام لفي الفؤاد وإنما ... جعل اللسان على الفؤاد دليلا
ومن لم يعقله عقله ولا نهاه نهاه عن أن يقول لساني حادث ولكن ما يحدث فيه
بقدرتي الحادثة قديم فاقطع عن عقلة طمعك وكف عن خطابه لسانك
ومن لم يفهم أن القديم عبارة عما ليس قبله شيء
وأن الباء قبل السين في قولك بسم الله فلا يكون السين المتأخر عن الباء
قديما فنزه عن الالتفات إليه قلبك فلله سبحانه سر في إبعاد بعض العباد ومن
يضلل الله فما له من هاد ومن استبعد أن يسمع موسى عليه السلام في الدنيا
كلاما ليس بصوت ولا حرف فليستنكر أن يرى في الآخرة موجودا ليس بجسم ولا لون
وإن عقل أن يرى ما ليس بلون ولا جسم ولا قدر ولا كمية وهو إلى الآن لم ير
غيره فليعقل في حاسة السمع ما عقله في حاسة البصر
وإن عقل على أن يكون له علم واحد هو علم بجميع الموجودات فليعقل صفة
واحدة للذات هو كلام بجميع ما دل عليه من العبارات
وإن عقل كون السموات السبع وكون الجنة والنار مكتوبة في ورقة صغيرة
ومحفوظة في مقدار ذرة من القلب وأن كل ذلك مرئي في مقدار عدسة من الحدقة من
غير أن تحل ذات السموات والأرض والجنة والنار في الحدقة والقلب والورقة
فليعقل كون الكلام مقروءا بالألسنة محفوظا في القلوب مكتوبا في المصاحف من
غير حلول ذات الكلام فيها إذ لو حلت بكتاب الله ذات الكلام في الورق لحل
ذات الله تعالى بكتابة اسمه في الورق وحلت ذات النار بكتابه اسمها في الورق
ولاحترق
الأصل السابع أن الكلام القائم بنفسه قديم وكذا جميع صفاته إذ يستحيل أن
يكون محلا
PageV01P109
للحوادث داخلا تحت التغير بل يجب للصفات من نعوت القدم ما يجب للذات فلا
تعتريه التغيرات ولا تحله الحادثات بل لم يزل في قدمه موصوفا بمحامد

- Root: ق-د-ر (q-d-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Capacity, measure, power to bring about with precise determination
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Divine omnipotence as exhaustive causal efficacy over all existents
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Ḥaqīqah — power as real attribute, not mere metaphor of ability
- Root: ع-ل-م (ʿ-l-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Knowledge, perception, distinguishing mark (ʿalamah)
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Comprehensive divine knowledge encompassing all particulars without temporal acquisition
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Ḥaqīqah — knowledge as essential attribute, not figurative awareness
- Root: ح-ي-و (ḥ-y-w)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Life, vitality, the opposite of death
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Divine life as necessary concomitant of knowledge and power
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Ḥaqīqah — life as real attribute, not metaphorical animation
- Root: إ-ر-د (ʾ-r-d)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Will, intention, desire directed toward a purpose
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Divine will as the differentiator (mukhaṣṣiṣ) selecting among equally possible alternatives
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Ḥaqīqah — will as essential attribute, distinct from mere inclination
- Root: س-م-ع (s-m-ʿ) / ب-ص-ر (b-ṣ-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Hearing and sight as perceptual faculties
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Divine hearing and sight as all-encompassing perception without organs
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Ḥaqīqah — real attributes, not metaphorical "awareness"
- Root: ك-ل-م (k-l-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Speech, utterance, wounding (effect on the recipient)
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Divine speech as eternal attribute of the essence (kalām nafsī), not letters or sounds
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Distinction between ḥaqīqah (inner speech) and majāz (vocal expression as sign)
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Taʿlīq (Suspension) — conditional clauses with law/la-walā establishing hypothetical necessity; Rule of Muḍāriʿ Istimrārī (continuous present) for eternal attributes; Rule of Taṣāruf (governance) — verbs governing accusatives in argumentative sequences
chapters.translation:
I say: The second pillar is knowledge of God's attributes, and its scope revolves around ten principles.

**The First Principle:** Knowledge that the Maker of the world is powerful (qādir), and that He — exalted — is truthful in His saying {«and He is over all things powerful»} (Q. 2:20), because the world is precise in its craftsmanship, ordered in its creation. Whoever sees a garment of fine brocade, beautiful in weave and composition, proportionate in embroidery and edging, then supposes that its weaving issued from a corpse having no capacity, or from a human being having no power — such a one would be stripped of the instinct of reason and threaded into the cord of the dull-witted and ignorant.

**The Second Principle:** Knowledge that He — exalted — is knowing (ʿālim) of all existents and encompassing of every creature. There escapes not His knowledge the weight of an atom in the earth nor in the heaven. He is truthful in His saying {«and He is over all things knowing»} (Q. 2:29), and He guides to His truthfulness by His saying — exalted — {«Does He who created not know, and He is the Subtle, the Aware?»} (Q. 67:14). He guided you to infer from creation to knowledge, such that you do not doubt that the subtle creation and the craftsmanship adorned with order — even in the mean and weak thing — indicates the Maker's knowledge of the manner of ordering and arrangement. So what God — glory to Him — mentioned is the ultimate in guidance and definition.

**The Third Principle:** Knowledge that He — might and majesty be His — is living (ḥayy). For whoever's knowledge and power are established, his life is established by necessity. If one could conceive a powerful, knowing agent and manager without being living, then one could doubt the life of animals in their alternating movements and stillnesses — nay, even the life of craftsmen and artisans — and that is immersion in the depths of ignorances and errors.

**The Fourth Principle:** Knowledge that He — exalted — is willing (murīd) for His acts. There is no existent except that it is dependent upon His will and issues from His intention. He is the Originator, the Restorer, {«the Doer of what He wills»} (Q. 85:16). How could He not be willing, when every act that issued from Him could have issued from Him its opposite, and that which has no opposite could have issued from Him that very thing before or after its time? Power relates to the two opposites and the two times with one single relation. There must, therefore, be a will that directs power to one of the two possible objects. And if knowledge sufficed over will in specifying the known — such that one might say, "It only came to be at the time preceded by its existence in knowledge" — then it would be permissible for knowledge to suffice over power, such that one might say, "It came to be without power, because knowledge preceded its existence in it."

**The Fifth Principle:** Knowledge that He — exalted — is hearing (samīʿ) and seeing (baṣīr). There escapes not His sight the whisperings of conscience, nor the hidden things of imagination and thought. There slips not from His hearing the sound of the crawling of a black ant upon the hard rock in the dark night. How could He not be hearing and seeing, when hearing and sight are perfection without doubt, not deficiency? How, then, could the creature be more perfect than the Creator, and the made thing more exalted and complete than the Maker? How could the division be equitable when deficiency falls on His side and perfection on His creation and craftsmanship? Or how could the argument of Abraham — peace be upon him — against his father stand, when he worshipped idols in ignorance and error, saying to him: {«Why do you worship what neither hears nor sees, nor avails you anything?»} (Q. 19:42)? Were that turned back upon him regarding his own object of worship, his argument would become invalid, his proof fallen, and there would be no confirmation of His saying — exalted — {«And that is Our argument which We gave to Abraham against his people»} (Q. 6:83). And just as reason grasped that He is an agent without a limb, and knowing without a heart and brain, so let it grasp that He is seeing without a pupil and hearing without an ear — for there is no difference between the two.

**The Sixth Principle:** That He — glory to Him and exalted — is speaking (mutakallim) with speech (kalām), which is an attribute subsisting in His essence, neither sound nor letter. Rather, His speech resembles not the speech of others, just as His existence resembles not the existence of others. Speech in truth is the speech of the soul (kalām al-nafs); sounds are merely letters cut for indications, just as one sometimes indicates by movements and gestures. How did this become confused upon a group of the stupid, yet was not confused upon the ignorant poets, one of whom said:

"Indeed speech is in the heart, and only — the tongue was made a sign upon the heart."

Whoever's intellect did not grasp it, and whose forbearance did not restrain him from saying, "My tongue is originated, but what occurs in it by my originated power is eternal" — cut off your hope from his intellect, and withhold your tongue from addressing him. And whoever did not understand that "eternal" (qadīm) means that before which there is nothing — and that the bāʾ precedes the sīn in your saying "bismillāh," so that the sīn which comes after the bāʾ cannot be eternal — then purify your heart from paying attention to him. For God — glory to Him — has a secret in distancing some servants, {«and whom God leads astray, for him there is no guide»} (Q. 13:33). And whoever deems it far-fetched that Moses — peace be upon him — heard in this world speech that is neither sound nor letter, let him deem it far-fetched that he will see in the hereafter an existent that is neither body nor color. And if he grasped that one can see what is neither color nor body nor magnitude nor quantity — though he has not yet seen other than that — then let him grasp in the sense of hearing what he grasped in the sense of sight. And if he grasped that God has one knowledge that is knowledge of all existents, let him grasp one attribute of the essence that is speech concerning all that the expressions indicate. And if he grasped that the seven heavens, and paradise and hellfire, are written in a small leaf and preserved in the measure of an atom of the heart, and that all of that is visible in the measure of a lentil of the pupil — without the essences of the heavens and earth and paradise and hellfire entering into the pupil, heart, and leaf — then let him grasp that speech is recited by tongues, preserved in hearts, written in codices, without the essence of speech entering into them. For were the essence of speech to enter into the paper by God's book, then the essence of God would enter into the paper by the writing of His name, and the essence of fire would enter into the paper by the writing of its name — and it would burn.

**The Seventh Principle:** That the speech subsisting in His essence is eternal (qadīm), and likewise all His attributes. For it is impossible that He be a locus for originated things (maḥall li-l-ḥawādith), falling under change. Rather, the attributes must have of the descriptions of eternity what the essence must have. So no changes befall Him, and no originated things enter into Him. Rather, He has never ceased in His eternity to be described with praiseworthy attributes, and shall not cease in His perpetuity to be so — transcendent above the change of states. For whatever is a locus for originated things is not free of them, and whatever is not free of originated things is itself originated. Origination (ḥudūth) is only established for bodies by virtue of their being subject to change and the turning of descriptions. How, then, could their Creator share with them in the acceptance of change? Upon this is built that His speech is eternal, subsisting in His essence, and that only the sounds indicating it are originated. And just as reason grasped the subsistence of the request for learning and the will for it in the essence of a parent toward his child before the child's creation — such that when the child is created and understands, and God creates for him knowledge pertaining to what is in his father's heart of the request, he becomes commanded by that request which subsisted in his father's essence and whose existence endured until the time of his child's knowing it — so let it grasp the subsistence of the request indicated by His saying — might and majesty be His — {«Take off your sandals»} (Q. 20:12) in God's essence, and Moses' — peace be upon him — becoming addressed by it after his existence, when knowledge was created for him of that request, and he heard that eternal speech.

**The Eighth Principle:** That His knowledge is eternal. He has never ceased to be knowing of His essence, His attributes, and what He originates of His creatures. Whenever creatures come to be, there does not originate for Him knowledge of them; rather, they become disclosed to Him by the eternal knowledge. For if knowledge were created in us of Zayd's arrival at sunrise, and that knowledge endured hypothetically until the sun rose, then Zayd's arrival at sunrise would be known to us by that knowledge without the renewal of another knowledge. Thus should the eternity of God's knowledge be understood.

**The Ninth Principle:** That His will (irādah) is eternal, and in eternity it was attached to the origination of originated things at their fitting times, in accordance with the precedence of eternal knowledge. For were it originated, He would become a locus for originated things; and were it originated outside His essence, He would not be willing by it — just as you are not moving by a motion not in your essence. However you suppose it, its origination would require another will, and that other will would require yet another, and the matter would regress infinitely. And if it were permissible that a will originate without a will, then it would be permissible that the world originate without a will.

**The Tenth Principle:** That God — exalted — is knowing by knowledge, living by life, powerful by power, willing by will, speaking by speech, hearing by hearing, seeing by sight. He has these descriptions by these eternal attributes. The saying of one who says "knowing without knowledge" is like his saying "rich without wealth," and "knowledge without a knower," and "a knower without a known." For knowledge, the known, and the knower are mutually entailed (mutalāzimah) — like killing, the killed, and the killer. Just as one cannot conceive a killer without killing and a killed, nor a killed without a killer and killing, so too one cannot conceive a knower without knowledge, nor knowledge without a known, nor a known without a knower. Rather, these three are mutually entailed in the intellect, none of them separable from the other. Whoever permits the separation of the knower from knowledge, let him permit his separation from the known, and the separation of knowledge from the knower — for there is no difference between these descriptions.

chapters.title_en: The Third Pillar: Knowledge of God's Acts, Comprising Ten Principles

||| الركن الثالث العلم بأفعال الله تعالى ومداره على عشرة أصول

الأصل الأول العلم بأن كل حادث في العالم فهو فعله وخلقه واختراعه لا
خالق له سواه ولا محدث له إلا إياه
خلق الخلق وصنعهم وأوجد قدرتهم وحركتهم فجميع أفعال عبادة مخلوقة له
ومتعلقة بقدرته تصديقا له في قوله تعالى الله خالق كل شيء وفي قوله تعالى
والله خلقكم وما تعملون وفي قوله تعالى وأسروا قولكم أو اجهروا به إنه عليم
بذات الصدور ألا يعلم من خلق وهو اللطيف الخبير أمر العباد بالتحرز في
أقوالهم وأفعالهم وإسرارهم وإضمارهم لعلمه بموارد أفعالهم
واستدل على العلم بالخلق وكيف لا يكون خالقا لفعل العبد وقدرته تامة لا
قصور فيها وهي متعلقة بحركة أبدان العباد والحركات متماثلة وتعلق القدرة
بها لذاتها فما الذي يقصر تعلقها عن بعض الحركات دون البعض مع تماثلها أو
كيف يكون الحيوان مستبدا بالاختراع ويصدر من العنكبوت والنحل وسائر
الحيوانات من لطائف الصناعات ما يتحير فيه عقول ذوي الألباب فكيف انفردت هي
باختراعها دون رب الأرباب وهي غير عالمة بتفصيل ما يصدر منها من الاكتساب
هيهات هيهات ذلت المخلوقات وتفرد بالملك والملكوت
PageV01P110
جبار الأرض والسموات
الأصل الثاني أن انفراد الله سبحانه باختراع حركات العباد لا يخرجها عن
كونها مقدورة للعباد على سبيل الاكتساب بل الله تعالى خلق القدرة والمقدور
جميعا وخلق الاختيار والمختار جميعا
فأما القدرة فوصف للعبد وخلق للرب سبحانه وليست بكسب له
وأما الحركة فخلق للرب تعالى ووصف للعبد وكسب له فإنها خلقت مقدورة بقدرة
هي وصفه وكانت للحركة نسبة إلى  صفة أخرى تسمى قدرة فتسمى باعتبار تلك
النسبة كسبا وكيف تكون جبرا محضا وهو بالضرورة يدرك التفرقة بين الحركة
المقدورة والرعدة الضرورية أو كيف يكون خلقا للعبد وهو لا يحيط علما
بتفاصيل أجزاء الحركات المكتسبة وأعدادها وإذا بطل الطرفان لم يبق إلا
الاقتصاد في الاعتقاد وهو أنها مقدورة بقدرة الله تعالى اختراعا وبقدرة
العبد على وجه آخر من التعليق يعبر عنه بالاكتساب
وليس من ضرورة تعلق القدرة بالمقدور أن يكون بالاختراع فقط إذ قدره الله
تعالى في الأزل قد كانت متعلقة بالعالم ولم يكن الاختراع حاصلا بها وهي عند
الاختراع متعلقة به نوعا آخر من التعلق فيه يظهر أن تعلق القدرة ليس مخصوصا
بحصول المقدور بها
الأصل الثالث أن فعل العبد وإن كان كسبا للعبد فلا يخرج عن كونه مرادا
لله سبحانه
فلا يجري في الملك والملكوت طرفة عين ولا لفتة خاطر ولا فلتة ناظر إلا
بقضاء الله وقدرته وبإرادته ومشيئته
ومنه الشر والخير والنفع والضر والإسلام والكفر والعرفان والنكر والفوز
والخسران والغواية والرشد والطاعة والعصيان والشرك والإيمان لا راد لقضائه
ولا معقب لحكمه يضل من يشاء ويهدي من يشاء لا يسئل عما يفعل وهم يسألون
ويدل عليه من النقل قول الأمة قاطبة ما شاء كان وما لم يشأ لم يكن وقول
الله عز وجل أن لو يشاء الله لهدى الناس جميعا وقوله تعالى ولو شئنا لآتينا
كل نفس هداها ويدل عليه من جهة العقل أن المعاصي والجرائم إن كان الله
يكرهها ولا يريدها وإنما هي جارية على وفق إرادة العدو إبليس لعنه الله مع
أنه عدو لله سبحانه والجاري على وفق إرادة العدو أكثر من الجاري على وفق
إرادته تعالى فليت شعري كيف يستجيز المسلم أن يرد ملك الجبار ذي الجلال
والإكرام إلى رتبة لو ردت إليها رياسة زعيم ضيعة لاستنكف منها إذ لو كان ما
يستمر لعدو الزعيم في القرية أكثر مما يستقيم له لاستنكف من زعامته وتبرأ
عن ولايته
والمعصية هي الغالبة على الخلق وكل ذلك جار  عند المبتدعة على خلاف إرادة
الحق تعالى وهذا غاية الضعف والعجز تعالى رب الأرباب عن قول الظالمين علوا
كبيرا
ثم مهما ظهر أن أفعال العباد مخلوقة لله صح أنها مرادة له
فإن قيل فكيف ينهى عما يريد ويأمر بما لا يريد قلنا الأمر غير الإرادة
ولذلك إذا ضرب السيد عبده فعاتبه السلطان عليه فاعتذر بتمرد عبده عليه
فكذبه السلطان فأراد إظهار حجته بأن يأمر العبد بفعل ويخالفه بين يديه فقال
له أسرج هذه الدابة بمشهد من السلطان فهو يأمره بما لايريد امتثاله ولو لم
يكن آمرا لما كان عذره عند السلطان ممهدا ولو كان مريدا لامتثاله لكان
مريدا لهلاك نفسه وهو محال
الأصل الرابع أن الله تعالى متفضل بالخلق والاختراع ومتطول بتكليف العباد
ولم يكن الخلق والتكليف واجبا عليه
وقالت المعتزلة وجب عليه ذلك لما فيه من مصلحة العباد وهو محال إذ هو
الموجب والآمر والناهي وكيف يتهدف لإيجاب أو يتعرض للزوم وخطاب والمراد
بالواجب أحد أمرين إما الفعل الذي في تركه ضرر إما آجل كما يقال يجب على
العبد أن يطيع الله حتى لا يعذبه في الآخرة بالنار أو ضرر عاجل كما يقال
يجب على العطشان أن يشرب حتى لا يموت
وإما أن يراد به الذي يؤدي عدمه إلى محال كما يقال وجود المعلوم واجب إذ
عدمه يؤدي إلى محال وهو أن يصير العلم جهلا فإن
chapters.anchors:
- Root: خ-ل-ق (kh-l-q)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Originating, creating from nothing; measuring and proportioning (taqdīr)
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Exclusive divine act of bringing into existence (ījād) without prior matter or model
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Ḥaqīqah — literal divine origination; never metaphorical for human acts
- Root: ك-س-ب (k-s-b)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Acquiring, earning; what one gains through effort
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Ashʿarī technical term — human acquisition of an act created by God
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Majāz — relational attribution, not literal creation
- Root: إ-ر-ا-د (i-r-ā-d)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Will, intention, desire
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Divine will encompassing all existents, good and evil alike
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Distinction between command (amr) and will (irādah) — literal divergence
- Sībawayh Rule: Taʿlīq al-ṣifah (Attribution of a predicate to multiple subjects) — the same act can be described as created by God and acquired by man without contradiction, as the predicate applies to each subject under a different aspect (min wajh)
chapters.translation:
I say: The third pillar is knowledge of God's acts, and its scope revolves around ten principles.

**The First Principle:** Knowledge that every originated thing in the world is His act, His creation, and His invention. There is no creator of it other than Him, and no originator of it except Him alone. He created the creatures and fashioned them, and brought into existence their power and their movement. Thus all the acts of His servants are created by Him and attached to His power — in confirmation of His saying, the Exalted: {«الله خالق كل شيء»} ("God is the Creator of all things"), and His saying, the Exalted: {«والله خلقكم وما تعملون»} ("And God created you and what you do"), and His saying, the Exalted: {«وأسروا قولكم أو اجهروا به إنه عليم بذات الصدور ألا يعلم من خلق وهو اللطيف الخبير»} ("And conceal your speech or proclaim it openly — indeed, He is Knower of what is in the breasts. Does He who created not know, and He is the Subtle, the Aware"). He commanded the servants to be cautious in their words, their acts, their secrets, and their hidden intentions, because of His knowledge of the sources of their acts.

He argued for knowledge through creation. And how could He not be the creator of the servant's act, when His power is complete with no deficiency in it, and it is attached to the movements of the servants' bodies — and movements are mutually similar, and the attachment of power to them is by their very essence? So what would restrict its attachment to some movements rather than others, given their similarity? Or how could the animal be independent in invention, when from the spider, the bee, and the rest of the animals there issue such refined crafts that the intellects of the discerning are bewildered by them? How then could they alone be singled out for inventing them, apart from the Lord of lords — while they have no knowledge of the detailed particulars of what issues from them by acquisition? Far be it, far be it! The creatures are humbled, and He alone is singled out for dominion and sovereignty — the Compeller of the earth and the heavens.

**The Second Principle:** That God's being singled out for inventing the movements of the servants does not remove those movements from being within the servants' power by way of acquisition (kasb). Rather, God the Exalted created both the power and the empowered thing together, and created both the choice and the chosen thing together.

As for the power (qudrah), it is a description of the servant but a creation of the Lord, Glorified be He — and it is not an acquisition of the servant. As for the movement, it is a creation of the Lord, the Exalted, and a description of the servant and an acquisition of his. For it was created as empowered by a power that is his description, and the movement had a relation to another attribute called "power," so by virtue of that relation it is called "acquisition." And how could it be pure compulsion (jabr), when he necessarily perceives the difference between the empowered movement and the involuntary tremor? Or how could it be a creation of the servant, when he does not encompass knowledge of the detailed parts of acquired movements and their number? And when both extremes are refuted, nothing remains but moderation in belief — namely, that it is empowered by the power of God the Exalted by way of invention, and by the power of the servant in another mode of attachment expressed as "acquisition."

And it is not a necessary condition of power's attachment to the empowered thing that it be by invention alone. For God's power in eternity was attached to the world, and invention was not yet produced by it; and at the moment of invention it is attached to it in another mode of attachment, in which it becomes apparent that the attachment of power is not confined to the production of the empowered thing by it.

**The Third Principle:** That the servant's act, even if it is an acquisition of the servant, does not thereby fall outside being willed by God, Glorified be He.

For nothing runs in the dominion and the sovereignty — not the blink of an eye, nor the flash of a thought, nor the darting of a glance — except by God's decree and His power, and by His will and His volition. From Him comes evil and good, benefit and harm, Islam and unbelief, knowledge and denial, success and loss, misguidance and right guidance, obedience and disobedience, polytheism and faith. There is no repeller of His decree, and no reverser of His judgment. He leads astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills. {«لا يسأل عما يفعل وهم يسألون»} ("He is not asked about what He does, while they are asked").

What indicates this from transmitted evidence is the saying of the entire community (ummah): "What God willed came to be, and what He did not will did not come to be," and the saying of God, Mighty and Majestic: {«أن لو يشاء الله لهدى الناس جميعا»} ("If God had willed, He would have guided all people together"), and His saying, the Exalted: {«ولو شئنا لآتينا كل نفس هداها»} ("And had We willed, We would have given every soul its guidance").

What indicates it from the standpoint of reason is that if acts of disobedience and crimes were something God detests and does not will, and they run only in accordance with the will of the enemy — Iblis, may God curse him — while he is an enemy of God, Glorified be He, then what runs in accordance with the enemy's will would be more than what runs in accordance with His will, the Exalted. Would that I knew how a Muslim could permit himself to reduce the dominion of the Compeller, the Possessor of Majesty and Honor, to a rank which, if the chieftainship of a village were reduced to it, its leader would disdain! For if what continues for the enemy of the village leader were more than what goes right for him, he would disdain his leadership and disavow his authority.

And disobedience is what prevails over creation, and all of that, according to the innovators (al-mubtadiʿah), runs contrary to the will of the Truth, the Exalted. This is the utmost weakness and incapacity. Exalted be the Lord of lords, with a great exaltation, above what the wrongdoers say!

Then, whenever it becomes apparent that the acts of the servants are created by God, it is established that they are willed by Him.

If it is said: "How does He forbid what He wills, and command what He does not will?" — we say: Command (amr) is other than will (irādah). For this reason, when a master strikes his slave and the ruler reproaches him for it, and he excuses himself by the slave's defiance of him, and the ruler calls him a liar — he wants to display his proof by commanding the slave to do an act and have him disobey it before the ruler's eyes. So he says to him: "Saddle this beast in the presence of the ruler." He commands him to do what he does not will him to comply with. Had he not been a commander, his excuse before the ruler would not have been prepared; and had he willed his compliance, he would have willed his own destruction — which is impossible.

**The Fourth Principle:** That God the Exalted is gracious (mutafaḍḍil) in creation and invention, and bestows favor (mutatawwil) by charging the servants with obligation (taklīf). Creation and obligation were not obligatory upon Him.

The Muʿtazilah said: It was obligatory upon Him because of what it contains of the servants' welfare (maṣlaḥah). This is impossible, for He is the One who obligates, the Commander, and the Prohibiter. How could He be exposed to being obligated, or subject to necessity and address? The meaning of "obligatory" (wājib) is one of two things: either an act whose omission entails harm — either deferred, as it is said "it is obligatory upon the servant to obey God so that He does not punish him in the hereafter with fire," or immediate, as it is said "it is obligatory upon the thirsty one to drink so that he does not die" — or it means that whose non-existence leads to an impossibility, as it is said "the existence of the known thing is necessary (wājib)," since its non-existence leads to an impossibility, namely knowledge becoming ignorance.

If the opponent means by "creation is obligatory upon God" the first sense, then he has exposed Him to harm. If he means the second sense, it is conceded — for after the precedence of knowledge, the existence of the known thing is unavoidable. And if he means a third sense, it is unintelligible.

His saying "it is obligatory for the welfare of the servants" is corrupt speech. For if He is not harmed by omitting the servants' welfare, then obligation has no meaning in His regard. Moreover, the servants' welfare would lie in His creating them in Paradise. As for His creating them in the abode of trials, exposing them to sins, then aiming them at the peril of punishment and the terror of the presentation and the reckoning — there is no delight in that for the discerning.

**The Fifth Principle:** That it is permissible for God, Glorified be He, to charge the creatures with what they cannot bear — contrary to the Muʿtazilah. And were that not permissible, the request to avert it would be impossible — yet they requested it, saying: {«ربنا ولا تحملنا ما لا طاقة لنا به»} ("Our Lord, do not burden us with what we have no capacity for"). And because God the Exalted informed His Prophet, peace be upon him, that Abū Jahl would not believe him, then commanded him to command Abū Jahl to believe him in all his statements — and among his statements was that he would not believe him. So how could he believe him in his statement that he would not believe him? Is this anything but an impossibility of existence?

**The Sixth Principle:** That God, Mighty and Majestic, may inflict pain upon the creatures and torment them without any prior sin and without any subsequent reward — contrary to the Muʿtazilah. For He disposes freely in His own dominion, and it is inconceivable that His disposal should exceed His dominion. Injustice (ẓulm) is the expression for disposing in another's dominion without his permission — and that is impossible for God the Exalted, for He encounters no dominion belonging to another such that His disposal in it would be injustice.

What indicates the permissibility of this is its actual occurrence. For the slaughtering of beasts is an infliction of pain upon them, and the various kinds of torment poured upon them at the hands of human beings was not preceded by any crime on their part.

If it is said: "God the Exalted will gather them and recompense them according to what they endured of pains, and that is obligatory upon God, Glorified be He" — then the one who claims that it is obligatory upon God to revive every ant that was trodden upon and every bug that was crushed, so as to reward them for their pains, has departed from both the Law and reason. For it is said: describing reward and gathering as obligatory upon Him — if what is meant is that He would be harmed by omitting it, that is impossible; and if something else is meant, it has already been established that it is unintelligible, having fallen outside the aforementioned meanings of "obligatory."

**The Seventh Principle:** That He, the Exalted, does with His servants what He wills, and it is not obligatory upon Him to observe what is most beneficial (al-aṣlaḥ) for His servants — for the reason we have mentioned: nothing is obligatory upon Him, Glorified be He; rather, obligation is not even conceivable in His regard. For {«لا يسأل عما يفعل وهم يسألون»} ("He is not asked about what He does, while they are asked").

Would that I knew what answer the Muʿtazilite would give to his claim that "the most beneficial is obligatory upon Him" in a question I would pose to him: Suppose a disputation in the hereafter between a child and an adult, both having died as Muslims. God the Exalted increases the degrees of the adult and favors him over the child, because he labored in faith and acts of obedience after reaching maturity — and that is obligatory upon Him according to the Muʿtazilite. If the child said: "O Lord, why did You raise his station above mine?" — He says: "Because he reached maturity and strove in acts of obedience." The child says: "You caused me to die in childhood. It was incumbent upon You to prolong my life until I reached maturity, so that I might strive. You have then deviated from justice in favoring him with length of life over me — so why did You favor him?" God the Exalted says: "Because I knew that had you reached maturity, you would have associated partners with Me or disobeyed, and death in childhood was more beneficial for you." This is the Muʿtazilite's excuse on behalf of God, Mighty and Majestic.

And at this point the disbelievers cry out from the depths of the Blaze, saying: "O Lord, did You not know that had we reached maturity we would have associated partners with You? Why then did You not cause us to die in childhood? For we would have been content with a station below that of the Muslim child!" With what would that be answered? And is there anything at this point except the decisive conclusion that divine matters are exalted, by the judgment of majesty, above being weighed on the scale of the people of iʿtizāl?

If it is said: "Whenever He is able to observe what is most beneficial for the servants, then lets loose upon them the causes of torment, that is ugliness (qubḥ) unbefitting wisdom" — we say: Ugliness is what does not accord with an aim (gharaḍ). Indeed, a thing may be ugly for one person and beautiful for another, when it accords with the aim of one and not the other — just as the killing of a person is deemed ugly by his allies and beautiful by his enemies.

If what is meant by "ugly" is what does not accord with the aim of the Creator, Glorified be He — that is impossible, for He has no aim. Thus ugliness is inconceivable from Him, just as injustice is inconceivable from Him, since disposal in another's dominion is inconceivable from Him.

And if what is meant by "ugly" is what does not accord with the aim of another — then why do you say that is impossible for Him? Is this anything but mere caprice, contradicted by what we have posited of the disputation of the people of the Fire? Then "the wise" (al-ḥakīm) means the one who knows the realities of things and is able to perfect His act of them in accordance with His will. From where does this entail observing what is most beneficial? As for the wise one among us, he observes what is most beneficial out of regard for himself — to gain thereby praise in this world and reward in the hereafter, or to repel from himself some harm. And all of that is impossible for God, Glorified be He and Exalted.

**The Eighth Principle:** That knowledge of God, Glorified be He, and obedience to Him are obligatory by God's own imposition and His Law, not by reason — contrary to the Muʿtazilah. For reason, even if it deems obedience obligatory, either deems it obligatory for no benefit — which is impossible, for reason does not deem frivolity obligatory — or it deems it obligatory for a benefit and an aim. That benefit either reverts to the Worshipped One — which is impossible in His regard, the Exalted, for He is sanctified above aims and benefits; rather, unbelief and faith, obedience and disobedience are equal in His regard, the Exalted — or it reverts to the interest of the servant — which is also impossible, for he has no aim in the present state; rather, he is wearied by it and diverted from appetites because of it, and in the final outcome there is nothing but reward and punishment.

And from where would he know that God the Exalted rewards for obedience and punishes for disobedience — when obedience and disobedience are equal in His regard, since He has no inclination toward one of them and no special relation to one of them? Rather, the distinction of that is known only through the Law. Indeed, he who took this from an analogy between the Creator and the creature has slipped — for the creature distinguishes between gratitude and ingratitude because of the comfort, thrill, and delight he finds in one of them and not the other.

If it is said: "If reflection (naẓar) and knowledge are not obligatory except by the Law, and the Law is not established unless the obligated one reflects in it — so if the obligated one says to the Prophet: 'Reason does not make reflection obligatory upon me, and the Law is not established for me except through reflection, and I will not undertake reflection' — that would lead to silencing the Messenger, peace be upon him" — we say: This resembles the saying of one who says to a man standing in a certain place: "Behind you is a predatory lion. If you do not move from the spot, it will kill you; and if you turn behind you and look, you will know I am truthful." The standing man says: "Your truthfulness is not established unless I turn behind me, and I will not turn behind me nor look unless your truthfulness is established." This indicates the foolishness of this speaker and his exposure to destruction — with no harm to the guide and director. Likewise, the Prophet, peace be upon him, says: "Behind you is death, and before it are predatory beasts and blazing fires. If you do not take caution against them and come to know my truthfulness by turning to my miracle, you will perish." Whoever turns, knows, takes caution, and is saved; and whoever does not turn and persists, perishes and falls. And there is no harm if all people together perish — upon him is only the clear delivery (al-balāgh al-mubīn).

So the Law makes known the existence of the predatory beasts after death; reason conveys the understanding of his speech and the apprehension of the possibility of what he says about the future; and nature (al-ṭabʿ) urges caution against harm. The meaning of a thing being obligatory (wājib) is that its omission entails harm; and the meaning of the Law being an obligator is that it makes known the anticipated harm. For reason does not guide to the exposure to harm after death in following appetites. This, then, is the meaning of the Law and reason and their effect in determining the obligatory. And were it not for the fear of punishment for omitting what is commanded, obligation would not be established — for there is no meaning of "obligatory" except what is tied, in its omission, to harm in the hereafter.

**The Ninth Principle:** That the sending of the Prophets, peace be upon them, is not impossible — contrary to the Barāhimah, who said there is no benefit in their sending, since reason is a substitute for them. For reason does not guide to the acts that save in the hereafter, just as it does not guide to the medicines beneficial for health. Thus the creatures' need for the Prophets is like their need for physicians. But the truthfulness of the physician is known by experiment, while the truthfulness of the Prophet is known by miracle (muʿjizah).

**The Tenth Principle:** That God, Glorified be He, sent Muhammad, peace be upon him, as the seal of the Prophets and the abrogator of what preceded him of the laws of the Jews, the Christians, and the Sabians; and supported him with manifest miracles and dazzling signs — such as the splitting of the moon, the glorification of the pebbles, the speaking of the dumb animal, and the water that gushed forth from between his fingers.

And among his manifest signs, with which he challenged all the Arabs, is the Mighty Qur'an. For they, despite their distinction in eloquence and rhetoric, aimed at reviling him, forbidding him, killing him, and expelling him — as God, Mighty and Majestic, reported of them — yet they were unable to produce anything to rival the like of the Qur'an. For it was not within human power to combine the grandeur of the Qur'an's diction with its arrangement — this, along with what it contains of the reports of the ancients, while he was illiterate, unversed in the books, and the announcement of the unseen in matters whose truthfulness was verified in the future — such as His saying, the Exalted: {«لتدخلن المسجد الحرام إن شاء الله آمنين محلقين رؤوسكم ومقصرين»} ("You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque, if God wills, in security, with your heads shaved and shortened"), and His saying: {«ألم غلبت الروم في أدنى الأرض وهم من بعد غلبهم سيغلبون في بضع سنين»} ("Alif Lām Mīm. The Romans have been vanquished in the nearer land, and they, after their vanquishing, will vanquish in a few years").

The manner in which the miracle indicates the truthfulness of the Messengers is that everything that humans are incapable of is nothing but an act of God the Exalted. So whenever it is conjoined with the Prophet's challenge, peace be upon him, it takes the rank of His saying "You have spoken truthfully." This is like a man standing before a king, claiming to the king's subjects that he is the king's messenger to them — for whenever he says to the king: "If you are truthful, then stand upon your throne three times and sit contrary to your custom," and the king does that, there arises for those present a necessary knowledge that this takes the rank of His saying "You have spoken truthfully."

chapters.title_en: The Fourth Pillar: On Matters of the Unseen (Samʿiyyāt) and Affirming the Prophet's Truthfulness — Ten Fundamental Principles

|||  الركن الرابع في السمعيات وتصديقه صلى الله عليه وسلم فيما أخبر عنه ومداره على عشرة أصول

الأصل الأول الحشر والنشر (1) وقد ورد بهما الشرع وهو حق والتصديق بهما
واجب لأنه في العقل ممكن ومعناه الإعادة بعد الإفناء وذلك مقدور لله تعالى
كابتداء الإنشاء قال الله تعالى قال من يحيي العظام وهي رميم قل يحييها
الذي أنشأها أول مرة فاستدل بالابتداء على الإعادة وقال عز وجل ما خلقكم
ولا بعثكم إلا كنفس واحدة والإعادة ابتداء ثان فهو ممكن كالابتداء الأول
الأصل الثاني سؤال منكر ونكير (2) وقد وردت به الأخبار فيجب التصديق به
لأنه ممكن إذ ليس يستدعي إلا إعادة الحياة إلى جزء من الأجزاء الذي به فهم
الخطاب وذلك ممكن في نفسه ولا يدفع ذلك ما يشاهد من سكون أجزاء الميت وعدم
سماعنا للسؤال له فإن النائم ساكن بظاهره ويدرك بباطنه من الآلام واللذات
ما يحس بتأثيره عند التنبه وقد كان رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم يسمع كلام
جبريل عليه السلام ويشاهده ومن حوله لا يسمعونه ولا يرونه (3) ولا يحيطون
بشيء من علمه إلا بما شاء فإذا لم يخلق لهم السمع والرؤية لم يدركوه
الأصل الثالث عذاب القبر وقد ورد الشرع به قال الله تعالى النار يعرضون
عليها غدوا وعشيا ويوم تقوم الساعة أدخلوا آل فرعون أشد العذاب واشتهر عن
رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم والسلف الصالح الاستعاذة من عذاب القبر (4)
وهو ممكن فيجب التصديق به ولا يمنع من التصديق به تفرق أجزاء الميت في بطون
السباع وحواصل الطيور فإن المدرك لألم العذاب من الحيوان أجزاء مخصوصة يقدر
الله تعالى على إعادة الإدراك إليها
الأصل الرابع الميزان وهو حق قال الله تعالى ونضع الموازين القسط ليوم
القيامة وقال تعالى فمن ثقلت موازينه فأولئك هم المفلحون ومن خفت موازينه
الآية ووجهها أن الله تعالى  يحدث في صحائف الأعمال وزنا بحسب درجات الأعمال
عند الله تعالى فتصير مقادير أعمال العباد معلومة PageV01P114
للعباد حتى يظهر لهم العدل في العقاب أو الفضل في العفو وتضعيف الثواب
الأصل الخامس الصراط وهو جسر ممدود على متن جهنم أرق من الشعرة وأحد من
السيف قال الله تعالى فاهدوهم إلى صراط الجحيم وقفوهم إنهم مسئولون وهذا
ممكن فيجب التصديق به فإن القادر على أن يطير الطير في الهواء قادر على أن
يسير الإنسان على الصراط
الأصل السادس أن الجنة والنار مخلوقتان قال الله تعالى وسارعوا إلى مغفرة
من ربكم وجنة عرضها السموات والأرض أعدت للمتقين فقوله تعالى أعدت دليل على
أنها مخلوقة فيجب إجراؤه على الظاهر إذ لا استحالة فيه ولا يقال لا فائدة
في خلقهما قبل يوم الجزاء لأن الله تعالى لا يسأل عما يفعل وهم يسألون
الأصل السابع أن الإمام الحق بعد رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم أبو بكر
ثم عمر ثم عثمان ثم علي رضي الله عنهم ولم يكن نص رسول الله صلى الله عليه
وسلم على إمام أصلا إذ لو كان لكان أولى بالظهور من نصبه آحاد الولاة
والأمراء على الجنود في البلاد ولم يخف ذلك فكيف خفي هذا وإن ظهر فكيف
اندرس حتى لم ينقل إلينا فلم يكن أبو بكر إماما إلا بالاختيار والبيعة وأما
تقدير النص على غيره فهو نسبة للصحابة كلهم إلى مخالفة رسول الله صلى الله
عليه وسلم وخرق الإجماع وذلك مما لا يستجرىء على اختراعه إلا الروافض
واعتاد أهل السنة تزكية جميع الصحابة والثناء عليهم كما أثنى الله سبحانه
وتعالى ورسوله صلى الله عليه وسلم
وما جرى بين معاوية وعلي رضي الله عنهما كان مبنيا على الاجتهاد لا
منازعة من معاوية في الإمامة إذ ظن علي رضي الله عنه أن تسليم قتلة عثمان
مع كثرة عشائرهم واختلاطهم بالعسكر يؤدي إلى اضطراب أمر الإمامة في بدايتها
فرأى التأخير أصوب وظن معاوية أن تأخير أمرهم مع عظم جنايتهم يوجب الإغراء
بالأئمة ويعرض الدماء  للسفك
وقد قال أفاضل العلماء كل مجتهد مصيب
وقال قائلون المصيب واحد ولم يذهب إلى تخطئة على ذو تحصيل أصلا
الأصل الثامن أن فضل الصحابة رضي الله عنهم على ترتيبهم في الخلافة إذ
حقيقة الفضل ما هو فضل عند الله عز وجل وذلك لا يطلع عليه إلا رسول الله
صلى الله عليه وسلم
وقد ورد في الثناء على جميعهم آيات وأخبار كثيرة (1) وإنما يدرك دقائق
الفضل والترتيب فيه المشاهدون للوحي والتنزيل بقرائن الأحوال ودقائق
التفصيل فلولا فهمهم ذلك لما رتبوا الأمر كذلك إذ كانوا لا تأخذهم في الله
لومة لائم ولا يصرفهم عن الحق صارف
الأصل التاسع أن شرائط الإمامة بعد الإسلام والتكليف خمسة الذكورة والورع
والعلم والكفاية ونسبة قريش لقوله صلى الله عليه وسلم الأئمة من قريش (2)
وإذا اجتمع عدد من الموصوفين بهذه الصفات فالإمام من انعقدت له البيعة من
أكثر الخلق والمخالف للأكثر باغ يجب رده إلى الانقياد إلى الحق
الأصل العاشر أنه لو تعذر وجود الورع والعلم فيمن يتصدى للإمامة وكان في
صرفه إثارة فتنة لا تطاق حكمنا بانعقاد إمامته لأنا بين أن نحرك فتنة
بالاست
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ح-ش-ر (ḥ-sh-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To gather, assemble, muster; the act of driving forth for assembly
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The eschatological gathering of creation for reckoning — a divine act of re-assembly after dispersion
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) in Quranic usage; no metaphorical extension here — it denotes actual physical reconstitution
- Root: ن-ك-ر (n-k-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To disavow, deny, or question; the intensive form (nakkara) implies stern interrogation
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The two angels' questioning in the grave — a test of faith through divine agency
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal event, though its modality (kayfiyyah) is imperceptible to the living — not metaphorical
- Root: م-ي-ز (m-y-z)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To separate, distinguish, weigh out; the balance as an instrument of discrimination
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The divine scale (mīzān) on the Day of Judgment — a real entity by which deeds are weighed, not a mere metaphor
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal in scripture; the "weight" is a divinely-created accident manifesting degrees of worth
- Root: ص-ر-ط (ṣ-r-ṭ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The straight path; a bridge or road (borrowed from Syriac/Aramaic usage)
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The eschatological bridge over Hell — a literal traversable structure, distinct from the metaphorical "straight path" of guidance
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Here literal (ḥaqīqah) in the afterlife context; the Quranic "ṣirāṭ al-jahīm" is a physical reality, unlike "ṣirāṭ mustaqīm" which is often metaphorical
- Sībawayh Rule: The Rule of Conditional Possibility (Qāʿidat al-Imkān) — In verifying reports of the unseen, the grammatical and logical criterion is: if the predicate is not inherently impossible (mustaḥīl), affirmation is obligatory. This mirrors the syntactic principle that a valid proposition requires no contradiction between subject and predicate.
chapters.translation:
I say: The fourth pillar concerns the matters of the unseen (samʿiyyāt) and the affirmation of his truthfulness — peace be upon him — regarding what he reported. Its scope revolves around ten fundamental principles.

**The First Principle: The Gathering and Resurrection (al-ḥashr wa al-nashr).** (1) The Sacred Law has come with both, and they are true; affirmation of them is obligatory, for they are possible in reason. Their meaning is the restoration (iʿādah) after annihilation (ifnāʾ), and that is within the power of God — exalted be He — just as the initial origination (ibtidāʾ al-inshāʾ) was. God — exalted be He — said: {«قَالَ مَنْ يُحْيِي الْعِظَامَ وَهِيَ رَمِيمٌ ۝ قُلْ يُحْيِيهَا الَّذِي أَنْشَأَهَا أَوَّلَ مَرَّةٍ»} ("He said: Who will give life to bones when they are decayed? Say: He will give them life who brought them forth the first time.") Thus He argued from the initial creation for the restoration. And He said — mighty and majestic: {«مَا خَلْقُكُمْ وَلَا بَعْثُكُمْ إِلَّا كَنَفْسٍ وَاحِدَةٍ»} ("Your creation and your raising are but as a single soul.") Restoration is a second beginning, so it is possible just as the first beginning was possible.

**The Second Principle: The Questioning of Munkar and Nakīr.** (2) The reports (akhbār) have come with this, so affirmation of it is obligatory, for it is possible — since it requires only the restoration of life to a part of the parts by which the address is comprehended. That is possible in itself. Nor does what is observed of the stillness of the dead one's parts and our failure to hear the questioning for him refute this; for the sleeper is still in his outward aspect yet perceives inwardly pains and pleasures whose effect he senses upon awakening. And the Messenger of God — peace be upon him — used to hear the speech of Gabriel — peace be upon him — and see him, while those around him neither heard nor saw him. (3) {«وَلَا يُحِيطُونَ بِشَيْءٍ مِنْ عِلْمِهِ إِلَّا بِمَا شَاءَ»} ("And they encompass nothing of His knowledge except what He wills.") So when He does not create for them the hearing and the sight, they do not perceive it.

**The Third Principle: The Punishment of the Grave.** The Sacred Law has come with it. God — exalted be He — said: {«النَّارُ يُعْرَضُونَ عَلَيْهَا غُدُوًّا وَعَشِيًّا وَيَوْمَ تَقُومُ السَّاعَةُ أَدْخِلُوا آلَ فِرْعَوْنَ أَشَدَّ الْعَذَابِ»} ("The Fire — they are exposed to it morning and evening, and on the Day the Hour arises: Enter, O family of Pharaoh, into the severest punishment.") And it is well-known from the Messenger of God — peace be upon him — and the righteous predecessors (al-salaf al-ṣāliḥ) that they sought refuge from the punishment of the grave. (4) It is possible, so affirmation of it is obligatory. Nor does the dispersal of the dead one's parts in the bellies of beasts of prey and the crops of birds prevent affirmation of it; for the perceiver of the pain of punishment among living beings is specific parts, and God — exalted be He — has power to restore perception to them.

**The Fourth Principle: The Balance (al-mīzān).** It is true. God — exalted be He — said: {«وَنَضَعُ الْمَوَازِينَ الْقِسْطَ لِيَوْمِ الْقِيَامَةِ»} ("And We shall set up the just balances for the Day of Resurrection.") And He said — exalted be He: {«فَمَنْ ثَقُلَتْ مَوَازِينُهُ فَأُولَٰئِكَ هُمُ الْمُفْلِحُونَ وَمَنْ خَفَّتْ مَوَازِينُهُ»} ("Then whoever's scales are heavy — those are the successful; and whoever's scales are light...") — the verse. Its interpretation is that God — exalted be He — creates in the scrolls of deeds a weight corresponding to the degrees of the deeds with God — exalted be He — so that the measures of the servants' deeds become known to the servants themselves, so that justice in punishment or bounty in pardon and the multiplication of reward may appear to them.

**The Fifth Principle: The Bridge (al-ṣirāṭ).** It is a bridge stretched over the back of Hell, finer than a hair and sharper than a sword. God — exalted be He — said: {«فَاهْدُوهُمْ إِلَىٰ صِرَاطِ الْجَحِيمِ ۝ وَقِفُوهُمْ إِنَّهُمْ مَسْئُولُونَ»} ("Then guide them to the path of Hell, and stop them — indeed they are to be questioned.") This is possible, so affirmation of it is obligatory; for He who is able to make the bird fly in the air is able to make man walk upon the bridge.

**The Sixth Principle: That Paradise and Hell are Created.** God — exalted be He — said: {«وَسَارِعُوا إِلَىٰ مَغْفِرَةٍ مِنْ رَبِّكُمْ وَجَنَّةٍ عَرْضُهَا السَّمَاوَاتُ وَالْأَرْضُ أُعِدَّتْ لِلْمُتَّقِينَ»} ("And hasten to forgiveness from your Lord and a Garden whose width is the heavens and the earth, prepared (uʿiddat) for the God-fearing.") His saying — exalted be He — "prepared" is evidence that they are created. It must be taken at its apparent meaning (ẓāhir), for there is no impossibility in it. Nor should it be said there is no benefit in creating them before the Day of Recompense, for God — exalted be He — is not asked about what He does, while they will be asked.

**The Seventh Principle: That the rightful Imam after the Messenger of God — peace be upon him — was Abū Bakr, then ʿUmar, then ʿUthmān, then ʿAlī — may God be pleased with them all.** There was no explicit designation (naṣṣ) from the Messenger of God — peace be upon him — for any Imam at all; for had there been, it would have been more fitting to be made public than the appointment of individual governors and commanders over armies in the provinces. That was not concealed — so how could this have been concealed? And if it had appeared, how could it have been effaced until it was not transmitted to us? Thus Abū Bakr was not Imam except through choice (ikhtiyār) and the oath of allegiance (bayʿah). As for positing designation for someone else, that is attributing to all the Companions opposition to the Messenger of God — peace be upon him — and a breach of consensus (kharq al-ijmāʿ). None would dare invent such a thing except the Rāfiḍah. The people of the Sunnah (ahl al-sunnah) are accustomed to declaring all the Companions virtuous and praising them, just as God — glorified and exalted be He — and His Messenger — peace be upon him — praised them.

As for what occurred between Muʿāwiyah and ʿAlī — may God be pleased with them both — it was based on independent judgment (ijtihād), not on any contestation from Muʿāwiyah regarding the imamate. For ʿAlī — may God be pleased with him — thought that surrendering the killers of ʿUthmān, given the multitude of their clans and their intermingling with the army, would lead to disorder in the imamate at its inception; so he saw delay as more correct. And Muʿāwiyah thought that delaying their matter, given the enormity of their crime, would embolden against the Imams and expose blood to being shed.

The eminent scholars have said: "Every mujtahid is correct." And some said: "The correct one is only one." But no one of attainment has ever gone so far as to declare ʿAlī mistaken.

**The Eighth Principle: That the virtue of the Companions — may God be pleased with them — follows their order in the caliphate.** For the reality of virtue is what is virtue with God — mighty and majestic — and that is not known except through the Messenger of God — peace be upon him. Many verses and reports have come praising all of them. (1) Only those who witnessed the revelation and the sending-down, through the indications of circumstances and the subtleties of detail, perceive the finer points of virtue and its ordering. Had they not understood that, they would not have arranged the matter thus — for they were not seized by the blame of any blamer in God's cause, nor did any turner turn them from the truth.

**The Ninth Principle: That the conditions of the imamate, after Islam and legal responsibility (taklīf), are five: masculinity, righteousness (waraʿ), knowledge, competence (kifāyah), and Qurayshī lineage.** This is due to his saying — peace be upon him: "The Imams are from Quraysh." (2) When a number of those described with these qualities are gathered, the Imam is the one for whom the oath of allegiance is concluded by the majority of the people. The one who opposes the majority is a rebel (bāghī) who must be returned to submission to the truth.

**The Tenth Principle: That if the existence of righteousness and knowledge in one who undertakes the imamate becomes unattainable, and in removing him there would be an unbearable sedition (fitnah), we rule the validity of his imamate.** For we are between two options: either we stir up a sedition by replacement, in which case the harm that befalls the Muslims exceeds what they lose from the deficiency of these conditions — which were established for the advantage of benefit (maṣlaḥah), so the root of benefit is not demolished out of passion for its advantages, like one who builds a palace and destroys a city — or we rule that the lands are devoid of an Imam and that judicial rulings are corrupted, which is impossible.

We rule the validity of the judgments of the people of rebellion (ahl al-baghy) in their lands due to the pressing of their need — so how should we not rule the validity of the imamate in times of need and necessity? These four pillars, encompassing the forty principles, are the foundations of the creeds (qawāʿid al-ʿaqāʾid). Whoever believes them is in agreement with the people of the Sunnah and separate from the partisans of innovation (rahṭ al-bidʿah).

May God — exalted be He — direct us with His grace and guide us to the truth and its verification, through His bounty, the vastness of His generosity, and His favor. And may God's blessings be upon our master Muḥammad, upon his family, and upon every chosen servant.

chapters.title_en: The Fourth Chapter on the Foundations of Creed: On Faith (Īmān) and Submission (Islām), Their Interconnection, What Pertains to Them of Increase and Decrease, and the Manner of the Predecessors’ Exception Therein — Containing Three Questions
chapters.arabic_text: || الفصل الرابع من قواعد العقائد في الإيمان والإسلام وما بينهما من الاتصال وما يتطرق إليه من الزيادة والنقصان ووجه استثناء السلف فيه وفيه ثلاث مسائل
chapters.anchors:
- Root: أ-م-ن (ʾ-m-n)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning of security, safety, and trustworthiness; īmān as the heart’s secure assent (taṣdīq) that dispels doubt.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Īmān is the theological act of affirming truth (taṣdīq) with the heart, entailing submission of the limbs; distinct from mere verbal confession.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) usage denotes inner conviction; metaphorical (majāz) usage may extend to outward acts as signs of that conviction.
- Root: س-ل-م (s-l-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Root meaning of peace, safety, and surrender; islām as wholehearted yielding to God’s command.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Islām is the outward compliance (inqiyād) and submission to divine law, forming the practical counterpart to īmān’s inner assent.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal usage denotes physical surrender; metaphorical usage extends to spiritual obedience, yet the two are inseparable in the Sharīʿah.
- Root: ز-ي-د (z-y-d)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning of increase, growth, and augmentation; nuqṣān (decrease) as its lexical opposite.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Increase and decrease of īmān are understood via the intensity of taṣdīq and the multiplicity of obedient acts, not as quantitative change in the essence of belief.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal usage applies to measurable quantities; metaphorical usage applies to spiritual states, where increase signifies deeper certainty and decrease signifies weakness.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of ʿAṭf al-Bayān (Appositional Clarification) — The phrase "wa-mā baynahumā min al-ittiṣāl" functions as an explicative apposition, clarifying the precise relational nexus between īmān and islām, while "wa-mā yataṭarraqu ilayhi" introduces a subordinate clause governed by the implicit verb of possibility, requiring careful parsing of the genitive chain (muḍāf ilayh) to preserve the author’s intended logical sequence.
chapters.translation: I say: This is the fourth chapter of the foundations of creed, concerning faith (īmān) and submission (islām), and what connects them to one another, and what may pertain to them of increase and decrease, and the manner in which the predecessors (al-salaf) made exception therein. It contains three questions.

chapters.title_en: On the Relationship Between Islam and Faith (al-Islām wa al-Īmān)
