||| مسألة

اختلفوا في أن الإسلام هو الإيمان أو  غيره وإن كان غيره فهل هو
منفصل عنه يوجد دونه أو مرتبط به يلازمه فقيل إنهما شيء واحد وقيل إنهما
شيئان لا يتواصلان وقيل إنهما شيئان ولكن يرتبط أحدهما بالآخر
وقد أورد أبو طالب المكي في هذا كلاما شديد الاضطراب كثير التطويل فلنهجم
الآن على التصريح بالحق من غير تعريج على نقل ما لا تحصيل له فنقول في هذا
ثلاثة مباحث بحث عن موجب اللفظين في اللغة وبحث عن المراد بهما في إطلاق
الشرع وبحث عن حكمهما في الدنيا والآخرة والبحث الأول لغوي والثاني تفسيري
والثالث فقهي شرعي
البحث الأول في موجب اللغة والحق فيه أن الإيمان عبارة عن التصديق قال
الله تعالى وما أنت بمؤمن لنا أي بمصدق والإسلام عبارة عن التسليم
والاستسلام بالإذعان والانقياد وترك التمرد والإباء والعناد وللتصديق محل
خاص وهو القلب واللسان ترجمان
وأما التسليم فإنه عام في القلب واللسان والجوارح فإن كل تصديق بالقلب
فهو تسليم وترك الإباء والجحود وكذلك الاعتراف باللسان وكذلك الطاعة
والانقياد بالجوارح
فموجب اللغة أن الإسلام أعم والإيمان أخص فكان الإيمان عبارة عن أشرف
أجزاء الإسلام فإذن كل تصديق تسليم وليس كل تسليم تصديقا
البحث الثاني عن إطلاق الشرع والحق فيه أن الشرع قد ورد باستعمالهما على
سبيل الترادف والتوارد وورد على سبيل الاختلاف وورد على سبيل التداخل أما
الترادف ففيقوله تعالى فأخرجنا من كان فيها من المؤمنين فما وجدنا فيها غير
بيت من المسلمين ولم يكن بالاتفاق إلا بيت واحد وقال تعالى يا قوم إن كنتم
آمنتم بالله فعليه توكلوا إن كنتم مسلمين وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم بني
الإسلام على خمس (1)
وسئل رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم مرة عن الإيمان فأجاب بهذه الخمس (2)
وأما الاختلاف فقوله تعالى {قالت الأعراب آمنا قل لم تؤمنوا ولكن قولوا
أسلمنا} ومعناه استسلمنا في الظاهر فأراد بالإيمان ههنا التصديق بالقلب فقط
وبالإسلام الاستسلام ظاهرا باللسان والجوارح وفي حديث جبرائيل عليه السلام
لما سأله عن الإيمان فقال أن تؤمن بالله وملائكته وكتبه ورسله واليوم  الآخر
وبالبعث بعد الموت وبالحساب وبالقدر خيره وشره فقال فما الإسلام فأجاب بذكر
الخصال الخمس (3) فعبر بالإسلام عن تسليم الظاهر بالقول والعمل
وفي الحديث عن سعد أنه صلى الله عليه وسلم أعطى رجلا عطاء ولم يعط الآخر
فقال له سعد يا رسول الله تركت فلانا لم تعطه وهو مؤمن فقال صلى الله عليه
وسلم أو مسلم فأعاد عليه فأعاد رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم حديث سعد أعطى
رجلا عطاء ولم يعط الآخر فقال له سعد يا رسول الله تركت فلانا لم تعطه وهو
مؤمن فقال أو مسلم الحديث أخرجاه بنحوه // وأما التداخل فما روى أيضا أنه
PageV01P116
سئل فقيل أي الأعمال أفضل فقال صلى الله عليه وسلم الإسلام فقال أي
الإسلام أفضل فقال صلى الله عليه وسلم الإيمان (1) وهذا دليل على الاختلاف
وعلى التداخل وهو أوفق الاستعمالات في اللغة لأن الإيمان عمل من الأعمال
وهو أفضلها والإسلام هو تسليم إما بالقلب وإما باللسان وإما بالجوارح
وأفضلها الذي بالقلب وهو التصديق الذي يسمى إيمانا والاستعمال لهما على
سبيل الاختلاف وعلى سبيل التداخل وعلى سبيل الترادف كله غير خارج عن طريق
التجوز في اللغة
أما الاختلاف فهو أن يجعل الإيمان عبارة عن التصديق بالقلب فقط وهو موافق
للغة والإسلام عبارة عن التسليم ظاهرا وهو أيضا موافق للغة فإن التسليم
ببعض محال التسليم ينطلق عليه اسم التسليم فليس من شرط حصول الاسم عموم
المعنى لكل محل يمكن أن يوجد المعنى فيه فإن من لمس غيره ببعض بدنه يسمى
لامسا وإن لم يستغرق جميع بدنه فإطلاق اسم الإسلام على التسليم الظاهر عند
عدم تسليم الباطن مطابق للسان وعلى هذا الوجه جرى قوله تعالى {قالت الأعراب
آمنا قل لم تؤمنوا ولكن قولوا أسلمنا} وقوله صلى الله عليه وسلم في حديث
سعد أو مسلم لأنه فضل أحدهما على الآخر ويريد بالاختلاف تفاضل المسميين
وأما التداخل فموافق أيضا للغة في خصوص الإيمان وهو أن يجعل الإسلام
عبارة عن التسليم بالقلب والقول والعمل جميعا والإيمان عبارة عن بعض  ما دخل
في الإسلام وهو التصديق بالقلب وهو الذي عنيناه بالتداخل وهو موافق للغة في
خصوص الإيمان وعموم الإسلام للكل وعلى هذا خرج قوله {الإيمان} في جواب قول
السائل أي الإسلام أفضل لأنه جعل الإيمان خصوصا من الإسلام فأدخله فيه وأما
استعماله فيه على سبيل الترادف بأن يجعل الإسلام عبارة عن التسليم بالقلب
والظاهر جميعا فإن كل ذلك تسليم وكذا الإيمان ويكون التصرف في الإيمان على
الخصوص بتعميمه وإدخال الظاهر في معناه وهو جائز لأن تسليم الظاهر بالقول
والعمل ثمرة تصديق الباطن ونتيجته وقد يطلق اسم الشجر ويراد به الشجر مع
ثمره على سبيل التسامح فيصير بهذا القدر من التعميم مرادفا لاسم الإسلام
ومطابقا له فلا يزيد عليه ولا ينقص وعليه خرج قو
chapters.anchors:
- Root: س-ل-م (s-l-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning of safety, soundness, and surrender; the verbal noun islām denotes yielding and submission without resistance.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, islām signifies outward compliance and peace-making with God through obedience, distinct from inward conviction.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense is physical surrender; metaphorically extended to verbal confession and bodily acts of worship, as in «قالت الأعراب آمنا قل لم تؤمنوا ولكن قولوا أسلمنا».
- Root: أ-م-ن (ʾ-m-n)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Root denotes security from fear; īmān is the act of granting trust and inner certainty.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Technical term for heartfelt assent (taṣdīq) to God, His angels, books, messengers, and the Last Day—the inward pillar of religion.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal usage is inner conviction; metaphorical extension occurs when īmān is used for the whole of religion, including works, as in «فما وجدنا فيها غير بيت من المسلمين».
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Taḍmīn (Semantic Inclusion) — When two nouns are conjoined or contrasted, their scopes may overlap or diverge based on contextual qarāʾin (indicators); the part may be named by the whole (kul) and vice versa, as in the tree-and-fruit analogy.
chapters.translation:
I say: Know that the scholars have differed concerning whether Islam is identical with faith (īmān) or something other than it. If it is other, then is it separate from faith, existing without it, or is it connected to faith and inseparable from it? Some said they are one single thing; others said they are two things that never meet; and others said they are two things, but one is linked to the other. Abū Ṭālib al-Makkī has presented on this matter discourse of extreme confusion and great prolixity. Let us now proceed to declare the truth plainly, without pausing to transmit what yields no profit. We say concerning this: there are three investigations—an investigation into what the two terms require in language, an investigation into what is meant by them in the usage of the Sacred Law, and an investigation into their rulings in this world and the Hereafter. The first investigation is linguistic, the second is exegetical, and the third is jurisprudential and legal.

The First Investigation: What Language Requires. The truth in this is that faith (īmān) is an expression for assent (taṣdīq). God Most High said: {وما أنت بمؤمن لنا} — that is, "you are not one who assents to us." And Islam is an expression for surrender (taslīm) and submission (istislām) through compliance (idhʿān) and obedience (inqiyād), and the abandonment of stubbornness, refusal, and obstinacy. Assent has a specific locus, namely the heart, and the tongue is its interpreter. As for surrender, it is general across the heart, the tongue, and the bodily members. For every assent of the heart is a surrender and an abandonment of refusal and denial; likewise, verbal acknowledgment is surrender; likewise, obedience and compliance of the bodily members is surrender. Thus what language requires is that Islam is more general and faith is more specific; faith is an expression for the noblest part of Islam. Therefore, every assent is a surrender, but not every surrender is an assent.

The Second Investigation: The Usage of the Sacred Law. The truth in this is that the Sacred Law has come using them synonymously (tarāduf), using them distinctively (ikhtilāf), and using them with mutual inclusion (tadākhul). As for synonymy, it is in His saying: {فأخرجنا من كان فيها من المؤمنين فما وجدنا فيها غير بيت من المسلمين} — and there was by agreement only one house. And His saying: {يا قوم إن كنتم آمنتم بالله فعليه توكلوا إن كنتم مسلمين}. And the Prophet ﷺ said: "Islam is built upon five." And the Messenger of God ﷺ was asked once about faith, and he answered with these five. As for the distinctive usage, it is His saying: {قالت الأعراب آمنا قل لم تؤمنوا ولكن قولوا أسلمنا} — meaning "we have submitted outwardly." He meant by faith here only the assent of the heart, and by Islam the outward submission of the tongue and bodily members. And in the ḥadīth of Gabriel (peace be upon him), when he asked about faith, he said: "That you believe in God, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day, the resurrection after death, the reckoning, and the divine decree, its good and its evil." Then he said: "What is Islam?" And he answered by mentioning the five practices, thereby expressing by Islam the surrender of the outward through speech and action. And in the ḥadīth of Saʿd, that the Prophet ﷺ gave a gift to one man and not to another, and Saʿd said: "O Messenger of God, you left so-and-so without giving him, and he is a believer." The Prophet ﷺ said: "Or a Muslim?" He repeated it, and the Messenger of God ﷺ repeated the ḥadīth of Saʿd. Both al-Bukhārī and Muslim transmitted it in similar wording. As for mutual inclusion, it is also transmitted that he was asked: "Which deeds are best?" He ﷺ said: "Islam." Then it was said: "Which Islam is best?" He ﷺ said: "Faith." This is evidence for both distinction and inclusion. And this is the most fitting of usages in language, because faith is a deed among deeds and the best of them, and Islam is a surrender—either by the heart, or by the tongue, or by the bodily members—and the best of these is that of the heart, which is the assent called faith. Their usage in the modes of distinction, inclusion, and synonymy is all not outside the path of figurative extension (tajawwuz) in language.

As for distinction, it is making faith an expression for assent of the heart only—which agrees with language—and making Islam an expression for outward surrender—which also agrees with language. For surrender by some of its loci is still called surrender; it is not a condition for the name's attainment that the meaning encompass every locus in which the meaning could exist. For one who touches another with part of his body is called "touching," even if he does not cover his entire body. Thus applying the name "Islam" to outward surrender when inward surrender is absent conforms to the tongue. On this basis ran His saying: {قالت الأعراب آمنا قل لم تؤمنوا ولكن قولوا أسلمنا}, and his saying ﷺ in the ḥadīth of Saʿd: "Or a Muslim?"—because he preferred one over the other, intending by the distinction the superiority of the two named things.

As for mutual inclusion, it also conforms to language in the specificity of faith. It is making Islam an expression for surrender by heart, speech, and action all together, and making faith an expression for a part of what enters into Islam, namely assent of the heart. This is what we mean by inclusion, and it conforms to language in the specificity of faith and the generality of Islam over the whole. On this basis came his saying "faith" in answer to the questioner's "Which Islam is best?"—because he made faith a specific part of Islam and included it therein.

As for their usage synonymously—making Islam an expression for surrender by heart and outward together, for all of that is surrender, and likewise faith—then this involves a manipulation of faith toward generality, extending it to include the outward in its meaning. This is permissible, because the outward surrender by speech and action is the fruit of inward assent and its result. The name "tree" may be applied meaning the tree with its fruit, by way of tolerance (tasāmuḥ). By this degree of generalization, it becomes synonymous with the name "Islam" and corresponds to it, neither exceeding nor falling short. On this basis came His saying: {فما وجدنا فيها غير بيت من المسلمين}.

The Third Investigation: The Legal Ruling. Islam and faith are two rulings—one pertaining to the Hereafter and one to this world. As for the Hereafter, it is the extraction from the Fire and the prevention of eternal abiding therein, for the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "There will come out of the Fire one who has in his heart the weight of a grain of faith." They have differed as to what this ruling is attached to, expressing it as: "What is faith?" Some say it is mere conviction (ʿaqd); some say it is conviction of the heart plus testimony of the tongue; some add a third, namely action upon the pillars. We shall lift the veil from this and say: whoever combines these three, there is no disagreement that his final abode is Paradise. This is the first degree.

The Second Degree: That two and part of the third exist—namely speech and conviction, and some works—but its possessor committed a major sin or some of the major sins. At this point the Muʿtazilites said: he has left faith by this, yet has not entered unbelief; rather his name is "corrupt sinner" (fāsiq), and he is in a station between the two stations, eternally abiding in the Fire. This is false, as we shall mention.

The Third Degree: That assent of the heart and testimony of the tongue exist without the works of the bodily members. They have differed concerning its ruling. Abū Ṭālib al-Makkī said: the works of the bodily members are part of faith and it is not complete without them, and he claimed consensus (ijmāʿ) on this, adducing evidences that suggest the opposite of his purpose—such as His saying: {الذين آمنوا وعملوا الصالحات}, for this indicates that works are beyond faith, not of the very essence of faith; otherwise works would be in the position of a repetition. It is astonishing that he claimed consensus on this while he also transmits his saying ﷺ: "No one is rendered an unbeliever except after denying what he has affirmed," and he criticizes the Muʿtazilites for their doctrine of eternal abiding in the Fire due to major sins. Yet the one who says this is himself saying the very doctrine of the Muʿtazilites. For it is said to him: "If one affirms with his heart and testifies with his tongue and dies at that very moment, is he in Paradise?" He must say yes—and in this is a ruling that faith exists without works. Then we add and say: "If he remained alive until the time of one prayer entered upon him, and he abandoned it, then died—or committed adultery, then died—is he eternally abiding in the Fire?" If he says yes, that is the very doctrine of the Muʿtazilites. If he says no, then this is an explicit declaration that works are neither a pillar of faith itself, nor a condition of its existence, nor of deserving Paradise through it. If he says: "I mean that he lives a long time without praying and without undertaking any of the legal works," then we say: what is the measure of that duration, and what is the number of those acts of obedience by whose abandonment faith is nullified, and what is the number of major sins by whose commission faith is nullified? This cannot be determined by arbitrary stipulation, and no one has ever resorted to it at all.

The Fourth Degree: That assent of the heart exists before the tongue utters or works are undertaken, and he dies. Do we say he died a believer between him and God Most High? This is a point of disagreement. Those who stipulate speech for the completion of faith say: he died before faith—and this is corrupt, for he ﷺ said: "There will come out of the Fire one who has in his heart the weight of a grain of faith," and this man's heart is overflowing with faith—so how could he be eternally abiding in the Fire? And in the ḥadīth of Gabriel (peace be upon him), nothing was stipulated for faith except assent to God Most High, His angels, His books, and the Last Day, as has preceded.

The Fifth Degree: That one assents with the heart, and his lifespan grants him the opportunity to utter the two words of testimony, and he knows their obligation, yet he does not utter them. It is possible to make his refusal to utter like his refusal to pray, and we say: he is a believer, not eternally abiding in the Fire. Faith is pure assent, and the tongue is the interpreter of faith—so faith must exist in its entirety before the tongue, so that the tongue may interpret it. This is the more apparent view, for there is no basis except following what the terms require, and the convention of the tongue is that faith is an expression for assent of the heart. And he ﷺ said: "There will come out one who has in his heart the weight of a grain"—and faith is not annihilated from the heart by silence from obligatory speech, just as it is not annihilated by silence from obligatory action. Some said: speech is a pillar, for the two words of testimony are not a report about the heart, but rather the origination of another covenant, the commencement of testimony, and a commitment. The first view is more apparent. A faction of the Murjiʾah went to excess in this and said: such a one will not enter the Fire at all, and they said: the believer, even if he disobeys, will not enter the Fire. We shall refute this against them.

The Sixth Degree: That one says with his tongue "There is no god but God, Muhammad is the Messenger of God," but does not assent with his heart. We do not doubt that in the ruling of the Hereafter he is among the unbelievers and eternally abiding in the Fire. And we do not doubt that in the ruling of this world—concerning what pertains to the imams and governors—he is among the Muslims, because his heart is not visible to them, and it is incumbent upon us to think well of him: that he did not say with his tongue except what he conceals in his heart. We only doubt concerning a third matter: the worldly ruling between him and God Most High. That is: if a Muslim relative of his dies at that moment, and then afterward he assents with his heart, and then he seeks a legal opinion and says: "I was not assenting with my heart at the moment of death, and the inheritance is now in my hand—is it lawful for me between me and God Most High?" Or: he married a Muslim woman, then assented with his heart—is he required to renew the marriage? This is a place of reflection. It is possible to say: the rulings of this world are attached to the outward speech, outwardly and inwardly. And it is possible to say: they are attached to the outward with respect to others, because his inward is not apparent to others, while his inward is apparent to himself between him and God Most High. The more apparent view—and God knows best—is that this inheritance is not lawful for him, and he is required to renew the marriage. For this reason, Ḥudhayfah (may God be pleased with him) would not attend the funeral of anyone who died among the hypocrites, and ʿUmar (may God be pleased with him) would defer to him in this, not attending if Ḥudhayfah did not attend. And prayer is an outward act in this world, even though it is among the acts of worship. And abstaining from the unlawful is also among what is obligatory upon one for God, like prayer, for his saying ﷺ: "Seeking the lawful is an obligation after obligation." This does not contradict our saying that inheritance is a ruling of Islam, which is submission—rather, complete submission is what encompasses both the outward and the inward. These are jurisprudential, probabilistic investigations, built upon the outward meanings of terms, generalities, and analogies. It should not be thought by one deficient in the sciences that certainty is sought here, merely because of the custom of presenting such matters in the art of kalām, where certainty is sought. Never has one prospered who looked to customs and formalities in the sciences.

If you say: What then is the doubt of the Muʿtazilites and the Murjiʾah, and what is the proof of the falsity of their doctrine? I say: Their doubt is the generalities of the Qurʾān. As for the Murjiʾah, they said: the believer will not enter the Fire even if he commits every disobedience, due to His saying, Mighty and Majestic: {فمن يؤمن بربه فلا يخاف بخسا ولا رهقا}, and His saying, Glorified and Exalted: {والذين آمنوا بالله ورسله أولئك هم الصديقون}, and His saying, Most High: {كلما ألقى فيها فوج سألهم خزنتها} up to His saying {فكذبنا وقلنا ما نزل الله من شيء}. His saying {كلما ألقى فيها فوج} is general, so it should include everyone cast into the Fire as a denier. And due to His saying, Most High: {لا يصلاها إلا الأشقى الذي كذب وتولى}—and this is a restriction, an affirmation, and a negation. And due to His saying, Most High: {من جاء بالحسنة فله خير منها وهم من فزع يومئذ آمنون}—for faith is the head of good deeds. And due to His saying, Most High: {والله يحب المحسنين}, and His saying: {إنا لا نضيع أجر من أحسن عملا}. But they have no proof in this. For wherever faith is mentioned in these verses, what is meant is faith together with works, since we have shown that faith may be used meaning Islam, which is compliance by heart, speech, and action. The proof of this interpretation is the many reports concerning the punishment of sinners and the measures of punishment, and his saying ﷺ: "There will come out of the Fire one who has in his heart the weight of a grain of faith"—for how could he come out if he never entered? And from the Qurʾān, His saying, Most High: {إن الله لا يغفر أن يشرك به ويغفر ما دون ذلك لمن يشاء}—and the exception by will indicates division. And His saying, Most High: {ومن يعص الله ورسوله فإن له نار جهنم خالدين فيها}—and restricting it to unbelief is arbitrary. And His saying, Most High: {ألا إن الظالمين في عذاب مقيم}, and His saying: {ومن جاء بالسيئة فكبت وجوههم في النار}. These generalities stand in opposition to their generalities, and it is necessary to apply specification and interpretation to both sides, because the reports explicitly state that sinners are punished. Indeed, His saying, Most High: {وإن منكم إلا واردها} is nearly explicit that this is inevitable for everyone, for no believer is free of a sin he commits. And His saying, Most High: {لا يصلاها إلا الأشقى الذي كذب وتولى}—He meant by it a specific group, or He meant by "the most wretched" a specific person as well. And His saying, Most High: {كلما ألقى فيها فوج سألهم خزنتها}—that is, a group of the unbelievers. And the specification of generalities is readily acceptable. From this verse, al-Ashʿarī and a group of theologians came to deny the forms of generality (ṣiyagh al-ʿumūm), holding that these terms must be suspended until a contextual indicator appears to clarify their meaning.

As for the Muʿtazilites, their doubt is His saying, Most High: {وإني لغفار لمن تاب وآمن وعمل صالحا ثم اهتدى}, and His saying, Most High: {والعصر إن الإنسان لفي خسر إلا الذين آمنوا وعملوا الصالحات}, and His saying, Most High: {وإن منكم إلا واردها كان على ربك حتما مقضيا} then His saying: {ثم ننجي الذين اتقوا}, and His saying, Most High: {ومن يعص الله ورسوله فإن له نار جهنم}—and every verse in which God Most High mentions righteous works conjoined with faith. And His saying, Most High: {ومن يقتل مؤمنا متعمدا فجزاؤه جهنم خالدا فيها}. These generalities are also specified by the proof of His saying, Most High: {ويغفر ما دون ذلك لمن يشاء}—so His will must remain operative in forgiving what is other than polytheism. Likewise, his saying ﷺ: "There will come out of the Fire one who has in his heart the weight of a grain of faith," and His saying, Most High: {إنا لا نضيع أجر من أحسن عملا}, and His saying, Most High: {إن الله لا يضيع أجر المحسنين}—so how could He waste the reward of the very root of faith and all acts of obedience because of a single disobedience? And His saying, Most High: {ومن يقتل مؤمنا متعمدا}—that is, "because of his faith," and it was revealed on such an occasion.

If you say: The choice has inclined to the view that faith is attained without works, yet it is well-known from the Salaf their saying: "Faith is conviction, speech, and action." What does this mean? We say: It is not far-fetched that works are counted as part of faith, because they complete it and perfect it—just as one says "the head and the hands are part of the human," and it is known that one ceases to be human by the absence of the head, but does not cease by being amputated of hand. Likewise, one says "the glorifications and the takbīrs are part of the prayer," even though the prayer is not invalidated by their absence. So assent of the heart is to faith as the head is to human existence—it is annihilated by its absence—while the rest of the acts of obedience are like the limbs, some higher than others. And he ﷺ said: "The adulterer does not commit adultery while he is a believer." And the Companions (may God be pleased with them) did not hold the Muʿtazilite doctrine of leaving faith through adultery; rather, its meaning is: he is not a true believer with complete, perfect faith—just as one says of the helpless one with amputated limbs: "This is not a human," meaning he does not possess the perfection that lies beyond the reality of humanity.

chapters.title_en: On the Increase and Decrease of Faith (Ziyādat al-Īmān wa Nuqṣānuhu)
chapters.arabic_text:
||| مسألة

فإن قلت فقد اتفق السلف على أن الإيمان يزيد وينقص يزيد بالطاعة
وينقص بالمعصية فإذا كان التصديق هو الإيمان فلا يتصور فيه زيادة ولا نقصان
فأقول السلف هم الشهود العدول وما لأحد عن قولهم عدول فما ذكروه حق وإنما
الشأن في فهمه وفيه دليل على أن العمل ليس من أجزاء الإيمان وأركان وجوده
بل هو مزيد عليه يزيد به والزائد موجود والناقص موجود والشيء لا يزيد بذاته
فلا يجوز أن يقال الإنسان يزيد برأسه بل يقال يزيد بلحيته وسمنه ولا يجوز
أن يقال الصلاة تزيد بالركوع والسجود بل تزيد بالآداب والسنن فهذا تصريح
بأن الإيمان له وجود ثم بعد الوجود يختلف حاله بالزيادة والنقصان
فإن قلت فالإشكال قائم في أن التصديق كيف يزيد وينقص وهو خصلة واحدة
فأقول إذا تركنا المداهنة ولم نكترث بتشغيب من تشغب وكشفنا الغطاء ارتفع
الإشكال فنقول الإيمان اسم مشترك يطلق من ثلاثة أوجه الأول أنه أنه يطلق
للتصديق بالقلب على سبيل الاعتقاد والتقليد من غير كشف وانشراح صدر وهو
إيمان العوام بل إيمان الخلق كلهم إلا الخواص وهذا الاعتقاد عقدة عن القلب
تارة تشتد وتقوى وتارة تضعف وتسترخي كالعقدة على الخيط مثلا ولا تستبعد هذا
واعتبره باليهودي وصلابته في عقيدته التي لا يمكن  نزوعه عنها بتخويف وتحذير
ولا بتخييل ووعظ ولا تحقيق وبرهان وكذلك النصراني والمبتدعة وفيهم من يمكن
تشكيكه بأدنى كلام ويمكن استنزاله عن اعتقاده بأدنى استمالة أو تخويف مع
أنه غير شاك في عقده كالأول ولكنهما متفاوتان في شدة التصميم
وهذا موجود في الاعتقاد الحق أيضا والعمل يؤثر في نماء هذا التصميم
وزيادته كما يؤثر سقي الماء في نماء الأشجار ولذلك قال الله تعالى فزادتهم
إيمانا وقال تعالى ليزدادوا إيمانا مع إيمانهم وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم
فيما يروى في بعض الأخبار الإيمان يزيد وينقص (2) وذلك بتأثير الطاعات في
القلب وهذا لا يدركه إلا من راقب أحوال نفسه في أوقات المواظبة على العبادة
والتجرد لها بحضور القلب مع أوقات الفتور وإدراك التفاوت في السكون إلى
عقائد الإيمان في هذه الأحوال حتى يزيد عقده استعصاء على من يريد حله
بالتشكيك بل من يعتقد في اليتيم معنى الرحمة إذا عمل بموجب اعتقاده فمسح
رأسه وتلطف به أدرك PageV01P120
من باطنه تأكيد الرحمة وتضاعفها بسبب العمل وكذلك معتقد التواضع إذا عمل
بموجبه عملا مقبلا أو ساجدا لغيره أحس من قلبه بالتواضع عند إقدامه على
الخدمة
وهكذا جميع صفات القلب تصدر منها أعمال الجوارح ثم يعود أثر الأعمال
عليها فيؤكدها ويزيدها وسيأتي هذا في ربع المنجيات والمهلكات عند بيان وجه
تعلق الباطن بالظاهر والأعمال بالعقائد والقلوب فإن ذلك من جنس تعلق الملك
بالملكوت وأعني بالملك عالم الشهادة المدرك بالحواس وبالملكوت عالم الغيب
المدرك بنور البصيرة والقلب من عالم الملكوت والأعضاء وأعمالها من عالم
الملك
ولطف الارتباط ودقته بين العالمين انتهى إلى حد ظن بعض الناس اتحاد
أحدهما بالآخر وظن آخرون أنه لا عالم إلا عالم الشهادة وهو هذه الأجسام
المحسوسة
ومن أدرك الأمرين وأدرك تعددهما ثم ارتباطهما عبر عنه فقال
رق الزجاج ورقت الخمر ... وتشابها فتشاكل الأمر
فكأنما خمر ولا قدح ... وكأنما قدح ولا خمر
ولنرجع إلى المقصود فإن هذا العلم خارج عن علم المعاملة ولكن بين العلمين
أيضا اتصال وارتباط فلذلك ترى علوم المكاشفة تتسلق  كل ساعة على علوم
المعاملة إلى أن تنكشف عنها بالتكليف فهذا وجه زيادة الإيمان بالطاعة بموجب

chapters.anchors:
- Root: ز-ي-د (z-y-d)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is "to increase, grow, exceed" — applied to quantity, intensity, or degree; its opposite is nuqṣān (decrease), from n-q-ṣ meaning "deficiency, diminution."
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, ziyādah in īmān denotes intensification of certitude (yaqīn) and the soul's tranquility (ṭuma'nīnah), not addition of a new essence; it is a modal strengthening of the same reality.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) for quantitative growth; metaphorical (majāz) when applied to qualities like faith — yet Ghazālī here insists on a real, non-metaphorical intensification, akin to a knot's tightening.
- Root: ع-ق-د (ʿ-q-d)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: "To tie, bind, knot" — ʿaqd is a firm tying; ʿaqīdah (creed) is what the heart is bound to.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): ʿAqd al-qalb is the heart's firm resolve (jazm) — admitting degrees of strength and weakness, as a physical knot tightens or loosens.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for physical knots; metaphorical for conviction — but Ghazālī exploits the analogy to show real variation in firmness.
- Root: ك-ش-ف (k-sh-f)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: "To uncover, reveal, disclose" — kashf is removal of a covering.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Technical term for unveiling (mukāshafah) — direct vision by the light of insight (nūr al-baṣīrah), the highest mode of certitude.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for removing a veil; metaphorical for intellectual apprehension — here used in its technical mystical sense.
- Sībawayh Rule: Ism Mushtarak (Homonymous Noun) — A single term (īmān) with multiple distinct senses (ishtirāk lafẓī), each requiring separate parsing; Ghazālī applies this to resolve the apparent contradiction between the Salaf's consensus and the unicity of taṣdīq.
chapters.translation:
I say: If you say, "The Salaf (the righteous predecessors) have agreed that faith (īmān) increases and decreases — it increases through obedience and decreases through disobedience. Now if taṣdīq (assent of the heart) is itself faith, then no increase or decrease is conceivable in it," — then I reply: The Salaf are the upright witnesses (al-shuhūd al-ʿudūl), and no one may deviate from their word. What they mentioned is true; the only matter is in understanding it. And in their statement there is proof that works (aʿmāl) are not a part of faith nor among the pillars of its existence, but rather something additional to it, by which it increases. The increaser exists, and the decreaser exists; and a thing does not increase by its own essence. Thus one may not say, "A man increases by his head," but rather, "He increases by his beard and his corpulence." Nor may one say, "The prayer increases by its bowing and prostration," but rather, "It increases by its etiquettes and supererogatory practices (ādāb wa sunan)." This is an explicit declaration that faith has an existence, and after existence its state varies by increase and decrease.

If you say, "The difficulty remains: how can taṣdīq increase and decrease, being a single trait?" — I reply: If we abandon flattery (mudāhanah), pay no heed to the clamor of the contentious, and lift the veil, the difficulty is removed. So I say: Faith (īmān) is a homonymous name (ism mushtarak), applied in three respects.

The first respect: It is applied to assent of the heart (taṣdīq bil-qalb) by way of belief and imitation (iʿtiqād wa taqlīd), without unveiling (kashf) or expansion of the breast (inshirāḥ al-ṣadr). This is the faith of the common folk — nay, the faith of all creatures except the elite (khawāṣṣ). This belief is a knot (ʿuqdah) upon the heart: at times it tightens and strengthens, at times it weakens and loosens — like a knot on a thread, for example. Do not deem this remote. Consider the Jew and the firmness of his creed, from which he cannot be drawn away by intimidation or warning, nor by fancy or exhortation, nor by verification or demonstration. Likewise the Christian and the innovator (mubtadiʿ). Among them there is one who can be thrown into doubt by the slightest speech, and can be brought down from his belief by the least allure or fear — though he is no less certain of his knot than the first. Yet the two differ in the intensity of resolve (shiddat al-taṣmīm). And this exists also in the true belief. Works affect the growth of this resolve and its increase, just as the watering of plants affects their growth. For this reason God Most High said: {«فزادتهم إيمانا»} ("And it increased them in faith") and said: {«ليزدادوا إيمانا مع إيمانهم»} ("That they may increase in faith upon their faith"). And the Prophet (peace be upon him) said, as narrated in some reports: "Faith increases and decreases." This is by the effect of acts of obedience upon the heart. None perceives this save one who watches over the states of his own soul — in times of persevering in worship and devoting oneself to it with presence of heart, versus times of languor — and perceives the disparity in his tranquility (sukūn) toward the creeds of faith in these states, until his knot becomes more resistant to anyone who would undo it by skepticism. Nay, consider one who holds the meaning of mercy toward an orphan: if he acts upon the requirement of his belief — wiping the orphan's head and showing kindness — he perceives from his inner self the strengthening of mercy and its multiplication due to the act. Likewise one who holds the belief of humility: if he acts upon its requirement — bowing or prostrating before another — he feels in his heart the humility when he undertakes the service.

And so it is with all the attributes of the heart: from them issue the works of the bodily members, then the effect of the works returns upon them, confirming and increasing them. This will come in the Quarter of Deliverance and Destruction (rubʿ al-munjiyāt wa al-muhlikāt) when explaining the manner of the attachment of the inner to the outer, and of works to creeds and hearts. For that is of the kind of attachment of the Kingdom (mulk) to the Dominion (malakūt). By "mulk" I mean the world of testimony (ʿālam al-shahādah), perceived by the senses; by "malakūt" I mean the world of the unseen (ʿālam al-ghayb), perceived by the light of insight (nūr al-baṣīrah). The heart is of the world of malakūt; the members and their works are of the world of mulk. The subtlety and delicacy of the connection between the two worlds reached such a limit that some people imagined the union of one with the other, and others imagined that there is no world but the world of testimony — namely, these perceived bodies. And one who perceived both matters — perceived their duality, then their connection — expressed it, saying:

"The glass became fine and the wine became fine, and they resembled each other, so the matter became alike. As if there is wine and no cup, and as if there is a cup and no wine."

Let us return to the purpose. For this knowledge is outside the knowledge of practical dealing (ʿilm al-muʿāmalah), but between the two sciences there is also connection and attachment. For this reason you see the sciences of unveiling (ʿulūm al-mukāshafah) climbing every hour upon the sciences of practical dealing, until they are unveiled from them by the divine command (taklīf). This then is the aspect of the increase of faith through obedience, according to this first application. For this reason ʿAlī (may God honor his face) said: "Faith indeed appears as a white gleam; when the servant performs righteous deeds, it grows and increases until the whole heart becomes white. And hypocrisy indeed appears as a black spot; when one violates the sacred prohibitions, it grows and increases until the whole heart becomes black, and then it is sealed over it — and that is the sealing (khatm)." And he recited the saying of God Most High: {«كلا بل ران على قلوبهم»} ("Nay, but that which they earned has rusted upon their hearts").

The second application: That by it is meant both assent and works together, as the Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "Faith has seventy-odd branches," and said: "The fornicator does not fornicate while he is a believer." When works enter into the import of the word "faith," its increase and decrease are not obscure. But does that affect the increase of faith which is mere taṣdīq? This is a matter of consideration — and we have indicated that it does affect it.

The third application: That by it is meant certain assent (taṣdīq yaqīnī) by way of unveiling (kashf), expansion of the breast (inshirāḥ al-ṣadr), and direct witnessing (mushāhadah) by the light of insight. This is the farthest of the divisions from admitting increase. But I say: The certain matter in which there is no doubt — the soul's tranquility toward it varies. For the soul's tranquility toward the fact that two is more than one is not like its tranquility toward the fact that the world is made, originated (ḥādith) — though there be no doubt in either. For certainties vary in their degrees of clarity and in the degrees of the soul's tranquility toward them. We have touched upon this in the chapter on certainty (yaqīn) in the Book of Knowledge, in the section on the signs of the scholars of the Hereafter — no need to repeat.

And it has become manifest in all the applications that what they said — of the increase and decrease of faith — is true. How could it be otherwise, when in the reports it is stated that there will come out of the Fire one in whose heart was a grain's weight (mithqāl dharrāh) of faith, and in another report, in some places, a dinar's weight (mithqāl dīnār)? What meaning could there be for the difference of its measures, if what is in the heart did not vary?

chapters.anchors:
- Root: ث ن ي (th-n-y)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Bending, folding, doubling; the act of returning upon a thing; hence istithnāʾ as the grammatical "exception" that doubles back upon a prior assertion.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, the exception signals epistemic humility before divine decree—an acknowledgment that ultimate verification of one's state rests with God alone.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense is syntactic exclusion; metaphorical sense (majāz) shifts to expressing hope (rajāʾ) or adab (courtesy), not doubt—as in "in shāʾ Allāh" for future matters.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Taʿlīq (Suspension) — The conditional particle "in" suspends the apodosis, rendering the assertion contingent without negating its truth-value; here applied to the predicate "muʾmin" to suspend self-praise, not the reality of faith.
chapters.translation:
I say: If you ask: "What is the meaning of the Salaf's saying, 'I am a believer, if God wills'—for the exception implies doubt, and doubt in faith is unbelief? Yet they all refrained from giving an unqualified answer concerning faith and guarded against it. Sufyān al-Thawrī (may God have mercy on him) said: 'Whoever says, "I am a believer before God," is among the liars; and whoever says, "I am a believer truly," is an innovator.' How then can one be a liar while knowing himself to be a believer inwardly? For whoever is a believer inwardly is a believer before God, just as whoever is tall or generous inwardly, and knows this, is so before God. Likewise, one who is joyful, sorrowful, hearing, or seeing. And if a man were asked, 'Are you an animal?' it would not be fitting for him to say, 'I am an animal, if God wills.' When Sufyān said this, he was asked: 'Then what should we say?' He replied: 'Say: We believe in God and in what has been sent down to us.' And what difference is there between saying 'We believe in God and what has been sent down to us' and saying 'I am a believer'?"

It was said to al-Ḥasan: "Are you a believer?" He said: "If God wills." It was said to him: "Why do you make the exception, O Abū Saʿīd, concerning faith?" He replied: "I fear to say 'Yes,' and then God (glorified be He) says: 'You have lied, O Ḥasan,' and the word of doom is verified against me." He used to say: "What assures me that God (glorified be He) has not looked upon me in some matter He dislikes, and abhorred me, and said: 'Go, I accept no deed from you'? So I labor in a place where labor is not accepted."

Ibrāhīm ibn Adham said: "When it is said to you, 'Are you a believer?' say: 'There is no god but God.'" And on another occasion he said: "Say: 'I do not doubt in faith; your asking me is an innovation.'" It was said to ʿAlqamah: "Are you a believer?" He said: "I hope so, if God wills." Al-Thawrī said: "We believe in God, His angels, His books, and His messengers—but we do not know what we are before God (exalted be He)."

So what is the meaning of these exceptions? The answer: This exception is sound and has four aspects—two based on doubt, not in the root of faith, but in its final outcome or its perfection; and two not based on doubt.

The first aspect, which does not rest on opposing doubt, is the guarding against unqualified assertion out of fear of what it contains of self-purification (tazkiyat al-nafs). God (exalted be He) says: {«فَلَا تُزَكُّوا أَنفُسَكُمْ»} "Do not purify yourselves" (Q 53:32), and {«أَلَمْ تَرَ إِلَى الَّذِينَ يُزَكُّونَ أَنفُسَهُمْ»} "Have you not seen those who purify themselves?" (Q 4:49), and He says: {«انظُرْ كَيْفَ يَفْتَرُونَ عَلَى اللَّهِ الْكَذِبَ»} "See how they invent lies against God" (Q 4:50). It was said to a sage: "What is ugly truthfulness?" He said: "A man's praising himself." Faith is among the highest attributes of glory, and unqualified assertion is an absolute self-purification; the form of the exception is, as it were, a burden borne by one who recognizes self-purification. Thus one says to a man: "You are a physician, a jurist, or an exegete," and he replies: "Yes, if God wills"—not in the mode of doubting, but to remove himself from self-praise. So the form is the form of hesitation and weakening of the very report, and its meaning is the weakening that is a necessary concomitant of the report—namely, self-praise. By this interpretation, if he were asked about a blameworthy attribute, the exception would not be fitting.

The second aspect is the courtesy (adab) of mentioning God (exalted be He) in every state and referring all matters to the will of God (glorified be He). For God (exalted be He) taught His Prophet (peace be upon him) courtesy, saying: {«وَلَا تَقُولَنَّ لِشَيْءٍ إِنِّي فَاعِلٌ ذَٰلِكَ غَدًا إِلَّا أَن يَشَاءَ اللَّهُ»} "And do not say of anything, 'I will do that tomorrow,' except 'if God wills'" (Q 18:23-24). Then He did not limit this to what is not doubted, but said: {«لَتَدْخُلُنَّ الْمَسْجِدَ الْحَرَامَ إِن شَاءَ اللَّهُ آمِنِينَ مُحَلِّقِينَ رُءُوسَكُمْ وَمُقَصِّرِينَ»} "You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque, if God wills, secure, heads shaved and hair cut short" (Q 48:27). God (exalted be He) knew they would enter inevitably and that He had willed it—but the purpose was to teach this courtesy. So the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) observed courtesy in what he reported, whether known or doubted, until he said (peace be upon him) upon entering the graves: "Peace be upon you, O people of a believing abode; and we, if God wills, shall join you." Joining them is not doubted, but the requirement of courtesy is to mention God and bind matters to Him. This form indicates that, until by customary usage it became an expression of desire and hope. Thus if it is said to you: "So-and-so will die soon," and you say: "If God wills," your desire is understood, not your doubt. And if it is said: "So-and-so's illness will pass and he will recover," and you say: "If God wills," meaning desire—so the word has been diverted from the meaning of doubt to the meaning of desire, and likewise diverted to the meaning of courtesy in mentioning God (exalted be He), however the matter may be.

The third aspect is based on doubt, and its meaning is: "I am a believer truly, if God wills," since God (exalted be He) said to a people specified by their very selves: {«أُولَٰئِكَ هُمُ الْمُؤْمِنُونَ حَقًّا»} "Those are the believers truly" (Q 8:4). So they are divided into two categories. This reverts to doubt concerning the perfection of faith, not its root. Every person doubts the perfection of his faith, and that is not unbelief. Doubt concerning the perfection of faith is sound from two angles: first, because hypocrisy (nifāq) removes the perfection of faith, and it is hidden—one cannot ascertain one's innocence from it; second, because faith is perfected by acts of obedience, and one does not know whether they exist in perfection. As for works, God (exalted be He) has said: {«إِنَّمَا الْمُؤْمِنُونَ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا بِاللَّهِ وَرَسُولِهِ ثُمَّ لَمْ يَرْتَابُوا وَجَاهَدُوا بِأَمْوَالِهِمْ وَأَنفُسِهِمْ فِي سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ ۚ أُولَٰئِكَ هُمُ الصَّادِقُونَ»} "The believers are only those who believe in God and His Messenger, then do not doubt, and strive with their wealth and selves in the way of God—those are the truthful" (Q 49:15). So doubt concerns this truthfulness. Likewise God (exalted be He) said: {«وَلَٰكِنَّ الْبِرَّ مَنْ آمَنَ بِاللَّهِ وَالْيَوْمِ الْآخِرِ وَالْمَلَائِكَةِ وَالْكِتَابِ وَالنَّبِيِّينَ»} "But righteousness is one who believes in God, the Last Day, the angels, the Book, and the prophets" (Q 2:177), stipulating twenty attributes, such as fulfilling covenants and patience in hardship. Then He said: {«أُولَٰئِكَ الَّذِينَ صَدَقُوا»} "Those are the truthful" (Q 2:177). And He said: {«يَرْفَعِ اللَّهُ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا مِنكُمْ وَالَّذِينَ أُوتُوا الْعِلْمَ دَرَجَاتٍ»} "God raises those who believe among you and those given knowledge in degrees" (Q 58:11), and {«لَا يَسْتَوِي مِنكُم مَّنْ أَنفَقَ مِن قَبْلِ الْفَتْحِ وَقَاتَلَ»} "Not equal among you are those who spent before the conquest and fought" (Q 57:10), and He said: {«هُمْ دَرَجَاتٌ عِندَ اللَّهِ»} "They are degrees before God" (Q 3:163). The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "Faith is naked, and its garment is piety," and he said (peace be upon him): "Faith has seventy-odd branches; the lowest is removing harm from the path." All this indicates the connection of faith's perfection to works. As for its connection to innocence from hypocrisy and hidden polytheism (shirk khafī), there is his saying (peace be upon him): "Four traits, whoever has them is a pure hypocrite, even if he fasts, prays, and claims to be a believer: when he speaks he lies, when he promises he breaks, when he is entrusted he betrays, and when he disputes he acts obscenely." In some narrations: "And when he covenants he treacherously breaks." In the hadith of Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī: "Hearts are four: a polished heart with a lamp shining therein—that is the believer's heart; and a covered heart in which are faith and hypocrisy—the likeness of faith therein is like a herb watered by sweet water, and the likeness of hypocrisy therein is like a sore fed by pus and blood; whichever of the two substances prevails, it rules over him." In another wording: "If it prevails, it carries him away." He (peace be upon him) said: "Most of the hypocrites of this community are its reciters (qurrāʾ)." And in the hadith: "Hidden polytheism in my community is more concealed than the crawling of an ant upon a rock." Ḥudhayfah (may God be pleased with him) said: "A man would speak a word in the time of the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) by which he would become a hypocrite until he died; and I hear it from one of you ten times a day." Some scholars said: "The closest of people to hypocrisy is one who sees himself innocent of it." Ḥudhayfah said: "The hypocrites today are more numerous than they were in the time of the Prophet (peace be upon him); then they concealed it, and today they display it." This hypocrisy opposes the truthfulness and perfection of faith, and it is hidden; the farthest of people from it is one who fears it, and the closest to it is one who sees himself innocent of it.

It was said to al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī: "They say there is no hypocrisy today." He said: "O my brother, if the hypocrites had perished, you would feel lonely on the road." He or another said: "If the hypocrites grew tails, we could not tread the earth with our feet." Ibn ʿUmar (may God be pleased with him) heard a man speaking against al-Ḥajjāj and said: "Do you see—if he were present and heard you, would you speak of him thus?" He said: "No." He said: "We used to count this as hypocrisy in the time of the Messenger of God (peace be upon him)." He (peace be upon him) said: "Whoever has two tongues in this world, God will make him have two tongues in the Hereafter." And he said (peace be upon him): "The worst of people is the double-faced one, who comes to these with one face and to those with another." It was said to al-Ḥasan: "Some people say we do not fear hypocrisy." He said: "By God, that I should know I am innocent of hypocrisy is dearer to me than the earth filled with gold." Al-Ḥasan said: "Part of hypocrisy is the divergence of tongue and heart, secret and public, entry and exit." A man said to Ḥudhayfah (may God be pleased with him): "I fear I am a hypocrite." He said: "If you were a hypocrite, you would not fear hypocrisy; the hypocrite feels secure from hypocrisy." Ibn Abī Mulaykah said: "I met one hundred and thirty—in another narration, one hundred and fifty—of the Companions of the Prophet (peace be upon him), all of them fearing hypocrisy."

It is narrated that the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) was sitting with a group of his Companions, and they mentioned a man and praised him profusely. While they were thus, the man appeared before them, his face dripping water from the traces of ablution, his sandal hanging from his hand, and between his eyes the mark of prostration. They said: "O Messenger of God, this is the man we described." He (peace be upon him) said: "I see on his face a black fleck from Satan." The man came, greeted, and sat with the people. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "I adjure you by God—did you say to yourself when you approached the people that there was none among them better than you?" He said: "O God, yes." He (peace be upon him) said in his supplication: "O God, I seek Your forgiveness for what I know and what I do not know." It was said to him: "Do you fear, O Messenger of God?" He said: "And what assures me, when hearts are between two fingers of the Merciful, He turns them as He wills?" And He (glorified be He) said: {«وَبَدَا لَهُم مِّنَ اللَّهِ مَا لَمْ يَكُونُوا يَحْتَسِبُونَ»} "And there will appear to them from God what they had never reckoned" (Q 39:47). It is said in the interpretation: "They did deeds they thought were good, and they were placed in the scale of evil deeds." Al-Sarī al-Saqaṭī said: "If a man entered a garden containing all kinds of trees, upon which were all kinds of birds, and each bird addressed him in its language, saying: 'Peace be upon you, O friend of God,' and his soul was tranquilized by that—he would be a captive in its hands."

These reports and traditions make known to you the gravity of the matter, due to the subtleties of hypocrisy and hidden polytheism, and that one is not secure from it—so much so that ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb (may God be pleased with him) used to ask Ḥudhayfah about himself, whether he was mentioned among the hypocrites. Abū Sulaymān al-Dārānī said: "I heard something from one of the commanders and wanted to denounce it, but I feared he would order my execution. I did not fear death, but I feared that my heart would be tempted to adorn itself before creatures at the moment my soul departed, so I refrained." This is of the hypocrisy that opposes the reality of faith, its truthfulness, perfection, and purity—not its root. For hypocrisy is of two kinds: one that expels from religion, joins the unbelievers, and is mustered in the company of those eternally in the Fire; the second leads its possessor to the Fire for a period, or diminishes his degrees in ʿIlliyyīn and lowers his rank among the Ṣiddīqīn. This second kind is doubtful, and therefore the exception is fitting concerning it. The root of this hypocrisy is the divergence between secret and public, security from God's deception (makr Allāh), self-admiration (ʿujb), and other matters from which none are free except the Ṣiddīqīn.

The fourth aspect, also based on doubt, concerns the fear of the final outcome (khātima): one does not know whether faith will be preserved for him at death or not. For if he is sealed with unbelief, his prior works are nullified, because they are contingent upon the soundness of the end. If a fasting person were asked in the forenoon about the soundness of his fast and said: "I am fasting, definitively," and then he broke his fast during the day, his claim would be shown false—since soundness is contingent upon completion until sunset at the day's end. Just as the day is the term for completing the fast, so the lifespan is the term for completing the soundness of faith. Describing it as sound before its end is based on presumption of continuity (istisḥāb), which is doubtful; the outcome is feared. For this reason, the weeping of most of the fearful was for the outcome, because it is the fruit of the prior decree and the eternal will, which appears only with the appearance of the decreed thing, and no human has access to it. So fear of the final outcome is like fear of the prior decree; perhaps what appears in the present is the opposite of what the word preceded. Who knows that he is among those for whom the goodly word has preceded from God? It is said concerning His saying: {«وَجَاءَتْ سَكْرَةُ الْمَوْتِ بِالْحَقِّ»} "And the stupor of death comes with the truth" (Q 50:19)—that is, with the prior decree, meaning it reveals it. Some of the Salaf said: "Only the final parts of deeds are weighed." Abū al-Dardāʾ (may God be pleased with him) used to swear by God: "No one who feels secure from having his faith snatched away is safe from it being snatched." It is said: "Among sins are sins whose punishment is an evil final outcome—we seek refuge in God from that." And it is said: "They are punishments for claiming friendship (wilāya) and honor (karāma) by falsehood." Some of the knowers (ʿārifūn) said: "If martyrdom were offered to me at the door of the house, and death upon tawḥīd at the door of the chamber, I would choose death upon tawḥīd at the door of the chamber—because I do not know what change might occur in my heart from tawḥīd by the time I reach the door of the house." Another said: "If I knew a man upon tawḥīd for fifty years, then a wall intervened between me and him and he died, I would not judge that he died upon tawḥīd."

In the hadith: "Whoever says 'I am a believer' is an unbeliever, and whoever says 'I am a scholar' is ignorant." It is said concerning His saying: {«وَتَمَّتْ كَلِمَتُ رَبِّكَ صِدْقًا وَعَدْلًا»} "And the word of your Lord is fulfilled in truth and justice" (Q 6:115)—"truth" for one who dies upon faith, and "justice" for one who dies upon polytheism. And He (exalted be He) said: {«وَلِلَّهِ عَاقِبَةُ الْأُمُورِ»} "And to God is the final outcome of all matters" (Q 31:22). Whenever doubt is of this magnitude, the exception becomes obligatory—because faith is an expression of what secures Paradise, just as fasting is an expression of what discharges the obligation. What is corrupted before sunset does not discharge the obligation and thus exits from being fasting; likewise faith. Indeed, it is not far-fetched to ask about a past fast that is not doubted after its completion, and one says: "Did you fast yesterday?" and he replies: "Yes, if God wills"—for the true fast is the accepted one, and the accepted is hidden from him, known only to God (exalted be He). From this, the exception is fitting in all acts of righteousness, being a doubt concerning acceptance—since acceptance is prevented, after the apparent conditions of soundness are fulfilled, by subtle causes known only to the Lord of lords (majestic is His glory). So doubt therein is fitting.

These, then, are the aspects of the fittingness of the exception in answering concerning faith. And with this we conclude the Book of the Foundations of Belief (Qawāʿid al-ʿAqāʾid). The book is completed by the praise of God (exalted be He), and may He bless and grant peace upon our master Muḥammad and upon every chosen servant.

chapters.title_en: The Book of the Mysteries of Purification — Section 35: The Four Ranks of Purification and the Conduct of the Early Muslims
chapters.arabic_text:
| كتاب أسرار الطهارة وهو الكتاب الثالث من ربع العبادات

بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم
الحمد لله الذي تلطف بعباده فتعبدهم بالنظافة وأفاض على قلوبهم تزكية
لسرائرهم أنواره وألطافه وأعد لظواهرهم تطهيرا لها الماء المخصوص بالرقة
واللطافة وصلى الله على النبي محمد المستغرق بنور الهدى أطراف العالم
وأكنافه وعلى آله الطيبين الطاهرين صلاة تنجينا بركاتها يوم المخافة وتنتصب
جنة بيننا وبين كل آفة
أما بعد
فقد قال النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم بنى الدين على النظافة (2) وقال صلى
الله عليه وسلم مفتاح الصلاة الطهور (3) وقال الله تعالى {فيه رجال يحبون
أن يتطهروا والله يحب المطهرين} وقال النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم الطهور نصف
الإيمان (4) وقال الله تعالى {ما يريد الله ليجعل عليكم من حرج ولكن يريد
ليطهركم} فتفطن ذوو البصائر بهذه الظواهر أن أهم الأمور تطهير السرائر إذ
يبعد أن يكون المراد بقوله صلى الله عليه وسلم الطهور نصف الإيمان عمارة
الظاهر بالتنظيف بإفاضة الماء وإلقائه وتخريب الباطن وإبقائه مشحونا
بالأخباث والأقذار هيهات PageV01P125
هيهات والطهارة لها أربع مراتب
المرتبة الأولى تطهير الظاهر عن الأحداث وعن الأخباث والفضلات
المرتبة الثانية تطهير الجوارح عن الجرائم والآثام
المرتبة الثالثة تطهير القلب عن الأخلاق المذمومة والرذائل الممقوتة
المرتبة الرابعة تطهير السر عما سوى الله تعالى وهي طهارة الأنبياء صلوات
الله عليهم والصديقين والطهارة في كل رتبة نصف العمل الذي فيها فإن الغاية
القصوى في عمل السر أن ينكشف له جلال الله تعالى وعظمته ولن تحل معرفة الله
تعالى بالحقيقة في السر ما لم يرتحل ما سوى الله تعالى عنه
ولذلك قال الله عز وجل {قل الله ثم ذرهم في خوضهم يلعبون} لأنهما لا
يجتمعان في قلب وما جعل الله لرجل من قلبين في جوفه وأما عمل القلب فالغاية
القصوى  عمارته بالأخلاق المحمودة والعقائد المشروعة ولن يتصف بها ما لم
ينظف عن نقائضها من العقائد الفاسدة والرذائل الممقوتة فتطهيره أحد الشطرين
وهو الشطر الأول الذي هو شرط في الثاني فكان الطهور شطر الإيمان بهذا
المعنى وكذلك تطهير الجوارح عن المناهي أحد الشطرين وهو الشطر الأول الذي
هو شرط في الثاني فتطهيره أحد الشطرين وهو الشطر الأول وعمارتها بالطاعات
الشطر الثاني فهذه مقامات الإيمان ولكل مقام طبقة ولن ينال العبد الطبقة
العالية إلا أن يجاوز الطبقة السافلة فلا يصل إلى طهارة السر عن الصفات
المذمومة وعمارته بالمحمودة ما لم يفرغ من طهارة القلب عن الخلق المذموم
وعمارته بالخلق المحمود ولن يصل إلى ذلك من لم يفرغ عن طهارة الجوارح عن
المناهي وعمارتها بالطاعات وكلما عز المطلوب وشرف صعب مسلكه وطال طريقه
وكثرت عقباته فلا تظن أن هذا الأمر يدرك وينال بالهوينى نعم من عميت بصيرته
عن تفاوت هذه الطبقات لم يفهم من مراتب الطهارة إلا الدرجة الأخيرة التي هي
كالقشرة الأخيرة الظاهرة بالإضافة إلى اللب المطلوب فصار يمعن فيها ويستقصى
في مجاريها ويستوعب جميع أوقاته في الاستنجاء وغسل الثياب وتنظيف الظاهر
وطلب المياه الجارية الكثيرة ظنا منه بحكم الوسوسة وتخيل العقل أن الطهارة
المطلوبة الشريفة هي هذه فقط وجهالة بسيرة الأولين واستغراقهم جميع الهم
والفكر في تطهير القلب وتساهلهم في أمر الظاهر حتى إن عمر رضي الله عنه مع
علو منصبه توضأ من ماء في جرة نصرانية وحتى إنهم ما كانوا يغسلون اليد من
الدسومات والأطعمة بل كانوا يمسحون أصابعهم بأخمص أقدامهم وعدوا الأشنان من
البدع المحدثة ولقد كانوا يصلون على الأرض في المساجد ويمشون حفاة في
الطرقات ومن كان لا يجعل بينه وبين الأرض حاجزا في مضجعه كان من أكابرهم
وكانوا يقتصرون على الحجارة في الاستنجاء
وقال أبو هريرة وغيره من أهل الصفة كنا نأكل الشواء فتقام الصلاة فندخل
أصابعنا في الحصى ثم نفركها بالتراب ونكبر (1) وقال عمر رضي الله عنه ما
كنا نعرف الأشنان في عصر رسول الله صلى  الله عليه وسلم وإنما كانت مناديلنا
بطون أرجلنا (2) كنا إذا أكلنا الغمر مسحنا بها ويقال أول ما ظهر من البدع
بعد رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم أربع المناخل والأشنان والموائد والشبع
فكانت عنايتهم كلها بنظافة الباطن حتى قال بعضهم الصلاة في النعلين أفضل
لأن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم لما نزع نعليه في صلاته بإخبار جبريل
عليه السلام له أن بهما نجاسة وخلع الناس نعالهم قال صلى الله عليه وسلم لم
خلعتم نعالكم (3) وقال النخعي في الذين يخلعون نعالهم وددت لو أن محتاجا
جاء إليها فأخذها منكرا لخلع النعال
فهكذا كان تساهلهم في هذه الأمور بل كانوا يمشون في طين الشوارع حفاة
ويجلسون عليها ويصلون PageV01P126
في المساجد على الأرض ويأكلون من دقيق البر والشعير وهو يداس بالدواب
وتبول عليه ولا يحترزون من عرق الإبل والخيل مع كثرة تمرغها في النجاسات
ولم ينقل قط عن أحد منهم سؤال في دقائق
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ط-ه-ر (ṭ-h-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is cleanliness and freedom from filth, both physical (khabath) and ritual (ḥadath); the root denotes removal of impurity in all its forms.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, ṭahārah is graded: purification of the body (ẓāhir), the limbs (jawāriḥ), the heart (qalb), and the innermost secret (sirr) — the last being the highest, reserved for prophets and the veracious (ṣiddīqūn).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) refers to physical cleansing with water; metaphorical (majāz) extends to spiritual purification from vices — the Prophet's saying "purification is half of faith" is understood metaphorically, as the outward act alone cannot be half of faith while the inner self remains defiled.
- Root: س-ر-ر (s-r-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The innermost secret or hidden core of the self; that which is concealed from others and even from oneself.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The sirr is the deepest faculty of the soul where divine knowledge (maʿrifah) is unveiled; it must be emptied of all save God for true gnosis to occur.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Used metaphorically here — "purification of the sirr" is not physical but signifies total orientation toward God alone.
- Root: ب-ذ-ذ (b-dh-dh)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Roughness or coarseness of dress and manner; simplicity and lack of ostentation in appearance.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In the prophetic tradition, budhādhah (simplicity) is described as part of faith (īmān) — a deliberate rejection of worldly adornment.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): The early Muslims' simplicity is literal (ḥaqīqah) — they walked barefoot and ate plainly; the later Sufis' elaborate cleanliness is metaphorical ostentation (majāz) mislabeled as piety.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Constructions (al-sharṭ wa al-istithnāʾ) — The text employs complex conditional sentences (e.g., "if you say... I say...") and exceptive clauses (illā bi-) to delineate the precise conditions under which outward cleanliness is praiseworthy, blameworthy, or permissible, requiring careful parsing of the protasis and apodosis.
chapters.translation:
I say: Know that the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Religion is built upon cleanliness," and he said, peace be upon him: "The key to prayer is purification," and God Most High said: {«In it are men who love to purify themselves, and God loves those who purify themselves»} and the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Purification is half of faith," and God Most High said: {«God does not intend to make difficulty for you, but He intends to purify you»}. Those possessed of insight perceived through these outward expressions that the most important of matters is the purification of the inner secrets, for it is far-fetched that the meaning of his saying, peace be upon him, "Purification is half of faith," should be the cultivation of the outward by cleansing with the pouring and casting of water, while the inward is left ruined, stuffed with filths and impurities. Far be it! Far be it!

Purification has four ranks:
The first rank: purifying the outward from ritual impurities (aḥdāth) and from filths and bodily excesses.
The second rank: purifying the limbs from crimes and sins.
The third rank: purifying the heart from blameworthy character traits and abhorred vices.
The fourth rank: purifying the innermost secret from all save God Most High — and this is the purification of the prophets, God's blessings be upon them, and the veracious (ṣiddīqīn).

Purification in every rank is half of the work belonging to that rank. For the ultimate goal in the work of the secret is that the majesty and grandeur of God Most High be unveiled to it; and the knowledge of God Most High will never truly settle in the secret so long as anything other than God Most High has not departed from it. For this reason God, Mighty and Majestic, said: {«Say: God — then leave them in their vain play»} — because the two cannot coexist in one heart, and God has not made for any man two hearts within his breast.

As for the work of the heart, the ultimate goal is its cultivation with praiseworthy character traits and lawful beliefs; and it will never be so described unless it is cleansed of their opposites — corrupt beliefs and abhorred vices. Thus its purification is one of the two halves, and it is the first half which is a condition for the second. So purification is half of faith in this sense. Likewise, purifying the limbs from forbidden things is one of the two halves — the first half which is a condition for the second; and their cultivation with acts of obedience is the second half.

These are the stations of faith, and for every station there is a level. The servant will never attain the higher level unless he passes beyond the lower level. He will not reach the purification of the secret from blameworthy traits and its cultivation with praiseworthy ones unless he has completed the purification of the heart from blameworthy character and its cultivation with praiseworthy character. And he will not reach that unless he has completed the purification of the limbs from forbidden things and their cultivation with acts of obedience. Whenever the sought object is more precious and nobler, its path becomes harder, its road longer, and its obstacles more numerous. Do not think that this matter is attained and reached with ease and indolence.

Indeed, whoever's inner sight is blind to the disparity of these levels understands of the ranks of purification only the last degree — which is like the outermost shell in relation to the sought kernel. So he plunges into it, exhausts himself in its details, and spends all his time in cleansing after relieving oneself, washing garments, cleaning the outward, and seeking abundant running waters — imagining, by the judgment of obsessive whisperings (waswasah) and the delusion of the intellect, that the noble, sought purification is only this. This is ignorance of the conduct of the early generations (salaf), and of their devoting all concern and thought to purifying the heart while being lenient in outward matters — so much so that ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, despite his lofty station, performed ablution from water in a Christian woman's jar. They did not wash their hands from greases and foods, but rather wiped their fingers on the soles of their feet, and counted soapwort (ushnān) among the innovated novelties (bidaʿ). They prayed on the ground in mosques, walked barefoot in the roads, and whoever had no barrier between himself and the earth in his sleeping place was among their great ones. They sufficed with stones for cleansing after relieving oneself.

Abū Hurayrah and others of the People of the Suffah (ahl al-ṣuffah) said: "We would eat roasted meat, then the prayer would be established, so we would thrust our fingers into the pebbles, then rub them with earth, and say the takbīr." ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, said: "We did not know soapwort in the era of the Messenger of God, peace be upon him; rather, our napkins were the soles of our feet — when we ate greasy food, we wiped them with them." It is said that the first novelties to appear after the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, were four: sieves, soapwort, dining tables, and eating one's fill.

Their entire concern was with the cleanliness of the inward, until one of them said: "Prayer in sandals is superior, because when the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, removed his sandals in his prayer upon the information of Gabriel, peace be upon him, that there was filth on them, and the people removed their sandals, he said, peace be upon him: 'Why did you remove your sandals?'" Al-Nakhaʿī said regarding those who remove their sandals: "I wish that a needy person would come and take them," disapproving of the removal of sandals.

Thus was their leniency in these matters. Indeed, they walked barefoot in the mud of the streets, sat upon it, prayed in mosques on the ground, ate from the flour of wheat and barley which was trodden by beasts and urinated upon, and did not guard against the sweat of camels and horses despite their frequent rolling in impurities. It has never been transmitted from any of them a question concerning the subtleties of impurities. Thus was their leniency in them.

Now the turn has come to a group who call foolish vanity (ruʿūnah) "cleanliness" and say it is the foundation of religion. So most of their time is spent in adorning their outward appearances, like the act of a beautician with her bride, while the inward is ruined, stuffed with the vilenesses of pride, self-admiration, ignorance, ostentation (riyāʾ), and hypocrisy — and they neither disapprove of this nor marvel at it. If anyone were to suffice with a stone for cleansing, or walk on the ground barefoot, or pray on the earth or on the reed mats of the mosque without a spread carpet, or walk on carpets without a leather covering for the feet, or perform ablution from the vessel of an old woman or a man not given to excessive refinement — they would raise a great outcry against him, rebuke him severely, meet him with disgust, expel him from their company, and disdain eating with him and mixing with him.

So they named simplicity (budhādhah), which is part of faith, "filth," and foolish vanity "cleanliness." See how the disapproved has become the approved and the approved has become the disapproved, and how the vestige of religion has been effaced just as its reality and knowledge have been effaced.

If you say: "Do you then say that these habits which the Sufis have innovated in their appearances and their cleanliness are among the prohibited or disapproved things?" — I say: God forbid that I should make an unqualified statement about this without detail. Rather, I say: This cleaning and self-imposed hardship, the preparation of vessels and tools, the use of foot coverings and the wrapped waist-wrapper to repel dust, and other such means — if one looks at them in themselves, abstractly, they are among the permissible things (mubāḥāt). But there may attach to them states and intentions that sometimes make them among the approved things (maʿrūfāt) and sometimes among the disapproved things (munkarāt).

As for their being permissible in themselves, it is not hidden that their practitioner is disposing of his own wealth, body, and garments, doing with them what he wills, so long as there is no wastefulness or extravagance in it. As for their becoming disapproved, it is by making this a root of religion and interpreting by it the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him, "Religion is built upon cleanliness" — so that one disapproves thereby of those who are lenient in it from the early generations — or by intending thereby the adornment of the outward for creatures and the improvement of their gaze upon one; for that is the prohibited ostentation (riyāʾ). So it becomes disapproved by these two considerations.

As for its being approved, it is that the intention therein be goodness without adornment, that one not disapprove of those who abandon it, that one not delay prayer from its earliest times because of it, and that one not occupy oneself with it instead of a work better than it, or instead of knowledge or other things. When none of these things attach to it, it is permissible, and it can be made an act of drawing near (qurbah) by intention. But this is not facilitated except for the idle (baṭṭālīn) who, if they did not occupy themselves with spending their times in it, would occupy themselves with sleep or idle talk about what does not concern them. So their occupation with it becomes more appropriate, because occupying oneself with purifications renews the remembrance of God Most High and the remembrance of acts of worship. There is no harm in it so long as it does not lead to something disapproved or to extravagance.

As for the people of knowledge and action, they should not divert from their times to it except the measure of need. Anything beyond that is disapproved in their case, and a waste of the life which is the most precious and dearest of jewels, in the case of one who is able to benefit from it. Do not marvel at this, for the good deeds of the righteous (abrār) are the evil deeds of those brought near (muqarrabūn).

Nor should the idle person abandon cleanliness and disapprove of the Sufis, claiming that he is imitating the Companions — for imitating them consists in not being free except for what is more important than it, as was said to Dāwūd al-Ṭāʾī: "Why do you not trim your beard?" He said: "Then I would indeed be free [for trivialities]."

For this reason, I do not see for the scholar, nor for the student, nor for the worker, that he should waste his time in washing garments — guarding against wearing unwashed clothes and imagining that the launderer has been negligent in the washing. For in the first era they prayed in tanned furs, and none of them is known to have distinguished between washed and tanned garments regarding purity and impurity. Rather, they avoided impurity when they saw it, and did not refine their gaze to extract subtle probabilities. But they did reflect on the subtleties of ostentation and injustice — until Sufyān al-Thawrī said to a companion who was walking with him and looked at the raised, well-built door of a house: "Do not do that! For if people did not look at it, its owner would not engage in this extravagance. The one who looks at it is his helper in extravagance." So they counted the sharpness of the mind for extracting such subtleties, not for the probabilities of impurity.

If the scholar finds a commoner (ʿāmmī) who occupies himself with washing garments out of caution, that is better — for in comparison to leniency it is good. And that commoner benefits from his occupation, for he occupies his soul that commands to evil with a permissible act in itself, and thus is prevented from sins in that state. And the soul — if it is not occupied with something, it occupies its owner. And if he intends thereby drawing near to God, it becomes for him among the best of acts of drawing near.

So the scholar's time is too noble to spend on such a thing — thus it remains preserved for him. And the best time of the commoner is to occupy himself with such a thing — thus goodness accrues to him from all sides. Let one reflect by this example on its parallels among works, the ordering of their virtues, and the manner of preferring some over others. For the precise reckoning in preserving the moments of life by spending them on what is best is more important than precise reckoning in the affairs of this world in their entirety.

When you have understood this preamble and discerned that purification has four ranks, know that in this book we speak only of the fourth rank — namely, the cleanliness of the outward — for in the first half of the book we do not intentionally address anything but the outward matters.

So we say: The purification of the outward is of three kinds: purification from filth (khabath), purification from ritual impurity (ḥadath), and purification from bodily excesses — which is achieved by trimming the nails, shaving the pubic hair, using depilatory lime (nūrah), circumcision, and other such things.

chapters.title_en: The First Division: On the Purification from Filth (Ṭahārat al-Khabath) — Its Subject, Agent, and Act
chapters.arabic_text: || القسم الأول في طهارة الخبث والنظر فيه يتعلق بالمزال والمزال به والإزالة
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ط-ه-ر (ṭ-h-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is "purity" and "cleanliness" — both physical (from dirt) and spiritual (from sin); the verbal noun ṭahārah denotes removal of impurity (khabath) and ritual purification (ṭahūr).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, ṭahārah is twofold: purification of the body from sensory filth (khabath) and purification of the soul from moral and spiritual defilement (ḥadath). Here, it is the former — the removal of tangible impurity.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) sense is physical cleansing; metaphorical (majāz) sense is spiritual purity. In this context, the literal sense governs, as the text specifies "filth" (khabath), not "event" (ḥadath).
- Root: خ-ب-ث (kh-b-th)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Means "badness," "corruption," and "uncleanness" — specifically that which is repugnant to sound nature (ṭabʿ) and prohibited by law (sharʿ). It contrasts with ṭayyib (good, pure).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Khabath is the sensory impurity that invalidates prayer and requires removal — distinct from ḥadath (ritual impurity from bodily events), which requires ablution or bathing.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: physical filth (e.g., blood, urine, wine). Metaphorical: moral corruption (e.g., evil deeds). Here, literal.
- Root: ز-و-ل (z-w-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Means "to depart," "to cease," "to be removed." The noun izālah (removal) implies an act of causing something to leave its place or state.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal contexts, izālah is the active removal of impurity — the third element in the tripartite analysis (the impurity, the remover, and the act of removal).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: physical displacement. Metaphorical: nullification of a ruling. Here, literal — the physical act of cleansing.
- Sībawayh Rule: The Construct Phrase (al-Idāfah) — The phrase "المزال والمزال به والإزالة" (the removed, the remover, and the removal) forms a coordinated series of nominal predicates governed by the prepositional phrase "في" (concerning). The passive participle (ism al-mafʿūl) "المزال" (that which is removed) and the instrumental "المزال به" (that by which removal occurs) are syntactically parallel, each governed by the same verbal root (z-w-l), demonstrating the tripartite division of the subject matter.
chapters.translation: I say: The first division concerns the purification from filth (ṭahārat al-khabath). The examination of this matter pertains to three things: the impurity that is removed (al-muzāl), the agent by which removal is effected (al-muzāl bihī), and the act of removal itself (al-izālah).

chapters.title_en: The First Aspect Concerning That Which Must Be Removed (Al-Muzāl) — Impurity (Najāsah)
