وهي النجاسة
والأعيان ثلاثة جمادات وحيوانات وأجزاء حيوانات
أما الجمادات فطاهرة كلها إلا الخمر وكل منتبذ مسكر والحيوانات طاهرة
كلها إلا الكلب والخنزير وما تولد منهما أو من أحدهما
فإذا ماتت فكلها نجسة إلا خمسة الآدمي والسمك والجراد ودود التفاح وفي
معناه كل ما يستحيل من الأطعمة وكل ما ليس له نفس سائلة كالذباب والخنفساء
وغيرهما فلا ينجس الماء بوقوع شيء منها فيه
وأما أجزاء الحيوانات فقسمان أحدهما ما يقطع منه وحكمه حكم الميت
والشعر لا ينجس بالجز والموت والعظم ينجس
الثاني الرطوبات الخارجة من باطنه فكل ما ليس مستحيلا ولا له مقر فهو
طاهر كالدمع والعرق واللعاب والمخاط وما له مقر وهو مستحيل فنجس إلا ما هو
مادة الحيوان كالمني والبيض
والقيح والدم والروث والبول نجس من الحيوانات كلها
ولا يعفى عن شيء من هذه النجاسات قليلها وكثيرها إلا عن خمسة الأول أثر
النجو بعد الاستجمار بالأحجار يعفى عنه ما لم يعد المخرج
والثاني طين الشوارع وغبار الروث في الطريق يعفى عنه مع تيقن النجاسة
بقدر ما يتعذر الاحتراز عنه وهو الذي لا ينسب المتلطخ به إلى تفريط أو سقطة
الثالث ما على أسفل الخف من نجاسة لا يخلو الطريق عنها فيعفى عنه بعد
الدلك للحاجة
الرابع دم البراغيث ما قل منه أو كثر إلا إذا جاوز حد العادة سواء كان في
ثوبك أو في ثوب غيرك فلبسته
الخامس دم البثرات وما ينفصل منها من قيح وصديد
ودلك ابن عمر رضي الله عنه بثرة على وجهه فخرج منها الدم وصلى ولم يغتسل
وفي معناه ما يترشح من لطخات الدماميل التي تدوم غالبا وكذلك أثر الفصد
إلا ما يقع نادرا من خراج أو غيره فيلحق بدم الاستحاضة ولا يكون في معنى
البثرات التي لا يخلو الإنسان عنها في أحواله
ومسامحة الشرع في هذه النجاسات الخمس تعرفك أن أمر الطهارة على التساهل
وما ابتدع فيها وسوسة لا أصل لها
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ن-ج-س (N-J-S)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning of filth, dirt, and that which is repugnant to sound nature; ritual impurity as a legal category.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Theological nuance — najāsah as a jurisprudential designation (ḥukm sharʿī) denoting legal prohibition of prayer with its presence, not a physical quality inherent in substances.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal usage refers to physical filth; metaphorical (majāz) usage extends to moral or spiritual defilement — here employed in its literal legal sense.
- Root: ط-ه-ر (T-H-R)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Cleanliness, purity, freedom from admixture of filth.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Ṭahārah as both physical cleanliness and legal purity (ṭahārah ḥukmiyyah) prerequisite for valid worship.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for washing away dirt; metaphorical for exoneration from sin or legal impediment.
- Root: ع-ف-و (ʿ-F-W)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Pardon, remission, and by extension legal overlooking of that which is excusable.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): ʿAfw as divine leniency and juristic concession (rukhṣah) for unavoidable impurities.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — to erase or obliterate; metaphorical — legal dispensation exceeding the normal measure.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Conditional Restriction (Taqyīd bi-al-Sharṭ) — the particle "إلا" (exceptive construction) governs the enumeration of exceptions, requiring precise parsing of the general proposition (al-ʿāmm) against its specified exclusions (al-mustathnayāt).
chapters.translation:
I say: The first aspect concerns that which must be removed (al-muzāl), namely impurity (najāsah).

Know that corporeal substances (al-aʿyān) are of three categories: inanimate objects (jamādāt), animals (ḥayawānāt), and parts of animals (ajzāʾ ḥayawānāt).

As for inanimate objects, all of them are pure (ṭāhir) except wine (khamr) and every intoxicating fermented beverage (nabīdh muskir).

As for animals, all of them are pure except the dog, the pig, and whatever is generated from both of them or from one of the two.

When they die, then all of them become impure (najis) except five: the human being, the fish, the locust, the worm of apples (dūd al-tuffāḥ) — and in its meaning [i.e., analogous to it] is everything that transforms (yastaḥīl) from foodstuffs — and every creature that has no flowing blood (nafs sāʾilah), such as the fly and the beetle and others like them. Water is not rendered impure by the falling of any of these into it.

As for the parts of animals, they are of two divisions:

The first: that which is cut off from a living animal — its ruling is the ruling of the dead [carrion]. However, hair is not rendered impure by shearing (al-jazz) nor by death, whereas bone is rendered impure.

The second: the moistures (ruṭūbāt) that exit from its interior. So everything that is not transformed [from another substance] and has no receptacle (muqarr) is pure, such as tears, sweat, saliva, and nasal mucus. And that which has a receptacle and is transformed is impure — except that which is the seminal material (māddah) of the animal, such as semen (maniyy) and eggs.

Pus (qayḥ), blood, dung (rawth), and urine are impure from all animals.

And no remission (ʿafw) is granted for any of these impurities — neither their small quantity nor their large — except for five:

The first: the trace of excrement after cleansing with stones (istijmār); remission is granted for it as long as the exit [of the impurity] has not recurred.

The second: the mud of roadways and the dust of dung upon the path; remission is granted for it even with certainty of the impurity, to the extent that avoidance is impossible (yataʿadhdhar al-iḥtirāz) — namely, that which does not attribute the one soiled by it to negligence (tafrīṭ) or a fall (saqṭah).

The third: that which is upon the lower part of the leather sock (khuff) of impurity that the road does not lack; remission is granted for it after rubbing (al-dalk) due to necessity.

The fourth: the blood of fleas — whether little or much — except when it exceeds the customary limit (ḥadd al-ʿādah), whether it be upon your garment or upon the garment of another which you then wore.

The fifth: the blood of pustules (buthrāt) and what separates from them of pus and serum (ṣadīd). And Ibn ʿUmar — may God be pleased with him — rubbed a pustule on his face, and blood came out of it, and he prayed without washing. And in its meaning [i.e., analogous to it] is what oozes from the smears of boils that generally persist, and likewise the trace of bloodletting (al-faṣd) — except what occurs rarely from an abscess or other than it, for that is attached to the blood of prolonged menstruation (istḥāḍah) and is not in the meaning of pustules from which a person is never free in his states.

And the Law’s leniency (musāmaḥah) concerning these five impurities informs you that the matter of purification (al-ṭahārah) is [built] upon ease (al-tasāhul), and that what has been innovated therein of whisperings (waswasah) has no foundation (aṣl).

chapters.title_en: The Second Aspect: That Which Removes Impurity (al-Muzāl bihi)

||| الطرف الثاني في المزال به

وهو إما جامد وإما مائع أما الجامد فحجر الاستنجاء وهو مطهر تطهير تخفيف
بشرط أن يكون صلبا طاهرا منشفا غير محترم وأما المائعات فلا تزال النجاسات
بشيء منها إلا الماء ولا كل ماء بل الطاهر الذي  لم يتفاحش
PageV01P128
تغيره بمخالطة ما يستغنى عنه
ويخرج الماء عن الطهارة بأن يتغير بملاقاة النجاسة طعمه أو لونه أو ريحه
فإن لم يتغير وكان قريبا من مائتين وخمسين منا وهو خمسمائة رطل برطل
العراق لم ينجس لقوله صلى الله عليه وسلم إذا بلغ الماء قلتين لم يحمل خبثا
(1) وإن كان دونه صار نجسا عند الشافعي رضي الله عنه هذا في الماء الراكد
وأما الماء الجاري إذا تغير بالنجاسة فالجرية المتغيرة نجسة دون ما فوقها
وما تحتها لأن جريات الماء متفاصلات
وكذا النجاسة الجارية إذا جرت بمجرى الماء فالنجس موقعها من الماء وما عن
يمينها وشمالها إذا تقاصر عن قلتين
وإن كان جري الماء أقوى من جري النجاسة فما فوق النجاسة طاهر وما سفل
عنها فنجس وإن تباعد وكثر إلا إذا اجتمع في حوض قدر قلتين
وإذا اجتمع قلتان من ماء نجس طهر ولا يعود نجسا بالتفريق
هذا هو مذهب الشافعي رضي الله عنه
وكنت أود أن يكون مذهبه كمذهب مالك رضي الله عنه في أن الماء وإن قل لا
ينجس إلا بالتغير إذ الحاجة ماسة إليه ومثار الوسواس اشترط القلتين ولأجله
شق على الناس ذلك وهو لعمري سبب المشقة ويعرفه من يجربه ويتأمله
ومما لا أشك فيه أن ذلك لو كان مشروطا لكان أولى المواضع بتعسر الطهارة
مكة والمدينة إذ لا يكثر فيهما المياه الجارية ولا الراكدة الكثيرة
ومن أول عصر رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم إلى آخر عصر أصحابه لم تنقل
واقعة في الطهارة ولا سؤال عن كيفية حفظ الماء عن النجاسات
وكانت أواني مياههم يتعاطاها الصبيان والإماء الذين لا يحترزون عن
النجاسات
وقد توضأ عمر رضي الله عنه بماء في جرة نصرانية وهذا كالصريح في أنه لم
يعول إلا على عدم تغير الماء وإلا فنجاسة النصرانية وإنائها غالبة تعلم بظن
قريب فإذا عسر القيام بهذا المذهب
وعدم وقوع السؤال في تلك الأعصار دليل أول
وفعل عمر رضي الله عنه دليل ثان
والدليل الثالث إصغاء رسول الله صلى  الله عليه وسلم الإناء للهرة (2)
وعدم تغطية الأواني منها بعد أن يرى أنها تأكل الفأرة ولم يكن في بلادهم
حياض تلغ السنانير فيها وكانت لا تنزل الآبار
والرابع أن الشافعي رضي الله عنه نص على أن غسالة النجاسة طاهرة إذا لم
تتغير ونجسة إن تغيرت وأي فرق بين أن يلاقي الماء النجاسة بالورود عليها أو
بورودها عليه وأي معنى لقول القائل إن قوة الورود تدفع النجاسة مع ان
الورود لم يمنع مخالطة النجاسة وإن أحيل ذلك على الحاجة فالحاجة أيضا ماسة
إلى هذا فلا فرق بين طرح الماء في إجانة فيها ثوب نجس أو طرح الثوب النجس
في الإجانة وفيها ماء وكل ذلك معتاد في غسل الثياب والأواني والخامس أنهم
كانوا يستنجون على أطراف المياه الجارية القليلة ولا خلاف في مذهب الشافعي
رضي الله عنه أنه إذا وقع بول في ماء جار ولم يتغير أنه يجوز التوضؤ به وإن
كان قليلا
وأي فرق بين الجاري والراكد وليت شعري هل الحوالة على عدم التغير أولى أو
على قوة الماء بسبب الجريان ثم ما حد تلك القوة أتجري في المياه الجارية في
أنابيب الحمامات أم لا فإن لم تجر فما الفرق وإن جرت فما الفرق بين ما يقع
فيها وبين ما يقع في مجرى الماء من الأواني على الأبدان وهي أيضا جارية ثم
البول أشد اختلاطا بالماء الجاري من نجاسة جامدة ثابتة إذا قضى بأن ما يجري
عليها وإن لم يتغير نجس أن يجتمع في مستنقع قلتان فأي فرق بين الجامد
والمائع والماء واحد والاختلاط أشد من المجاورة
والسادس أنه إذا وقع رطل من البول في قلتين ثم فرقتا فكل كوز يغترف منه
طاهر ومعلوم أن البول منتشر فيه وهو قليل وليت شعري هل تعليل طهارته بعدم
التغير أولى أو بقوة الماء بعد انقطاع الكثرة وزوالها مع PageV01P129
تحقق بقاء أجزاء النجاسة فيها
والسابع أن الحمامات لم تزل في الأعصار الخالية يتوضأ فيها المتقشفون
ويغمسون الأيدي والأواني في تلك الحياض مع قلة الماء  ومع العلم بأن الأيدي
النجسة والطاهرة كانت تتوارد عليها
فهذه الأمور مع الحاجة الشديدة تقوى في النفس أنهم كانوا ينظرون إلى عدم
التغير معولين على قوله صلى الله عليه وسلم خلق الماء طهورا لا ينجسه شيء
إلا ما غير طعمه أو لونه أو ريحه (1) وهذا فيه تحقيق وهو أن طبع كل مائع أن
يقلب إلى صفة نفسه كل ما يقع فيه وكان مغلوبا من جهته فكما ترى الكلب يقع
في المملحة فيستحيل ملحا ويحكم بطهارته بصيرورته ملحا وزوال صفة الكلبية
عنه فكذلك الخل يقع في الماء وكذا اللبن يقع فيه وهو قليل فتبطل صفته
ويتصور بصفة الماء وينطبع بطبعه إلا إذا كثر وغلب وتعرف غلبته بغلبة طعمه
أو لونه أو ريحه فهذا المعيار
وقد أشار الشرع إليه في الماء القوي على إزالة النجاسة وهو جدير بأن يعول
عليه فيند
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ز-و-ل (z-w-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning of departure, removal, and cessation of a state; al-zawāl is the passing away of a thing from its place or condition.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In juristic-theological usage, izālat al-najāsah denotes the elimination of ritual impurity as a legal qualification (ḥukm), not merely physical removal.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) sense is physical displacement; metaphorical (majāz) sense is the legal purification effected by a purifying agent.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Constructions (al-sharṭ wa al-istithnāʾ) — the text employs repeated conditionals (in kāna... fa-) and exceptions (illā) that govern legal rulings, requiring precise parsing of protasis and apodosis.
chapters.translation:
I say: The second aspect concerns that by which impurity is removed (al-muzāl bihi). It is either solid (jāmid) or liquid (māʾiʿ). As for the solid, it is the stone of istinjāʾ (cleansing after excretion), and it is a purifier effecting a purification of alleviation (taṭhīr takhfīf), on the condition that it be hard, pure (ṭāhir), absorbent, and not venerated (ghayr muḥtaram). As for liquids, impurities are not removed by any of them except water — and not by every water, but only by pure water whose alteration has not become excessive (lam yatafāḥash) through admixture with something that can be dispensed with.

Water departs from purity (ṭahārah) when, through contact with impurity (najāsah), its taste, color, or odor changes. If it does not change, and it is close to two hundred and fifty manns (mudd), which is five hundred raṭls by the Iraqi raṭl, it is not rendered impure, due to his saying, peace and blessings be upon him: {«إِذَا بَلَغَ الْمَاءُ قُلَّتَيْنِ لَمْ يَحْمِلْ خَبَثًا»} ("When water reaches two qullas, it does not carry impurity"). If it is less than that, it becomes impure according to al-Shāfiʿī, may God be pleased with him. This concerns still water (al-māʾ al-rākid).

As for running water (al-māʾ al-jārī), if it becomes altered by impurity, then the altered current (al-jaryah al-mutaghayyirah) is impure, but not what is above it or below it, because the currents of water are discrete entities (mutafāṣilāt). Likewise, if flowing impurity runs in the course of water, then the impure part is its location in the water, and what is to its right and left — if it falls short of two qullas. If the flow of the water is stronger than the flow of the impurity, then what is above the impurity is pure, and what is below it is impure, even if it is distant and abundant — unless it collects in a basin (ḥawḍ) to the measure of two qullas. And if two qullas of impure water collect together, it becomes pure, and it does not revert to impurity by being divided afterward.

This is the school (madhhab) of al-Shāfiʿī, may God be pleased with him.

I had wished that his school were like the school of Mālik, may God be pleased with him — namely, that water, however little, is not rendered impure except by alteration (al-taghayyur) — for the need for it is pressing, and the source of obsessive scruples (waswās) is the stipulation of the two qullas, and for its sake hardship has befallen people in this matter. It is, by my life, a cause of difficulty, and he who tests and contemplates it knows this.

Among what I do not doubt is that if this condition had been stipulated, then the places most deserving of difficulty in purification would be Mecca and Medina, for in them there are neither abundant running waters nor abundant still waters. And from the beginning of the era of the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, to the end of the era of his Companions, no incident concerning purification has been transmitted, nor any question about how to preserve water from impurities. Their water vessels were handled by boys and slave-girls who did not guard against impurities. And ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, performed ablution with water from a jar belonging to a Christian woman. This is almost explicit (ka-al-ṣarīḥ) that he relied only on the non-alteration of the water — for otherwise, the impurity of the Christian woman and her vessel is predominant, known by near-certain conjecture (ẓann qarīb).

So when adherence to this school becomes difficult, and the absence of questioning in those eras is the first proof, and the act of ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, is a second proof, and the third proof is the Messenger of God's, peace and blessings be upon him, tilting his vessel for the cat {«إِصْغَاءُ الْإِنَاءِ لِلْهِرَّةِ»} and not covering the vessels from it after he saw that it eats mice — and in their lands there were no basins in which cats lapped, nor did they descend into wells — and the fourth is that al-Shāfiʿī, may God be pleased with him, explicitly ruled that the washing-water of impurity (ghusālah) is pure if it has not changed, and impure if it has changed. What difference is there between water meeting impurity by its flowing upon it (al-wurūd ʿalayhā) or by impurity flowing upon it (wurūduhā ʿalayhi)? And what meaning is there in one's saying that the force of the flow repels impurity, given that the flow does not prevent the admixture of impurity? And if this is referred to necessity (al-ḥājah), then necessity is equally pressing here — there is no difference between throwing water into a basin containing a garment soiled with impurity, or throwing the soiled garment into a basin containing water. All of this is customary in washing clothes and vessels.

And the fifth is that they used to perform istinjāʾ at the edges of small running waters, and there is no disagreement in the school of al-Shāfiʿī, may God be pleased with him, that if urine falls into running water and it does not change, it is permissible to perform ablution with it, even if it is little. What difference is there between running and still water? Would that I knew — is the reliance upon non-alteration more appropriate, or upon the strength of water due to its flow? Then what is the limit of that strength? Does it flow in the waters of bathhouses' pipes or not? If it does not flow, what is the difference? And if it flows, what is the difference between what falls into it and what falls into the course of water poured from vessels upon bodies — which is also flowing? Moreover, urine mixes with running water more thoroughly than a solid, fixed impurity. If one rules that what flows over it, even without alteration, is impure — unless it collects in a pool to two qullas — what difference is there between the solid and the liquid? Water is one, and admixture is more intense than mere adjacency (mujāwarah).

And the sixth is that if a raṭl of urine falls into two qullas, and then they are divided, every jug scooped from it is pure. It is known that the urine is dispersed within it, and it is little. Would that I knew — is the attribution of its purity to non-alteration more appropriate, or to the strength of water after the cessation and removal of abundance, while the persistence of the parts of impurity within it is verified?

And the seventh is that bathhouses have not ceased in bygone eras to be places where the scrupulously devout (al-mutaqashshifūn) performed ablution, dipping hands and vessels into those basins, despite the scarcity of water, and with the knowledge that impure and pure hands would successively come upon them.

These matters, combined with the pressing necessity, strengthen in the soul that they looked to non-alteration, relying upon his saying, peace and blessings be upon him: {«خُلِقَ الْمَاءُ طَهُورًا لَا يُنَجِّسُهُ شَيْءٌ إِلَّا مَا غَيَّرَ طَعْمَهُ أَوْ لَوْنَهُ أَوْ رِيحَهُ»} ("Water was created purifying; nothing renders it impure except that which changes its taste, color, or odor"). And in this there is a verification (taḥqīq), namely: the nature (ṭabʿ) of every liquid is to convert to its own attribute everything that falls into it, when that thing is overpowered by it. Just as you see a dog falling into a salt-marsh (mamlaḥah) and becoming salt, and one rules its purity by its becoming salt and the departure of the attribute of dogness from it — likewise vinegar falls into water, and likewise milk falls into it while little, so its attribute is nullified, and it is formed by the attribute of water and imprinted by its nature — except when it is abundant and overpowers, and its overpowering is known by the dominance of its taste, color, or odor. This, then, is the criterion (miʿyār).

The Law (al-sharʿ) has pointed to this in the case of water strong enough to remove impurity, and it is worthy of reliance. By it, hardship is repelled, and by it the meaning of its being purifying (ṭahūr) becomes manifest — for the impurity is overpowered by it, and it purifies it, just as it became so in the case of what exceeds two qullas, in the washing-water (ghusālah), in running water, and in the tilting of the vessel for the cat. Do not think this is incidental (ʿafwan), for if it were so, it would be like the trace of istinjāʾ and the blood of fleas, such that the water meeting it would become impure — yet it is not rendered impure by the washing-water, nor by the lapping of a cat in little water.

As for his saying, peace and blessings be upon him, {«لَا يَحْمِلُ خَبَثًا»} ("it does not carry impurity"), it is in itself ambiguous (mubham), for it does carry it when it changes. If one says: "He meant when it does not change," then it may be said: He meant that in the usual case it does not change through customary impurities. Then it is an appeal to the implied meaning (al-mafhūm) in the case of what does not reach two qullas, and abandoning the implied meaning in favor of the lesser of the proofs we have mentioned is possible. And his saying "it does not carry impurity" — its apparent sense is the negation of carrying, i.e., it converts it to its own attribute, just as it is said of the salt-marsh: "it does not carry a dog or anything else," i.e., it is converted. This is because people used to perform istinjāʾ in little waters and in pools, and dip impure vessels into them, then hesitate as to whether they had changed with an effective change or not. So it was clarified that when it is two qullas, it does not change through these customary impurities.

If you say: "The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: 'It does not carry impurity' — and whenever it carries much, this turns against you, for whenever it carries much, it carries it legally (ḥukman) just as it carries it sensibly (ḥissan)." Then specification (takhṣīṣ) to customary impurities is unavoidable on both schools alike.

In sum, my inclination in matters of customary impurities is toward leniency (al-tasāhuL), in accordance with the practice (sīrah) of the early generations, and to cut off the very source of obsessive scruples (waswās). And on this basis, I have issued legal rulings (aftaytu) of purity in what has been disputed in such matters.

chapters.title_en: On the Manner of Removing Impurity (Kayfiyyat al-Izālah)
chapters.arabic_text:
||| الطرف الثالث في كيفية الإزالة

والنجاسة إن كانت حكمية وهي التي ليس لها جرم محسوس فيكفي إجراء الماء
على جميع مواردها وإن كانت عينية فلا بد من إزالة العين وبقاء الطعم يدل
على بقاء العين وكذا بقاء اللون إلا فيما يلتصق به فهو معفو عنه بعد الحت
والقرص
أما الرائحة فبقاؤها يدل على بقاء العين ولا يعفى عنها إلا إذا كان الشيء
له رائحة فائحة يعسر إزالتها فالدلك والعصر مرات متواليات يقوم مقام الحت
والقرص في اللون والمزيل للوسواس أن يعلم أن الأشياء خلقت طاهرة بيقين فما
لا يشاهد عليه نجاسة ولا يعلمها يقينا يصلي معه ولا ينبغي أن يتوصل
بالاستنباط إلى تقدير النجاسات
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ز-و-ل (z-w-l) — *Note: This root is prohibited per constraints; substituting with root: ح-ك-م (ḥ-k-m) for "ḥukmiyyah" (legal/ruling-based impurity).
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: ḥ-k-m: to judge, decide, or render a legal ruling; hence "ḥukmiyyah" = that which is established by legal ruling, not by sensory perception.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In fiqh, "ḥukmiyyah" contrasts with "ʿayniyyah" (corporeal) — the former is a juridical construct (ḥukm sharʿī) lacking physical substrate.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) for legal rulings; metaphorical (majāz) when applied to impurity — i.e., impurity by legal estimation, not by physical presence.
- Root: ع-ي-ن (ʿ-y-n) for "ʿayniyyah" (corporeal impurity).
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: ʿayn = the eye, the very substance, the physical essence of a thing.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): ʿayniyyah = impurity having a tangible, perceptible substance (jirm maḥsūs).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — the physical trace remains; metaphorical — when only color or smell remains, it may be excused.
- Root: ح-ت (ḥ-t) for "ḥatt" (scraping) and ق-ر-ص (q-r-ṣ) for "qarṣ" (pinching/rubbing).
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: ḥatt = to scrape off; qarṣ = to pinch or squeeze out.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Both denote physical removal of the corporeal impurity from the surface.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal actions for removing ʿayn; metaphorical when extended to washing and wringing.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional clause (sharṭ) with "in kānat" — the protasis introduces a dichotomy (ḥukmiyyah vs. ʿayniyyah), and the apodosis gives the legal consequence. Also, the exception (istithnāʾ) with "illā fīmā yaltaṣiqu bihī" — a restrictive clause limiting the general rule.
chapters.translation:
I say: The third aspect concerns the manner of removing impurity.

If the impurity is legal-ruling-based (ḥukmiyyah) — that is, having no perceptible corporeal substance — then it suffices to let water flow over all its locations. But if it is corporeal (ʿayniyyah), then the removal of the substance itself is obligatory. The persistence of taste indicates the persistence of the substance, and likewise the persistence of color — except in what adheres [to the fabric] after scraping and pinching, for that is excused.

As for odor, its persistence indicates the persistence of the substance, and it is not excused — unless the thing has a penetrating smell whose removal is difficult. In that case, rubbing and wringing repeatedly take the place of scraping and pinching for color. What dispels obsessive doubt (waswās) is to know that things are created pure with certainty. So whatever one does not observe as impure, nor know with certainty to be impure, one may pray with it. One should not resort to speculative inference to estimate impurities.

chapters.title_en: The Second Division: Purification from Ritual Impurities — Ablution, Full Bath, Dry Ablution, and Preceding Cleansing
chapters.arabic_text:
|| القسم الثاني طهارة الأحداث ومنها الوضوء والغسل والتيمم ويتقدمها الاستنجاء

فلنورد كيفيتها على الترتيب مع آدابها وسننها مبتدئين بسبب الوضوء وآداب
قضاء الحاجة إن شاء الله تعالى
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ط-ه-ر (ṭ-h-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning of cleanliness and purity, both physical and spiritual; removal of filth or ritual impurity.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, ṭahārah denotes ritual purity (ṭahārah al-ḥadath) as a prerequisite for valid worship, distinguishing outward cleanliness from inward sanctity.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) for physical cleansing; metaphorical (majāz) for spiritual purification from sin.
- Root: ح-د-ث (ḥ-d-th)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Origination, occurrence; in legal context, a state of ritual impurity arising from bodily events.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Ḥadath signifies the contingent state that interrupts ritual purity, requiring ablution (wuḍūʾ) or full bath (ghusl) for restoration.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for temporal occurrence; metaphorical for the juridical state of impurity.
- Root: ن-ج-و (n-j-w)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Salvation, deliverance; in this context, istinjāʾ refers to cleansing after answering the call of nature.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Istinjāʾ is the prescribed act of removing filth (najāsah) from the private parts, a preparatory act for ritual purity.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for physical cleansing; metaphorical for spiritual deliverance from defilement.
- Sībawayh Rule: ʿAṭf al-Bayān (Appositional Coordination) — The phrase "ومنها الوضوء والغسل والتيمم" employs coordination (ʿaṭf) to enumerate the types of purification, while "ويتقدمها الاستنجاء" uses a verbal sentence to indicate temporal precedence, governed by the rule of faṣl (separation) between coordinate clauses.
chapters.translation:
I say: The second division concerns purification from ritual impurities (ṭahārah al-ḥadath), which includes ablution (wuḍūʾ), full bath (ghusl), and dry ablution (tayammum), and is preceded by cleansing after answering the call of nature (istinjāʾ).

Let us now present their modalities in due order, along with their etiquettes (ādāb) and established practices (sunan), beginning with the cause of ablution and the etiquettes of relieving oneself, if God Most High wills.

chapters.title_en: Section 41 — On the Etiquette of Relieving Oneself (Ādāb Qaḍāʾ al-Ḥājah)
chapters.arabic_text:
||| باب آداب قضاء الحاجة

ينبغي أن يبعد عن أعين الناظرين في الصحراء وأن يستتر بشيء إن وجده وأن
لا يكشف عورته قبل الانتهاء PageV01P130
إلى موضع الجلوس وأن لا يستقبل الشمس والقمر وأن لا يستقبل القبلة ولا
يستدبرها إلا إذا كان في بناء والعدول أيضا عنها في البناء أحب وإن استتر
في الصحراء براحلته جاز وكذلك بذيله وأن يتقي الجلوس في متحدث الناس وأن لا
يبول في الماء الراكد ولا تحت الشجرة المثمرة ولا في الجحر وأن يتقي الموضع
الصلب ومهاب الرياح في البول استنزاها من رشاشه وأن يتكىء في جلوسه على
الرجل اليسرى وإن كان في بنيان يقدم الرجل اليسرى في الدخول واليمنى في
الخروج ولا يبول قائما
قالت عائشة رضي الله عنها من حدثكم  أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم كان يبول
قائما فلا تصدقوه (1) وقال عمر رضي الله عنه رآني رسول الله صلى الله عليه
وسلم وأنا أبول قائما فقال يا عمر لا تبل قائما (2) قال عمر فما بلت قائما
بعد وفيه رخصة إذ روى حذيفة رضي الله عنه أنه عليه الصلاة والسلام بال
قائما فأتيته بوضوء فتوضأ ومسح على خفيه (3) ولا يبول في المغتسل قال صلى
الله عليه وسلم عامة الوسواس منه (4) وقال ابن المبارك قد وسع في البول في
المغتسل إذا جرى الماء عليه ذكره الترمذي وقال عليه الصلاة والسلام لا
يبولن أحدكم في مستحمه ثم يتوضأ فيه فإن عامة الوسواس منه وقال ابن المبارك
إن كان الماء جاريا فلا باس به ولا يستصحب شيئا عليه اسم الله تعالى أو
رسوله صلى الله عليه وسلم ولا يدخل بيت الماء حاسر الرأس
وأن يقول عند الدخول بسم الله أعوذ بالله من الرجس النجس الخبيث المخبث
الشيطان الرجيم وعند الخروج الحمد لله الذي أذهب عني ما يؤذيني وأبقى علي
ما ينفعني ويكون ذلك خارجا عن بيت الماء وأن يعد النبل قبل الجلوس وأن لا
يستنجي بالماء في موضع الحاجة وأن يستبرىء من البول بالتنحنح والنثر ثلاثا
وإمرار اليد على أسفل القضيب ولا يكثر التفكر في الاستبراء فيتوسوس ويشق
عليه الأمر وما يحس به من بلل فليقدر أنه بقية الماء
فإن كان يؤذيه ذلك فليرش عليه الماء حتى يقوى في نفسه ذلك ولا يتسلط عليه
الشيطان بالوسواس
وفي الخبر أنه صلى الله عليه وسلم فعله أعني رش الماء (5) وقد كان أخفهم
استبراء أفقههم فتدل الوسوسة فيه على قلة الفقه
وفي حديث سلمان رضي الله عنه علمنا رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم كل شيء
حتى الخراءة فأمرنا أن لا نستنجي بعظم ولاروث ونهانا أن نستقبل القبلة
بغائط أو بول (6) وقال رجل لبعض الصحابة من الأعراب وقد خاصمه لا أحسبك
تحسن الخراء قال بلى وأبيك إني لأحسنها وإني بها لحاذق أبعد الأثر وأعد
المدر وأستقبل  الشيح وأستدبر الريح وأقعي إقعاء الظبي وأجفل إجفال النعام
الشيح نبت طيب الرائحة بالبادية والإقعاء ههنا أن يستوفز على صدور قدميه
والإجفال أن يرفع عجزه
ومن الرخصة أن يبول الإنسان قريبا من صاحبه مستترا عنه (7) فعل ذلك رسول
الله صلى الله عليه وسلم مع شدة حيائه ليبين للناس ذلك PageV01P131
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ق-ض-ي (qaḍā)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To accomplish, fulfill, or settle a matter; completion of a need.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, qaḍāʾ denotes the divine decree or the execution of an act; here, the "need" (ḥājah) is a euphemism for excretion, aligning with Quranic reticence.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) for "fulfilling"; metaphorical (majāz) for the bodily act, as the Shariah veils it in decorous language.
- Root: ع-و-ر (ʿawrah)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: A vulnerable, exposed part; defect or breach.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): That which must be concealed; in ritual law, the parts of the body forbidden to expose.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for bodily exposure; metaphorical for moral or spiritual vulnerability.
- Root: ن-ج-و (najwā)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Private counsel or secret conversation.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In Quranic usage, intimate whispering, often with negative connotation (e.g., {«إِنَّ النَّجْوَىٰ مِنَ الشَّيْطَانِ»}); here, the act of withdrawing for privacy.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for seclusion; metaphorical for the soul's retreat from public gaze.
- Sībawayh Rule: The Rule of ʿAṭf (Coordination) — The text employs frequent conjunction (wa) to sequence imperatives and prohibitions, each clause governed by the implicit verb "should" (yanbaghī), maintaining parallel syntactic structure across the etiquette list.
chapters.translation:
I say: Know that the seeker of religious excellence must observe the following etiquettes when relieving himself.

He should distance himself from the eyes of onlookers when in the open desert, and conceal himself with something if he finds it. He should not uncover his private parts (ʿawrah) before reaching the place of sitting. He should not face the sun or the moon, nor face the qiblah or turn his back to it, except when within a building; and even within a building, turning away from it is more beloved. If he conceals himself in the desert with his riding beast, that is permissible, and likewise with the tail of his garment. He should avoid sitting in the places where people gather and converse. He should not urinate in stagnant water, nor under a fruit-bearing tree, nor into a burrow. He should avoid hard ground and windy spots when urinating, as a precaution against the spray splashing back on him. He should lean in his sitting upon his left leg. If he is within a building, he should put forward his left foot when entering and his right foot when exiting. He should not urinate standing.

ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "Whoever tells you that the Prophet, peace be upon him, urinated standing, do not believe him." (1) And ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "The Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him, saw me urinating standing and said: 'O ʿUmar, do not urinate standing.'" ʿUmar said: "So I never urinated standing after that." (2) Yet there is a concession (rukhṣah) in this, for Ḥudhayfah, may Allah be pleased with him, narrated that the Prophet, peace be upon him, urinated standing, and I brought him water for ablution, and he performed ablution and wiped over his leather socks (khuffayn). (3) He should not urinate in the bathing place (al-mughtasal). The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Most of the whisperings (waswās) come from it." (4) Ibn al-Mubārak said: "It has been made permissible to urinate in the bathing place if water flows over it." Al-Tirmidhī mentioned this. And the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Let none of you urinate in his bathing place, then perform ablution in it, for most whisperings come from it." Ibn al-Mubārak said: "If the water is flowing, there is no harm."

He should not carry with him anything upon which is the name of Allah, Exalted is He, or the name of His Messenger, peace be upon him. He should not enter the place of water (i.e., the latrine) with an uncovered head.

He should say upon entering: "In the name of Allah. I seek refuge in Allah from the filthy, the impure, the wicked, the corrupting, the accursed devil." And upon exiting: "Praise be to Allah who has removed from me what harms me and preserved for me what benefits me." And this supplication should be made outside the place of relief. He should count the stones (for cleansing) before sitting. He should not cleanse himself with water in the very place of need. He should seek to be free of urine (istibrāʾ) by clearing the throat and blowing the nose three times, and by passing his hand along the underside of the penis. He should not overthink the istibrāʾ, lest he fall into whisperings (waswās) and the matter becomes burdensome upon him. Whatever moisture he perceives, let him deem it to be the remainder of water (from ablution).

If that bothers him, let him sprinkle water upon it, so that this conviction is strengthened in his soul, and the devil does not overpower him with whisperings. It is reported in the narration that the Prophet, peace be upon him, did this — I mean, sprinkling water. (5) And the lightest of them in istibrāʾ was the most knowledgeable of them in jurisprudence (fiqh). Thus, whisperings in this matter indicate a deficiency in fiqh.

In the ḥadīth of Salmān, may Allah be pleased with him: "The Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him, taught us everything, even the manner of relieving oneself. He commanded us not to cleanse ourselves with bone or dung, and forbade us from facing the qiblah when passing stool or urine." (6) A man from the Bedouins said to one of the Companions, having argued with him: "I do not think you know how to relieve yourself properly." He replied: "Yes, by your father, I do know it well, and I am skilled in it. I distance the trace (of urine), I count the stones, I face the shrub (al-shīḥ), I turn my back to the wind, I squat like the squatting of a gazelle, and I startle like the startle of an ostrich." Al-shīḥ is a fragrant plant in the desert. "Squatting" (iqqāʾ) here means perching upon the balls of the feet. "Startling" (ijfāl) means raising the buttocks.

Among the concessions is that a man may urinate near his companion while concealing himself from him. (7) The Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him, did this despite his intense modesty, to clarify this matter for the people.

chapters.title_en: On the Manner of Cleansing After Relieving Oneself (Kayfiyyat al-Istinjā’)
chapters.arabic_text:
||| كيفية الاستنجاء

ثم يستنجي لمقعدته بثلاثة أحجار فإن أنقى وإلا استعمل رابعا فإن أنقى
وإلا استعمل خامسا لأن الإنقاء واجب والإيتار مستحب
قال صلى الله عليه وسلم من استجمر فليوتر (1) ويأخذ الحجر بيساره ويضعه
على مقدم المقعدة قبل موضع النجاسة ويمره بالمسح والإدارة إلى المؤخر ويأخذ
الثاني ويضعه على المؤخر كذلك ويمره إلى المقدمة ويأخذ الثالث فيديره حول
المسربة إدارة فإن عسرت الإدارة ومسح من المقدمة إلى المؤخرة أجزأه ثم يأخذ
حجرا كبيرا بيمينه والقضيب بيساره ويمسح الحجر بقضيبه ويحرك اليسار فيمسح
ثلاثا في ثلاثة مواضع أوفى ثلاثة أحجار أو في ثلاثة مواضع من جدار إلى أن
لا يرى الرطوبة في محل المسح فإن حصل ذلك بمرتين أتى بالثالثة ووجب ذلك إن
أراد الاقتصار على الحجر وإن حصل بالرابعة استحب الخامسة للإيتار
ثم ينتقل من ذلك الموضع إلى موضع آخر ويستنجي بالماء بأن يفيضه باليمنى
على محل النجو ويدلك باليسرى حتى لا يبقى أثر يدركه الكف بحس اللمس ويدرك
الاستقصاء فيه بالتعرض للباطن فإن ذلك منبع الوسواس وليعلم أن كل ما لا يصل
إليه الماء فهو باطن ولا يثبت حكم النجاسة للفضلات الباطنة ما لم تظهر وكل
ما هو ظاهر وثبت له حكم النجاسة فحد ظهوره أن يصل الماء إليه فيزيله ولا
معنى للوسواس
ويقول عند الفراغ من الاستنجاء اللهم طهر قلبي من النفاق وحصن فرجي من
الفواحش ويدلك يده بحائط أو بالأرض إزالة للرائحة إن بقيت
والجمع بين الماء والحجر مستحب فقد روي أنه لما نزل قوله تعالى {فيه رجال
يحبون أن يتطهروا والله يحب المطهرين} قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
لأهل قباء ما هذه الطهارة التي أثنى  الله بها عليكم قالوا كنا نجمع بين
الماء والحجر (2)
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ن-ج-و (n-j-w)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is "to be saved, to escape"; in this context, istinjā’ denotes the act of removing filth (najāsah) from the private parts, deriving from the notion of "cutting off" the impurity.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In juristic-theological usage, istinjā’ is the ritual purification (ṭahārah) of the excretory orifices, a condition for the validity of prayer (ṣalāh), distinguishing physical purity from spiritual purity.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) refers to physical wiping with stones or water; metaphorical (majāz) extends to "cleansing the heart" from hypocrisy (nifāq), as in the supplication cited.
- Root: و-ت-ر (w-t-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The root denotes oddness, singularity; al-witr is the odd number, and ītār is the act of making something odd.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In ritual law, ītār is a recommended (mustaḥabb) practice of using an odd count (three, five) for istinjā’, reflecting the divine love for odd numbers as a sign of divine unity (tawḥīd).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: odd numerical count; metaphorical: the spiritual virtue of concluding acts with an odd number to emulate prophetic practice.
- Root: و-س-و-س (w-s-w-s)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The root denotes a faint, whispering sound; waswās is the subtle insinuation of Satan or the self.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological ethics, waswās is the pathological obsession in ritual matters, arising from ignorance of legal limits (ḥudūd) and leading to excessive scrupulosity (tanattu‘) beyond the Law.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: whispering; metaphorical: intrusive doubts in purification, which the author here refutes by defining the legal boundary of apparent vs. internal filth.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Condition and Exception (al-sharṭ wa’l-jawāb) — The phrase "فإن أنقى وإلا استعمل رابعا" employs a conditional clause (in) with an implied apodosis, governing the permissibility of escalation; also the rule of ʿaṭf (coordination) with fa- to sequence successive actions (tarattub), as in "ثم يستنجي... ثم يأخذ... ثم ينتقل".
chapters.translation:
I say: Then he cleanses his seat with three stones. If they purify, [well and good]; otherwise, he uses a fourth, and if it purifies, [he stops]; otherwise, he uses a fifth — because purification (al-inqā’) is obligatory, while making the count odd (al-ītār) is recommended. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: {«من استجمر فليوتر»} — "Whoever uses stones for cleansing, let him make it odd." He takes the stone in his left hand and places it on the front part of the seat, before the site of the filth, and passes it with wiping and rotation toward the rear. He takes the second and places it on the rear similarly, passing it toward the front. He takes the third and rotates it around the anus (al-masrabah) in a circular motion. If the rotation proves difficult, and he wipes from front to rear, that suffices him. Then he takes a large stone in his right hand and the penis (al-qadīb) in his left, and wipes the stone over his penis, moving the left [hand] — thus wiping three times in three places, or with three stones, or in three places on a wall — until no moisture is seen in the place of wiping. If this is achieved with two [wipes], he performs the third, and this is obligatory if he intends to limit himself to stones. If it is achieved with the fourth, a fifth is recommended for the sake of making it odd.

Then he moves from that place to another, and cleanses with water by pouring it with his right hand over the site of the filth, and rubbing with his left until no trace remains that the palm can perceive by the sense of touch. He should not seek thoroughness by probing the interior (al-bāṭin), for that is the source of obsessive doubt (al-waswās). Let him know that whatever water does not reach is "interior," and the ruling of impurity (ḥukm al-najāsah) does not attach to internal residues so long as they have not appeared. Whatever is apparent and has the ruling of impurity attached to it, the limit of its appearance is that water reaches it and removes it — and there is no meaning to obsessive doubt.

He says upon completing the cleansing: "O Allah, purify my heart from hypocrisy (al-nifāq), and guard my private parts from indecencies (al-fawāḥish)." Then he rubs his hand on a wall or on the ground to remove any lingering odor.

Combining water and stones is recommended (mustaḥabb). For it has been narrated that when the verse was revealed: {«فيه رجال يحبون أن يتطهروا والله يحب المطهرين»} — "In it are men who love to purify themselves, and Allah loves those who purify themselves" — the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) said to the people of Qubā’: "What is this purification for which Allah has praised you?" They said: "We used to combine water with stones."

chapters.title_en: The Manner of Ablution (Kayfiyyat al-Wuḍūʾ)
chapters.arabic_text:
||| كيفية الوضوء

إذا فرغ من الاستنجاء اشتغل بالوضوء فلم ير رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
قط خارجا من الغائط إلا توضأ ويبتدىء بالسواك فقد قال رسول الله صلى الله
عليه وسلم إن أفواهكم طرق القرآن فطيبوها بالسواك (3) فينبغي أن ينوي عند
السواك تطهير فمه لقراءة القرآن وذكر الله تعالى في الصلاة وقال صلى الله
عليه وسلم صلاة على أثر سواك أفضل من خمس وسبعين صلاة بغير سواك {حديث}
صلاة على أثر سواك أفضل من خمس وسبعين صلاة بغير سواك رواه أبو نعيم في
كتاب السواك من حديث ابن عمر بإسناد ضعيف ورواه أبو داود والحاكم وصححه
والبيهقي وضعفه من حديث عائشة وضعفه بلفظ من سبعين صلاة (4) حديث لولا أن
أشق على أمتي لأمرتهم بالسواك عند كل صلاة متفق عليه من حديث أبي هريرة (5)
حديث ما لي أراكم تدخلون علي قلحا استاكوا أخرجه البزار والبيهقي من حديث
العباس بن عبد المطلب وأبو داود والبغوي من حديث تمام بن العباس والبيهقي
من حديث عبد الله بن عباس وهو مضطرب (6) حديث كان يستاك من الليل مرارا
أخرجه مسلم من حديث ابن عباس (7) حديث ابن عباس لم يزل يأمرنا رسول الله
صلى الله عليه وسلم بالسواك حتى ظننا أنه سينزل عليه فيه شيء رواه أحمد //
وقال عليه السلام عليكم بالسواك فإنه PageV01P132
مطهرة للفم ومرضاة للرب (1) وقال علي بن أبي طالب كرم الله وجهه السواك
يزيد في الحفظ ويذهب البلغم (2) وكان أصحاب النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
يروحون والسواك على آذانهم
وكيفيته أن يستاك بخشب الأراك أو غيره من قضبان الأشجار مما يخشن ويزيل
القلح ويستاك عرضا وطولا وإن اقتصر فعرضا
ويستحب السواك عند كل صلاة وعند كل وضوء وإن لم يصل عقيبه وعند تغير
النكهة بالنوم أو طول الأزم أو كل ما تكره رائحته ثم عند الفراغ من السواك
يجلس للوضوء مستقبل القبلة ويقول بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم قال صلى الله عليه
وسلم لا  وضوء لمن لم يسم الله تعالى (3) أي لا وضوء كامل
ويقول عند ذلك أعوذ بك من همزات الشياطين وأعوذ بك رب أن يحضرون ثم يغسل
يديه ثلاثا قبل أن يدخلهما الإناء ويقول اللهم إني أسألك اليمن والبركة
وأعوذ بك من الشؤم والهلكة ثم ينوي رفع الحدث أو استباحة الصلاة ويستديم
النية إلى غسل الوجه فإن نسيها عند الوجه لم يجزه ثم يأخذ غرفة لفيه بيمينه
فيتمضمض بها ثلاثا ويغرغر بأن يرد الماء إلى الغلصمة إلا أن يكون صائما
فيرفق ويقول اللهم أعني على تلاوة كتابك وكثرة الذكر لك ثم يأخذ غرفة لأنفه
ويستنشق ثلاثا ويصعد الماء بالنفس إلى خياشيمه ويستنثر ما فيها ويقول في
الاستنشاق اللهم أوجد لي رائحة الجنة وأنت عني راض وفي الاستنثار اللهم إني
أعوذ بك من روائح النار ومن سوء الدار لأن الاستنشاق إيصال والاستنثار
إزالة ثم يغرف غرفة لوجهه فيغسله من مبدإ سطح الجبهة إلى منتهى ما يقبل من
الذقن في الطول ومن الأذن إلى الأذن في العرض ولا يدخل في حد الوجه
النزعتان اللتان على طرفي الجبينين فهما من الرأس ويوصل الماء إلى موضع
التحذيف وهو ما يعتاد النساء تنحية الشعر عنه وهو القدر الذي يقع في جانب
الوجه مهما وضع طرف الخيط على رأس الأذن والطرف الثاني على زاوية الجبين
ويوصل الماء إلى منابت الشعور الأربعة الحاجبان والشاربان والعذاران
والأهداب لأنها خفيفة في الغالب
والعذاران هما ما يوازيان الأذنين من مبدإ اللحية
ويجب إيصال الماء إلى منابت اللحية الخفيفة أعني ما يقبل من الوجه وأما
الكثيفة فلا وحكم العنفقة حكم اللحية في الكثافة والخفة ثم يفعل ذلك ثلاثا
ويفيض الماء على ظاهر ما استرسل من اللحية ويدخل الأصابع في محاجر العينين
وموضع الرمص ومجتمع الكحل وينقيهما
فقد روي أنه صلى الله عليه وسلم فعل ذلك (4) ويأمل عند ذلك خروج الخطايا
من عينيه وكذلك عند كل عضو ويقول عنده اللهم بيض وجهي بنورك يوم تبيض وجوه
أوليائك ولا تسود وجهي بظلماتك يوم تسود وجوه  أعدائك ويخلل اللحية الكثيفة
عند غسل الوجه فإنه مستحب ثم يغسل يديه إلى مرفقيه ثلاثا ويحرك الخاتم
ويطيل الغرة ويرفع الماء إلى أعلى العضد فإنهم يحشرون يوم القيامة غرا
محجلين من آثار الوضوء كذلك ورد الخبر
قال صلى الله عليه وسلم من استطاع أن PageV01P133
يطيل غرته فليفعل (1) وروي أن الحلية تبلغ مواضع الوضوء (2) ويبدأ
باليمنى ويقول اللهم أعطني كتابي بيميني وحاسبني حسابا يسيرا ويقول عند غسل
الشمال اللهم إني أعوذ بك أن تعطيني كتابي بشمالي أو من وراء ظهري ثم
يستوعب رأسه بالمسح بأن يبل يديه ويلصق رءوس أصابع يديه اليمنى باليسرى
ويضعهما على مقدمة الرأس ويمدهما إلى القفا ثم يردهما إلى المقدمة وهذه
مسحة واحدة يفعل ذلك ثلاثا ويقول اللهم اغشني برحمتك وأنزل علي من بركاتك
وأظلني تحت ظل عرشك يوم لا ظل إلا ظلك ثم يمسح أذنيه ظاهرهما وباطنهما بماء
جديد بأن يدخل مسبحتيه في صماخي أذنيه ويدير إبهاميه على ظاهر أذنيه ثم يضع
الكف على الأذنين استظهارا ويكرره ثلاثا
chapters.anchors:
- Root: و-ض-أ (w-ḍ-ʾ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is cleanliness and brightness; al-wuḍūʾ is the specific act of washing the limbs for prayer, derived from waḍāʾa meaning "to be clean and radiant."
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In the religious law, wuḍūʾ denotes the purification of the four limbs as a prerequisite for the validity of prayer, symbolizing the outward counterpart to inward purification (taṭhīr al-qalb).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Used literally (ḥaqīqah) for the physical washing; metaphorically (majāz) extended to spiritual purification, as in "wuḍūʾ of the heart" from sins.
- Root: س-و-ك (s-w-k)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The act of rubbing or cleansing the teeth with a stick (miswāk); derived from sāka, meaning to rub or polish.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A recommended purification of the mouth, preparing the believer for the recitation of the Qurʾān and remembrance of God, aligning the physical with the spiritual act of worship.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for the physical cleansing; metaphorical for the "polishing" of the tongue from vain or sinful speech.
- Root: م-س-ح (m-s-ḥ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To wipe or pass the hand over something; in ritual law, specifically wiping the head, ears, and neck with wet hands.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A lighter form of purification, signifying the permissibility of wiping over the head as a mercy (raḥmah) from God, easing the burden of full washing.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for the physical act; metaphorical for the "wiping away" of sins through the ritual.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of ʿAṭf al-Bayān (Appositional Clarification) — When the author lists sequential actions (e.g., "then he washes his hands... then he rinses his mouth"), the conjunctive particles (thumma, fa) govern the temporal order, requiring strict adherence to the sequence in translation to preserve the legal (fiqhī) precision of the ritual.
chapters.translation:
I say: The Manner of Ablution

When one has finished the cleansing after relieving oneself, he occupies himself with the ablution (wuḍūʾ). The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, was never seen coming out from the privy except that he performed the ablution. He begins with the tooth-stick (siwāk), for the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: "Verily, your mouths are the pathways of the Qurʾān, so perfume them with the siwāk." Thus, one should intend at the siwāk the purification of his mouth for the recitation of the Qurʾān and the remembrance of God, the Exalted, in prayer. And he, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: "A prayer following a siwāk is better than seventy-five prayers without a siwāk." {Ḥadīth: "A prayer following a siwāk is better than seventy-five prayers without a siwāk" — narrated by Abū Nuʿaym in the Book of the Siwāk from the ḥadīth of Ibn ʿUmar with a weak chain; also narrated by Abū Dāwūd and al-Ḥākim who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqī who weakened it from the ḥadīth of ʿĀʾishah with the wording "seventy prayers."} {Ḥadīth: "Were it not that I would burden my community, I would have commanded them to use the siwāk at every prayer" — agreed upon (muttafaq ʿalayh) from the ḥadīth of Abū Hurayrah.} {Ḥadīth: "Why do I see you entering upon me with yellowed teeth? Use the siwāk!" — narrated by al-Bazzār and al-Bayhaqī from the ḥadīth of al-ʿAbbās ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, and by Abū Dāwūd and al-Baghawī from the ḥadīth of Tammām ibn al-ʿAbbās, and al-Bayhaqī from the ḥadīth of ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbbās, and it is disordered (muḍṭarib).} {Ḥadīth: "He used the siwāk multiple times during the night" — narrated by Muslim from the ḥadīth of Ibn ʿAbbās.} {Ḥadīth of Ibn ʿAbbās: "The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, never ceased commanding us to use the siwāk until we thought that something of it would be revealed upon him" — narrated by Aḥmad.} And he, peace be upon him, said: "Upon you is the siwāk, for it is a purification for the mouth and a cause of the Lord's pleasure." And ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, may God honor his face, said: "The siwāk increases memory and removes phlegm." And the companions of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, would go forth in the evening with the siwāk placed upon their ears.

Its manner is that one uses the siwāk with the wood of the arāk tree or other tree branches, whatever is rough and removes the yellow film (qalaḥ). He uses it horizontally and vertically, and if he limits himself, then horizontally.

The siwāk is recommended at every prayer, at every ablution even if no prayer follows it, and at the change of breath due to sleep, prolonged silence, or anything whose odor is disliked. Then, upon finishing the siwāk, he sits for the ablution facing the qiblah and says: "In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate." The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: "There is no ablution for one who does not mention the name of God, the Exalted" — meaning, no complete ablution. And he says at that moment: "I seek refuge in You from the whisperings of the devils, and I seek refuge in You, my Lord, lest they attend me." Then he washes his hands three times before inserting them into the vessel, and says: "O God, I ask You for blessedness (yumn) and blessing (barakah), and I seek refuge in You from misfortune and destruction." Then he intends the lifting of the state of minor impurity (rafʿ al-ḥadath) or the permitting of prayer (istibāḥat al-ṣalāh), and he maintains the intention until the washing of the face. If he forgets it at the face, it does not suffice him. Then he takes a handful of water for his mouth with his right hand and rinses it three times, gargling by returning the water to the throat (ghalṣamah), unless he is fasting, in which case he is gentle. And he says: "O God, help me in the recitation of Your Book and the abundant remembrance of You." Then he takes a handful for his nose and snuffs water up three times, drawing the water by breath into his nostrils, and he expels what is within them. He says during the snuffing: "O God, make me find the fragrance of Paradise while You are pleased with me," and during the expulsion: "O God, I seek refuge in You from the odors of the Fire and from the evil abode." For the snuffing is a bringing in (īṣāl), and the expulsion is a removal (izālah). Then he takes a handful for his face and washes it from the beginning of the surface of the forehead to the end of what is accepted of the chin in length, and from ear to ear in breadth. The two temples (nazʿatān) at the sides of the forehead do not enter into the limit of the face, for they are of the head. He conveys the water to the place of the hairline (taḥdhīf) — which is what women customarily push the hair away from — and it is the measure that falls at the side of the face whenever the tip of a thread is placed at the top of the ear and its other end at the corner of the forehead. He conveys the water to the four growths of hair: the two eyebrows, the two mustaches, the two sideburns (ʿadhārān), and the eyelashes, for they are mostly light.

The two sideburns are what parallel the ears from the beginning of the beard. It is obligatory to convey the water to the roots of the light beard — meaning what is accepted of the face — but as for the thick beard, no. The rule of the chin-tuft (ʿanfaqah) follows the rule of the beard in thickness and lightness. Then he does this three times, and he pours the water over the exterior of what hangs down of the beard, and he inserts his fingers into the corners of the eyes, the place of rheum (ramaṣ), and the gathering of kohl, and cleans them. For it has been narrated that he, may God bless him and grant him peace, did this. And he hopes at that moment for the exit of sins from his eyes, and likewise at every limb. And he says at it: "O God, whiten my face with Your light on the day when the faces of Your friends are whitened, and do not blacken my face with Your darknesses on the day when the faces of Your enemies are blackened." And he thoroughly interlaces the thick beard during the washing of the face, for it is recommended. Then he washes his hands up to the elbows three times, moves the ring, lengthens the white blaze (ghurrah), and raises the water to the upper part of the upper arm. For they will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection with white blazes and white fetlocks (muḥajjalīn) from the traces of the ablution — thus has the report come.

He, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: "Whoever is able to lengthen his white blaze, let him do so." And it is narrated that the adornment (ḥilyah) reaches the places of the ablution. He begins with the right hand and says: "O God, give me my book in my right hand, and reckon with me an easy reckoning." And he says upon washing the left: "O God, I seek refuge in You from giving me my book in my left hand or from behind my back." Then he wipes his entire head by wetting his hands and pressing the fingertips of his right hand against his left, placing them at the front of the head and drawing them to the nape, then returning them to the front — this is one single wipe. He does this three times and says: "O God, cover me with Your mercy, and send down upon me from Your blessings, and shade me under the shade of Your Throne on the day when there is no shade but Your shade." Then he wipes his ears, their exteriors and interiors, with new water, by inserting his index fingers into the openings of his ears and rotating his thumbs over the exteriors of his ears. Then he places his palms over the ears for thoroughness, repeating this three times, and says: "O God, make me of those who listen to the word and follow the best of it. O God, make me hear the caller of Paradise with the righteous." Then he wipes his neck with new water, due to his saying, may God bless him and grant him peace: "The wiping of the neck is a security from the collar (ghull) on the Day of Resurrection." And he says: "O God, free my neck from the Fire, and I seek refuge in You from the chains and the fetters." Then he washes his right foot three times, interlacing with the left hand from beneath the toes of the right foot, beginning with the little toe of the right foot and ending with the little toe of the left foot. And he says: "O God, make firm my foot upon the Straight Path on the day when feet slip in the Fire." And he says upon washing the left: "I seek refuge in You from my foot slipping from the Path on the day when the feet of the hypocrites slip therein." And he raises the water to the middle of the shanks.

When he finishes, he raises his head to the sky and says: "I bear witness that there is no god but God alone, with no partner, and I bear witness that Muḥammad is His servant and His Messenger. Glory be to You, O God, and with Your praise; there is no god but You. I have done evil and wronged myself; I seek Your forgiveness, O God, and I repent to You. So forgive me and relent upon me, for You are the Oft-Relenting, the Most Merciful. O God, make me of the repentant, and make me of the purified, and make me of Your righteous servants, and make me a patient, thankful servant, and make me remember You much and glorify You in the morning and the evening." It is said that whoever says this after the ablution, a seal is placed upon his ablution, and it is raised for him beneath the Throne, and it does not cease glorifying God, the Exalted, and sanctifying Him, and he is written the reward of that until the Day of Resurrection.

Disliked matters in the ablution include: exceeding three washes — for whoever exceeds has wronged; extravagance in water — he, peace be upon him, performed the ablution with three washes and said: "Whoever exceeds has wronged and done ill." And he said: "There will be people from this community who transgress in supplication and in purification." And it is said: "From the weakness of a man's knowledge is his obsession with water in purification." And Ibrāhīm ibn Adham said: "It is said that the first thing by which whisperings (waswās) begin is from purification." And al-Ḥasan said: "There is a devil who laughs at people in the ablution, called al-Walahān."

It is disliked to flick the hand and spray water, to speak during the ablution, and to slap the face with water. Some people disliked drying oneself, saying: "The ablution is weighed" — this was said by Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib and al-Zuhrī. However, it is narrated that Muʿādh, may God be pleased with him, said that he, peace be upon him, wiped his face with the edge of his garment. And ʿĀʾishah, may God be pleased with her, narrated that he, may God bless him and grant him peace, had a towel — but this narration from ʿĀʾishah has been criticized.

It is disliked to perform the ablution from a brass vessel (ināʾ ṣufr) and to perform the ablution with sun-heated water (māʾ mushammas) — this is from the perspective of medicine. It has been narrated from Ibn ʿUmar and Abū Hurayrah, may God be pleased with them both, the dislike of the brass vessel. And some said: "I brought water to Shuʿbah in a brass vessel, and he refused to perform the ablution from it." The dislike of that has been transmitted from Ibn ʿUmar and Abū Hurayrah, may God be pleased with them both.

Whenever one finishes his ablution and turns to prayer, he should bring to mind that he has purified his exterior — which is the place of the gaze of creation — so that he may be ashamed to whisper in intimate counsel with God, the Exalted, without purifying his heart — which is the place of the gaze of the Lord, Glorified be He. And let him realize the purification of the heart through repentance, and being free of blameworthy traits, and adorning oneself with praiseworthy traits is more fitting. And whoever limits himself to the purification of the exterior is like one who invites a king to his house, then leaves it filled with filth and occupies himself with plastering the exterior of the outer door of the dwelling. How deserving is such a man of exposure to wrath and ruin! And God, Glorified and Exalted, knows best.

chapters.title_en: The Virtue of Ablution (Faḍīlat al-Wuḍūʾ)
chapters.arabic_text:
||| فضيلة الوضوء

قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم من توضأ فأحسن الوضوء وصلى ركعتين لم
يحدث نفسه فيهما بشيء من الدنيا خرج من ذنوبه كيوم ولدته أمه (1) وفي لفظ
آخر ولم يسه فيهما غفر له ما تقدم من ذنبه وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم أيضا
ألا أنبئكم بما يكفر الله به الخطايا ويرفع به الدرجات إسباغ الوضوء على
المكاره ونقل الأقدام إلى المساجد وانتظار الصلاة بعد الصلاة فذلكم الرباط
ثلاث مرات (2) وتوضأ صلى الله عليه وسلم مرة مرة وقال هذا وضوء لا يقبل
الله الصلاة إلا به وتوضأ مرتين مرتين وقال من توضأ مرتين مرتين أتاه الله
أجره مرتين وتوضأ ثلاثا ثلاثا وقال هذا وضوئي ووضوء الأنبياء من قبلي ووضوء
خليل الرحمن إبراهيم عليه السلام (3) وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم من ذكر الله
عند وضوئه طهر الله جسده كله ومن لم يذكر الله لم يطهر منه إلا ما أصاب
الماء (4) وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم من توضأ على طهر كتب الله له به عشر
حسنات (5) وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم الوضوء على الوضوء نور على نور (6) وهذا
كله حث على تجديد الوضوء وقال عليه السلام إذا توضأ العبد المسلم فتمضمض
خرجت الخطايا من فيه فإذا استنثر خرجت الخطايا من أنفه فإذا غسل وجهه خرجت
الخطايا من وجهه حتى تخرج من تحت أشفار عينيه فإذا غسل يديه خرجت الخطايا
من يديه حتى تخرج من تحت أظفاره فإذا مسح برأسه خرجت الخطايا من رأسه حتى
تخرج من تحت أذنيه وإذا غسل رجليه خرجت الخطايا من رجليه حتى تخرج من تحت
أظفار رجليه ثم كان مشيه إلى المسجد وصلاته نافلة له (7) ويروى إن الطاهر
كالصائم (8) قال صلى الله عليه وسلم من توضأ فأحسن الوضوء ثم رفع طرفه إلى
السماء فقال أشهد أن لا إله إلا الله وحده لا شريك له وأشهد أن محمدا عبده
ورسوله فتحت له أبواب الجنة الثمانية يدخل من أيها شاء (9) وقال عمر رضي
الله عنه PageV01P135
إن  الوضوء الصالح يطرد عنك الشيطان
وقال مجاهد من استطاع أن لا يبيت إلا طاهرا ذاكرا مستغفرا فليفعل فإن
الأرواح تبعث على ما قبضت عليه
chapters.anchors:
- Root: و-ض-أ (w-ḍ-ʾ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Cleanliness and brightness; the act of washing specific limbs for purification; derived from waḍuʾa (to be clean, radiant).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Ritual purification (ṭahārah) as a prerequisite for prayer (ṣalāh), symbolizing both physical and spiritual cleansing from minor impurities (ḥadath).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) — washing with water; metaphorical (majāz) — purification of the soul from sins, as sins are described as "emerging" from limbs.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Clause (al-Sharṭ) — The repeated "man" (whoever) constructions introduce protases with apodoses, requiring precise temporal sequencing (e.g., "whoever performs ablution... then prays... emerges").
chapters.translation: I say: The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: "Whoever performs ablution and perfects it, then prays two units (rakʿatayn) without letting his soul speak to him therein of any worldly matter, emerges from his sins as on the day his mother bore him." (1) In another wording: "And does not err therein, his prior sins are forgiven him." He, peace be upon him, also said: "Shall I not inform you of that by which God erases sins and elevates degrees? Perfecting ablution despite hardships, taking many steps to the mosques, and awaiting prayer after prayer — that is the ribāṭ (garrisoning the frontier)." — repeated three times. (2) And he, peace be upon him, performed ablution once each (limb), saying: "This is an ablution without which God accepts no prayer." And he performed it twice each, saying: "Whoever performs ablution twice each, God gives him his reward twice." And he performed it three times each, saying: "This is my ablution, and the ablution of the prophets before me, and the ablution of the Friend of the Merciful (khalīl al-Raḥmān), Abraham, peace be upon him." (3) And he, peace be upon him, said: "Whoever mentions God during his ablution, God purifies his entire body; and whoever does not mention God, only that which the water touches is purified of him." (4) And he, peace be upon him, said: "Whoever performs ablution while already in a state of purity, God writes for him thereby ten good deeds." (5) And he, peace be upon him, said: "Ablution upon ablution is light upon light (nūr ʿalā nūr)." (6) All of this is an urging toward renewing ablution. And he, peace be upon him, said: "When the Muslim servant performs ablution and rinses his mouth, sins exit from his mouth; when he snuffs water into his nose, sins exit from his nose; when he washes his face, sins exit from his face until they emerge from beneath his eyelashes; when he washes his hands, sins exit from his hands until they emerge from beneath his fingernails; when he wipes his head, sins exit from his head until they emerge from beneath his ears; and when he washes his feet, sins exit from his feet until they emerge from beneath his toenails. Then his walking to the mosque and his prayer are an additional supererogatory act (nāfilah) for him." (7) And it is narrated that the one in a state of purity is like the one fasting. (8) He, peace be upon him, said: "Whoever performs ablution and perfects it, then raises his gaze to the sky and says: 'I bear witness that there is no god but God alone, with no partner, and I bear witness that Muḥammad is His servant and His Messenger' — the eight gates of Paradise are opened for him, and he enters through whichever of them he wishes." (9) And ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, said: "Sound ablution drives the devil away from you." And Mujāhid said: "Whoever is able to not spend the night except in a state of purity, remembering God and seeking His forgiveness, let him do so — for souls are resurrected according to the state in which they were seized."

chapters.title_en: The Manner of the Major Ablution (Kīfiyyat al-Ghusl)
chapters.arabic_text:
||| كيفية الغسل

وهو أن يضع الإناء عن يمينه ثم يسمي الله تعالى ويغسل يديه ثلاثا ثم
يستنجي كما وصفت لك ويزيل ما على بدنه من نجاسة إن كانت ثم يتوضأ وضوءه
للصلاة كما وصفنا إلا غسل القدمين فإنه يؤخرهما فإن غسلهما ثم وضعهما على
الأرض كان إضاعة للماء ثم يصب الماء على رأسه ثلاثا ثم على شقه الأيمن
ثلاثا ثم على شقه الأيسر ثلاثا ثم يدلك ما أقبل من بدنه ويخلل شعر الرأس
واللحية ويوصل الماء إلى منابت ما كثف منه أو خف وليس على المرأة نقض
الضفائر إلا إذا علمت أن الماء لا يصل إلى خلال الشعر ويتعهد معاطف البدن
وليتق أن يمس ذكره في أثناء ذلك فإن فعل ذلك فليعد الوضوء وإن توضأ قبل
الغسل فلا يعيده بعد الغسل
فهذه سنن الوضوء والغسل ذكرنا منها ما لا بد لسالك طريق الآخرة من علمه
وعمله وما عداه من المسائل التي يحتاج إليها في عوارض الأحوال فليرجع فيها
إلى كتب الفقه
والواجب من جملة ما ذكرناه في الغسل أمران النية واستيعاب البدن بالغسل
وفروض الوضوء النية وغسل الوجه وغسل اليدين إلى المرفقين ومسح ما ينطلق
عليه الاسم من الرأس وغسل الرجلين إلى الكعبين والترتيب
وأما الموالاة فليست بواجبة
والغسل الواجب بأربعة بخروج المني والتقاء الختانين والحيض والنفاس وما
عداه من الأغسال سنة كغسل العيدين والجمعة والأعياد والإحرام والوقوف بعرفة
ومزدلفة ولدخول مكة وثلاثة أغسال أيام التشريق ولطواف الوداع على قول
والكافر إذا أسلم غير جنب والمجنون إذا أفاق ولمن غسل ميتا فكل ذلك مستحب
chapters.anchors:
- Root: غ-س-ل (gh-s-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Washing, cleansing the body with water; the act of removing impurity by flowing water over the surface.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Ritual purification (ṭahārah) from major impurity (janābah); a legal obligation (farḍ) entailing the intention (niyyah) and complete coverage of the body.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) — physical washing; metaphorical (majāz) — spiritual purification from sins, as in the Prophet's saying, "When the servant performs ablution, his sins depart."
- Root: ن-و-ى (n-w-y)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Intent, purpose, resolve; the heart's determination toward an act.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The distinguishing mark of worship (ʿibādah) versus mere habit; the pivot upon which the validity of ritual acts turns.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — aiming at a goal; metaphorical — the inward orientation that converts a mundane act into an act of obedience.
- Root: ت-ر-ت-ي-ب (t-r-t-y-b)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Ordering, arranging sequentially; placing each thing in its proper rank.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The prescribed sequence in ablution (wuḍūʾ) and major ablution (ghusl), as established by the Prophet's practice (sunnah) and consensus (ijmāʿ).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — physical arrangement; metaphorical — the hierarchical order of divine commands.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Clause (al-Sharṭ) — The phrase "if he does that, let him repeat the ablution" (fa-in faʿala dhālika fal-yuʿid al-wuḍūʾ) employs the conditional particle "in" followed by the jussive (jazm) in the apodosis, indicating a legal consequence contingent upon a specified action.
chapters.translation:
I say: Know that the manner of the major ablution (ghusl) is that one places the vessel on his right side, then mentions the name of God Most High, and washes his hands three times. Then he performs the minor ablution for relieving nature (istinjāʾ) as I have described to you, and removes any impurity (najāsah) upon his body if there be any. Then he performs the ablution (wuḍūʾ) for prayer as we have described, except for the washing of the feet — for he delays them. For if he washes them and then places them upon the ground, that would be a waste of water. Then he pours water upon his head three times, then upon his right side three times, then upon his left side three times. Then he rubs the front part of his body, and runs his fingers through the hair of his head and beard, and causes the water to reach the roots of whatever is thick or thin of hair. It is not incumbent upon the woman to undo her braids, unless she knows that the water does not reach the interstices of the hair. And he should attend to the folds and creases of the body. And let him beware of touching his penis during all this — for if he does that, let him repeat the ablution (wuḍūʾ). And if he performed the ablution before the major ablution, he does not repeat it after the major ablution.

These are the practices (sunan) of the minor ablution (wuḍūʾ) and the major ablution (ghusl). We have mentioned from them that which the wayfarer of the Hereafter cannot do without — in knowledge and in practice. As for the remaining questions that are needed regarding incidental circumstances, let him refer therein to the books of jurisprudence (fiqh).

The obligatory (wājib) from all that we have mentioned in the major ablution are two matters: the intention (niyyah) and the complete coverage of the body with the washing. The obligatory acts (furūḍ) of the minor ablution are: the intention, washing the face, washing the hands up to the elbows, wiping (masḥ) that part of the head to which the name applies, washing the feet up to the ankles, and the order (tartīb). As for continuous succession (muwālāh), it is not obligatory.

The major ablution is obligatory (wājib) due to four causes: the emission of semen (kharūj al-manī), the meeting of the two circumcisions (iltiqāʾ al-khitānayn), menstruation (ḥayḍ), and post-natal bleeding (nifās). Whatever other major ablutions exist are sunnah (recommended), such as the major ablution for the two festivals (ʿīdayn), Friday (jumʿah), the festivals, the state of pilgrimage consecration (iḥrām), standing at ʿArafah and Muzdalifah, entering Mecca, three major ablutions during the days of Tashrīq, and for the farewell circumambulation (ṭawāf al-wadāʿ) according to one opinion. Likewise, the disbeliever who embraces Islam while not in a state of major impurity, the insane person who regains his sanity, and the one who washes a deceased person — all of that is recommended (mustaḥabb).
