- Root: ع م م (ʿamma)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To encompass, include, or cover generally; generality as opposed to particularity.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): General applicability of a ruling (ʿumūm al-balwā) — that which afflicts the common masses, necessitating public instruction.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense of encompassing; here used metaphorically for the widespread nature of the need.
- Root: ق ل ل (qalla)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Fewness, smallness, scarcity.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The minimal action (al-fiʿl al-qalīl) — legally negligible in quantity yet morally significant in intent.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal quantity vs. metaphorical extension to legal tolerance.
- Root: ر خ ص (rakhuṣa)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Softness, ease; legally, a concession (rukhṣah) relaxing a primary ruling.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Divine leniency in secondary matters versus strictness in fundamentals.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal softness; metaphorical for legal dispensation.
- Root: و س و س (waswasa)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Faint sound; whisper; intrusive thought.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Satanic insinuation (waswās) disrupting devotional acts, rooted in ignorance of legal principles.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal whispering; metaphorical for psychological disturbance in worship.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Condition and Exception (al-sharṭ wa al-jawāb) — conditional clauses governing legal permissibility, as in "if X, then Y," requiring precise parsing of protasis and apodosis.
chapters.translation:
I say: The sixth chapter concerns miscellaneous matters of widespread affliction (ʿumūm al-balwā) which the seeker (murīd) needs to know. As for matters that occur rarely, we have already exhausted them in the books of jurisprudence (fiqh).

**On the Minor Action (al-fiʿl al-qalīl):**
Know that the minor action, even if it does not nullify the prayer, is nevertheless disliked (makrūh) — except when necessitated by need. This applies to repelling a passerby, or killing a scorpion that is feared, when it can be dispatched with one or two blows. If it reaches three blows, the action has become excessive and the prayer is nullified. Likewise with the louse and the flea: whenever one is harmed by them, it is permissible to repel them. Similarly, one's need to scratch an itch that disturbs one's humility (khushūʿ).

Muʿādh used to remove lice and fleas during prayer. Ibn ʿUmar used to kill lice in prayer until blood appeared on his hand. Al-Nakhaʿī said: "He takes it and weakens it, and there is nothing against him if he kills it." Ibn al-Musayyib said: "He takes it, numbs it, then casts it away." Mujāhid said: "It is more beloved to me that he leaves it — unless it harms him and distracts him from his prayer, in which case he weakens it just enough that it no longer harms, then casts it away."

This is a concession (rukhṣah); otherwise, perfection lies in abstaining from action entirely, however slight. For this reason, some of the pious would not even shoo away a fly, saying: "I will not train myself to do that, lest I corrupt my prayer." I have heard that the wicked, standing before kings, endure much harm without moving.

When one yawns, there is no harm in placing his hand over his mouth — and this is preferable. If he sneezes, let him praise God — Mighty and Majestic — inwardly, without moving his tongue. If he belches, he should not raise his head toward the sky. If his cloak falls, he should not straighten it, nor the ends of his turban — all of this is disliked (makrūh) except under necessity.

**On Praying in Sandals:**
Praying in sandals (naʿlayn) is permissible, even if removing them is easy. The concession is not granted for the difficulty of removal, as with leather socks (khuff), but rather because such impurity is pardoned. In this same sense is the madas (a type of footwear). The Messenger of God — may God bless him and grant him peace — prayed in his sandals, then removed them, and the people removed theirs. He said: "Why did you remove your sandals?" They replied: "We saw you remove yours, so we removed ours." He — peace and blessings be upon him — said: "Gabriel — peace be upon him — came to me and informed me that there was filth upon them. So when any of you intends to enter the mosque, let him turn over his sandals and inspect them; if he sees filth, let him wipe it against the ground, and then pray in them." {«أن جبرائيل عليه السلام أتاني فأخبرني أن بهما خبثا فإذا أراد أحدكم المسجد فليقلب نعليه ولينظر فيهما فإن رأى خبثا فليمسحه بالأرض وليصل فيهما»}

Some scholars said that praying in sandals is superior, citing his saying — peace be upon him — "Why did you remove your sandals?" But this is an exaggeration, for he — peace be upon him — asked them only to explain to them the reason for his own removal, knowing that they had removed theirs in imitation of him. ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Sāʾib narrated that the Prophet — peace be upon him — did remove his sandals. Thus he did both. So whoever removes them should not place them to his right or left, thereby constricting the space and breaking the row; rather, he should place them before him. Nor should he leave them behind him, lest his heart be distracted toward them. Perhaps the one who deemed praying in them superior had in view this very consideration — namely, the heart's distraction toward them.

Abū Hurayrah — may God be pleased with him — narrated that the Prophet — peace be upon him — said: "When any of you prays, let him place his sandals between his feet." {«إذا صلى أحدكم فليجعل نعليه بين رجليه»} Abū Hurayrah said to another: "Place them between your feet, and do not harm a Muslim with them." The Messenger of God — peace be upon him — placed his sandals to his left, and he was the imam. Thus the imam may do this, since no one stands to his left. The preferable course, however, is not to place them between one's feet, for they would occupy one's attention, but rather before one's feet — and perhaps this is what the hadith means. Jubayr ibn Muṭʿim said: "A man's placing his sandals between his feet is an innovation (bidʿah)."

**On Spitting in Prayer:**
If one spits during his prayer, his prayer is not nullified, for it is a minor action. What produces no sound is not counted as speech, nor does it take the form of articulated letters — yet it is disliked (makrūh). One should guard against it, except as the Messenger of God — peace be upon him — permitted. Some Companions narrated that the Messenger of God — peace be upon him — saw phlegm on the qiblah wall, became intensely angry, then scraped it off with a palm-branch he held, and said: "Bring me saffron." He smeared the trace with saffron, then turned to us and said: "Which of you would love to spit in his own face?" We said: "No one." He said: "When any of you enters into prayer, God — Mighty and Majestic — is between him and the qiblah." {«أيكم يحب أن يبزق في وجهه فقلنا لا أحد قال فإن أحدكم إذا دخل في الصلاة فإن الله عز وجل بينه وبين القبلة»} In another wording: "God faces him, so let none of you spit in front of his face, nor to his right, but rather to his left or beneath his left foot. If a spurt overcomes him, let him spit into his garment and rub it thus" — and he rubbed one part against another.

**On the Standing of the Follower (al-muqtadī):**
Know that the follower's position involves both sunnah and obligation (farḍ). As for the sunnah: a single man stands to the right of the imam, slightly behind him; a single woman stands behind the imam. If she stands beside the imam, this does not harm her, but she has contravened the sunnah. If a man is with her, the man stands to the imam's right and she stands behind the man. No one should stand alone behind the row; rather, he should enter the row or draw one person from the row back to himself. If he stands alone, his prayer is valid, albeit with dislike (karāhah).

As for the obligation: it is the connection of the row (ittiṣāl al-ṣaff) — namely, that there be a linking bond between the follower and the imam, such that they are in congregation (jamāʿah). If both are in the mosque, that suffices as a bond, for the mosque was built for this purpose; no physical row-connection is needed, only knowledge of the imam's actions. Abū Hurayrah — may God be pleased with him — prayed on the roof of the mosque following the imam's prayer. If the follower is in the mosque's courtyard (fanāʾ), on a road, or in shared open land, with no dividing structure between them, then proximity of a bow-shot's distance suffices as a bond, for each one's action reaches the other. The condition applies when one stands in a house-court (ṣaḥn) to the right or left of the mosque, with its door opening into the mosque: then the condition is that the mosque's row extends through its vestibule (dihlīz) without interruption into the court. Then the prayer of those in that row and those behind them is valid, but not of those ahead of them. Such is the ruling for differing structures. As for a single structure and a single open space, it is like open land.

**On the One Overtaken (al-masbūq):**
If one catches the last part of the imam's prayer, that is the beginning of his own prayer. Let him follow the imam and build upon it. Let him perform the qunūt in the dawn prayer at the end of his own prayer, even if he performed it with the imam. If he catches part of the standing with the imam, he should not occupy himself with supplication; rather, he should begin with the Fātiḥah and shorten it. If the imam bows before he completes it, and he is able to catch up with him in the imam's rising from the bow, let him complete it. If he cannot, let him follow the imam and bow — for part of the Fātiḥah has the ruling of the whole, and it is dropped from him by virtue of being overtaken. If the imam bows while he is in the additional surah, let him cut it off. If he catches the imam in prostration or in the tashahhud, he says the takbīr of consecration (takbīr al-iḥrām), then sits, without a second takbīr — unlike when he catches him in the bowing, where he says a second takbīr while descending, for that transition is counted for him. The takbīrs are for the original transitions of the prayer, not for incidental ones arising from following the imam. He is not considered to have caught the rakʿah unless he attains tranquility (ṭumaʾnīnah) in the bow while the imam is still within the bounds of the bower. If he does not complete his tranquility until after the imam has passed beyond the bounds of the bower, that rakʿah is lost to him.

**On Missed Prayers and Congregation:**
If one misses the noon prayer (ẓuhr) until the time of the afternoon prayer (ʿaṣr), let him pray the noon first, then the afternoon. If he begins with the afternoon, it suffices him, but he has abandoned the preferable and entered into a sphere of scholarly disagreement. If he finds an imam, let him pray the afternoon with him, then pray the noon afterward — for congregation with the timely prayer takes precedence. If he prays alone at the beginning of the time, then catches a congregation, let him pray with the congregation intending the prayer of the time — and God will reckon whichever He wills. If he intends a missed prayer (fāʾitah) or a supererogatory prayer (taṭawwuʿ), that is permissible. If he has already prayed in congregation and then catches another congregation, let him intend a missed prayer or a voluntary one — for repeating an already-performed prayer in congregation a second time has no basis, and it is only tolerated for the sake of attaining the virtue of congregation.

**On Discovering Impurity on One's Garment:**
If one prays, then sees impurity (najāsah) on his garment, the more beloved course is to repeat the prayer, though it is not obligatory upon him. If he sees the impurity during the prayer, let him cast off the garment and complete the prayer — though repeating is more beloved. The basis of this is the story of removing the sandals when Gabriel — peace be upon him — informed the Messenger of God — peace be upon him — that there was impurity upon them, for he — peace be upon him — did not restart his prayer.

**On Forgetfulness and Prostration of Forgetfulness (sujūd al-sahw):**
If one omits the first tashahhud, or the qunūt, or the salutation upon the Messenger of God — peace be upon him — in the first tashahhud, or commits an act forgetfully which would nullify the prayer if done deliberately, or doubts whether he prayed three or four rakʿahs — let him take the certain (al-yaqīn) and perform two prostrations of forgetfulness before the salutation. If he forgets, then after the salutation, whenever he remembers — provided it is soon. If he prostrates after the salutation but after having broken his ablution, his prayer is nullified — for when he entered into the prostration, it was as if his salutation had been a forgetful act in the wrong place, so no dissolution (taḥallul) was achieved by it, and he returned to the prayer; therefore he must repeat the salutation after the prostration. If he remembers the prostration of forgetfulness after leaving the mosque, or after a long interval, it is lost.

**On Whispering (waswās) in the Intention of Prayer:**
Know that whispering in the intention of prayer stems from a defect in the intellect or ignorance of the Sacred Law (al-sharʿ) — for compliance with the command of God — Mighty and Majestic — is like compliance with the command of any other, and reverencing Him is like reverencing another, with respect to purpose (qaṣd). If a scholar entered upon a man and he stood up for him, and he were to say: "I intend to stand upright, reverencing the entry of Zayd the virtuous, on account of his virtue, facing him with my face" — that would be foolishness in his intellect. Rather, just as he sees him and knows his virtue, the motive of reverence arises and stands him up, and he is reverencing — unless he stood for some other business or in heedlessness. The condition that the prayer be noon, timely, and obligatory, in order to constitute compliance, is like the condition that the standing be conjoined with the entry, with the face turned toward the entrant, with no other motive present, and with the purpose of reverence thereby — so that it be reverence. For if he stood turning away from him, or waited and then stood after a while, he would not be reverencing.

Then these attributes must be known and must be intended. Yet their presence in the soul need not be prolonged in a single moment; rather, what is prolonged is the articulation of the words denoting them — either by utterance of the tongue or by reflection of the heart. Whoever does not understand the intention of prayer in this manner is as if he did not understand intention at all. For you have merely been summoned to pray at a time, and you responded and stood — so the whispering is pure ignorance. For these purposes and these knowledges gather in the soul in a single state, without being detailed individually in the mind such that the soul surveys and contemplates them. There is a difference between a thing's presence in the soul and its detailed articulation by thought. Presence is opposed to absence and heedlessness, even if not detailed. For whoever knows "the originated" (al-ḥādith), for example, knows it by a single knowledge in a single state, and this knowledge encompasses knowledges that are present though not detailed. For whoever knows the originated has known the existent and the non-existent, priority and posteriority, and time — that priority belongs to non-existence and posteriority to existence. These knowledges are folded within the knowledge of the originated, as evidenced by the fact that if one who knows the originated — knowing nothing else — were asked: "Did you know priority alone, or posteriority, or non-existence, or the priority of non-existence, or the posteriority of existence, or time divided into prior and posterior?" and he said: "I never knew that" — he would be a liar, and his statement would contradict his claim "I know the originated."

From ignorance of this subtlety arises whispering. For the one afflicted with waswās burdens himself to present in his heart the noon-ness, the timeliness, and the obligatoriness in a single state, detailed with their words, while he surveys them — and that is impossible. If he burdened himself with that in standing for the scholar, it would prove impossible for him. By this knowledge the whispering is repelled — namely, that compliance with the command of God — Glorified be He — in intention is like compliance with the command of another. Then I add, by way of facilitation and concession: I say that even if the one afflicted with waswās does not understand intention except by presenting these matters in detail, and cannot represent compliance to himself all at once — let him present the whole of it during the takbīr, from its beginning to its end, such that he does not finish the takbīr until the intention is achieved. That suffices him, and we do not burden him to conjoin all of it with the beginning of the takbīr or its end — for that would be an excessive burden (taklīf shaṭaṭ). Had it been commanded, the early generations would have been questioned about it, and some Companion would have been afflicted with waswās in intention. The fact that this did not occur is proof that the matter is one of leniency. However the intention becomes easy for the one afflicted, he should be content with it, until he becomes accustomed to it and the whispering departs from him. He should not demand of himself the realization (taḥqīq) of that — for realization only increases the whispering. We have mentioned in the fatāwā various aspects of realization concerning the knowledges and purposes pertaining to intention, which the scholars need to know. As for the common folk, perhaps hearing them would harm them and stir up whispering against them — therefore we have omitted them.

**On Not Preceding the Imam:**
The follower should not precede the imam in bowing, prostration, or rising from them, nor in any other act. Nor should he equal him; rather, he should follow him and trace his footsteps — this is the meaning of following (iqtidāʾ). If he equals him deliberately, his prayer is not nullified, just as if he stood beside him without lagging behind. If he precedes him, there is disagreement over the nullification of his prayer — and it is not far-fetched to rule nullification, by analogy with preceding him in position — indeed, this is more apt, for congregation is following in action, not in position, so following in action is more important. The condition of not preceding in position was only stipulated to facilitate following in action and to achieve the form of subordination, since it befits the one followed to be ahead. Preceding him in action has no justification except forgetfulness. For this reason the Messenger of God — peace be upon him — issued a severe rebuke, saying: "Does not the one who raises his head before the imam fear that God will transform his head into the head of a donkey?" {«أما يخشى الذي يرفع رأسه قبل الإمام أن يحول الله رأسه رأس حمار»} As for lagging behind him by one pillar (rukn), this does not nullify the prayer — namely, when the imam rises from his bow while the follower has not yet bowed. But lagging to this extent is disliked. If the imam places his forehead on the ground while the follower has not yet reached the bounds of the bower, his prayer is nullified. Likewise, if the imam places his forehead for the second prostration while the follower has not yet performed the first.

**On Enjoining Right and Forbidding Wrong in Prayer:**
It is incumbent upon whoever attends the prayer, when he sees another's error in his prayer, to correct it and disapprove of it. If it issues from an ignorant person, let him be gentle with the ignorant one and teach him. This includes commanding the straightening of the rows, preventing one who stands alone outside the row, and disapproving of one who raises his head before the imam — among other matters. For he — peace be upon him — said: "Woe to the scholar from the ignorant one, when he does not teach him." {«ويل للعالم من الجاهل حيث لا يعلمه»} Ibn Masʿūd — may God be pleased with him — said: "Whoever sees one who prays badly and does not forbid him is his partner in its sin." It is narrated from Bilāl ibn Saʿd that he said: "The sin, when concealed, harms only its owner; but when it is made public and not corrected, it harms the general public." It has come in the hadith that Bilāl used to straighten the rows and strike their shins with a whip. ʿUmar — may God be pleased with him — said: "Check on your brothers in prayer; if you find them missing — if they are sick, visit them; if they are healthy, rebuke them." The rebuke is a disapproval of one who abandons the congregation, and one should not be lenient in it. The early generations were extreme in this, to the point that some of them would carry a funeral bier to one who had lagged behind the congregation — indicating that the dead one is he who lags behind the congregation, not the living.

Whoever enters the mosque should aim for the right side of the row. For this reason, people crowded toward it in the time of the Messenger of God — peace be upon him — until it was said to him: "The left side is neglected." He — peace be upon him — said: "Whoever populates the left side of the mosque shall have a double portion of reward." {«من عمر ميسرة المسجد كان له كفلان من الأجر»} Whenever one finds a boy in the row and finds no place for himself, he may remove him to the back and enter in his place — I mean, when the boy has not reached puberty. This is what we intended to mention of the matters of widespread affliction. The rulings on the various prayers will follow, God willing, in the Book of Liturgies (Kitāb al-Awrād).

chapters.arabic_text:
|| الباب السابع في النوافل من الصلوات

اعلم أن ما عدا الفرائض
من الصلوات ينقسم إلى ثلاثة أقسام سنن ومستحبات وتطوعات
ونعني بالسنن ما نقل عن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم المواظبة عليه
كالرواتب عقيب الصلوات وصلاة الضحى والوتر والتهجد وغيرها لأن السنة عبارة
عن الطريق المسلوكة
ونعني بالمستحبات ما ورد الخبر بفضله ولم ينقل المواظبة عليه كما سننقله
في صلوات الأيام والليالي في الأسبوع وكالصلاة عند الخروج من المنزل
والدخول فيه وأمثاله
ونعني بالتطوعات ما وراء ذلك مما لم يرد في عينه أثر ولكنه تطوع به العبد
من حيث رغب في مناجاة الله عز وجل بالصلاة التي ورد الشرع بفضلها مطلقا
فكأنه متبرع به إذا لم يندب إلى تلك الصلاة بعينها وإن ندب إلى الصلاة
مطلقا والتطوع عبارة عن التبرع
وسميت الأقسام الثلاثة نوافل من حيث إن النفل هو الزيادة وجملتها زائد
على الفرائض
فلفظ النافلة والسنة والمستحب والتطوع أردنا الاصطلاح  عليه لتعريف هذه
المقاصد
ولا حرج على من يغير هذا الاصطلاح فلا مشاحة في الألفاظ بعد فهم المقاصد
وكل قسم من هذه الأقاسم تتفاوت درجاته في PageV01P192
الفضل بحسب ما ورد فيها من الأخبار والآثار المعرفة لفضلها وبحسب طول
مواظبة رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم عليها وبحسب صحة الأخبار الواردة فيها
واشتهارها ولذلك يقال سنن الجماعات أفضل من سنن الانفراد
وأفضل سنن الجماعات صلاة العيد ثم الكسوف ثم الاستسقاء
وأفضل سنن الانفراد الوتر ثم ركعتا الفجر ثم ما بعدهما من الرواتب على
تفاوتها
واعلم أن النوافل باعتبار الإضافة إلى معلقاتها تنقسم إلى ما يتعلق
بأسباب كالكسوف والاستسقاء وإلى ما يتعلق بأوقات والمتعلق بالأوقات ينقسم
إلى ما يتكرر بتكرر اليوم والليلة أو بتكرر الأسبوع أو بتكرر السنة فالجملة
أربعة أقسام
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ن-ف-ل (N-F-L)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Additional gain beyond what is obligatory; spoils of war taken as surplus; that which exceeds the due portion.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In devotional context, denotes voluntary acts exceeding the prescribed minimum, drawing the servant nearer to God through supererogation.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense is 'increase/surplus' (ziyādah); applied metaphorically (majāz) to prayers beyond the farāʾiḍ, as they are an 'extra' over the obligatory.
- Root: س-ن-ن (S-N-N)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: A trodden path, a clear way; to establish a practice or custom that is followed.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The prophetic way (sunnah) as the normative model of worship, transmitted by continuous practice.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: a beaten track; metaphorical: the Prophet's established practice, since it is a 'path' to be traversed.
- Root: ح-ب-ب (Ḥ-B-B)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To love, to prefer; that which is beloved and desirable.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Mustaḥabb — that which the Lawgiver loves but does not command with binding force; recommended acts.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: beloved; technical: recommended, distinguished from obligatory by absence of compulsion.
- Root: ت-ط-و-ع (T-T-W-ʿ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To volunteer, to offer freely without being asked; voluntary obedience.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Taṭawwuʿ — supererogatory devotion performed out of free choice, not mandated by a specific command.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: spontaneous giving; metaphorical: any voluntary worship beyond the prescribed, as it is a 'gift' from the servant.
- Sībawayh Rule: Taqdīr al-ʿAwāmil (Ellipsis of Governing Elements) — In classifying the divisions, the nominal predicates are governed by implicit copulas (e.g., 'the sunan are...'), requiring the reader to supply the omitted operator for correct parsing of the categorical statements.
chapters.translation:
I say: Know that whatever lies beyond the obligatory prayers (al-farāʾiḍ) divides into three categories: sunan (established practices), mustaḥabbāt (recommended acts), and taṭawwuʿāt (voluntary devotions).

By 'sunan' I mean that which has been transmitted from the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) as his continuous practice (muwāẓabah) — such as the regular supererogatory prayers (rawātib) following the obligatory prayers, the forenoon prayer (ḍuḥā), the witr prayer, the night vigil (tahajjud), and the like. For 'sunnah' is an expression denoting the trodden path (al-ṭarīq al-maslūkah).

By 'mustaḥabbāt' I mean that concerning which a report (khabar) has come regarding its virtue, yet continuous practice upon it has not been transmitted — as we shall relate concerning the prayers of the days and nights throughout the week, and like the prayer upon leaving the house and entering it, and similar examples.

By 'taṭawwuʿāt' I mean that which lies beyond these — that for which no specific tradition (athar) has come concerning its particular form, but the servant volunteers it out of his desire for intimate communion (munājāh) with God, Mighty and Majestic, through prayer — that prayer whose virtue the Sacred Law has commended in absolute terms (muṭlaqan). Thus it is as if he freely offers it (mutabarriʿ), since he was not specifically summoned to that particular prayer, though he was summoned to prayer in general. And 'taṭawwuʿ' is an expression for voluntary giving (tabarruʿ).

These three categories are all termed 'nawāfil' (supererogatory) because 'nafl' means increase (ziyādah), and all of them together are an increase over the obligatory prayers.

So by the terms 'nāfilah,' 'sunnah,' 'mustaḥabb,' and 'taṭawwuʿ,' I intend only a conventional usage (iṣṭilāḥ) for the purpose of defining these objectives. There is no blame upon one who alters this convention, for there is no quibbling over words once the objectives are understood.

Each of these categories has degrees of merit that vary — as recorded on PageV01P192 — according to what has come down concerning them of reports (akhbār) and traditions (āthār) that make known their virtue, according to the length of the Messenger of God's (peace and blessings be upon him) continuous practice upon them, and according to the authenticity (ṣiḥḥah) of the reports concerning them and their widespread renown (ishtihār). For this reason it is said: the sunan of congregations are more excellent than the sunan of individual seclusion.

The most excellent of the congregational sunan is the prayer of the two festivals (ʿīd), then the eclipse prayer (kusūf), then the rain-seeking prayer (istisqāʾ).

The most excellent of the individual sunan is the witr prayer, then the two rakʿahs of the dawn (fajr), then what follows them of the rawātib, according to their varying degrees.

Know that the nawāfil, considered in relation to that to which they are attached, divide into: that which is attached to causes (asbāb) — like the eclipse and rain-seeking prayers — and that which is attached to times (awqāt). And that which is attached to times divides into: that which recurs with the recurrence of the day and night, or with the recurrence of the week, or with the recurrence of the year. Thus the total is four categories.

chapters.title_en: Section 80 — The First Category: Supererogatory Prayers (Rawātib) That Recur with the Recurrence of Days and Nights

chapters.anchors:
- Root: ر-ت-ب (r-t-b)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To establish firmly, to set in order, to make permanent and regular; a rawtibah is that which is fixed and steadfast in its sequence.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The supererogatory prayers attached to the obligatory ones, functioning as their completion (takmilah) and reparation (jabar) for any deficiency.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense is "fixed in rank/order"; metaphorically applied to prayers that are permanently appended to the obligatory rites.
- Root: ز-و-ل (z-w-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Departure, cessation, decline; the sun's declension from its meridian zenith.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The moment marking the legal entry of the ẓuhr prayer; a cosmic sign (āyah) of divine order.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: "to cease being in a place"; technical: the sun's departure from the meridian arc.
- Root: و-ت-ر (w-t-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Odd number; the single unit that makes a count uneven.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The witr prayer — the seal of the night prayer, making the preceding even units odd.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: oddness in number; metaphorical: the concluding act that renders the night worship complete.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Constructions (al-sharṭ wa al-istithnāʾ) — governing the legal distinctions between "performance within time" (adāʾ) versus "making up" (qaḍāʾ), and the conditional validity of the witr prayer upon prior connected units.
chapters.translation:
I say: The first category comprises what recurs with the recurrence of days and nights, and these are eight: five are the fixed supererogatory prayers (rawātib) of the five obligatory prayers, and three lie beyond them — namely, the forenoon prayer (ḍuḥā), the revival of the interval between the two evening prayers (al-ʿishāʾayn), and the night vigil (tahajjud).

**The First: The Fixed Prayer of Dawn (Ṣubḥ)** — two units (rakʿatān). The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, said: «Two units of the dawn prayer are better than the world and all that it contains» (1). Its time enters with the rising of the true dawn (al-fajr al-ṣādiq) — that which spreads horizontally (al-mustatīr), not the vertical column (al-mustatīl). Perceiving this by direct observation is difficult at its very beginning, unless one learns the lunar mansions (manāzil al-qamar) or knows the correlation of its rising with stars visible to the eye, thereby inferring the dawn from the stars; or one knows it by the moon on two nights of the month — for the moon rises with the dawn on the twenty-sixth night, and the dawn breaks with the setting of the moon on the twelfth night of the month. This is the predominant pattern, though variation occurs in certain zodiacal signs, and the detailed explanation of that would be lengthy.

Learning the lunar mansions is among the important matters for the spiritual seeker (murīd), for through it he becomes acquainted with the measures of the times by night and with the dawn. The time of the two dawn units lapses with the lapse of the time of the obligatory dawn prayer, which is at sunrise. However, the Sunnah is to perform them before the obligatory prayer. If one enters the mosque while the congregational prayer has already commenced, let him occupy himself with the obligatory prayer, for he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: «When the prayer has been established, there is no prayer except the obligatory one» (2). Then, when he finishes the obligatory prayer, he rises and prays them.

The correct position is that they are performed within their time (adāʾ) as long as they occur before sunrise, because they are subordinate to the obligatory prayer in its time. The ordering between them is merely a Sunnah of precedence and delay — when one does not encounter the congregation. But when one encounters the congregation, the order is inverted, and they remain valid as adāʾ.

It is recommended (mustaḥabb) that one pray them at home and make them brief, then enter the mosque and pray two units as a greeting of the mosque (taḥiyyat al-masjid), then sit and not pray until he has performed the obligatory prayer. Between dawn and sunrise, the most beloved act is remembrance (dhikr), reflection (fikr), and restricting oneself to the two dawn units and the obligatory prayer.

**The Second: The Fixed Prayer of Noon (Ẓuhr)** — six units: two after it, which are also an emphatic Sunnah, and four before it, which are likewise Sunnah, though of lesser rank than the two final ones. Abū Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, narrated from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, that he said: «Whoever prays four units after the sun's declension (zawāl), perfecting their recitation, bowing, and prostration, seventy thousand angels pray alongside him, seeking forgiveness for him until the night» (3) — this is from the ḥadīth of Abū Masʿūd; I have not seen it from the ḥadīth of Abū Hurayrah. He, peace and blessings be upon him, would not abandon four units after the declension, lengthening them, saying: «The gates of heaven are opened at this hour, and I love that a deed of mine be raised up therein» (4) — narrated by Abū Ayyūb al-Anṣārī, who was alone in transmitting it. This is also indicated by what Umm Ḥabībah, the wife of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, narrated: that he said: «Whoever prays twelve units daily besides the obligatory, a house will be built for him in Paradise» — two units before dawn, four before noon, two after it, two before the afternoon prayer, and two after the evening prayer (1). Ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: «I preserved from the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, ten units daily» (2), and he mentioned what Umm Ḥabībah mentioned, except the two dawn units, for he said: «That was an hour in which he did not enter upon the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him; but my sister Ḥafṣah, may Allah be pleased with her, told me that he, peace and blessings be upon him, used to pray two units in her house, then go out.» And in his narration he said: «Two units before noon and two after the night prayer» — thus the two units before noon became more emphatic than the rest of the four.

The time of this enters with the declension (zawāl). The declension is known by the increase of the shadow of upright objects inclining toward the east. For an object casts a shadow at sunrise on the western side, which lengthens; the sun continues to rise and the shadow decreases, deviating from the western direction, until the sun reaches the limit of its elevation — which is the arc of midday (niṣf al-nahār) — and that is the limit of the shadow's decrease. When the sun declines from the limit of elevation, the shadow begins to increase. From the very point where the increase becomes perceptible to the senses, the time of noon enters. One knows with certainty that the declension in the knowledge of Allah, glorified be He, occurred before that, but legal obligations (takālīf) are tied only to what falls under sensory perception.

The remaining portion of the shadow from which it begins to increase lengthens in winter and shortens in summer. The limit of its length is the sun's reaching the beginning of Capricorn (al-jady), and the limit of its shortness is its reaching the beginning of Cancer (al-saraṭān). This is known by feet and measures.

Among the methods closest to verification, for one who excels in observing it, is to observe the North Pole (al-quṭb al-shamālī) at night, and place upon the ground a square board in a level position, such that one of its sides faces the direction of the Pole — such that if one imagined a stone falling from the Pole to the ground, then imagined a line from the stone's point of impact to the nearest side of the board, the line would stand upon the side at two right angles, i.e., the line would not incline toward either of the two sides. Then one erects a vertical staff upon the board at a marked position, and it faces the Pole. Its shadow falls upon the board at the beginning of the day inclining toward the west, in the direction of line (a). It continues to incline until it coincides with line (b), such that if its tip were extended, it would end in a straight line at the stone's point of impact, being parallel to the eastern and western sides, not inclining toward either. When its inclination toward the western side ceases, the sun is at the limit of its elevation. When the shadow deviates from the line upon the board toward the east, the sun has declined. This is perceived by the senses with certainty at a time close to the beginning of the declension in the knowledge of Allah, exalted be He. Then one marks the tip of the shadow at its deviation. When the shadow from that mark becomes equal to the staff, the time of the afternoon prayer (ʿaṣr) enters. This much is sufficient to know regarding the science of declension. And this is its diagram.

**The Third: The Fixed Prayer of Afternoon (ʿAṣr)** — four units before the afternoon prayer. Abū Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, narrated from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, that he said: «May Allah have mercy upon a servant who prays four units before the afternoon prayer» (3). Acting upon this, hoping to be included in the supplication of the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, is recommended with emphatic recommendation — for his supplication is surely answered. Yet his, peace and blessings be upon him, constancy upon the Sunnah before the afternoon prayer was not like his constancy upon the two units before noon.

**The Fourth: The Fixed Prayer of Sunset (Maghrib)** — two units after the obligatory prayer, concerning which there is no divergence in the narrations. As for two units before it, between the caller's adhān and the caller's iqāmah, by way of hastening — this has been transmitted from a group of the Companions, such as Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, ʿUbādah ibn al-Ṣāmit, Abū Dharr, Zayd ibn Thābit, and others. ʿUbādah or another said: «When the caller gave the adhān for the sunset prayer, the companions of the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, would hasten to the pillars, praying two units» (1). Some of them said: «We used to pray the two units before sunset until a person entering would think we had prayed, and ask: "Have you prayed the sunset prayer?"» (2). This falls under the general scope of his saying, peace and blessings be upon him: «Between every two adhāns there is a prayer, for whoever wishes» (3). Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal used to pray them, but people criticized him, so he abandoned them. When asked about this, he said: «I did not see the people praying them, so I abandoned them.» And he said: «If a man prays them in his house, or where people do not see him, that is good.»

The time of sunset enters with the sun's disappearance from sight in level lands not surrounded by mountains. If they are surrounded by mountains on the western side, one waits until he sees the darkness advancing from the east. He, peace and blessings be upon him, said: «When the night approaches from here and the day retreats from here, the faster has broken his fast» (4). The most beloved is hastening in the sunset prayer specifically. Even if it is delayed and prayed before the disappearance of the red twilight, it occurs as adāʾ, but it is disliked (makrūh). ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, delayed the sunset prayer one night until a star appeared, so he freed a slave. Ibn ʿUmar delayed it until two stars appeared, so he freed two slaves.

**The Fifth: The Fixed Prayer of the Final Night Prayer (ʿIshāʾ al-Ākhirah)** — four units after the obligatory prayer. ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, said: «The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, used to pray four units after the final night prayer, then sleep» (5). Some scholars chose, from the totality of the reports, that the number of the rawātib should be seventeen, equal to the number of the obligatory prayers: two before dawn, four before noon, two after it, four before the afternoon prayer, two after sunset, and three after the final night prayer — which is the witr (6). Whenever one has come to know the ḥadīths transmitted concerning this, there is no meaning in fixed estimation, for he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: «Prayer is a good place — whoever wishes may increase, and whoever wishes may decrease» (7). Thus, each seeker's choice from these prayers is according to his desire for good. It has become clear from what we have mentioned that some of them are more emphatic than others, and abandoning the more emphatic is more remote — especially since the obligatory prayers are completed by the supererogatory ones. Whoever does not multiply them may well find that no obligatory prayer remains sound for him without a reparation (jābir).

**The Sixth: The Witr Prayer.** Anas ibn Mālik said: «The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, used to pray the witr after the night prayer with three units, reciting in the first "Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High," in the second "Say: O disbelievers," and in the third "Say: He is Allah, the One"» (8). It has come in the report that he, peace and blessings be upon him, used to pray two units after the witr while sitting, and in some versions, sitting cross-legged (9). In some reports: «When he wished to enter his bed, he would crawl to it and pray two units upon it before sleeping, reciting in them "When the earth is shaken with its earthquake" and the sūrah of "Rivalry in wealth"» (10). In another narration: «Say: O disbelievers.» It is permissible to pray the witr separated (mafṣūl) or connected (mawṣūl), with a single taslīm or two taslīms. The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, prayed the witr with one unit (1), with three (2), with five (3), and so on with the odd numbers (4) up to eleven units (5). The narration is uncertain regarding thirteen (6), and in an anomalous (shādhdh) report, seventeen units (7). These units — I mean the totality of what we have named as witr — constitute prayer by night, which is the tahajjud. The tahajjud by night is an emphatic Sunnah, and its virtues will be mentioned in the Book of Liturgies (Kitāb al-Awrād). There is disagreement concerning what is superior: it is said that performing the witr as a single odd unit is superior, since it is established that he, peace and blessings be upon him, was constant upon performing the witr as a single odd unit. And it is said that the connected form is superior, to exit from the suspicion of disagreement — especially for the prayer leader (imām), for one who does not consider the single odd unit a valid prayer may follow him. If he prays connected, he intends the witr by all of it. If he restricts himself to a single unit after the two units of the night prayer, or after the obligatory night prayer, he intends the witr and it is valid — for the condition of the witr is that it be odd in itself and that it render odd what preceded it. The obligatory prayer has already rendered the preceding even. If one prayed the witr before the night prayer, it is not valid — meaning he does not attain the virtue of the witr, which is «better for him than red camels» (8), as has come in the report. Otherwise, a single odd unit is valid at any time. It is only invalid before the night prayer because it breaches the consensus (ijmāʿ) of the people in practice, and because nothing preceded it to render it odd.

As for one who wishes to pray the witr as three separated units, there is consideration regarding his intention in the two units. If he intends by them the tahajjud or the Sunnah of the night prayer, they are not part of the witr. If he intends the witr, they are not odd in themselves — rather, the witr is what follows them. But the more apparent view is that he intends the witr, just as he intends the witr in the three connected units. For the witr has two meanings: one is that it be odd in itself, and the other is that it be initiated to render odd what follows it — thus the totality of the three is odd, and the two units are part of the three, except that their oddness is contingent upon the third unit. When one is resolved to render them odd by a third, he may intend the witr by them — and the third unit is odd by itself and renders odd what precedes it. The two units do not render odd what precedes them, nor are they odd in themselves, but they are rendered odd by what follows them.

The witr should be the last prayer of the night, occurring after the tahajjud. The virtues of the witr and the tahajjud, and the manner of ordering between them, will come in the Book on the Ordering of Liturgies (Kitāb Tartīb al-Awrād).

**The Seventh: The Forenoon Prayer (Ḍuḥā).** Constancy upon it is among the firm resolutions of action and their most virtuous. As for the number of its units, the most transmitted is eight. Umm Hāniʾ, the sister of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, may Allah be pleased with them both, narrated that he, peace and blessings be upon him, prayed the forenoon prayer with eight units, lengthening and perfecting them (9). No one else transmitted this number. As for ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, she mentioned that he, peace and blessings be upon him, used to pray the forenoon prayer with four units, increasing whatever Allah, glorified be He, willed (10) — she did not limit the increase, but he was constant upon the four, not diminishing from them, and he would sometimes add increases. It is narrated in an isolated (mufrad) report that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, used to pray the forenoon prayer with six units (11). As for its time, ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him, narrated that he, peace and blessings be upon him, used to pray the forenoon prayer with six units at two times: when the sun shone brightly and rose high, he would stand and pray two units — this being the first portion (wird) of the second set of the day's portions, as will come — and when the sun spread out and was in the quarter of the sky on the eastern side, he would pray four (1). The first occurs when the sun has risen to the measure of half a spear; the second when a quarter of the day has passed — corresponding to the afternoon prayer, whose time is when a quarter of the day remains. Noon is at the midpoint of the day, and the forenoon prayer is at the midpoint between sunrise and declension, just as the afternoon prayer is at the midpoint between declension and sunset. This is the most virtuous of the times. From the time of the sun's rising high until just before the declension, the entire period is a time for the forenoon prayer in general.

**The Eighth: The Revival of the Interval Between the Two Evening Prayers (al-ʿishāʾayn).** This is an emphatic Sunnah. What has been transmitted of its number from the practice of the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, between the two evening prayers is six units (2). This prayer has tremendous virtue. It is said that it is what is meant by His saying, exalted be He: {«Their sides forsake their beds»} (Quran 32:16). It is narrated from him, peace and blessings be upon him, that he said: «Whoever prays between sunset and the night prayer, it is among the prayers of the penitent (al-awwābīn)» (3). And he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: «Whoever confines himself between sunset and the night prayer in a mosque in congregation, speaking nothing but prayer or Quran, it is incumbent upon Allah to build for him two palaces in Paradise, each palace a journey of a hundred years, and to plant for him between them plantings that, if the inhabitants of the earth were to traverse them, would encompass them» (4). The remainder of its virtues will come in the Book of Liturgies, if Allah, exalted be He, wills.

chapters.anchors:
- Root: ص-ل-و (ṣ-l-w)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning of supplication, blessing, and the ritual prayer (al-ṣalāh) as an act of devotion with prescribed postures and recitations.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, al-ṣalāh denotes the specific act of worship (ʿibādah) comprising standing, bowing, and prostration, established as a pillar of faith; its reward (thawāb) is contingent upon sincerity (ikhlāṣ) and conformity to prophetic practice.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) for the ritual prayer; metaphorical (majāz) when extended to supplication (duʿāʾ) or blessing upon the Prophet (al-ṣalāh ʿalā al-nabī).
- Root: ح-س-ن (ḥ-s-n)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Beauty, goodness, and excellence; a good deed (ḥasanah) as a unit of divine reward.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In Kalām, al-ḥasanah is the act that accrues merit (thawāb) in the afterlife, contrasted with al-sayyiʾah (misdeed); its multiplication reflects divine generosity (faḍl).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for moral beauty; metaphorical for the recorded reward in the divine ledger.
- Root: غ-ف-ر (gh-f-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Covering, veiling, and forgiving; al-maghfirah as the divine act of concealing sins and pardoning the sinner.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Theological nuance of forgiveness as removal of the consequence of sin (ʿiqāb), contingent upon repentance (tawbah) and divine mercy (raḥmah).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for covering; metaphorical for the obliteration of sin's record.
- Root: ث-و-ب (th-w-b)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Return, reward, and recompense; al-thawāb as the divine recompense for obedience.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In eschatological context, thawāb is the eternal reward in the Hereafter, graded by the quality and quantity of deeds.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for return; metaphorical for the recompense granted by God.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Construction (al-Sharṭ wa al-Jawāb) — The protasis (sharṭ) introduced by "man" (whoever) is followed by an apodosis (jawāb) that specifies the reward, often with "kāna ḥaqqan ʿalā Allāh" (it is incumbent upon God), indicating a divine promise (waʿd) rather than obligation (wujūb) in the theological sense.
chapters.translation:
I say: The second division concerns what recurs with the recurrence of weeks, namely, the prayers of the days of the week and their nights, for each day and each night.

As for the days, we begin with Sunday.

**Sunday:** Abū Hurayrah (may God be pleased with him) narrated from the Prophet (peace be upon him) that he said: "Whoever prays on Sunday four rakʿahs, reciting in each rakʿah the Opening of the Book (Fātiḥah) and 'The Messenger believes' (Āman al-Rasūl) once, God writes for him, for every Christian male and female, good deeds, and God gives him the reward of a prophet, and writes for him a Pilgrimage (Ḥajj) and an ʿUmrah, and writes for him for every rakʿah a thousand prayers, and God gives him in Paradise, for every letter, a city of fragrant musk." It is also narrated from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib (may God be pleased with him) from the Prophet (peace be upon him) that he said: "Declare the Oneness of God (tawḥīd) abundantly through prayer on Sunday, for He, glorified be He, is One, having no partner. Whoever prays on Sunday after the noon prayer (Ẓuhr), four rakʿahs after the obligatory and the sunnah, reciting in the first (rakʿah) the Opening of the Book and 'The Prostration' (Sajdah), and in the second the Opening of the Book and 'Blessed is the Kingdom' (Tabārak al-Mulk), then makes the tashahhud and salutation, then stands and prays two further rakʿahs, reciting in them the Opening of the Book and the Chapter of Friday (al-Jumuʿah), and asks God, glorified be He, for his need — it is incumbent upon God to fulfill his need."

**Monday:** Jābir narrated from the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) that he said: "Whoever prays on Monday at the height of the forenoon two rakʿahs, reciting in each rakʿah the Opening of the Book once, the Throne Verse (Āyat al-Kursī) once, 'Say: He is God, One' (Qul Huwa Allāhu Aḥad) and the two refuge-seeking chapters (al-Muʿawwidhatayn) once each — then when he salutes, seeks forgiveness from God ten times and sends blessings upon the Prophet (peace be upon him) ten times — God, exalted be He, forgives all his sins." Anas ibn Mālik narrated from the Prophet (peace be upon him) that he said: "Whoever prays on Monday twelve rakʿahs, reciting in each rakʿah the Opening of the Book and the Throne Verse once, then when he finishes recites 'Say: He is God, One' twelve times and seeks forgiveness twelve times, a caller will call on the Day of Resurrection: 'Where is so-and-so, son of so-and-so? Let him stand and take his reward from God, mighty and majestic.' The first of the reward he is given is a thousand garments (ḥullah), and he is crowned, and it is said to him: 'Enter Paradise.' A hundred thousand angels will meet him, each angel bearing a gift, escorting him until he circles a thousand palaces of light, radiant."

**Tuesday:** Yazīd al-Raqqāshī narrated from Anas ibn Mālik, who said: The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "Whoever prays on Tuesday ten rakʿahs at midday — and in another narration, at the height of the forenoon — reciting in each rakʿah the Opening of the Book, the Throne Verse once, and 'Say: He is God, One' three times, no sin will be recorded against him for seventy days; and if he dies within seventy days, he dies a martyr, and sins of seventy years are forgiven him."

**Wednesday:** Abū Idrīs al-Khawlānī narrated from Muʿādh ibn Jabal (may God be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of God (peace be upon him) said: "Whoever prays on Wednesday twelve rakʿahs at the height of the forenoon, reciting in each rakʿah the Opening of the Book, the Throne Verse once, 'Say: He is God, One' three times, and the two refuge-seeking chapters three times, a caller will call from beside the Throne: 'O servant of God, resume your deeds, for your past sin has been forgiven you.' God, glorified be He, will lift from him the punishment of the grave, its constriction and darkness, and will lift from him the severities of the Resurrection, and there will be raised for him from that day the deed of a prophet."

**Thursday:** From ʿIkrimah, from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: The Messenger of God (peace be upon him) said: "Whoever prays on Thursday between the noon (Ẓuhr) and afternoon (ʿAṣr) prayers two rakʿahs, reciting in the first the Opening of the Book and the Throne Verse a hundred times, and in the second the Opening of the Book and 'Say: He is God, One' a hundred times, and sends blessings upon Muḥammad a hundred times, God gives him the reward of one who fasted Rajab, Shaʿbān, and Ramaḍān, and he has a reward like that of the pilgrims to the House, and there is written for him, for every one who believed in God, glorified be He, and relied upon Him, a good deed."

**Friday:** It is narrated from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib (may God be pleased with him) from the Prophet (peace be upon him) that he said: "Friday is entirely a prayer. No believing servant stands when the sun has risen and ascended the measure of a spear or more, then performs ablution and perfects it, then prays the forenoon prayer (ṣubḥat al-ḍuḥā) two rakʿahs in faith and seeking reward, except that God writes for him two hundred good deeds and erases from him two hundred misdeeds. Whoever prays four rakʿahs, God, glorified be He, raises him four hundred degrees in Paradise; whoever prays eight rakʿahs, God, exalted be He, raises him eight hundred degrees in Paradise and forgives him all his sins; whoever prays twelve rakʿahs, God writes for him two thousand two hundred good deeds, erases from him two thousand two hundred misdeeds, and raises him two thousand two hundred degrees in Paradise." And from Nāfiʿ, from Ibn ʿUmar (may God be pleased with them both), from the Prophet (peace be upon him), that he said: "Whoever enters the congregational mosque on Friday and prays four rakʿahs before the Friday prayer, reciting in each rakʿah 'Praise be to God' (al-Ḥamd) and 'Say: He is God, One' fifty times, he will not die until he sees his seat in Paradise, or it is shown to him."

**Saturday:** Abū Hurayrah narrated that the Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "Whoever prays on Saturday four rakʿahs, reciting in each rakʿah the Opening of the Book once and 'Say: He is God, One' three times, then when he finishes recites the Throne Verse, God writes for him for every letter a Pilgrimage (Ḥajj) and an ʿUmrah, and raises for him for every letter the reward of a year of fasting its days and standing its nights, and God, mighty and majestic, gives him for every letter the reward of a martyr, and he will be beneath the shade of God's Throne with the prophets and the martyrs."

As for the nights:

**Sunday Night:** Anas ibn Mālik narrated concerning Sunday night that the Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "Whoever prays on Sunday night twenty rakʿahs, reciting in each rakʿah the Opening of the Book, 'Say: He is God, One' fifty times, and the two refuge-seeking chapters once each, then seeks forgiveness from God, mighty and majestic, a hundred times, and seeks forgiveness for himself and his parents a hundred times, and sends blessings upon the Prophet (peace be upon him) a hundred times, and disavows his own power and strength and seeks refuge in God, then says: 'I bear witness that there is no god but God, and I bear witness that Adam is the chosen one of God and His primordial nature, Abraham is the friend (khalīl) of God, Moses is the interlocutor (kalīm) of God, Jesus is the spirit (rūḥ) of God, and Muḥammad is the beloved (ḥabīb) of God' — he will have a reward equal to the number of those who ascribed a son to God and those who did not ascribe a son to God, and God, mighty and majestic, will raise him on the Day of Resurrection with the secure ones, and it is incumbent upon God, exalted be He, to admit him to Paradise with the prophets."

**Monday Night:** Al-Aʿmash narrated from Anas, who said: The Messenger of God (peace be upon him) said: "Whoever prays on Monday night four rakʿahs, reciting in the first rakʿah 'Praise be to God' and 'Say: He is God, One' eleven times, in the second rakʿah 'Praise be to God' and 'Say: He is God, One' twenty times, in the third 'Praise be to God' and 'Say: He is God, One' thirty times, and in the fourth 'Praise be to God' and 'Say: He is God, One' forty times, then salutes and recites 'Say: He is God, One' seventy-five times, and seeks forgiveness from God for himself and his parents seventy-five times, then asks God for his need — it is incumbent upon God to grant him his request, whatever he asks." This is the prayer of need (ṣalāt al-ḥājah).

**Tuesday Night:** Whoever prays two rakʿahs, reciting in each rakʿah the Opening of the Book, 'Say: He is God, One', and the two refuge-seeking chapters fifteen times, and recites after the salutation the Throne Verse fifteen times, and seeks forgiveness from God, exalted be He, fifteen times, will have a great reward and a mighty recompense. It is also narrated from ʿUmar (may God be pleased with him) from the Prophet (peace be upon him) that he said: "Whoever prays on Tuesday night two rakʿahs, reciting in each rakʿah the Opening of the Book once, 'Indeed, We sent it down' (Innā Anzalnāhu) and 'Say: He is God, One' seven times, God frees his neck from the Fire, and on the Day of Resurrection he will have a leader and a guide to Paradise."

**Wednesday Night:** Fāṭimah (may God be pleased with her) narrated from the Prophet (peace be upon him) that he said: "Whoever prays on Wednesday night two rakʿahs, reciting in the first the Opening of the Book and 'Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the Dawn' (Qul Aʿūdhu bi-Rabb al-Falaq) ten times, and in the second after the Opening 'Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of Mankind' (Qul Aʿūdhu bi-Rabb al-Nās) ten times, then when he salutes seeks forgiveness from God ten times, then sends blessings upon Muḥammad (peace be upon him) ten times, seventy thousand angels descend from each heaven, writing his reward until the Day of Resurrection." In another narration: sixteen rakʿahs, reciting after the Opening whatever God wills, and reciting at the end of the last two rakʿahs the Throne Verse thirty times, and in the first two 'Say: He is God, One' thirty times — he will intercede for ten of his household, all of whom were destined for the Fire. Fāṭimah (may God be pleased with her) also narrated that she said: The Messenger of God (peace be upon him) said: "Whoever prays on Wednesday night six rakʿahs, reciting in a rakʿah after the Opening 'Say: O God, Possessor of the Kingdom' (Qul Allāhumma Mālik al-Mulk) to the end of the verse, then when he finishes his prayer says: 'May God reward Muḥammad on our behalf as he deserves' — sins of seventy years are forgiven him, and a writ of freedom from the Fire is written for him."

**Thursday Night:** Abū Hurayrah (may God be pleased with him) said: The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "Whoever prays on Thursday night between the sunset (Maghrib) and night (ʿIshāʾ) prayers two rakʿahs, reciting in each rakʿah the Opening of the Book, the Throne Verse five times, 'Say: He is God, One' five times, and the two refuge-seeking chapters five times, then when he finishes his prayer seeks forgiveness from God, exalted be He, fifteen times and assigns its reward to his parents — he has fulfilled the right of his parents upon him, even if he had been undutiful to them, and God, exalted be He, gives him what He gives to the truthful (ṣiddīqīn) and the martyrs."

**Friday Night:** Jābir said: The Messenger of God (peace be upon him) said: "Whoever prays on Friday night between the sunset (Maghrib) and night (ʿIshāʾ) prayers twelve rakʿahs, reciting in each rakʿah the Opening of the Book once and 'Say: He is God, One' eleven times, it is as if he worshipped God, exalted be He, for twelve years, fasting its days and standing its nights." Anas said: The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "Whoever prays on Friday night the final night prayer (ʿIshāʾ al-ākhirah) in congregation, prays the two sunnah rakʿahs, then prays after them ten rakʿahs, reciting in each rakʿah the Opening of the Book, 'Say: He is God, One', and the two refuge-seeking chapters once each, then performs the witr with three rakʿahs and sleeps on his right side facing the qiblah — it is as if he revived the Night of Decree (Laylat al-Qadr)." And he (peace be upon him) said: "Send abundant blessings upon me on the radiant night and the luminous day — the night of Friday and the day of Friday."

**Saturday Night:** Anas said: The Messenger of God (peace be upon him) said: "Whoever prays on Saturday night between the sunset (Maghrib) and night (ʿIshāʾ) prayers twelve rakʿahs, a palace is built for him in Paradise, and it is as if he gave charity to every believing male and female, and he disavows the Jews, and it is incumbent upon God to forgive him."
