- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Clause (al-Sharṭ wa al-Jawāb) — The particle "in" (if) governs a protasis and apodosis; here, "if the cash was a full niṣāb" sets the legal condition for the ḥawl's commencement, with the apodosis implied in the ruling that follows.
chapters.translation:
I say: The fourth kind is the zakāh on trade goods (zakat al-tijārah).

It is like the zakāh on the two currencies (al-naqdayn) [gold and silver]. The annual cycle (al-ḥawl) is only reckoned from the moment one possesses the cash with which the merchandise was purchased — if that cash constituted a full niṣāb. But if it was deficient [of the niṣāb], or if one purchased [the goods] with a commodity (ʿaraḍ) intending trade, then the ḥawl is reckoned from the time of purchase.

The zakāh is paid from the currency of the land (naqd al-balad), and by it the goods are valued. However, if the means of purchase was cash and it was a complete niṣāb, then valuation by that [same cash] is more appropriate than by the currency of the land.

Whoever intends trade with wealth that was [originally] for personal use (māl qunyah) — the ḥawl does not commence by mere intention alone, until he purchases something with it. And whenever he abandons the intention of trade before the completion of the ḥawl, the zakāh lapses.

The preferred [practice] is that the zakāh of that year be paid [from the goods themselves]. Whatever profit (ribḥ) accrues in the commodity at the end of the ḥawl, the zakāh becomes obligatory upon it by virtue of the ḥawl of the principal capital — no new ḥawl is initiated for it, just as in the case of livestock offspring (al-nitāj).

The wealth of money-changers (al-ṣayārifah) — its ḥawl is not interrupted by the exchanges (al-mubādalah) that occur among them, just as in all other trades.

The zakāh on the profit of partnership capital (māl al-qirāḍ) falls upon the working partner (al-ʿāmil), even if [it is assessed] before division — this is the more sound analogy (al-aqyas).

chapters.title_en: The Fifth Type: Buried Treasure (Rikāz) and Mines (Maʿdin)
chapters.arabic_text:
||| النوع الخامس الركاز والمعدن

والركاز مال دفن في الجاهلية ووجد في أرض لم يجر عليها في الإسلام ملك
فعلى واجده في الذهب والفضة منه الخمس والحول غير معتبر
والأولى أن لا يعتبر النصاب أيضا لأن إيجاب الخمس يؤكد شبهه بالغنيمة
واعتباره أيضا ليس ببعيد لأن مصرف الزكاة ولذلك يخصص على الصحيح بالنقدين
وأما المعادن فلا زكاة فيما استخرج منها سوى الذهب والفضة ففيها بعد
الطحن والتخليص ربع العشر على أصح القولين وعلى هذا يعتبر النصاب
وفي الحول قولان وفي قول يجب الخمس فعلى هذا لا يعتبر
وفي النصاب قولان والأشبه والعلم عند الله تعالى أن يلحق في قدر الواجب
بزكاة التجارة فإنه نوع اكتساب
وفي الحول بالمعشرات فلا يعتبر لأنه عين الرفق ويعتبر النصاب كالمعشرات
والاحتياط أن يخرج الخمس من القليل والكثير ومن عين النقدين أيضا خروجا عن
شبهة هذه الاختلافات فإنها ظنون قريبة من التعارض وجزم الفتوى فيها خطر
لتعارض الاشتباه
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ر-ك-ز (r-k-z)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To fix firmly, implant, or bury in the earth; a buried hoard (rikāz) is that which is deposited and concealed in the ground.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal-theological usage, rikāz denotes pre-Islamic buried wealth, treated as a category akin to spoils of war (ghanīmah) due to its unowned, extracted nature.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense is 'fixed in place' (ḥaqīqah); the legal application to buried treasure is a transferred usage (majāz) by customary extension, as the wealth is 'fixed' in the earth.
- Root: ع-د-ن (ʿ-d-n)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To abide, remain, or settle; a mine (maʿdin) is a place where minerals are permanently lodged in the earth.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Denotes a natural source of extracted substances; in fiqh, it contrasts with rikāz as a continuous, non-buried deposit.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal 'permanent abode'; metaphorically applied to the earth's mineral-bearing strata.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Conditional Restriction (Taqyīd bi-al-Sharṭ) — The phrase "found in land over which no Muslim ownership has passed" restricts the legal scope of rikāz, requiring the condition of unowned, pre-Islamic land for the obligation to apply.
chapters.translation:
I say: The fifth type is buried treasure (rikāz) and mines (maʿdin).

Buried treasure is wealth buried in the pre-Islamic era (jāhiliyyah) and found in land over which no ownership has passed in Islam. Upon its finder, in gold and silver from it, is the fifth (khums), and the lapse of a full year (ḥawl) is not considered. It is preferable that the minimum threshold (niṣāb) also not be considered, because the obligation of the fifth strengthens its resemblance to spoils of war (ghanīmah). Yet considering it is not far-fetched either, because its disbursement is that of alms (zakāh), and for this reason it is restricted, on the soundest view, to the two coinages (gold and silver).

As for mines, there is no alms on what is extracted from them save gold and silver. In these, after grinding and purification, is a quarter of a tenth (rubʿ al-ʿushr) on the sounder of the two opinions. On this view, the niṣāb is considered. Regarding the ḥawl, there are two opinions. In one opinion, the fifth is obligatory, and on this view it is not considered. Regarding the niṣāb, there are two opinions. The most fitting—and knowledge is with God most High—is that it be annexed, in the measure of the obligatory amount, to the alms of trade (zakāh al-tijārah), for it is a type of acquisition. And in the ḥawl, it is annexed to the tithed crops (al-muʿashsharāt), so it is not considered, because it is the very essence of leniency; and the niṣāb is considered, as with tithed crops. The cautious course is to pay the fifth from little and much, and from the very substance of the two coinages, in departure from the shadow of these disagreements—for they are conjectures close to mutual contradiction, and issuing a definitive legal verdict therein is perilous, due to the conflict of ambiguities.

chapters.title_en: The Sixth Kind: The Alms of Fast-Breaking (Ṣadaqat al-Fiṭr)
chapters.arabic_text:
||| النوع السادس في صدقة الفطر

وهي واجبة على لسان رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم على كل مسلم فضل عن
قوته وقوت من يقوته يوم الفطر وليلته صاع مما يقتات (1) بصاع رسول الله صلى
الله عليه وسلم وهو منوان وثلثا من يخرجه من جنس قوته أو من أفضل منه
فإن اقتات بالحنطة لم يجز الشعير
وإن اقتات حبوبا مختلفة اختار خيرها ومن أيها أخرج أجزأه
وقسمتها كقسمة زكاة الأموال فيجب فيها استيعاب الأصناف ولا يجوز إخراج
الدقيق والسويق
ويجب على الرجل المسلم فطرة زوجته ومماليكه وأولاده وكل قريب هو في نفقته
أعني من تجب عليه نفقته من الآباء والأمهات والأولاد قال صلى الله عليه
وسلم أدوا صدقة الفطر عمن تمونون (2) وتجب  صدقة العبد المشترك على الشريكين
ولا تجب صدقة العبد الكافر
وإن تبرعت الزوجة بالإخراج عن نفسها أجزأها وللزوج الإخراج عنها دون
إذنها
وإن فضل عنه ما يؤدى عن بعضهم أدى عن بعضهم وأولاهم بالتقديم من كانت
نفقته آكد
وقد PageV01P211
قدم رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم نفقة الولد على نفقة الزوجة ونفقتها
على نفقة الخادم (1) فهذه أحكام فقهية لا بد للغني من معرفتها وقد تعرض له
وقائع نادرة خارجة عن هذا فله أن يتكل فيها على الاستفتاء عند نزول الواقعة
بعد إحاطته بهذا المقدار
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ف-ط-ر (fa-ṭā-ra)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The act of breaking a fast; the innate disposition (fiṭrah) upon which creation is formed; the beginning of a thing.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The obligatory alms tied to the completion of Ramaḍān, purifying the faster from indecency and feeding the needy—a divinely ordained act of gratitude.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense is 'splitting' or 'cleaving' (as in dawn breaking); here it is metaphorical (majāz) for the festival marking the end of fasting.
- Root: ق-و-ت (q-w-t)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Sustenance, nourishment; that which maintains life and bodily strength.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The staple foodstuff (qūt) by which one sustains himself and his dependents—the baseline for determining surplus wealth.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: physical nourishment; metaphorical: the measure of one's daily provision as the threshold of sufficiency.
- Root: ن-ف-ق (n-f-q)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Expenditure, spending; the means by which one maintains another.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The obligatory maintenance (nafaqah) owed to dependents—a legal duty rooted in kinship and ownership.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: disbursement of wealth; metaphorical: the legal obligation of support that binds the provider.
- Sībawayh Rule: The Rule of Conditional Precedence (Taqdīm al-Sharṭ)—the clause "if he has surplus" (fa-in faḍala) establishes a conditional framework governing the obligation, with the apodosis (jawāb al-sharṭ) determining the scope of duty.
chapters.translation:
I say: The sixth kind concerns the alms of fast-breaking (ṣadaqat al-fiṭr).

It is obligatory by the tongue of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, upon every Muslim who possesses a surplus beyond his own sustenance and the sustenance of those whom he maintains on the day of fast-breaking and its night—a ṣāʿ (measure) of that which serves as his staple food, measured by the ṣāʿ of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, which is two mudds and two-thirds. He must give it from the same kind as his staple food, or from what is superior to it. For if his staple is wheat, barley is not permissible for him. And if his staple consists of various grains, he chooses the best of them, and whichever of them he gives, it suffices him.

Its distribution is like the distribution of the alms of wealth (zakāt al-amwāl): it is obligatory therein to cover all eight categories [of recipients], and it is not permissible to give flour or toasted grain (sawīq).

It is obligatory upon the Muslim man to pay the fiṭr alms for his wife, his slaves, his children, and every relative who is under his maintenance—I mean, those whose maintenance is obligatory upon him, from fathers, mothers, and children. He said, may Allah bless him and grant him peace: "Pay the alms of fast-breaking on behalf of those whom you maintain" {أدوا صدقة الفطر عمن تمونون}. The alms of a jointly-owned slave is obligatory upon both partners [in proportion to their shares], but the alms of an unbelieving slave is not obligatory.

If the wife voluntarily gives on her own behalf, it suffices her; and the husband may give on her behalf without her permission.

And if there remains surplus [sufficient] to pay for some of them, he pays for some of them, and the most deserving of precedence is the one whose maintenance is more firmly incumbent. The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, gave precedence to the maintenance of the child over the maintenance of the wife, and her maintenance over that of the servant. These are jurisprudential rulings (aḥkām fiqhiyyah) which the wealthy man must know. Rare cases may befall him beyond this, and he may rely in them upon seeking a formal legal opinion (istiftāʾ) when the case arises, after he has encompassed this measure [of knowledge].

chapters.title_en: Section 92 — On the Payment of Zakāh and Its Inward and Outward Conditions
chapters.arabic_text:
|| الفصل الثاني في الأداء وشروطه الباطنة والظاهرة

اعلم أنه يجب على مؤدى الزكاة خمسة أمور
الأول النية وهو أن ينوي بقلبه زكاة الفرض ويسن عليه تعيين الأموال
فإن كان له مال غائب فقال هذا عن مالي الغائب إن كان سالما وإلا فهو
نافلة جاز لأنه إن لم يصرح به فكذلك يكون عند إطلاقه
ونية الولي تقوم مقام نية المجنون والصبي
ونية السلطان تقوم مقام نية المالك الممتنع عن الزكاة ولكن في ظاهر حكم
الدنيا أعني في قطع المطالبة عنه أما في الآخرة فلا بل تبقى ذمته مشغولة
إلى أن يستأنف الزكاة وإذا وكل بأداء الزكاة ونوى عند التوكيل أو وكل
الوكيل بالنية كفاه لأن توكيله بالنية نية
الثاني البدار عقيب الحول وفي زكاة الفطر لا يؤخرها عن يوم الفطر
ويدخل وقت وجوبها بغروب الشمس من آخر يوم من شهر رمضان ووقت تعجيلها شهر
رمضان كله
ومن أخر زكاة ماله مع التمكن عصى ولم يسقط عنه بتلف ماله وتمكنه بمصادقة
المستحق
وإن أخر لعدم المستحق فتلف ماله سقطت الزكاة عنه
وتعجيل الزكاة جائز بشرط أن يقع بعد كمال النصاب وانعقاد الحول
ويجوز تعجيل زكاة حولين
ومهما عجل فمات المسكين قبل الحول أو ارتد أو صار غنيا بغير ما عجل إليه
أو تلف مال المالك أو مات فالمدفوع ليس بزكاة واسترجاعه غير ممكن إلا إذا
قيد الدفع بالاسترجاع فليكن المعجل مراقبا آخر الأمور وسلامة العاقبة
الثالث أن لا  يخرج بدلا باعتبار القيمة بل يخرج المنصوص عليه فلا يجزىء
ورق عن ذهب ولا ذهب عن ورق وإن زاد عليه في القيمة
ولعل بعض من لا يدرك غرض الشافعي رضي الله عنه يتساهل في ذلك ويلاحظ
المقصود من سد الخلة وما أبعده عن التحصيل فإن سد الخلة مقصود وليس هو كل
المقصود بل واجبات الشرع ثلاثة أقسام قسم هو تعبد محض لا مدخل للحظوظ
والأغراض فيه
وذلك كرمي الجمرات مثلا إذ لا حظ للجمرة في وصول الحصى إليها فمقصود
الشرع فيه الابتلاء بالعمل ليظهر العبد رقه وعبودته بفعل ما لا يعقل له
معنى لأن ما يعقل معناه فقد يساعده الطبع عليه ويدعوه إليه فلا يظهر به
خلوص الرق والعبودية إذ العبودية تظهر بأن تكون الحركة لحق أمر المعبود فقط
لا لمعنى آخر وأكثر أعمال الحج كذلك ولذلك قال صلى الله عليه وسلم في
إحرامه لبيك بحجة حقا تعبدا ورقا (2) تنبيها على أن ذلك إظهار للعبودية
بالانقياد لمجرد الأمر وامتثاله كما أمر من غير استئناس العقل منه بما يميل
إليه ويحث عليه
القسم الثاني من واجبات الشرع ما المقصود منه حظ معقول وليس يقصد منه
التعبد كقضاء دين الآدميين ورد المغصوب فلا جرم لا يعتبر فيه فعله ونيته
ومهما وصل الحق إلى مستحقه بأخذ المستحق أو ببدل عنه عند رضاه تأدى
الوجوب وسقط خطاب الشرع
فهذان قسمان لا تركيب فيهما يشترك في دركهما جميع الناس
والقسم الثالث هو المركب الذي يقصد منه الأمران جميعا وهو حظ العباد
وامتحان المكلف بالاستعباد فيجتمع فيه تعبد رمي الجمار وحظ رد الحقوق فهذا
قسم في نفسه معقول فإن ورد الشرع به وجب الجمع بين المعنيين ولا ينبغي أن
PageV01P212
ينسى أدق المعنيين وهو التعبد والاسترقاق بسبب أجلاهما ولعل الأدق هو
الأهم والزكاة من هذا القبيل ولم ينتبه له غير الشافعي رضي الله عنه فحظ
الفقير مقصود في سد الخلة وهو جلي سابق إلى الأفهام وحق التعبد في اتباع
التفاصيل مقصود للشرع
وباعتباره صارت الزكاة قرينة للصلاة  والحج في كونها من مباني الإسلام
ولا شك في أن على المكلف تعبا في تمييز أجناس ماله وإخراج حصة كل مال من
نوعه وجنسه وصفته ثم توزيعه على الأصناف الثمانية كما سيأتي والتساهل فيه
غير قادح في حظ الفقير لكنه قادح في التعبد
ويدل على أن التعبد مقصود بتعيين الأنواع أمور ذكرناها في كتب الخلاف من
الفقهيات
ومن أوضحها أن الشرع أوجب في خمس من الإبل شاة فعدل من الإبل إلى الشاة
ولم يعدل إلى النقدين والتقويم وإن قدر أن ذلك لقلة النقود في أيدي العرب
بطل بذكره عشرين درهما في الجبران مع الشاتين فلم يذكر في الجبران قدر
النقصان من القيمة ولمقدر بعشرين درهما وشاتين وإن كانت الثياب والأمتعة
كلها في معناها
فهذا وأمثاله من التخصيصات يدل على أن الزكاة لم تترك خالية عن التعبدات
كما في الحج ولكن جمع بين المعنيين والأذهان الضعيفة تقصر عن درك المركبات
فهذا شأن الغلط فيه
الرابع أن لا ينقل الصدقة إلى بلد آخر فإن أعين المساكين في كل بلدة تمتد
إلى أموالها وفي النقل تخييب للظنون فإن فعل ذلك أجزأه في قول ولكن الخروج
عن شبهة الخلاف أولى فليخرج زكاة كل مال في تلك البلدة ثم لا بأس أن يصرف
إلى الغرباء في تلك البلدة
الخامس أن يقسم ماله بعدد الأصناف الموجودين في بلده فإن استيعاب الأصناف
واجب وعليه يدل ظاهر قوله تعالى إنما الصدقات للفقراء والمساكين الآية فإنه
يشبه قول المريض إنما ثلث مال للفقراء والمساكين وذلك يقتضي التشريك في
التمليك
والعبادات ينبغي أن يتوقى عن الهجوم فيها على الظواهر
وقد عدم من الثمانية
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ن-و-ي (n-w-y)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Intent, purpose, resolve directed toward an object; the heart's aim.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The distinguishing mark of worship (ʿibādah) separating it from mere habit; intention is the soul's orientation toward the command.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal in the heart's resolve; metaphorical when applied to the tongue's utterance alone.
- Root: ع-ج-ل (ʿ-j-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Haste, promptness, precedence in time.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal context, performing an obligation before its appointed time (taʿjīl) versus at its due moment (badar).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for temporal acceleration; metaphorical for eagerness of compliance.
- Root: ب-د-ل (b-d-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Substitution, exchange, replacement of one thing for another.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In worship, substituting the specified species (jins) with another violates the servitude (ʿubūdiyyah) inherent in following detailed prescriptions.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for exchange of goods; metaphorical for deviating from the revealed command.
- Root: ق-س-م (q-s-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Division, apportionment, distribution into parts.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The equitable distribution among the eight categories (aṣnāf) as a legal obligation, not a discretionary act.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for dividing shares; metaphorical for the comprehensive coverage of all entitled classes.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Constructions (al-sharṭ wa al-istithnāʾ) — The phrase "إن كان سالما وإلا فهو نافلة" employs a conditional protasis with an implicit apodosis, governing the legal validity of the payment's classification.
chapters.translation:
Know that five matters are obligatory upon the payer of zakāh.

The first is intention (niyyah), namely that he intend in his heart the obligatory zakāh (zakāt al-farḍ). It is recommended (sunna) for him to specify the wealth [from which it is paid]. If he has absent wealth and says, "This is from my absent wealth — if it is safe [and reaches me], then it is zakāh; otherwise it is supererogatory (nāfilah)," this is permissible, because even if he does not explicitly state this, the same [conditional] result obtains when he makes an unqualified utterance.

The intention of the guardian (walī) stands in place of the intention of the insane person and the minor. The intention of the ruler (sulṭān) stands in place of the intention of the owner who refuses to pay zakāh — but only in the outward ruling of this world, namely in absolving him from being pursued [by the authorities]. As for the Hereafter, no; rather his liability (dhimmah) remains burdened until he renews the zakāh. If he appoints an agent (wakīl) to pay the zakāh and intends [the zakāh] at the time of appointment, or the agent intends on his behalf, this suffices him, because his appointment of the agent with the intention is itself an intention.

The second is promptness (bidār) immediately upon the completion of the year (ḥawl). As for the zakāh of the Fast-Breaking (zakāt al-fiṭr), he must not delay it past the day of Fiṭr. Its time of obligation enters with the setting of the sun on the last day of Ramaḍān, and its time of acceleration (taʿjīl) is the entire month of Ramaḍān.

Whoever delays the zakāh of his wealth while able [to pay it] has sinned, and it is not remitted from him by the destruction of his wealth, nor by his ability [to pay] being nullified through the absence of a deserving recipient. But if he delayed it due to the unavailability of a deserving recipient and his wealth was then destroyed, the zakāh is remitted from him.

Accelerating the zakāh (taʿjīl) is permissible on the condition that it occurs after the completion of the niṣāb and the full formation of the year. It is permissible to accelerate the zakāh of two years. Whenever he accelerates [the payment] and the poor person dies before the year [completes], or apostatizes, or becomes wealthy by means other than what was given to him, or the owner's wealth is destroyed, or he dies — then what was paid is not zakāh, and its retrieval is not possible unless he conditioned the payment upon retrieval. Thus the one who accelerates should be watchful of the final outcomes and the safety of the end.

The third is that he should not pay a substitute (badal) based on value, but rather pay what is specified by the text (al-manṣūṣ ʿalayh). Thus silver (waraq) does not suffice for gold, nor gold for silver, even if it exceeds it in value.

Perhaps some who do not grasp the purpose of al-Shāfiʿī — may God be pleased with him — are lenient in this matter, observing only the aim of filling need (sadd al-khallah). How far they are from true attainment! For filling need is an aim, but it is not the whole aim. Rather, the obligations of the Sacred Law are of three divisions:

The first division is pure devotion (taʿabbud) with no entry for interests or purposes. This is like the stoning of the jamarāt, for example, since the jamrah has no interest in the pebbles reaching it. The Law's purpose therein is trial through the act, so that the servant manifests his servitude and bondage (riqq) by doing what he comprehends no meaning for — because what he comprehends its meaning, nature may assist him in it and call him to it, so pure servitude and bondage are not manifested thereby. For servitude is manifested when the movement is solely for the right of the command of the Master, not for any other meaning. Most of the acts of the Pilgrimage are likewise. For this reason, he — peace and blessings be upon him — said in his iḥrām: "Labbayk with a true ḥajj, in devotion and servitude," {«لبيك بحجة حقا تعبدا ورقا»} — alerting that this is a manifestation of servitude through submission to the bare command and compliance with it as commanded, without the intellect deriving from it any inclination or incitement.

The second division of the Law's obligations is that whose purpose is a rational interest, with devotion not intended — like repaying the debts of human beings and returning usurped property. Hence, no account is taken of the agent's act and intention; whenever the right reaches its possessor — whether by the possessor's taking it or by a substitute for it with his consent — the obligation is discharged and the address of the Law is lifted.

These two divisions contain no composition, and all people share in comprehending them.

The third division is the composite (al-murakkab), which intends both matters together: the interest of the servants and the trial of the obligated one through enslavement (istirqāq). Thus there combine in it the devotion of stoning the jamarāt and the interest of returning rights. This division is in itself intelligible; when the Law has brought it, it is obligatory to combine both meanings. One should not forget the subtler of the two meanings — namely devotion and enslavement — because of their being more manifest; perhaps the subtler is the more important. Zakāh is of this kind, and none but al-Shāfiʿī — may God be pleased with him — has attended to this. The poor person's interest in filling need is intended, and it is manifest, preceding to the understandings; but the right of devotion in following the detailed prescriptions is intended by the Law. By virtue of this, zakāh became paired with prayer and pilgrimage in being among the foundations of Islam.

There is no doubt that upon the obligated one there is toil in distinguishing the species of his wealth and extracting the share of each wealth from its type, kind, and description, then distributing it among the eight categories as will come. Leniency in this does not harm the poor person's interest, but it harms the devotion.

That devotion is intended by the specification of the types is indicated by matters we have mentioned in the books of legal disagreement (khilāf) among the jurisprudential works. Among the clearest of them is that the Law obligated in five camels one sheep — it turned from camels to sheep and did not turn to the two currencies or valuation. If one supposed that this was due to the scarcity of coins in the hands of the Arabs, this is refuted by its mentioning twenty dirhams in the compensation (jabrān) along with the two sheep — for it did not mention in the compensation the amount of the deficiency in value, though it could have been estimated by twenty dirhams and two sheep, even if garments and goods were all equivalent to it. This and its like, from the specifications, indicate that zakāh was not left devoid of devotions as in the pilgrimage, but rather combined both meanings. Weak minds fall short of comprehending composites — this is the matter of error therein.

The fourth is that he should not transfer the charity (ṣadaqah) to another town. For the eyes of the poor in every town extend to its own wealth, and in transfer there is a disappointment of expectations. If he does this, it suffices him according to one opinion, but exiting from the doubt of disagreement is more appropriate. So let him pay the zakāh of each wealth in that town; then there is no harm in disbursing it to strangers within that town.

The fifth is that he should divide his wealth according to the number of categories (aṣnāf) present in his town. For covering all the categories is obligatory, and the apparent meaning of His saying — exalted be He — {«إِنَّمَا الصَّدَقَاتُ لِلْفُقَرَاءِ وَالْمَسَاكِينِ»} "The charities are only for the poor and the needy..." indicates this. For it resembles the saying of a sick person: "Only a third of my wealth is for the poor and the needy" — and that entails sharing in ownership.

In acts of worship, one should be wary of rushing into apparent meanings. Two of the eight categories are absent in most lands — namely those whose hearts are reconciled (al-muʾallafah qulūbuhum) and the workers upon the zakāh. Four categories are found in all lands: the poor (fuqarāʾ), the needy (masākīn), the debtors (ghārimūn), and the travelers (musāfirūn) — I mean the wayfarers (abnāʾ al-sabīl). Two categories are found in some lands but not others: the fighters (ghuzāh) and the slaves contracting manumission (mukātabūn).

If, for example, five categories are found, he divides his zakāh among them into five equal or approximate portions, assigns to each category its portion, then divides each portion into three shares or more — either equal or varying. He is not obligated to equalize among the individuals of a single category, for he may divide it among ten or twenty, thereby reducing each one's share. As for the categories, they do not admit increase or decrease; he should not reduce any category below three [recipients] if they are found. Then, if only one ṣāʿ of Fiṭr is obligatory and five categories are found, he must deliver it to fifteen persons. If he reduces one of them while able, he forfeits the share of that one. If this is difficult for him due to the smallness of the obligation, then let a group of those upon whom zakāh is obligatory participate, mixing his wealth with theirs, gathering the deserving recipients, and handing it to them so that they draw lots among themselves for it — for this is unavoidable.

chapters.title_en: Exposition of the Subtleties of the Inward Etiquettes of Alms (Zakāh)
chapters.arabic_text:
||| بيان دقائق الآداب الباطنة في الزكاة

اعلم أن على مريد طريق الآخرة بزكاته وظائف الوظيفة الأولى فهم وجوب
الزكاة ومعناها ووجه الامتحان فيها وأنها لم جعلت من مباني الإسلام مع أنها
تصرف مالي وليست من عبادة الأبدان وفيه ثلاث معان الأول أن التلفظ بكلمتي
الشهادة التزام للتوحيد وشهادة بإفراد المعبود وشرط تمام الوفاء به أن لا
يبقى للموحد محبوب سوى الواحد الفرد فإن المحبة لا تقبل الشركة والتوحيد
باللسان قليل الجدوى وإنما يمتحن به درجة المحب بمفارقة المحبوب والأموال
محبوبة عند الخلائق لأنها آلة تمتعهم بالدنيا وبسببها يأنسون بهذا العالم
وينفرون عن الموت مع أن فيه لقاء المحبوب فامتحنوا بتصديق دعواهم في
المحبوب واستنزلوا عن المال الذي هو مرموقهم ومعشوقهم ولذلك قال
PageV01P213
{الله تعالى} إن الله اشترى من المؤمنين أنفسهم وأموالهم بأن لهم الجنة
وذلك بالجهاد وهو مسامحة بالمهجة شوقا إلى لقاء الله عز وجل والمسامحة
بالمال أهون
ولما فهم هذا المعنى في بذل الأموال انقسم الناس إلى ثلاثة أقسام قسم
صدقوا التوحيد ووفوا بعهدهم ونزلوا عن جميع أموالهم فلم يدخروا دينارا ولا
درهما فأبوا أن يتعرضوا لوجوب الزكاة عليهم حتى قيل لبعضهم كم يجب من
الزكاة في مائتي درهم فقال أما على العوام بحكم الشرع فخمسة دراهم وأما نحن
فيجب علينا بذل الجميع ولهذا تصدق أبو بكر رضي الله عنه بجميع ماله وعمر
رضي الله عنه  بشطر ماله فقال صلى الله عليه وسلم ما أبقيت لأهلك فقال مثله
وقال لأبي بكر رضي الله عنه ما أبقيت لأهلك قال الله ورسوله فقال صلى الله
عليه وسلم بينكما ما بين كلمتيكما (1) فالصديق وفي بتمام الصدق فلم يمسك
سوى المحبوب عنده وهو الله ورسوله
القسم الثاني درجتهم دون درجة هذا وهم الممسكون أموالهم المراقبون
لمواقيت الحاجات ومواسم الخيرات فيكون قصدهم في الادخار الإنفاق على قدر
الحاجة دون التنعم وصرف الفاضل عن الحاجة إلى وجوه البر مهما ظهر وجوهها
وهؤلاء لا يقتصرون على مقدار الزكاة
وقد ذهب جماعة من التابعين إلى أن في المال حقوقا سوى الزكاة كالنخعي
والشعبي وعطاء ومجاهد قال الشعبي بعد أن قيل له هل في المال حق سوى الزكاة
قال نعم أما سمعت قوله عز وجل وآتى المال على حبه ذوي القربى الآية
واستدلوا بقوله عز وجل ومما رزقناهم ينفقون وبقوله تعالى وأنفقوا مما
رزقناكم وزعموا أن ذلك غير منسوخ بآية الزكاة بل هو داخل في حق المسلم على
المسلم ومعناه أنه يجب على الموسر مهما وجد محتاجا أن يزيل حاجته فضلا عن
مال الزكاة والذي يصح في الفقه من هذا الباب أنه مهما أرهقته حاجته كانت
إزالتها فرض كفاية إذ لا يجوز تضييع مسلم ولكن يحتمل أن يقال ليس على
الموسر إلا تسليم ما يزيل الحاجة فرضا ولا يلزمه بذله بعد أن أسقط الزكاة
عن نفسه ويحتمل أن يقال يلزمه بذله في الحال ولا يجوز له الاقتراض أي لا
يجوز له تكليف الفقير قبول القرض وهذا مختلف فيه والاقتراض نزول إلى الدرجة
الأخيرة من درجات العوام وهي درجة القسم الثالث الذين يقتصرون على أداء
الواجب فلا يزيدون عليه ولا ينقصون عنه وهي أقل الرتب وقد اقتصر جميع
العوام عليه لبخلهم بالمال وميلهم إليه وضعف حبهم للآخرة قال الله تعالى إن
يسألكموها فيحفكم تبخلوا يحفكم أي يستقص عليكم فكم بين عبد اشترى منه ماله
ونفسه بأن له الجنة وبين عبد لا يستقصي عليه لبخله فهذا أحد  معاني أمر الله
سبحانه عباده ببذل الأموال
المعنى الثاني التطهير من صفة البخل فإنه من المهلكات قال صلى الله عليه
وسلم ثلاث مهلكات شح مطاع وهوى متبع وإعجاب المرء بنفسه (2) وقال تعالى ومن
يوق شح نفسه فأولئك هم المفلحون وسيأتي في ربع المهلكات وجه كونه مهلكا
وكيفية التقصي منه وإنما تزول صفة البخل بأن تتعود بذل المال فحب الشيء لا
ينقطع إلا بقهر النفس على مفارقته حتى يصير ذلك اعتيادا فالزكاة بهذا
المعنى طهرة أي تطهر صاحبها عن خبث البخل المهلك وإنما طهارته بقدر بذله
وبقدر فرحه بإخراجه واستبشاره بصرفه إلى الله تعالى
المعنى الثالث شكر النعمة فإن لله عز وجل على عبده نعمة في نفسه وفي ماله
فالعبادات البدنية شكر لنعمة البدن والمالية شكر لنعمة المال وما أخس من
ينظر إلى الفقير وقد ضيق عليه الرزق وأحوج إليه ثم لا تسمح نفسه بأن يؤدي
شكر الله تعالى على إغنائه عن السؤال وإحواج غيره إليه بربع العشر أو العشر
من ماله PageV01P214
الوظيفة الثانية في وقت الأداء ومن آداب ذوي الدين التعجيل عن وقت الوجوب
إظهارا للرغبة في الامتثال بإيصال السرور إلى قلوب الفقراء ومبادرة لعوائق
الزمان أن تعوقه عن الخيرات وعلما بأن في التأخير آفات مع ما يتعرض العبد
له من العصيان لو أخر عن وقت الوجوب
ومهما ظهرت داعية الخير من الباطن فينبغي أن يغتنم فإن ذلك لمة الملك
وقلب المؤمن بين أصبعين من أصابع الرحمن فما أسرع تقلبه والشيطان يعد الفقر
ويأمر بالفحشاء والمنكر وله لمة
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ز-ك-و (z-k-w)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Growth, increase, purification; the core sense is that of a thing becoming pure and thriving.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Zakāh is that which purifies the soul from avarice (shuḥḥ) and causes the wealth to grow in divine reckoning; it is a spiritual cultivation.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Used literally (ḥaqīqah) for purification of the soul; metaphorically (majāz) for the growth of wealth through divine blessing.
- Root: م-ح-ن (m-ḥ-n)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To test, to try, to refine; the root implies a trial that distinguishes the sincere from the insincere.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The divine trial (imtiḥān) that manifests the degree of one's love for God against love of worldly things.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal testing by affliction; here, a metaphorical testing of the heart's claim to love God alone.
- Root: ب-خ-ل (b-kh-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Avarice, withholding what one possesses; a blameworthy trait of hoarding.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A destructive vice (muhlikah) that opposes the virtue of generosity and trust in God's provision.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal stinginess with wealth; metaphorically, a spiritual disease of the heart that withholds love from God.
- Sībawayh Rule: The Rule of Conditional Emphasis (al-Sharṭ wa al-Jazā') — In sentences like "if you give, you are purified," the protasis and apodosis are structured to emphasize the causal link between the act and its spiritual consequence, requiring precise parsing of the conditional particles (in, idhā) to convey the necessary outcome.
chapters.translation:
I say: Know that upon the aspirant to the path of the Hereafter, with respect to his alms (zakāh), there are certain duties. The first duty is the understanding of the obligation of zakāh, its meaning, and the aspect of trial (imtiḥān) contained within it — namely, why it was made one of the foundations of Islam, despite being a financial expenditure and not a bodily act of worship. In this there are three meanings.

The first: The utterance of the two words of the testimony (shahādatayn) is a commitment to divine unity (tawḥīd) and a witness to the singling out of the Worshipped One. The condition for the complete fulfillment of this is that no beloved remains for the unitarian (muwaḥḥid) save the One, the Singular — for love does not admit of partnership. Unity by the tongue alone is of little avail; rather, the degree of the lover is tested by his separation from the beloved. Wealth is beloved among creatures because it is the instrument of their enjoyment of this world; through it they find comfort in this world and shrink from death, even though in death lies the meeting with the Beloved. Thus they are tested in the truthfulness of their claim regarding the Beloved, and are asked to descend from wealth, which is their object of aspiration and their beloved. For this reason, God Most High said: {«إِنَّ اللَّهَ اشْتَرَىٰ مِنَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ أَنفُسَهُمْ وَأَمْوَالَهُم بِأَنَّ لَهُمُ الْجَنَّةَ»} — "Indeed, God has purchased from the believers their lives and their properties, in exchange for Paradise" — and that is through jihad, which is a relinquishing of the lifeblood out of longing for the meeting with God, Mighty and Majestic. And the relinquishing of wealth is easier.

When this meaning was understood regarding the expenditure of wealth, people divided into three categories. A category who were truthful in their unity and fulfilled their covenant, descending from all their wealth, not storing up a single dinar or dirham; they refused to subject themselves to the obligation of zakāh upon them, until it was said to one of them: "How much zakāh is due on two hundred dirhams?" He replied: "As for the common folk, by the ruling of the Law, five dirhams. But as for us, the expenditure of all is obligatory upon us." For this reason, Abū Bakr, may God be pleased with him, gave in charity all his wealth, and ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, gave half his wealth. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said to ʿUmar: "What have you left for your family?" He said: "The like of it." And he said to Abū Bakr, may God be pleased with him: "What have you left for your family?" He said: "God and His Messenger." The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "The difference between you two is the difference between your words." Thus the Ṣiddīq (the most truthful) was faithful in the perfection of truthfulness, retaining nothing save the Beloved with him — namely, God and His Messenger.

The second category: Their rank is below this one. They are those who retain their wealth but are watchful of the times of need and the seasons of good deeds. Their intention in saving is to spend according to need, not for luxury, and to direct the surplus beyond need toward the various aspects of righteousness whenever such aspects appear. These do not confine themselves to the measure of zakāh. A group of the Followers (tābiʿūn) held that in wealth there are rights besides zakāh — such as al-Nakhaʿī, al-Shaʿbī, ʿAṭā', and Mujāhid. Al-Shaʿbī said, after being asked, "Is there in wealth a right besides zakāh?": "Yes. Have you not heard His saying, Mighty and Majestic: {«وَآتَى الْمَالَ عَلَىٰ حُبِّهِ ذَوِي الْقُرْبَىٰ»} — 'And gives wealth, despite his love for it, to relatives'?" They also adduced His saying, Mighty and Majestic: {«وَمِمَّا رَزَقْنَاهُمْ يُنفِقُونَ»} — "And from what We have provided them, they spend," and His saying, Exalted: {«وَأَنفِقُوا مِمَّا رَزَقْنَاكُم»} — "And spend from what We have provided you." They claimed that this is not abrogated by the verse of zakāh; rather, it falls within the right of a Muslim upon a Muslim. Its meaning is that it is obligatory upon the affluent, whenever a needy person is found, to remove his need — beyond the wealth of zakāh. What is sound in jurisprudence (fiqh) from this chapter is that whenever need presses upon someone, its removal is a communal obligation (farḍ kifāyah), for it is not permissible to neglect a Muslim. However, it may be said that upon the affluent is only the delivery of what removes the need, as an obligation, and he is not bound to expend it after having discharged zakāh from himself. And it may be said that he is bound to expend it immediately, and it is not permissible for him to offer a loan — that is, it is not permissible for him to task the poor man with accepting a loan. This is a point of divergence. And offering a loan is a descent to the lowest rank of the ranks of the common folk — namely, the rank of the third category.

The third category: Those who confine themselves to the performance of the obligatory duty, neither increasing nor decreasing from it. This is the least of the ranks, and all the common folk have confined themselves to it due to their avarice for wealth, their inclination toward it, and the weakness of their love for the Hereafter. God Most High said: {«إِن يَسْأَلْكُمُوهَا فَيُحْفِكُمْ تَبْخَلُوا»} — "If He asks you for them and then presses you, you would withhold out of avarice" — i.e., He would exact from you to the utmost. How great is the difference between a servant from whom his wealth and his self were purchased, with Paradise as his due, and a servant from whom nothing is exacted due to his avarice! This, then, is one of the meanings of God's command to His servants to expend wealth.

The second meaning: Purification from the attribute of avarice (bukhl), for it is among the destructive vices. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Three are destructive: avarice obeyed, desire followed, and a man's self-admiration." And God, Exalted, said: {«وَمَن يُوقَ شُحَّ نَفْسِهِ فَأُولَٰئِكَ هُمُ الْمُفْلِحُونَ»} — "And whoever is protected from the avarice of his soul — it is those who are the successful." The aspect of its being destructive, and the manner of extricating oneself from it, will come in the Quarter of the Destructive Vices. The attribute of avarice is only removed by accustoming oneself to the expenditure of wealth; for the love of a thing does not cease except by compelling the soul to part with it, until this becomes a habit. Zakāh, in this sense, is a purification (ṭuhrah) — that is, it purifies its possessor from the foulness of destructive avarice. Its purification is in proportion to one's expenditure, and in proportion to one's joy in giving it out and one's gladness in directing it to God Most High.

The third meaning: Gratitude for the blessing (shukr al-niʿmah). For God, Mighty and Majestic, has upon His servant a blessing in his self and in his wealth. Thus, bodily acts of worship are gratitude for the blessing of the body, and financial ones are gratitude for the blessing of wealth. How base is he who looks at the poor man, upon whom provision has been straitened and who has been made needy of him, and then his soul does not permit him to render thanks to God Most High for enriching him against asking, and for making others in need of him, by a quarter of a tenth or a tenth of his wealth!

The second duty: Concerning the time of payment. Among the etiquettes of people of religion is hastening (taʿjīl) beyond the time of obligation, as a display of eagerness for compliance by bringing joy to the hearts of the poor, and as a precaution against the obstacles of time that might hinder one from good deeds, and as knowledge that in delay there are afflictions — along with the disobedience the servant incurs if he delays beyond the time of obligation. Whenever the call to good arises from within, one should seize it, for that is a touch (lammah) of the angel. The heart of the believer is between two fingers of the fingers of the Merciful — how swift is its turning! And Satan promises poverty and commands indecency and evil, and he has a touch that follows the touch of the angel. So let one seize the opportunity, and let him designate for his zakāh, if he pays it all at once, a known month, striving that it be among the most virtuous of times, so that this may be a cause for the growth of his village and the multiplication of his alms. Such is the month of Muḥarram, for it is the first of the year and is among the sacred months; or Ramaḍān, for the Prophet, peace be upon him, was the most generous of people, and in Ramaḍān he was like the unleashed wind, retaining nothing. And Ramaḍān has the virtue of the Night of Decree (laylat al-qadr), and in it the Qur'an was revealed. Mujāhid used to say: "Do not say 'Ramaḍān,' for it is a name among the names of God Most High; rather, say 'the month of Ramaḍān.'" And Dhū al-Ḥijjah is also among the months of great virtue, for it is a sacred month, and in it is the Greater Pilgrimage (al-ḥajj al-akbar), and in it are the "known days" (ayyām maʿlūmāt) — which are the first ten — and the "numbered days" (ayyām maʿdūdāt) — which are the days of tashrīq. The most virtuous days of the month of Ramaḍān are its last ten, and the most virtuous days of Dhū al-Ḥijjah are its first ten.

The third duty: Concealment (al-isrār). For that is further from ostentation (riyā') and reputation (sumʿah). The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "The best charity is that of the man of scant means, given secretly to a poor man." And some scholars said: "Three are among the treasures of righteousness, among them the concealment of charity." It has also been related as an unbroken (musnad) tradition. And the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Indeed, a servant performs a deed in secret, and God writes it for him as secret. If he reveals it, it is transferred from the secret and written as public. If he then speaks of it, it is transferred from the secret and the public, and is written as ostentation." And in the well-known hadith: "Seven are shaded by God on the day when there is no shade but His shade — among them a man who gave charity such that his left hand did not know what his right hand gave." And in the report: "The charity given in secret extinguishes the wrath of the Lord." And God, Exalted, said: {«وَإِن تُخْفُوهَا وَتُؤْتُوهَا الْفُقَرَاءَ فَهُوَ خَيْرٌ لَّكُمْ»} — "And if you conceal them and give them to the poor, that is better for you." The benefit of concealment is deliverance from the afflictions of ostentation and reputation. For the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "God does not accept from one who seeks reputation, nor from one who seeks ostentation, nor from one who reminds of his gift." The one who speaks of his charity seeks reputation, and the one who gives in a gathering of people seeks ostentation; concealment and silence are what deliver from this. A group went to great lengths in the virtue of concealment, striving that the recipient not know the giver. Some of them would place it in the hand of a blind man; some would place it on the path of the poor man or in his sitting place, where he would see it but not see the giver; some would tie it in the garment of the poor man while he slept; and some would deliver it to the poor man's hand through another, such that the giver was not known, entrusting the intermediary with his affair and charging him not to divulge it. All of this was a means to extinguishing the wrath of the Lord, Glorified, and a precaution against ostentation and reputation.

If one cannot manage except that a single person knows him, then delivering it to an agent to give to the poor man, while the poor man does not know, is more appropriate — for in the poor man's knowledge there is both ostentation and reminder of the gift (mann), whereas in the intermediary's knowledge there is only ostentation. And if fame is his very intention, his deed is void — for zakāh is the removal of avarice and the weakening of the love of wealth, and the love of status (jāh) is more overpowering over the soul than the love of wealth. Each of the two is destructive in the Hereafter. But the attribute of avarice is transformed in the grave, in the realm of the similitude (ḥukm al-mithāl), into a stinging scorpion, and the attribute of ostentation is transformed in the grave into a serpent among serpents. He is commanded to weaken them or kill them, to repel their harm or lighten it. So whenever he intends ostentation and reputation, it is as if he has strengthened some of the scorpion's limbs for the serpent; to the extent that the scorpion is weakened, the serpent's strength increases. Had he left the matter as it was, it would have been easier for him. The strength of these attributes — that by which they are strengthened — is acting in accordance with them; and these attributes are weakened by struggling against them, opposing them, and acting contrary to their dictates. So what benefit is there in opposing the promptings of avarice while answering the promptings of ostentation, thereby weakening the lesser and strengthening the greater? The secrets of these meanings will come in the Quarter of the Destructive Vices.

The fourth duty: That he should display it where he knows that displaying it will encourage people to follow his example, while guarding his inner self from the prompting of ostentation by the method we will mention in the Book of Ostentation in treating it. For God, Mighty and Majestic, said: {«إِن تُبْدُوا الصَّدَقَاتِ فَنِعِمَّا هِيَ»} — "If you disclose your charities, that is good" — and that is where the situation calls for disclosure, either for the sake of emulation, or because the asker has asked in a gathering of people, in which case one should not abandon charity out of fear of ostentation in displaying it. Rather, one should give and guard his inner self against ostentation as much as possible. This is because in display there is a third hazard besides the reminder of the gift and ostentation — namely, the tearing of the poor man's veil, for he may be harmed by being seen in the guise of a needy person. But whoever displays his asking is the one who has torn his own veil, so this meaning is not feared in his case. This is like the display of immorality (fisq) by one who has concealed it — for it is prohibited, and spying into it and habitually mentioning it are forbidden. As for the one who displays it, the establishment of the prescribed punishment upon him is a publicizing, but he himself is the cause of it. And with a similar meaning, the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Whoever casts off the cloak of modesty, there is no backbiting against him." And God, Exalted, said: {«وَأَنفِقُوا مِمَّا رَزَقْنَاهُم سِرًّا وَعَلَانِيَةً»} — "And spend from what We have provided them, secretly and publicly" — He also encouraged publicity for the benefit of encouragement contained in it. So let the servant be precise in weighing this benefit against the hazard contained in it, for that varies with circumstances and persons. Publicity may be better in some circumstances for some persons. And whoever knows the benefits and the harms, and does not look with the eye of desire, the more appropriate and fitting course in every situation becomes clear to him.

The fifth duty: That he not corrupt his charity by reminding of the gift (mann) and by injury (adhan). God, Exalted, said: {«لَا تُبْطِلُوا صَدَقَاتِكُم بِالْمَنِّ وَالْأَذَىٰ»} — "Do not invalidate your charities by reminder and injury." They differed over the reality of reminder and injury. It was said: The reminder is that he mentions it, and the injury is that he displays it. Sufyān said: "Whoever reminds, his charity is corrupted." It was said to him: "How is the reminder?" He said: "That he mentions it and speaks of it." It was said: The reminder is that he employs the recipient through the gift, and the injury is that he reproaches him for his poverty. It was said: The reminder is that he acts arrogantly toward him because of his giving, and the injury is that he rebukes him or reproaches him for asking. And the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "God does not accept the charity of one who reminds." In my view, the reminder has a root and a planting-ground, and it is among the states of the heart and its attributes; then from it branch outward states upon the tongue and the limbs. Its root is that he sees himself as the benefactor to the poor man and the bestower of favor upon him. His due is to see the poor man as the benefactor to him, by accepting from him the right of God, Mighty and Majestic — which is his purification and his deliverance from the Fire — and that had he not accepted it, it would have remained pledged against him. Thus his due is to regard the poor man as having conferred a favor upon him, since he made his hand a deputy for God, Mighty and Majestic, in receiving the right of God, Mighty and Majestic. The Messenger of God, peace be upon him, said: "Indeed, charity falls into the hand of God, Mighty and Majestic, before it falls into the hand of the asker." So let him be certain that he is delivering to God, Mighty and Majestic, His right, and that the poor man is taking from God, Exalted, his provision after it has come to God, Mighty and Majestic. Were a debt owed to him by a man, and he assigned it to his slave or servant who was responsible for his provision, it would be foolishness and ignorance for the debtor to think that the recipient was under his favor — for the benefactor is the one responsible for his provision. As for him, he is merely discharging what was incumbent upon him, in exchange for what he loves; he is pursuing his own interest, so he does not remind anyone of a favor.

Whenever one understands the three meanings we mentioned regarding the obligation of zakāh — or even one of them — he does not see himself as a benefactor except to himself: either by expending his wealth as a display of love for God Most High, or as a purification of his soul from the vice of avarice, or as gratitude for the blessing of wealth, seeking increase. However it may be, there is no transaction between him and the poor man such that he should see himself as a benefactor to him. And whenever this ignorance occurs — that he sees himself as a benefactor to him — there branches from it upon his outward state what was mentioned regarding the meaning of the reminder: namely, speaking of it, displaying it, and seeking recompense from him through thanks, supplication, service, veneration, glorification, fulfillment of rights, precedence in gatherings, and compliance in affairs. All these are fruits of the sense of favor (mannah). And the meaning of mannah inwardly is what we have mentioned.

As for injury (adhan), its outward form is reproach, rebuke, harshness of speech, frowning of the face, tearing of the veil by display, and various forms of belittlement. Its inward form — its source — is two things. One is his dislike of lifting his hand from wealth and the severity of that upon his soul, for that inevitably narrows one's character. The second is his seeing that he is better than the poor man, and that the poor man, by reason of his need, is baser than him. Both have their origin in ignorance. As for disliking the delivery of wealth, that is foolishness — for whoever dislikes expending a dirham in exchange for what is worth a thousand is intensely foolish. It is known that he expends wealth seeking the pleasure of God, Mighty and Majestic, and the reward in the abode of the Hereafter — and that is nobler than what he has expended or will expend, whether for purifying his soul from the vice of avarice or as gratitude seeking increase. However it is supposed, there is no ground for dislike. As for the second, it is also ignorance — for were he to know the virtue of poverty over wealth, and the peril of the rich, he would not belittle the poor man; rather, he would seek blessing through him and wish for his rank. The righteous rich enter Paradise five hundred years after the poor. For this reason, the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "They are the losers, by the Lord of the Kaʿbah!" Abū Dharr said: "Who are they?" He said: "Those who are most abundant in wealth" — the hadith. Then how can he belittle the poor man, whom God Most High has made a merchandise (tijārah) for him — for he acquires wealth by his effort, seeks much of it, and strives to preserve it to the measure of need — and he is obligated to deliver to the poor man the measure of his need, and to withhold from him the surplus that would harm him were it delivered to him? Thus the rich man is employed in seeking the provision of the poor man, and is distinguished by bearing the burdens of wrongs, undertaking hardships, and guarding the surplus until he dies, whereupon his enemies consume it. For whenever dislike is transformed and replaced by joy and gladness at God Most High's granting him success to perform the obligation, and His preferring the poor man so that he is delivered from his liability by the poor man's acceptance — then injury, reproach, and frowning are negated, and are replaced by gladness, praise, and acceptance of the favor. This, then, is the source of the reminder and the injury.

If you say: "His seeing himself in the rank of the benefactor is a subtle matter — is there a sign by which he may test his heart and thereby know that he does not see himself as a benefactor?" Know that it has a subtle and clear sign: namely, that he imagine the poor man had committed an offense against him, or become an enemy to him — would his disapproval and rejection of him increase beyond his disapproval before the charity? If it increased, then his charity is not free of the taint of the sense of favor, because he expects from him, by reason of it, what he did not expect before.

If you say: "This is a subtle matter, and no heart is free of it — what is its remedy?" Know that it has an inward remedy and an outward remedy. As for the inward, it is the knowledge of the realities we mentioned in understanding the obligation — that the poor man is the benefactor to him, in purifying him by acceptance. As for the outward, it is the acts that the one bearing the sense of favor undertakes — for the acts that issue from character traits dye the heart with those traits, as its secrets will come in the latter half of the book. For this reason, some of them would place the charity before the poor man and stand before him in the posture of a supplicant, until he asked him to accept it, so that he himself would be in the guise of the askers — while sensing, at the same time, a dislike were he to refuse it. And some of them would spread out his palm so that the poor man would take from his hand, with the poor man's hand being the upper one. And ʿĀ'ishah and Umm Salamah, may God be pleased with them both, when they sent a gift of kindness to a poor man, would say to the messenger: "Preserve what he supplicates with." Then they would return to him the like of his words, saying: "This for that," so that their charity would be pure for them. They did not expect supplication, because it resembles recompense, and they would meet supplication with its like. Thus did ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb and his son ʿAbd Allāh, may God be pleased with them both, do. And thus did the masters of hearts treat their hearts. There is no remedy from the outward aspect except these acts that indicate self-abasement, humility, and acceptance of the favor; and from the inward aspect, the cognitions we have mentioned. This is from the aspect of action, and that from the aspect of knowledge. The heart is not treated except with the compound of knowledge and action. This condition of zakāh runs in the course of humility (khushūʿ) in prayer. This is established by his saying, peace be upon him: "A man has nothing of his prayer except what he comprehends of it." And this is like his saying, peace be upon him: "God does not accept the charity of one who reminds," and like His saying, Mighty and Majestic: {«لَا تُبْطِلُوا صَدَقَاتِكُم بِالْمَنِّ وَالْأَذَىٰ»} — "Do not invalidate your charities by reminder and injury." As for the jurist's fatwa that it falls in its place and that his liability is discharged without this condition — that is another matter, and we have indicated its meaning in the Book of Prayer.

The sixth duty: That he deem his gift small. For if he deems it great, he will be amazed by it — and self-amazement (ʿujb) is among the destructive vices and is that which voids deeds. God, Exalted, said: {«وَيَوْمَ حُنَيْنٍ إِذْ أَعْجَبَتْكُمْ كَثْرَتُكُمْ فَلَمْ تُغْنِ عَنكُمْ شَيْئًا»} — "And on the day of Ḥunayn, when your multitude pleased you, but it availed you nothing." And it is said: The act of obedience, the more it is deemed small, the greater it becomes with God, Mighty and Majestic; and the act of disobedience, the more it is deemed great, the smaller it becomes with God, Mighty and Majestic. And it was said: A good deed is not perfected except by three things: deeming it small, hastening it, and concealing it. Deeming it great is not the same as the reminder and injury — for were one to spend his wealth on the construction of a mosque or a hostel (ribāṭ), deeming it great would be possible therein, while the reminder and injury would not be possible. Rather, self-amazement and deeming great run through all acts of worship. Its remedy is knowledge and action.

As for the knowledge: It is that he know that a tenth or a quarter of a tenth is little from much, and that he has contented himself with the basest of the degrees of expenditure, as we mentioned in understanding the obligation. He is worthy of being ashamed of it — so how can he deem it great? And if he ascends to the higher rank, expending all his wealth or most of it, let him reflect: From where did the wealth come to him, and to what is he directing it? The wealth belongs to God, Mighty and Majestic, and upon him is His favor, since He gave it to him and granted him success to expend it. So let him not deem great, in the right of God Most High, what is itself the very right of God, Glorified. And if his station requires that he look to the Hereafter and that he expends it for reward, let him not deem great the expenditure of that upon which he awaits its multiples.

As for the action: It is that he give with the giving of one ashamed of his avarice in withholding the rest of his wealth from God, Mighty and Majestic. Thus his bearing would be one of brokenness and shame, like the bearing of one who is demanded to return a deposit and withholds some of it while returning the rest — for all wealth belongs to God, Mighty and Majestic, and the expenditure of all of it is the most beloved to God, Glorified. He only did not command His servant to do so because it is hard upon him due to his avarice, as God, Mighty and Majestic, said: {«فَيُحْفِكُمْ تَبْخَلُوا»} — "Then He would press you, and you would withhold out of avarice."

The seventh duty: That he select from his wealth its best, most beloved, most precious, and most lawful (ṭayyib) portion. For God Most High is Good (ṭayyib) and accepts only what is good. And if what is given out is from a doubtful source, perhaps it is not his property at all, and thus it does not fall in its proper place. In the hadith of Abān, from Anas ibn Mālik: "Blessed is a servant who spends from wealth he has earned without disobedience." And if what is given out is not from the best of his wealth, that is a breach of good manners — for he may be keeping the best for himself, or for his slave, or for his family, thus preferring over God, Mighty and Majestic, someone other than Him. Were he to do this with his guest, offering him the worst food in his house, it would fill his breast with rancor. This is if his regard is toward God, Mighty and Majestic. And if his regard is toward himself and his reward in the Hereafter, then he is not intelligent who prefers another over himself — for he has nothing of his wealth except what he gave in charity and thus stored up, or what he ate and thus consumed. And what he eats is the satisfaction of a desire in the present moment; it is not of intelligence to confine one's regard to the immediate and abandon the storing up. And God, Exalted, said: {«يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا أَنفِقُوا مِن طَيِّبَاتِ مَا كَسَبْتُمْ وَمِمَّا أَخْرَجْنَا لَكُم مِّنَ الْأَرْضِ ۖ وَلَا تَيَمَّمُوا الْخَبِيثَ مِنْهُ تُنفِقُونَ وَلَسْتُم بِآخِذِيهِ إِلَّا أَن تُغْمِضُوا فِيهِ»} — "O you who believe, spend from the good things you have earned and from what We have brought forth for you from the earth, and do not aim at the bad from it to spend — while you would not take it yourselves except with closed eyes" — i.e., you would not take it except with dislike and shame, and that is the meaning of closing the eyes. So do not prefer your Lord with it.

And in the report: "A dirham preceded a hundred thousand dirhams." That is when a man gives it out from the most lawful and best of his wealth, and it issues from satisfaction and joy in the expenditure. And one may give out a hundred thousand dirhams from what he dislikes of his wealth, and that indicates that he does not prefer God, Mighty and Majestic, with anything he loves. With this, God Most High censured a people who assigned to God what they disliked, saying, Exalted: {«وَيَجْعَلُونَ لِلَّهِ مَا يَكْرَهُونَ وَتَصِفُ أَلْسِنَتُهُمُ الْكَذِبَ أَنَّ لَهُمُ الْحُسْنَىٰ ۖ لَا جَرَمَ أَنَّ لَهُمُ النَّارَ»} — "And they assign to God what they dislike, and their tongues utter the lie that for them is the best. No doubt — for them is the Fire." Some reciters paused at the negation, as a denial of them, then began anew: "No doubt that for them is the Fire" — i.e., their assigning to God what they dislike earned them the Fire.

The eighth duty: That he seek for his charity one by whom the charity is purified, and not be content that it be from the general categories of the eight classes. For within their generality there are particular attributes. Let him observe the particularity of those attributes, which are six.

The first: That he seek the God-fearing (atqiyā'), those turned away from this world, devoted to the commerce of the Hereafter. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Do not eat except the food of a God-fearing man, and let no one eat your food except a God-fearing man." This is because the God-fearing man uses it as aid upon piety, and thus the giver becomes a partner in his obedience by aiding him. And the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Feed your food to the God-fearing, and direct your kindness to the believers." In another wording: "Host with your food whom you love for the sake of God Most High." And some scholars would prefer with their food the poor of the Sufis over others.

chapters.title_en: Chapter Three on the Receiver of the Soul (al-Qābiḍ), the Causes of His Entitlement, and the Functions of His Taking
chapters.arabic_text: || الفصل الثالث في القابض وأسباب استحقاقه ووظائف قبضه
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ق-ب-ض (q-b-ḍ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is "to take, grasp, seize, or contract" — used for taking hold of something with the hand, and also for constriction or contraction (as opposed to bast, expansion).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, qabḍ refers to God’s act of taking the soul at death (qabḍ al-rūḥ), and also to the divine attribute of constricting provision or hearts — a deliberate, sovereign act, not a physical seizure.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) is physical grasping; metaphorical (majāz) is God’s decree of death or spiritual contraction. Here, it is used in the technical sense of the Angel of Death’s function.
- Sībawayh Rule: Nominal sentence with definite article (al-qābiḍ) functioning as a technical agent noun; the genitive construction (asbāb istiḥqāqihi) indicates causal entitlement, and the following genitive (waẓāʾif qabḍihi) specifies the functional duties — all governed by the implicit predicate "this chapter concerns."
chapters.translation: I say: This is the third chapter, concerning the Receiver of the soul (al-qābiḍ) — namely, the Angel of Death — the causes that render a servant deserving of his taking, and the functions incumbent upon him in the act of seizing the soul.

chapters.title_en: Exposition of the Causes of Eligibility (Bayān Asbāb al-Istīḥqāq)
chapters.arabic_text:
||| بيان أسباب الاستحقاق

اعلم أنه لا يستحق الزكاة إلا حر مسلم ليس بهاشمي ولا مطلبي اتصف بصفة من
صفات الأصناف الثمانية المذكورين في كتاب الله عز وجل
ولا تصرف زكاة إلى كافر ولا إلى عبد ولا إلى هاشمي ولا إلى مطلبي
أما الصبي والمجنون فيجوز الصرف إليهما إذا قبض وليهما فلنذكر صفات
الأصناف الثمانية
الصنف الأول الفقراء والفقير هو الذي ليس له مال ولا قدرة له على الكسب
فإن كان معه قوت يومه وكسوة حاله فليس بفقير ولكنه مسكين وإن كان معه نصف
قوت يومه فهو فقير وإن كان معه قميص وليس معه منديل ولا خف ولا سراويل ولم
تكن قيمة القميص بحيث تفي بجميع ذلك كما يليق بالفقراء فهو فقير لأنه في
الحال قد عدم ما هو محتاج إليه وما هو عاجز عنه فلا ينبغي أن يشترط في
الفقير أن لا يكون له كسوة سوى ساتر العورة فإن هذا غلو والغالب أنه لا
يوجد مثله ولا يخرجه عن الفقر كونه معتادا للسؤال فلا يجعل السؤال كسبا
بخلاف ما لو قدر على كسب فإن ذلك يخرجه عن الفقر فإن قدر على الكسب بآلة
فهو فقير ويجوز أن يشتري له آلة وإن قدر على كسب لا يليق بمروءة وبحال مثله
فهو فقير وإن كان متفقها ويمنعه الاشتغال بالكسب عن التفقه فهو فقير ولا
تعتبر قدرته وإن كان متعبدا يمنعه الكسب من وظائف العبادات وأوراد الأوقات
فليكتسب لأن الكسب أولى من ذلك قال صلى الله عليه وسلم طلب الحلال فريضة
بعد  الفريضة (1) وأراد به السعي في الاكتساب وقال عمر رضي الله عنه كسب في
شبهة خير من مسألة وإن كان مكتفيا بنفقة أبيه أو من تجب عليه نفقته فهذا
أهون من الكسب فليس بفقير
الصنف الثاني المساكين والمسكين هو الذي لا يفي دخله بخرجه فقد يملك ألف
درهم وهو مسكين وقد لا يملك إلا فأسا وحبلا وهو غني والدويرة التي يسكنها
والثوب الذي يستره على قدر حاله لا يسلبه اسم المسكين وكذا أثاث البيت أعني
ما يحتاج إليه وذلك ما يليق به وكذا كتب الفقه لا تخرجه عن المسكنة وإذا لم
يملك إلا الكتب فلا تلزمه صدقة الفطر
وحكم الكتاب حكم الثوب وأثاث البيت فإنه محتاج إليه ولكن ينبغي أن يحتاط
في قطع الحاجة بالكتاب فالكتاب محتاج إليه لثلاثة أغراض التعليم والاستفادة
والتفرج بالمطالعة
أما حاجة التفرج فلا تعتبر كاقتناء كتب الأشعار وتواريخ الأخبار وأمثال
ذلك مما لا ينفع في الآخرة ولا يجري في الدنيا إلا مجرى التفرج والاستئناس
فهذا يباع في الكفارة وزكاة الفطر وتمنع اسم المسكنة
وأما حاجة التعليم إن كان لأجل الكسب كالمؤدب والمعلم والمدرس بأجره فهذه
آلته فلا تباع في الفطرة كأدوات الخياط وسائر المحترفين وإن كان يدرس
للقيام بفرض PageV01P221
الكفاية فلا تباع ولا يسلبه ذلك اسم المسكين لأنها حاجة مهمة
وأما حاجة الاستفادة والتعلم من الكتاب كادخاره كتب طب ليعالج بها نفسه
أو كتاب وعظ ليطالع فيه ويتعظ به فإن كان في البلد طبيب وواعظ فهذا مستغنى
عنه وإن لم يكن فهو محتاج إليه ثم ربما لا يحتاج إلى مطالعة الكتاب إلا بعد
مدة فينبغي أن يضبط مدة الحاجة والأقرب أن يقال ما لا يحتاج إليه في السنة
فهو مستغنى عنه فإن من فضل من قوت يومه شيء لزمته الفطرة فإذا قدرنا القوت
باليوم فحاجة أثاث البيت وثياب البدن ينبغي أن تقدر بالسنة فلا تباع ثياب
الصيف في الشتاء والكتب بالثياب والأثاث أشبه وقد يكون له من كتاب نسختان
فلا حاجة إلى إحداهما
فإن قال إحداهما  أصح والأخرى أحسن فأنا محتاج إليهما قلنا اكتف بالأصح
وبع الأحسن ودع التفرج والترفه وإن كان نسختان من علم واحد إحداهما بسيطة
والأخرى وجيزة فإن كان مقصوده الاستفادة فليكتف بالبسيطة وإن كان قصده
التدريس فيحتاج إليهما إذ في كل واحدة فائدة ليست في الأخرى
وأمثال هذه الصور لا تنحصر ولم يتعرض له في فن الفقه وإنما أوردناه لعموم
البلوى والتنبيه بحسن هذا النظر على غيره فإن استقصاء هذه الصور غير ممكن
إذ يتعدى مثل هذا النظر في أثاث البيت في مقدارها وعددها ونوعها وفي ثياب
البدن وفي الدار وسعتها وضيقها وليس لهذه الأمور حدود محدودة ولكن الفقيه
يجتهد فيها برأيه ويقرب في التحديدات بما يراه ويقتحم فيه خطر الشبهات
والمتورع يأخذ فيه بالأحوط ويدع ما يريبه إلى ما لا يريبه والدرجات
المتوسطة المشكلة بين الأطراف المتقابلة الجلية كثيرة ولا ينجي منها إلا
الاحتياط والله أعلم
الصنف الثالث العاملون وهم السعاة الذين يجمعون الزكوات سوى الخليفة
والقاضي ويدخل فيه العريف والكاتب والمستوفى والحافظ والنقال ولا يزاد واحد
منهم على أجرة المثل فإن فضل شيء من الثمن عن أجر مثلهم رد على بقية
الأصناف وإن نقص كمل من مال المصالح
الصنف الرابع المؤلفة قلوبهم على الإسلام وهم الأشراف الذين أسلموا وهم
مطاعون في قومهم وفي إعطائهم تقريرهم على الإسلام وترغيب نظائرهم وأتباعهم
الصنف الخامس المكاتبون فيدفع إلى السيد سهم المكاتب وإن دفع إلى المكاتب
جاز ولا يدفع السيد زكاته إلى مكاتب نفسه لأنه يعد عبد
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ح-ق-ق (Ḥ-Q-Q)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is "truth, reality, due, and that which is firmly established and obligatory." Al-ʿAyn notes it signifies the opposite of falsehood (bāṭil) and that which is incumbent (wājib).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, ḥaqq denotes the "due" or "entitlement" that is firmly established by divine command, distinguishing it from mere discretionary giving. It carries the sense of a fixed right (istīḥqāq) that the recipient has earned through a specific attribute.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literally, istīḥqāq means "deserving" or "being worthy of." In this context, it is used in its ḥaqīqah (literal) sense regarding legal entitlement, not metaphorically, as the eligibility is a concrete legal status determined by specified criteria.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Condition and Consequence (al-Sharṭ wa al-Jazāʾ) — The opening sentence "لا يستحق الزكاة إلا حر مسلم..." employs the restrictive particle (innamā/illā) which functions to negate all other possibilities, establishing a strict conditional framework for the legal ruling that follows.
chapters.translation:
I say: Know that Zakat is not deserved except by a free Muslim, who is neither a Hāshimī nor a Muṭṭalibī, and who is characterized by one of the attributes of the eight categories mentioned in the Book of God, Mighty and Majestic. And Zakat is not disbursed to a disbeliever, nor to a slave, nor to a Hāshimī, nor to a Muṭṭalibī. As for the child and the insane person, it is permissible to disburse to them when their guardian receives it on their behalf. Let us now mention the attributes of the eight categories.

The first category: The Poor (al-Fuqarāʾ). The poor person (faqīr) is one who possesses no wealth and has no ability to earn. If he has with him his sustenance for the day and clothing suitable for his state, he is not poor (faqīr) but rather a needy person (miskīn). If he has with him half of his day's sustenance, he is poor (faqīr). If he has a shirt but does not have a handkerchief, nor socks, nor trousers, and the value of the shirt is not sufficient to cover all of these as befits the poor, then he is poor (faqīr), because at that moment he lacks what he is in need of and what he is incapable of obtaining. It should not be stipulated for the poor person that he have no clothing other than what covers his nakedness, for this is extremism, and such a person is rarely found. Nor does his being accustomed to begging remove him from poverty, for begging is not considered earning. This is contrary to the case where he is able to earn, for that ability removes him from poverty. If he is able to earn but lacks the tool, he is poor, and it is permissible to purchase a tool for him. If he is able to earn in a manner unbefitting his honor (murūʾah) and his like, he is poor. If he is a student of jurisprudence (mutafaqqih) and being occupied with earning would prevent him from his studies, he is poor, and his ability [to earn] is not considered. If he is a devotee and earning would prevent him from the duties of worship and the litanies of the times, let him earn, for earning takes precedence over that. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: {«طلب الحلال فريضة بعد الفريضة»} "Seeking the lawful is an obligation after the obligation." He meant by this striving in earning. And ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, said: "Earning from something doubtful is better than begging." If he is sufficiently provided for by the expenditure of his father or of one whose maintenance is obligatory upon him, then this is easier than earning, so he is not poor.

The second category: The Needy (al-Masākīn). The needy person (miskīn) is one whose income does not suffice for his expenditure. He may own a thousand dirhams and still be needy (miskīn), and he may own nothing but an axe and a rope and yet be rich. The small house he dwells in and the garment that covers him, according to his state, do not strip him of the name "needy" (miskīn). Likewise, the household furnishings — I mean what he needs — and that which befits him, and likewise books of jurisprudence, do not remove him from neediness (maskanah). If he owns nothing but books, the alms of breaking the fast (ṣadaqat al-fiṭr) is not obligatory upon him. The ruling on books is the ruling on garments and household furnishings, for he is in need of them. However, one should be cautious in determining the need for books, for the book is needed for three purposes: teaching, benefiting oneself, and amusement through reading.

As for the need of amusement, it is not considered, like possessing books of poetry, historical chronicles, and the like, which benefit nothing in the Hereafter and serve in this world only as amusement and companionship. Such books are sold for the expiation (kaffārah) and the alms of breaking the fast (zakāt al-fiṭr), and they prevent the name of neediness (maskanah).

As for the need of teaching — if it is for the sake of earning, like the tutor, the teacher, and the professor who teaches for a wage — then it is his tool, so it is not sold for the alms of breaking the fast, just like the tools of the tailor and the implements of other professionals. If he teaches to fulfill the communal obligation (farḍ al-kifāyah), then it is not sold, and it does not strip him of the name "needy" (miskīn), because it is an important need.

As for the need of benefiting and learning from the book — like storing books of medicine to treat himself with them, or a book of admonition to read and be admonished by — if there is in the town a physician and a preacher, then he is independent of it; but if there is none, then he is in need of it. Then perhaps he does not need to read the book except after a period of time, so one should determine the period of need. The closest [view] is to say: whatever he does not need within the year is something he is independent of. For whoever has surplus from his day's sustenance, the alms of breaking the fast is obligatory upon him. So if we measure sustenance by the day, then the need for household furnishings and body garments should be measured by the year. Thus summer garments are not sold in winter. And books are more similar to garments and furnishings. He may have two copies of a book, and he has no need for one of them.

If he says: "One of them is more correct and the other is more beautiful, and I am in need of both," we say: Be content with the more correct one, sell the more beautiful one, and abandon amusement and luxury. If he has two copies of one science, one detailed and the other abridged — if his purpose is to benefit himself, let him be content with the detailed one; but if his purpose is teaching, then he needs both, for in each one there is a benefit not found in the other.

Such cases are not limited, and this has not been addressed in the science of jurisprudence. We have only mentioned it due to the generality of affliction and to draw attention, by the excellence of this consideration, to other matters. For an exhaustive enumeration of these cases is not possible, since such consideration extends to household furnishings in their quantity, number, and type, and to body garments, and to the house in its spaciousness and narrowness. These matters have no fixed limits, but the jurist exerts his judgment (ijtihād) regarding them, approximates in the determinations what he deems fit, and plunges into the danger of ambiguities (shubuhāt). The scrupulous one (mutawarriʿ) takes the more cautious course and abandons what makes him doubt for what does not make him doubt. The intermediate degrees that are problematic between the opposing clear extremes are many, and nothing saves from them except caution (iḥtiyāṭ). And God knows best.

The third category: The Workers (al-ʿĀmilūn). They are the collectors who gather the Zakat, excluding the Caliph and the judge. Included among them are the overseer (ʿarīf), the scribe, the accountant, the keeper, and the transporter. None of them is given more than the equivalent wage (ujrat al-mithl). If anything remains of the amount beyond their equivalent wages, it is returned to the remaining categories; and if it falls short, it is completed from the funds of the public interest (maṣāliḥ).

The fourth category: Those Whose Hearts are Reconciliated (al-Muʾallafah Qulūbuhum) to Islam. They are the nobles who have embraced Islam and are obeyed among their people. In giving to them is the confirmation of their adherence to Islam and the encouragement of their peers and followers.

The fifth category: The Mukātabūn (slaves under contract of manumission). The share of the mukātab is paid to the master. If it is paid to the mukātab himself, it is permissible. The master does not pay his Zakat to his own mukātab, because he is considered his slave.

The sixth category: The Debtors (al-Ghārimūn). The debtor (ghārim) is one who has borrowed in obedience [to God] or in something permissible, and he is poor. If he borrowed in disobedience, he is not given until he repents. If he is rich, his debt is not paid unless he borrowed for the sake of reconciliation or extinguishing a sedition (fitnah).

The seventh category: The Warriors (al-Ghuzāh) who have no fixed stipend in the register of mercenaries (dīwān al-murtaziqah). A share is disbursed to them even if they are rich, as assistance to them for the raid (ghazw).

The eighth category: The Son of the Path (Ibn al-Sabīl). He is one who has departed from his town to travel in something not involving disobedience, or who has passed through it. He is given if he is poor. If he has wealth in another town, he is given up to the amount of his destination (bulghah).

If you say: "By what means are these attributes known?" We say: As for poverty (faqr) and neediness (maskanah), [they are known] by the statement of the recipient, and he is not required to produce evidence, nor is he made to take an oath. Rather, it is permissible to rely on his statement when his falsehood is not known. As for raiding (ghazw) and travel, it is a future matter, so he is given based on his statement "I am a raider." If he does not fulfill it, it is taken back. As for the remaining categories, evidence is indispensable for them. These are the conditions of eligibility. As for the amount disbursed to each one, it will follow.

chapters.title_en: The Functions of the Recipient of Alms (Zakāh) — Five Duties
chapters.arabic_text:
||| بيان وظائف القابض وهي خمسة

الأولى أن يعلم إن الله عز وجل أوجب صرف الزكاة إليه ليكفي همه ويجعل
همومه هما واحدا فقد تعبد الله عز وجل الخلق بأن يكون همهم واحدا وهو الله
سبحانه واليوم الآخر وهو المعني بقوله تعالى {وما خلقت الجن والإنس إلا
ليعبدون} ولكن لما اقتضت الحكمة أن يسلط على العبد الشهوات والحاجات وهي
تفرق همه
PageV01P222
اقتضى الكرم إفاضة نعمة تكفي الحاجات فأكثر الأموال وصبها في أيدي عباده
لتكون آلة لهم في دفع حاجاتهم ووسيلة لتفرغهم لطاعاتهم فمنهم من أكثر ماله
فتنة وبلية فأقحمه في الخطر ومنهم من أحبه فحماه عن الدنيا كما يحمي المشفق
مريضه فزوى عنه فضولها وساق إليه قدر حاجته على يد الأغنياء ليكون سهل
الكسب والتعب في الجمع والحفظ عليهم وفائدته تنصب إلى الفقراء فيتجردون
لعبادة الله والاستعداد لما بعد الموت فلا تصرفهم عنها فضول الدنيا ولا
تشغلهم عن التأهب الفاقة وهذا منتهى النعمة فحق الفقير أن يعرف قدر نعمة
