chapters.translation:
I say: When the pilgrim departs from ʿArafāt after sunset, he should maintain tranquility and dignity, and he must avoid the rapid galloping of horses and the hurried pace of camels, as is the custom of some people. For the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, forbade the galloping of horses and the hurried pace of camels, and he said: "Fear God, and travel with a beautiful manner of travel, neither treading upon the weak nor harming a Muslim." {«اتقوا الله وسيروا سيرا جميلا لا تطأوا ضعيفا ولا تؤذوا مسلما»}

When he reaches Muzdalifah, he should perform the major ablution (ghusl) for it, because Muzdalifah is within the Sacred Precinct (al-ḥaram); thus, let him enter it in a state of purity. If he is able to enter it walking, that is more virtuous and closer to revering the sanctity of the Sacred Precinct. Along the way, he should raise his voice with the talbiyah (proclamation of "Here I am, O God"). When he reaches Muzdalifah, he should say: "O God, this is Muzdalifah, wherein You have gathered diverse tongues asking You for newly-commenced needs; so make me among those who called upon You and You answered them, and who relied upon You and You sufficed them."

Then he combines the sunset prayer (maghrib) and the night prayer (ʿishāʾ) at Muzdalifah, at the time of the night prayer, shortening them, with one call to prayer (adhān) and two commencements (iqāmah), with no supererogatory prayer between them. However, he combines the supererogatory prayers of maghrib, ʿishāʾ, and the witr after the two obligatory prayers. He begins with the supererogatory of maghrib, then the supererogatory of ʿishāʾ, just as with the two obligatory prayers. For abandoning the supererogatory prayers during travel is a manifest loss, and the obligation of performing them at their appointed times would be harmful and would sever the connection of subordination (tabaʿiyyah) between them and the obligatory prayers. Since it is permissible to perform the supererogatory prayers with the obligatory ones with a single dry ablution (tayammum) by virtue of subordination, then it is all the more fitting that they be performed on the basis of combination (jamʿ) through subordination. Nor is this prevented by the fact that the supererogatory prayer may be performed upon a mount, given what we have indicated regarding subordination and need.

Then he remains that night at Muzdalifah, for the overnight stay there is a ritual act (nusuk). Whoever departs from it during the first half of the night without staying overnight owes a sacrificial offering (dam). Reviving this noble night is among the excellent acts of devotion (qurubāt) for whoever is able to do so. Then, when the night reaches its midpoint, he begins to prepare for departure, and he gathers pebbles (ḥaṣā) from it, for therein are soft stones. Let him take seventy pebbles, for that is the sufficient amount, and there is no harm in taking extra as a precaution, for perhaps some of them may fall. Let the pebbles be light, such that the tips of the finger joints can contain them.

Then let him perform the dawn prayer (ṣubḥ) in the darkness of early morning, and let him proceed on his way until he reaches the Sacred Monument (al-Mashʿar al-Ḥarām), which is the end of Muzdalifah. There he stands and supplicates until the morning light spreads, saying: "O God, by the right of the Sacred Monument, the Sacred House, the Sacred Month, the Corner (al-rukn), and the Station (al-maqām), convey to the soul of Muḥammad from us greetings and peace, and admit us into the Abode of Peace (Dār al-Salām), O Possessor of Majesty and Honor." Then he departs from it before sunrise until he reaches a place called the Valley of Muḥassir. It is recommended for him to urge his mount so as to cross the width of the valley swiftly; if he is on foot, he should hasten his walking.

Then, when the morning of the Day of Sacrifice (yawm al-naḥr) comes, he mixes the talbiyah with the takbīr (proclamation of God's greatness), uttering the talbiyah at times and the takbīr at others. He proceeds to Minā and the locations of the stoning pillars (jamarāt), which are three. He passes by the first and the second without engaging with them on the Day of Sacrifice, until he reaches the Pillar of ʿAqabah, which is to the right of one facing the qiblah, on the main road. The place of stoning is slightly elevated at the base of the mountain, and it is visible at the sites of the stoning pillars. He stones the Pillar of ʿAqabah after sunrise by the measure of a spear's length. Its manner is that he stands facing the qiblah; if he faces the pillar, there is no harm. He casts seven pebbles, raising his hand, and he replaces the talbiyah with the takbīr, saying with each pebble: "God is Most Great, in obedience to the Most Merciful and in defiance of Satan. O God, in affirmation of Your Book and in following the Sunnah of Your Prophet." When he has stoned, he ceases the talbiyah and the takbīr, except for the takbīr following the obligatory prayers, from the noon prayer (ẓuhr) of the Day of Sacrifice until after the dawn prayer of the last of the Days of Tashrīq. He does not stand for supplication on this day; rather, he supplicates in his dwelling.

The description of the takbīr is that he says: "God is Most Great, God is Most Great, God is Most Great, abundantly great. Praise be to God, abundantly. Glory be to God morning and evening. There is no god but God alone, with no partner, sincere to Him in religion, even if the disbelievers detest it. There is no god but God alone; He fulfilled His promise, aided His servant, and defeated the confederates alone. There is no god but God, and God is Most Great."

Then let him slaughter the sacrificial offering (hady) if he has one. It is preferable that he slaughter it himself, and let him say: "In the name of God, and God is Most Great. O God, from You and to You; accept from me as You accepted from Your friend Abraham." Sacrificing a camel (badanah) is more virtuous, then a cow, then a sheep. A sheep is more virtuous than sharing in a camel or a cow among six partners. Sheep (ḍaʾn) are more virtuous than goats (maʿz). The Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "The best sacrificial animal is the horned ram." {«خير الأضحية الكبش الأقرن»} The white is more virtuous than the gray and the black. Abū Hurayrah said: "A white animal is better in sacrifice than the blood of two black ones." Let him eat from it if it is a voluntary offering (hady al-taṭawwuʿ). He should not sacrifice an animal that is lame (ʿarjāʾ), one with a severed ear or horn (jadʿāʾ), one with a broken horn (ʿaḍbāʾ), one with mange (jarbāʾ), one with a split ear from above (sharqāʾ), one with a split ear from below (kharqāʾ), one with a hole in the front of the ear (muqābalah), one with a hole in the back of the ear (mudābarah), or one that is emaciated (ʿajfāʾ). The jadʿ is the severing of the nose and ear; the ʿaḍb is in the horn and in the deficiency of the limbs; the sharqāʾ is the one with a split ear from above; the kharqāʾ is from below; the muqābalah is the one pierced in the front of the ear; the mudābarah is from behind; and the ʿajfāʾ is the emaciated one that has no marrow in its bones due to leanness.

Then let him shave his head after that. The Sunnah is that he faces the qiblah and begins with the front of his head, shaving the right side down to the two bones overlooking the nape, then shaves the rest, saying: "O God, establish for me a good deed for every hair, erase from me a sin through it, and raise for me a degree with You through it." The woman shortens her hair. For the bald man, it is recommended to pass the razor over his head. Whenever he has shaved after stoning the pillar, he has achieved the first release (al-taḥallul al-awwal), and all prohibitions become permissible for him except women and hunting.

Then he departs to Mecca and circumambulates as we have described. This circumambulation is a pillar (rukn) of the pilgrimage and is called the Circumambulation of Visitation (ṭawāf al-ziyārah). Its earliest time is after the middle of the night of the Day of Sacrifice, and its most virtuous time is the Day of Sacrifice itself. There is no final limit to its time; rather, he may delay it to any time he wishes, but he remains bound by the ties of iḥrām, and women are not permissible for him until he circumambulates. When he has circumambulated, the release is complete, sexual intercourse becomes permissible, and the iḥrām is entirely lifted. Nothing remains except the stoning of the Days of Tashrīq and the overnight stay at Minā, which are obligatory duties after the lifting of iḥrām, by way of following the truth. The manner of this circumambulation with its two units of prayer is as previously described in the Circumambulation of Arrival (ṭawāf al-qudūm). When he finishes the two units, he performs the running (saʿy) as we described, if he had not already performed it after the Circumambulation of Arrival. If he had already performed it, then that has counted as the pillar, and he should not repeat the running.

The causes of release (taḥallul) are three: the stoning, the shaving, and the circumambulation, which is the pillar. Whenever he performs two of these three, he has achieved one of the two releases, and there is no blame upon him in the precedence or delay of these three with the sacrifice. However, the most excellent order is that he stones, then slaughters, then shaves, then circumambulates.

The Sunnah for the leader (imām) on this day is to deliver a sermon after the sun's decline (zawāl). It is the Farewell Sermon of the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him. In the pilgrimage there are four sermons: the sermon of the seventh day, the sermon of the Day of ʿArafah, the sermon of the Day of Sacrifice, and the sermon of the Day of the First Departure. All of them are after the sun's decline, and all are single sermons, except the sermon of the Day of ʿArafah, which is two sermons with a sitting between them.

Then, when he finishes the circumambulation, he returns to Minā for the overnight stay and the stoning. He stays that night at Minā, which is called the Night of Settling (laylat al-qarr), because on the morrow the people settle at Minā and do not depart.

When the second day of the Festival dawns and the sun declines, he performs the major ablution for the stoning and heads to the first pillar, which is nearest to ʿArafāt, located to the right of the main road. He stones it with seven pebbles. When he has passed it, he turns slightly to the right of the road and stands facing the qiblah, praising God, declaring His oneness, magnifying Him, and supplicating with a present heart and humble limbs. He stands facing the qiblah for the measure of reciting Sūrat al-Baqarah, devoting himself to supplication. Then he advances to the middle pillar and stones it as he stoned the first, and stands as he stood for the first. Then he advances to the Pillar of ʿAqabah and stones it with seven pebbles, not tarrying for any matter, but rather returning to his dwelling. He stays that night at Minā, and this night is called the Night of the First Departure. He rises in the morning, and when he has prayed the noon prayer on the second of the Days of Tashrīq, he stones on this day twenty-one pebbles, just as on the day before.

Then he is given the choice between remaining at Minā and returning to Mecca. If he departs from Minā before sunset, nothing is incumbent upon him. But if he waits until night, it is not permissible for him to depart; rather, the overnight stay becomes obligatory upon him, until he stones on the Day of the Second Departure twenty-one stones, as previously mentioned. In the omission of the overnight stay and the stoning, there is the shedding of blood (i.e., a sacrificial offering), and let him give the meat in charity.

He may visit the House (the Kaʿbah) during the nights of Minā, on the condition that he does not stay overnight except at Minā. The Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, used to do this. {«كان رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم يفعل ذلك»} He should not abandon attending the obligatory prayers with the imām in the Mosque of al-Khayf, for its merit is immense. When he departs from Minā, it is preferable that he stay at al-Muḥaṣṣab of Minā, praying the afternoon prayer (ʿaṣr), the sunset prayer (maghrib), and the night prayer (ʿishāʾ), and taking a brief rest. {«ويصلي العصر والمغرب والعشاء ويرقد رقدة»} This is the Sunnah, as narrated by a group of the Companions, may God be pleased with them. If he does not do this, nothing is incumbent upon him.

chapters.title_en: The Eighth Discourse on the Description of the Minor Pilgrimage (ʿUmrah) and What Follows It Until the Farewell Circumambulation (Ṭawāf al-Wadāʿ)
chapters.arabic_text:
||| الجملة الثامنة في صفة العمرة وما بعدها إلى طواف الوداع

من أراد أن يعتمر قبل حجه أو بعده كيفما أراد فليغتسل ويلبس ثياب الإحرام
كما سبق في الحج ويحرم بالعمرة من ميقاتها وأفضل مواقيتها الجعرانة ثم
التنعيم ثم الحديبية
وينوي العمرة ويلبي ويقصد مسجد عائشة رضي الله PageV01P257
عنها ويصلي ركعتين ويدعو بما شاء ثم يعود إلى مكة وهو يلبي حتى يدخل
المسجد الحرام فإذا دخل المسجد ترك التلبية وطاف سبعا وسعى سبعا كما وصفنا
فإذا فرغ حلق رأسه وقد تمت عمرته والمقيم بمكة ينبغي أن يكثر الاعتمار
والطواف وليكثر النظر إلى البيت فإذا دخله فليصل ركعتين  بين العمودين فهو
الأفضل وليدخله حافيا موقرا
قيل لبعضهم هل دخلت بيت ربك اليوم فقال والله ما أرى هاتين القدمين أهلا
للطواف حول بيت ربي فكيف أراهما أهلا لأن أطأ بهما بيت ربي وقد علمت حيث
مشيتا وإلى أين مشيتا وليكثر شرب ماء زمزم وليستق بيده من غير استنابة إن
أمكنه وليرتو منه حتى يتضلع وليقل اللهم اجعله شفاء من كل داء وسقم وارزقني
الإخلاص واليقين والمعافاة في الدنيا والآخرة قال صلى الله عليه وسلم ماء
زمزم لما شرب له (1) أي يشفي ما قصد به
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ع-م-ر (ʿ-m-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning of visitation, cultivation, and inhabiting a place; the ʿumrah as a visit to the Sacred House distinct from the ḥajj.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The ʿumrah signifies the intentional visitation of the Kaʿbah as an act of devotion, emphasizing the renewal of servitude (ʿubūdiyyah) outside the fixed hajj season.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) usage denotes physical visitation; metaphorical (majāz) usage extends to the soul's "inhabiting" the precincts of divine proximity.
- Root: ج-ع-ر (j-ʿ-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Al-Jiʿrānah — a place near Mecca; root evokes the idea of a hollow or basin, here a topographical marker for miqāt.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Designated station (mīqāt) for entering the state of iḥrām, carrying jurisprudential weight in determining the validity of the ʿumrah.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Proper noun usage, literal and fixed; no metaphorical extension.
- Root: ت-ل-ب (t-l-b)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Talbiyah — the vocal proclamation of readiness; root conveys continuous response and presence.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The verbal declaration of intention (niyyah) made manifest, aligning the tongue with the heart's resolve in the sacred rite.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal speech act; metaphorically, the soul's perpetual answering of the divine call beyond the ritual.
- Root: ض-ل-ع (ḍ-l-ʿ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Iḍṭalaʿa — to drink until the ribs are saturated; root denotes fullness and satiation.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Physical satiation as a symbol of spiritual quenching through the blessed water of Zamzam.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal bodily satiation; metaphorical usage points to the soul's yearning for complete spiritual fulfillment.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Imperative Sequencing (al-Sharṭ wa al-Jazāʾ) — The text employs a series of coordinated imperatives (fa-l-yaghtasil, wa-l-yalbas, wa-l-yuḥrim) following the conditional clause (man arāda), requiring the apodosis to be parsed as a chain of obligatory actions governed by the initial intent.
chapters.translation:
I say: The eighth discourse concerns the description of the minor pilgrimage (ʿumrah) and what follows it until the farewell circumambulation (ṭawāf al-wadāʿ).

Know that whoever desires to perform the ʿumrah before his ḥajj or after it, in whatever manner he wishes, let him perform the major ablution (ghusl) and don the garments of iḥrām, just as was previously described in the ḥajj. And let him enter the state of iḥrām for the ʿumrah from its appointed station (mīqāt). The most excellent of its stations is al-Jiʿrānah, then al-Tanʿīm, then al-Ḥudaybiyyah.

And let him intend the ʿumrah, and utter the talbiyah, and make his way to the mosque of ʿĀʾishah — may God be pleased with her — and pray two rakʿahs therein, and supplicate with whatever he wishes. Then let him return to Mecca while still uttering the talbiyah, until he enters the Sacred Mosque. When he enters the mosque, let him cease the talbiyah, and circumambulate seven circuits, and run between al-Ṣafā and al-Marwah seven times, just as we have described. When he finishes, let him shave his head, and his ʿumrah is thereby completed.

The one residing in Mecca ought to multiply the performance of ʿumrah and circumambulation, and let him multiply his gazing upon the House. When he enters it, let him pray two rakʿahs between the two pillars, for that is most virtuous. And let him enter it barefoot, with reverence and awe.

It was said to one of the pious: "Have you entered the House of your Lord today?" He replied: "By God, I do not deem these two feet worthy of circumambulating around the House of my Lord — how then do I deem them worthy of treading with them inside the House of my Lord, when I know where they have walked and to where they have walked?"

And let him drink abundantly of the water of Zamzam, and let him draw it with his own hand, without delegating to another, if he is able. And let him drink deeply of it until he is satiated. And let him say: "O God, make it a healing from every ailment and sickness, and grant me sincerity (ikhlāṣ), certainty (yaqīn), and well-being in this world and the Hereafter." The Prophet — peace be upon him — said: {«مَاءُ زَمْزَمَ لِمَا شُرِبَ لَهُ»} — "The water of Zamzam is for whatever purpose it is drunk" — meaning, it brings healing for that which was intended by drinking it.

chapters.title_en: The Ninth Section on the Farewell Circumambulation (Ṭawāf al-Wadāʿ)
chapters.arabic_text:
||| الجملة التاسعة في طواف الوداع

مهما عن له الرجوع إلى الوطن بعد الفراغ من إتمام الحج والعمرة فلينجز
أولا أشغاله وليشد رحاله وليجعل آخر أشغاله وداع البيت ووداعه بأن يطوف به
سبعا ما سبق ولكن من غير رمل واضطباع فإذا فرغ منه صلى ركعتين خلف المقام
وشرب من ماء زمزم ثم يأتي الملتزم ويدعو ويتضرع ويقول اللهم إن البيت بيتك
والعبد عبدك وابن عبدك وابن أمتك حملتني على ما سخرت لي من خلقك حتى سيرتني
في بلادك وبلغتني بنعمتك حتى أعنتني على قضاء مناسكك فإن كنت رضيت عني
فازدد عني رضا وإلا فمن الآن قبل تباعدي عن بيتك هذا أوان انصرافي إن أذنت
لي غير مستبدل بك ولا ببيتك ولا راغب عنك ولا عن بيتك
اللهم أصحبني العافية في بدني والعصمة في ديني وأحسن منقلبي وارزقني
طاعتك أبدا ما أبقيتني واجمع لي خير الدنيا والآخرة إنك على كل شيء قدير
اللهم لا تجعل هذا آخر عهدي ببيتك الحرام وإن جعلته آخر عهدي فعوضني عنه
الجنة والأحب أن لا يصرف بصره عن البيت حتى يغيب عنه
chapters.anchors:
- Root: و-د-ع (w-d-ʿ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning of "bidding farewell," "leaving behind," or "departing from" — signifying the final act of separation from a venerated place.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In ritual context, denotes the concluding devotional act (ʿibādah) that seals the pilgrim's state of iḥrām and formalizes the termination of the sacred journey (nusuk).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) usage refers to physical parting; here it is metaphorical (majāz) for the soul's reluctant severance from the sanctified precinct, emphasizing emotional and spiritual detachment.
- Root: ل-ت-ز-م (l-t-z-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Root meaning "to cling," "to adhere," or "to hold fast" — referring to the physical embrace of the wall between the Black Stone and the Door of the Kaʿbah.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Symbolizes the servant's desperate attachment to Divine mercy, a gesture of humble supplication (duʿāʾ) and seeking refuge (istiʿādhah).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal clinging to a physical object; metaphorically, the soul's clinging to God's covenant (ʿahd) and forgiveness.
- Root: ص-ر-ف (ṣ-r-f)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning "to turn away," "to divert," or "to avert" — used here for averting the gaze.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Indicates the discipline of the senses (ḥifẓ al-jawāriḥ) in maintaining spiritual focus until the sacred site vanishes from sight.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal turning of the eyes; metaphorically, the heart's continued orientation (tawajjuh) toward the Divine even after physical departure.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Supplicatory Clauses (al-sharṭ wa al-duʿāʾ) — The text employs conditional particles (in, law) and imperative-optative verbs (rabbī, allāhumma) to structure a sequence of contingent requests, requiring careful parsing of protasis and apodosis to preserve the logical and devotional flow.
chapters.translation:
I say: The Ninth Section on the Farewell Circumambulation (ṭawāf al-wadāʿ).

Whenever the intention arises in him to return to his homeland after completing the Hajj and the ʿUmrah, let him first finish all his pending affairs and strap his baggage, and let him make the very last of his deeds the farewell to the House — and his farewell to it is that he circumambulate it seven times, as previously described, but without the hurried pace (ramal) and without the draping of the cloak (iḍṭibāʿ). When he finishes this, let him pray two rakʿahs behind the Station of Abraham (maqām Ibrāhīm), and drink from the water of Zamzam. Then let him come to the Place of Clinging (multazam), and supplicate and humble himself, saying: "O God, verily the House is Your House, and the servant is Your servant, the son of Your servant, the son of Your maidservant. You have carried me upon what You subjected to me of Your creation, until You made me journey through Your lands, and You conveyed me by Your grace until You aided me in fulfilling Your rites. If You are pleased with me, then increase Your pleasure in me; and if not, then from this very moment, before my distance from Your House, this is the time of my departure, if You permit me — not exchanging You nor Your House, nor turning away from You nor from Your House.

O God, accompany me with well-being in my body, and protection in my religion, and make excellent my final return, and grant me Your obedience forever as long as You keep me alive, and gather for me the good of this world and the Hereafter; verily You are over all things Omnipotent. O God, do not make this my last covenant with Your Sacred House; but if You make it my last covenant, then compensate me for it with Paradise."

And it is beloved that he not avert his gaze from the House until it disappears from his sight.

وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم من وجد سعة ولم يفد إلي فقد جفاني (3) وقال صلى
الله عليه وسلم من جاءني زائرا لا يهمه إلا زيارتي كان حقا على الله سبحانه

عليك
