chapters.anchors:
- Root: ز-و-ر (z-w-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Intentional turning toward a place or person for encounter; visitation implying purposeful approach.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Pilgrimage-visitation (ziyārah) as an act of devotional proximity, distinct from mere travel.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) in physical approach; metaphorical (majāz) in spiritual nearness to the Prophet ﷺ after death.
- Root: و-ق-ي (w-q-y)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Preservation, shielding from harm; protective barrier.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Divine safeguard (wiqāyah) from chastisement, tied to seeking intercession.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal in physical protection; metaphorical in eschatological deliverance.
- Root: ش-ف-ع (sh-f-ʿ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Pairing or doubling; intercession as joining one's plea to another's.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Prophetic intercession (shafāʿah) as divinely granted mediation on Judgment Day.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal in legal advocacy; metaphorical in the Prophet's ﷺ role as pleader for the ummah.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional-Protasis Construction (al-sharṭ wa-l-jawāb) — The phrase "whoever visits me... it is as if" employs a conditional clause where the apodosis equates posthumous visitation with living encounter, requiring the subjunctive mood in the implied verb.
chapters.translation:
I say: The Tenth Discourse concerns the visitation of Madīnah and its etiquettes.

The Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever visits me after my death, it is as if he visited me in my life." (2)
And he ﷺ said: "Whoever finds ample means and does not come to me has indeed been remiss toward me." (3)
And he ﷺ said: "Whoever comes to me as a visitor, with no concern other than my visitation, it is incumbent upon Allah the Exalted that I be an intercessor for him." (4)

So whoever intends to visit Madīnah, let him send abundant blessings upon the Messenger of Allah ﷺ along his way.

When his gaze falls upon the walls of Madīnah and its trees, let him say: "O Allah, this is the sanctuary of Your Messenger, so make it for me a protection from the Fire, and a security from chastisement and an evil reckoning."

Let him perform the major ablution (ghusl) before entering, from the well of al-Ḥarrah, and let him apply perfume, and wear his cleanest garments. When he enters it, let him enter with humility and veneration, and let him say: "In the name of Allah, and upon the creed of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. O my Lord, admit me with an honorable admission, and bring me out with an honorable exit, and grant me from Yourself an assisting authority."

Then let him proceed to the mosque, enter it, and pray two units (rakʿatayn) beside the pulpit (minbar), placing the pillar of the pulpit opposite his right shoulder, facing the column beside which is the chest (ṣundūq), with the circle in the qiblah of the mosque between his eyes — for that is the standing place of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ before the mosque was altered. Let him strive to pray in the original mosque before its expansion.

Then let him come to the grave of the Prophet ﷺ and stand at its face — that is, by turning his back to the qiblah and facing the wall of the grave, at about four cubits from the column at the corner of the grave's wall, placing the lantern above his head. It is not from the Sunnah to touch the wall nor to kiss it; rather, standing at a distance is closer to reverence. Let him stand and say:

"Peace be upon you, O Messenger of Allah. Peace be upon you, O Prophet of Allah. Peace be upon you, O Trustworthy One of Allah. Peace be upon you, O Beloved of Allah. Peace be upon you, O Chosen One of Allah. Peace be upon you, O Best of Allah's creation. Peace be upon you, O Aḥmad. Peace be upon you, O Muḥammad. Peace be upon you, O Abū al-Qāsim. Peace be upon you, O Eraser (of disbelief). Peace be upon you, O Final (Prophet). Peace be upon you, O Gatherer (of mankind). Peace be upon you, O Bringer of glad tidings. Peace be upon you, O Warner. Peace be upon you, O Pure one. Peace be upon you, O Purified one. Peace be upon you, O Most noble of Adam's children. Peace be upon you, O Master of the Messengers. Peace be upon you, O Seal of the Prophets. Peace be upon you, O Messenger of the Lord of the Worlds. Peace be upon you, O Leader of goodness. Peace be upon you, O Opener of virtue. Peace be upon you, O Prophet of Mercy. Peace be upon you, O Guide of the Ummah. Peace be upon you, O Leader of the bright-faced (al-ghurr al-muḥajjalīn). Peace be upon you, and upon your Household, from whom Allah has removed all impurity and purified them thoroughly. Peace be upon you, and upon your righteous Companions, and upon your pure wives, the Mothers of the Believers. May Allah reward you on our behalf with the best that He has rewarded any Prophet for his people, or any Messenger for his nation. And may Allah send blessings upon you whenever those who remember you remember you, and whenever those who are heedless of you are heedless. And may Allah send blessings upon you among the first and the last, with the best, most complete, most exalted, most noble, most wholesome, and most pure blessings that He has bestowed upon any of His creation — just as He rescued us through you from misguidance, and gave us sight through you from blindness, and guided us through you from ignorance. I bear witness that there is no god but Allah alone, with no partner, and I bear witness that you are His servant, His Messenger, His Trustworthy One, His Chosen One, and His Best of creation. And I bear witness that you have conveyed the message, fulfilled the trust, advised the Ummah, struggled against your enemy, guided your Ummah, and worshipped your Lord until certainty came to you. So may Allah bless you and your pure Household, and grant you peace, honor, nobility, and veneration."

And if someone has entrusted him to convey a greeting, let him say: "Peace be upon you from so-and-so. Peace be upon you from so-and-so."

Then let him step back about a cubit and greet Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq (may Allah be pleased with him), for his head is at the shoulder of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and the head of ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) is at the shoulder of Abū Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him).

Then let him step back about a cubit and greet al-Fārūq ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him), and say: "Peace be upon you both, O ministers of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and his helpers in upholding the religion while he lived, and those who stood after him over the affairs of the religion among his Ummah, following his traces therein and acting upon his Sunnah. May Allah reward you both with the best that He has rewarded any ministers of a Prophet for his religion."

Then let him return and stand at the head of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, between the grave and the column today, facing the qiblah. Let him praise Allah the Mighty and Majestic, magnify Him, and send abundant blessings upon the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Then let him say:

"O Allah, You have said — and Your word is the truth: {«And if they, when they wronged themselves, had come to you and asked forgiveness of Allah, and the Messenger had asked forgiveness for them, they would have found Allah Accepting of repentance and Merciful»} (Q 4:64). O Allah, we have heard Your word and obeyed Your command, and we have come to Your Prophet seeking his intercession with You for our sins and for what weighs heavily upon our backs of our burdens, repenting from our slips, confessing our faults and our shortcomings. So relent upon us, O Allah, and grant Your Prophet this intercession for us, and raise us by his station with You and his right upon You.

O Allah, forgive the Emigrants (Muhājirūn) and the Helpers (Anṣār), and forgive us and our brothers who preceded us in faith. O Allah, do not make this the last of our visits to the grave of Your Prophet and to Your Sacred Sanctuary, O Most Merciful of the merciful."

Then let him come to the Rawḍah (the Garden) and pray two units therein, and multiply supplication as much as he is able, for the Prophet ﷺ said: "What is between my grave and my pulpit is a garden from the gardens of Paradise, and my pulpit is upon my cistern (ḥawḍ)." (1)

Let him supplicate at the pulpit, and it is recommended that he place his hand upon the lower pommel (al-rummānah) upon which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to place his hand during the sermon. (2)

It is recommended that he go to Uḥud on Thursday and visit the graves of the martyrs, praying the dawn prayer (ghadāh) in the Prophet's mosque, then go out and return to the mosque for the noon prayer, so that he does not miss the congregational obligatory prayer in the mosque.

It is recommended that he go out every day to al-Baqīʿ after greeting the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and visit the grave of ʿUthmān (may Allah be pleased with him), and the grave of al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with them both). Therein also are the graves of ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn, Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī, and Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad (may Allah be pleased with them). Let him pray in the mosque of Fāṭimah (may Allah be pleased with her), and visit the grave of Ibrāhīm, the son of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and the grave of Ṣafiyyah, the aunt of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ — all of these are in al-Baqīʿ.

It is recommended that he come to the mosque of Qubā every Saturday and pray therein, for it is narrated that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever goes out from his house until he comes to the mosque of Qubā and prays therein, it is equivalent to an ʿumrah." (3)

Let him come to the well of Arīs — it is said that the Prophet ﷺ spat into it — and it is near the mosque. Let him perform ablution from it and drink from its water. (4)

Let him come to the mosque of al-Fatḥ, which is upon the trench (al-khandaq).

Likewise, let him visit the rest of the mosques and sacred sites. It is said that all the sacred sites and mosques in Madīnah number thirty places, known to the people of the city. Let him visit what he is able to. Likewise, let him visit the wells from which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to perform ablution, bathe, and drink — (5) these are seven wells — seeking healing and blessing (tabarruk) through him ﷺ.

If he is able to reside in Madīnah while observing its sanctity, it has great virtue. The Prophet ﷺ said: "No one endures its hardships and severity except that I will be an intercessor for him on the Day of Resurrection." (1)
And he ﷺ said: "Whoever is able to die in Madīnah, let him die there, for no one dies therein except that I will be an intercessor or a witness for him on the Day of Resurrection." (2)

Then, when he has finished his affairs and resolves to depart from Madīnah, it is recommended that he come to the noble grave, repeat the visitation supplication as previously mentioned, bid farewell to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, ask Allah the Mighty and Majestic to grant him return to it, and ask for safety in his journey.

Then let him pray two units in the small Rawḍah — which is the place of the standing of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ before the enclosure (maqṣūrah) was added to the mosque. When he exits, let him put out his left foot first, then his right, and say: "O Allah, send blessings upon Muḥammad and upon the family of Muḥammad, and do not make this the last of my visits to Your Prophet. Remove my burdens through my visitation of him, and accompany me in my journey with safety, and make easy my return to my family and homeland in security, O Most Merciful of the merciful."

Let him give charity to the neighbors of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ as much as he is able, and let him visit the mosques between Madīnah and Makkah, praying therein — these number twenty places.

chapters.title_en: Section on the Sunnas of Returning from Travel
chapters.arabic_text:
||| فصل في سنن الرجوع من السفر

كان رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم إذا
قفل من غزو أو حج أو عمرة يكبر على رأس كل شرف من الأرض ثلاث تكبيرات
ويقول لا إله إلا الله وحده لا شريك له له الملك وله الحمد وهو على كل شيء
قدير آيبون تائبون عابدون ساجدون لربنا حامدون صدق الله وعده ونصر عبده
وهزم الأحزاب وحده (3) وفي بعض الروايات وكل شيء هالك إلا وجهه له الحكم
وإليه ترجعون فينبغي أن يستعمل هذه السنة في رجوعه
وإذا أشرف على مدينته يحرك الدابة ويقول اللهم اجعل لنا بها قرارا ورزقا
حسنا
ثم ليرسل إلى أهله من يخبرهم بقدومه كي لا يقدم عليهم بغتة فذلك هو السنة
(4) ولا ينبغي أن يطرق أهله ليلا فإذا دخل البلد فليقصد المسجد أولا وليصل
ركعتين فهو السنة (5) كذلك كان يفعل  رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم فإذا دخل
بيته قال توبا توبا لربنا أو با لا يغادر علينا حوبا فإذا استقر في منزله
فلا ينبغي أن ينسى ما أنعم الله به عليه من زيارة بيته وحرمه وقبر نبيه صلى
الله عليه وسلم فيكفر تلك النعمة بأن يعود إلى الغفلة واللهو والخوض في
المعاصي فما ذلك علامة الحج المبرور بل علامته أن يعود زاهدا في الدنيا
راغبا في الآخرة متأهبا للقاء رب البيت بعد لقاء البيت
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ق-ف-ل (q-f-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Return from a journey; the act of turning back to one's origin or home.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological context, denotes the soul's reversion to its primordial state or the physical return from a sacred expedition, implying completion of a ritual cycle.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) for physical return; metaphorical (majāz) for spiritual reversion to obedience after a state of absence.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional-Response Construction (al-sharṭ wa-l-jawāb) — the protasis (idhā) governs the apodosis sequence, requiring the verb to be in the past tense for habitual actions, as in "kāna idhā qafala... kabbara."
chapters.translation:
I say: The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, when he returned from a raid, or a pilgrimage, or a lesser pilgrimage, would proclaim the takbīr (saying "God is Great") three times upon every elevated point of the land, and he would say: "There is no god but God alone, with no partner; His is the dominion, and His is the praise, and He is over all things powerful. Returning, repentant, worshipping, prostrating to our Lord, praising. God has fulfilled His promise, aided His servant, and defeated the confederates alone" {«لا إله إلا الله وحده لا شريك له له الملك وله الحمد وهو على كل شيء قدير آيبون تائبون عابدون ساجدون لربنا حامدون صدق الله وعده ونصر عبده وهزم الأحزاب وحده»} (3). In some narrations, it adds: "And everything is perishing except His Face; His is the judgment, and to Him you shall return" {«وكل شيء هالك إلا وجهه له الحكم وإليه ترجعون»}. Thus, one ought to practice this sunna upon his return.

And when he comes in sight of his city, he should urge his mount onward and say: "O God, grant us therein settledness and goodly provision" {«اللهم اجعل لنا بها قرارا ورزقا حسنا»}.

Then let him send ahead to his family one who will inform them of his arrival, so that he does not come upon them suddenly—for that is the sunna (4). Nor should he approach his family by night. When he enters the town, let him head first to the mosque and pray two rakʿahs—that is the sunna (5). Thus did the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, do. When he entered his house, he would say: "Repentance, repentance to our Lord; O pardoner, leave no sin upon us" {«توبا توبا لربنا أو با لا يغادر علينا حوبا»}.

Then, when he settles in his abode, he must not forget the grace God has bestowed upon him—the visitation of His House, His Sacred Precinct, and the grave of His Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace—such that he repays that blessing by reverting to heedlessness, frivolity, and plunging into sins. For that is not the mark of an accepted pilgrimage (ḥajj mabrūr); rather, its mark is that he returns abstinent (zāhid) in this world, desirous of the Hereafter, and prepared for the meeting with the Lord of the House after the visitation of the House.

chapters.title_en: The Third Book on Subtle Etiquettes and Inward Works
chapters.arabic_text: || الباب الثالث في الآداب الدقيقة والأعمال الباطنة
chapters.anchors:
- Root: أ-د-ب (ʾ-d-b)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning of refined conduct, discipline, and cultivated propriety—both outward manners and inward training of the soul.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, adab signifies the disciplined alignment of the heart’s intentions with divine command, transcending mere social custom.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) refers to the training of character; metaphorical (majāz) extends to the subtle inward states that govern outward acts.
- Root: د-ق-ق (d-q-q)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Root denotes fineness, subtlety, and precision—that which is too delicate for coarse perception.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In the spiritual path, daqīqah points to the hidden nuances of devotional practice that escape the heedless.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: thinness or smallness; metaphorical: the inward subtleties of the heart’s movements.
- Root: ب-ط-ن (b-ṭ-n)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning of the inner, concealed, or hidden aspect—opposed to ẓāhir (outward).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Bāṭin denotes the inward dimension of deeds—intentions, sincerity, and the heart’s states—which are the true locus of divine acceptance.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: the belly or interior of a thing; metaphorical: the hidden spiritual reality behind outward forms.
- Sībawayh Rule: ʾIḍāfah (Construct State) — The phrase "ādāb al-daqīqah" and "al-aʿmāl al-bāṭinah" employ genitive construction and adjectival agreement, respectively, to bind outward discipline to inward subtlety, indicating that the etiquettes are themselves the vehicles for the hidden works.
chapters.translation: I say: This is the third book, concerning the subtle etiquettes and the inward works.

chapters.title_en: The Exposition of the Subtleties of the Pilgrimage Etiquettes — Ten Principles
chapters.arabic_text:
||| بيان دقائق الآداب وهي عشرة

الأول أن تكون النفقة حلالا وتكون اليد خالية من تجارة تشغل القلب وتفرق
الهم حتى يكون الهم مجردا PageV01P261
لله تعالى والقلب مطمئنا منصرفا إلى ذكر الله تعالى وتعظيم شعائره
وقد روي في خبر من طريق أهل البيت إذا كان آخر الزمان خرج الناس إلى الحج
أربعة أصناف سلاطينهم للنزهة وأغنياؤهم للتجارة وفقراؤهم للمسألة وقراؤهم
للسمعة (1) وفي الخبر إشارة إلى جملة أغراض الدنيا التي يتصور أن تتصل
بالحج فكل ذلك مما يمنع فضيلة الحج ويخرجه عن حيز حج الخصوص لا سيما إذا
كان متجردا بنفس الحج بأن يحج لغيره بأجرة فيطلب الدنيا بعمل الآخرة
وقد كره الورعون وأرباب القلوب ذلك إلا أن يكون قصده المقام بمكة ولم يكن
له ما يبلغه فلا بأس أن يأخذ ذلك على هذا القصد لا ليتوصل بالدين إلى
الدنيا بل بالدنيا إلى الدين
فعند ذلك ينبغي أن يكون قصده زيارة بيت الله عز وجل ومعاونة أخيه المسلم
بإسقاط الفرض عنه
وفي مثله ينزل قول رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم يدخل الله سبحانه بالحجة
الواحدة ثلاثة الجنة الموصي بها والمنفذ لها ومن حج بها عن أخيه (2) ولست
أقول لا تحل الأجرة أو يحرم ذلك بعد أن أسقط فرض الإسلام عن نفسه ولكن
الأولى أن لا يفعل ولا يتخذ ذلك مكسبه ومتجره فإن الله عز وجل يعطي الدنيا
بالدين ولا يعطي الدين بالدنيا
وفي الخبر مثل الذي يغزو في سبيل  الله عز وجل ويأخذ أجرا مثل أم موسى
عليه السلام ترضع ولدها وتأخذ أجرها (3) فمن كان مثاله في أخذ الأجرة على
الحج مثال أم موسى فلا بأس بأخذه فإنه يأخذ ليتمكن من الحج والزيارة فيه
وليس يحج ليأخذ الأجرة بل يأخذ الأجرة ليحج كما كانت تأخذ أم موسى ليتيسر
لها الإرضاع بتلبيس حالها عليهم
الثاني أن لا يعاون أعداء الله سبحانه بتسليم المكس وهم الصادون عن
المسجد الحرام من أمراء مكة والأعراب المترصدين في الطريق
فإن تسليم المال إليهم إعانة على الظلم وتيسير لأسبابه عليهم فهو
كالإعانة بالنفس فليتلطف في حيلة الخلاص فإن لم يقدر فقد قال بعض العلماء
ولا بأس بما قاله إن ترك التنفل بالحج والرجوع عن الطريق أفضل من إعانة
الظلمة فإن هذه بدعة أحدثت وفي الانقياد لها ما يجعلها سنة مطردة وفيه ذل
وصغار على المسلمين ببذل جزية
ولا معنى لقول القائل إن ذلك يؤخذ مني وأنا مضطر فإنه لو قعد في البيت أو
رجع من الطريق لم يؤخذ منه شيء بل ربما يظهر أسباب الترفه فتكثر مطالبته
فلو كان في زي الفقراء لم يطالب فهو الذي ساق نفسه إلى حالة الاضطرار
الثالث التوسع في الزاد وطيب النفس بالبذل والإنفاق من غير تقتير ولا
إسراف بل على اقتصاد وأعني بالإسراف التنعم بأطيب الأطعمة والترفه بشرب
أنواعها على عادة المترقين
فأما كثرة البذل فلا سرف فيه إذ لا خير في السرف ولا سرف في الخير كما
قيل وبذل الزاد في طريق الحج نفقته في سبيل عز وجل والدرهم بسبعمائة درهم
قال ابن عمر رضي الله عنهما من كرم الرجل طيب زاده في سفره وكان يقول
أفضل الحاج أخلصهم نية وأزكاهم نفقة وأحسنهم يقينا وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم
الحج المبرور ليس له جزاء إلا الجنة فقيل له يا رسول الله ما بر الحج فقال
طيب الكلام وإطعام الطعام (4)
الرابع ترك الرفث والفسوق PageV01P262
والجدال كما نطق به القرآن
والرفث اسم جامع لكل لغو وخنى وفحش من الكلام ويدخل  فيه مغازلة النساء
ومداعبتهن والتحدث بشأن الجماع ومقدماته فإن ذلك يهيج داعية الجماع المحظور
والداعي إلى المحظور محظور
والفسق اسم جامع لكل خروج عن طاعة الله عز وجل
والجدال هو المبالغة في الخصومة والمماراة بما يورث الضغائن ويفرق في
الحال الهمة ويناقض حسن الخلق وقد قال سفيان من رفث فسد حجه
وقد جعل رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم طيب الكلام مع إطعام الطعام من بر
الحج
والمماراة تناقض طيب الكلام فلا ينبغي أن يكون كثير الاعتراض على رفيقه
وجماله وعلى غيره من أصحابه بل يلين جانبه ويخفض جناحه للسائرين إلى بيت
الله عز وجل ويلزم حسن الخلق وليس حسن الخلق كف الأذى بل احتمال الأذى وقيل
سمي السفر سفرا لأنه يسفر عن أخلاق الرجال ولذلك قال عمر رضي الله عنه لمن
زعم أنه يعرف رجلا هل صحبته في السفر الذي يستدل به على مكارم الأخلاق قال
لا فقال ما أراك تعرفه
الخامس أن يحج ماشيا إن قدر عليه فذلك الأفضل أوصى عبد الله بن عباس رضي
الله عنهما بنيه عند موته فقال يا بني حجوا مشاة فإن للحاج الماشي بكل خطوة
يخطوها سبعمائة حسنة من حسنات الحرم قيل وما حسنات الحرم قال الحسنة بمائة
ألف والاستحباب في المشي في المناسك والتردد من مكة إلى الموقف وإلى منى
آكد منه في الطريق
وإن أضاف إلى المشي الإحرام من دويرة أهله فقد قيل إن ذلك من إتمام الحج
قاله عمر وعلي وابن مسعود رضي الله عنهم في معنى قوله عز وجل وأتموا الحج
والعمرة لله وقال بعض العلماء الركوب أفضل لما فيه من الإنفاق والمؤنة
ولأنه أبعد عن ضجر النفس وأقل لأذاه
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ن-ف-ق (n-f-q)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Expenditure, disbursement; the root denotes the outflow of provisions and wealth.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Spending in the path of obedience; specifically the provision (zād) that sustains the pilgrim's journey.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense is monetary outlay; metaphorical extension applies to expending one's effort and soul in devotion.
- Root: ر-ف-ث (r-f-th)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Obscene, lewd speech; any utterance that is foul or indecent.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Comprehensive term for all forbidden speech during the state of iḥrām, including sexual innuendo and frivolous talk.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal meaning is filth and obscenity; metaphorically, it designates every word that corrupts the sanctity of the pilgrimage.
- Root: ج-د-ل (j-d-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Disputation, argumentation; the root implies twisting and knotting in speech.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Quarrelsome contention that breeds rancor and diverts the heart from devotion.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense is the act of wrestling in debate; metaphorically, it is the excessive wrangling prohibited in the Quranic verse.
- Root: ش-ع-ر (sh-ʿ-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Ritual marks, symbols; the root denotes awareness and the distinctive signs of devotion.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The sacred rites and sacrificial animals that manifest the glorification of Allah.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal meaning is the physical mark or banner; metaphorically, it is the outward emblem of religious veneration.
- Sībawayh Rule: The Rule of Conditional Restriction (al-Sharṭ wa al-Jazāʾ) — In the phrase "if he is unable, then..." the protasis governs the apodosis, requiring the apodosis to be contingent upon the fulfillment of the condition, as in the permissibility of taking wages for pilgrimage only when the intention is pure.
chapters.translation:
I say: The exposition of the subtleties of the etiquettes, and they are ten.

The first is that the expenditure be lawful (ḥalāl), and that the hand be free from any commerce that occupies the heart and disperses the concern, so that the concern is purely directed to Allah the Exalted, and the heart is tranquil, turned to the remembrance of Allah the Exalted and the veneration of His sacred rites (shaʿāʾir). It has been narrated in a report from the path of the People of the House (Ahl al-Bayt): "When the end of time arrives, people will go out to the pilgrimage in four categories: their kings for leisure, their wealthy for commerce, their poor for begging, and their reciters for reputation." In this report there is an indication of the totality of worldly aims that can conceivably attach themselves to the pilgrimage. All of that is what prevents the virtue of the pilgrimage and removes it from the domain of the pilgrimage of the elite (ḥajj al-khuṣūṣ), especially if one is devoted solely to the pilgrimage itself by performing it for another for a wage, thereby seeking the world through the work of the Hereafter. The pious (waraʿah) and the masters of hearts have disapproved of this, except when one's intention is to reside in Mecca and one has no means to reach it — then there is no harm in taking that [wage] with this intention, not to reach the world through religion, but rather to reach religion through the world.

At that point, his intention should be the visitation of the House of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and the assistance of his Muslim brother by discharging the obligation (farḍ) on his behalf. In a similar case is the descent of the saying of the Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him: "Allah the Glorified will admit three persons to Paradise through a single pilgrimage: the one who bequeaths it, the one who executes it, and the one who performs it on behalf of his brother." I do not say that the wage is unlawful (ḥarām) or that it is forbidden after one has discharged the obligation of Islam from himself, but the preferable course is not to do it, nor to make it one's livelihood and trade. For Allah, Mighty and Majestic, gives the world through religion, but He does not give religion through the world.

In the report, the example of one who fights in the path of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and takes a wage is like the mother of Moses, peace be upon him, who nursed her child and took her wage. Whoever's example in taking the wage for the pilgrimage is the example of the mother of Moses — there is no harm in his taking it, for he takes it to be enabled to perform the pilgrimage and the visitation therein, and he does not perform the pilgrimage to take the wage. Rather, he takes the wage to perform the pilgrimage, just as the mother of Moses took [her wage] so that nursing would be facilitated for her by concealing her situation from them.

The second is that he not assist the enemies of Allah the Glorified by surrendering the toll (maks) to them — and they are those who bar [others] from the Sacred Mosque, namely the governors of Mecca and the Bedouins lying in wait on the road. For surrendering wealth to them is assistance in injustice and facilitation of its means for them; it is like assistance with one's own person. Let him, therefore, be subtle in devising a means of escape. If he is unable, then some scholars have said — and there is no harm in what they said — that abandoning the supererogatory pilgrimage and turning back from the road is better than assisting the oppressors. For this is an innovation (bidʿah) that has been introduced, and in submitting to it there is what makes it a continuous sunnah, and in it there is humiliation and abasement for the Muslims by the payment of a tribute (jizyah).

There is no meaning to the saying of one who says: "This is taken from me, and I am compelled (muḍṭarr)." For if he had remained at home or turned back from the road, nothing would have been taken from him. Rather, perhaps he displays the appearances of luxury, and so his demands multiply. Had he been in the garb of the poor, he would not have been demanded. It is he who has driven himself into a state of compulsion.

The third is the abundance of provision (zād) and the cheerfulness of the soul in giving and spending, without stinginess (taqtīr) nor extravagance (isrāf), but rather with moderation (iqtiṣād). By extravagance I mean the indulgence in the finest foods and the luxury of drinking their varieties, following the custom of the upwardly mobile. As for the abundance of giving, there is no extravagance in it, for there is no good in extravagance, nor is there extravagance in good, as it has been said. And the expenditure of provision on the path of the pilgrimage is one's expenditure in the path of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and the dirham is [multiplied] by seven hundred dirhams. Ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "Part of a man's generosity is the goodness of his provision on his journey." And he used to say: "The best of pilgrims are the most sincere of them in intention, the purest of them in expenditure, and the best of them in certainty." And he, peace be upon him, said: "The accepted pilgrimage (al-ḥajj al-mabrūr) has no reward except Paradise." It was said to him: "O Messenger of Allah, what is the acceptance (birr) of the pilgrimage?" He said: "The goodness of speech and the feeding of food."

The fourth is the abandonment of lewdness (rafath), wickedness (fusūq), and disputation (jidal), as the Quran has pronounced. Rafath is a comprehensive name for every idle, obscene, and foul utterance of speech, and into it enters the flirtation with women, jesting with them, and speaking about the matter of intercourse and its preliminaries. For that stirs the impulse toward forbidden intercourse, and the caller to the forbidden is itself forbidden. Fusūq is a comprehensive name for every departure from obedience to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. And jidal is the exaggeration in contention and wrangling (mirāʾ) with what engenders grudges, disperses in the present moment the resolve, and contradicts good character. Sufyān said: "Whoever commits rafath, his pilgrimage is corrupted." And the Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him, made the goodness of speech along with the feeding of food part of the acceptance (birr) of the pilgrimage. Wrangling contradicts the goodness of speech, so one should not be excessive in objecting to his companion and his beauty, nor to others among his fellows. Rather, he should soften his side and lower his wing to those journeying to the House of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and adhere to good character. And good character is not the mere withholding of harm, but rather the endurance of harm. It has been said: "The journey (safar) was named safar because it unveils (yusfiru) the characters of men." For this reason, ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, said to one who claimed to know a man: "Have you accompanied him on a journey by which one may infer noble character traits?" He said: "No." He said: "I do not think you know him."

The fifth is that he perform the pilgrimage on foot if he is able, for that is more virtuous. ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, bequeathed to his sons at his death, saying: "O my sons, perform the pilgrimage on foot, for the walking pilgrim has for every step he takes seven hundred good deeds from the good deeds of the Sanctuary (al-ḥaram)." It was said: "And what are the good deeds of the Sanctuary?" He said: "The good deed is [multiplied by] one hundred thousand." And the recommendation of walking in the rites (manāsik) and the going back and forth from Mecca to the Standing Place (al-mawqif) and to Minā is more emphatic than it is on the road.

And if he adds to walking the assumption of iḥrām from the vicinity of his family, it has been said that this is part of the completion of the pilgrimage. ʿUmar, ʿAlī, and Ibn Masʿūd, may Allah be pleased with them, said this regarding the meaning of His saying, Mighty and Majestic: {«And complete the pilgrimage and the ʿumrah for Allah»}. And some scholars said that riding is more virtuous because of what it entails of expenditure and expense, and because it is further from the vexation of the soul, lesser in its harm, and closer to one's safety and the completion of his pilgrimage. This, upon investigation, is not contrary to the first [view]. Rather, one should make a distinction and say: Whoever finds walking easy, it is more virtuous for him. But if he is weakened by it and it leads him to bad character and deficiency in [other] works, then riding is more virtuous for him, just as fasting is more virtuous for the traveler and for the sick person as long as it does not lead to weakness and bad character.

Some scholars were asked about the ʿumrah: "Should one walk in it, or hire a donkey for a dirham?" He said: "If the weight of the dirham is heavier upon him, then hiring is more virtuous than walking; and if walking is heavier upon him, like the wealthy, then walking is more virtuous for him." It is as if he went in this to the path of struggling against the soul (mujāhadat al-nafs), and this has a basis. But the more virtuous for him is to walk and to spend that dirham on good — that is more fitting than spending it on the muleteer in exchange for the debasement of the beast. And if his soul does not expand to combine the hardship of walking and the diminution of wealth, then what he mentioned is not far off in this matter.

The sixth is that he ride only a saddle-beast (zāmilah). As for the howdah (maḥmil), let him avoid it, except when he fears that he cannot hold himself steady upon the zāmilah due to an excuse. In this there are two meanings: one is the lightening of the burden upon the camel, for the howdah harms it; and the second is the avoidance of the garb of the luxurious and the arrogant. The Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him, performed the pilgrimage upon a riding beast, and beneath him was a worn saddle and a threadbare saddle-cloth worth four dirhams. And he circumambulated upon the riding beast so that the people might look upon his guidance and his noble traits. And he, peace be upon him, said: "Take from me your rites (manāsik)." It has been said that these howdahs were introduced by al-Ḥajjāj, and the scholars of his time used to disapprove of them. Sufyān al-Thawrī narrated from his father that he said: "I set out from Kufa to al-Qādisiyyah for the pilgrimage, and I met the caravans from the various lands, and I saw all the pilgrims upon zāmilahs, saddle-bags (jawāliq), and riding camels, and I saw among all of them only two howdahs." And Ibn ʿUmar, when he looked upon what al-Ḥajjāj had introduced of attire and howdahs, would say: "The pilgrims are few, and the riders are many." Then he looked upon a poor man of shabby appearance beneath whom was a saddle-bag and said: "This is one of the best of the pilgrims."

The seventh is that he be of shabby appearance, disheveled (ashʿath), and dust-covered (aghbar), not seeking abundance of adornment, nor inclining to the causes of boasting and multiplying [possessions], lest he be written in the register of the arrogant and the luxurious and depart from the party of the weak, the poor, and the elite of the righteous. For he, peace be upon him, commanded dishevelment and concealment, and forbade indulgence and comfort in the hadith of Fuḍālah ibn ʿUbayd. And in the hadith: "The pilgrim is only the disheveled and dust-covered one." And Allah the Exalted says: "Look upon the visitors of My House — they have come to Me disheveled and dust-covered from every deep valley." And He the Exalted said: {«Then let them complete their rites (tafath)»} — and tafath is the dishevelment and dustiness, and its completion is by shaving the head, trimming the mustache, and clipping the nails.

And ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, may Allah be pleased with him, wrote to the commanders of the armies: "Wear worn garments (ikhlaulaqū) and be rough (ikhshawshanū)" — that is, wear the threadbare clothes and employ roughness in matters. It has been said: "The adornment of the pilgrims is the people of Yemen, for they are upon the appearance of humility, weakness, and the way of the predecessors (salaf)." One should, therefore, avoid the color red in his attire in particular, and notoriety (shuhrah) in whatever form in general. For it has been narrated that he, peace be upon him, was on a journey, and his companions alighted at a way-station and let the camels loose. He looked upon red cloths upon the saddles and said, peace be upon him: "I see that this redness has overcome you." They said: "So we rose to them and pulled them off their backs until some of the camels bolted."

The eighth is that he be gentle with the beast, not loading upon it what it cannot bear — and the howdah is beyond the limit of its capacity — and sleeping upon it harms it and weighs heavily upon it. The people of piety (waraʿ) would not sleep upon beasts except a doze while sitting, and they would not stand upon them for a long standing. He, peace be upon him, said: "Do not take the backs of your beasts as chairs." And it is recommended that he dismount from his beast morning and evening to give it rest, for that is a sunnah, and there are reports about this from the predecessors. Some of the predecessors would hire [a beast] on the condition that he not dismount, and he would pay the full hire, then he would dismount from it, so that by this he would be doing good to the beast, and it would be in his good deeds and placed in his scale, not in the scale of the muleteer.

And whoever harms an animal and loads upon it what it cannot bear will be called to account for it on the Day of Resurrection. Abū al-Dardāʾ said to his camel at the time of death: "O camel, do not litigate against me to your Lord, for I never loaded upon you beyond your capacity." And in sum, in every moist liver there is a reward, so let him observe the right of the beast and the right of the muleteer together. And in his dismounting for an hour there is the resting of the beast and the joy of the muleteer's heart. A man said to Ibn al-Mubārak: "Carry this book with me to deliver it." He said: "Until I seek permission from the camel-driver, for I have hired [the beast]." See how he was scrupulous (waraʿ) about carrying a book of no weight — and this is the path of prudence in piety, for when the door of the little is opened, it drags to the much, little by little.

The ninth is that he draw near [to Allah] by the shedding of blood [of sacrifice], even if it is not obligatory upon him, and he should strive that it be from the fat and precious of the cattle. Let him eat from it if it is voluntary (taṭawwuʿ), and let him not eat from it if it is obligatory. It has been said in the interpretation of His saying, the Exalted: {«That is so; and whoever venerates the sacred rites (shaʿāʾir) of Allah»} — that it is the beautifying of it and the fattening of it. And the driving of the sacrificial animal (hady) from the miqāt is more virtuous if it does not exhaust him nor weary him. And let him abandon haggling in its purchase, for they used to be extravagant in three things and disliked haggling in them: the hady, the udḥiyyah, and the slave — for the most virtuous of that is the highest in price and the most precious to its owner. Ibn ʿUmar narrated that ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both, offered a fine camel (bukhtiyyah), and it was demanded of him for three hundred dinars. He asked the Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him, to sell it and buy with its price a number of sacrificial camels (budn), but he forbade him from that and said: "Rather, offer it." This is because the little that is excellent is better than the much that is inferior. And in three hundred dinars is the value of thirty sacrificial camels, and in that is the multiplication of meat — but the intended object is not the meat. The intended object is only the purification of the soul and its cleansing from the attribute of miserliness, and its adornment with the beauty of veneration for Allah, Mighty and Majestic. For {«Never will their flesh nor their blood reach Allah, but piety from you reaches Him»}. And that is attained by observing the preciousness in value, whether the number is many or few. And the Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him, was asked: "What is the acceptance (birr) of the pilgrimage?" He said: "The raising of the voice (al-ʿajj) and the shedding of blood (al-thajj)" — al-ʿajj is the raising of the voice in the talbiyah, and al-thajj is the slaughtering of the budn. And ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, narrated that the Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him, said: "No son of Adam performs a deed on the Day of Sacrifice more beloved to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, than the shedding of blood, and it will come on the Day of Resurrection with its horns and its hooves, and the blood falls from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, in a station before it falls to the earth. So cheer your souls with it." And in the report: "For you, for every tuft of its skin, is a good deed, and for every drop of its blood, a good deed, and it is placed in the scale — so rejoice." And he, peace be upon him, said: "Seek aid with your sacrificial animals (hadāyā), for they are your mounts on the Day of Resurrection."

The tenth is that he be cheerful of soul with what he has spent of expenditure and hady, and with what has befallen him of loss and calamity in wealth or body, if that befalls him. For that is among the signs of the acceptance of his pilgrimage. For the calamity on the path of the pilgrimage is equivalent to the expenditure in the path of Allah, Mighty and Majestic — the dirham by seven hundred dirhams — just like the hardships on the path of jihad. So for him, for every harm he endures and every loss that befalls him, there is a reward, and nothing of it is lost with Allah, Mighty and Majestic. And it is said that among the signs of the acceptance of the pilgrimage is also the abandonment of what one was upon of sins, and that he exchange his idle companions for righteous companions, and his gatherings of frivolity and heedlessness for gatherings of remembrance and wakefulness.

chapters.title_en: The Exposition of the Inward Works, the Essence of Sincerity in Intention, and the Method of Contemplation upon the Noble Rites — from the Beginning of the Pilgrimage to Its End
chapters.arabic_text:
||| بيان الأعمال الباطنة ووجه الإخلاص في النية وطريق الاعتبار بالمشاهد

الشريفة وكيفية الافتكار فيها والتذكر لأسرارها ومعانيها من أول الحج إلى
آخره
اعلم أن أول الحج الفهم أعني فهم موقع الحج في الدين ثم الشوق إليه ثم
العزم عليه ثم قطع العلائق المانعة منه ثم شراء ثوب الإحرام ثم شراء الزاد
ثم اكتراء الراحلة ثم الخروج ثم المسير في البادية ثم الإحرام من الميقات
بالتلبية ثم دخول مكة ثم استتمام الأفعال كما سبق
وفي كل واحد من هذه الأمور تذكرة للمتذكر وعبرة للمعتبر وتنبيه للمريد
الصادق وتعريف وإشارة للفطن
فلنرمز إلى مفاتحها حتى إذا انفتح بابها وعرفت أسبابها انكشفت لكل حاج من
أسرارها ما يقتضيه صفاء قلبه وطهارة باطنه وغزارة فهمه
أما الفهم اعلم أنه لا وصول إلى الله سبحانه وتعالى إلا بالتنزه عن
الشهوات والكف عن اللذات والاقتصار على الضرورات فيها والتجرد لله سبحانه
في جميع الحركات والسكنات
ولأجل هذا انفرد الرهبانيون في الملل السالفة PageV01P265
عن الخلق وانحازوا إلى قلل الجبال وآثروا التوحش عن الخلق لطلب الأنس
بالله عز وجل فتركوا لله عز وجل اللذات الحاضرة وألزموا أنفسهم المجاهدات
الشاقة طمعا في الآخرة وأثنى الله عز وجل عليهم في كتابه فقال {ذلك بأن
منهم قسيسين ورهبانا وأنهم لا يستكبرون} فلما اندرس ذلك وأقبل الخلق على
اتباع الشهوات وهجروا التجرد لعبادة الله عز وجل وفتروا عنه بعث الله عز
وجل نبيه محمدا صلى الله عليه وسلم لإحياء طريق الآخرة وتجديد سنة المرسلين
في سلوكها
فسأله أهل الملل عن الرهبانية والسياحة في دينه فقال صلى الله عليه وسلم
أبدلنا الله بها الجهاد والتكبير على كل شرف (1) يعني الحج
وسئل صلى الله عليه وسلم عن السائحين فقال هم الصائمون (2) فأنعم الله عز
وجل على هذه الأمة بأن جعل الحج رهبانية لهم فشرف البيت العتيق بالإضافة
إلى نفسه تعالى
ونصبه مقصدا لعباده وجعل ما حواليه حرما  لبيته تفخيما لأمره
وجعل عرفات كالميزاب على فناء حوضه وأكد حرمة الموضع بتحريم صيده وشجره
ووضعه على مثال حضرة الملوك يقصده الزوار من كل فج عميق ومن كل أوب سحيق
شعثا غبرا متواضعين لرب البيت ومستكينين له خضوعا لجلاله واستكانة لعزته مع
الاعتراف بتنزيهه عن أن يحويه بيت أو يكتنفه بلد ليكون ذلك أبلغ في رقهم
وعبوديتهم وأتم في إذعانهم وانقيادهم
ولذلك وظف عليهم فيها أعمالا لا تأنس بها النفوس ولا تهتدي إلى معانيها
العقول كرمي الجمار بالأحجار والتردد بين الصفا والمروة على سبيل التكرار
وبمثل هذه الأعمال يظهر كمال الرق والعبودية
فإن الزكاة إرفاق ووجهه مفهوم وللعقل إليه ميل
والصوم كسر للشهوة التي هي آلة عدو الله وتفرغ للعبادة بالكف عن الشواغل
والركوع والسجود في الصلاة تواضع لله عز وجل بأفعال هي هيئة التواضع
وللنفوس أنس بتعظيم الله عز وجل
فأما ترددات السعي ورمي الجمار وأمثال هذه الأعمال فلا حظ للنفوس ولا أنس
فيها ولا اهتداء للعقل إلى معانيها فلا يكون في الإقدام عليها باعث إلا
الأمر المجرد وقصد الامتثال للأمر من حيث إنه أمر واجب الاتباع فقط وفيه
عزل للعقل عن تصرفه وصرف النفس والطبع عن محل أنسه فإن كل ما أدرك العقل
معناه مال الطبع إليه ميلا ما فيكون ذلك الميل معينا للأمر وباعثا معه على
الفعل فلا يكاد يظهر به كمال الرق والانقياد ولذلك قال صلى الله عليه وسلم
في الحج على الخصوص لبيك بحجة حقا تعبدا ورقا (3) ولم يقل ذلك في صلاة ولا
غيرها
وإذا اقتضت حكمة الله سبحانه وتعالى ربط نجاة الخلق بأن تكون أعمالهم على
خلاف هوى طباعهم وأن يكون زمامها بيد الشرع فيترددون في أعمالهم على سنن
الانقياد وعلى مقتضى الاستعباد كان ما لا يهتدي إلى معانيه أبلغ أنواع
التعبدات في تزكية النفوس وصرفها عن مقتضى الطباع والأخلاق مقتضى الاسترقاق
وإذا تفطنت لهذا فهمت أن تعجب النفوس من هذه الأفعال العجيبة مصدره
الذهول عن أسرار التعبدات وهذا القدر كاف في تفهم أصل  الحج إن شاء الله
تعالى
وأما الشوق فإنما ينبعث بعد الفهم والتحقق بأن البيت بيت الله عز وجل
وأنه وضع على مثال حضرة الملوك PageV01P266
فقاصده قاصد إلى الله عز وجل وزائر له وأن من قصد البيت في الدنيا جدير
بأن لا يضيع زيارته فيرزق مقصود الزيارة في ميعاده المضروب له وهو النظر
إلى وجه الله الكريم في دار القرار من حيث إن العين القاصرة الفانية في دار
الدنيا لا تتهيألقبول النظر إلى وجه الله عز وجل ولا تطيق احتماله ولا
تستعد للاكتحال به لقصورها وأنها إن أمدت في الدار الآخرة بالبقاء ونزهت عن
أسباب التغير والفناء استعدت للنظر والإبصار ولكنها بقصد البيت والنظر إليه
تستحق لقاء رب البيت بحكم الوعد الكريم
فالشوق إلى لقاء الله عز وجل يشوقه إلى أسباب اللقاء لا محالة هذا مع أن
المحب مشتاق إلى كل ماله إلى محبوبه إضافة والبيت مضاف إلى الله عز وجل
فبالحري أن يشتاق إليه لمجرد هذه الإ
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ف-ه-م (f-h-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Comprehension, grasping the reality of a thing; the faculty by which meaning is apprehended.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The intellectual apprehension (taṣawwur) that precedes volitional movement; in the religious path, it is the perception of the station (maqām) of an act within the divine order.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — mental grasp; metaphorical — the "understanding" that ignites longing (shawq), as understanding is the seed of all spiritual motion.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional-Clause Fronting (Taqdīm al-Sharṭ) — The repeated "if... then" constructions (fa-idhā...) establish a causal sequence where each inward state is the necessary condition for the next, mirroring the graded ascent of the pilgrim.

- Root: ش-و-ق (sh-w-q)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Intense yearning that draws one toward the beloved; the stirring of the heart toward reunion.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The longing that arises only after knowledge (maʿrifah) of the object's excellence; in the divine path, it is the heart's movement toward the vision of God (ruʾyah).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — the neck stretching toward what is desired; metaphorical — the soul's aspiration toward the celestial encounter.
- Sībawayh Rule: Causative Sequence (Sababiyyah) — The particle "innamā" restricts the cause of longing to prior understanding, establishing a strict logical priority.

- Root: ع-ز-م (ʿ-z-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Firm resolve, the knotting of the heart upon a course of action; severing hesitation.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The volitional determination (jazm al-irādah) that follows understanding and longing; it is the point where intention (niyyah) becomes operative.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — biting upon something firmly; metaphorical — the soul's decisive commitment to the journey, excluding all vacillation.
- Sībawayh Rule: Emphasis by Repetition (Tawkīd) — The imperative "fal-yuṣaḥḥiḥ" (let him rectify) followed by explanatory clauses reinforces the necessity of purifying resolve.

- Root: ق-ط-ع (q-t-ʿ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Severing, cutting off; separation from what binds.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The detachment from worldly attachments (ʿalāʾiq) that obstruct the path; it is the negative precondition for spiritual travel.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — cutting a rope or bond; metaphorical — severing the heart's ties to possessions, status, and sin.
- Sībawayh Rule: Parallelism (Muqābalah) — The pairing of "cutting ties" with "returning injustices" (radd al-maẓālim) creates a balanced dual requirement for valid departure.

- Root: ز-و-د (z-w-d)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Provision for a journey; sustenance stored for the road.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The metaphorical provision (zād al-taqwā) for the journey to the afterlife; the only provision that endures beyond death.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — food and supplies; metaphorical — piety (taqwā) as the sole viable sustenance for the eternal voyage.
- Sībawayh Rule: Comparative Construction (Tafḍīl) — The comparison between the earthly journey and the journey to the hereafter is framed by "afʿal" (longer, more certain), establishing the priority of the latter.

- Root: ر-ح-ل (r-h-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The riding beast; departure from a place; the mount that carries one.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The means of conveyance; in the spiritual sense, the bier (janāzah) that carries one to the final abode.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — the camel; metaphorical — any vehicle of transit, including the body itself as a mount for the soul.
- Sībawayh Rule: Antithesis (Ṭibāq) — The contrast between the riding beast (rāḥilah) and the bier (janāzah) highlights the inversion of worldly and otherworldly priorities.

- Root: خ-ر-ج (kh-r-j)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Going forth, exiting; emergence from a place.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The physical departure that mirrors the soul's emigration (hijrah) from sin to obedience.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — leaving one's town; metaphorical — the soul's exodus from the homeland of heedlessness.
- Sībawayh Rule: Inchoative Clause (Ibtidāʾiyyah) — The command "fal-yaʿlam" (let him know) introduces a new cognitive state that governs the subsequent emotional disposition.

- Root: ب-د-و (b-d-w)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The desert; appearing, becoming manifest.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The wilderness as a place of trial and solitude, mirroring the intermediate state (barzakh) between death and resurrection.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — the open desert; metaphorical — the desolate expanse of the grave and its terrors.
- Sībawayh Rule: Analogical Extension (Qiyās) — The terrors of the desert (highway robbers, wild beasts) are mapped onto the terrors of the grave (Munkar and Nakīr, scorpions, serpents) through structured analogy.

- Root: ح-ر-م (h-r-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To forbid, make sacred; the state of pilgrimage consecration (iḥrām).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The sacred precinct (ḥaram) as a zone of divine sanctity; iḥrām as the ritual entry into that sanctity.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — the forbidden; metaphorical — the consecrated state that strips the pilgrim of worldly adornment.
- Sībawayh Rule: Vocative Response (Nidāʾ) — The talbiyah ("Labbayk") is analyzed as a response to a divine call, structured as an answer to an implied vocative.

- Root: ط-و-ف (t-w-f)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To go around, encircle; circumambulation.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The physical circumambulation as a symbol of the heart's encircling of divine remembrance.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — walking around the Kaʿbah; metaphorical — the heart's orbit around the remembrance of God, as the angels circle the Throne.
- Sībawayh Rule: Simile (Tashbīh) — The pilgrim's circumambulation is likened to the angels' circumambulation of the Throne, establishing a hierarchy of imitation.

- Root: س-ع-ي (s-ʿ-y)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To strive, run, exert effort.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The running between Ṣafā and Marwah as an act of pure obedience, devoid of rational appeal.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — rapid walking; metaphorical — the soul's oscillation between hope and fear, as between the scales of judgment.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Alternation (Tardīd) — The repeated "between... and..." constructions (bayna... wa-bayna...) express the pilgrim's suspended state.

- Root: و-ق-ف (w-q-f)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Standing, halting; the vigil at ʿArafāt.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The standing as a foretaste of the standing before God on the Day of Resurrection.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — pausing in a place; metaphorical — the soul's halt before the divine tribunal.
- Sībawayh Rule: Accumulation (Tardīf) — The piling of descriptive clauses (crowds, voices, languages, sects) creates a sensory overload mirroring the Day of Gathering.

- Root: ر-م-ي (r-m-y)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To throw, cast; pelting stones.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The casting of stones as an act of pure submission (taʿabbud), with no rational or natural appeal.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — throwing pebbles; metaphorical — casting stones at the face of Satan, crushing his back.
- Sībawayh Rule: Apparent vs. Real (Ẓāhir wa-Bāṭin) — The grammatical distinction between the apparent object (the pillar) and the real object (Satan) is parsed through double accusative structures.

- Root: ذ-ب-ح (dh-b-h)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To slaughter; the sacrificial offering (hady).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The offering as a ransom (fidāʾ) for the self from the Fire.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — animal sacrifice; metaphorical — the surrender of the lower self.
- Sībawayh Rule: Proportionality (Munāsabah) — The correspondence between the size of the offering and the extent of redemption is expressed through correlative clauses.

- Root: ز-ي-ر (z-y-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To visit; the visitation (ziyārah) of the Prophet's grave.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The visit as an act of love and longing, distinct from mere tourism.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — visiting a person; metaphorical — the soul's approach to the Prophet's presence, alive in his grave.
- Sībawayh Rule: Hypothetical (Taqdīr) — The conditional "as if he were alive" (ka-annahu ḥayy) governs the etiquette of approach.
chapters.translation:
I say: Know that the beginning of the pilgrimage is understanding (al-fahm) — I mean, understanding the station of the pilgrimage within the religion — then longing for it (al-shawq), then resolve upon it (al-ʿazm), then the severing of the impediments that prevent it (qaṭʿ al-ʿalāʾiq), then the purchase of the two garments of iḥrām, then the purchase of provision (al-zād), then the hiring of the riding beast (al-rāḥilah), then departure, then travel through the desert, then the assumption of iḥrām from the mīqāt with the talbiyah, then entry into Mecca, then the completion of the rites as previously detailed.

In each of these matters there is a reminder (tadhkirah) for the mindful, a lesson (ʿibrah) for the one who takes heed, an awakening (tanbīh) for the sincere seeker, and an indication and sign (taʿrīf wa-ishārah) for the perceptive.

Let us gesture toward their keys, so that when their door is opened and their causes are known, there will be unveiled to every pilgrim of the secrets thereof what his heart's purity, his inner cleanliness, and the abundance of his understanding require.

As for understanding (al-fahm): Know that there is no reaching God — Glorified and Exalted be He — except by abstaining from appetites, refraining from pleasures, restricting oneself to necessities therein, and devoting oneself entirely to God — Glorified and Exalted be He — in all movements and stillnesses.

For this reason, the monks (al-ruhbāniyyūn) in the past religions isolated themselves from creation and withdrew to the peaks of mountains, preferring wild solitude over human company in pursuit of intimacy (uns) with God — Mighty and Majestic is He. They abandoned present pleasures for God — Mighty and Majestic is He — and imposed upon themselves arduous struggles, hoping for the Hereafter. God — Glorified and Exalted be He — praised them in His Book, saying: {«That is because among them are priests and monks, and because they do not behave arrogantly»} (Q 5:82). When that practice became extinct, and creation turned to following appetites, abandoned self-devotion to the worship of God — Glorified and Exalted be He — and grew languid therein, God — Glorified and Exalted be He — sent His Prophet Muḥammad — may God bless him and grant him peace — to revive the path of the Hereafter and renew the way of the messengers in traversing it.

The people of the religions asked him about monasticism and wandering (al-siyāḥah) in his religion, and he — may God bless him and grant him peace — said: "God has replaced it for us with jihad and the takbīr upon every elevated place" — meaning the pilgrimage. And he — may God bless him and grant him peace — was asked about the wanderers (al-sāʾiḥūn), and he said: "They are the fasters." Thus God — Glorified and Exalted be He — bestowed favor upon this community by making the pilgrimage their monasticism. He honored the Ancient House (al-bayt al-ʿatīq) by attributing it to Himself — Exalted is He — and erected it as a destination for His servants. He made its surroundings a sanctuary (ḥaram) for His House, magnifying its affair. He made ʿArafāt like a spout upon the courtyard of His basin, and He emphasized the sanctity of the place by forbidding its game and its trees. He placed it on the model of the courts of kings, which visitors seek from every deep ravine and every distant path — disheveled and dust-covered, humble before the Lord of the House, submissive to Him, in humility before His majesty and submission to His might, while acknowledging His transcendence above being contained by any house or encompassed by any land — that this might be more complete in their servitude and bondage, and more perfect in their compliance and obedience.

For this reason, He imposed upon them therein acts with which souls find no familiarity and to whose meanings intellects do not attain — such as the pelting of the pillars with stones (ramy al-jimār) and the repeated going between Ṣafā and Marwah. By such acts the perfection of servitude and bondage becomes manifest.

For the alms-tax (zakāh) is a kindness, its rationale is understood, and the intellect has an inclination toward it. Fasting is a breaking of appetite, which is the instrument of the enemy of God, and a vacating for worship by refraining from distractions. The bowing and prostration in prayer are humility before God — Mighty and Majestic is He — through acts that are the very posture of humility, and souls find intimacy in magnifying God — Glorified and Exalted be He.

But as for the repeated traversals of the saʿy, the pelting of the pillars, and similar acts — souls have no share in them, no intimacy with them, and the intellect finds no path to their meanings. Thus there is no motive for undertaking them except the bare command (al-amr al-mujarrad) and the intention of complying with the command insofar as it is a command that must be obeyed — and nothing else. In this there is a deposing of the intellect from its governance and a turning of the soul and nature away from their familiar ground. For whenever the intellect grasps the meaning of something, nature inclines toward it with some inclination, and that inclination becomes an aid to the command and a co-motive for the act — so that the perfection of servitude and submission is hardly manifested thereby. For this reason, he — may God bless him and grant him peace — said specifically regarding the pilgrimage: "I respond to You, O God, for a true pilgrimage, in worship and servitude" — and he did not say this for prayer or anything else.

And when the wisdom of God — Glorified and Exalted be He — requires that the salvation of creation be tied to their acts being contrary to the inclination of their natures, and that their reins be in the hand of the Sacred Law, so that they oscillate in their acts upon the path of submission and the requirement of enslavement — then that which the intellect cannot penetrate is the most powerful type of devotional act (taʿabbudāt) in purifying souls and turning them from the requirements of nature and character to the requirement of servitude. If you discern this, you will understand that the wonder of souls at these strange acts stems from heedlessness of the secrets of devotional acts. This suffices for understanding the foundation of the pilgrimage, God willing — Exalted is He.

As for longing (al-shawq): It arises only after understanding and the realization that the House is the House of God — Mighty and Majestic is He — and that it is placed on the model of the courts of kings. Thus its seeker is a seeker of God — Glorified and Exalted be He — and a visitor to Him. And whoever seeks the House in this world is worthy that his visit not be wasted, and that he be granted the purpose of the visit at its appointed time — namely, the vision of the noble Face of God in the abode of permanence. For the deficient, perishable eye in the abode of this world is not prepared to receive the vision of the Face of God — Glorified and Exalted be He — nor can it bear it, nor is it ready for the collyrium thereof, due to its deficiency. But if it is prolonged in the Hereafter with permanence and purified from the causes of change and annihilation, it becomes prepared for vision and sight. Yet by seeking the House and gazing upon it, one becomes worthy of meeting the Lord of the House by virtue of the noble promise.

Thus longing for the meeting of God — Glorified and Exalted be He — inevitably draws one to the means of that meeting. Moreover, the lover yearns for everything that has an attribution to his Beloved, and the House is attributed to God — Glorified and Exalted be He. So it is fitting that one yearn for it merely for this attribution, let alone for seeking the attainment of what is promised upon it of abundant reward.

As for resolve (al-ʿazm): Let him know that by his resolve he intends to depart from family and homeland, to emigrate from appetites and pleasures, and to set out for the visitation of the House of God — Glorified and Exalted be He. Let him magnify in his soul the worth of the House and the worth of the Lord of the House. Let him know that he has resolved upon a matter of lofty station and grave import, and that whoever seeks something great risks something great.

Let him make his resolve pure for the Face of God — Glorified and Exalted be He — far from the admixtures of ostentation (riyāʾ) and reputation (sumʿah). Let him realize that nothing is accepted of his intention and deed except the pure, and that among the most heinous abominations is to intend the House of God and His sanctuary while the intended object is other than Him.

Let him rectify his resolve within himself, and its rectification is through sincerity, and its sincerity is through avoiding everything in which there is ostentation and reputation. Let him beware of exchanging that which is lower for that which is better.

As for the severing of impediments (qaṭʿ al-ʿalāʾiq): Its meaning is the restitution of injustices (radd al-maẓālim) and sincere repentance to God — Exalted is He — from all sins. For every injustice is an impediment, and every impediment is like a present creditor seizing his collar, calling out against him and saying: "Where are you heading? Do you intend the House of the King of Kings while you have neglected His command in your own home, treating it lightly and abandoning it? Are you not ashamed to approach Him with the approach of a disobedient servant, so that He turns you away and does not accept you? If you desire the acceptance of your visit, then execute His commands, return the injustices, and repent to Him first from all sins. Sever your heart's attachment from looking back at what is behind you, so that you face Him with the face of your heart just as you face His House with the face of your outward self."

For if you do not do this, you will have nothing from your journey — first — except toil and misery, and — finally — except expulsion and rejection.

Let him sever his attachments to his homeland as one who has been cut off from it, and let him suppose that he will not return to it. Let him write his will for his children and family, for the traveler and his wealth are in peril — except for him whom God — Glorified and Exalted be He — protects. Let him remember, when severing his attachments for the journey of pilgrimage, the severing of attachments for the journey of the Hereafter — for that is before him, near at hand. What he sends ahead from this journey is hope for the facilitation of that journey, for that is the final abode and to it is the return.

So he should not be heedless of that journey while preparing for this one.

As for provision (al-zād): Let him seek it from a lawful source. And when he senses in himself eagerness to amass it, seeking what will remain over the long journey and will not change or spoil before reaching the destination — let him remember that the journey of the Hereafter is longer than this journey, and that its provision is piety (taqwā), and that everything else which he supposes to be his provision will lag behind him at death and betray him, not remaining with him — like moist food that spoils at the first waystation of the journey, leaving him at the time of need bewildered, needy, with no recourse.

Let him beware that his deeds, which are his provision to the Hereafter, do not accompany him after death, but rather are spoiled by the admixtures of ostentation and the turbidities of shortcoming.

As for the riding beast (al-rāḥilah): When he brings it, let him thank God with his heart for God — Mighty and Majestic is He — subjugating the beasts to him, to bear from him the hardship and lighten the difficulty. Let him remember at that point the mount he will ride to the abode of the Hereafter — namely, the bier (al-janāzah) upon which he will be carried. For the affair of the pilgrimage in one respect parallels the affair of the journey to the Hereafter. Let him consider whether his journey upon this mount will be fit to serve as provision for that journey upon that mount. How near it is to him! And what does he know — perhaps death is near, and his riding of the bier will precede his riding of the camel. Riding the bier is certain, while the facilitation of the means of travel is doubtful. So how can he be cautious about the means of a doubtful journey, securing his provision and mount, while neglecting the affair of the certain journey?

As for the purchase of the two garments of iḥrām: Let him remember at that point the shroud (al-kafan) and the wrapping therein — for in it he will be wrapped. He dons the two garments of iḥrām when near the House of God — Glorified and Exalted be He — and perhaps his journey to it will not be completed. And he will meet God — Glorified and Exalted be He — wrapped in the garments of the shroud, inevitably. Just as he does not meet the House of God — Glorified and Exalted be He — except in a manner contrary to his customs in dress and appearance, so too he will not meet God — Glorified and Exalted be He — after death except in a dress contrary to the dress of this world. And this garment is near to that garment, for there is no stitching in it, just as in the shroud.

As for departure from the town: Let him know at that point that he has left family and homeland, heading toward God — Glorified and Exalted be He — in a journey that bears no resemblance to the journeys of this world. Let him bring to his heart: What does he intend? Where is he heading? Whose visitation does he seek? — that he is heading to the King of Kings in the company of His visitors, those who were called and answered, who were made to yearn and so yearned, who were roused and so rose, who severed attachments and parted from creatures, and turned toward the House of God — Glorified and Exalted be He — whose affair He magnified, whose station He exalted, and whose worth He raised — seeking consolation in the meeting of the House from the meeting of the Lord of the House, until they are granted the utmost of their hopes and are blessed with the vision of their Master. Let him bring to his heart the hope of arrival and acceptance — not relying on his deeds in departing and leaving family and wealth, but trusting in the bounty of God — Glorified and Exalted be He — and hoping for the fulfillment of His promise to those who visit His House. Let him hope that if he does not reach it and death overtakes him on the road, he will meet God — Glorified and Exalted be He — as one arriving to Him, for He — Majestic is His Glory — said: {«And whoever leaves his home emigrating to God and His Messenger, then death overtakes him — his reward has fallen upon God»} (Q 4:100).

As for entering the desert up to the mīqāt and witnessing those mountain passes: Let him recall therein what lies between leaving this world by death and the mīqāt of the Day of Resurrection, and what is between them of terrors and demands. Let him recall, from the terror of highway robbers, the terror of the questioning of Munkar and Nakīr; from the wild beasts of the deserts, the scorpions of the grave and its worms, and what is in it of vipers and serpents; and from his solitude from his family and relatives, the desolation of the grave, its distress, and its loneliness. Let him, amidst these fears, be in his deeds and words one who provisions himself for the fears of the grave.

As for the iḥrām and the talbiyah from the mīqāt: Let him know that its meaning is the answering of the call of God — Glorified and Exalted be He. So hope that you are accepted, and fear that it may be said to you: "No response to you, and no blessedness for you." So be oscillating between hope and fear, disavowing your own strength and power, and relying upon the bounty of God — Glorified and Exalted be He — and His generosity. For the time of the talbiyah is the beginning of the affair, and it is the place of peril.

Sufyān ibn ʿUyaynah said: ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn — may God be pleased with them both — performed the pilgrimage. When he assumed iḥrām and his mount stood still with him, his face turned pale, he trembled, and a shudder fell upon him, and he could not utter the talbiyah. It was said to him: "Why do you not say the talbiyah?" He said: "I fear that it will be said to me: 'No response to you, and no blessedness for you.'" When he did say the talbiyah, he fainted and fell from his mount, and this condition continued to afflict him until he completed his pilgrimage.

Aḥmad ibn Abī al-Ḥawārī said: I was with Abū Sulaymān al-Dārānī — may God be pleased with him — when he intended to assume iḥrām. He did not say the talbiyah until we had traveled a mile, then a swoon overtook him. Then he regained consciousness and said: "O Aḥmad, God — Glorified and Exalted be He — revealed to Moses — peace be upon him: 'Command the oppressors of the Children of Israel to speak little of My remembrance, for I remember with curse whoever of them remembers Me.' Woe to you, O Aḥmad! It has reached me that whoever performs the pilgrimage from other than its proper place, then says the talbiyah, God — Glorified and Exalted be He — says: 'No response to you, and no blessedness for you, until you return what is in your hands.' So we are not safe from having that said to us."

Let the one saying the talbiyah remember, when raising his voice with the talbiyah at the mīqāt, his answering of the call of God — Glorified and Exalted be He — when He said: {«And proclaim the pilgrimage to the people»} (Q 22:27) — and the calling of creation by the blast of the Trumpet, and their mustering from the graves, and their crowding in the plains of the Resurrection, answering the call of God — Glorified and Exalted be He — and divided into those brought near and those abhorred, those accepted and those rejected, oscillating at the beginning of the affair between fear and hope — like the oscillation of the pilgrim at the mīqāt, where they do not know whether the completion of the pilgrimage and its acceptance will be facilitated for them or not.

As for entering Mecca: Let him remember at that point that he has arrived at the sanctuary of God — Exalted is He — in safety. Let him hope at that point that by his entry he will be safe from the punishment of God — Glorified and Exalted be He — and let him fear that he may not be worthy of nearness, so that by his entry into the sanctuary he becomes disappointed and deserving of abhorrence. Let his hope be predominant at all times — for generosity is vast, the Lord is merciful, the honor of the House is great, the right of the visitor is preserved, and the protection of the seeker of refuge who clings is not neglected.

As for the falling of the eye upon the House: He should bring to mind at that point the greatness of the House in the heart, and suppose as if he were witnessing the Lord of the House, due to the intensity of his magnification of it. Hope that God — Exalted is He — will grant you the vision of His noble Face, just as He granted you the vision of His great House. Thank God — Exalted is He — for conveying you to this rank and joining you to the company of those arriving to Him. Remember at that point the pouring of people on the Day of Resurrection toward the direction of Paradise, hoping for entry into it all together, then their division into those permitted to enter and those turned away — like the division of the pilgrims into the accepted and the rejected. Do not be heedless of remembering the matters of the Hereafter in everything you see, for all the states of the pilgrim are indications of the states of the Hereafter.

As for the circumambulation of the House (al-ṭawāf): Know that it is a prayer (ṣalāh). So bring to your heart therein the magnification, fear, hope, and love that we detailed in the Book of Prayer. Know that by circumambulating you are imitating the angels brought near, who surround the Throne and circle around it. Do not suppose that the purpose is the circumambulation of your body around the House — rather, the purpose is the circumambulation of your heart around the remembrance of the Lord of the House, so that you begin remembrance only from Him and end only with Him, just as you begin the circumambulation from the House and end with the House.

Know that the noble circumambulation is the circumambulation of the heart in the presence of the Lordship (al-rubūbiyyah), and that the House is an apparent exemplar in the world of dominion (ʿālam al-mulk) for that Presence which is not seen by the eye — namely, the world of the unseen dominion (ʿālam al-malakūt) — just as the body is an apparent exemplar in the world of witness (ʿālam al-shahādah) for the heart, which is not seen by the eye and is in the world of the unseen (ʿālam al-ghayb).

The world of dominion and witness is a ladder to the world of the unseen and the malakūt for him for whom God opens the door. To this correspondence the indication points: that the Much-Frequented House (al-bayt al-maʿmūr) in the heavens is opposite the Kaʿbah — for the circumambulation of the angels around it is like the circumambulation of humans around this House. When the rank of most creatures fell short of such circumambulation, they were commanded to imitate them as much as possible, and were promised that whoever imitates a people is of them. And the one who is capable of such circumambulation is the one of whom it is said that the Kaʿbah visits him and circumambulates him — as some of those with unveiling (mukāshifūn) saw regarding some of the saints of God — Glorified and Exalted be He.

As for the touching of the Black Stone (al-istilām): Believe at that point that you are pledging allegiance (mubāyaʿah) to God — Mighty and Majestic is He — upon His obedience. So firm your resolve upon fulfilling your pledge, for whoever betrays in the pledge deserves abhorrence. Ibn ʿAbbās — may God be pleased with him — narrated from the Messenger of God — may God bless him and grant him peace — that he said: "The Black Stone is the right hand of God — Mighty and Majestic is He — upon the earth, by which He shakes hands with His creatures, just as a man shakes hands with his brother."

As for clinging to the curtains of the Kaʿbah and pressing against the Multazam: Let your intention in pressing be the seeking of nearness, out of love and longing for the House and the Lord of the House, seeking blessing through contact, and hoping for protection from the Fire for every part of your body — not for the House. Let your intention in clinging to the curtain be importunity in seeking forgiveness and asking for safety — like the sinner clinging to the garments of the one he has wronged, imploring him for pardon, showing him that he has no refuge from him except to him, no escape except to his generosity and pardon, and that he will not release his hem except with pardon and the granting of safety for the future.

As for the running between Ṣafā and Marwah (al-saʿy) in the courtyard of the House: It resembles the oscillation of the servant in the courtyard of the king's palace, coming and going, time after time — displaying sincerity in service and hoping to be noticed with the eye of mercy — like one who entered upon the king and exited, not knowing what the king will decree regarding him, acceptance or rejection. So he keeps oscillating in the courtyard, time after time, hoping to be shown mercy the second time if not the first. Let him remember, during his oscillation between Ṣafā and Marwah, his oscillation between the two pans of the Scale in the plains of the Resurrection. Let him represent Ṣafā as the pan of good deeds and Marwah as the pan of evil deeds. Let him remember his oscillation between the two pans, looking at the preponderance and deficiency, oscillating between chastisement and forgiveness.

As for the standing at ʿArafāt (al-wuqūf): Recall, by what you see of the crowding of creation, the raising of voices, the diversity of languages, and the following of the sects of their im

| كتاب آداب تلاوة القرآن

بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم
الحمد لله الذي امتن على عباده بنبيه المرسل صلى الله عليه وسلم وكتابه
المنزل الذي لا يأتيه الباطل من بين يديه ولا من خلفه تنزيل من حكيم حميد
حتى اتسع على أهل الأفكار طريق الاعتبار بما فيه من القصص والأخبار واتضح
به سلوك المنهج القويم والصراط المستقيم بما فصل فيه من الأحكام وفرق بين
الحلال والحرام فهو الضياء والنور وبه النجاة من الغرور وفيه شفاء لما في
الصدور ومن خالفه من الجبابرة قصمه الله ومن ابتغى العلم في غيره أضله الله
هو حبل الله المتين ونوره المبين والعروة الوثقى والمعتصم الأوفى وهو
المحيط بالقليل والكثير والصغير والكبير لا تنقضي عجائبه ولا تتناهى غرائبه
لا يحيط بفوائده عند أهل العلم تحديد ولا يخلقه عند أهل التلاوة كثرة
الترديد هو الذي أرشد الأولين والآخرين ولما سمعه الجن لم يلبثوا أن ولوا
إلى قومهم منذرين {فقالوا إنا سمعنا قرآنا عجبا يهدي إلى الرشد فآمنا به
ولن نشرك بربنا أحدا} فكل من آمن به فقد وفق ومن قال به فقد صدق ومن تمسك
به فقد هدي ومن عمل به فقد فاز وقال تعالى {إنا نحن نزلنا الذكر وإنا له
لحافظون} ومن أسباب حفظه في القلوب والمصاحف استدامة تلاوته والمواظبة على
دراسته مع القيام بآدابه وشروطه والمحافظة على ما فيه من الأعمال الباطنة
والآداب الظاهرة وذلك لا  بد من بيانه وتفصيله وتنكشف مقاصده في أربعة أبواب
الباب الأول في فضل القرآن وأهله
الباب الثاني في آداب التلاوة في الظاهر
الباب الثالث في الأعمال الباطنة عند التلاوة
