chapters.anchors:
- Root: ف-ه-م (f-h-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Comprehension, grasping the intended meaning; the faculty by which one apprehends signification
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The intellectual apprehension of meaning (fahm) as distinct from mere hearing (samāʿ); the divinely-granted capacity to penetrate the intent of divine discourse
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense of intellectual grasp; metaphorically extended to the heart's reception of divine address
- Sībawayh Rule: ʿAṭf al-Bayān (Appositional Clarification) — the ten enumerated principles are set in appositional series, each term specifying a distinct stage of the spiritual ascent in recitation
chapters.translation:
**Section 135 — The Third Book on the Inner Works of Recitation, Being Ten in Number**

I say: The ten inner works of recitation are: first, understanding the origin of the discourse; second, magnification; third, presence of heart; fourth, reflection; fifth, comprehension; sixth, self-emptying of the obstacles to understanding; seventh, self-application; eighth, being affected; ninth, ascent; tenth, self-disavowal.

**The First: Understanding the Greatness of the Discourse**

The first is understanding the greatness of the discourse, its exaltedness, and the favor of God—glorified and exalted be He—and His gentleness toward His creation in its descent from the throne of His majesty to the level of His creatures' comprehension.

Let the reciter consider how God was gentle with His creation in conveying the meanings of His discourse—which is an eternal attribute subsisting in His essence—to the understandings of His creatures, and how that attribute manifested itself to them wrapped in letters and sounds that are attributes of human beings. For humans are incapable of attaining to the understanding of God's attributes—mighty and majestic is He—except through the medium of their own attributes.

Were it not that the inner reality of the majesty of His discourse is veiled by the garment of letters, neither throne nor earth would endure the hearing of it, and all that lies between them of the grandeur of His dominion and the splendors of His light would be annihilated. And were it not for God's strengthening of Moses—peace be upon him—he would not have been able to endure the hearing of His discourse, just as the mountain could not endure the beginnings of His self-disclosure and became crushed to dust.

The greatness of the discourse cannot be conveyed except through parables commensurate with the understanding of creatures. For this reason, one of the knowers (ʿārifīn) expressed it saying: "Every letter of God's discourse in the Preserved Tablet is greater than Mount Qāf, and were the angels—peace be upon them—to gather upon a single letter to lift it, they could not, until Isrāfīl—peace be upon him, who is the angel of the Tablet—comes and lifts it by God's permission and mercy, not by his own strength and capacity. Rather, God—mighty and majestic is He—empowered him for it and employed him in it."

One of the sages (ḥukamāʾ) shone brilliantly in expressing the aspect of gentleness in conveying the meanings of the discourse, despite its exalted rank, to human understanding, and in establishing it despite the deficiency of the human station. He struck for it a parable that did not fall short. He summoned a certain king to the law of the prophets—peace be upon them. The king asked him about matters, and he answered with what the king's understanding could not bear. The king said: "Tell me about what the prophets bring when they claim it is not the speech of men but the speech of God—mighty and majestic is He—how then can men bear to carry it?"

The sage said: "We have seen that when people wanted to make certain beasts and birds understand what they desired of them—their coming forward and going back, their approaching and departing—and they saw that the beasts fell short in their discernment of understanding their speech, which issued from the lights of their intellects despite its beauty, adornment, and wondrous composition, they descended to the level of the beasts' discernment and conveyed their purposes to the inner faculties of the beasts through sounds they devised suitable to them—of tapping, whistling, and sounds close to the beasts' own sounds—so that they might be able to carry them. Likewise, people are incapable of carrying the speech of God—mighty and majestic is He—in its full reality and the perfection of its attributes. So they resorted to the sounds they exchanged among themselves, by which they heard wisdom, like the sound of tapping and whistling by which the beasts heard from men."

This did not prevent the meanings of wisdom hidden in those sounds from conferring honor upon the speech—that is, the sounds—by their honor, and greatness by their magnification. For the sound is to wisdom as a body and dwelling, and wisdom is to the sound as a soul and spirit.

Just as the bodies of humans are honored and revered for the sake of the soul within them, so likewise the sounds of speech are ennobled for the wisdom contained in them.

Discourse is lofty in station, elevated in degree, overpowering in dominion, penetrating in judgment over truth and falsehood. It is the just judge and the approved witness. It commands and forbids, and falsehood has no power to stand before the discourse of wisdom, just as the shadow cannot stand before the rays of the sun. Nor do humans have the power to penetrate the depths of wisdom, just as they have no power to penetrate with their eyes the very light of the sun's disc. But they attain from the light of the sun's disc that by which their eyes live and by which they are guided to their needs only.

So discourse is like a king whose face is veiled and hidden but whose command is penetrating; like the abundant sun whose element is concealed though it is manifest; like the bright stars by which one who does not know their courses is guided. It is the key to precious treasuries, the water of life—whoever drinks from it does not die—and the medicine for ailments—whoever is given it to drink does not fall sick.

This is what the sage mentioned—a sample of conveying the meaning of discourse. To add more upon it is not fitting for the science of practical religion (ʿilm al-muʿāmalah); one should be content with it.

**The Second: Magnification of the Speaker**

The second is magnification of the Speaker. The reciter, at the beginning of reciting the Qur'an, should bring into his heart the greatness of the Speaker and know that what he recites is not the speech of humans, and that in reciting the speech of God—mighty and majestic is He—there is utmost peril. For He—exalted is He—said: {«لَا يَمَسُّهُ إِلَّا الْمُطَهَّرُونَ»} ("None touch it except the purified"). Just as the outward skin of the muṣḥaf and its pages are guarded from the outward skin of the toucher unless he is purified, so likewise its inner meaning, by virtue of its might and majesty, is veiled from the inner heart unless it is purified of every filth and illuminated with the light of magnification and reverence. And just as not every hand is fit to touch the skin of the muṣḥaf, so not every tongue is fit to recite its letters, nor every heart to attain its meanings.

It was for such magnification that ʿIkrimah ibn Abī Jahl—when he would spread open the muṣḥaf—would fall into a swoon and say: "It is the speech of my Lord! It is the speech of my Lord!"

Magnification of the discourse is magnification of the Speaker. The greatness of the Speaker will not be present in one's heart unless one reflects upon His attributes, His majesty, and His acts. When the Throne, the Footstool, the heavens, the earth, and all that is between them—of jinn, humans, beasts, and trees—come to mind, and one knows that the Creator of all of them, the Omnipotent over them, the Provider for them, is One; that all are in the grasp of His power, oscillating between His bounty and His mercy and His vengeance and His severity; that if He bestows, it is by His bounty, and if He punishes, it is by His justice; and that He is the One who says: "These are for Paradise, and I care not," and "These are for the Fire, and I care not"—this is the utmost of greatness and exaltation. By reflecting upon such things, the magnification of the Speaker becomes present, and then the magnification of the discourse.

**The Third: Presence of Heart and Abandoning Self-Talk**

The third is presence of heart and abandoning the whispering of the self. It was said in explanation of {«يَا يَحْيَىٰ خُذِ الْكِتَابَ بِقُوَّةٍ»} ("O John, take the Book with strength")—that is, with seriousness and exertion. Taking it with seriousness means that one is wholly devoted to it during one's recitation, with one's concern turned entirely to it apart from all else.

It was said to one of them: "When you recite the Qur'an, does your self speak to you of anything?" He said: "Is there anything more beloved to me than the Qur'an that I should speak to myself of it?" And some of the Salaf, when reciting a verse in which his heart was not present, would repeat it a second time.

This quality is generated from what precedes it, namely magnification. For one who magnifies the discourse he recites rejoices in it and finds intimacy with it and does not become heedless of it. In the Qur'an there is that with which the heart finds intimacy, if the reciter is worthy of it. How then should one seek intimacy by thinking of other things while he is in a garden and a place of delight?

One who strolls in gardens does not think of other things. It has been said that in the Qur'an there are fields (mayādīn), gardens (basātīn), chambers (maqāṣīr), brides (ʿarāʾis), brocades (dayābīj), meadows (riyāḍ), and pavilions (khānāt). The mīm-s are the fields of the Qur'an, the rāʾ-s are its gardens, the ḥāʾ-s are its chambers, the musabbiḥāt are its brides, the ḥawāmīm are its brocades, the mufaṣṣal is its meadows, and the pavilions are what is other than that. When the reciter enters the fields, plucks from the gardens, enters the chambers, witnesses the brides, dons the brocades, strolls in the meadows, and dwells in the chambers of the pavilions, that overwhelms him and occupies him from all else, so his heart does not wander and his thought does not scatter.

**The Fourth: Reflection (Tadabbur)**

The fourth is reflection, which lies beyond presence of heart. For one may not think of other than the Qur'an, yet confine oneself to hearing the Qur'an from oneself without reflecting upon it.

The purpose of recitation is reflection. For this reason, tartīl (measured recitation) was prescribed—tartīl in the outward form—so that reflection might be possible in the inward.

ʿAlī—may God be pleased with him—said: "There is no good in worship without understanding, nor in recitation without reflection."

If reflection cannot be achieved except by repetition, let him repeat—unless he is behind an imam. For if he remains in reflecting upon one verse while the imam has moved on to another verse, he is doing wrong, like one who occupies himself with marveling at a single word from someone conversing with him, to the neglect of understanding the rest of his speech. Likewise, if he is in the tasbīḥ of the bowing while reflecting upon a verse his imam recited, this is an intrusive whisper (waswās).

It is related of ʿĀmir ibn ʿAbd Qays that he said: "The waswās afflicts me in prayer." It was said: "Concerning worldly matters?" He said: "That spears should pierce me is more beloved to me than that. Rather, my heart is occupied with my standing before my Lord—mighty and majestic is He—and how I shall depart." This was counted as waswās, and so it is, for it occupies him from understanding what he is in. Satan cannot do such a thing except by occupying him with a religious concern, but thereby prevents him from what is more excellent.

When this was mentioned to al-Ḥasan, he said: "If you are truthful about him, then God has not made such a thing for us." It is related that the Prophet—peace be upon him—recited "Bismillāh al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm" and repeated it twenty times. He only repeated it—peace be upon him—for reflection upon its meanings.

It is related of Abū Dharr that he said: "The Messenger of God—peace be upon him—stood with us one night, repeating a single verse: {«إِن تُعَذِّبْهُمْ فَإِنَّهُمْ عِبَادُكَ ۖ وَإِن تَغْفِرْ لَهُمْ»} ('If You punish them, they are Your servants; and if You forgive them...')." Tamīm al-Dārī stood a night with this verse: {«أَمْ حَسِبَ الَّذِينَ اجْتَرَحُوا السَّيِّئَاتِ»} ("Or do those who commit evil deeds think..."). Saʿīd ibn Jubayr stood a night repeating this verse: {«وَامْتَازُوا الْيَوْمَ أَيُّهَا الْمُجْرِمُونَ»} ("And separate yourselves today, O criminals").

One of them said: "I open a sūrah, and something of what I witness in it stops me from finishing it until dawn breaks." Some of them said: "A verse I do not comprehend and in which my heart is not present—I count no reward for it." It is related of Abū Sulaymān al-Dārānī that he said: "I recite a verse and remain in it four or five nights. Were I not to cut off my thought in it, I would not pass beyond it to another."

It is related of one of the Salaf that he remained in Sūrat Hūd for six months, repeating it and not finishing his reflection upon it.

One of the knowers said: "For me there is a complete recitation (khatmah) every Friday, a khatmah every month, and a khatmah every year—and I have had a khatmah for thirty years that I have not yet finished." This is according to the degrees of his reflection and investigation. This same man also said: "I have placed myself in the position of hired laborers; I work by the day, by the week, by the month, and by the year."

**The Fifth: Comprehension (Tafahhum)**

The fifth is comprehension, which is to seek clarification from each verse of what befits it. For the Qur'an comprises the mention of God's attributes—mighty and majestic is He—the mention of His acts, the mention of the conditions of the prophets—peace be upon them—the mention of the conditions of those who denied them and how they were destroyed, the mention of His commands and prohibitions, and the mention of Paradise and the Fire.

As for God's attributes—mighty and majestic is He—such as His saying—exalted is He: {«لَيْسَ كَمِثْلِهِ شَيْءٌ ۖ وَهُوَ السَّمِيعُ الْبَصِيرُ»} ("Nothing is like Him, and He is the Hearing, the Seeing"), and His saying—exalted is He: {«الْمَلِكُ الْقُدُّوسُ السَّلَامُ الْمُؤْمِنُ الْمُهَيْمِنُ الْعَزِيزُ الْجَبَّارُ الْمُتَكَبِّرُ»} ("The King, the Holy, the Peace, the Faithful, the Guardian, the Mighty, the Compeller, the Proud"). Let him contemplate the meanings of these names and attributes so that their secrets may be unveiled to him, for beneath them are meanings buried that are not unveiled except to the divinely aided. To this ʿAlī—may God be pleased with him—pointed in his saying: "The Messenger of God—peace be upon him—did not confide to me anything that he concealed from the people, except that God grants a servant understanding (fahm) in His Book." So let one be eager in seeking that understanding.

Ibn Masʿūd—may God be pleased with him—said: "Whoever desires the knowledge of the first and the last, let him stir up the Qur'an." The greatest of the sciences of the Qur'an lies beneath the names of God—mighty and majestic is He—and His attributes, for most of creation have grasped from them only matters befitting their understandings and have not stumbled upon their depths.

As for His acts—exalted is He—such as His mention of the creation of the heavens and the earth and other things, let the reciter understand from them the attributes of God—mighty and majestic is He—and His majesty. For the act indicates the agent, so its greatness indicates His greatness. He should witness in his intellect the Agent rather than the act. For whoever knows the Truth sees Him in everything, since everything is from Him, to Him, by Him, and for Him. He is, in truth, the All. Whoever does not see Him in all that he sees, it is as though he has not known Him. And whoever knows Him knows that everything other than God is falsehood, and that everything is perishing except His Face—not that it will become void in a second state, but that it is now falsehood if one considers its essence in itself, unless one considers its existence insofar as it exists by God—mighty and majestic is He—and by His power. Then it has, by way of derivation, a certain stability, and by way of independence, pure falsehood. This is one of the beginnings of the science of unveiling (ʿilm al-mukāshafah).

For this reason, when the reciter reads His saying—mighty and majestic is He: {«أَفَرَأَيْتُم مَّا تَحْرُثُونَ»} ("Have you seen what you sow?"), {«أَفَرَأَيْتُم مَّا تُمْنُونَ»} ("Have you seen what you emit?"), {«أَفَرَأَيْتُمُ الْمَاءَ الَّذِي تَشْرَبُونَ»} ("Have you seen the water you drink?"), {«أَفَرَأَيْتُمُ النَّارَ الَّتِي تُورُونَ»} ("Have you seen the fire you kindle?"), he should not confine his gaze to water, fire, sowing, and semen. Rather, let him contemplate the semen—a drop of uniform parts—then consider how it divides into flesh, bone, veins, and nerves; how its organs are formed in various shapes of head, hand, foot, liver, heart, and others; then what appears in it of noble attributes—hearing, sight, intellect, and others; then what appears in it of blameworthy attributes—anger, lust, pride, ignorance, denial, and disputation—as God—exalted is He—said: {«أَوَلَمْ يَرَ الْإِنسَانُ أَنَّا خَلَقْنَاهُ مِن نُّطْفَةٍ فَإِذَا هُوَ خَصِيمٌ مُّبِينٌ»} ("Does man not see that We created him from a drop, and behold, he is a manifest adversary?"). Let him contemplate these wonders to ascend from them to the wonder of wonders—the attribute from which these marvels issued. Thus he continues looking at the craftsmanship until he sees the Craftsman.

As for the conditions of the prophets—peace be upon them—when he hears how they were denied, struck, and some of them killed, let him understand from it the attribute of God's—mighty and majestic is He—self-sufficiency from the messengers and those to whom they were sent, and that were He to destroy them all, it would not affect His dominion in the least. And when he hears of their victory in the end, let him understand God's power—mighty and majestic is He—and His will to support the truth.

As for the conditions of the deniers—like ʿĀd and Thamūd and what befell them—let his understanding from it be the sensing of fear of His severity and vengeance. Let his portion from it be taking heed in himself, that if he is heedless, ill-mannered, and deluded by the respite given him, perhaps vengeance will overtake him and the decree will be executed upon him.

Likewise, when he hears the description of Paradise and the Fire and the rest of what is in the Qur'an—it is not possible to exhaust what is understood from it, for that has no end. Each servant has only according to his provision. {«وَلَا رَطْبٍ وَلَا يَابِسٍ إِلَّا فِي كِتَابٍ مُّبِينٍ»} ("No moist thing and no dry thing but is in a manifest Book"). {«قُل لَّوْ كَانَ الْبَحْرُ مِدَادًا لِّكَلِمَاتِ رَبِّي لَنَفِدَ الْبَحْرُ قَبْلَ أَن تَنفَدَ كَلِمَاتُ رَبِّي وَلَوْ جِئْنَا بِمِثْلِهِ مَدَدًا»} ("Say: Were the sea ink for the words of my Lord, the sea would be exhausted before the words of my Lord were exhausted, even if We brought the like of it as replenishment"). For this reason ʿAlī—may God be pleased with him—said: "Were I to wish, I would load seventy camels with the commentary of the Opening Sūrah."

The purpose of what we have mentioned is to point to the path of comprehension so that its door may open. As for exhaustiveness, there is no hope of it. Whoever has no understanding of what is in the Qur'an, even at the lowest degree, enters into His saying—exalted is He: {«وَمِنْهُم مَّن يَسْتَمِعُ إِلَيْكَ حَتَّىٰ إِذَا خَرَجُوا مِنْ عِندِكَ قَالُوا لِلَّذِينَ أُوتُوا الْعِلْمَ مَاذَا قَالَ آنِفًا ۚ أُولَٰئِكَ الَّذِينَ طَبَعَ اللَّهُ عَلَىٰ قُلُوبِهِمْ»} ("And among them are those who listen to you until, when they depart from you, they say to those who have been given knowledge: 'What did he say just now?' Those are the ones upon whose hearts God has set a seal"). The seal is the obstacles we shall mention among the obstacles to understanding. It has been said: "The seeker is not a seeker until he finds in the Qur'an everything he desires, and knows from it the deficient from the abundant, and is rendered independent by the Master from servants."

**The Sixth: Self-Emptying of the Obstacles to Understanding**

The sixth is self-emptying of the obstacles to understanding. For most people are prevented from understanding the meanings of the Qur'an by causes and veils that Satan has cast over their hearts, so that the wonders of the Qur'an's secrets are blinded to them. The Prophet—peace be upon him—said: "Were it not that the devils hover around the hearts of the children of Adam, they would look upon the Kingdom (malakūt)." The meanings of the Qur'an are among the things of the malakūt. Everything that is hidden from the senses and is not perceived except by the light of inner vision is of the malakūt.

The veils of understanding are four:

**The first** is that one's concern be turned to perfecting the letters by extracting them from their points of articulation. A devil is appointed over this, assigned to the reciters to divert them from understanding the meanings of God's speech—mighty and majestic is He. He keeps driving them to repeat a letter, making them imagine it did not come out from its point of articulation. Such a one's reflection is confined to the points of articulation—how then can meanings be unveiled to him? The greatest laughter for Satan is one who is obedient to such deception.

**The second** is that one be a blind follower (muqallid) of a school heard by way of blind imitation, frozen upon it, with partisanship fixed in his soul by mere adherence to what was heard, without reaching it by inner vision and direct witnessing. Such a person is bound by his belief from going beyond it; he cannot conceive in his mind other than his belief. His gaze is stopped at what he has heard. If a lightning flash gleams from afar and a meaning appears to him among the meanings that diverge from what he has heard, the devil of blind imitation attacks him and says: "How can this occur to your mind, when it contradicts the belief of your fathers?" So he sees that as a deception from Satan, distances himself from it, and guards against the like of it.

It was for this that the Sufis said: "Knowledge is a veil." By "knowledge" they meant the beliefs upon which most people persist by mere blind imitation, or by mere dialectical words that partisans of schools have polished and cast to them. As for true knowledge, which is unveiling and direct witnessing by the light of inner vision—how could it be a veil, when it is the ultimate goal of seeking?

This blind imitation may be false and thus an obstacle—like one who believes in "establishment upon the Throne" as physical sitting and settling. If it occurs to him, for example, that "the Holy" (al-Quddūs) means "sanctified above everything that is possible for His creatures," his blind imitation cannot prevent that from settling in his soul. Were it to settle in his soul, it would lead to a second and third unveiling, and so on continuously. But he hastens to repel that from his mind because it contradicts his false blind imitation.

And it may be true, yet also an obstacle to understanding and unveiling. For the truth that creatures are charged to believe has ranks and degrees; it has a manifest beginning and a hidden depth. Freezing upon the manifest prevents reaching the hidden depth, as we mentioned in the distinction between outward and inward knowledge in the Book of the Foundations of Belief (Qawāʿid al-ʿAqāʾid).

**The third** is that one be persistent upon a sin, or characterized by pride, or afflicted generally with an obeyed passion for the world. For that is a cause of the heart's darkness and rust. It is like filth upon a mirror, preventing the clarity of truth from being reflected in it. It is the greatest veil of the heart, and by it most people are veiled. The more intensely lusts accumulate, the more intensely the meanings of the discourse are concealed. The lighter the burdens of the world upon the heart, the nearer the reflection of meaning in it.

The heart is like a mirror; lusts are like rust; the meanings of the Qur'an are like the images reflected in the mirror. The discipline of the heart by removing lusts is like polishing and cleansing the mirror. For this reason the Prophet—peace be upon him—said: "When my community magnifies the dinar and the dirham, the awe of Islam is stripped from it; and when they abandon commanding the good and forbidding the evil, they are deprived of the blessing of revelation." Al-Fuḍayl said: "That is, they are deprived of understanding the Qur'an."

God—mighty and majestic is He—has made turning in repentance (inābah) a condition for understanding and remembrance. He said—exalted is He: {«تَبْصِرَةً وَذِكْرَىٰ لِكُلِّ عَبْدٍ مُّنِيبٍ»} ("An insight and a reminder for every servant who turns in repentance"), and He said—mighty and majestic is He: {«وَمَا يَتَذَكَّرُ إِلَّا مَن يُنِيبُ»} ("None remembers except one who turns in repentance"), and He said—exalted is He: {«إِنَّمَا يَتَذَكَّرُ أُولُو الْأَلْبَابِ»} ("Only those of sound intellect remember"). Whoever prefers the delusion of the world over the bliss of the Hereafter is not among those of sound intellect, and therefore the secrets of the Book are not unveiled to him.

**The fourth** is that one has read an outward commentary (tafsīr ẓāhir) and believes that the words of the Qur'an have no meaning beyond what the transmitted reports from Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, and others convey, and that what lies beyond that is "interpretation by opinion" (tafsīr bi-l-raʾy), and that "whoever interprets the Qur'an by his opinion has taken his seat in the Fire." This too is among the great veils.

We shall explain the meaning of "interpretation by opinion" in the Fourth Book, and that it does not contradict the saying of ʿAlī—may God be pleased with him: "Except that God grants a servant understanding in His Book." For were the meaning only the outward transmitted one, people would not have differed about it.

**The Seventh: Self-Application (Takhṣīṣ)**

The seventh is self-application, which is that one deem oneself the intended addressee of every address in the Qur'an. If one hears a command or prohibition, one deems oneself the commanded and prohibited one. If one hears a promise or threat, likewise. If one hears the stories of the ancients and the prophets, one knows that mere storytelling is not intended; rather, the intent is that one take heed and extract from its folds what one needs. There is no story in the Qur'an except that its context is for a benefit regarding the Prophet—peace be upon him—and his community. For this reason He said—exalted is He: {«مَا نُثَبِّتُ بِهِ فُؤَادَكَ»} ("That by which We strengthen your heart"). Let the servant deem that God strengthens his heart by what He narrates to him of the conditions of the prophets and their patience under harm and their steadfastness in religion, awaiting God's victory.

How should one not deem this, when the Qur'an was not sent down to the Messenger of God—peace be upon him—for the Messenger alone, but is a healing, a guidance, a mercy, and a light for the worlds? For this reason God—exalted is He—commanded all people to give thanks for the blessing of the Book. He said—exalted is He: {«وَاذْكُرُوا نِعْمَتَ اللَّهِ عَلَيْكُمْ وَمَا أَنزَلَ عَلَيْكُم مِّنَ الْكِتَابِ وَالْحِكْمَةِ يَعِظُكُم بِهِ»} ("And remember God's favor upon you and what He sent down to you of the Book and the Wisdom, admonishing you thereby"), and He said—mighty and majestic is He: {«لَقَدْ أَنزَلْنَا إِلَيْكُمْ كِتَابًا فِيهِ ذِكْرُكُمْ ۖ أَفَلَا تَعْقِلُونَ»} ("We have sent down to you a Book in which is your remembrance—will you not then reason?"), and {«وَأَنزَلْنَا إِلَيْكَ الذِّكْرَ لِتُبَيِّنَ لِلنَّاسِ مَا نُزِّلَ إِلَيْهِمْ»} ("And We sent down to you the Remembrance that you may make clear to the people what was sent down to them"), and {«كَذَٰلِكَ يَضْرِبُ اللَّهُ لِلنَّاسِ أَمْثَالَهُمْ»} ("Thus God strikes for the people their parables"), and {«وَاتَّبِعُوا أَحْسَنَ مَا أُنزِلَ إِلَيْكُم مِّن رَّبِّكُم»} ("And follow the best of what was sent down to you from your Lord"), and {«هَٰذَا بَصَائِرُ لِلنَّاسِ وَهُدًى وَرَحْمَةٌ لِّقَوْمٍ يُوقِنُونَ»} ("This is insights for the people, and a guidance and mercy for a people who are certain"), and {«هَٰذَا بَيَانٌ لِّلنَّاسِ وَهُدًى وَمَوْعِظَةٌ لِّلْمُتَّقِينَ»} ("This is an explanation for the people, and a guidance and admonition for the God-fearing").

When the address is intended for all people, it is intended for each individual. So this single reciter is intended—what has he to do with other people? Let him deem himself the intended one. God—exalted is He—said: {«وَأُوحِيَ إِلَيَّ هَٰذَا الْقُرْآنُ لِأُنذِرَكُم بِهِ وَمَن بَلَغَ»} ("And this Qur'an was revealed to me that I may warn you thereby and whomsoever it reaches"). Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Quraẓī said: "Whoever the Qur'an reaches, it is as though God spoke to him directly."

When one deems this, he does not make the study of the Qur'an his mere occupation, but recites it as a servant recites the letter of his master, which was written to him to contemplate and act upon. For this reason one of the scholars said: "This Qur'an is letters that have come to us from our Lord—mighty and majestic is He—with His covenants. We reflect upon them in the prayers, pause upon them in seclusion, and execute them in acts of obedience and the followed Sunnahs."

Mālik ibn Dīnār used to say: "What has the Qur'an sown in your hearts, O people of the Qur'an? The Qur'an is the spring of the believer, just as rain is the spring of the earth."

Qatādah said: "No one has sat with this Qur'an but that he rose with an increase or a decrease." God—exalted is He—said: {«هُوَ شِفَاءٌ وَرَحْمَةٌ لِّلْمُؤْمِنِينَ وَلَا يَزِيدُ الظَّالِمِينَ إِلَّا خَسَارًا»} ("It is a healing and a mercy for the believers, and it increases the wrongdoers only in loss").

**The Eighth: Being Affected (Taʾaththur)**

The eighth is being affected, which is that one's heart be affected by various impressions according to the variety of the verses. One should have, according to each understanding, a state and a finding (wajd) with which the heart is characterized—of sorrow, fear, hope, and other things. Whenever one's knowledge is more complete, reverential fear (khashyah) predominates over the states of the heart. For the constricting is predominant over the verses of the Qur'an. One does not see the mention of forgiveness and mercy except coupled with conditions that the knower falls short of attaining—like His saying—mighty and majestic is He: {«وَإِنِّي لَغَفَّارٌ»} ("And indeed I am most forgiving"), then He followed it with four conditions: {«لِّمَن تَابَ وَآمَنَ وَعَمِلَ صَالِحًا ثُمَّ اهْتَدَىٰ»} ("for whoever repents, believes, does righteous work, and then is guided"). And His saying—exalted is He: {«وَالْعَصْرِ * إِنَّ الْإِنسَانَ لَفِي خُسْرٍ * إِلَّا الَّذِينَ آمَن

chapters.title_en: Book IV: On Understanding the Qur'an and Its Interpretation by Personal Opinion (Tafsīr bi al-Ra'y) Without Transmission
