|| الباب الرابع في فهم القرآن وتفسيره بالرأي من غير نقل

لعلك تقول عظمت الأمر فيما سبق في فهم أسرار القرآن وما ينكشف لأرباب
القلوب الزكية من معانيه
PageV01P288
فكيف يستحب ذلك وقد قال صلى الله عليه وسلم من فسر القرآن برأيه فليتبوأ
مقعده من النار (1) وعن هذا شنع أهل العلم بظاهر التفسير على أهل التصوف من
المقصرين المنسوبين إلى التصوف في تأويل كلمات في القرآن على خلاف ما نقل
عن ابن عباس وسائر المفسرين وذهبوا إلى أنه كفر فإن صح ما قاله أهل التفسير
فما معنى فهم القرآن سوى حفظ تفسيره وإن لم يصح ذلك فما معنى قوله صلى الله
عليه وسلم من فسر القرآن برأيه فليتبوأ مقعده  من النار فاعلم أن من زعم أن
لا معنى للقرآن إلا ما ترجمه ظاهر التفسير فهو مخبر عن حد نفسه وهو مصيب في
الإخبار عن نفسه ولكنه مخطئ في الحكم برد الخلق كافة إلى درجته التي هي حده
ومحطه بل الأخبار والآثار تدل على أن في معاني القرآن متسعا لأرباب الفهم
(2) قال علي رضي الله عنه إلا أن يؤتى الله عبدا فهما في القرآن فإن لم يكن
سوى الترجمة المنقولة فما ذلك الفهم وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم إن للقرآن
ظهرا وبطنا وحدا ومطلعا (3) ويروى أيضا عن ابن مسعود موقوفا عليه وهو من
علماء التفسير فما معنى الظهر والبطن والحد والمطلع وقال علي كرم الله وجهه
لو شئت لأوقرت سبعين بعيرا من تفسير فاتحة الكتاب فما معناه وتفسير ظاهرها
في غاية الاقتصار وقال أبو الدرداء لا يفقه الرجل حتى يجعل للقرآن وجوها
وقد قال بعض العلماء لكل آية ستون ألف فهم وما بقي من فهمها أكثر وقال
آخرون القرآن يحوي سبعة وسبعين ألف علم ومائتي علم إذ كل كلمة علم ثم
يتضاعف ذلك أربعة أضعاف إذ لكل كلمة ظاهر وباطن وحد ومطلع وترديد رسول الله
صلى الله عليه وسلم بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم عشرين مرة (4) لا يكون إلا
لتدبره باطن معانيها وإلا فترجمتها وتفسيرها ظاهر لا يحتاج مثله إلى تكرير
وقال ابن مسعود رضي الله عنه من أراد علم الأولين والآخرين فليتدبر القرآن
وذلك لا يحصل بمجرد تفسير الظاهر وبالجملة فالعلوم كلها داخلة في أفعال
الله عز وجل وصفاته وفي القرآن شرح ذاته وأفعاله وصفاته وهذه العلوم لا
نهاية لها وفي القرآن إشارة إلى مجامعها والمقامات في التعمق في تفصيله
راجع إلى فهم القرآن ومجرد ظاهره التفسير لا يشير إلى ذلك بل كل ما أشكل
فيه على النظار واختلف فيه الخلائق في النظريات والمعقولات ففي القرآن إليه
رموز ودلالات عليه يختص أهل الفهم بدركها فيكف يفي بذلك ترجمة ظاهره
وتفسيره ولذلك قال صلى الله عليه وسلم اقرءوا القرآن والتمسوا غرائبه  (5)
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم في حديث علي كرم الله وجهه والذي بعثني بالحق نبيا
ليفترقن أمتي عن أصل دينها وجماعتها على اثنتين وسبعين فرقة كلها ضالة مضلة
يدعون إلى النار فإذا كان ذلك فعليكم بكتاب الله عز وجل فإن فيه نبأ من كان
قبلكم ونبأ ما يأتي بعدكم وحكم ما بينكم من خالفه من الجبابرة قصمه الله عز
وجل ومن ابتغى العلم في غيره أضله الله عز وجل وهو حبل الله المتين ونوره
المبين وشفاؤه النافع عصمة لمن تمسك به ونجاة لمن اتبعه لا يموج فيقوم ولا
يزيغ فيستقيم ولا تنقضي عجائبه ولا يخلقه كثرة الترديد (6) PageV01P289
الحديث وفي حديث حذيفة لما أخبره رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم بالاختلاف
والفرقة بعده قال فقلت يا رسول الله فماذا تأمرني إن أدركت ذلك فقال تعلم
كتاب الله واعمل بما فيه فهو المخرج من ذلك قال فأعدت عليه ذلك ثلاثا فقال
صلى الله عليه وسلم ثلاثا تعلم كتاب الله عز وجل واعمل بما فيه ففيه النجاة
(1) وقال علي كرم الله وجهه من فهم القرآن فسر به جمل العلم أشار به إلى أن
القرآن يشير إلى مجامع العلوم كلها وقال ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما في قوله
تعالى ومن يؤت الحكمة فقد أوتي خيرا كثيرا يعني الفهم في القرآن وقال عز
وجل ففهمناها سليمان وكلا آتينا حكما وعلما سمى ما آتاهما علما وحكما وخصص
ما انفرد به سليمان بالتفطن له باسم الفهم وجعله مقدما على الحكم والعلم
فهذه الأمور تدل على أن في فهم معاني القرآن مجالا رحبا ومتسعا بالغا وأن
المنقول من ظاهر التفسير ليس منتهى الإدراك فيه
فأما قوله صلى الله عليه وسلم من فسر القرآن برأيه ونهيه عنه (2) صلى
الله عليه وسلم وقول أبي بكر رضي الله عنه أي أرض تقلني وأي سماء تظلني إذا
قلت في القرآن برأيي إلى غير ذلك مما ورد في الأخبار والآثار في النهي عن
تفسير القرآن بالرأي فلا يخلو إما أن يكون المراد به  الاقتصار على النقل
والمسموع وترك الاستنباط والاستقلال بالفهم أو المراد به أمرا آخر وباطل
قطعا أن يكون المراد به أن لا يتكلم أحد في القرآن إلا بما يسمعه لوجوه
أحدها أنه يشترط أن يكون ذلك مسموعا من رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
ومسندا إليه وذلك مما لا يصادف إلا في بعض القرآن فأما ما يقوله ابن عباس
وابن مسعود من أنفسهم فينبغي أن ل
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ف-ه-م (f-h-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Comprehension, grasping the reality of a thing; deep intellectual penetration into meaning.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Understanding (fahm) is the perception of the meaning of speech, distinct from mere hearing (samāʿ); it implies an act of the intellect upon the received words.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) is the direct conveyance of meaning; metaphorical (majāz) is the extension. Here, 'fahm' is used literally for intellectual apprehension, not mere sensory reception.
- Root: ر-أ-ي (r-'-y)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Opinion, view, judgment formed by reflection; also 'to see' — hence a mental vision.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Ra'y is the considered opinion arrived at through ijtihād, but it is often contrasted with transmitted knowledge (naql); it can be sound (ṣawāb) or corrupt (fāsid).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): The literal sense is 'sight'; metaphorically, it denotes intellectual insight. The prohibition targets the corrupt opinion (al-ra'y al-fāsid) that follows caprice (hawā), not sound ijtihād.
- Root: ظ-ه-ر (ẓ-h-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Apparent, outward, manifest surface of a thing.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The ẓāhir is the external aspect of the Qur'anic text; its bāṭin (inner) is the deeper reality. Both are valid, but the ẓāhir requires transmission (naql) to be secured.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal usage for the visible exterior; here, 'ẓāhir al-tafsīr' is the transmitted exegesis of the outward wording, as opposed to the inner meanings (asrār).
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Taqdīr (Ellipsis and Supposition) — In complex periodic sentences, omitted elements (e.g., 'love' in 'they were made to drink the calf in their hearts') must be supplied by the interpreter based on syntactic context, preventing misreading of the ẓāhir.
chapters.translation:
I say: You might say, "You have magnified the matter in what preceded regarding the understanding of the secrets of the Qur'an and what is unveiled to the possessors of pure hearts of its meanings. How then is that commendable, given that he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: 'Whoever interprets the Qur'an by his own opinion, let him take his seat in the Fire'?" And upon this, the scholars of outward exegesis have denounced the Sufis — those deficient ones attributed to Sufism — for their interpretation of words in the Qur'an contrary to what was transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās and the rest of the exegetes, deeming it unbelief. If what the exegetes say is sound, then what is the meaning of 'understanding the Qur'an' other than memorizing its exegesis? And if that is not sound, then what is the meaning of his saying, peace and blessings be upon him: 'Whoever interprets the Qur'an by his own opinion, let him take his seat in the Fire'?

Know that whoever claims that there is no meaning for the Qur'an except what the outward exegesis has rendered is reporting about the limit of his own self. He is correct in reporting about himself, but he errs in judging all creatures to be reduced to his own level, which is his limit and his resting place. Rather, the reports (akhbār) and traditions (āthār) indicate that in the meanings of the Qur'an there is ample scope for the possessors of understanding. ʿAlī, may God be pleased with him, said: "Except that God grants a servant understanding (fahm) in the Qur'an." For if there were nothing but the transmitted rendering, what would that understanding be? And he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Indeed, the Qur'an has an outward (ẓahr) and an inward (baṭn), a limit (ḥadd) and a point of ascent (muṭṭalaʿ)." It is also related from Ibn Masʿūd as a stopped tradition (mawqūf), and he is among the scholars of exegesis. So what is the meaning of 'outward,' 'inward,' 'limit,' and 'point of ascent'? And ʿAlī, may God honor his face, said: "If I wished, I could load seventy camels with the exegesis of the Opening Chapter (Fātiḥah)." What is its meaning, when the exegesis of its outward is extremely brief? And Abū al-Dardā' said: "A man does not attain true understanding (fiqh) until he makes for the Qur'an multiple facets." And some scholars have said: "For every verse there are sixty thousand understandings, and what remains of its understanding is even more." Others said: "The Qur'an contains seventy-seven thousand and two hundred sciences, for every word is a science, then that multiplies fourfold, for every word has an outward, an inward, a limit, and a point of ascent." And the repetition of the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, of "In the name of God, the Merciful, the Compassionate" twenty times could only be for his pondering the inner meanings of it. Otherwise, its rendering and outward exegesis are apparent and do not require such repetition. And Ibn Masʿūd, may God be pleased with him, said: "Whoever desires the knowledge of the first and the last, let him ponder the Qur'an." And that is not attained by mere outward exegesis. In sum, all the sciences are included in the acts of God, Mighty and Majestic, and His attributes; and in the Qur'an is the explanation of His essence, His acts, and His attributes. These sciences have no end, and in the Qur'an is an indication of their summaries. The stations of deep penetration into its details revert to the understanding of the Qur'an. The mere outward exegesis does not indicate that. Rather, everything that perplexed the thinkers and over which creatures differed in theoretical and intellectual matters — in the Qur'an there are symbols and indications of it, which the possessors of understanding are singled out to grasp. How then can the rendering of its outward and its exegesis suffice for that? Therefore, he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Recite the Qur'an and seek its wonders." And he, peace and blessings be upon him, said in the hadith of ʿAlī, may God honor his face: "By Him who sent me as a prophet with the truth, my community will split from the foundation of its religion and its main body into seventy-two sects, all of them erring and leading astray, calling to the Fire. When that occurs, cling to the Book of God, Mighty and Majestic, for in it is the news of those before you and the news of what comes after you, and the judgment of what is between you. Whoever opposes it among the tyrants, God will crush him; whoever seeks knowledge in other than it, God will lead him astray. It is the firm rope of God, the clear light, the beneficial healing, a protection for whoever clings to it, and a deliverance for whoever follows it. It does not waver so as to need straightening, nor does it deviate so as to need correction. Its wonders do not cease, nor does frequent repetition wear it out." And in the hadith of Ḥudhayfah, when the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, informed him of the disagreement and division after him, he said: "I said, 'O Messenger of God, what do you command me if I reach that?' He said: 'Learn the Book of God and act by what is in it, for it is the way out of that.' He said: 'I repeated it to him three times, and he said three times: Learn the Book of God, Mighty and Majestic, and act by what is in it, for in it is deliverance.'" And ʿAlī, may God honor his face, said: "Whoever understands the Qur'an, by it he interprets the sum of knowledge," indicating that the Qur'an points to the summaries of all sciences. And Ibn ʿAbbās, may God be pleased with them both, said regarding His saying, Exalted is He: {«And whoever is given wisdom has been given abundant good»} — meaning understanding in the Qur'an. And He, Mighty and Majestic, said: {«And We gave understanding of it to Solomon, and to each We gave judgment and knowledge»} — He named what He gave them 'judgment' and 'knowledge,' and singled out what Solomon uniquely possessed of discernment with the name 'understanding' (fahm), making it precede judgment and knowledge. These matters indicate that in understanding the meanings of the Qur'an there is a wide field and a far-reaching scope, and that what is transmitted of the outward exegesis is not the limit of perception therein.

As for his saying, peace and blessings be upon him: "Whoever interprets the Qur'an by his own opinion," and his prohibition of it, and the saying of Abū Bakr, may God be pleased with him: "Which earth would carry me and which sky would shade me if I said about the Qur'an by my own opinion," and other such reports and traditions prohibiting the interpretation of the Qur'an by opinion — this cannot be free from one of two possibilities: either the intent is restriction to transmission and what is heard, abandoning derivation (istinbāṭ) and independent understanding, or the intent is something else. It is absolutely false that the intent is that no one should speak about the Qur'an except with what he has heard, for several reasons.

First: That would require it to be heard from the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, and attributed to him — and that is only found in part of the Qur'an. As for what Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn Masʿūd say from themselves, it should then not be accepted, and it would be said it is interpretation by opinion, because they did not hear it from the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him. Likewise for others among the Companions, may God be pleased with them.

Second: The Companions and exegetes differed in interpreting some verses, stating divergent opinions that cannot be reconciled, and hearing all of them from the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, is impossible. If one were heard, the rest would be rejected. Thus it is decisively established that every exegete spoke about the meaning according to what appeared to him through his own derivation, until they said about the letters at the beginnings of the chapters seven divergent opinions that cannot be reconciled. It was said that 'Alif-Lām-Rā' are letters from 'al-Raḥmān' (the Merciful); and it was said that 'Alif' is God (Allāh), 'Lām' is the Subtle (Laṭīf), and 'Rā' is the Merciful (Raḥīm); and other opinions were given. Reconciling all of them is impossible — so how could all be heard?

Third: He, peace and blessings be upon him, prayed for Ibn ʿAbbās, may God be pleased with him, saying: "O God, give him understanding in religion and teach him the interpretation (ta'wīl)." If interpretation were heard like the revelation and preserved like it, what would be the meaning of singling him out for that?

Fourth: He, Mighty and Majestic, said: {«...to those among them who derive it (yastanbiṭūnahu)»} — thus affirming for the people of knowledge a derivation (istinbāṭ), and it is known that this is beyond mere hearing.

The sum of what we have transmitted of the traditions on understanding the Qur'an contradicts this illusion. Thus it is nullified that hearing is a condition in interpretation, and it is permissible for everyone to derive from the Qur'an according to the measure of his understanding and the limit of his intellect.

As for the prohibition, it is to be applied to one of two aspects:

The first: That one has an opinion about a matter and an inclination toward it from his nature and caprice (hawā), so he interprets the Qur'an in accordance with his opinion and caprice, seeking thereby to argue for the correctness of his purpose — even if he did not have that opinion and caprice, that meaning would not have occurred to him from the Qur'an. This is sometimes with knowledge, like one who cites certain verses of the Qur'an to validate his innovation (bidʿah) while knowing that the intended meaning of the verse is not that, but he obscures it against his opponent. And sometimes it is with ignorance, but when the verse is susceptible to multiple meanings, his understanding inclines to the aspect that agrees with his purpose, and he weights that side by his opinion and caprice. Thus he has interpreted by his opinion — i.e., his opinion is what drove him to that interpretation, and were it not for his opinion, that aspect would not have been weighted for him. And sometimes one may have a sound purpose and seek a proof for it from the Qur'an, citing what he knows was not intended by it — like one who calls to seeking forgiveness in the last hours of the night, citing his saying, peace and blessings be upon him: "Take the pre-dawn meal (saḥūr), for in the pre-dawn meal is blessing," claiming that the intent is the pre-dawn meal of remembrance (dhikr), while knowing that the intent is eating. Or like one who calls to struggling against the hard heart, saying: "God, Mighty and Majestic, said: {«Go to Pharaoh, for he has transgressed»}," pointing to his heart and indicating that 'Pharaoh' is meant thereby. This kind is sometimes used by some preachers for sound purposes, to beautify speech and entice the listener — and it is prohibited. And the Bāṭiniyyah use it for corrupt purposes, to deceive people and call them to their false doctrine, applying the Qur'an in accordance with their opinion and doctrine to matters they know with certainty are not intended by it. These kinds are one of the two aspects of the prohibition of interpretation by opinion, and the meaning of 'opinion' here is the corrupt opinion that follows caprice, not sound ijtihād. For 'opinion' encompasses both sound and corrupt, and what follows caprice may be specifically named 'opinion.'

The second aspect: That one rushes to interpret the Qur'an by the outward of the Arabic language without seeking support from hearing and transmission regarding the wonders of the Qur'an — what it contains of ambiguous words, altered forms, abbreviation, ellipsis, implication, and advance and delay. Whoever does not master the outward exegesis and hastens to derive meanings by mere understanding of Arabic will err frequently and enter the ranks of those who interpret by opinion.

Thus transmission and hearing are indispensable in the outward exegesis first, to guard against the places of error. Then after that, understanding and derivation expand. The wonders that are not understood except by hearing are many, and we will gesture to a sum of them so that one may infer their like, and know that it is not permissible to be negligent in preserving the outward exegesis first, nor is there any hope of reaching the inward before mastering the outward. Whoever claims to understand the secrets of the Qur'an without mastering the outward exegesis is like one who claims to reach the inner chamber of the house before passing through the door, or claims to understand the purposes of the Turks from their speech while not understanding the Turkish language. For the outward exegesis is like teaching the language that is indispensable for understanding.

Among what requires hearing are many kinds:

From them, the abbreviated by ellipsis and implication — like His saying, Exalted is He: {«And We gave Thamūd the she-camel as a visible sign, but they wronged it»} — meaning 'a visible sign,' and 'they wronged themselves by killing it.' The one who looks at the outward of the Arabic thinks the intent is that the she-camel was seeing and not blind, and does not realize by what they wronged others or themselves. And His saying, Exalted is He: {«And they were made to drink into their hearts the calf, by their unbelief»} — i.e., the love of the calf, with 'love' omitted. And His saying, Mighty and Majestic: {«Then We would have made you taste double the life and double the death»} — i.e., double the punishment of the living and double the punishment of the dead, with 'punishment' omitted and 'the living' and 'the dead' replaced by the mention of 'life' and 'death.' All of that is permissible in eloquent language.

And His saying, Exalted is He: {«And ask the town in which we were and the caravan in which we returned»} — i.e., the people of the town and the people of the caravan, with 'people' omitted and implied in both. And His saying, Mighty and Majestic: {«It weighs heavily upon the heavens and the earth»} — meaning it is hidden from the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth; and when a thing is hidden, it is heavy, so the word was substituted for it and placed in the position of 'upon,' with 'inhabitants' implied and omitted.

And His saying, Exalted is He: {«And you make your provision that you deny»} — i.e., the thanks for your provision. And His saying, Mighty and Majestic: {«And give us what You promised us upon Your messengers»} — i.e., upon the tongues of Your messengers, with 'tongues' omitted. And His saying, Exalted is He: {«Indeed, We sent it down on the Night of Decree»} — intending the Qur'an, though no prior mention of it occurred.

And He said, Mighty and Majestic: {«Until it concealed itself behind the veil»} — intending the sun, with no prior mention of it. And His saying, Exalted is He: {«And those who take besides Him protectors, 'We do not worship them except to bring us nearer to God in rank'»} — i.e., they say, 'We do not worship them.'

And His saying, Mighty and Majestic: {«So what is with these people that they scarcely understand any statement? Whatever good befalls you is from God, and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself»} — meaning they do not understand a statement, saying, 'Whatever good befalls you is from God, and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself.' For if this were not intended, it would contradict His saying: {«Say: All is from God»} — and the doctrine of the Qadariyyah would be understood from it.

From them, the transmitted and altered — like His saying, Exalted is He: {«And the Mount of Sīnīn»} — i.e., the Mount of Sinai; {«Peace upon Āl Yāsīn»} — i.e., upon Elijah (al-Yāsaʿ); and it was said, upon Idrīs, because in the reading of Ibn Masʿūd it is: "Peace upon Idrāsīn."

From them, the repeated that cuts the connection of speech in the outward — like His saying, Mighty and Majestic: {«And those they call upon besides God do not follow partners; they follow nothing but conjecture»} — and His saying, Mighty and Majestic: {«The chiefs who were arrogant among his people said to those who were oppressed, to those who believed among them»} — meaning the arrogant ones said to those who believed among the oppressed.

From them, the advanced and delayed, which is a locus of error — like His saying, Mighty and Majestic: {«Were it not for a word that preceded from your Lord, it would have been a necessary consequence, and an appointed term»} — meaning, were it not for the word and the appointed term, it would have been a necessary consequence; and were it not for it, it would be accusative like 'lizām.' And His saying, Exalted is He: {«They ask you as if you were wary of it»} — i.e., they ask you about it as if you were wary of it. And His saying, Mighty and Majestic: {«For them is forgiveness and a noble provision, just as your Lord brought you out of your house with the truth»} — this speech is not connected; rather, it reverts to His earlier saying: {«Say: The spoils are for God and the Messenger, just as your Lord brought you out of your house with the truth»} — i.e., so the spoils of war became yours, as you were content with your departure while they were averse. Between the two statements, the command to piety and other things intervened. And of this type is His saying, Mighty and Majestic: {«Until you believe in God alone — except the saying of Abraham to his father»} — the verse.

From them, the ambiguous — which is the word shared between meanings, whether a noun or a particle. As for the noun, it is like 'al-shay' (thing), 'al-qarīn' (companion), 'al-ummah' (community), 'al-rūḥ' (spirit), and their like. God, Exalted is He, said: {«God strikes a parable: a slave owned, unable to do anything»} — intending thereby spending from what is provided. And His saying, Mighty and Majestic: {«And God strikes a parable: two men, one of them mute, unable to do anything»} — i.e., the command to justice and uprightness. And His saying, Mighty and Majestic: {«If you follow me, do not ask me about anything»} — intending thereby the attributes of lordship, which are the sciences about which it is not lawful to ask until the knower initiates them at the time of their merit.

And His saying, Mighty and Majestic: {«Or were they created from nothing, or are they the creators?»} — i.e., from no creator. One might mistakenly think it indicates that nothing is created except from something.

As for 'al-qarīn' — like His saying, Mighty and Majestic: {«And his companion said, 'This is what I have ready. Cast into Hell every obstinate disbeliever'»} — intending the angel appointed over him. And His saying, Exalted is He: {«His companion said, 'Our Lord, I did not make him transgress, but he was in deep error'»} — intending the devil.

As for 'al-ummah,' it is used in eight aspects: 'al-ummah' is the group — like His saying, Exalted is He: {«And he found upon it a community of people watering»}; and the followers of the prophets — like your saying, 'the community of Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him'; and a man who gathers good and is followed as an exemplar — like His saying, Exalted is He: {«Indeed, Abraham was a community (ummah), devoutly obedient to God»}; and 'al-ummah' is the religion — like His saying, Mighty and Majestic: {«Indeed, we found our fathers upon a religion (ummah)»}; and 'al-ummah' is the time and period — like His saying, Mighty and Majestic: {«To an appointed term (ummah) counted»} and His saying, Exalted is He: {«And he remembered after a time (ummah)»}; and 'al-ummah' is the stature — it is said, 'So-and-so is handsome in stature (ummah)'; and 'ummah' is a man alone in a religion in which no one shares with him — he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Zayd ibn ʿAmr ibn Nufayl will be raised as a single community (ummah)"; and 'al-ummah' — it is said, 'this is the ummah of Zayd,' i.e., the mother (umm) of Zayd. And 'al-rūḥ' (spirit) also occurs in the Qur'an with many meanings, and we will not lengthen by listing them.

Likewise, ambiguity may occur in particles — like His saying, Mighty and Majestic: {«And raised thereby a dust cloud, and penetrated thereby into the midst of a host»} — the first pronoun refers to the hooves, which are the 'striking sparks' — i.e., they raised by the hooves a dust cloud; and the second refers to the raid, which is the 'dawn raiders' — i.e., they penetrated by it into the midst of a host, the polytheists, and raided with their host. And His saying, Exalted is He: {«And We sent down from it water»} — meaning the clouds; {«And We brought forth from it fruits of every kind»} — meaning the water. And examples of this in the Qur'an are not limited.

From them, the gradation in clarification — like His saying, Mighty and Majestic: {«The month of Ramadan in which the Qur'an was sent down»} — for it did not make clear whether it was night or day; and it became clear by His saying, Mighty and Majestic: {«Indeed, We sent it down on a blessed night»} — but it did not make clear which night; and it became clear by His saying, Exalted is He: {«Indeed, We sent it down on the Night of Decree»}. One might think in the outward there is a contradiction between these verses. This and its like are such that nothing suffices for them except transmission and hearing.

For the Qur'an, from its beginning to its end, is not free of this kind, because it was sent down in the language of the Arabs, and thus it includes the varieties of their speech — abbreviation, elongation, implication, ellipsis, substitution, advance, and delay — so that it would be a challenge to them and a miracle against them. Therefore, whoever is content with understanding the outward of the Arabic and rushes to interpret the Qur'an without seeking support from hearing and transmission in these matters is included among those who interpret the Qur'an by their opinion — like one who understands from 'al-ummah' the most famous meaning of it, and his nature and opinion incline to it; then when he hears it in another place, he inclines by his opinion to what he has heard of its famous meaning, abandoning the pursuit of transmission in many of its meanings. This is what may be prohibited — not the understanding of the secrets of the meanings, as preceded.

So when hearing is attained for such matters, the outward exegesis is known, which is the rendering of the words — but that does not suffice for understanding the realities of the meanings. The difference between the realities of the meanings and the outward exegesis is grasped by an example: God, Mighty and Majestic, said: {«And you did not throw when you threw, but God threw»} — its outward is a clear exegesis, but the reality of its meaning is obscure, for it affirms throwing and negates it, which are contradictory in the outward, until one understands that he threw in one respect and did not throw in another, and from the respect in which he did not throw, God, Mighty and Majestic, threw.

Likewise, He said, Exalted is He: {«Fight them; God will punish them by your hands»} — for if they are the fighters, how is God, Exalted is He, the punisher? And if God, Exalted is He, is the punisher by moving their hands, then what is the meaning of commanding them to fight? The reality of this is drawn from a vast sea of the sciences of unveiling (mukāshafāt), which the outward exegesis does not suffice for — namely, to know the aspect of the connection of acts to the originated power (al-qudrah al-ḥādithah), and to understand the aspect of the connection of that power to the power of God, Mighty and Majestic, until after clarifying many obscure matters, the truth of His saying, Mighty and Majestic: {«And you did not throw when you threw, but God threw»} is unveiled. Perhaps if a lifetime were spent in uncovering the secrets of this meaning and what is connected to its premises and consequences, the lifetime would expire before exhausting all its consequences. And there is no word in the Qur'an whose verification does not require the like of this. It is only unveiled to those firmly rooted in knowledge of its secrets according to the abundance of their sciences, the purity of their hearts, the fullness of their motives for pondering, and their detachment for seeking. Each one has a limit in ascending to a degree higher than it. As for complete attainment, there is no hope in it — {«Were the sea ink and the trees pens, the secrets of God's words would have no end; the seas would be exhausted before the words of God, Mighty and Majestic, were exhausted»}.

From this aspect, creatures differ in understanding after sharing in the knowledge of the outward exegesis — and the outward exegesis is not dispensed with. An example of this is the understanding of some possessors of hearts from his saying, peace and blessings be upon him, in his prostration: "I seek refuge in Your pleasure from Your wrath, and I seek refuge in Your pardon from Your punishment, and I seek refuge in You from You. I cannot enumerate praise of You; You are as You have praised Yourself." He was told: "Prostrate and draw near." He found nearness in prostration, so he looked at the attributes and sought refuge in some from others — for pleasure and wrath are two attributes. Then his nearness increased, and the first nearness was subsumed in it, so he ascended to the Essence and said: "I seek refuge in You from You." Then his nearness increased by what he was ashamed of in seeking refuge on the carpet of nearness, so he resorted to praise and said: "I cannot enumerate praise of You." Then he knew that was a shortcoming and said: "You are as You have praised Yourself." These are thoughts that open to the possessors of hearts. Then for them there are depths beyond this — namely, understanding the meaning of nearness and its specificity to prostration, and the meaning of seeking refuge from one attribute by another, and from Him by Him. Its secrets are many, and the outward exegesis does not indicate them. Nor is the wording contradictory to the outward exegesis; rather, it is a completion of it and an arrival at its core from its outward. This is what we present for understanding the inner meanings — not what contradicts the outward. And God knows best.

The Book of the Etiquettes of Recitation is completed, and praise be to God, Lord of the worlds, and prayers and peace be upon Muhammad, the Seal of the Prophets, and upon every chosen servant from all the worlds, and upon the family of Muhammad and his Companions, and peace. It will be followed, God willing, by the Book of Remembrances and Supplications. And God is the one whose help is sought; there is no Lord but Him.

chapters.title_en: The Book of Remembrances and Supplications — Section 137
chapters.arabic_text:
| كتاب الأذكار والدعوات

بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم الحمد لله الشاملة
رأفته العامة رحمته الذي جازى عباده عن ذكرهم بذكرهم فقال تعالى فاذكروني
أذكركم PageV01P293
ورغبهم في السؤال والدعاء بأمره فقال ادعوني أستجب لكم فأطمع المطيع
والعاصي والداني والقاصي في الانبساط إلى حضرة جلاله برفع الحاجات والأماني
بقوله فإني قريب أجيب دعوة الداع إذا دعان والصلاة على محمد سيد أنبيائه
وعلى آله وأصحابه خيرة أصفيائه وسلم تسليما كثيرا
أما بعد
فليس بعد تلاوة كتاب الله عز وجل عبادة تؤدى باللسان أفضل من ذكر الله
تعالى ورفع الحاجات بالأدعية الخالصة إلى الله تعالى فلا بد من شرح فضيلة
الذكر على الجملة  ثم على التفصيل في أعيان الأذكار
وشرح فضيلة الدعاء وشروطه وآدابه ونقل المأثور من الدعوات الجامعة لمقاصد
الدين والدنيا والدعوات الخاصة لسؤال المغفرة والاستعاذة وغيرها
ويتحرر المقصود من ذلك بذكر أبواب خمسة
الباب الأول في فضيلة الذكر وفائدته جملة وتفصيلا
الباب الثاني في فضيلة الدعاء وآدابه وفضيلة الاستغفار والصلاة على رسول
الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
الباب الثالث في أدعية مأثورة ومعزية إلى أصحابها وأسبابها
الباب الرابع في أدعية منتخبة محذوفة الإسناد من الأدعية الماثورة
الباب الخامس في الأدعية المأثورة عند حدوث الحوادث
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ذ-ك-ر (dhakara)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Remembrance, recollection, invocation; the tongue's utterance and the heart's presence
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The act of keeping something present in mind; in theological terms, the servant's remembrance of God through praise and the divine response of God's remembrance of the servant
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) for mental recall; metaphorical (majāz) for verbal praise and glorification
- Root: د-ع-و (daʿā)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Calling, summoning, supplication; the raising of need toward the one who can fulfill it
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The servant's petition to God, combining humility of heart with utterance of request; God's "call" to servants is His command and invitation
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for vocal calling; metaphorical for earnest petition and worshipful entreaty
- Root: ج-ز-ي (jazā)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Recompense, requital, repayment — whether good or evil
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Divine recompense that befits the act; here, God's recompense for remembrance is a greater remembrance, showing His generosity
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for exchange; metaphorical for divine favor exceeding the deed
- Sībawayh Rule: The Rule of Inceptive Clauses (al-ibtidāʾ) — the opening "amā baʿd" (to proceed) marks the transition from praise to the treatise's subject, functioning as a syntactic pivot between the doxology and the exposition.
chapters.translation:
I say: This is the Book of Remembrances and Supplications.

In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Ever-Merciful. Praise be to God, whose compassion is all-encompassing, whose mercy is universal, who recompensed His servants for their remembrance of Him with His own remembrance of them, for He — exalted be His statement — said: {«فاذكروني أذكركم»} ("So remember Me; I will remember you"). And He urged them toward asking and supplication by His command, saying: {«ادعوني أستجب لكم»} ("Call upon Me; I will respond to you"). Thus He made both the obedient and the disobedient, the near and the far, aspire to stretch forth toward the presence of His majesty by raising their needs and hopes, through His saying: {«فإني قريب أجيب دعوة الداع إذا دعان»} ("For I am near; I answer the call of the caller when he calls Me"). And blessings upon Muhammad, the master of His prophets, and upon his family and companions, the choicest of His elect, with abundant peace.

To proceed: After the recitation of the Book of God — mighty and majestic is He — there is no act of worship performed by the tongue more excellent than the remembrance of God — exalted is He — and the raising of needs through supplications sincerely directed to God — exalted is He. Thus it is necessary to explain the virtue of remembrance in general, then in detail concerning the specific forms of remembrances; and to explain the virtue of supplication, its conditions, and its proprieties; and to transmit the transmitted supplications that gather the purposes of religion and this world, as well as the specific supplications for seeking forgiveness, seeking refuge, and other matters.

The aim of all this is achieved through the mention of five chapters:

Chapter One: On the virtue of remembrance and its benefit, in general and in detail.

Chapter Two: On the virtue of supplication and its proprieties, the virtue of seeking forgiveness, and blessings upon the Messenger of God — may God bless him and grant him peace.

Chapter Three: On transmitted supplications attributed to their narrators and the occasions of their origin.

Chapter Four: On selected supplications, with chains of transmission omitted, drawn from the transmitted supplications.

Chapter Five: On the transmitted supplications to be said upon the occurrence of events.

chapters.title_en: On the Virtue of Remembrance (Dhikr) and Its Benefit in General and in Detail, from Verses, Reports, and Traditions
chapters.arabic_text:
|| الباب الأول في فضيلة الذكر وفائدته على الجملة والتفصيل من الآيات والأخبار والآثار

ويدل على فضيلة الذكر على الجملة من الآيات قوله سبحانه وتعالى فاذكروني
أذكركم قال ثابت البناني رحمه الله إني أعلم متى يذكرني ربي عز وجل ففزعوا
منه وقالوا كيف تعلم ذلك فقال إذا ذكرته ذكرني وقال تعالى اذكروا الله ذكرا
كثيرا وقال تعالى فإذا أفضتم من عرفات فاذكروا الله عند المشعر الحرام
واذكروه كما هداكم وقال عز وجل فإذا قضيتم مناسككم فاذكروا الله كذكركم
آباءكم أو أشد ذكرا وقال تعالى الذين يذكرون الله قياما وقعودا وعلى جنوبهم
وقال تعالى فإذا قضيتم الصلاة فاذكروا الله قياما وقعودا وعلى جنوبكم قال
ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما أي بالليل والنهار في البر والبحر والسفر والحضر
والغنى والفقر والمرض والصحة والسر والعلانية
وقال تعالى في ذم المنافقين ولا يذكرون الله إلا قليلا وقال عز وجل واذكر
ربك في نفسك تضرعا وخيفة ودون الجهر من القول بالغدو والآصال ولا تكن من
الغافلين وقال تعالى ولذكر الله أكبر قال ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما له وجهان
أحدهما أن ذكر الله تعالى لكم أعظم من ذكرككم إياه والآخر أن ذكر الله أعظم
من كل عبادة سواه إلى غير ذلك من الآيات
وأما الأخبار فقد قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم ذاكر الله في
الغافلين كالشجرة في وسط الهشيم (1) وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم ذاكر الله في
الغافلين كالمقاتل بين الفارين  وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم يقول الله عز وجل
أنا مع عبدي ما ذكرني وتحركت شفتاه بي (2) وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم ما عمل
ابن آدم من عمل أنجى له من عذاب الله من ذكر الله عز وجل قالوا يا رسول
الله ولا الجهاد في سبيل الله قال ولا الجهاد في سبيل الله إلا أن تضرب
بسيفك حتى ينقطع ثم PageV01P294
تضرب به حتى ينقطع ثم تضرب به حتى ينقطع (1) فقال صلى الله عليه وسلم من
أحب أن يرتع في رياض الجنة فليكثر ذكر الله عز وجل (2) وسئل رسول الله صلى
الله عليه وسلم أي الأعمال أفضل فقال أن تموت ولسانك رطب بذكر الله عز وجل
(3) وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم أصبح وأمس ولسانك رطب بذكر الله تصبح وتمسي
وليس عليك خطيئة (4) وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم لذكر الله عز وجل بالغداة
والعشي أفضل من حطم السيوف في سبيل الله ومن إعطاء المال سحا (5) وقال صلى
الله عليه وسلم يقول الله تبارك وتعالى إذا ذكرني عبدي في نفسه ذكرته في
نفسي وإذا ذكرني في ملأ ذكرته في ملأ خير من ملئه وإذا تقرب مني شبرا تقربت
منه ذراعا وإذا تقرب مني ذراعا تقربت منه باعا وإذا مشى إلي هرولت إليه (6)
يعني بالهرولة سرعة الإجابة
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم سبعة يظلهم الله عز وجل في ظله يوم لا ظل إلا
ظله من جملتهم رجل ذكر الله خاليا ففاضت عيناه من خشية الله (7) وقال أبو
الدرداء قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم ألا أنبئكم بخير أعمالكم وأزكاها
عند مليككم وأرفعها في درجاتكم وخير لكم من إعطاء الورق والذهب وخير لكم من
أن تلقوا عدوكم فتضربون أعناقهم ويضربون أعناقكم قالوا وما ذاك يا رسول
الله قال ذكر الله عز وجل دائما (8) وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم قال الله عز
وجل من شغله ذكري عن مسألتي أعطيته أفضل ما أعطي السائلين (9) وأما الآثار
فقد قال الفضيل بلغنا إن الله عز وجل قال عبدي  اذكرني بعد الصبح ساعة وبعد
العصر ساعة أكفك ما بينهما
وقال بعض العلماء إن الله عز وجل يقول أيما عبد اطلعت على قلبه فرأيت
الغالب عليه التمسك بذكرى توليت سياسته وكنت جليسه ومحادثه وأنيسه
وقال الحسن الذكر ذكران ذكر الله عز وجل بين نفسك وبين الله عز وجل ما
أحسنه وأعظم أجره وأفضل من ذلك ذكر الله سبحانه عند ما حرم الله عز وجل
ويروى إن كل نفس تخرج من الدنيا عطشى إلا ذاكر الله عز وجل وقال معاذ بن
جبل رضي الله عنه ليس يتحسر أهل الجنة على شيء إلا على ساعة مرت بهم لم
يذكروا الله سبحانه فيها والله تعالى أعلم PageV01P295
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ذ-ك-ر (dhikr)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is "presence of something in the mind" or "uttering with the tongue"; also "honor" and "renown" (as in dhikr = fame). It entails both inward recollection and outward articulation.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, dhikr is the heart's vigilance toward God, ranging from verbal praise (tasbīḥ, taḥmīd) to silent contemplation; its highest form is the heart's absorption in divine majesty, which the Qur'an calls "the greater remembrance" (al-dhikr al-akbar).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) = verbal utterance or mental recall; metaphorical (majāz) = obedience and worship itself, as in "remembrance of God" standing for all acts of devotion. The phrase "remembrance of God is greater" (wa-la-dhikru llāhi akbar) admits both literal and figurative readings.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Conditional Clauses (al-sharṭ wa-l-jawāb) — In "If My servant remembers Me in himself, I remember him in Myself" (fa-idhā dhakaranī fī nafsihi dhakartuhu fī nafsī), the protasis and apodosis are parallel in structure, indicating mutual correspondence; the doubling of "remembrance" (dhikr) in both clauses signals reciprocity, not mere sequence.
chapters.translation:
I say: The first chapter concerns the virtue of remembrance (dhikr) and its benefit, in general and in detail, as established by verses, reports (akhbār), and traditions (āthār).

As for what indicates the virtue of remembrance in general from the verses, there is His saying, exalted and majestic: {«فَاذْكُرُونِي أَذْكُرْكُمْ»} ("So remember Me; I will remember you"). Thābit al-Bunānī (may God have mercy on him) said: "I know when my Lord, mighty and majestic, remembers me." They were alarmed by this and said: "How do you know that?" He replied: "When I remember Him, He remembers me." And He, exalted, said: {«اذْكُرُوا اللَّهَ ذِكْرًا كَثِيرًا»} ("Remember God with much remembrance"). And He, exalted, said: {«فَإِذَا أَفَضْتُمْ مِنْ عَرَفَاتٍ فَاذْكُرُوا اللَّهَ عِنْدَ الْمَشْعَرِ الْحَرَامِ وَاذْكُرُوهُ كَمَا هَدَاكُمْ»} ("When you pour forth from ʿArafāt, remember God at the Sacred Monument, and remember Him as He has guided you"). And He, mighty and majestic, said: {«فَإِذَا قَضَيْتُمْ مَنَاسِكَكُمْ فَاذْكُرُوا اللَّهَ كَذِكْرِكُمْ آبَاءَكُمْ أَوْ أَشَدَّ ذِكْرًا»} ("When you have completed your rites, remember God as you remember your fathers, or with even more intense remembrance"). And He, exalted, said: {«الَّذِينَ يَذْكُرُونَ اللَّهَ قِيَامًا وَقُعُودًا وَعَلَى جُنُوبِهِمْ»} ("Those who remember God standing, sitting, and on their sides"). And He, exalted, said: {«فَإِذَا قَضَيْتُمُ الصَّلَاةَ فَاذْكُرُوا اللَّهَ قِيَامًا وَقُعُودًا وَعَلَى جُنُوبِكُمْ»} ("When you have completed the prayer, remember God standing, sitting, and on your sides"). Ibn ʿAbbās (may God be pleased with them both) said: "That is, by night and by day, on land and at sea, in travel and at home, in wealth and poverty, in sickness and health, in secret and in public."

And He, exalted, said in censure of the hypocrites: {«وَلَا يَذْكُرُونَ اللَّهَ إِلَّا قَلِيلًا»} ("And they do not remember God except a little"). And He, mighty and majestic, said: {«وَاذْكُرْ رَبَّكَ فِي نَفْسِكَ تَضَرُّعًا وَخِيفَةً وَدُونَ الْجَهْرِ مِنَ الْقَوْلِ بِالْغُدُوِّ وَالْآصَالِ وَلَا تَكُنْ مِنَ الْغَافِلِينَ»} ("And remember your Lord within yourself, in supplication and fear, and without loudness of speech, in the mornings and the evenings, and be not among the heedless"). And He, exalted, said: {«وَلَذِكْرُ اللَّهِ أَكْبَرُ»} ("And the remembrance of God is greater"). Ibn ʿAbbās (may God be pleased with them both) said: "This has two aspects: one is that God's remembrance of you is greater than your remembrance of Him; the other is that remembrance of God is greater than every act of worship besides it." And there are further verses beyond these.

As for the reports (akhbār), the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "The one who remembers God among the heedless is like a tree in the midst of dry brushwood." And he (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "The one who remembers God among the heedless is like a fighter among those who flee." And he (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "God, mighty and majestic, says: 'I am with My servant as long as he remembers Me and his lips move with Me.'" And he (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "No deed of the son of Adam is more saving for him from God's punishment than remembrance of God, mighty and majestic." They said: "O Messenger of God, not even jihad in the path of God?" He said: "Not even jihad in the path of God, unless you strike with your sword until it breaks, then strike with it until it breaks, then strike with it until it breaks." Then he (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "Whoever loves to graze in the meadows of Paradise, let him increase his remembrance of God, mighty and majestic." And the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) was asked: "Which deed is most excellent?" He said: "That you die with your tongue moist with the remembrance of God, mighty and majestic." And he (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "Enter the morning and the evening with your tongue moist with the remembrance of God, and you will enter morning and evening without sin upon you." And he (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "Remembrance of God, mighty and majestic, in the morning and the evening is better than the clashing of swords in the path of God, and better than pouring out wealth in abundance." And he (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "God, blessed and exalted, says: 'When My servant remembers Me in himself, I remember him in Myself; and when he remembers Me in a gathering, I remember him in a gathering better than his; and when he draws near to Me by a span, I draw near to him by a cubit; and when he draws near to Me by a cubit, I draw near to him by a fathom; and when he comes to Me walking, I come to him running.'" — meaning by "running" the swiftness of response.

And he (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "Seven are shaded by God, mighty and majestic, in His shade on the day when there is no shade but His shade" — among them being "a man who remembers God in solitude, and his eyes overflow with tears from fear of God." And Abū al-Dardāʾ said: The Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "Shall I not inform you of the best of your deeds, the most pure of them before your King, the highest of them in your ranks, better for you than giving silver and gold, and better for you than meeting your enemy so that you strike their necks and they strike your necks?" They said: "What is that, O Messenger of God?" He said: "The constant remembrance of God, mighty and majestic." And he (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "God, mighty and majestic, says: 'Whoever is occupied by My remembrance from asking of Me, I give him the best of what I give to those who ask.'"

As for the traditions (āthār), al-Fuḍayl said: "It has reached us that God, mighty and majestic, said: 'My servant, remember Me for an hour after the dawn prayer and an hour after the afternoon prayer, and I will suffice you for what is between them.'" And some scholars said: "God, mighty and majestic, says: 'Any servant upon whose heart I look and find that the dominant thing is clinging to My remembrance, I undertake his governance, and I am his companion, his intimate converser, and his familiar friend.'" And al-Ḥasan said: "Remembrance is of two kinds: remembrance of God, mighty and majestic, between yourself and God — how excellent it is and how great its reward! And better than that is remembrance of God, glorified and exalted, at the moment of what God has forbidden." And it is narrated that "every breath that leaves this world is thirsty, except the breath of the one who remembers God, mighty and majestic." And Muʿādh ibn Jabal (may God be pleased with him) said: "The people of Paradise will not regret anything except an hour that passed them by in which they did not remember God, glorified and exalted." And God, exalted, knows best.

chapters.title_en: The Excellence of Assemblies of Remembrance (Faḍīlat Majālis al-Dhikr)
chapters.arabic_text:
||| فضيلة مجالس الذكر

قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم ما جلس قوم مجلسا يذكرون الله عز وجل
إلا حفت بهم الملائكة وغشيتهم الرحمة وذكرهم الله تعالى فيمن عنده (1) وقال
صلى الله عليه وسلم ما من قوم اجتمعوا يذكرون الله تعالى لا يريدون بذلك
إلا وجهه إلا ناداهم مناد من السماء قوموا مغفورا لكم قد بدلت لكم سيئاتكم
حسنات (2) وقال أيضا صلى الله عليه وسلم ما قعد قوم مقعدا لم يذكروا الله
سبحانه وتعالى فيه ولم يصلوا على النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم ألا كان عليهم
حسرة يوم القيامة (3) وقال داود صلى الله عليه وسلم إلهي إذا رأيتني أجاوز
مجالس الذاكرين إلى مجالس الغافلين فاكسر رجلي دونهم فإنها نعمة تنعم بها
علي
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم المجلس الصالح يكفر عن المؤمن ألفي ألف مجلس من
مجالس السوء (4) وقال أبو هريرة رضي الله عنه إن أهل السماء ليتراءون بيوت
أهل الأرض التي يذكر فيها اسم الله تعالى كما تتراءى النجوم
وقال سفيان بن عيينة رحمه الله إذا اجتمع قوم يذكرون الله تعالى اعتزل
الشيطان والدنيا فيقول الشيطان للدنيا ألا ترين ما يصنعون فتقول الدنيا
دعهم فإنهم إذا تفرقوا أخذت بأعناقهم إليك
وعن أبي هريرة رضي الله عنه أنه إذا دخل السوق وقال أراكم ههنا وميراث
رسول الله  صلى الله عليه وسلم يقسم في المسجد فذهب الناس إلى المسجد وتركوا
السوق فلم يروا ميراثا فقالوا يا أبا هريرة ما رأينا ميراثا يقسم في المسجد
قال فماذا رأيتم قالوا رأينا قوما يذكرون الله عز وجل ويقرءون القرآن قال
فذلك ميراث رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم (5) وروى الأعمش عن أبي صالح عن
أبي هريرة وأبي سعيد الخدري عنه صلى الله عليه وسلم أنه قال إن لله عز وجل
ملائكة سياحين في الأرض فضلا عن كتاب الناس فإذا وجدوا قوما يذكرون الله عز
وجل تنادوا هلموا بغيتكم فيجيئون فيحفون بهم إلى السماء فيقول الله تبارك
وتعالى أي شيء تركتم عبادي يصنعونه فيقولون تركناهم يحمدونك ويمجدونك
ويسبحونك فيقول الله تبارك وتعالى وهل رأوني فيقولون لا فيقول جل جلاله كيف
لو رأوني فيقولون لو رأوك لكانوا أشد تسبيحا وتحميدا وتمجيدا فيقول لهم من
أي شيء يتعوذون فيقولون من النار فيقول تعالى وهل رأوها فيقولون لا فيقول
الله عز وجل فكيف لو رأوها فيقولون لو رأوها لكانوا أشد هربا منها وأشد
نفورا فيقول الله عز وجل وأي شيء يطلبون فيقولون الجنة فيقول تعالى وهل
رأوها فيقولون لا فيقول تعالى فكيف لو رأوها فيقولون لو رأوها لكانوا أشد
عليها حرصا فيقول جل جلاله إني أشهدكم أني قد غفرت لهم فيقولون كان فيهم
فلان لم يردهم إنما جاء لحاجة فيقول الله عز وجل هم القوم لا يشقى جليسهم
(6) PageV01P296
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ج-ل-س (j-l-s)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is 'to sit' or 'to remain seated'; a majlis is the place or act of sitting together in company.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, majlis al-dhikr denotes a gathering whose purpose is the conscious invocation and remembrance of God, elevating the act from mere physical sitting to spiritual communion.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) refers to physical sitting; metaphorical (majāz) extends to 'abiding in a state' or 'occupying a spiritual station'—here, the assembly is a locus of divine mercy.
- Root: ذ-ك-ر (dh-k-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Root signifies 'to mention', 'to remember', or 'to be mindful'; dhikr is both verbal utterance and inward recollection.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Dhikr in the Quranic and theological frame is the antithesis of forgetfulness (nisyān); it is the heart's vigilance toward God, often manifested in praise (ḥamd), glorification (tasbīḥ), and magnification (tamjīd).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal usage is verbal mention; metaphorical usage is the soul's persistent awareness of God, as in the hadith 'to remember Me'—implying intimate knowledge and love.
- Root: ح-ف-ف (ḥ-f-f)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Means 'to surround', 'to encircle', or 'to encompass on all sides'.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Used here to depict angels encircling the assembly—a physical metaphor for comprehensive divine protection and witness.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal is physical encirclement; metaphorical is the encompassing mercy and angelic presence that 'covers' the gathering.
- Root: غ-ش-ي (gh-sh-y)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Means 'to cover', 'to envelop', or 'to overwhelm'.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological context, ghishāyah is the divine mercy (raḥmah) that descends as an enveloping shroud over the participants.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal is a physical covering; metaphorical is the spiritual state of being wholly immersed in divine compassion.
- Root: ح-س-ر (ḥ-s-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Means 'regret', 'remorse', or 'grief over loss'.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In eschatological usage, ḥasrah on the Day of Resurrection is the acute anguish of missed opportunity—here, the failure to remember God in assemblies.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal is the feeling of loss; metaphorical is the eternal consequence of negligence in worldly gatherings.
- Root: س-ي-ح (s-y-ḥ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Means 'to travel', 'to roam', or 'to traverse freely'.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Angels described as sayyāḥīn (roaming) signifies their appointed mission to seek out gatherings of dhikr—a divine search for the faithful.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal is physical wandering; metaphorical is the angels' purposeful quest, unbound by earthly limits.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Ḥāl (Circumstantial Clause) — In the hadith 'ما جلس قوم مجلسا يذكرون الله', the verb 'yadhkurūna' functions as a ḥāl (circumstantial qualifier) describing the state of the subjects while sitting, indicating that the remembrance is concurrent with the act of assembly, not a separate event.
chapters.translation:
I say: Know that the merit of assemblies of remembrance (majālis al-dhikr) is established by the unequivocal texts of the prophetic traditions (aḥādīth). The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: «ما جلس قوم مجلسا يذكرون الله عز وجل إلا حفت بهم الملائكة وغشيتهم الرحمة وذكرهم الله تعالى فيمن عنده» — 'No people sit in an assembly wherein they remember God, Mighty and Majestic, except that the angels surround them, mercy envelops them, and God, Exalted is He, mentions them among those who are with Him.' And he, peace be upon him, said: «ما من قوم اجتمعوا يذكرون الله تعالى لا يريدون بذلك إلا وجهه إلا ناداهم مناد من السماء قوموا مغفورا لكم قد بدلت لكم سيئاتكم حسنات» — 'There is no people who gather remembering God, Exalted is He, desiring thereby nothing but His Face, except that a caller from heaven calls out to them: "Arise, for you have been forgiven; your evil deeds have been exchanged for good deeds."' And he, peace be upon him, also said: «ما قعد قوم مقعدا لم يذكروا الله سبحانه وتعالى فيه ولم يصلوا على النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم ألا كان عليهم حسرة يوم القيامة» — 'No people sit in a place wherein they do not remember God, Glorified and Exalted is He, and do not send blessings upon the Prophet, peace be upon him, except that it will be a cause of regret (ḥasrah) for them on the Day of Resurrection.' And David, peace be upon him, said: 'My God, when You see me passing by the assemblies of those who remember You toward the assemblies of the heedless, break my leg before them—for that is a blessing You bestow upon me.'

And he, peace be upon him, said: «المجلس الصالح يكفر عن المؤمن ألفي ألف مجلس من مجالس السوء» — 'A righteous assembly expiates for the believer two thousand thousand assemblies of evil.' And Abū Hurayrah, may God be pleased with him, said: 'The inhabitants of heaven indeed behold the houses of the people of the earth in which the name of God, Exalted is He, is mentioned, just as the stars are beheld.' And Sufyān ibn ʿUyaynah, may God have mercy on him, said: 'When a people gather remembering God, Exalted is He, Satan and the world withdraw, and Satan says to the world: "Do you not see what they are doing?" The world replies: "Leave them, for when they disperse, I shall seize them by their necks and bring them to you."'

And it is related from Abū Hurayrah, may God be pleased with him, that he entered the marketplace and said: 'I see you here while the inheritance of the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, is being divided in the mosque.' So the people went to the mosque and left the marketplace, but they saw no inheritance. They said: 'O Abū Hurayrah, we saw no inheritance being divided in the mosque.' He said: 'Then what did you see?' They replied: 'We saw a people remembering God, Mighty and Majestic, and reciting the Quran.' He said: 'That is the inheritance of the Messenger of God, peace be upon him.' And al-Aʿmash related from Abū Ṣāliḥ, from Abū Hurayrah and Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī, from him, peace be upon him, that he said: «إن لله عز وجل ملائكة سياحين في الأرض فضلا عن كتاب الناس فإذا وجدوا قوما يذكرون الله عز وجل تنادوا هلموا بغيتكم فيجيئون فيحفون بهم إلى السماء فيقول الله تبارك وتعالى أي شيء تركتم عبادي يصنعونه فيقولون تركناهم يحمدونك ويمجدونك ويسبحونك فيقول الله تبارك وتعالى وهل رأوني فيقولون لا فيقول جل جلاله كيف لو رأوني فيقولون لو رأوك لكانوا أشد تسبيحا وتحميدا وتمجيدا فيقول لهم من أي شيء يتعوذون فيقولون من النار فيقول تعالى وهل رأوها فيقولون لا فيقول الله عز وجل فكيف لو رأوها فيقولون لو رأوها لكانوا أشد هربا منها وأشد نفورا فيقول الله عز وجل وأي شيء يطلبون فيقولون الجنة فيقول تعالى وهل رأوها فيقولون لا فيقول تعالى فكيف لو رأوها فيقولون لو رأوها لكانوا أشد عليها حرصا فيقول جل جلاله إني أشهدكم أني قد غفرت لهم فيقولون كان فيهم فلان لم يردهم إنما جاء لحاجة فيقول الله عز وجل هم القوم لا يشقى جليسهم» — 'Indeed, God, Mighty and Majestic, has angels who roam the earth, beyond the recording scribes of people. When they find a people remembering God, Mighty and Majestic, they call out to one another: "Come to your quest!" So they come and surround them, ascending to heaven. Then God, Blessed and Exalted is He, says: "What did you leave My servants doing?" They reply: "We left them praising You, magnifying You, and glorifying You." God, Blessed and Exalted is He, says: "Have they seen Me?" They say: "No." He, Glorious is His Majesty, says: "How would it be if they had seen Me?" They say: "If they had seen You, they would be more intense in glorification, praise, and magnification." He says to them: "From what do they seek refuge?" They say: "From the Fire." He, Exalted is He, says: "Have they seen it?" They say: "No." God, Mighty and Majestic, says: "How would it be if they had seen it?" They say: "If they had seen it, they would flee from it more intensely and be more averse to it." God, Mighty and Majestic, says: "And what do they seek?" They say: "Paradise." He, Exalted is He, says: "Have they seen it?" They say: "No." He, Exalted is He, says: "How would it be if they had seen it?" They say: "If they had seen it, they would be even more eager for it." He, Glorious is His Majesty, says: "I call you to witness that I have forgiven them." They say: "Among them was so-and-so who did not intend them; he only came for a need." God, Mighty and Majestic, says: "They are a people whose companion is not wretched."'

قال صلى الله عليه وسلم أفضل ما قلته أنا والنبيون من قبلي لا إله إلا
الله وحده لا شريك له (1) وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم من قال لا إله إلا الله
وحده لا شريك له له الملك وله الحمد وهو على كل شيء قدير كل يوم مائة مرة
كانت له عدل عشر رقاب وكتبت له مائة حسنة ومحيت عنه مائة سيئة وكانت له
حرزا من الشيطان يومه ذلك حتى يمسي ولم يأت أحد بأفضل مما جاء به إلا أحد
عمل أكثر من ذلك (2) وقال صلى  الله عليه وسلم ما من عبد توضأ فأحسن الوضوء
ثم رفع طرفه إلى السماء فقال أشهد أن لا إله إلا الله وحده لا شريك له
وأشهد أن محمدا عبده ورسوله إلا فتحت له أبواب الجنة يدخل من أيها شاء (3)
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم ليس على أهل لا إله إلا الله وحشة في قبورهم ولا
في نشورهم كأني أنظر إليهم عند الصيحة ينفضون رؤوسهم من التراب ويقولون
الحمد لله الذي أذهب عنا الحزن إن ربنا لغفور شكور (4) وقال صلى الله عليه
وسلم أيضا لأبي هريرة يا أبا هريرة إن كل حسنة تعملها توزن يوم القيامة إلا
شهادة أن لا إله إلا الله فإنها لا توضع في ميزان لأنها لو وضعت في ميزان
من قالها صادقا ووضعت السموات السبع والأرضون السبع وما فيهن كان لا إله
إلا الله أرجح من ذلك (5) وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم لو جاء قائل لا إله إلا
الله صادقا بقراب الأرض ذنوبا لغفر الله له ذلك (6) وقال صلى الله عليه
وسلم يا أبا هريرة لقن الموتى شهادة أن لا إله إلا الله فإنها تهدم الذنوب
هدما قلت يا رسول الله هذا للموتى فكيف للأحياء قال صلى الله عليه وسلم هي
أهدم وأهدم (7) وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم من قال لا إله إلا الله مخلصا دخل
الجنة (8) وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم لتدخلن الجنة كلكم إلا من أبى وشرد عن
الله عز وجل شراد البعير عن أهله فقيل يا رسول الله من الذي يأبى ويشرد عن
الله قال من لم يقل لا إله إلا الله (9) فأكثروا من قول لا إله إلا الله
قبل أن PageV01P297
يحال بينكم وبينها فإنها كلمة التوحيد وهي كلمة الإخلاص وهي كلمة التقوى
وهي كلمة طيبة وهي دعوة الحق وهي العروة الوثقى وهي ثمن الجنة وقال الله عز
وجل {هل جزاء الإحسان إلا الإحسان} فقيل الإحسان في الدنيا قول لا إله إلا
الله وفي الآخرة الجنة وكذا قوله تعالى {للذين أحسنوا الحسنى وزيادة} وروى
البراء بن عازب أنه صلى الله عليه وسلم قال من قال لا إله إلا الله وحده لا
شريك له له الملك وله الحمد وهو على كل شيء قدير عشر مرات كانت له عدل رقبة
أو قال نسمة (1) وروى عمرو بن شعيب عن أبيه عن جده أنه قال قال رسول الله
صلى الله عليه وسلم من قال في يوم مائتي مرة لا إله إلا الله وحده لا شريك
له له الملك وله الحمد وهو على كل شيء قدير لم يسبقه أحد كان قبله ولا
يدركه أحد بعده إلا من عمل بأفضل من عمله (2) وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم من
قال في سوق من الأسواق لا إله إلا الله وحده لا شريك له له الملك وله الحمد
يحيي ويميت وهو على كل شيء قدير كتب الله له ألف ألف حسنة ومحا عنه ألف الف
سيئة وبنى له بيتا في الجنة ويروى إن العبد إذا قال لا إله إلا الله أتت
إلى صحيفته فلا تمر على خطيئة إلى محتها حتى تجد حسنة مثلها فتجلس إلى
جنبها (3) وفي الصحيح عن أيوب عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم أنه قال من قال
لا إله إلا الله وحده لا شريك له له الملك وله الحمد وهو على كل شيء قدير
عشر مرات كان كمن أعتق أربعة أنفس من ولد إسماعيل صلى الله عليه وسلم (4)
وفي الصحيح أيضا عن عبادة بن الصامت عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم أنه قال
من تعار من الليل فقال لا إله إلا الله وحده لا شريك له له الملك وله الحمد
وهو على كل شيء قدير سبحان الله والحمد لله ولا إله إلا الله والله أكبر
ولا حول ولا قوة إلا بالله العلي العظيم ثم قال اللهم اغفر لي غفر له أو
دعا استجيب له فإن توضأ وصلى قبلت صلاته (5)
chapters.anchors:
- Root: هـ-ل-ل (h-l-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The root denotes the raising of the voice in proclamation; al-tahlīl is the utterance of "lā ilāha illā Allāh" — the verbal declaration that negates all false deities and affirms the One.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological terms, al-tahlīl is the verbal embodiment of tawḥīd (divine unity), the foundational confession that distinguishes faith (īmān) from unbelief (kufr), and the "word of sincerity" (kalimat al-ikhlāṣ).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literally, it is the act of proclaiming; metaphorically, it signifies the heart's purification from all associations (shirk) with God, making the tongue's utterance a true reflection of inner conviction.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Conditional Emphasis (al-Sharṭ wa al-Jawāb) — In constructions like "man qāla... kāna lahu," the protasis (condition) is followed by an apodosis (result) that is grammatically independent, emphasizing the guaranteed reward contingent upon the sincere act.
chapters.translation: I say: The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "The most excellent words that I and the prophets before me have uttered are: There is no god but Allah alone, with no partner." (1) And he, peace be upon him, said: "Whoever says, 'There is no god but Allah alone, with no partner; to Him belongs the dominion and to Him belongs all praise, and He is over all things omnipotent,' one hundred times each day, it will be for him the equivalent of freeing ten slaves, and one hundred good deeds will be recorded for him, and one hundred evil deeds will be erased from him, and it will be a protection for him from Satan for that day until evening; and no one will bring anything better than what he has brought, except one who has done more than that." (2) And he, peace be upon him, said: "No servant performs ablution and perfects his ablution, then raises his gaze to the sky and says, 'I bear witness that there is no god but Allah alone, with no partner, and I bear witness that Muhammad is His servant and His messenger,' except that the gates of Paradise are opened for him, and he enters through whichever of them he wishes." (3) And he, peace be upon him, said: "There is no loneliness upon the people of 'lā ilāha illā Allāh' in their graves, nor in their resurrection. As if I see them at the Blast, shaking the dust from their heads and saying, 'Praise be to Allah who has removed from us all sorrow; indeed, our Lord is Forgiving, Appreciative.'" (4) And he, peace be upon him, also said to Abū Hurayrah: "O Abū Hurayrah, every good deed you perform will be weighed on the Day of Resurrection, except the testimony that there is no god but Allah — for it will not be placed in the balance, because if it were placed in the balance of one who utters it truthfully, and the seven heavens and the seven earths and all that is in them were placed [on the other side], 'lā ilāha illā Allāh' would outweigh all of that." (5) And he, peace be upon him, said: "If one who utters 'lā ilāha illā Allāh' truthfully were to come with sins filling the earth, Allah would forgive him for that." (6) And he, peace be upon him, said: "O Abū Hurayrah, prompt the dying with the testimony that there is no god but Allah, for it demolishes sins utterly." I said: "O Messenger of Allah, this is for the dying — what about the living?" He, peace be upon him, said: "It is even more demolishing, and more demolishing." (7) And he, peace be upon him, said: "Whoever says 'lā ilāha illā Allāh' sincerely enters Paradise." (8) And he, peace be upon him, said: "You will all enter Paradise, except one who refuses and strays from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, as a camel strays from its people." It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, who is it that refuses and strays from Allah?" He said: "One who does not say 'lā ilāha illā Allāh.'" (9) So multiply your utterance of 'lā ilāha illā Allāh' before a barrier is placed between you and it — for it is the word of divine unity (tawḥīd), the word of sincerity (ikhlāṣ), the word of piety (taqwā), the goodly word (al-kalimah al-ṭayyibah), the call of truth (daʿwat al-ḥaqq), the firmest handhold (al-ʿurwah al-wuthqā), and the price of Paradise. And Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: {«Hal jazāʾ al-iḥsān illā al-iḥsān»} — "Is the reward of goodness anything but goodness?" (Q 55:60) — and it was said: goodness in this world is the utterance of 'lā ilāha illā Allāh,' and in the Hereafter it is Paradise. Likewise is His saying, Exalted is He: {«Lilladhīna aḥsanū al-ḥusnā wa ziyādah»} — "For those who do good is the best [reward] and more" (Q 10:26). And al-Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib narrated that he, peace be upon him, said: "Whoever says 'lā ilāha illā Allāh alone, with no partner; to Him belongs the dominion and to Him belongs all praise, and He is over all things omnipotent' ten times, it will be for him the equivalent of freeing a slave" — or he said, "a living soul." (1) And ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb narrated from his father, from his grandfather, that he said: The Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him, said: "Whoever says two hundred times in a day, 'lā ilāha illā Allāh alone, with no partner; to Him belongs the dominion and to Him belongs all praise, and He is over all things omnipotent,' no one before him will surpass him, and no one after him will overtake him, except one who does better than his deed." (2) And he, peace be upon him, said: "Whoever says in one of the marketplaces, 'lā ilāha illā Allāh alone, with no partner; to Him belongs the dominion and to Him belongs all praise; He gives life and causes death, and He is over all things omnipotent,' Allah will record for him a thousand thousand good deeds, and erase from him a thousand thousand evil deeds, and build for him a house in Paradise." And it is narrated that when a servant says 'lā ilāha illā Allāh,' it comes to his scroll [of deeds] and does not pass by any sin without erasing it, until it finds a good deed like it and sits beside it. (3) And in the Ṣaḥīḥ, from Ayyūb, from the Prophet, peace be upon him, that he said: "Whoever says 'lā ilāha illā Allāh alone, with no partner; to Him belongs the dominion and to Him belongs all praise, and He is over all things omnipotent' ten times, it is as if he freed four souls from the descendants of Ismāʿīl, peace be upon him." (4) And in the Ṣaḥīḥ also, from ʿUbādah ibn al-Ṣāmit, from the Prophet, peace be upon him, that he said: "Whoever wakes in the night and says, 'lā ilāha illā Allāh alone, with no partner; to Him belongs the dominion and to Him belongs all praise, and He is over all things omnipotent; glory be to Allah (subḥān Allāh), and praise be to Allah (al-ḥamdu lillāh), and there is no god but Allah (lā ilāha illā Allāh), and Allah is Greater (Allāhu akbar), and there is no might and no power except through Allah, the Exalted, the Magnificent (lā ḥawla wa lā quwwata illā billāh al-ʿaliyy al-ʿaẓīm)' — then says, 'O Allah, forgive me,' he will be forgiven; or if he supplicates, his supplication will be answered; and if he performs ablution and prays, his prayer will be accepted." (5)
