||| فضيلة الأوراد وبيان أن المواظبة عليها هي الطريق إلى الله تعالى

اعلم أن الناظرين بنور البصيرة علموا أنه لا نجاة إلا في لقاء الله تعالى
وأنه لا سبيل إلى اللقاء إلا بأن يموت العبد محبا لله تعالى وعارفا بالله
سبحانه
وأن المحبة والأنس لا تحصل إلا من دوام ذكر المحبوب والمواظبة عليه وأن
المعرفة به لا تحصل إلا بدوام الفكر فيه وفي صفاته وأفعاله وليس في الوجود
سوى الله تعالى  وأفعاله ولن يتيسر دوام الذكر والفكر إلا بوداع الدنيا
وشهواتها والاجتزاء منها بقدر البلغة والضرورة وكل ذلك لا يتم إلا باستغراق
أوقات الليل والنهار في وظائف الأذكار والأفكار والنفس لما جبلت عليه من
السآمة والملال لا تصبر على فن واحد من الأسباب المعينة على الذكر والفكر
بل إذا ردت إلى نمط واحد أظهرت الملال والاستثقال وأن الله تعالى لا يمل
حتى تملوا فمن ضرورة اللطف بها أن تروح بالتنقل من فن إلى فن ومن نوع إلى
نوع بحسب كل وقت لتغزر بالانتقال لذتها وتعظم باللذة رغبتها وتدوم بدوام
الرغبة مواظبتها فلذلك تقسم الأوراد قسمة مختلفة فالذكر والفكر ينبغي أن
يستغرقا جميع الأوقات أو أكثرها فإن النفس بطبعها مائلة إلى ملاذ الدنيا
فإن صرف العبد شطر أوقاته إلى تدبيرات الدنيا وشهواتها المباحة مثلا والشطر
الآخر إلى العبادات رجح جانب الميل إلى الدنيا لموافقتها الطبع إذ يكون
الوقت متساويا فأنى يتقاومان والطبع لأحدهما مرجح إذ الظاهر والباطن
يتساعدان على أمور الدنيا ويصفو في طلبها القلب ويتجرد وأما الرد إلى
العبادات فمتكلف ولا يسلم إخلاص القلب فيه وحضوره إلا في بعض الأوقات فمن
أراد أن يدخل الجنة بغير حساب فليستغرق أوقاته في الطاعة ومن أراد أن تترجح
كفة حسناته وتثقل موازين خيراته فليستوعب في الطاعة أكثر أوقاته فإن خلط
عملا صالحا وآخر سيئا فأمره مخطر ولكن الرجاء غير منقطع والعفو من كرم الله
منتظر فعسى الله تعالى أن يغفر له بجوده وكرمه فهذا ما انكشف للناظرين بنور
البصيرة فإن لم تكن من أهله فانظر إلى خطاب الله تعالى لرسوله واقتبسه بنور
الإيمان فقد قال الله تعالى لأقرب عباده إليه وأرفعهم درجة لديه {إن لك في
النهار سبحا طويلا واذكر اسم ربك وتبتل إليه تبتيلا} وقال تعالى {واذكر اسم
ربك بكرة وأصيلا ومن الليل فاسجد له وسبحه ليلا طويلا} وقال تعالى {وسبح
بحمد ربك قبل طلوع الشمس وقبل الغروب ومن الليل فسبحه وأدبار السجود} وقال
سبحانه {وسبح بحمد ربك حين تقوم ومن الليل فسبحه  وإدبار النجوم} وقال تعالى
{إن ناشئة الليل هي أشد وطأ وأقوم قيلا} وقال تعالى {ومن آناء الليل فسبح
وأطراف النهار لعلك ترضى} وقال عز وجل {وأقم الصلاة طرفي النهار وزلفا من
الليل أن الحسنات يذهبن السيئات} ثم انظر كيف وصف الفائزين من عباده وبماذا
وصفهم فقال تعالى {أم من هو قانت}
PageV01P330
{آناء الليل ساجدا وقائما يحذر الآخرة ويرجو رحمة ربه قل هل يستوي الذين
يعلمون والذين لا يعلمون} وقال تعالى {تتجافى جنوبهم عن المضاجع يدعون ربهم
خوفا وطمعا} وقال عز وجل {والذين يبيتون لربهم سجدا وقياما} وقال عز وجل
{كانوا قليلا من الليل ما يهجعون وبالأسحار هم يستغفرون} وقال عز وجل
{فسبحان الله حين تمسون وحين تصبحون} وقال تعالى {ولا تطرد الذين يدعون
ربهم بالغداة والعشي يريدون وجهه} فهذا كله يبين لك أن الطريق إلى تعالى
مراقبة الأوقات وعمارتها بالأوراد على سبيل الدوام
ولذلك قال صلى الله عليه وسلم أحب عباد الله إلى الله الذين يراعون الشمس
والقمر والأظلة لذكر الله تعالى (1) وقد قال تعالى {الشمس والقمر بحسبان}
وقال تعالى {ألم تر إلى ربك كيف مد الظل ولو شاء لجعله ساكنا ثم جعلنا
الشمس عليه دليلا ثم قبضناه إلينا قبضا يسيرا} وقال تعالى {والقمر قدرناه
منازل} وقال تعالى {وهو الذي جعل لكم النجوم لتهتدوا بها في ظلمات البر
والبحر} فلا تظنن أن المقصود من سير الشمس والقمر بحسبان منظوم مرتب ومن
خلق الظل والنور والنجوم أن يستعان بها على أمور الدنيا بل لتعرف بها
مقادير الأوقات فتشتغل فيها بالطاعات والتجارة للدار الآخرة يدلك عليه قوله
تعالى {وهو الذي جعل الليل والنهار خلفة لمن أراد أن يذكر أو أراد شكورا}
أي يخلف أحدهما الآخر ليتدارك في أحدهما ما فات في الآخر وبين أن ذلك للذكر
والشكر لا غير وقال تعالى {وجعلنا الليل والنهار آيتين فمحونا آية الليل
وجعلنا آية النهار مبصرة لتبتغوا فضلا من ربكم ولتعلموا عدد السنين
والحساب} وإنما الفضل المبتغى هو الثواب والمغفرة ونسأل الله حسن التوفيق
لما يرضيه
chapters.anchors:
- Root: و-ر-د (w-r-d)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The root denotes arriving at water, a place of watering, or a point of access; hence a "ward" (wird) is a portion of recitation or devotion assigned to a fixed time, like a scheduled arrival at a watering-place.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In the theological sense, the wird is the appointed portion of invocation (dhikr) and reflection (fikr) by which the servant arrives at the presence of God—an ordered discipline of approach (wurūd) to the Divine.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literally, "arriving at water" (ḥaqīqah); metaphorically (majāz), the assigned devotional portion that quenches the soul's thirst for nearness to God.
- Root: ب-ت-ل (b-t-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Severance, cutting off, or pure devotion; tabattul is the utter severance of oneself from worldly attachments for exclusive dedication to God.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In Quranic usage (e.g. {«وَتَبَتَّلْ إِلَيْهِ تَبْتِيلًا»}), it signifies the complete isolation of the heart for God alone, a total orientation of intention.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal severance of a limb or bond; metaphorical severance of all worldly concerns in devotional absorption.
- Root: ن-ش-أ (n-sh-')
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To arise, commence, or raise up; nāshi'ah al-layl is the night-time rising (for prayer), the hour when one arises from sleep.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The night vigil (tahajjud) as the most potent time for aligning the soul with the divine—its "treading" (waṭ') is firmer and its speech (qīl) more upright.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal "rising up"; metaphorically, the spiritual ascent of the soul in nocturnal devotion.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Taqdīm wa Ta'khīr (Fronting and Delaying) — In the verse {«إِنَّ لَكَ فِي النَّهَارِ سَبْحًا طَوِيلًا»}, the fronting of "for you" (laka) restricts the long "swimming" (sabḥ) to the day, implying the night is reserved for tabattul; likewise, the conditional structure "if... then" (fa-in... fa-) in the author's exhortations establishes a cause-effect syntactic bond.
chapters.translation:
I say: Know that those who gaze with the light of inner vision (nūr al-baṣīrah) have come to know that there is no deliverance save in the encounter with Allah Most High, and that there is no path to that encounter save that the servant die as a lover of Allah Most High and a knower of Allah, Glorified be He. And that love (maḥabbah) and intimacy (uns) are not attained except through the constant remembrance of the Beloved and perseverance therein, and that knowledge (maʿrifah) of Him is not attained except through constant reflection (fikr) upon Him, His attributes, and His acts—and there is nothing in existence save Allah Most High and His acts. And constant remembrance and reflection will not be facilitated except by bidding farewell to this world and its lusts, and being content therefrom with only the measure of sustenance and necessity. And all of that is not completed except by saturating the hours of night and day with the functions of invocations (adhkār) and reflections (afkār).

Now the soul, by its very constitution, is disposed to weariness (sa'āmah) and boredom (malāl); it does not endure patiently upon a single mode of the means that aid remembrance and reflection. Rather, when it is confined to one pattern, it displays boredom and aversion—and Allah Most High is not weary, but rather it is you who grow weary. Therefore, it is a necessity of gentleness (luṭf) toward the soul that it be refreshed by moving from one mode to another, and from one type to another, according to each time, so that its delight may be enriched by the transition, its desire may be magnified by the delight, and its perseverance may endure through the continuity of desire. For this reason, the litanies (awrād) are divided into varied portions.

Thus remembrance and reflection ought to saturate all times, or most of them. For the soul is by nature inclined toward the pleasures of this world. If the servant were to direct half of his times to the management of worldly affairs and its permissible lusts, for example, and the other half to acts of worship, the scale of inclination toward the world would outweigh, because it accords with nature—for when the time is equal, how can the two be balanced, while nature tips the scale for one of them? For the outward and the inward cooperate upon worldly matters, and the heart becomes pure and stripped in seeking them; whereas the return to acts of worship is burdensome, and the sincerity of the heart and its presence therein is not secured except in some moments.

So whoever desires to enter Paradise without reckoning, let him saturate all his times in obedience. And whoever desires that the scale of his good deeds be weighted and the balances of his virtues be heavy, let him occupy most of his times in obedience. For if he mixes a righteous deed with another evil one, his affair is perilous—yet hope is not cut off, and pardon from the generosity of Allah is awaited. Perhaps Allah Most High will forgive him through His bounty and generosity.

This is what has been unveiled to those who gaze with the light of inner vision. But if you are not among its people, then look to the address of Allah Most High to His Messenger and derive it by the light of faith. For Allah Most High said to the most beloved of His servants to Him and the highest of them in rank before Him: {«إِنَّ لَكَ فِي النَّهَارِ سَبْحًا طَوِيلًا وَاذْكُرِ اسْمَ رَبِّكَ وَتَبَتَّلْ إِلَيْهِ تَبْتِيلًا»} — "Indeed, for you in the day is prolonged swimming [in occupation], and remember the name of your Lord and devote yourself to Him with complete devotion." And He said: {«وَاذْكُرِ اسْمَ رَبِّكَ بُكْرَةً وَأَصِيلًا وَمِنَ اللَّيْلِ فَاسْجُدْ لَهُ وَسَبِّحْهُ لَيْلًا طَوِيلًا»} — "And remember the name of your Lord in the morning and the evening, and from the night prostrate to Him and glorify Him a long night." And He said: {«وَسَبِّحْ بِحَمْدِ رَبِّكَ قَبْلَ طُلُوعِ الشَّمْسِ وَقَبْلَ الْغُرُوبِ وَمِنَ اللَّيْلِ فَسَبِّحْهُ وَأَدْبَارَ السُّجُودِ»} — "And glorify the praise of your Lord before the rising of the sun and before its setting, and from the night glorify Him and at the ends of the prostrations." And He, Glorified be He, said: {«وَسَبِّحْ بِحَمْدِ رَبِّكَ حِينَ تَقُومُ وَمِنَ اللَّيْلِ فَسَبِّحْهُ وَإِدْبَارَ النُّجُومِ»} — "And glorify the praise of your Lord when you arise, and from the night glorify Him and at the departure of the stars." And He said: {«إِنَّ نَاشِئَةَ اللَّيْلِ هِيَ أَشَدُّ وَطْأً وَأَقْوَمُ قِيلًا»} — "Indeed, the rising of the night is severer in tread and more upright in speech." And He said: {«وَمِنْ آنَاءِ اللَّيْلِ فَسَبِّحْ وَأَطْرَافَ النَّهَارِ لَعَلَّكَ تَرْضَى»} — "And from the hours of the night glorify, and at the ends of the day, that you may be pleased." And He, Mighty and Majestic, said: {«وَأَقِمِ الصَّلَاةَ طَرَفَيِ النَّهَارِ وَزُلَفًا مِنَ اللَّيْلِ إِنَّ الْحَسَنَاتِ يُذْهِبْنَ السَّيِّئَاتِ»} — "And establish prayer at the two ends of the day and in the near hours of the night; indeed, good deeds remove evil deeds."

Then observe how He described the triumphant ones among His servants, and with what He described them. He said: {«أَمَّنْ هُوَ قَانِتٌ آنَاءَ اللَّيْلِ سَاجِدًا وَقَائِمًا يَحْذَرُ الْآخِرَةَ وَيَرْجُو رَحْمَةَ رَبِّهِ قُلْ هَلْ يَسْتَوِي الَّذِينَ يَعْلَمُونَ وَالَّذِينَ لَا يَعْلَمُونَ»} — "Is one who is devoutly obedient during the hours of the night, prostrating and standing, fearing the Hereafter and hoping for the mercy of his Lord... Say: Are those who know equal to those who do not know?" And He said: {«تَتَجَافَى جُنُوبُهُمْ عَنِ الْمَضَاجِعِ يَدْعُونَ رَبَّهُمْ خَوْفًا وَطَمَعًا»} — "Their sides forsake their beds, calling upon their Lord in fear and hope." And He, Mighty and Majestic, said: {«وَالَّذِينَ يَبِيتُونَ لِرَبِّهِمْ سُجَّدًا وَقِيَامًا»} — "And those who pass the night prostrating and standing before their Lord." And He, Mighty and Majestic, said: {«كَانُوا قَلِيلًا مِنَ اللَّيْلِ مَا يَهْجَعُونَ وَبِالْأَسْحَارِ هُمْ يَسْتَغْفِرُونَ»} — "They used to sleep but little of the night, and in the dawn hours they would seek forgiveness." And He, Mighty and Majestic, said: {«فَسُبْحَانَ اللَّهِ حِينَ تُمْسُونَ وَحِينَ تُصْبِحُونَ»} — "So glorify Allah when you enter the evening and when you enter the morning." And He said: {«وَلَا تَطْرُدِ الَّذِينَ يَدْعُونَ رَبَّهُمْ بِالْغَدَاةِ وَالْعَشِيِّ يُرِيدُونَ وَجْهَهُ»} — "And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord in the morning and the evening, desiring His Face."

All of this makes clear to you that the path to Allah Most High is the watchfulness over times (murāqabat al-awqāt) and their cultivation with litanies (awrād) in a perpetual manner. For this reason, he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "The most beloved of Allah's servants to Allah are those who observe the sun, the moon, and the shadows for the remembrance of Allah Most High." And He said: {«الشَّمْسُ وَالْقَمَرُ بِحُسْبَانٍ»} — "The sun and the moon are by precise calculation." And He said: {«أَلَمْ تَرَ إِلَى رَبِّكَ كَيْفَ مَدَّ الظِّلَّ وَلَوْ شَاءَ لَجَعَلَهُ سَاكِنًا ثُمَّ جَعَلْنَا الشَّمْسَ عَلَيْهِ دَلِيلًا ثُمَّ قَبَضْنَاهُ إِلَيْنَا قَبْضًا يَسِيرًا»} — "Have you not seen how your Lord stretched the shadow, and had He willed He would have made it still? Then We made the sun an indicator upon it, then We drew it to Ourselves with an easy drawing." And He said: {«وَالْقَمَرَ قَدَّرْنَاهُ مَنَازِلَ»} — "And the moon—We have measured for it stations." And He said: {«وَهُوَ الَّذِي جَعَلَ لَكُمُ النُّجُومَ لِتَهْتَدُوا بِهَا فِي ظُلُمَاتِ الْبَرِّ وَالْبَحْرِ»} — "And it is He who made for you the stars that you may be guided by them in the darknesses of land and sea."

Do not suppose that the purpose of the sun's and moon's course by precise, ordered calculation, and of the creation of shadow, light, and stars, is merely that they be used for worldly affairs. Rather, it is that by them the measures of times may be known, so that one may occupy them with acts of obedience and trade for the abode of the Hereafter. That is indicated to you by His saying: {«وَهُوَ الَّذِي جَعَلَ اللَّيْلَ وَالنَّهَارَ خِلْفَةً لِمَنْ أَرَادَ أَنْ يَذَّكَّرَ أَوْ أَرَادَ شُكُورًا»} — "And it is He who made the night and the day alternate for whoever desires to remember or desires gratitude"—that is, one succeeds the other, so that what was missed in one may be made up in the other. And He made clear that this is for remembrance and gratitude, and nothing else. And He said: {«وَجَعَلْنَا اللَّيْلَ وَالنَّهَارَ آيَتَيْنِ فَمَحَوْنَا آيَةَ اللَّيْلِ وَجَعَلْنَا آيَةَ النَّهَارِ مُبْصِرَةً لِتَبْتَغُوا فَضْلًا مِنْ رَبِّكُمْ وَلِتَعْلَمُوا عَدَدَ السِّنِينَ وَالْحِسَابَ»} — "And We made the night and the day two signs, and We erased the sign of the night and made the sign of the day visible, that you may seek bounty from your Lord and that you may know the number of years and the reckoning." And the bounty sought is none other than reward and forgiveness. And we ask Allah for good success (tawfīq) in what pleases Him.

chapters.title_en: Exposition of the Enumeration of the Daily Liturgies (Awrād) and Their Ordering
chapters.arabic_text:
||| بيان أعداد الأوراد وترتيبها

اعلم أن أوراد النهار سبعة فما بين طلوع الصبح إلى طلوع قرص الشمس ورد
وما بين طلوع الشمس إلى الزوال وردان وما بين الزوال إلى وقت العصر وردان
وما بين العصر إلى المغرب وردان والليل ينقسم إلى أربعة أوراد وردان من
المغرب إلى وقت نوم الناس ووردان من النصف الأخير من الليل إلى طلوع الفجر
فلنذكر فضيلة كل ورد ووظيفته وما يتعلق به
فالورد الأول ما بين طلوع الصبح إلى طلوع الشمس وهو وقت شريف ويدل على
شرفه وفضله إقسام الله تعالى به إذ قال {والصبح إذا تنفس} وقدحه به إذ قال
{فالق الإصباح} وقال تعالى {قل أعوذ برب الفلق} وإظهاره القدرة بقبض الظل
فيه إذ قال تعالى {ثم قبضناه إلينا قبضا يسيرا} وهو وقت قبض ظل الليل ببسط
نور الشمس وإرشاده الناس إلى التسبيح فيه بقوله تعالى {فسبحان الله حين
تمسون وحين تصبحون} وبقوله تعالى فسبح بحمد ربك قبل طلوع الشمس وقبل غروبها
وقوله عز وجل {ومن آناء الليل فسبح وأطراف النهار لعلك ترضى} وقوله تعالى
{واذكر اسم ربك بكرة وأصيلا}
فأما ترتيبه فليأخذ من وقت انتباهه من النوم فإذا انتبه فينبغي أن يبتدىء
بذكر الله تعالى فيقول الحمد لله الذي أحيانا بعد ما أماتنا وإليه النشور
إلى آخر الأدعية والآيات التي ذكرناها في دعاء الاستيقاظ من كتاب الدعوات
PageV01P331
وليلبس ثوبه وهو في الدعاء وينوي به ستر عورته امتثالا لأمر الله تعالى
واستعانة به على عبادته من غير قصد رياء ولا رعونة ثم يتوجه إلى بيت الماء
إن كان به حاجة إلى بيت الماء ويدخل أولا رجله اليسرى ويدعو بالأدعية التي
ذكرناها فيه في كتاب الطهارة عند الدخول والخروج ثم يستاك على السنة كما
سبق ويتوضأ مراعيا لجميع السنن والأدعية التي ذكرناها في الطهارة فإنا إنما
قدمنا آحاد العبادات لكي نذكر في هذا الكتاب وجه التركيب والترتيب فقط فإذا
فرغ من الوضوء صلى ركعتي الفجر أعني السنة في منزله (1) كذلك كان يفعل رسول
الله صلى  الله عليه وسلم ويقرأ بعد الركعتين سواء أداهما في البيت أو
المسجد الدعاء الذي رواه ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما ويقول اللهم إني أسألك
رحمة من عندك تهدي بها قلبي إلا آخر الدعاء (2) ثم يخرج من البيت متوجها
إلى المسجد ولا ينسى دعاء الخروج إلى المسجد لا يسعى إلى الصلاة سعيا بل
يمشي وعليه السكينة والوقار (3) كما ورد به الخبر ولا يشبك بين أصابعه
ويدخل المسجد ويقدم رجله اليمنى ويدعو بالدعاء المأثور لدخول المسجد (4) ثم
يطلب من المسجد الصف الأول إن وجد متسعا ولا يتخطى رقاب الناس ولا يزاحم
كما سبق ذكره في كتاب الجمعة ثم يصلي ركعتي الفجر إن لم يكن صلاهما في
البيت ويشتغل بالدعاء المذكور بعدهما وإن كان قد صلى ركعتي الفجر صلى ركعتي
التحية وجلس منتظرا للجماعة والأحب التغليس بالجماعة فقد كان صلى الله عليه
وسلم يغلس بالصبح (5) ولا ينبغي أن يدع الجماعة في الصلاة عامة وفي الصبح
والعشاء خاصة فلهما زيادة فضل
فقد روى أنس بن مالك رضي الله عنه عن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم أنه
قال في صلاة الصبح من توضأ ثم توجه إلى المسجد ليصلي فيه الصلاة كان له بكل
خطوة حسنة ومحي عنه سيئة والحسنة بعشر أمثالها فإذا صلى ثم انصراف عند طلوع
الشمس كتب له بكل شعرة في جسده حسنة وانقلب بحجة مبرورة فإن جلس حتى يركع
الضحى كتب له بكل ركعة ألفا ألف حسنة ومن صلى العتمة فله مثل ذلك وانقلب
بعمرة مبرورة (6) وكان من عادة السلف دخول المسجد قبل طلوع الفجر
قال رجل من التابعين دخلت المسجد قبل طلوع الفجر فلقيت أبا هريرة قد
سبقني فقال لي يا ابن أخي لأي شيء خرجت من منزلك في هذه الساعة فقلت لصلاة
الغداة فقال أبشر فإنا كنا نعد خروجنا وقعودنا في المسجد في هذه الساعة
بمنزلة غزوة في سبيل الله تعالى (7) أو قال مع رسول الله صلى الله عليه
وسلم وعن علي رضي الله عنه أن النبي صلى الله  عليه وسلم طرقه وفاطمة رضي
الله عنهما وهما نائمان فقال ألا تصليان قال علي فقلت يا رسول الله إنما
أنفسنا بيد الله تعالى فإذا شاء أن يبعثها بعثها فانصرف صلى الله عليه وسلم
فسمعته وهو منصرف يضرب فخذه ويقول وكان الإنسان أكثر شيء جدلا (8) ثم ينبغي
أن يشتغل بعد ركعتي الفجر ودعائه بالاستغفار والتسبيح إلى أن تقام الصلاة
فيقول أستغفر الله الذي لا إله إلا هو الحي القيوم وأتوب إليه سبعين مرة
PageV01P332
وسبحان الله والحمد لله ولا إله إلا الله والله أكبر مائة مرة ثم يصلي
الفريضة مراعيا جميع ما ذكرناه من الآداب الباطنة والظاهرة في الصلاة
والقدوة فإذا فرغ منها قعد في المسجد إلى طلوع الشمس في ذكر الله تعالى كما
سنرتبه فقد قال صلى الله عليه وسلم لأن أقعد في مجلسي أذكر الله تعالى فيه
من صلاة الغداة إلى طلوع الشمس أحب إلي من أن أعتق أربع رقاب (1) وروي أنه
صلى الله عليه وسلم كان إذا صلى الغداة قعد في مصلاه حتى تطلع الشمس وفي
بعضها ويصلي ركعتين (2) أي بعد الطلو
chapters.anchors:
- Root: و-ر-د (w-r-d)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The root denotes arriving at water, approaching a watering-place; hence a portion, turn, or appointed round of devotion.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In the spiritual path, the wird is the appointed portion of worship apportioned to a time-segment, marking the soul's approach to its Lord as to a source of life.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal usage is the approach to water; metaphorical (majāz) usage transfers this to the soul's approach to divine mercy through prescribed devotional acts.
- Root: ف-ج-ر (f-j-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Splitting, cleaving open; the dawn as the splitting of night's darkness.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The divine act of cleaving the dawn (falaq al-iṣbāḥ) signifies origination of light from darkness—a sign of God's creative power.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: the physical splitting of dawn; metaphorical: the emergence of spiritual illumination after the darkness of heedlessness.
- Root: ض-ح-و (ḍ-ḥ-w)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The spreading of the sun's light over the earth; the forenoon (ḍuḥā).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The time of full solar manifestation, used in the Qur'anic oath {«والضحى»} as a sign of divine beneficence.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: the sun's expansion above the horizon; metaphorical: the state of the soul when divine light fully manifests after the dawn of initial awakening.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of ʿAṭf al-Bayān (Appositional Coordination) — When enumerating the awrād, the temporal segments are coordinated as explanatory appositions, each defined by its boundary markers (from X to Y), requiring precise parsing of the time-intervals as non-verbal predicates of implicit nominal sentences.
chapters.translation:
Know that the liturgies (awrād) of the day are seven. Between the rising of dawn and the rising of the sun's disk is one wird. Between sunrise and the zenith (zawāl) are two awrād. Between the zenith and the time of ʿAṣr are two awrād. Between ʿAṣr and sunset (maghrib) are two awrād. The night is divided into four awrād: two from sunset to the time when people sleep, and two from the latter half of the night to the rising of dawn. Let us now mention the excellence (faḍīlah) of each wird, its prescribed function (waẓīfah), and what pertains to it.

As for the first wird—that between the rising of dawn and the rising of the sun—it is a noble time. Its nobility and excellence are indicated by God's swearing by it, for He said {«والصبح إذا تنفس»} [By the dawn when it breathes], and by His cleaving it, for He said {«فالق الإصباح»} [Cleaver of the dawn], and He said {«قل أعوذ برب الفلق»} [Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the dawn]. And His manifestation of power in contracting the shadow therein, for He said {«ثم قبضناه إلينا قبضا يسيرا»} [Then We contracted it to Us with an easy contraction]—this being the time of contracting the shadow of night by the spreading of the light of the sun. And His guidance of people to glorification (tasbīḥ) therein, by His saying {«فسبحان الله حين تمسون وحين تصبحون»} [So glory be to God when you enter the evening and when you enter the morning], and His saying {«فسبح بحمد ربك قبل طلوع الشمس وقبل غروبها»} [So glorify the praise of your Lord before the rising of the sun and before its setting], and His saying {«ومن آناء الليل فسبح وأطراف النهار لعلك ترضى»} [And in the hours of the night glorify, and at the ends of the day, that you may be pleased], and His saying {«واذكر اسم ربك بكرة وأصيلا»} [And remember the name of your Lord morning and evening].

As for its ordering: let him begin from the moment of his awakening from sleep. When he awakens, he should commence with the remembrance of God, saying: "Praise be to God who gave us life after He caused us to die, and to Him is the resurrection," up to the rest of the supplications and verses which we mentioned in the supplication of awakening in the Book of Supplications. And let him put on his garment while engaged in supplication, intending thereby the covering of his nakedness in obedience to God's command and seeking His aid upon His worship, without any intention of ostentation or vanity. Then let him proceed to the lavatory if he has need of it, entering with his left foot first, and uttering the supplications we mentioned therein in the Book of Purification upon entering and exiting. Then let him use the tooth-stick (siwāk) according to the Sunnah as previously mentioned, and perform the ablution (wuḍūʾ) observing all the Sunnas and supplications we mentioned in the Book of Purification—for we have only presented the individual acts of worship individually so that in this book we might mention the manner of composition and ordering alone. When he finishes the ablution, let him pray the two rakʿahs of Fajr—I mean the Sunnah—in his dwelling; thus did the Messenger of God ﷺ do. And after the two rakʿahs, whether he performs them in the house or the mosque, let him recite the supplication narrated by Ibn ʿAbbās (may God be pleased with them both), saying: "O God, I ask You for mercy from Your presence with which You guide my heart..." to the end of the supplication. Then let him exit the house heading toward the mosque, not forgetting the supplication of exiting to the mosque. Let him not hasten to the prayer with rapid running, but rather walk with tranquility and dignity, as reported in the tradition. And let him not interlace his fingers. Let him enter the mosque, advancing his right foot, and utter the transmitted supplication for entering the mosque. Then let him seek the first row in the mosque if he finds space, and let him not step over people's necks nor jostle, as previously mentioned in the Book of Friday. Then let him pray the two rakʿahs of Fajr if he had not prayed them at home, and occupy himself with the aforementioned supplication after them. If he had already prayed the two rakʿahs of Fajr, let him pray the two rakʿahs of greeting (taḥiyyah) and sit awaiting the congregation. And it is beloved to perform the congregational prayer in the darkness of early dawn (taghlīs), for the Prophet ﷺ used to pray the morning prayer in the darkness of dawn. And he should not abandon the congregational prayer in general, and especially in the morning (Ṣubḥ) and evening (ʿIshāʾ) prayers, for they have additional excellence.

It has been narrated that Anas ibn Mālik (may God be pleased with him) reported from the Messenger of God ﷺ that he said concerning the morning prayer: "Whoever performs ablution, then sets out to the mosque to pray therein, has for every step a good deed, and an evil deed is erased from him, and the good deed is multiplied tenfold. Then when he prays and departs at sunrise, there is written for him for every hair of his body a good deed, and he returns with an accepted pilgrimage (ḥajjah mabrūrah). If he sits until he prays the forenoon (ḍuḥā), there is written for him for every rakʿah a thousand thousand good deeds. And whoever prays the night prayer (ʿAtamah) has the like of that, and returns with an accepted minor pilgrimage (ʿumrah mabrūrah)." And it was the custom of the Salaf to enter the mosque before the rising of dawn.

A man of the Tābiʿīn said: "I entered the mosque before dawn and found Abū Hurayrah had preceded me. He said to me: 'O son of my brother, for what purpose did you leave your dwelling at this hour?' I said: 'For the morning prayer.' He said: 'Rejoice, for we used to count our going out and our sitting in the mosque at this hour as equivalent to a campaign (ghazwah) in the path of God.'" Or he said: "with the Messenger of God ﷺ." And it is narrated from ʿAlī (may God be pleased with him) that the Prophet ﷺ came upon him and Fāṭimah (may God be pleased with them both) while they were sleeping, and said: "Will you not pray?" ʿAlī said: "I said: O Messenger of God, our souls are in the hand of God; when He wills to send them forth, He sends them forth." So the Prophet ﷺ turned away, and I heard him as he was departing striking his thigh and saying: {«وكان الإنسان أكثر شيء جدلا»} [And man is the most disputatious of things].

Then after the two rakʿahs of Fajr and his supplication, he should occupy himself with seeking forgiveness (istighfār) and glorification (tasbīḥ) until the prayer is established. Let him say: "I seek forgiveness of God, there is no god but He, the Living, the Self-Subsisting, and I repent to Him" seventy times. And "Glory be to God, and praise be to God, and there is no god but God, and God is Greater" one hundred times. Then let him pray the obligatory prayer, observing all that we have mentioned of the inward and outward etiquettes in prayer and in following the imam. When he finishes it, let him sit in the mosque until sunrise in the remembrance of God, as we shall order it. For the Prophet ﷺ said: "That I should sit in my place of prayer remembering God from the morning prayer until sunrise is more beloved to me than freeing four slaves." And it is narrated that he ﷺ, when he prayed the morning prayer, would sit in his place of prayer until the sun rose, and in some narrations, "and he would pray two rakʿahs"—that is, after sunrise. And there has come regarding the excellence of that what cannot be enumerated. Al-Ḥasan narrated that the Messenger of God ﷺ, in what he would mention of his Lord's mercy, said: "He said: O son of Adam, remember Me for an hour after the dawn prayer and an hour after the ʿAṣr prayer, and I will suffice you for what is between them."

Since the excellence of this has become manifest, let him sit and not speak until sunrise. Rather, his function until sunrise should be of four kinds: supplications (adʿiyah) and remembrances (adhkār) which he repeats, recitation of the Qur'an, and reflection (tafakkur).

As for the supplications: whenever he finishes his prayer, let him begin and say: "O God, bless Muḥammad and the family of Muḥammad and grant them peace. O God, You are Peace, and from You is peace, and to You returns peace. Revive us, our Lord, with peace, and admit us to the Abode of Peace. Blessed are You, O Possessor of Majesty and Honor." Then let him open the supplication with what the Messenger of God ﷺ used to open with, namely his saying: "Glory be to my Lord, the Most High, the Most Exalted, the Bestower. There is no god but God alone, with no partner; to Him belongs the dominion and to Him belongs praise; He gives life and causes death, and He is Living and dies not; in His hand is all good, and He is over all things Omnipotent. There is no god but God, Possessor of bounty, grace, and beautiful praise. There is no god but God, and we worship none but Him, making sincere for Him the religion, even though the disbelievers dislike it." Then let him proceed to the supplications we have presented in the third and fourth chapters of the Book of Supplications, supplicating with all of them if he is able, or memorizing from among them what he deems most fitting to his state, most tender to his heart, and lightest upon his tongue.

As for the repeated remembrances (adhkār), they are words regarding whose repetition there have come excellences which we shall not prolong by citing. The least that he should repeat each one is three or seven times; the most is one hundred or seventy; and the middle is ten. Let him repeat them according to his free time and the breadth of his hour. The excellence of the more is greater, and the middle is the most moderate—that he repeat them ten times, for that is more deserving of his perseverance upon it. The best of affairs is the most constant, even if little. And every function whose abundant performance cannot be maintained—its little with constancy is better and more powerfully effective upon the heart than its much with interruption. The example of the little constant is like drops of water falling upon the earth in succession, which produce in it a hollow—even if that fell upon stone. And the example of the much interrupted is water poured at once or in separate pourings with far-apart intervals, which shows no apparent trace.

These words are ten. The first: his saying "There is no god but God alone, with no partner; to Him belongs the dominion and to Him belongs praise; He gives life and causes death, and He is Living and dies not; in His hand is all good, and He is over all things Omnipotent." The second: his saying "Glory be to God, and praise be to God, and there is no god but God, and God is Greater, and there is no might and no power except with God, the Most High, the Magnificent." The third: his saying "Glory be to the Most Holy, the Most Holy, Lord of the angels and the Spirit." The fourth: his saying "Glory be to God the Magnificent and with His praise." The fifth: his saying "I seek forgiveness of God the Magnificent, there is no god but He, the Living, the Self-Subsisting, and I ask Him for repentance." The sixth: his saying "O God, there is no preventer of what You have given, nor giver of what You have withheld, and the possessor of wealth does not benefit from You his wealth." The seventh: his saying "There is no god but God, the King, the Truth, the Manifest." The eighth: his saying "In the name of God, with whose name nothing harms in the earth nor in the heaven, and He is the Hearing, the Knowing." The ninth: "O God, bless Muḥammad, Your servant, Your Prophet, and Your Messenger, the unlettered Prophet, and upon his family and companions, and grant them peace." The tenth: his saying "I seek refuge with God, the Hearing, the Knowing, from the accursed Satan. My Lord, I seek refuge with You from the whisperings of the devils, and I seek refuge with You, my Lord, lest they attend me."

These ten words—if he repeats each one ten times, he obtains one hundred repetitions. That is better than repeating a single remembrance one hundred times, for each of these words has an excellence of its own, and for the heart with each one there is a type of awakening and delight, and for the soul in transitioning from one word to another there is a type of rest and security from boredom.

As for recitation, it is recommended for him to recite a number of verses whose excellence has been reported in the traditions: that he recite Sūrat al-Ḥamd, and the Throne Verse (Āyat al-Kursī), and the conclusion of Sūrat al-Baqarah from His saying {«آمن الرسول»} [The Messenger believes], and {«شهد الله»} [God bears witness], and {«قل اللهم مالك الملك»} [Say: O God, Possessor of the Kingdom]—the two verses—and His saying {«لقد جاءكم رسول من أنفسكم»} [Indeed, there has come to you a Messenger from among yourselves] to its end, and His saying {«لقد صدق الله رسوله الرؤيا بالحق»} [Indeed, God has fulfilled for His Messenger the vision in truth] to its end, and His saying {«الحمد لله الذي لم يتخذ ولدا»} [Praise be to God who has not taken a son]—the verse—and five verses from the beginning of Sūrat al-Ḥadīd, and three from the end of Sūrat al-Ḥashr. And if he recites the ten "Musammiʿāt" (the tenfold glorifications) which al-Khaḍir (peace be upon him) gifted to Ibrāhīm al-Taymī (may God have mercy on him) and advised him to say morning and evening, then he has completed the excellence, and that gathers for him the excellence of the entirety of the aforementioned supplications.

It has been narrated from Karz ibn Wabrah (may God have mercy on him)—and he was among the abdāl—that he said: "A brother of mine from the people of Syria came to me and gifted me a gift, saying: 'O Karz, accept this gift from me, for it is an excellent gift.' I said: 'O my brother, who gifted this to you?' He said: 'Ibrāhīm al-Taymī gave it to me.' I said: 'Did you not ask Ibrāhīm who gave it to him?' He said: 'I was sitting in the courtyard of the Kaʿbah engaged in tahlīl, tasbīḥ, taḥmīd, and tamjīd, when a man came to me, greeted me, and sat to my right. I have not seen in my time anyone more handsome of face, nor better of garments, nor whiter, nor more fragrant than him. I said: O servant of God, who are you, and from where have you come? He said: I am al-Khaḍir. I said: For what purpose have you come to me? He said: I came to greet you and out of love for you in God, and I have a gift I wish to give you. I said: What is it? He said: That you say, before the rising of the sun and before its spreading upon the earth and before sunset: Sūrat al-Ḥamd, and {«قل أعوذ برب الناس»}, and {«قل أعوذ برب الفلق»}, and {«قل هو الله أحد»}, and {«قل يا أيها الكافرون»}, and the Throne Verse—each one seven times. And you say: Glory be to God, and praise be to God, and there is no god but God, and God is Greater—seven times. And you send blessings upon the Prophet ﷺ seven times. And you seek forgiveness for yourself, your parents, the believing men, and the believing women—seven times. And you say: O God, do with me and with them, immediately and later, in religion, this world, and the Hereafter, what is worthy of You, and do not do with us, O our Master, what we are worthy of; indeed, You are Forgiving, Forbearing, Generous, Noble, Kind, Merciful—seven times. And see that you do not abandon this morning and evening.' I said: 'I would love for you to tell me who gave you this great gift.' He said: 'Muḥammad ﷺ gave it to me.' I said: 'Tell me of its reward.' He said: 'When you meet Muḥammad ﷺ, ask him of its reward, for he will tell you.'"

Ibrāhīm al-Taymī mentioned that one day he saw in his dream as though the angels came and carried him until they admitted him into Paradise, and he saw what was in it, and he described great matters of what he saw in Paradise. He said: "I asked the angels, saying: For whom is this?" They said: "For the one who does like your deed." And he mentioned that he ate of its fruits and was given to drink of its wine. He said: "Then the Prophet ﷺ came to me, and with him seventy prophets and seventy ranks of angels, each rank like the distance between the east and the west. He greeted me and took my hand. I said: O Messenger of God, al-Khaḍir told me that he heard this ḥadīth from you. He said: 'Al-Khaḍir spoke truthfully, al-Khaḍir spoke truthfully. And everything he narrates is true, and he is the scholar of the people of the earth, and he is the chief of the abdāl, and he is among the soldiers of God in the earth.' I said: O Messenger of God, whoever does this or acts upon it and does not see what I have seen in my dream—will he be given something of what I have been given? He said: 'By Him who sent me as a Prophet with the truth, the one who acts upon this—even if he does not see me and does not see Paradise—indeed, all the major sins (kabāʾir) he has committed are forgiven him, and God removes from him His anger and His wrath, and He commands the angel of the left not to record against him any sin of evil deeds for a year. By Him who sent me as a Prophet with the truth, none acts upon this except one whom God created fortunate, and none abandons it except one whom God created wretched.'"

And Ibrāhīm al-Taymī remained four months without eating or drinking—perhaps this was after this vision.

This is the function of recitation. If he adds to it something of what his wird of the Qur'an has reached, or confines himself to it, that is good—for the Qur'an encompasses the excellence of remembrance, reflection, and supplication whenever it is with contemplation, as we have mentioned its excellence and etiquettes in the chapter on recitation.

As for reflections (afkār), let that be one of his functions. The detailed account of what one reflects upon and its modality will come in the Book of Reflection from the Quarter of the Deliverers. But its comprehensive summary returns to two branches. The first: that he reflect upon what benefits him in his spiritual practice (muʿāmalah)—that he call his soul to account for its past shortcomings, and arrange his functions for the day before him, and deliberate upon repelling the distractions and obstacles that divert him from good, and recall his negligence and what defect creeps into his deeds so that he may rectify it, and bring to his heart the sound intentions of his deeds concerning himself and his dealings with the Muslims. The second branch: that he reflect upon what benefits him in the science of unveiling (ʿilm al-mukāshafah)—that he reflect once upon the blessings of God and the succession of His instruments, outward and inward, so that his knowledge of them increases and his gratitude for them multiplies; or upon His punishments and retributions, so that his knowledge of the power of the Divine and His self-sufficiency increases, and his fear of them increases. Each of these matters has many branches, and reflection upon them expands for some creatures without others. We shall only complete that in the Book of Reflection.

Whenever reflection is facilitated, it is the noblest of acts of worship, for in it is the meaning of remembrance of God plus two additional matters. One is the increase of knowledge (maʿrifah), for reflection is the key to knowledge and unveiling. The second is the increase of love (maḥabbah), for the heart loves none but one whose grandeur it believes in, and the grandeur of God and His majesty are not unveiled except through knowledge of His attributes, knowledge of His power, and the wonders of His acts. Thus from reflection comes knowledge, from knowledge comes veneration (taʿẓīm), and from veneration comes love. Remembrance also begets intimacy (uns), which is a type of love, but the love whose cause is knowledge is stronger, more firmly established, and greater. The proportion of the love of the knower (ʿārif) to the intimacy of the rememberer without complete insight is like the proportion of the passion of one who has beheld the beauty of a person with his eye and witnessed the excellence of his character, his deeds, his virtues, and his praiseworthy qualities by experience—to the intimacy of one who has had repeated to his hearing the description of a person absent from his eye as being beautiful in form and character in an absolute manner, without detailing the aspects of beauty in them. Thus his love for him is not like the love of the beholder. And news is not like direct vision (muʿāyanah).

Thus the servants who are constant upon the remembrance of God with heart and tongue, who affirm what the messengers brought with traditional faith (īmān taqlīdī)—with them there is nothing of the beautiful attributes of God except beautiful matters they have believed through affirmation of their description to them. But the knowers (ʿārifūn) are those who have witnessed that majesty and beauty with the eye of inner insight (baṣīrah), which is stronger than outward sight—for no one has encompassed the reality of His majesty and beauty, for that is not possible for any of creation. Rather, each one has witnessed according to what has been lifted of the veil for him. There is no end to the beauty of the presence of Lordship nor to its veils. The number of its veils that deserve to be called "light"—and he who reaches them nearly thinks he has completed his arrival at the Origin—is seventy veils. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed, God has seventy veils of light; were He to uncover them, the glories of His Face would burn everything that His sight perceives."

And those veils are also ordered, and those lights are differentiated in rank like the differentiation of the sun, the moon, and the stars. The smallest of them appears first, then what follows it. Upon this, some of the Sufis based the degrees of what appeared to Abraham the Friend (peace be upon him) in his ascent, when He said {«فلما جن عليه الليل»} [When the night covered him]—that is, the matter darkened upon him—{«رأى كوكبا»} [he saw a star]—that is, he reached a veil of the veils of light, and expressed it as a star. What is meant is not these luminous bodies, for even the common folk are not unaware that Lordship is not befitting of bodies; rather, they perceive that with the very beginnings of their reflection. So what does not mislead the common folk does not mislead the Friend (peace be upon him). And the veils called "lights"—what is meant by them is not the light perceived by sight, but rather what is meant by His saying {«الله نور السموات والأرض مثل نوره كمشكاة فيها مصباح»} [God is the light of the heavens and the earth; the likeness of His light is as a niche wherein is a lamp]—the verse.

Let us pass beyond these meanings, for they are outside the science of spiritual practice (ʿilm al-muʿāmalah), and their realities are not reached except by unveiling (kashf) that follows pure reflection. Few are those for whom its door opens. What is facilitated for the masses of creatures is reflection upon what benefits in the science of spiritual practice—and that too is abundant in benefit and great in utility.

These four functions—namely supplication, remembrance, recitation, and reflection—should be the function of the seeker (murīd) after the dawn prayer; indeed, in every wird after finishing the function of prayer. There is no function after prayer other than these four. And he is strengthened upon that by taking his weapon and his shield—and fasting is the shield (junnah) that narrows the passages of the accursed enemy who diverts him from the path of right guidance. There is no prayer after the rising of dawn other than the two rakʿahs of Fajr and the obligatory morning prayer until sunrise. The Messenger of God ﷺ and his companions (may God be pleased with them) used to occupy themselves at this time with remembrances—and that is more appropriate—until sleep overcomes him before the obligatory prayer, and he is not repelled except by prayer; so if he prays for that, there is no harm.

The second wird: that between sunrise and the mid-forenoon (ḍaḥwah). By "ḍaḥwah" I mean the midpoint between sunrise and the zenith—that is, after the passage of three hours of the day, if the day is reckoned as twelve hours. This is the fourth [of the day]. In this quarter of the day there are two additional functions. The first is the forenoon prayer (ṣalāt al-ḍuḥā), which we have mentioned in the Book of Prayer—that the preferred practice is to pray two rakʿahs at the time of brightness (ishrāq), that is, when the sun has spread and risen approximately half a spear's length; and to pray four, six, or eight when the young camels feel the heat of the sand (ramḍat al-fiṣāl) and the feet are scorched by the sun's heat. The time of the two rakʿahs is what God meant by His saying {«يسبحن بالعشي والإشراق»} [They glorify in the evening and at the brightness]—for it is the time of the sun's brightness, which is the appearance of its complete light by its rising above the level of the vapors and dusts upon the face of the earth, for these prevent its complete radiance. And the time of the four rakʿahs is the higher forenoon (al-ḍuḥā al-aʿlā), by which God swore, saying {«والضحى والليل إذا سجى»} [By the forenoon, and the night when it covers]. The Messenger of God ﷺ came out to his companions while they were praying at the time of brightness and called out with his loudest voice: "Indeed, the prayer of the penitent (awwābīn) is when the young camels feel the heat of the sand." Therefore we say: if one confines himself to a single time for prayer, this time is best for the forenoon prayer. Though the origin of excellence is obtained by praying between the two ends of the times of disapproval—that is, between the sun's rising by approximately half a spear and before the zenith at the hour of equinox. The name "ḍuḥā" applies to all of it. It is as though the two rakʿahs of ishrāq fall at the beginning of the time of permission for prayer and the end of disapproval, since the Prophet ﷺ said: "The sun rises and with it is the horn of Satan; when it rises high, he departs from it." The least of its rising is that it rise above the vapors and dust of the earth, and this is observed approximately.

The second function in this time: the acts of goodness pertaining to people that are customary in the early morning—visiting the sick, following funerals, assisting in righteousness and piety, attending a gathering of knowledge, and what runs in that course of fulfilling a Muslim's need and the like. If there is none of that, he returns to the four functions we have presented—supplications, remembrance, recitation, and reflection—and supererogatory prayers if he wishes, for they are disapproved after the morning prayer but are not disapproved now. Thus prayer becomes a fifth division of the functions of this time for whoever desires it. As for after the obligatory morning prayer, every prayer without a cause is disapproved. After the morning prayer, the beloved practice is to confine oneself to the two rakʿahs of Fajr and the greeting of the mosque, and not to occupy oneself with prayer but rather with remembrances, recitation, supplication, and reflection.

The third wird: from the mid-forenoon to the zenith. By "ḍaḥwah" I mean the midpoint and a little before it. Since after every three hours a prayer is commanded—when three hours after sunrise have elapsed, and before their passing, is the forenoon prayer; when another three hours pass, it is Ẓuhr; when another three pass, it is ʿAṣr; when another three pass, it is Maghrib—the station of the forenoon between the zenith and sunrise is like the station of ʿAṣr between the zenith and sunset, except that the forenoon was not made obligatory because it is a time when people are bent upon their occupations, so it was lightened for them. The fourth function in this time is the four divisions [already mentioned], with two matters added. One: occupation with earning a livelihood, managing one's sustenance, and attending the market. If he is a merchant, he should trade with truthfulness and trustworthiness; if he is a craftsman, with sincerity and compassion. And he should not forget the remembrance of God in all his occupations. And he should confine his earning to the measure of his need for his day, whenever he is able to earn each day his sustenance. When he obtains the sufficiency of his day, let him return to the house of his Lord and provision himself for his Hereafter—for the need for the provision of the Hereafter is more severe, and the enjoyment of it is more enduring. Thus his occupation with his earning is more important than seeking increase beyond the need of the hour. For it has been said: "The believer is not found except in three places: a mosque he frequents, a house that conceals him, or a need he cannot do without." And few know the measure of what is indispensable; rather, most people reckon as indispensable what they could do without—and that is because Satan promises them poverty and commands them to indecency, so they listen to him and amass what they do not eat out of fear of poverty. And God promises them forgiveness from Him and bounty, so they turn away from it and do not desire it.

The second matter: the midday nap (qaylūlah), which is a Sunnah by which one is aided in standing the night [in prayer], just as the pre-dawn meal (saḥūr) is a Sunnah by which one is aided in fasting the day. If he does not stand the night, but were he not to sleep he would not occupy himself with good—and perhaps he would mix with the people of heedlessness and converse with them—then sleep is more beloved for him if his vigor does not stir him to return to the remembrances and functions mentioned. For in sleep there is silence and safety. Some have said: "A time will come upon people when silence and sleep will be the best of their deeds." How many a worshiper has had sleep as his best state—that is, when he shows off in his worship and is not sincere in it—so how much more so the heedless sinner? Sufyān al-Thawrī (may God have mercy on him) said: "It used to please them, when they were free, to sleep, seeking safety." So if his sleep is with the intention of seeking safety and the intention of standing the night, his sleep is an act of drawing near (qurbah). But he should awaken before the zenith by the measure of preparing for prayer—the ablution and attending the mosque before the entry of the prayer time—for that is among the excellences of deeds. And if he does not sleep and does not occupy himself with earning, but occupies himself with prayer and remembrance, that is the best of the deeds of the day, for it is a time of people's heedlessness of God and their occupation with the cares of the world. A heart free for the service of its Lord at the time when servants turn away from His door is worthy that God should purify it and choose it for His nearness and knowledge. The excellence of that is like the excellence of reviving the night—for the night is a time of heedlessness through sleep, and this is a time of heedlessness through following passion and occupying oneself with the cares of the world.
