||| القسم الثاني في آداب حالة الأكل

وهو أن يبدأ ب بسم الله في أوله وب الحمد لله في أخره
ولو قال مع كل لقمة بسم الله فهو حسن حتى لا يشغله الشره عن ذكر الله
تعالى ويقول مع اللقمة الأولى بسم الله ومع الثانية بسم الله الرحمن ومع
الثالثة بسم  الله الرحمن الرحيم ويجهر به ليذكر غيره
ويأكل باليمنى ويبدأ بالملح ويختم به ويصغر اللقمة ويجود مضغها وما لم
يبتلعها لم يمد اليد إلى الأخرى فإن ذلك عجلة في الأكل وأن لا يذم مأكولا
كان صلى الله عليه وسلم لا يعيب مأكولا كان إذا أعجبه أكله وإلا تركه (3)
وأن يأكل مما يليه إلا الفاكهة فإن له أن يجيل يده فيها قال صلى الله
عليه وسلم كل مما يليك (4) حديث كان يدور على الفاكهة وقال ليس هو نوعا
واحدا أخرجه الترمذي وابن ماجه من حديث عكراش بن دويب وفيه وجالت يد رسول
الله صلى الله عليه وسلم في الطبق فقال يا عكراش كل من حيث شئت فإنه غير
لون واحد قال الترمذي غريب ورواه ابن حبان في الضعفاء (5) حديث النهي عن
قطع الخبز بالسكين رواه ابن حبان في الضعفاء من حديث أبي هريرة وفيه نوح
ابن أبي مريم وهو كذاب ورواه البيهقي في الشعب من حديث أم سلمة بسند ضعيف
(6)
ولا يوضع على الخبز قصعة ولا غيرها إلا ما يأكل به قال صلى الله عليه
وسلم أكرموا الخبز فإن الله تعالى أنزله من بركات السماء ولا يمسح يده
بالخبز
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم إذا وقعت لقمة أحدكم فليأخذها وليمط ما كان بها
من أذى ولا يدعها للشيطان ولا يمسح يده بالمنديل حتى يلعق أصابعه فإنه لا
يدري في أي طعامه البركة (7)
ولا ينفخ في الطعام الحار (8)
فهو منهي عنه بل يصبر إلى إن يسهل أكله ويأكل من التمر وترا سبعا أو إحدى
عشرة أو إحدى وعشرين أو ما اتفق ولا يجمع بين التمر والنوى في طبق ولا يجمع
في كفه بل يضع النواة من فيه على ظهر كفه ثم يلقيها وكذا كل ماله عجم وثفل
وأن لا يترك ما استرذله من الطعام ويطرحه في القصعة بل يتركه مع الثفل
حتى لا يلتبس على غيره فيأكله
وأن لا يكثر الشرب في أثناء الطعام إلا إذا غص بلقمة أو صدق عطشه فقد  قيل
إن ذلك مستحب في الطب وإنه دباغ المعدة
وأما الشرب فأدبه أن يأخذ الكوز بيمينه ويقول بسم الله ويشربه مصا لا عبا
قال صلى الله عليه وسلم PageV02P005
مصوا الماء مصا ولا تعبوه عبا فإنه الكباد من العب (1)
ولا يشرب قائما ولا مضطجعا فإنه صلى الله عليه وسلم نهى عن الشرب قائما
(2)
وروي أنه صلى الله عليه وسلم شرب قائما (3)
ولعله كان لعذر
ويراعي أسفل الكوز حتى لا يقطر عليه وينظر في الكوز قبل الشرب ولا يتجشأ
ولا يتنفس في الكوز بل ينحيه عن فمه بالحمد ويرده بالتسمية
وقد قال صلى الله عليه وسلم بعد الشرب الحمد لله الذي جعله عذبا فراتا
برحمته ولم يجعله ملحا أجاجا بذنوبنا (4)
والكوز وكل ما يدار على القوم يدار يمنة وقد شرب رسول الله صلى الله عليه
وسلم لبنا وأبو بكر رضي الله عنه عن شماله وأعرابي عن يمينه وعمر ناحيته
فقال عمر رضي الله عنه أعط أبا بكر فناول الأعرابي وقال الأيمن فالأيمن
ويشرب في ثلاثة أنفاس يحمد الله في أواخرها ويسمي الله في أوائلها ويقول في
آخر النفس الأول الحمد لله وفي الثاني رب العالمين وفي الثالث يزيد الرحمن
الرحيم فهذا قريب من عشرين أدبا في حالة الأكل والشرب دلت عليها الأخبار
والآثار
chapters.anchors:
- Root: أ-ك-ل (a-k-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is the act of consuming food; extends to tasting and partaking.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Denotes physical nourishment; metaphorically, the soul's reception of knowledge or divine grace.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) for mastication; metaphorical (majāz) for spiritual ingestion of wisdom.
- Root: ش-ر-ب (sh-r-b)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Drinking; sipping (maṣṣ) versus gulping (ʿabb) as distinct modes.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Physical hydration; symbolically, the quenching of spiritual thirst through divine remembrance.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for liquid intake; rhetorical contrast between measured sipping and hasty gulping.
- Root: ب-ر-ك-ة (b-r-k-h)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Blessing; abundance descending from the divine.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The hidden good (khayr) infused in creation, especially food.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for divine favor; metaphorical for the unseen locus of blessing in a meal.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Conditional Sequence (al-Sharṭ wa al-Jazāʾ) — The protasis (e.g., 'if a morsel falls') governs the apodosis ('let him take it'), requiring precise temporal ordering to convey legal and ethical imperatives.
chapters.translation:
The second section concerns the etiquette of the state of eating.

It is that one begins with «بسم الله» (In the name of Allah) at its commencement and concludes with «الحمد لله» (Praise be to Allah) at its end. If one says «بسم الله» with every morsel, that is virtuous, so that voracity does not distract him from the remembrance of Allah, the Exalted. He says with the first morsel «بسم الله», with the second «بسم الله الرحمن» (In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful), and with the third «بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم» (In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate), and he utters it audibly so that others may be reminded.

He eats with his right hand, begins with salt and concludes with it, makes the morsel small, and chews it thoroughly. As long as he has not swallowed it, he does not extend his hand to another [morsel], for that is haste in eating. He does not disparage any food — the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, never found fault with food; if it pleased him, he ate it, and if not, he left it (3).

He eats from what is before him, except fruit, for he may move his hand freely therein. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: «كل مما يليك» (Eat from what is before you) (4). A hadith is narrated that he used to circulate his hand over fruit and said, 'It is not of a single kind.' It was transmitted by al-Tirmidhī and Ibn Mājah from the hadith of ʿIkrimah ibn Dhuwayb, in which it is stated: 'The hand of the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, moved around the dish, and he said: O ʿIkrimah, eat from wherever you wish, for it is not of one color.' Al-Tirmidhī said it is gharīb (unfamiliar), and Ibn Ḥibbān narrated it among the weak narrations (5). The hadith prohibiting cutting bread with a knife was narrated by Ibn Ḥibbān among the weak narrations from the hadith of Abū Hurayrah, in which there is Nūḥ ibn Abī Maryam, who is a liar; al-Bayhaqī also narrated it in al-Shuʿab from the hadith of Umm Salamah with a weak chain (6).

One does not place upon the bread a bowl or anything else except what one eats with. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: «أكرموا الخبز فإن الله تعالى أنزله من بركات السماء» (Honor bread, for Allah, the Exalted, has sent it down from the blessings of heaven). He does not wipe his hand with bread. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: «إذا وقعت لقمة أحدكم فليأخذها وليمط ما كان بها من أذى ولا يدعها للشيطان ولا يمسح يده بالمنديل حتى يلعق أصابعه فإنه لا يدري في أي طعامه البركة» (When a morsel of one of you falls, let him take it, remove any harm that is upon it, and not leave it for Satan; and let him not wipe his hand with a napkin until he licks his fingers, for he does not know in which part of his food the blessing lies) (7).

He does not blow upon hot food (8), for that is prohibited; rather, he waits until it becomes easy to eat. He eats dates in odd numbers — seven, eleven, twenty-one, or whatever is convenient — and he does not combine dates and pits on a single dish, nor does he gather them in his palm. Rather, he places the pit from his mouth upon the back of his hand, then casts it away. Likewise, [he does] with everything that has a pit or residue. He does not leave what he deems inferior of the food and toss it into the bowl; rather, he leaves it with the residue, so that it is not confused for another who might eat it.

He does not drink excessively during the meal, except if he chokes on a morsel or his thirst becomes genuine, for it has been said that this is commendable in medicine and that it is a tanning of the stomach.

As for drinking, its etiquette is that he takes the vessel with his right hand, says «بسم الله», and drinks it by sipping (maṣṣ), not gulping (ʿabb). The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: «مصوا الماء مصا ولا تعبوه عبا فإنه الكباد من العب» (Sip water by sipping, and do not gulp it by gulping, for liver disease comes from gulping) (1). He does not drink standing or reclining, for the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, prohibited drinking while standing (2). It is narrated that he, peace and blessings be upon him, drank while standing (3), but perhaps that was due to an excuse.

He observes the bottom of the vessel so that nothing drips upon him, looks into the vessel before drinking, does not belch, and does not breathe into the vessel. Rather, he moves it away from his mouth with praise (al-ḥamd) and returns it with the tasmiyah (naming of Allah). The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said after drinking: «الحمد لله الذي جعله عذبا فراتا برحمته ولم يجعله ملحا أجاجا بذنوبنا» (Praise be to Allah who made it sweet and fresh by His mercy and did not make it salty and bitter due to our sins) (4).

The vessel, and everything circulated among a people, is passed to the right. The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, drank milk while Abū Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, was on his left, a Bedouin on his right, and ʿUmar was in his vicinity. ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: 'Give it to Abū Bakr,' but he handed it to the Bedouin and said: «الأيمن فالأيمن» (The rightmost, then the rightmost).

He drinks in three breaths, praising Allah at their ends and naming Allah at their beginnings. He says at the end of the first breath: «الحمد لله» (Praise be to Allah); at the second: «رب العالمين» (Lord of the worlds); and at the third, he adds: «الرحمن الرحيم» (The Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate). This amounts to nearly twenty etiquettes in the state of eating and drinking, as indicated by the reports (akhbār) and traditions (āthār).

chapters.title_en: The Third Section: What is Recommended After Eating

||| القسم الثالث ما يستحب بعد الطعام

وهو أن يمسك قبل الشبع ويلعق أصابعه ثم يمسح بالمنديل ثم يغسلها ويلتقط
فتات الطعام قال صلى الله عليه وسلم من أكل ما يسقط من المائدة عاش في سعة
وعوفي في ولده (5)
ويتخلل ولا يبتلع كل ما يخرج من بين أسنانه بالخلال إلا ما يجمع من أصول
أسنانه بلسانه أما المخرج بالخلال فيرميه وليتمضمض بعد الخلال ففيه أثر عن
أهل البيت عليهم السلام
وأن يلعق القصعة ويشرب ماءها
ويقال من لعق القصعة وغسلها وشرب ماءها كان له عتق رقبة
وأن التقاط الفتات مهور الحور العين وأن يشكر الله تعالى بقلبه على ما
أطعمه فيرى الطعام نعمة منه قال الله تعالى كلوا من طيبات  ما رزقناكم
واشكروا لله ومهما أكل حلالا قال الحمد لله الذي بنعمته تتم الصالحات وتنزل
البركات اللهم أطعمنا طيبا واستعملنا صالحا
وإن أكل شبهة فليقل الحمد لله على كل حال اللهم لا تجعله قوة لنا على
معصيتك ويقرأ بعد الطعام قل هو الله أحد ولإيلاف قريش
ولا يقوم عن المائدة حتى ترفع أولا فإن أكل طعام الغير فليدع له وليقل
اللهم أكثر خيره وبارك له فيما رزقته ويسر له أن يفعل فيه خيرا وقنعه بما
أعطيته واجعلنا وإياه من الشاكرين
وإن أفطر عند قوم فليقل أفطر عندكم الصائمون وأكل طعامكم الأبرار وصلت
عليكم الملائكة
وليكثر الاستغفار والحزن على ما أكل من شبهة ليطفيء بدموعه وحزنه حر
النار التي تعرض لها لقوله صلى الله عليه وسلم كل لحم نبت من حرام فالنار
أولى به (6) حديث القوم عند أكل اللبن اللهم بارك لنا فيما رزقتنا وزدنا
منه أخرجه أبو داود والترمذي وحسنه وابن ماجه من حديث ابن عباس إذا أكل
أحدكم طعاما فليقل اللهم بارك لنا فيه وأطعمنا خيرا منه ومن سقاه الله لبنا
فليقل اللهم بارك لنا فيه وزدنا منه //
فإن أكل غيره قال اللهم بارك لنا فيما رزقتنا وارزقنا خيرا PageV02P006
منه فذلك الدعاء مما خص به رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم اللبن لعموم
نفعه
ويستحب عقيب الطعام أن يقول الحمد لله الذي أطعمنا وسقانا وكفانا وآوانا
سيدنا ومولانا يا كافي من كل شيء ولا يكفى منه شيء أطعمت من جوع وآمنت من
خوف فلك الحمد آويت من يتم وهديت من ضلالة وأغنيت من عيلة فلك الحمد حمدا
كثيرا دائما طيبا نافعا مباركا فيه كما أنت أهله ومستحقه اللهم أطعمتنا
طيبا فاستعملنا صالحا واجعله عونا لنا عن طاعتك ونعوذ بك أن نستعين به على
معصيتك وأما غسل اليدين بالأشنان فكيفيته أن يجعل الأشنان في كفه اليسرى
ويغسل الأصابع الثلاث من اليد اليمنى أولا ويضرب أصابعه على الأشنان اليابس
فيمسح به شفتيه ثم ينعم غسل الفم بإصبعه ويدلك ظاهر أسنانه وباطنها  والحنك
واللسان ثم يغسل أصابعه من ذلك بالماء ثم يدلك ببقية الأشنان اليابس أصابعه
ظهرا وبطنا ويستغني بذلك عن إعادة الأشنان إلى الفم وإعادة غسله
chapters.anchors:
- Root: م-س-ك (masaka)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To hold, restrain, or grasp; to withhold onset
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Restraint from satiety as a discipline of the soul (riyāḍah) against appetitive excess
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal physical holding; metaphorical here for self-restraint before fullness
- Sībawayh Rule: ʿAṭf al-Bayān (Appositional Coordination) — Sequential verbs (yumsiku, yalʿaqu, yamṣaḥu, yaghsilu, yaltaqiṭu) are coordinated without conjunction to denote ordered, habitual praxis (sunan) rather than mere simultaneity.
chapters.translation:
I say: The third section concerns what is recommended after eating.

It is that one should withhold before satiety, lick his fingers, then wipe them with a napkin, then wash them, and pick up the crumbs of food that have fallen. The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said: {«Whoever eats what falls from the table shall live in abundance and his offspring shall be preserved from affliction»}.

He should also use a toothpick (khilāl), but not swallow whatever comes out from between his teeth by means of the toothpick — except what he gathers from the roots of his teeth with his tongue. As for what is extracted by the toothpick, he should discard it. And let him rinse his mouth (maḍmaḍah) after using the toothpick, for there is a tradition (athar) concerning this from the People of the House (Ahl al-Bayt), peace be upon them.

And he should lick the bowl and drink its water. It is said: Whoever licks the bowl, washes it, and drinks its water, it is for him as the emancipation of a slave.

And it is recommended to pick up the crumbs, for it is said they are the dowries (muhūr) of the Ḥūr al-ʿAyn. And he should thank Allah the Exalted in his heart for what He has fed him, so that he perceives the food as a blessing from Him. Allah the Exalted said: {«Eat of the good things We have provided you, and be grateful to Allah»} (Q 2:172).

Whenever he eats what is lawful (ḥalāl), let him say: "Praise be to Allah, by whose grace good deeds are perfected and blessings descend. O Allah, feed us with what is good and employ us in what is righteous."

And if he eats something doubtful (shubhah), let him say: "Praise be to Allah in every state. O Allah, do not make it a strength for us in disobeying You." And after eating, let him recite {«Say: He is Allah, the One»} (Q 112:1) and {«For the covenant of the Quraysh»} (Q 106:1).

And he should not rise from the table until it is lifted up first. And if he eats the food of another, let him supplicate for him and say: "O Allah, increase his good, bless him in what You have provided him, make it easy for him to do good therein, suffice him with what You have given him, and make us and him among the thankful."

And if he breaks his fast (ifṭār) with a people, let him say: "May the fasting ones break their fast with you, may the righteous eat your food, and may the angels send blessings upon you."

And let him multiply seeking forgiveness (istighfār) and sorrow over what he has eaten of doubtful substance, so that by his tears and his grief he may extinguish the heat of the Fire that he has exposed himself to — for the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said: {«Every flesh that has grown from what is unlawful, the Fire is more deserving of it»}.

Regarding the supplication of a people when eating milk: "O Allah, bless us in what You have provided us, and increase us from it." This was transmitted by Abū Dāwūd, al-Tirmidhī (who deemed it good), and Ibn Mājah, from the ḥadīth of Ibn ʿAbbās: "When one of you eats food, let him say: 'O Allah, bless us in it and feed us with what is better than it.' And whoever is given milk to drink by Allah, let him say: 'O Allah, bless us in it and increase us from it.'"

And if he eats something other than milk, let him say: "O Allah, bless us in what You have provided us, and provide us with what is better than it." For this supplication is something particular to the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) regarding milk, due to the generality of its benefit.

And it is recommended after food to say: "Praise be to Allah who fed us, gave us drink, sufficed us, and sheltered us. Our Master and our Lord, O Sufficer of everything, from whom nothing is sufficed. You fed us from hunger, gave us security from fear, so to You is praise. You sheltered the orphan, guided from error, and enriched from poverty, so to You is praise — abundant, perpetual, good, beneficial, and blessed in it, as is befitting of You and due to You. O Allah, You have fed us with what is good, so employ us in what is righteous, make it an aid for us in obeying You, and we seek refuge in You from using it in disobeying You."

As for washing the hands with cleansing ash (ushnān), its method is that one places the ushnān in his left palm, washes the three fingers of the right hand first, strikes his fingers upon the dry ushnān, and wipes his lips with it. Then he thoroughly washes his mouth with his finger, rubbing the outer and inner surfaces of his teeth, the palate, and the tongue. Then he washes his fingers from that with water, and then rubs with the remainder of the dry ushnān his fingers, both back and palm — thereby dispensing with returning the ushnān to the mouth and re-washing it.

|| الباب الثاني فيما يزيد بسبب الاجتماع والمشاركة في الأكل وهي سبعة

الأول أن لا يبتدئ بالطعام ومعه من يستحق التقديم بكبر سن أو زيادة فضل
إلا أن يكون هو المتبوع والمقتدى به فحينئذ ينبغي أن لا يطول عليهم
الانتظار إذا اشرأبوا للأكل واجتمعوا له
الثاني أن لا يسكتوا على الطعام فإن ذلك من سيرة العجم ولكن يتكلمون
بالمعروف ويتحدثون بحكايات الصالحين في الأطعمة وغيرها
الثالث أن يرفق برفيقه في القصعة فلا يقصد أن يأكل زيادة على ما يأكله
فإن ذلك حرام إن لم يكن موافقا لرضا رفيقه مهما كان الطعام مشتركا
بل ينبغي أن يقصد الإيثار ولا يأكل تمرتين في دفعة إلا إذا فعلوا ذلك أو
استأذنهم
فإن قلل رفيقه نشطه ورغبه في الأكل وقال له كل ولا يزيد في قوله كل على
ثلاث مرات فإن ذلك إلحاح وإفراط
كان رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم إذا خوطب في شيء ثلاثا لم يراجع بعد
ثلاث
حديث كان إذا خوطب في شيء ثلاثا لم يراجع بعد ثلاث أخرجه أحمد من حديث
جابر في حديث طويل ومن حديث أبي حدرد أيضا وإسنادهما حسن (1) حديث كان يكرر
الكلمة ثلاثا أخرجه البخاري من حديث أنس كان يعيد الكلمة ثلاثا //
فليس من الأدب الزيادة عليه
فأما الحلف عليه بالأكل فممنوع قال الحسن بن علي رضي الله عنهما الطعام
أهون من أن يحلف عليه
الرابع أن لا يحوج رفيقه إلى أن يقول له كل
قال بعض الأدباء أحسن الآكلين أكلا من لا يحوج صاحبه إلى أن يتفقده في
الأكل وحمل عن أخيه مؤنة القول
ولا ينبغي أن يدع شيئا مما يشتهيه لأجل نظر الغير إليه فإن ذلك تصنع بل
يجري على المعتاد ولا ينقص من عادته شيئا في الوحدة ولكن يعود نفسه حسن
الأدب في الوحدة حتى لا يحتاج إلى التصنع  عند الاجتماع
نعم لو قلل من أكله إيثارا لإخوانه ونظرا لهم عند الحاجة إلى ذلك فهو حسن
وإن زاد في الأكل على نية المساعدة وتحريك نشاط القوم في الأكل فلا بأس به
بل هو حسن وكان ابن المبارك يقدم فاخر الرطب إلى إخوانه ويقول من أكل أكثر
أعطيته بكل نواة درهما
وكان يعد النوى ويعطي كل من له فضل نوى بعدده دراهم وذلك لدفع الحياء
وزيادة النشاط في الإنبساط وقال جعفر بن محمد رضي الله عنهما
أحب إخواني إلي أكثرهم أكلا وأعظمهم لقمة وأثقلهم على من يحوجني إلى
تعهده في الأكل
وكل هذا إشارة إلى الجري على المعتاد وترك التصنع
وقال جعفر رحمه الله أيضا تتبين جودة محبة الرجل لأخيه بجودة أكله في
منزله
الخامس أن غسل اليد في الطست لا بأس به وله أن يتنخم فيه PageV02P007
إن أكل وحده وإن أكل مع غيره فلا ينبغي أن يفعل ذلك
فإذا قدم الطست إليه غيره إكراما له فليقبله
اجتمع أنس بن مالك وثابت البناني رضي الله عنهما على طعام فقدم أنس الطست
إليه فامتنع ثابت فقال أنس إذا أكرمك أخوك فاقبل كرامته ولا تردها فإنما
يكرم الله عز وجل وروي أن هارون الرشيد دعا أبا معاوية الضرير فصب الرشيد
على يده في الطست فلما فرغ قال يا أبا معاوية تدري من صب على يدك فقال لا
قال صبه أمير المؤمنين فقال
يا أمير المؤمنين إنما أكرمت العلم وأجللته فأجلك الله وأكرمك كما أجللت
العلم وأهله
ولا بأس أن يجتمعوا على غسل اليد في الطست في حالة واحدة فهو أقرب إلى
التواضع وأبعد عن طول الإنتظار
فإن لم يفعلوه فلا ينبغي أن يصب ماء كل واحد بل يجمع الماء في الطست قال
صلى الله عليه وسلم أجمعوا وضوءكم جمع الله شملكم (1)
قيل إن المراد هذا
وكتب عمر بن عبد العزيز إلى الأمصار لا يرفع الطست من بين يدي قوم إلا
مملوءة ولا تشبهوا بالعجم
وقال ابن مسعود اجتمعوا على غسل اليد في  طست واحد ولا تستنوا بسنة
الأعاجم
والخادم الذي يصب الماء على اليد كره بعضهم أن يكون قائما وأحب أن يكون
جالسا لأنه أقرب إلى التواضع وكره بعضهم جلوسه فروي أنه صب الماء على يد
واحد خادم جالسا فقام المصبوب عليه فقيل له لم قمت فقال أحدنا لا بد وأن
يكون قائما
وهذا أولى لأنه أيسر للصب وللغسل وأقرب إلى تواضع الذي يصب وإذا كان له
نية فيه فتمكينه من الخدمة ليس فيه تكبر فإن العادة جارية بذلك ففي الطست
إذا سبعة آداب أن لا يبزق فيه وأن يقدم به المتبوع وأن يقبل الإكرام
بالتقديم وأن يدار يمنة وأن يجتمع فيه جماعة وأن يجمع الماء فيه وأن يكون
الخادم قائما وأن يمج الماء من فيه ويرسله من يده برفق حتى لا يرش على
الفراش وعلى أصحابه وليصب صاحب المنزل بنفسه الماء على يد ضيفه هكذا فعل
مالك بالشافعي رضي الله عنهما في أول نزوله عليه وقال لا يروعك ما رأيت مني
فخدمة الضيف فرض
السادس أن لا ينظر إلى أصحابه ولا يراقب أكلهم فيستحيون بل يغض بصره عنهم
ويشتغل بنفسه ولا يمسك قبل إخوانه إذا كانوا يحتشمون الأكل بعده بل يمد
اليد ويقبضها ويتناول قليلا قليلا إلى أن يستوفوا فإن كان قليل الأكل توقف
في الابتداء وقلل الأكل حتى إذا توسعوا في الطعام أكل معهم أخيرا فقد فعل
ذلك كثير من الصحابة رضي الله عنهم فإن امتنع لسبب فليعتذر إليهم دفعا

chapters.anchors:
- Root: ق-د-م (q-d-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Precedence, priority, advancing forward; also 'the forepart' of a thing.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Merit-based precedence (taqdīm) in communal acts reflects the divine order of honoring excellence (faḍl).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense is spatial/sequential priority; here it is metaphorical (majāz) for social honor and deference.
- Root: أ-ث-ر (a-th-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Choosing, preferring, selecting; the trace or remnant of a thing.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Altruism (īthār) — preferring others over oneself, a praiseworthy trait in Islamic ethics.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: leaving a mark; metaphorical: self-sacrificial preference in sharing.
- Root: ص-ن-ع (ṣ-n-ʿ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Crafting, making; also affectation or artificial behavior.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Pretension (taṣannuʿ) — contrived conduct for show, opposed to sincerity (ikhlāṣ).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: skilled making; metaphorical: feigned mannerism in social settings.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Conditional Restriction (al-Sharṭ wa al-Jazāʾ) — The phrase "if not agreeing with the companion's consent" (fa-inna dhālika ḥarām... mā lam yakun muwāfiqan) uses a negative conditional to delimit the legal ruling, requiring parsing of the implied exception.
chapters.translation:
I say: The second book concerns what increases through gathering and sharing in eating, and these are seven [matters].

**The First:** That one should not begin eating while in his presence is someone deserving precedence (taqdīm) due to advanced age or superior merit — unless he himself is the one followed and imitated (al-mattabūʿ wa al-muqtadā bihī). In that case, he should not prolong their waiting when they have stretched their necks toward the food and gathered for it.

**The Second:** That they should not remain silent over food, for that is the custom of the non-Arabs (al-ʿajam). Rather, they should speak what is proper (al-maʿrūf) and converse with stories of the righteous (al-ṣāliḥīn) concerning foods and other matters.

**The Third:** That one should be gentle with his companion at the bowl (al-qaṣʿah), not intending to eat more than what his companion eats. For that is unlawful (ḥarām) if it is not in accord with the companion's consent, whenever the food is shared. Rather, he should intend altruism (al-īthār), and not eat two dates at once unless they do likewise or he seeks their permission.

If his companion eats little, he should encourage him, make eating desirable to him, and say to him: "Eat!" — but he should not exceed saying "Eat!" three times, for that is importunity (ilḥāḥ) and excess. The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) — when addressed about a matter three times, he did not return to it after the third. {«كان رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم إذا خوطب في شيء ثلاثا لم يراجع بعد ثلاث»} — a hadith recorded by Aḥmad from Jābir in a long narration, and also from Abū Ḥadrad; their chains are sound (ḥasan). {«حديث كان إذا خوطب في شيء ثلاثا لم يراجع بعد ثلاث أخرجه أحمد من حديث جابر في حديث طويل ومن حديث أبي حدرد أيضا وإسنادهما حسن»} And {«حديث كان يكرر الكلمة ثلاثا أخرجه البخاري من حديث أنس كان يعيد الكلمة ثلاثا»} — so exceeding this is not from good manners (al-adab).

As for swearing an oath upon him to eat, that is prohibited (mamnūʿ). Al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: "Food is too insignificant to swear an oath upon."

**The Fourth:** That one should not put his companion in need of saying to him: "Eat!" Some men of letters said: "The best of eaters in eating is the one who does not put his companion in need of attending to him in eating, and who spares his brother the burden of speech."

Nor should one leave something he desires because of another's gaze upon him, for that is affectation (taṣannuʿ). Rather, he should proceed according to his habit, and not diminish from his custom anything in solitude — but he should accustom himself to good manners in solitude so that he does not need to feign (al-taṣannuʿ) at gatherings.

Yes, if he reduces his eating out of altruism (īthāran) for his brothers and consideration for them when there is need for that, it is good. And if he increases in eating with the intention of helping and stirring the group's vigor in eating, there is no harm in it — rather, it is good. Ibn al-Mubārak used to present the choicest fresh dates to his brothers and say: "Whoever eats more, I will give him a dirham for every date-stone." He would count the stones and give to each one who had surplus stones dirhams in number — all to repel shyness (al-ḥayāʾ) and increase vigor in expansiveness. Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: "The most beloved of my brothers to me is the most eating among them, the greatest in morsel, and the heaviest upon me — the one who puts me in need of attending to him in eating." All of this points to proceeding according to habit and abandoning affectation. Jaʿfar (may Allah have mercy on him) also said: "The excellence of a man's love for his brother is discerned by the excellence of his eating in his home."

**The Fifth:** That washing the hand in the basin (al-ṭasht) is permissible, and one may spit phlegm into it if he eats alone. But if he eats with others, he should not do that.

When the basin is presented to him by another as an honor, let him accept it. Anas ibn Mālik and Thābit al-Bunānī (may Allah be pleased with them both) gathered over food, and Anas presented the basin to him; Thābit declined. Anas said: "When your brother honors you, accept his honor and do not refuse it, for Allah the Mighty and Majestic honors." It is narrated that Hārūn al-Rashīd invited Abū Muʿāwiyah al-Ḍarīr, and al-Rashīd poured water over his hand in the basin. When he finished, he said: "O Abū Muʿāwiyah, do you know who poured over your hand?" He said: "No." He said: "The Commander of the Faithful poured it." He said: "O Commander of the Faithful, I have only honored knowledge and venerated it — so may Allah venerate you and honor you, just as you venerated knowledge and its people."

There is no harm in their gathering together over washing the hand in one basin at a single time, for it is closer to humility (al-tawāḍuʿ) and farther from prolonged waiting. If they do not do that, then one should not pour water for each one separately, but rather collect the water in the basin. He (peace be upon him) said: {«أجمعوا وضوءكم جمع الله شملكم»} — "Gather your ablution water; may Allah gather your unity." It is said that this is what is meant.

ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz wrote to the provinces: "Do not raise the basin from before a people except filled, and do not imitate the non-Arabs." Ibn Masʿūd said: "Gather together over washing the hand in a single basin, and do not follow the custom of the foreigners (al-aʿājim)."

As for the servant who pours water over the hand, some disliked that he be standing and preferred that he be sitting, because it is closer to humility. Others disliked his sitting, for it is narrated that a servant poured water over the hand of someone while sitting, and the one being poured upon stood up. It was said to him: "Why did you stand?" He said: "One of us must necessarily be standing." This is more appropriate, for it is easier for pouring and for washing, and closer to the humility of the one pouring. If he has intention (niyyah) in it, then enabling him to serve is not arrogance, for custom runs with that.

In the basin, then, there are seven etiquettes: that one not spit into it; that the one followed be given precedence with it; that one accept the honor of its presentation; that it be passed to the right; that a group gather over it; that water be collected in it; that the servant be standing; and that one expel water from his mouth and release it from his hand gently so that it does not splash upon the carpet or upon his companions. Let the host himself pour water over the hand of his guest — thus did Mālik do with al-Shāfiʿī (may Allah be pleased with them both) at the beginning of his stay with him, saying: "Do not be alarmed by what you see from me, for serving the guest is an obligation (farḍ)."

**The Sixth:** That one should not look at his companions nor watch their eating, lest they become shy. Rather, he should lower his gaze from them and occupy himself with his own [eating]. Nor should he withhold his hand before his brothers if they are too diffident to eat after him. Rather, he should extend his hand and withdraw it, taking a little at a time, until they finish. If he is a small eater, let him pause at the beginning and reduce his eating, so that when they expand into the food, he eats with them at the end — for many of the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) did this. If he refrains for a reason, let him excuse himself to them, to repel embarrassment (al-khajalah) from them.

**The Seventh:** That one should not do what others find repugnant (yastaqdhirahu). So he should not flick his hand into the bowl, nor bring his head near it when placing the morsel in his mouth. If he removes something from his mouth, let him turn his face away from the food and take it with his left hand. Nor should he dip a greasy morsel into vinegar, nor vinegar into the greasy [dish], for another may dislike it. The morsel he has cut with his teeth — he should not dip its remainder into the broth or the vinegar. Nor should he speak of anything that recalls repugnant things.

|| الباب الثالث في آداب تقديم الطعام إلى الإخوان الزائرين

تقديم الطعام إلى الإخوان فيه فضل كثير
قال جعفر  بن محمد رضي الله عنهما إذا قعدتم مع الإخوان على المائدة
فأطيلوا الجلوس فإنها ساعة لا تحسب عليكم من أعماركم
وقال الحسن رحمه الله كل نفقة ينفقها الرجل على نفسه وأبويه فمن دونهم
يحاسب عليها البتة إلا نفقة الرجل على إخوانه في الطعام فإن الله يستحي أن
يسأل عن ذلك
هذا مع ما ورد من الأخبار في الإطعام قال صلى الله عليه وسلم لا تزال
الملائكة تصلي على أحدكم ما دامت مائدته موضوعة PageV02P008
بين يديه حتى ترفع (1)
وروي عن بعض علماء خراسان أنه كان يقدم إلى إخوانه طعاما كثيرا لا يقدرون
على أكل جميعه وكان يقول بلغنا عن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم أنه قال إن
الإخوان إذا رفعوا أيديهم عن الطعام لم يحاسب من أكل فضل ذلك (2)
فأنا أحب أن أستكثر مما أقدمه إليكم لنأكل فضل ذلك
وفي الخبر لا يحاسب العبد على ما يأكله مع إخوانه (3)
وكان بعضهم يكثر الأكل مع الجماعة لذلك ويقلل إذا أكل وحده وفي الخبر
ثلاثة لا يحاسب عليها العبد أكلة السحور وما أفطر عليه وما أكل مع الإخوان
(4)
وقال علي رضي الله عنه لأن أجمع إخواني على صاع من طعام أحب إلي من أن
أعتق رقبة
وكان ابن عمر رضي الله عنهما يقول من كرم المرء طيب زاده في سفره وبذله
لأصحابه وكان الصحابة رضي الله عنهم يقولون الاجتماع على الطعام من مكارم
الأخلاق وكانوا رضي الله عنهم يجتمعون على قراءة القرآن ولا يتفرقون إلا عن
ذواق
وقيل اجتماع الإخوان على الكفاية مع الأنس والألفة ليس هو من الدنيا
وفي الخبر يقول الله تعالى للعبد يوم القيامة يا ابن آدم جعت فلم تطعمني
فيقول كيف أطعمك وأنت رب العالمين فيقول جاع أخوك المسلم فلم تطعمه ولو
أطعمته كنت أطعمتني (5)
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم إذا جاءكم الزائر فأكرموه (6)
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم إن في الجنة غرفا يرى ظاهرها من باطنها وباطنها
من ظاهرها هي لمن ألان الكلام وأطعم الطعام وصلى بالليل  والناس نيام (7)
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم خيركم من أطعم الطعام (8)
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم من أطعم أخاه حتى يشبعه وسقاه حتى يرويه بعده
الله من النار بسبع خنادق ما بين كل خندقين مسيرة خمسمائة عام (9)
وأما آدابه فبعضها في الدخول وبعضها في تقديم الطعام
أما الدخول فليس من السنة أن يقصد قوما متربصا لوقت طعامهم فيدخل عليهم
وقت الأكل فإن ذلك من المفاجأة وقد نهي عنه قال الله تعالى {لا تدخلوا بيوت
النبي إلا أن يؤذن لكم إلى طعام غير ناظرين إناه} يعني منتظرين حينه ونضجه
وفي الخبر من مشى إلى طعام لم يدع إليه مشى فاسقا وأكل حراما (10)
ولكن حق الداخل إذا لم يتربص وأتفق أن صادفهم على طعام أن لا يأكل ما لم
يؤذن له فإذا قيل له كل
نظر فإن علم أنهم يقولونه على محبة لمساعدته فليساعد وإن PageV02P009
كانوا يقولونه حياء منه فلا ينبغي أن يأكل بل ينبغي أن يتعلل أما إذا كان
جائعا فقصد بعض إخوانه ليطعمه ولم يتربص به وقت أكله فلا بأس به
قصد رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم وأبو بكر وعمر رضي الله عنهما منزل أبي
الهيثم بن التيهان وأبي أيوب الأنصاري لأجل طعام يأكلونه وكانوا جياعا (1)
والدخول على مثل هذه الحالة إعانة لذلك المسلم على حيازة ثواب الإطعام
وهي عادة السلف
وكان عون بن عبد الله المسعودي له ثلاثمائة وستون صديقا يدور عليهم في
السنة
ولآخر ثلاثون يدور عليهم في الشهر
ولآخرة سبعة يدور عليهم في الجمعة
فكان إخوانهم معلومهم بدلا عن كسبهم وكان قيام أولئك بهم على قصد التبرك
عبادة لهم فإن دخل ولم يجد صاحب الدار وكان واثقا بصداقته عالما بفرحه إذا
أكل من طعامه فله أن يأكل بغير إذنه إذ المراد من الإذن الرضا لا سيما في
الأطعمة وأمرها على السعة
فرب رجل يصرح بالإذن ويحلف وهو غير راض فأكل طعامه مكروه
ورب غائب لم يأذن وأكل طعامه محبوب
وقد قال تعالى {أو صديقكم} ودخل رسول  الله صلى الله عليه وسلم دار بريرة
وأكل طعامها وهي غائبة وكان الطعام من الصدقة فقال بلغت الصدقة محلها (2)
وذلك لعلمه بسرورها بذلك
لذلك يجوز أن يدخل الدار بغير استئذان اكتفاء بعلمه بالإذن فإن لم يعلم
فلا بد من الاستئذان أولا ثم الدخول
وكان محمد بن واسع وأصحابه يدخلون منزل الحسن فيأكلون ما يجدون بغير إذن
وكان الحسن يدخل ويرى ذلك فيسر به ويقول هكذا كنا
وروي عن الحسن رضي الله عنه أنه كان قائما يأكل من متاع بقال في السوق
يأخذ من هذه الجونة تينة ومن هذه قسبة فقال له هشام ما بدا لك يا أبا سعيد
في الورع تأكل متاع الرجل بغير إذنه فقال
يا لكع اتل علي آية الأكل فتلا إلى قوله تعالى {أو صديقكم} فقال
فمن الصديق يا أبا سعيد قال من استروحت إليه النفس واطمأن إليه القلب
ومشى قوم إلى منزل سفيان الثوري فلم يجدوه ففتحوا الباب وأنزلوا السفرة
وجعلوا يأكلون فدخل الثوري وجعل يقول ذكرتموني أخلاق السلف
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ق-ر-ب (q-r-b)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Nearness in place, time, or rank; drawing close
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Spiritual proximity through righteous deeds; the act of presenting (taqdīm) as drawing the guest near through hospitality
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal physical nearness vs. metaphorical nearness of honor and favor
- Root: ض-ي-ف (ḍ-y-f)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To incline, lean toward; a guest (ḍayf) who inclines toward hospitality
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The guest as one who seeks shelter and provision; hospitality as a divine ordinance
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal act of hosting vs. metaphorical "hosting" of angels through righteous deeds
- Root: ك-ل-ف (k-l-f)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To burden, charge, or impose; takalluf as self-imposed burden
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Affectation and artificiality in worship and social dealings; blameworthy excess
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal burden-bearing vs. metaphorical burden of pretense and ostentation
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Constructions (al-sharṭ wa al-istithnāʾ) — Governing the nuanced legal distinctions between cases of permission and prohibition in hospitality, requiring precise parsing of protasis and apodosis.
chapters.translation:
I say: The third book concerns the etiquette of presenting food to visiting brethren.

**The presentation of food to brethren carries abundant merit.**
Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: "When you sit with your brethren at the table, prolong the sitting, for it is an hour that will not be reckoned against you from your lifespans."

Al-Ḥasan (may Allah have mercy on him) said: "Every expenditure a man makes upon himself, his parents, and those beneath them shall certainly be accounted for — except a man's expenditure upon his brethren in food, for Allah is too shy to ask about that."

This is in addition to what has been reported of traditions concerning feeding others. The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said: {«The angels continue to invoke blessings upon one of you as long as his table remains set before him, until it is lifted.»} (1)

It is related of one of the scholars of Khurāsān that he would present to his brethren abundant food that they could not finish eating, and he would say: "It has reached us from the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) that he said: {«When brethren lift their hands from food, the one who eats of the surplus thereof is not held to account.»} (2) So I love to increase what I present to you, that we may eat of that surplus."

And in the tradition: {«A servant is not held to account for what he eats with his brethren.»} (3)

Some of them would eat much in company for this reason, and eat little when alone. And in the tradition: {«Three things for which the servant is not held to account: the meal of suḥūr (pre-dawn meal), what he breaks his fast with, and what he eats with brethren.»} (4)

ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "That I gather my brethren over a ṣāʿ (measure) of food is dearer to me than freeing a slave."

Ibn ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with them both) would say: "Part of a man's nobility is the goodness of his provision on his journey and his generosity in sharing it with his companions." The Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) would say: "Gathering together over food is among the noble traits of character." They (may Allah be pleased with them) would gather over the recitation of the Qurʾān and would not disperse except after tasting something.

It was said: "The gathering of brethren over sufficiency, with intimacy and familiarity, is not of this world."

And in the tradition: {«Allah the Exalted says to the servant on the Day of Resurrection: "O son of Adam, I was hungry and you did not feed Me." He says: "How can I feed You, when You are the Lord of the worlds?" He says: "Your brother, the Muslim, was hungry and you did not feed him. Had you fed him, you would have fed Me."»} (5)

The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said: {«When a visitor comes to you, honor him.»} (6)

And he (peace and blessings be upon him) said: {«In Paradise there are chambers whose exterior is seen from their interior and their interior from their exterior — they are for the one who softens his speech, feeds food, and prays by night while people sleep.»} (7)

And he (peace and blessings be upon him) said: {«The best of you is the one who feeds food.»} (8)

And he (peace and blessings be upon him) said: {«Whoever feeds his brother until he is sated and gives him drink until he is quenched, Allah will distance him from the Fire by seven trenches, between each two trenches a distance of five hundred years' journey.»} (9)

**As for its etiquettes, some pertain to entering, and some to presenting food.**

**Regarding entering:** It is not of the Sunnah to intend a people, lying in wait for the time of their meal, and enter upon them at the time of eating — for that is a form of sudden intrusion, which has been prohibited. Allah the Exalted says: {«Do not enter the houses of the Prophet unless permission is given to you for a meal, not waiting for its readiness»} — meaning, waiting for its time and its cooking. And in the tradition: {«Whoever walks to a food to which he was not invited walks as a transgressor and eats unlawfully.»} (10)

Rather, the right of the one who enters — if he did not lie in wait and it so happened that he found them at food — is that he should not eat unless permission is given to him. If it is said to him, "Eat," he should consider: if he knows they say it out of love for his participation, let him participate. But if they say it out of shyness before him, he should not eat; rather, he should offer an excuse.

However, if he is hungry and intends one of his brethren to feed him, without lying in wait for his mealtime, there is no harm in it. The Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him), Abū Bakr, and ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with them) intended the home of Abū al-Haytham ibn al-Tayyihān and Abū Ayyūb al-Anṣārī for food they would eat, and they were hungry. (1) Entering in such a state is assistance to that Muslim in attaining the reward of feeding — and it was the practice of the Salaf (righteous predecessors).

ʿAwn ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Masʿūdī had three hundred and sixty friends, and he would circulate among them through the year. Another had thirty, circulating among them monthly. Another had seven, circulating among them weekly. Their brethren's provision was their known sustenance in place of their own earning, and the standing of those (hosts) in serving them, intending blessing, was an act of worship for them.

If one enters and does not find the master of the house, yet is confident of his friendship and knows of his joy when he eats of his food, he may eat without his permission — for the intent of permission is satisfaction (riḍā), especially regarding foods, whose matter is one of ease. For there is a man who explicitly grants permission and swears oaths while not being satisfied — eating his food is disliked. And there is an absent one who did not grant permission, yet eating his food is beloved. Allah the Exalted has said: {«Or your friends»} — and the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) entered the home of Barīrah and ate her food while she was absent, and the food was from charity, so he said: {«The charity has reached its place.»} (2) That was due to his knowledge of her delight in it.

Therefore, it is permissible to enter the house without seeking permission, relying on one's knowledge of permission. But if one does not know, then permission must first be sought, then entry.

Muḥammad ibn Wāsiʿ and his companions would enter the home of al-Ḥasan and eat whatever they found without permission. Al-Ḥasan would enter, see that, and rejoice, saying: "Thus we used to be."

It is related of al-Ḥasan (may Allah be pleased with him) that he stood eating from the goods of a grocer in the market, taking from this basket a fig and from that a cucumber. Hishām said to him: "What has come over you, O Abū Saʿīd, in scrupulousness (waraʿ)? You eat a man's goods without his permission?" He said: "O foolish one, recite to me the verse of eating." So he recited until he reached the saying of Allah the Exalted: {«Or your friends»} — then he said: "So who is the friend, O Abū Saʿīd?" He said: "The one to whom the soul is drawn and the heart is at rest."

A group walked to the home of Sufyān al-Thawrī and did not find him, so they opened the door, spread the tablecloth, and began eating. Al-Thawrī entered and began saying: "You have reminded me of the character of the Salaf — thus they used to be."

A group visited one of the Tābiʿīn (successors), and he had nothing to present to them. He went to the home of one of his brethren and did not find him in the house, so he entered, saw a pot that had been cooked, bread that had been baked, and other things — he carried it all, presented it to his companions, and said: "Eat." The master of the house came and saw nothing, and it was said to him: "So-and-so took it." He said: "So-and-so has done well." When he met him, he said: "O my brother, if they return, then return (to do the same)."

These are the etiquettes of entering.

**As for the etiquettes of presenting:** First, abandoning affectation (takalluf) and presenting what is available. If one has nothing present and owns nothing, he should not borrow for that purpose, troubling himself. And if he has what he needs for his own sustenance but his soul does not permit presenting it, he should not present it.

One of them entered upon a renunciant (zāhid) while he was eating, and he said: "Were it not that I took this on debt, I would feed you of it."

Some of the Salaf said in explanation of affectation (takalluf): "That you feed your brother what you yourself do not eat, intending something beyond it in quality and value."

Al-Fuḍayl used to say: "People only cut off relations through affectation — one of them invites his brother and goes to trouble for him, thus cutting him off from returning."

Some of them said: "I care not who comes to me of my brethren, for I do not go to trouble for him — I only present what I have. Were I to go to trouble for him, I would dislike his coming and grow weary of him."

Another said: "I used to visit a brother of mine, and he would go to trouble for me. I said to him: 'You do not eat this alone, nor do I — so why, when we gather, do we eat it? Either you cut off this affectation, or I cut off my coming.' So he cut off the affectation, and our gathering continued by reason of it."

And of affectation is presenting all that one has, thereby harming one's dependents and hurting their hearts. It is related that a man invited ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with him), and ʿAlī said: "I will answer you on three conditions: that you bring nothing from the market, that you do not store what is in the house, and that you do not harm your dependents."

Some of them would present of everything in the house, leaving no kind without bringing something of it.

One of them said: "We entered upon Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh, and he presented to us bread and vinegar, saying: 'Were we not forbidden from affectation, I would have gone to trouble for you.'" (1)

Another said: "If you intend a visit, present what is available; and if you invite, leave nothing stored and nothing left behind."

Salmān said: "The Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) commanded us not to go to trouble for the guest with what we do not have, and to present to him what is available to us." (2)

In the tradition of Yūnus the Prophet (peace be upon him): his brethren visited him, and he presented to them dry crumbs and cut for them a vegetable (buql) he had cultivated, then said to them: "Eat — were it not that Allah has cursed the affectatious, I would have gone to trouble for you."

It is related of Anas ibn Mālik (may Allah be pleased with him) and others of the Companions that they would present what was available — dry crumbs and poor-quality dates — and say: "We do not know which of the two bears the greater sin: the one who disdains what is presented to him, or the one who disdains what he has to present it."

**The second etiquette — and it is for the visitor:** that he should not propose or insist upon any specific thing, for perhaps its procurement is burdensome upon the one visited. If his brother gives him a choice between two foods, let him choose the lighter of the two upon him — thus was the Sunnah. For in the tradition: {«The Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) was never given a choice between two things except that he chose the lighter of them.»} (3)

Al-Aʿmash related from Abū Wāʾil that he said: "I went with a companion of mine to visit Salmān, and he presented to us barley bread and coarse salt. My companion said: 'Were there thyme in this salt, it would be more pleasant.' So Salmān went out, pawned his water-skin (miṭharah), and brought thyme. When we had eaten, my companion said: 'Praise be to Allah who has sufficed us with what He has provided.' Salmān said: 'Had you been sufficed with what you were provided, my water-skin would not have been pawned.'"

This applies when one suspects that procuring it is difficult for his brother or disliked by him. But if he knows that he delights in his proposal and that it is easy for him, then proposing is not disliked for him. Al-Shāfiʿī (may Allah be pleased with him) did this with al-Zaʿfarānī when he was staying with him in Baghdad. Al-Zaʿfarānī would write each day a note of the dishes to be cooked and hand it to the maidservant. Al-Shāfiʿī took the note one day and appended another dish in his own handwriting. When al-Zaʿfarānī saw that dish, he disapproved and said: "I did not order this." The note was shown to him with al-Shāfiʿī's handwriting appended. When his eye fell upon his handwriting, he rejoiced at that and freed the maidservant, delighting in al-Shāfiʿī's proposal upon him.

Abū Bakr al-Kattānī said: "I entered upon al-Sarī, and he brought crumbled bread (fatīt) and began putting half of it in the bowl. I said to him: 'What are you doing, when I will drink it all at once?' He laughed and said: 'This is better for you than a pilgrimage (ḥajjah).'"

One of them said: "Eating is of three kinds: with the poor, by giving preference (īthār); with brethren, by ease and expansiveness (inbisāṭ); and with the people of this world, by decorum (adab)."

**The third etiquette:** that the one visited should make his brother the visitor desire (food) and seek his proposal — whenever his soul is agreeable to doing what is proposed, that is good, and therein is abundant reward and merit. The Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) said: {«Whoever encounters a desire of his brother (and fulfills it), he is forgiven; and whoever delights his believing brother has delighted Allah the Exalted.»} (4)

And he (peace and blessings be upon him) said, as related by Jābir: {«Whoever delights his brother with what he desires, Allah writes for him a thousand thousand good deeds, erases from him a thousand thousand evil deeds, raises him a thousand thousand degrees, and feeds him from three gardens: the Garden of Firdaws, the Garden of ʿAdn, and the Garden of Khuld.»} (1)

**The fourth etiquette:** that one should not say to him, "Shall I present food to you?" Rather, he should present it. Al-Thawrī said: "When your brother visits you, do not say to him, 'Will you eat?' or 'Shall I present to you?' Rather, present — if he eats, (good); otherwise, lift it away."

And if one intends to feed them food, he should not make them aware of it beforehand, nor describe it to them. Al-Thawrī said: "If you intend not to feed your family from what you eat, do not mention it to them, nor let them see it with you."

One of the Sufis said: "When the poor enter upon you, present food to them; when the jurists (fuqahāʾ) enter, ask them a question; and when the reciters (qurrāʾ) enter, direct them to the miḥrāb."

chapters.title_en: The Fourth Book on the Etiquette of Hospitality
chapters.arabic_text:
|| الباب الرابع في آداب الضيافة

ومظان الآداب فيها ستة الدعوة أولا ثم الإجابة ثم الحضور ثم تقديم الطعام
ثم الأكل ثم الانصراف ولنقدم على شرحها إن شاء الله تعالى
فضيلة الضيافة قال صلى الله عليه وسلم لا تكلفوا للضيف فتبغضوه فإنه من
أبغض الضيف فقد أبغض الله ومن أبغض الله أبغضه الله (2)
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم لا خير فيمن لا يضيف (3)
ومر رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم برجل له إبل وبقر كثيرة فلم يضيفه ومر
بامرأة لها شويهات فذبحت له
فقال صلى الله عليه وسلم انظروا إليهما إنما هذه الأخلاق بيد الله فمن
شاء أن يمنحه خلقا حسنا فعل (4)
وقال أبو رافع مولى رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم أنه نزل به صلى الله
عليه وسلم ضيف فقال
قل لفلان اليهودي نزل بي ضيف فأسلفني شيئا من الدقيق إلى رجب فقال
اليهودي والله ما أسلفه إلا برهن فأخبرته فقال والله إني لأمين في السماء
أمين في الأرض ولو أسلفني لأديته فاذهب بدرعي وارهنه عنده (5)
وكان إبراهيم الخليل صلوات الله عليه وسلامه إذا أراد ان يأكل خرج ميلا
أو ميلين يلتمس من يتغدى معه وكان يكنى أبا الضيفان ولصدق نيته فيه دامت
ضيافته في مشهده إلى يومنا هذا فلا تنقضي ليلة إلا ويأكل عنده جماعة من بين
ثلاثة إلى عشرة إلى مائة
وقال قوام الموضع إنه لن يخل إلى الآن ليلة عن ضيف وسئل رسول الله صلى
الله عليه وسلم ما الإيمان فقال إطعام الطعام وبذل السلام (6)
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم في الكفارات والدرجات إطعام الطعام والصلاة
بالليل والناس نيام (7) PageV02P012
وسئل عن الحج المبرور فقال إطعام الطعام وطيب الكلام (1)
وقال أنس رضي الله عنه كل بيت لا  يدخله ضيف لا تدخله الملائكة
والأخبار الواردة في فضل الضيافة والإطعام لا تحصى فلنذكر آدابها
أما الدعوة فينبغي للداعي أن يعمد بدعوته الأتقياء دون الفساق قال صلى
الله عليه وسلم أكل طعامك الأبرار (2)
في دعائه لبعض من دعا له وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم لا تأكل إلا طعام تقي
ولا يأكل طعامك إلا تقي (3)
ويقصد الفقراء دون الأغنياء على الخصوص
قال صلى الله عليه وسلم شر الطعام طعام الوليمة يدعى إليها الأغنياء دون
الفقراء (4)
وينبغي أن لا يهمل أقاربه في ضيافته فإن إهمالهم إيحاش وقطع رحم وكذلك
يراعي الترتيب في أصدقائه ومعارفه فإن في تخصيص البعض إيحاشا لقلوب الباقين
وينبغي أن لا يقصد بدعوته المباهاة والتفاخر بل استمالة قلوب الإخوان
والتسنن بسنة رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم في إطعام الطعام وإدخال السرور
على قلوب المؤمنين
وينبغي أن لا يدعو من يعلم أنه يشق عليه الإجابة وإذا حضر تأذى بالحاضرين
بسبب من الأسباب
وينبغي أن لا يدعو إلا من يحب إجابته قال سفيان من دعا أحدا إلى طعام وهو
يكره الإجابة فعليه خطيئة فإن أجاب المدعو فعليه خطيئتان
لأنه حمله على الأكل مع كراهة ولو علم ذلك لما كان يأكله
وإطعام التقي إعانة على الطاعة وإطعام الفاسق تقوية على الفسق
قال رجل خياط لابن المبارك أنا أخيط ثياب السلاطين فهل تخاف أن أكون من
أعوان الظلمة قال لا إنما أعوان الظلمة من يبيع منك الخيط والإبرة أما أنت
فمن الظلمة نفسهم
وأما الإجابة فهي سنة مؤكدة وقد قيل بوجوبها في بعض المواضع
قال صلى الله عليه وسلم لو دعيت إلى كراع لأجبت ولو أهدي إلي ذراع لقبلت
(5)
وللإجابة خمسة آداب
الأول أن لا يميز الغني بالإجابة عن الفقير فذلك هو التكبر المنهي عنه
ولأجل ذلك امتنع بعضهم عن أصل الإجابة وقال انتظار المرقة ذل وقال آخر إذا
وضعت يدي في قصعة غيري فقد ذلت له رقبتي ومن المتكبرين من يجيب الأغنياء
دون الفقراء وهو خلاف السنة
كان رسول الله صلى  الله عليه وسلم يجيب دعوة العبد ودعوة المسكين (6)
ومر الحسن بن علي رضي الله عنهما بقوم من المساكين الذين يسألون الناس
على الطريق وقد نشروا كسرا على الأرض في الرمل وهم يأكلون وهو على بغلته
فسلم عليهم فقالوا له هلم إلى الغداء يا ابن بنت رسول الله صلى الله عليه
وسلم فقال نعم إن الله لا يحب المستكبرين فنزل وقعد معهم على الأرض وأكل ثم
سلم عليهم وركب وقال قد أجبتكم فأجيبوني قالوا نعم فوعدهم وقتا معلوما
فحضروا فقدم إليهم فاخر الطعام وجلس يأكل معهم
وأما قول القائل إن من وضعت يدي في قصعته فقد ذلت له رقبتي فقد قال بعضهم
هذا خلاف السنة وليس كذلك فإنه ذل إذا كان الداعي لا يفرح بالإجابة ولا
يتقلد منة وكان يرى ذلك يدا له على المدعو
ورسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم كان يحضر لعلمه أن الداعي له يتقلد منة
ويرى ذلك شرفا وذخرا لنفسه في الدنيا والآخرة فهذا يختلف باختلاف الحال فمن
ظن به أنه يستثقل الإطعام وإنما يفعل ذلك مباهاة أو تكلفا فليس من السنة
إجابته (7)
بل الأولى التعلل ولذلك قال بعض الصوفية
لا تجب إلا دعوة من يرى أنك أكلت رزقك وأنه PageV02P013
سلم إليك وديعة كانت لك عنده ويرى لك الفضل عليه في قبول تلك الوديعة منه

chapters.anchors:
- Root: ض-ي-ف (ḍ-y-f)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The core meaning is "to incline, to lean toward, to alight upon" — a guest (ḍayf) is one who inclines toward a host seeking shelter and provision.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Hospitality (ḍiyāfah) is a covenantal act of honoring the guest as a divine trust, mirroring the hospitality of Ibrāhīm (ʿalayhi al-salām) as a prophetic paradigm.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense is physical sheltering; metaphorical sense extends to spiritual sheltering — the guest is "one who leans" upon the host's generosity as the creature leans upon the Creator.
- Root: د-ع-و (d-ʿ-w)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To call, summon, invoke — the act of invitation (daʿwah) as a verbal summons that creates obligation.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The invitation to food is a microcosm of the divine call (daʿwah) to salvation — responding to it is a form of obedience.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: summoning to a meal; metaphorical: the summons of faith, as in {«يَدْعُونَ إِلَى الْخَيْرِ»} — the host's call mirrors the prophetic call.
- Root: أ-ك-ل (ʾ-k-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To eat, consume — the physical act of ingestion.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Eating is a divinely ordained means of sustaining the body for worship; its intention (niyyah) transforms it from animal act to act of devotion.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: mastication and swallowing; metaphorical: consuming what is lawful (ḥalāl) versus unlawful (ḥarām) — the "food of the pious" (ṭaʿām al-taqī) as spiritual nourishment.
- Root: ك-ر-م (k-r-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Nobility, generosity, honor — the quality of the one who gives freely without expectation.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Generosity (karam) is a divine attribute reflected in the host; honoring the guest (ikrām al-ḍayf) is honoring God's trust.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: noble lineage; metaphorical: nobility of character — the "honored guests" (ḍayf Ibrāhīm al-mukramīn) as those ennobled by swift provision.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of ʿAṭf al-Bayān (Appositional Clarification) — In the enumeration of the six loci of etiquette (al-daʿwah, al-ijābah, al-ḥuḍūr, taqdīm al-ṭaʿām, al-akl, al-inṣirāf), the sequential conjunction (thumma) marks a temporal-causal order, each stage conditioning the next, requiring the translator to preserve the architectonic progression.
chapters.translation:
I say: The fourth book on the etiquette of hospitality. The loci of etiquette therein are six: the invitation first, then the response, then the attendance, then the presentation of food, then the eating, then the departure. Let us proceed to their explanation, God willing.

On the virtue of hospitality: The Prophet (God's peace and blessings be upon him) said: "Do not burden the guest so that you make him hate you, for whoever hates the guest has hated God, and whoever hates God, God hates him." And he (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "There is no good in one who does not host." The Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) passed by a man who had many camels and cattle, yet he did not host him; and he passed by a woman who had a few sheep, and she slaughtered for him. He (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "Look at the two of them — these moral characters are in the hand of God; whomever He wills to grant a good character, He does."

Abū Rāfiʿ, the freed slave of the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him), said that a guest alighted upon him (peace and blessings be upon him), and he said: "Tell so-and-so the Jew: a guest has alighted upon me, so lend me some flour until Rajab." The Jew said: "By God, I will not lend it except with a pledge." He informed him (the Prophet), and he said: "By God, I am indeed trustworthy in heaven and trustworthy on earth; had he lent me, I would have repaid him. Go with my coat of mail and pledge it with him."

Ibrāhīm al-Khalīl (God's prayers and peace be upon him), whenever he wished to eat, would go out a mile or two seeking someone to dine with him. He was nicknamed "Abū al-Ḍayfān" (Father of Guests). Due to the sincerity of his intention therein, his hospitality has endured at his shrine to this very day — no night passes but a group of people, from three to ten to a hundred, eat at his place. The custodian of the site said that to this day no night has been devoid of a guest.

The Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) was asked: "What is faith?" He said: "Feeding food and spreading peace." And he (peace and blessings be upon him) said regarding expiations and degrees: "Feeding food and praying at night while people sleep." And he was asked about the accepted pilgrimage (ḥajj al-mabrūr), and he said: "Feeding food and speaking kindly." Anas (God be pleased with him) said: "Every house into which no guest enters — the angels do not enter it." The reports concerning the virtue of hospitality and feeding are innumerable; let us mention its etiquettes.

As for the invitation: The inviter ought to target the pious rather than the wicked in his invitation. The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said — in his supplication for one for whom he prayed — "May the righteous eat your food." And he (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "Do not eat except the food of a pious man, and let none eat your food except a pious man." He should intend the poor rather than the rich in particular. The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "The worst food is the food of the wedding feast (walīmah) to which the rich are invited and the poor are excluded."

He ought not to neglect his relatives in his hospitality, for neglecting them is alienation and severance of kinship. Likewise, he should observe order among his friends and acquaintances, for singling out some alienates the hearts of the rest. He ought not to intend by his invitation ostentation (mubāhāh) and self-glorification, but rather the drawing of the hearts of brethren, the emulation of the Sunnah of the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) in feeding food, and the bringing of joy into the hearts of the believers.

He ought not to invite one whom he knows would find it burdensome to respond, and who, if he attended, would be harmed by the attendees for some reason. He ought not to invite except one whose response he desires. Sufyān said: "Whoever invites someone to food while disliking his response bears a sin; and if the invitee responds, then upon him are two sins" — because he compelled him to eat with reluctance, and had he known, he would not have eaten. Feeding the pious is assistance upon obedience, and feeding the wicked is strengthening upon wickedness. A tailor said to Ibn al-Mubārak: "I sew the clothes of sultans — do you fear that I am among the helpers of the oppressors?" He said: "No — the helpers of the oppressors are only those who sell you the thread and needle. As for you, you are among the oppressors themselves."

As for the response: It is an emphatic Sunnah, and some have held it obligatory in certain contexts. The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "Were I invited to a trotter (kurāʿ), I would respond; and were a foreleg (dhirāʿ) gifted to me, I would accept."

The response has five etiquettes:

**First**: That he not distinguish the rich by responding while refusing the poor — for that is the pride (takabbur) that is prohibited. For this reason, some abstained from responding altogether, saying: "Waiting for the broth is humiliation." Another said: "When I place my hand in another's bowl, my neck has bowed to him." Among the proud are those who respond to the rich but not the poor — and that contradicts the Sunnah. The Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) used to respond to the invitation of a slave and the invitation of a poor man. Al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī (God be pleased with them both) passed by a group of poor beggars on the road who had spread out crumbs on the ground in the sand and were eating, while he was on his mule. He greeted them, and they said: "Come to the meal, O son of the daughter of the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him)!" He said: "Yes — indeed God does not love the proud." So he dismounted, sat with them on the ground, ate, then greeted them, mounted, and said: "I have responded to you, so respond to me." They said: "Yes." He promised them a known time; they attended, and he served them the finest food and sat eating with them.

As for the saying of one who said, "When I place my hand in his bowl, my neck has bowed to him" — some have said this contradicts the Sunnah, but it is not so. For it is humiliation only when the inviter does not rejoice in the response nor consider it a favor (minnah) upon himself, but rather views it as a favor he has done to the invitee. The Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) used to attend because he knew that the inviter would consider it a favor and view it as honor and treasure for himself in this world and the next. This thus varies with the variation of circumstance. Whoever is thought to find feeding burdensome, doing it only for ostentation or affectation — responding to him is not from the Sunnah; rather, the better course is to offer an excuse. For this reason, some of the Sufis said: "Do not respond except to the invitation of one who sees that you have eaten your own provision and that he has delivered to you a trust (wadīʿah) that was yours with him, and who sees that you have a favor upon him in accepting that trust from him." Sari al-Saqaṭī (God's mercy be upon him) said: "Alas for a morsel over which there is no liability upon God and no obligation (minnah) upon any creature toward me." When the invitee knows there is no favor in it, he ought not to refuse. Abū Turāb al-Nakhshī (God's mercy be upon him) said: "Food was offered to me and I refused, so I was afflicted with hunger for fourteen days — and I knew it was its punishment." It was said to Maʿrūf al-Karkhī (God be pleased with him): "Everyone who invites you, go to him." He said: "I am a guest — I alight wherever they make me alight."

**Second**: That he ought not to refrain from responding due to the distance of the journey, just as he does not refrain due to the poverty of the inviter or his lack of status. Rather, any distance that can be borne customarily — he ought not to refrain on its account. It is said in the Torah or some of the books: "Travel a mile to visit the sick; travel two miles to escort a funeral; travel three miles to respond to an invitation; travel four miles to visit a brother in God." The response to the invitation and the visit were placed first because therein is fulfilling the right of the living — and that takes precedence over the dead. The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "Were I invited to a trotter at al-Ghamīm, I would respond" — and it is a place several miles from Medina where the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) broke his fast in Ramadan when the news reached him, and he shortened the prayer there during his journey.

**Third**: That he not refrain because he is fasting, but rather attend. If he knows that it delights his brother for him to break the fast, let him break it and reckon in his breaking the intention of bringing joy to his brother's heart — what he reckons in fasting, and more excellent. This applies to voluntary fasting (ṣawm al-taṭawwuʿ). If he does not ascertain his brother's joy, let him affirm it outwardly and break the fast. If he ascertains that the host is being affected (mutakallif), let him offer an excuse. The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said to one who excused himself by fasting: "Your brother has gone to trouble for you, and you say, 'I am fasting'!" Ibn ʿAbbās (God be pleased with them both) said: "Among the best of good deeds is honoring the companions by breaking the fast." Thus breaking the fast is an act of worship with this intention and a good character — its reward surpasses the reward of fasting. And whenever he does not break the fast, his hospitality is the pleasant demeanor, the incense burner, and pleasant conversation. It has been said: "The kohl and the oil are one of the two readings (al-qirāʾayn)."

**Fourth**: That he refrain from responding if the food is of doubtful provenance (shubhah), or the place or the spread carpet is not from lawful means, or an abomination (munkar) is established in the place — such as spreading silk brocade (dībāj), using silver or gold vessels, depicting animals on the ceiling or wall, hearing flutes and instruments of amusement, occupying oneself with any kind of frivolity, play, jest, and sport, listening to backbiting, slander, falsehood, calumny, and lying, and the like — all of which prevents the response and its desirability and renders it forbidden or disliked. Likewise, if the inviter is an oppressor, an innovator (mubtadiʿ), a wicked person, an evil person, or one who is affected seeking ostentation and pride.

**Fifth**: That he not intend by his response the satisfaction of the belly's lust, thereby acting in the affairs of this world. Rather, let him beautify his intention so that by responding he acts for the Hereafter. That is by intending the emulation of the Sunnah of the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) in his saying: "Were I invited to a trotter, I would respond." And he intends caution against disobeying God Almighty, due to his saying (peace and blessings be upon him): "Whoever does not respond to the inviter has disobeyed God and His Messenger." And he intends honoring his believing brother, following his saying (peace and blessings be upon him): "Whoever honors his believing brother, it is as if he has honored God." And he intends bringing joy to his heart, complying with his saying (peace and blessings be upon him): "Whoever delights a believer has delighted God." And he intends with that his visitation, to be among those who love one another for God's sake, since the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) made mutual visitation and mutual giving (tabādhal) for God's sake a condition therein. The giving has been realized from one side, so the visitation is realized from his side as well. And he intends safeguarding himself from being ill-thought-of in his refusal, and from tongues being unleashed against him, attributing to him pride, bad character, contempt for a Muslim brother, or the like.

These are six intentions that attach his response to the acts of nearness (qurubāt) — each one singly, so how much more when combined! Some of the predecessors (salaf) used to say: "I love to have an intention in every act — even in food and drink." And in this vein, he (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "Actions are but by intentions, and every man shall have what he intended. So whoever's emigration (hijrah) was to God and His Messenger, his emigration is to God and His Messenger; and whoever's emigration was to a worldly gain he seeks or a woman he marries, his emigration is to that which he emigrated to."

The intention only takes effect in permissible acts (mubāḥāt) and acts of obedience. As for the prohibited acts, it does not. For if one intended to delight his brothers by assisting them in drinking wine or another unlawful thing, the intention would not benefit, and it is not permissible to say "actions are but by intentions." Rather, if one intended by raiding (ghazw) — which is an act of obedience — ostentation and seeking wealth, it turns away from the direction of obedience. Likewise, the permissible act that is wavering between aspects of goodness and other things is attached to the aspects of goodness by intention. Thus the intention takes effect in these two categories, not in the third.

As for the attendance: Its etiquette is that he enter the house and not take the seat of honor (taṣaddur), seizing the finest place, but rather humble himself. He should not prolong their waiting, nor hasten so as to surprise them before the preparation is complete. He should not constrict the place upon the attendees by crowding. Rather, if the master of the house gestures to him a place, he should not oppose him at all — for he may have arranged in his mind the place of each one, and opposing him would disturb him. And if some of the guests gesture to him to move up as an honor, let him humble himself. The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "Indeed, from humility before God is being content with the lowly place in the gathering." He ought not to sit facing the door of the women's chamber and their concealment. He should not gaze excessively at the place from which the food emerges, for that indicates greed (sharah). He should single out with greeting and inquiry those nearest to him when he sits.

When a guest enters for the night, the master of the house should inform him upon entry of the direction of the qiblah, the latrine, and the place of ablution — thus did Mālik do with al-Shāfiʿī (God be pleased with them both). Mālik washed his hand before the food, before the people, and said: "Washing before the food is for the master of the house first, because he invites people to his generosity — his ruling is to precede in washing; and at the end of the food, he delays in washing, to wait for one who enters to eat, so that he may eat with him."

When he enters and sees an abomination, let him change it if he is able; otherwise, let him denounce it with his tongue and depart. The abomination is the spreading of silk brocade, the use of silver and gold vessels, depiction on the walls, hearing instruments of amusement and flutes, the presence of unveiled women, and other forbidden things — until Aḥmad (God's mercy be upon him) said: "When he sees a kohl container whose tip is silver-plated, he should depart" — and he did not permit sitting except with a silver clasp (ḍabbah). And he said: "When he sees a canopy (kullah), he should depart, for that is affectation with no benefit — it neither repels heat nor cold, nor conceals anything." Likewise, he said: "He departs when he sees the walls of the house covered with silk brocade as the Kaʿbah is covered." And he said: "When he rents a house containing a depiction, or enters the bathhouse and sees a depiction, he should scratch it out; if he cannot, he departs."

All that he mentioned is sound. The consideration, however, is regarding the canopy and the adornment of walls with silk brocade — for that does not reach the degree of prohibition, since silk is forbidden to men. The Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "These two are forbidden to the males of my community and lawful for its females." What is on the wall is not attributed to males. Were this forbidden, the adornment of the Kaʿbah would be forbidden. Rather, the better course is its permissibility, due to His saying: {«قُلْ مَنْ حَرَّمَ زِينَةَ اللَّهِ»} ("Say: Who has forbidden the adornment of God...") — especially at times of adornment, when it is not taken as a habit of ostentation. And if one imagines that men benefit by looking at it — it is not forbidden for men to benefit by looking at silk brocade whenever women and slave girls wear it. And walls are in the meaning of women, for they are not described by masculinity.

As for the presentation of food: It has five etiquettes.

**First**: Hastening the food — for that is from honoring the guest. The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "Whoever believes in God and the Last Day, let him honor his guest." Whenever the majority have arrived and one or two are absent, delayed beyond the appointed time, the right of the present in hastening takes precedence over the right of the absent in delaying — unless the delayed one is poor or his heart would be broken by that, in which case there is no harm in delaying. One of the two meanings in His saying {«هَلْ أَتَاكَ حَدِيثُ ضَيْفِ إِبْرَاهِيمَ الْمُكْرَمِينَ»} ("Has the story of the honored guests of Abraham reached you?") is that they were honored by hastening the food to them. This is indicated by His saying {«فَمَا لَبِثَ أَن جَاءَ بِعِجْلٍ حَنِيذٍ»} ("And he did not tarry until he brought a roasted calf") and His saying {«فَرَاغَ إِلَىٰ أَهْلِهِ فَجَاءَ بِعِجْلٍ سَمِينٍ»} ("And he turned to his family and brought a fat calf") — and al-rawaghān is going swiftly; it was also said: in secret. It was said: he brought a haunch of meat. It was only called a calf (ʿijl) because he hastened it (ʿajjalahu) and did not tarry.

Ḥātim al-Aṣamm said: "Haste is from Satan, except in five things, for they are from the Sunnah of the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him): feeding the guest, preparing the dead, marrying the virgin, repaying the debt, and repenting from sin." Hastening is recommended in the wedding feast (walīmah). It was said: "The walīmah on the first day is Sunnah, on the second is generosity, and on the third is ostentation."

**Second**: Ordering the foods by presenting the fruit first, if there is fruit — for that is more fitting in medicine, since it transforms most quickly and thus should settle at the bottom of the stomach. In the Qur'an there is a hint at presenting the fruit in His saying: {«وَفَاكِهَةٍ مِّمَّا يَتَخَيَّرُونَ»} ("And fruit of what they choose") — then He said: {«وَلَحْمِ طَيْرٍ مِّمَّا يَشْتَهُونَ»} ("And flesh of birds of what they desire"). Then the best of what is presented after the fruit is meat and tharīd (bread soaked in broth). The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "The superiority of ʿĀʾishah over women is like the superiority of tharīd over all other food." If sweetness is added after it, then all the good things have been gathered.

The attainment of honor through meat is indicated by His saying regarding the guests of Ibrāhīm, when he brought the roasted calf (al-ʿijl al-ḥanīdh) — that is, the one well-roasted, which is one of the meanings of honor, namely presenting meat. And He said in describing the good things: {«وَأَنزَلْنَا عَلَيْكُمُ الْمَنَّ وَالسَّلْوَىٰ»} ("And We sent down upon you manna and quails") — al-mann is honey, and al-salwā is meat. It was called salwā because one is consoled (yatasallā) by it from all other condiments, and nothing else takes its place. For this reason, he (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "The master of condiments is meat." Then after mentioning manna and quails, He said: {«كُلُوا مِن طَيِّبَاتِ مَا رَزَقْنَاكُمْ»} ("Eat of the good things We have provided you") — so meat and sweetness are among the good things.

Abū Sulaymān al-Dārānī (God be pleased with him) said: "Eating good things (ṭayyibāt) begets contentment with God." These good things are completed by drinking cold water and pouring lukewarm water upon the hand when washing. Al-Maʾmūn said: "Drinking water with ice purifies gratitude." And some of the literati said: "When you invite your brothers and feed them ḥusrumiyyah and būrāniyyah and give them cold water to drink, you have perfected the hospitality." Some spent dirhams on hospitality, and a sage said: "We had no need of this — if your bread is good, your water cold, and your vinegar sour, that is sufficient." Another said: "Sweetness after food is better than a multitude of dishes, and being settled upon the table is better than adding two more dishes." It is said that the angels attend the table when there is greens upon it — that too is recommended, for the adornment with greenery therein. In the report: "The table that was sent down upon the Children of Israel had upon it every kind of greens except leeks." Upon it was a fish — at its head vinegar, at its tail salt — and seven loaves, upon each loaf an olive and a pomegranate seed. When all this is gathered, it is good for concordance.

**Third**: That he present the most delicate of the dishes first, so that whoever wishes may take his fill of it and not eat excessively afterward. The habit of the luxurious is to present the coarse first, so that the appetite is renewed by encountering the delicate afterward — and that contradicts the Sunnah, for it is a stratagem for eating excessively. It was from the Sunnah of the early generations to bring out all the dishes at once and to line up the bowls of food upon the table, so that each person eats what he desires. If he has only one dish, let him mention it so they may take their fill of it and not wait for something better. It is related of one of the men of magnanimity (murūʾah) that he would write a list of the dishes he would bring out and present it to the guests. One of the shaykhs said: "A dish was presented to one of the shaykhs in Syria, and I said: 'With us in Iraq, this is only presented last.' He said: 'And so with us in Syria' — and he had no other dish, so I was ashamed before him." Another said: "We were a group at a hospitality, and dishes of roasted heads were presented to us — cooked and dried. We did not eat, waiting for a dish or a roast lamb after them.
