Then he brought the basin and presented nothing else. We looked at one another, and one of the shaykhs — who was humorous — said: 'God Almighty is able to create heads without bodies.' He said: 'And we spent that night hungry, seeking crumbs until dawn.'" For this reason, it is recommended to present everything at once, or to inform of what one has.

**Fourth**: That he not hasten to remove the dishes before they have been able to take their fill, until they lift their hands from them. For perhaps among them is one for whom the remainder of that dish is more desirable than what was brought, or he still has a need to eat — and it would be spoiled for him by the hastening. This is part of being settled upon the table, which is said to be better than two dishes — perhaps the meaning intended is cutting off haste, and perhaps he meant the spaciousness of the place.

It is related of al-Sattūrī — who was a humorous Sufi — that he attended the table of one of the worldly people. A roast lamb was presented to them, and the master of the table was miserly. When he saw the people tearing the lamb apart, each tearing a piece, his chest tightened and he said: "O boy, raise it to the children!" The lamb was raised into the house, and al-Sattūrī stood up running after the lamb. It was said to him: "Where are you going?" He said: "I will eat with the children." The man was ashamed and ordered the lamb to be brought back.

From this art is that the master of the table should not lift his hand before the people, for they would be shy. Rather, he should be the last of them in eating. One of the generous men used to inform the people of all the dishes and leave them to take their fill. When they neared completion, he would kneel upon his knees, extend his hand to the food, eat, and say: "In the name of God — help me, may God bless you and upon you." The predecessors used to deem this excellent from him.

**Fifth**: That he present food in the measure of sufficiency. For falling short of sufficiency is a deficiency in magnanimity, and exceeding it is affectation and ostentation — especially when his soul does not permit them to eat it all. Unless he presents much while being well-disposed were they to take it all, intending to seek blessing in the leftover of their food — for in the hadith: "It will not be reckoned against him." Ibrāhīm ibn Adham (God's mercy be upon him) presented much food upon his table, and Sufyān said to him: "O Abū Isḥāq, do you not fear this is extravagance (sarf)?" Ibrāhīm said: "There is no extravagance in food." If this intention is not present, then multiplying is affectation. Ibn Masʿūd (God be pleased with him) said: "We were forbidden to respond to the invitation of one who boasts with his food." And a group of the Companions disliked eating the food of ostentation.

From this is that no leftover food was ever raised from before the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him), because they would not present except the measure of need, and they would not eat to full satiety. He ought to set aside first the portion of the household, so that their eyes are not straining toward the return of something from it — for perhaps it will not return, and their chests would constrict and their tongues would be unleashed against the guests, and he would have fed the guests what is followed by the dislike of a people — and that is treachery against them.

As for what remains of the foods, it is not for the guests to take — that which the Sufis call "the slip" (al-zallah) — unless the master of the food explicitly grants permission from a content heart, or it is known by an indication of his state that he delights in it. If he suspects his dislike, it should not be taken. And when his contentment is known, one should observe justice and fairness with the companions — one should not take except what is his share, or what his companion is pleased with willingly, not out of shyness.

As for the departure: It has three etiquettes.

**First**: That he go out with the guest to the door of the house — and that is Sunnah, and it is from honoring the guest, which has been commanded. The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "Whoever believes in God and the Last Day, let him honor his guest." And he (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "Indeed, from the Sunnah of the guest is that he be escorted to the door of the house." Abū Qatādah said: "The delegation of the Negus arrived upon the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him), and he stood up to serve them himself. His companions said: 'We will suffice you, O Messenger of God.' He said: 'No — they honored my companions, and I love to repay them.'" The completion of honor is a cheerful face and pleasant speech upon entry, exit, and at the table. It was said to al-Awzāʿī (God be pleased with him): "What is the honor of the guest?" He said: "A cheerful face and pleasant speech." Yazīd ibn Abī Ziyād said: "I never entered upon ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Laylā but he told us a good hadith and fed us good food."

**Second**: That the guest depart with a contented soul — even if there was a shortcoming in his treatment — for that is from good character and humility. The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "Indeed, a man attains by his good character the rank of the one who fasts and stands in prayer." One of the predecessors was invited by a messenger, but the messenger did not find him. When he heard, he attended — but they had already dispersed, finished, and left. The master of the house came out to him and said: "The people have left." He said: "Is there any remainder?" He said: "No." He said: "A crumb, if any remains?" He said: "None remains." He said: "The pot — let me wipe it." He said: "I have washed it." So he departed praising God Almighty. He was questioned about that and said: "The man did well — he invited us with intention and refused us with intention." This is the meaning of humility and good character.

It is related that the master of Abū al-Qāsim al-Junayd was invited by a boy to his father's invitation four times, and the father refused him all four times — while he (the master) returned each time to delight the boy's heart by his attendance and the father's heart by his departure. These are souls that have been tamed by humility before God Almighty and have found tranquility in tawḥīd, and have come to witness in every refusal and acceptance a lesson between themselves and their Lord. They are not broken by what occurs from servants of humiliation, just as they do not rejoice in what occurs from them of honor — rather, they see all from the One, the Subduer. For this reason, one of them said: "I do not respond to the invitation except because I am reminded by it of the food of Paradise" — that is, it is good food whose toil, burden, and reckoning are borne from us.

**Third**: That he not depart except with the contentment and permission of the master of the house, and he should observe his heart in the measure of the stay. When he alights as a guest, he should not exceed three days — for perhaps the host would become weary of him and need to expel him. The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "Hospitality is three days; whatever exceeds that is charity (ṣadaqah)." Yes — if the master of the house urges him insistently from a pure heart, then he may stay at that point. And it is recommended that he have a bed for the guest who alights. The Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "A bed for the man, a bed for the woman, a bed for the guest — and the fourth is for Satan."

chapters.title_en: A Chapter Gathering Scattered Virtuous and Lawful Etiquettes and Prohibitions
chapters.arabic_text:
|| فصل يجمع آدابا ومناهي طيبة وشرعية متفرقة

الأول حكي عن إبراهيم النخعي أنه قال الأكل في السوق دناءة (3)
وأسنده إلى رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم وإسناده قريب
وقد نقل ضده عن ابن عمر رضي الله عنهما أنه قال كنا نأكل عهد رسول الله
صلى الله عليه وسلم PageV02P018
ونحن نمشي ونشرب ونحن قيام (1)
ورؤي بعض المشايخ من المتصوفة المعروفين يأكل في السوق فقيل له في ذلك
فقال ويحك أجوع في السوق وآكل في البيت فقيل تدخل المسجد قال أستحي أن أدخل
بيته للأكل فيه
ووجه الجمع أن الأكل في السوق تواضع وترك تكلف من بعض الناس فهو حسن وخرق
مروءة من بعضهم فهو مكروه وهو مختلف بعادات البلاد وأحوال الأشخاص فمن لا
يليق ذلك بسائر أعماله حمل ذلك على قلة المروءة وفرط الشره ويقدح ذلك في
الشهادة ومن يليق ذلك بجميع أحواله وأعمالهفي ترك التكلف كان ذلك منه
تواضعا
الثاني قال علي رضي الله عنه من ابتدأ غذاءه بالملح أذهب الله عنه سبعين
نوعا من البلاء ومن أكل في يوم سبع تمرات عجوة قتلت كل دابة في بطنه ومن
أكل كل يوم إحدى وعشرين زبيبة حمرا لم ير في جسده شيئا يكرهه واللحم ينبت
اللحم والثريد طعام العرب والبسقارجات تعظم البطن وترخي الأليتين ولحم
البقر داء ولبنها شفاء وسمنها دواء والشحم يخرج مثله من الداء ولن تستشفي
النفساء بشيء أفضل من الرطب والسمك يذيب الجسد وقراءة القرآن والسواك
يذهبان البلغم ومن أراد البقاء ولا بقاء فليباكر بالغداء وليكرر العشاء
وليلبس الحذاء ولن يتداوى الناس بشيء مثل السمن وليقل غشيان النساء وليخف
الرداء وهو الدين
الثالث قال الحجاج لبعض الأطباء صف لي صفة آخذ بها ولا أعدوها قال
لا تنكح من النساء إلا فتاة ولا تأكل من اللحم إلا فتيا ولا تأكل المطبوخ
حتى يتم نضجه ولا تشربن دواء إلا من علة ولا تأكل من الفاكهة إلا نضيجها
ولا تأكلن طعاما إلا أجدت مضغه وكل ما أحببت من الطعام ولا تشربن عليه فإذا
شربت فلا تأكلن عليه شيئا ولا تحبس الغائط والبول وإذا أكلت بالنهار فنم
وإذا أكلت بالليل فامش قبل أن تنام ولو مائة خطوة
وفي معناه قول العرب تغد تمد تعش تمش يعني تمدد كما قال الله تعال ثم ذهب
إلى أهله يتمطى أي يتمطط
ويقال إن حبس البول يفسد الجسد كما يفسد النهر ما حوله إذا سد مجراه
الرابع في الخبر قطع العروق مسقمة وترك العشاء مهرمة (2)
والعرب تقول ترك الغداء يذهب بشحم الكاذة يعني الآلية وقال بعض الحكماء
لابنه يا بني لا تخرج من منزلك حتى تأخذ حلمك أي تتغذى إذ به يبقى الحلم
ويزول الطيش  وهو أيضا أقل لشهوته لما يرى في السوق
وقال حكيم لسمين أرى عليك قطيفة من نسج أضراسك فمم هي قال من أكل لباب
البر وصغار المعز وأدهن بجام بنفسج وألبس الكتان
الخامس الحمية تضر بالصحيح كما يضر تركها بالمريض هكذا قيل
وقال بعضهم من احتمى فهو على يقين من المكروه وعلى شك من العوافي وهذا
حسن في حال الصحة ورأى رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم صهيبا يأكل تمرا وإحدى
عينيه رمداء فقال
أتأكل التمر وأنت رمد فقال يا رسول الله إنما آكل بالشق الآخر (3)
يعني جانب السليمة فضحك رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
السادس أنه يستحب أن يحمل طعام إلى أهل الميت ولما جاء نعي جعفر بن أبي
طالب قال صلى الله عليه وسلم إن آل جعفر شغلوا بميتهم عن صنع طعامهم
فاحملوا إليهم ما يأكلون (4)
فذلك سنة
وإذا قدم ذلك إلى الجمع حل الأكل منه ما يهيأ للنوائح والمعينات عليه
بالبكاء والجزع PageV02P019
فلا ينبغي أن يؤكل معهم
السابع لا ينبغي أن يحضر طعام ظالم فإن أكره فليقلل الأكل ولا يقصد
الطعام الأطيب رد بعض المزكين شهادة من حضر طعام سلطان فقال كنت مكرها فقال
رأيتك تقصد الأطيب وتكبر اللقمة وما كنت مكرها عليه وأجبر السلطان هذا
المزكي على الأكل فقال إما أن آكل وأخلي التزكية أو أزكي ولا آكل فلم يجدوا
بدا من تزكيته فتركوه
وحكي أن ذا النون المصري حبس ولم يأكل أياما في السجن فكانت له أخت في
الله فبعثت إليه طعاما من مغزلها على يد السجان فامتنع فلم يأكل فعاتبته
المرأة بعد ذلك فقال كان حلالا ولكن جاءني على طبق ظالم وأشار به إلى يد
السجان وهذا غاية الورع
الثامن حكي عن فتح الموصلي رحمه الله أنه دخل على بشر الحافي زائرا فأخرج
بشر درهما فدفعه لأحمد الجلاء خادمه وقال اشتر به طعاما جيدا وأدما طيبا
قال فاشتريت خبزا نظيفا وقلت لم يقل رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم لشيء
اللهم بارك لنا فيه  وزدنا منه (1)
سوى اللبن فاشتريت اللبن واشتريت تمرا جيدا فقدمت إليه فأكل وأخذ الباقي
فقال بشر أتدرون لم قلت اشتر طعاما طيبا لأن الطعام الطيب يستخرج خالص
الشكر أتدرون لم لم يقل لي كل لأنه ليس للضيف أن يقول لصاحب الدار كل
أتدرون لم حمل ما بقي لأنه إذا صح التوكل لم يضر الحمل
وحكى أبو علي الروذباري رحمه الله تعالى أنه اتخذ ضيافة فأوقد فيها ألف
سراج فقال له رجل قد أسرفت فقال له ادخل فكل ما أوقدته لغير
chapters.anchors:
- Root: د-ن-و (danā'a)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Lowness, baseness, despicableness; a state of moral degradation.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A deficiency in religious and worldly honor (murū'a) that diminishes one's standing before God and men.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal in reference to physical lowness; metaphorical here for moral baseness in social conduct.
- Root: م-ر-ء (murū'a)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Complete manliness; integrity of character; social honorableness.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The composite virtue of piety, decency, and propriety that safeguards one's reputation.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Used literally for manly virtue; contextually shifts to social decorum (ḥaqīqah vs. majāz).
- Root: ش-ر-ه (sharah)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Excessive greed, voracious appetite, insatiable craving.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A blameworthy trait opposing contentment (qanā'a); linked to worldly attachment.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for gluttony; metaphorically for moral laxity in testimony.
- Root: ح-م-ي (ḥimyah)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Restraint, protection, guarding against harm.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Dietary abstention as a means of bodily preservation, a secondary virtue.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for medical regimen; metaphorical for spiritual self-discipline.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Constructions (al-sharṭ wa al-istithnā') — Governing clauses with 'man' (whoever) and 'law' (if) to express universal rulings and hypothetical cases, ensuring precise legal nuance.
chapters.translation:
I say: This section gathers scattered virtuous and lawful etiquettes and prohibitions.

The first: It is narrated from Ibrahim al-Nakha'i that he said: "Eating in the marketplace is baseness." He attributed this to the Messenger of God (peace be upon him), and its chain of transmission is close. Yet the opposite is transmitted from Ibn 'Umar (may God be pleased with them both), who said: "We used to eat during the era of the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) while walking, and drink while standing." And some renowned Sufi masters were seen eating in the marketplace, and it was said to him about that, so he replied: "Woe to you! I become hungry in the marketplace, so I eat in the house?" It was said: "Do you enter the mosque?" He said: "I am ashamed to enter His house to eat therein."

The reconciliation is that eating in the marketplace is humility and abandonment of affectation for some people, so it is good; but it is a breach of manliness for others, so it is disliked. It varies with the customs of lands and the conditions of persons. Whoever this does not befit in all his deeds, it is attributed to lack of manliness and excess of greed, and it impugns his testimony. Whoever this befits in all his states and deeds, in abandoning affectation, it is from him an act of humility.

The second: 'Ali (may God be pleased with him) said: "Whoever begins his meal with salt, God removes from him seventy types of affliction. Whoever eats seven 'ajwa dates in a day, they kill every creature in his belly. Whoever eats twenty-one red raisins each day, he sees nothing in his body that he dislikes. Meat grows flesh, and tharīd is the food of the Arabs. Large quantities of food enlarge the belly and slacken the buttocks. Beef is a disease, its milk is a cure, and its butter is a medicine. Fat expels its like of disease. A postpartum woman will never be healed by anything better than fresh dates. Fish dissolves the body. Reciting the Quran and using the toothstick remove phlegm. Whoever desires longevity—though there is no longevity—let him eat breakfast early, repeat the evening meal, wear sandals, and let people not treat themselves with anything like ghee. Let him reduce intercourse with women, and let him lighten the cloak—that is, the religion."

The third: Al-Hajjaj said to one of the physicians: "Describe for me a regimen I may adopt and not exceed." He said: "Do not marry any woman except a virgin, do not eat any meat except tender young meat, do not eat cooked food until it is fully done, do not drink any medicine except for an ailment, do not eat any fruit except its ripe one, and do not eat any food unless you chew it thoroughly. Eat whatever food you like, but do not drink over it; and if you drink, do not eat anything over it. Do not withhold stool or urine. If you eat during the day, sleep; and if you eat at night, walk before you sleep, even a hundred steps."

In its meaning is the saying of the Arabs: "Eat breakfast, stretch; eat dinner, walk"—meaning stretch out, as God (exalted be He) said: {«Then he went to his family, stretching himself»} (Q. 75:33), i.e., stretching languidly.

It is said that withholding urine corrupts the body just as a river corrupts what surrounds it when its channel is blocked.

The fourth: In the report: "Cutting the veins is sickening, and abandoning the evening meal is aging." The Arabs say: "Abandoning breakfast removes the fat of the kādha"—meaning the tail. One of the sages said to his son: "O my son, do not leave your house until you take your ḥilm"—meaning breakfast, for by it forbearance remains and rashness departs. It also lessens his appetite for what he sees in the marketplace.

A sage said to a fat man: "I see upon you a quilt woven by your molars—what is it made of?" He said: "From eating the core of wheat, young goats, anointing with violet oil, and wearing linen."

The fifth: Abstinence harms the healthy just as its abandonment harms the sick—thus it is said. Some said: "Whoever practices abstinence is certain of dislike and doubtful of well-being." This is good in a state of health. The Messenger of God (peace be upon him) saw Suhayb eating dates while one of his eyes was inflamed, so he said: "Do you eat dates while you are inflamed?" He replied: "O Messenger of God, I only eat with the other side"—meaning the healthy side. The Messenger of God (peace be upon him) laughed.

The sixth: It is recommended to carry food to the family of the deceased. When the news of Ja'far ibn Abi Talib's death came, he (peace be upon him) said: "The family of Ja'far are occupied with their dead from preparing their food, so carry to them what they may eat." That is the Sunnah.

When that is presented to a gathering, it is permissible to eat from it. But what is prepared for the wailing women and those who assist them with weeping and lamentation should not be eaten with them.

The seventh: One should not attend the food of a tyrant. If compelled, let him eat little and not seek the finest food. Some testifiers rejected the testimony of one who attended a sultan's meal. He said: "I was compelled." He replied: "I saw you seeking the finest and enlarging the morsel—you were not compelled in that." The sultan forced this testifier to eat, so he said: "Either I eat and relinquish the testimony, or I testify and do not eat." They found no alternative but to accept his testimony, so they left him.

It is narrated that Dhu al-Nun al-Misri was imprisoned and did not eat for days in jail. He had a sister in God, so she sent him food from her spinning work via the jailer's hand. He refused and did not eat. The woman reproached him afterward, and he said: "It was lawful, but it came to me on the tray of a tyrant"—pointing to the jailer's hand. This is the utmost scrupulousness (wara').

The eighth: It is narrated from Fath al-Mawsili (may God have mercy on him) that he entered upon Bishr al-Hafi as a visitor. Bishr brought out a dirham, gave it to Ahmad al-Jalla', his servant, and said: "Buy with it good food and fine relish." He said: "So I bought clean bread, and I said: The Messenger of God (peace be upon him) did not say for anything: 'O God, bless us in it and increase us from it'—except for milk. So I bought milk, and I bought good dates, and I presented it to him. He ate and took the remainder." Then Bishr said: "Do you know why I said, 'Buy good food'? Because good food extracts pure gratitude. Do you know why he did not say to me, 'Eat'? Because it is not for the guest to say to the host, 'Eat.' Do you know why he carried what remained? Because when trust in God (tawakkul) is sound, carrying does not harm."

Abu 'Ali al-Rudhbari (may God have mercy on him) narrated that he prepared a feast and lit a thousand lamps in it. A man said to him: "You have been extravagant." He said: "Enter and extinguish whatever I lit for other than God." The man entered and could not extinguish a single one, so he was silenced.

Abu 'Ali al-Rudhbari bought loads of sugar and ordered the confectioners until they built a wall of sugar with battlements and prayer niches on carved columns, all of sugar. Then he invited the Sufis until they demolished it and plundered it.

The ninth: Al-Shafi'i (may God be pleased with him) said: "Eating is of four kinds: eating with one finger is from hatred, with two fingers from pride, with three fingers from the Sunnah, and with four or five from greed. Four things strengthen the body: eating meat, smelling perfume, frequent washing without intercourse, and wearing linen. Four things weaken the body: frequent intercourse, excessive worry, drinking much water on an empty stomach, and eating much sour food. Four things strengthen the eyesight: sitting facing the qibla, applying kohl at sleep, looking at greenery, and cleaning one's garments. Four things weaken the eyesight: looking at filth, looking at a crucified person, looking at a woman's private parts, and sitting with one's back to the qibla. Four things increase intercourse: eating sparrows, eating the greater itrifal, eating pistachios, and eating watercress."

Sleep is of four kinds: sleeping on the back—the sleep of the prophets (peace be upon them), reflecting on the creation of the heavens and the earth; sleeping on the right side—the sleep of scholars and worshippers; sleeping on the left side—the sleep of kings, to digest their food; and sleeping on the face—the sleep of devils.

Four things increase intellect: abandoning excess speech, using the toothstick, sitting with the righteous and scholars. Four things are acts of worship: not taking a step except with ablution, frequent prostration, adhering to mosques, and frequent recitation of the Quran.

He also said: "I marvel at one who enters the bathhouse on an empty stomach, then delays eating after exiting—how does he not die? And I marvel at one who is cupped, then hastens to eat—how does he not die?" He said: "I have seen nothing more beneficial in an epidemic than violet—anointed with it and drunk."

And God knows best what is correct.

chapters.title_en: The Book of the Etiquettes of Marriage — Book Two of the Quarter of Customs from The Revival of the Religious Sciences
chapters.arabic_text:
| كتاب آداب النكاح وهو الكتاب الثاني من ربع العادات من كتاب إحياء علوم الدين

بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم
الحمد لله الذي لا تصادف سهام الأوهام في عجائب صنعه مجرى ولا ترجع
العقول عن أوائل بدائعها إلا والهة حيرى ولا تزال لطائف نعمه على العالمين
تترى فهي تتوالى عليهم اختيارا وقهرا
ومن بدائع ألطافه أن خلق من الماء بشرا فجعله نسبا وصهرا وسلط على الخلق
شهوة اضطرهم بها الحراثة جبرا واستبقى بهم نسلهم إقهارا وقسرا
ثم عظم أمر الأنساب وجعل لها قدرا فحرم بسببها السفاح وبالغ في تقبيحه
ردعا وزجرا وجعل اقتحامه جريمة فاحشة وأمر إمرا وندب إلى النكاح وحث عليه
استحبابا وأمرا فسبحان من كتب الموت على عباده فأذلهم به هدما وكسرا ثم بث
بذور النطف في أراضي الأرحام وأنشأ منها خلقا وجعله لكسر الموت جبرا تنبيها
على أن بحار المقادير فياضة على العالمين نفعا وضرا وخيرا وشرا وعسرا ويسرا
وطيا ونشرا والصلاة والسلام على محمد المبعوث بالإنذار والبشرى وعلى آله
وأصحابه صلاة لا يستطيع لها الحساب عدا ولا حصرا وسلم تسليما كثيرا
أما بعد فإن النكاح معين على الدين ومهين للشياطين وحصن دون عدو الله
حصين وسبب للتكثير الذي به مباهاة سيد المرسلين لسائر النبيين فما أحراه
بأن تتحرى أسبابه وتحفظ سننه وآدابه وتشرح مقاصده وآرابه وتفصل فصوله
وأبوابه
والقدر المهم من أحكامه ينكشف في ثلاثة أبواب
الباب الأول في الترغيب فيه وعنه
الباب الثاني في الآداب المرعية في العقد والعاقدين
الباب الثالث في آداب المعاشرة بعد العقد إلى الفراق
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ن-ك-ح (n-k-ḥ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The root denotes joining, coupling, or uniting; in marriage it signifies the contractual union of spouses, with a core sense of "pairing" or "interlocking" (as in the interlocking of teeth or the rising of rain-laden clouds).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, nikāḥ is the divinely sanctioned bond that channels the God-given sexual urge (shahwah) into lawful procreation, thereby serving as a means of preserving lineage (nasab) and fulfilling the command of the Prophet to multiply.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literally (ḥaqīqah) it is the marriage contract; metaphorically (majāz) it can denote the act of intercourse itself. Here al-Ghazālī employs it in its primary contractual sense, while weaving in its teleological purpose.
- Root: ش-ه-و (sh-h-w)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Desire, craving, or appetite; the innate inclination of the soul toward what pleases it, whether physical or otherwise.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The God-implanted appetite (shahwah) is a neutral faculty; its moral value derives from its direction—lawful marriage channels it toward divine ends, while unlawful indulgence (sifāḥ) corrupts it.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Used literally here for physical desire, but with a rhetorical twist: God "subjugated" (sallaṭa) it upon creation, making it a compelled instrument (jabr) for the preservation of the species.
- Root: ن-س-ب (n-s-b)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Lineage, kinship, or relation; the web of familial ties that binds individuals to ancestors and descendants.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In the Qur'anic frame, nasab and ṣihr (affinity by marriage) are divine signs (āyāt) of social order; their sanctity demands the prohibition of fornication (sifāḥ) to protect genealogical integrity.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for blood kinship; metaphorically extended to the "honor" (qadr) God bestows upon such ties, making their violation a grave offense.
- Sībawayh Rule: The Rule of Concessive Clauses (al-ḥāl wa al-tamyīz) — The opening employs a series of circumstantial accusatives (e.g., "اختيارا وقهرا," "جبرا," "إقهارا وقسرا," "ردعا وزجرا," "استحبابا وأمرا," "هدما وكسرا," "جبرا," "نفعا وضرا...") that function as modal qualifiers, specifying the manner of divine acts. These are maṣdar-based adverbs (al-mafʿūl al-muṭlaq) used to intensify and clarify the verbal action, a hallmark of Ghazālī's rhythmic, homiletic prose.
chapters.translation:
In the Name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

Praise be to God, against whose wondrous handiwork the arrows of vain imaginings find no course to run, and from whose primordial marvels the intellects recoil only bewildered and enamored. The subtle bounties of His grace continue upon all worlds in succession—they pour upon them by choice and by compulsion.

Among the marvels of His subtle kindness is that He created from water a human being, then made him kin by lineage and by marriage. He subjugated upon creation a lust by which He compelled them to till the soil, and through it He preserved their progeny by force and constraint. Then He magnified the matter of genealogies and assigned to them a station of honor; for their sake He forbade fornication and went to great lengths in vilifying it, as a deterrent and a rebuke. He made its commission a heinous crime and a grave affair. He summoned to marriage and urged it upon them, as a recommendation and a command. Glory be to Him who wrote death upon His servants and thereby humbled them, as demolition and shattering. Then He scattered the seeds of sperm into the furrows of wombs and brought forth from them a creation, making it a mending for the breaking of death—a notification that the seas of destinies overflow upon all worlds with benefit and harm, good and evil, ease and hardship, folding and unfolding.

And the blessings and peace be upon Muḥammad, sent forth with warning and glad tidings, and upon his family and companions—a blessing whose reckoning no arithmetic can count or encompass—and abundant peace.

To proceed: Verily, marriage is an aid to religion, a humiliator of devils, a fortress against the enemy of God, and a means to the multiplication by which the Master of the Messengers boasts over the rest of the prophets. How fitting it is that one should pursue its causes, preserve its normative practices (sunan) and etiquettes (ādāb), expound its purposes and aims, and detail its chapters and sections.

The essential portion of its rulings unfolds in three chapters:

Chapter One: On the encouragement of marriage and the discouragement from it.
Chapter Two: On the etiquettes observed in the contract and by the two contracting parties.
Chapter Three: On the etiquettes of cohabitation after the contract until separation.

chapters.title_en: The First Chapter on Encouragement and Discouragement of Marriage
chapters.arabic_text:
|| الباب الأول في الترغيب في النكاح والترغيب عنه

اعلم أن العلماء قد اختلفوا في فضل النكاح فبالغ بعضهم فيه حتى زعم أنه
أفضل من التخلي لعبادة الله واعترف آخرون بفضله ولكن قدموا عليه التخلي
لعبادة الله مهما لم تتق النفس إلى النكاح توقانا  يشوش الحال ويدعو إلى
الوقاع
وقال آخرون الأفضل تركه في زماننا هذا وقد كان له فضيلة من قبل إذ لم تكن
الأكساب محظورة وأخلاق النساء مذمومة
ولا ينكشف الحق فيه إلا بان نقدم أولا ما ورد من الأخبار والآثار في
الترغيب فيه والترغيب عنه ثم نشرح فوائد النكاح وغوائله حتى يتضح منها
فضيلة النكاح وتركه في حق كل من سلم من غوائله أو لم يسلم منه
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ن-ك-ح (n-k-ḥ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The root denotes the contractual union of marriage, with primary lexical sense of "joining" or "coupling" (al-ḍamm wa al-jamʿ), extending to the marital contract itself.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, nikāḥ signifies the licit bond (ʿaqd) sanctioned by divine law, distinct from mere carnal union; its virtue is assessed by intent (niyyah) and resultant spiritual state.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) refers to the legal contract; metaphorical (majāz) may extend to coitus, but here the discourse concerns the act of contracting marriage as a devotional choice.
- Root: خ-ل-و (kh-l-w)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is "emptiness" or "solitude" — being alone, free from occupation or company.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In ascetic theology, khalwah denotes seclusion for worship (tafarrugh li-ʿibādah), a state of devotional withdrawal from worldly entanglements.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: physical solitude; metaphorical: the heart's detachment from distractions, here contrasted with marriage as an occupation.
- Root: غ-و-ل (gh-w-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The root signifies "mischief," "harm," or "that which corrupts" — a destructive consequence or evil outcome.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In moral theology, ghāʾilah denotes the latent spiritual harm or corrupting effect of an act, often hidden until manifested.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: a calamity that befalls; metaphorical: the subtle detriments of marriage that undermine one's religious state.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Constructions (al-sharṭ wa al-istithnāʾ) — The sentence "مهما لم تتق النفس" employs the conditional particle (mā mā) governing a negated protasis, while "إلا بان نقدم" uses the exceptive (istithnāʾ) to restrict the means of clarification, requiring careful parsing of the apodosis.
chapters.translation:
I say: Know that the scholars have differed concerning the merit of marriage. Some among them went to extremes in it, even claiming that it is more excellent than devoting oneself exclusively to the worship of God. Others acknowledged its merit, but gave precedence to devoting oneself exclusively to the worship of God, whenever the soul does not crave marriage with a craving that would disturb one's state and summon one to coitus.

And others said: The better course is to abandon it in our present age, though it possessed merit in former times, when means of livelihood were not forbidden and the morals of women were not blameworthy.

The truth in this matter is not unveiled except by our first presenting what has come down of reports (akhbār) and traditions (āthār) concerning encouragement toward it and discouragement from it. Then we shall expound the benefits (fawāʾid) of marriage and its harms (ghawāʾil), so that thereby the merit of marriage and of abandoning it may become clear with respect to every person who is safe from its harms or is not safe from them.

chapters.title_en: Encouragement of Marriage (al-Targhīb fī al-Nikāḥ)
chapters.arabic_text:
||| ا الترغيب في النكاح

أما من الآيات فقد قال تعالى وانكحوا الأيامى منكم وهذا أمر وقال تعالى
فلا تعضلوهن أن ينكحن أزواجهن وهذا منع من العضل ونهي عنه
وقال تعالى في وصف الرسل ومدحهم ولقد أرسلنا رسلا من قبلك وجعلنا لهم
أزواجا وذرية فذكر ذلك في معرض الامتنان وإظهار الفضل
ومدح أولياءه بسؤال ذلك في الدعاء فقال والذين يقولون ربنا هب لنا من
أزواجنا وذرياتنا قرة أعين الآية ويقال أن الله تعالى لم يذكر
PageV02P021
في كتابه من الأنبياء إلا المتأهلين فقالوا إن يحيى صلى الله عليه وسلم
قد تزوج ولم يجامع قيل إنما فعل ذلك لنيل الفضل وإقامة السنة وقيل لغض
البصر وأما عيسى عليه السلام فإنه سينكح إذا نزل الأرض ويولد له
وأما الأخبار فقوله صلى الله عليه وسلم النكاح سنتي فمن رغب عن سنتي فقد
رغب عني وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم النكاح سنتي فمن أحب فطرتي فليستن بسنتي
(1)
وقال أيضا صلى الله عليه وسلم تناكحوا تكثروا فإني أباهي بكم الأمم يوم
القيامة حتى بالسقط (2)
وقال أيضا صلى الله عليه وسلم من رغب عن سنتي فليس مني وإن من سنتي
النكاح فمن أحبني فليستن بسنتي (3)
وقال النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم من ترك التزويج مخافة العيلة فليس منا (4)
وهذا ذم لعلة الامتناع لا لأصل الترك وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم من كان ذا
طول فليتزوج (5)
وقال من استطاع منكم الباءة فليتزوج فإنه أغض للبصر وأحصن للفرج ومن لا
فليصم فإن الصوم له وجاء (6)
وهذا يدل على أن سبب الترغيب فيه خوف الفساد  في العين والفرج
والوجاء هو عبارة عن رض الخصيتين للفحل حتى تزول فحولته فهو مستعار للضعف
عن الوقاع في الصوم
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم إذا أتاكم من ترضون دينه وأمانته فزوجوه إلا
تفعلوه تكن فتنة في الأرض وفساد كبير (7)
وهذا أيضا تعليل الترغيب لخوف الفساد
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم من نكح لله وأنكح لله استحق ولاية الله (8)
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم من تزوج فقد أحرز شطر دينه فليتق الله في الشطر
الثاني (9)
وهذا أيضا إشارة إلى أن فضيلته لأجل التحرز من المخالفة تحصنا من الفساد
فكأن المفسد لدين المرء في الأغلب فرجه وبطنه وقد كفى بالتزويج أحدهما
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم كل عمل ابن آدم ينقطع إلا ثلاث ولد صالح يدعو له
(10)
الحديث
ولا يوصل إلى هذا إلا بالنكاح PageV02P022
وأما الآثار فقال عمر رضي الله عنه لا يمنع من النكاح إلا عجز أو فجور
فبين أن الدين غير مانع منه وحصر المانع في أمرين مذمومين
وقال ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما لا يتم نسك الناسك حتى يتزوج
يحتمل أن جعله من النسك وتتمة له
ولكن الظاهر أنه أراد به أنه لا يسلم قلبه لغلبة الشهوة إلا بالتزويج ولا
يتم النسك إلا بفراغ القلب ولذلك كان يجمع غلمانه لما أدركوا عكرمة وكريبا
وغيرهما ويقول إن أردتم النكاح أنكحتكم فإن العبد إذا زنى نزع الإيمان من
قلبه
وكان ابن مسعود رضي الله عنه يقول لو لم يبق من عمري إلا عشرة أيام
لأحببت أن أتزوج لكيلا ألقى الله عزبا ومات امرأتان لمعاذ بن جبل رضي الله
عنه في الطاعون وكان هو أيضا مطعونا فقال زوجوني فإني أكره أن ألقى الله
عزبا
وهذا منهما يدل على أنهما رأيا في النكاح فضلا لا من حيث التحرز عن غائلة
الشهوة
وكان عمر رضي الله عنه يكثر النكاح ويقول ما أتزوج إلا لأجل الولد وكان
بعض الصحابة قد انقطع إلى رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم يخدمه ويبيت عنده
لحاجة إن طرقته  فقال له رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم ألا تتزوج فقال يا
رسول الله إني فقير لا شيء لي وأنقطع عن خدمتك فسكت
ثم عاد ثانيا فأعاد الجواب
ثم تفكر الصحابي وقال والله لرسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم أعلم بما
يصلحني في دنياي وآخرتي وما يقربني إلى الله مني ولئن قال لي الثالثة
لأفعلن
فقال له الثالثة ألا تتزوج قال فقلت يا رسول الله زوجني قال
اذهب إلى بني فلان فقل أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم يأمركم أن
تزوجوني فتاتكم قال فقلت يا رسول الله لا شيء لي فقال لأصحابه اجمعوا
لأخيكم وزن نواة من ذهب فجمعوا له فذهبوا به إلى القوم فأنكحوه فقال له
أولم وجمعوا له من الأصحاب شاة للوليمة (1)
وهذا التكرير يدل على فضل في نفس النكاح ويحتمل أنه توسم فيه الحاجة إلى
النكاح
وحكى أن بعض العباد في الأمم السالفة فاق أهل زمانه في العبادة فذكر لنبي
زمانه حسن عبادته فقال نعم الرجل هو لولا أنه تارك لشيء من السنة فاغتم
العابد لما سمع ذلك فسأل النبي عن ذلك فقال أنت تارك للتزويج فقال لست
أحرمه ولكني فقير وأنا عيال على الناس قال أنا أزوجك ابنتي فزوجه النبي
عليه السلام ابنته
وقال بشر بن الحرث فضل علي أحمد بن حنبل بثلاث بطلب الحلال لنفسه ولغيره
وأنا أطلبه لنفسي فقط ولاتساعه في النكاح وضيقي عنه ولأنه نصب إماما للعامة
ويقال إن أحمد رحمه الله تزوج في اليوم الثاني لوفاة أم ولده عبد الله
وقال أكره أن أبيت عزبا
وأما بشر فإنه لما قيل له
إن الناس يتكلمون فيك
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ن-ك-ح (n-k-ḥ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The root denotes the contractual union of marriage; linguistically it signifies "joining" or "coupling," and in legal usage, the marriage contract itself.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological terms, nikāḥ is the divinely ordained institution for lawful procreation (nasl) and the channeling of sexual desire (shahwah) within permissible bounds, serving both worldly and otherworldly ends.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Used literally (ḥaqīqah) for the marriage contract; metaphorically (majāz) for sexual intercourse itself, as in the verse {فَانكِحُوا مَا طَابَ لَكُم مِّنَ النِّسَاءِ}.
- Root: ع-ز-ب (ʿ-z-b)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: A state of being unmarried or without a spouse; solitude from conjugal life.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In ascetic discourse, ʿuzūbah (celibacy) is examined as a potential distraction from or aid to worship, depending on one's spiritual state.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for the unmarried state; metaphorically extended to denote spiritual isolation or lack of familial support.
- Root: ش-ه-و-ة (sh-h-w-h)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Desire or appetite, particularly sexual longing; the innate drive within the human constitution.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The divinely implanted urge (shahwah) that serves as a motive for procreation, yet requires regulation through marriage or fasting to prevent moral corruption (fasād).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for physical appetite; metaphorically, the soul's inclination toward worldly pleasures that must be disciplined.
- Root: و-ل-د (w-l-d)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Offspring, progeny; the act of begetting or giving birth.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The primary purpose (maqṣūd) of marriage—preserving the human species and securing righteous descendants who pray for their parents.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for biological offspring; metaphorically, spiritual legacy through righteous deeds and intercession.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Constructions (al-Sharṭ wa al-Istithnāʾ) — The text frequently employs conditional clauses (e.g., "من استطاع منكم الباءة فليتزوج") and exceptive particles (e.g., "إلا أن يعمل عملا لا يغفر له") to qualify rulings, requiring precise parsing to distinguish universal commands from context-bound exhortations.
chapters.translation:
I say: Now, regarding the encouragement to marry (al-targhīb fī al-nikāḥ).

As for the Quranic verses: Allah Most High has said: {وَأَنكِحُوا الْأَيَامَىٰ مِنكُمْ} "And marry the unmarried among you" — and this is a command. He also said: {فَلَا تَعْضُلُوهُنَّ أَن يَنكِحْنَ أَزْوَاجَهُنَّ} "Then do not hinder them from marrying their husbands" — and this is a prohibition against obstruction (al-ʿaḍl) and a forbiddance of it. And He said, describing the messengers and praising them: {وَلَقَدْ أَرْسَلْنَا رُسُلًا مِّن قَبْلِكَ وَجَعَلْنَا لَهُمْ أَزْوَاجًا وَذُرِّيَّةً} "And indeed We sent messengers before you and made for them spouses and offspring" — and He mentioned this in the context of bestowing favor and manifesting virtue. And He praised His saints for seeking this in supplication, saying: {وَالَّذِينَ يَقُولُونَ رَبَّنَا هَبْ لَنَا مِنْ أَزْوَاجِنَا وَذُرِّيَّاتِنَا قُرَّةَ أَعْيُنٍ} "And those who say: 'Our Lord, grant us from our spouses and our offspring comfort of eyes'" — and it is said that Allah Most High did not mention in His Book any of the prophets except those who were married. Thus they said concerning Yaḥyā (peace be upon him) that he married but did not consummate; it was said he did this to attain virtue and establish the Sunnah, and it was said to lower his gaze. As for ʿĪsā (peace be upon him), he will marry when he descends to earth and will have children.

As for the prophetic reports (al-akhbār): His saying (peace be upon him): "Marriage is my Sunnah; whoever turns away from my Sunnah has turned away from me." And he said (peace be upon him): "Marriage is my Sunnah; whoever loves my natural disposition (fiṭrah), let him follow my Sunnah." He also said (peace be upon him): "Marry and multiply, for I will boast of you before the nations on the Day of Resurrection, even by the miscarried fetus." And he said (peace be upon him): "Whoever turns away from my Sunnah is not of me; and indeed from my Sunnah is marriage, so whoever loves me, let him follow my Sunnah." And the Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "Whoever abandons marriage out of fear of poverty is not of us" — and this is a censure of the reason for abstention, not of the act of abstention itself. And he said (peace be upon him): "Whoever has means (ṭawl), let him marry." And he said: "Whoever among you has the ability (bāʾah), let him marry, for it is more lowering of the gaze and more protective of the private parts; and whoever cannot, let him fast, for fasting is a protection (wijāʾ) for him." This indicates that the cause of encouragement therein is the fear of corruption in the eye and the private parts. Al-wijāʾ is an expression for crushing the testicles of a stallion until its virility ceases — it is thus metaphorically used for the weakening of sexual capacity through fasting.

And he said (peace be upon him): "When one comes to you whose religion and trustworthiness you approve, then marry him; if you do not, there will be tribulation (fitnah) in the earth and great corruption" — and this too is an explanation of the encouragement due to fear of corruption. And he said (peace be upon him): "Whoever marries for Allah and gives in marriage for Allah has earned the guardianship (wilāyah) of Allah." And he said (peace be upon him): "Whoever marries has secured half of his religion; so let him fear Allah regarding the other half" — and this also points to the fact that its virtue is for the sake of guarding against transgression and protecting oneself from corruption, as if the corrupter of a man's religion is most often his private parts and his belly, and marriage suffices for one of them. And he said (peace be upon him): "Every deed of the son of Adam ceases except three: a righteous child who prays for him" — and one cannot attain this except through marriage.

As for the reports from the Companions (al-āthār): ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "Nothing prevents marriage except incapacity or lewdness" — thus clarifying that religion is not a preventer, and confining the preventer to two blameworthy matters. Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: "The devotional act (nusuk) of the devotee is not complete until he marries" — it is possible he made it part of the devotional act and its completion, but the apparent meaning is that he intended that one's heart is not safe from the dominance of desire except through marriage, and the devotional act is not complete except with a free heart. For this reason, he would gather his young servants when they reached maturity — ʿIkrimah, Kurayb, and others — and say: "If you wish marriage, I will marry you, for when a slave commits fornication, faith is pulled out of his heart." Ibn Masʿūd (may Allah be pleased with him) used to say: "If only ten days remained of my life, I would love to marry so that I do not meet Allah as an unmarried man (ʿazb)." And two wives of Muʿādh ibn Jabal (may Allah be pleased with him) died in the plague, and he himself was afflicted, yet he said: "Marry me, for I dislike meeting Allah as an unmarried man." This from both of them indicates that they saw in marriage a virtue beyond mere protection from the harm of desire.

ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) married frequently and said: "I marry only for the sake of offspring." And one of the Companions had devoted himself to the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him), serving him and spending the night at his door for any need that arose. The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) said to him: "Will you not marry?" He said: "O Messenger of Allah, I am poor, having nothing, and I would be cut off from your service." He fell silent. Then he returned a second time, and he repeated the answer. Then the Companion reflected and said: "By Allah, the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) knows better than I what is good for me in my worldly and otherworldly affairs, and what brings me nearer to Allah. If he says it a third time, I will do it." He said to him a third time: "Will you not marry?" He said: "I said, O Messenger of Allah, marry me." He said: "Go to such-and-such tribe and say: 'The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) commands you to marry me to your daughter.'" He said: "I said, O Messenger of Allah, I have nothing." He said to his Companions: "Gather for your brother the weight of a date-stone (nawāh) of gold." They gathered it for him, and they went with him to the people, and they married him. Then he said to him: "Hold a wedding feast (awlim)," and they gathered for him from the Companions a sheep for the feast. This repetition indicates a virtue in marriage itself, though it is possible he discerned in him a need for marriage.

It is narrated that one of the worshippers among previous nations surpassed the people of his time in worship. He was mentioned to the prophet of his time for his excellent worship, and he said: "What an excellent man he is, were it not that he has abandoned something of the Sunnah." The worshipper was grieved when he heard this and asked the prophet about it. He said: "You have abandoned marriage." He said: "I do not forbid it, but I am poor and dependent on people." He said: "I will marry you to my daughter." So the prophet (peace be upon him) married him to his daughter.

Bishr ibn al-Ḥārith said: "Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal surpassed me in three things: in seeking lawful sustenance (ḥalāl) for himself and for others, while I seek it only for myself; in his expansiveness in marriage while I am constrained from it; and because he was appointed as an Imām for the common people." It is said that Aḥmad (may Allah have mercy on him) married on the second day after the death of the mother of his son ʿAbdullāh, saying: "I dislike spending the night as an unmarried man." As for Bishr, when it was said to him: "People are speaking about you for abandoning marriage, saying he has abandoned the Sunnah," he said: "Tell them: he is occupied with the obligatory (farḍ) over the Sunnah." He was reproached another time and said: "Nothing prevents me from marriage except His saying: {وَلَهُنَّ مِثْلُ الَّذِي عَلَيْهِنَّ بِالْمَعْرُوفِ} 'And they have rights similar to those against them in accordance with what is recognized'." This was mentioned to Aḥmad, who said: "And where is the like of Bishr? He has sat upon the edge of a spear-point (ḥadd al-sinān)." Nevertheless, it is narrated that he was seen in a dream and asked: "What has Allah done with you?" He said: "My ranks in Paradise were raised, and I was shown the stations of the prophets, but I did not reach the stations of the married ones." In another narration, he said: "He said to me: 'I would not have liked you to meet Me as an unmarried man.'" We said to him: "What has Abu Naṣr al-Tammār done?" He said: "He was raised above me by seventy degrees." We said: "How, when we used to see you above him?" He said: "By his patience with his daughters and dependents."

Sufyān ibn ʿUyaynah said: "The multiplicity of women is not of the worldly life, for ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with him) was the most ascetic of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him), yet he had four wives and seventeen concubines. Thus marriage is an established Sunnah and a trait of the character of the prophets."

A man said to Ibrāhīm ibn Adham (may Allah have mercy on him): "Blessed are you, for you have devoted yourself to worship through celibacy." He replied: "A single moment of anxiety from you due to dependents is better than all that I am in." He said: "Then what prevents you from marriage?" He said: "I have no need for a woman, and I do not wish to deceive a woman with myself." And it has been said: "The virtue of the married man over the unmarried is like the virtue of the warrior (mujāhid) over the one who sits back." And: "One unit of prayer (rakʿah) from a married man is better than seventy units from an unmarried man."

As for what has come regarding discouragement from marriage (al-tarhīb): He said (peace be upon him): "The best of people after the two hundredth year is the light, swift one (al-khafīf al-ḥādhi) who has neither family nor child." And he said (peace be upon him): "A time will come upon people when a man's destruction will be at the hands of his wife, his parents, and his children, who reproach him for poverty and burden him with what he cannot bear, leading him into paths that destroy his religion, and thus he perishes." And in the report: "Fewness of dependents is one of the two riches, and their multiplicity is one of the two poverties." Abu Sulaymān al-Dārānī was asked about marriage and said: "Patience without them is better than patience with them, and patience with them is better than patience with the Fire." He also said: "The solitary one finds of the sweetness of work and freedom of heart what the married one does not find." And he said once: "I have not seen any of our companions who married and remained upon his former station." He also said: "Three things — whoever seeks them has inclined to the worldly life: whoever seeks a livelihood, or marries a woman, or writes ḥadīth." Al-Ḥasan (may Allah have mercy on him) said: "When Allah desires good for a servant, He does not occupy him with family or wealth." Ibn Abī al-Ḥawārī said: "A group debated this ḥadīth, and their conclusion settled upon that its meaning is not that he should not have them, but that he should have them and they should not occupy him" — and this points to the saying of Abu Sulaymān al-Dārānī: "Whatever occupies you from Allah — of family, wealth, or child — is ill-omened (mashʾūm) upon you." In sum, no one has transmitted an absolute discouragement from marriage except coupled with a condition. As for the encouragement to marry, it has come both absolutely and coupled with a condition. So let us unveil this by enumerating the harms (āfāt) of marriage and its benefits (fawāʾid).

The harms of marriage and its benefits. In it are five benefits: offspring, breaking desire, household management, multiplicity of kin, and self-struggle (mujāhadah) in upholding their rights.

The first benefit: offspring (al-walad). This is the foundation, and for it marriage was instituted. The purpose is the preservation of progeny (nasl) and that the world not be devoid of the human species. Desire was created as a motive and instigator — like an agent appointed over the male to emit the seed and over the female to enable the tilling — as a kindness to both in driving them toward the pursuit of offspring through intercourse, just as kindness is shown to birds by scattering the grain they crave to lure them into the net. The eternal power was not incapable of inventing persons initially without tilling and pairing, but wisdom necessitated the ordering of effects upon causes — while being independent of them — to manifest power, to complete the wonders of craftsmanship, and to realize what the will had preceded and the word had confirmed and the pen had run. In attaining offspring there is an act of nearness (qurbah) from four aspects, which are the foundation of the encouragement therein when safe from the harms of desire — such that none of them loved to meet Allah as an unmarried man.

The first: conformity with Allah's love by striving to obtain offspring for the preservation of the human species. The second: seeking the love of the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) in multiplying that by which he boasts. The third: seeking blessing through the prayer of a righteous child after him. The fourth: seeking intercession through the death of a young child if it dies before him.

As for the first aspect, it is the most subtle and the farthest from the understanding of the masses, yet it is the most worthy and strongest among those of penetrating insight into the wonders of Allah's craftsmanship and the courses of His wisdom. Its explanation: When a master hands to his slave the seed and the tools of tilling, and prepares for him a land ready for cultivation, and the slave is capable of tilling, and an agent is appointed over him to demand it of him — if he is sluggish, neglects the tool of tilling, leaves the seed wasted until it spoils, and repels the agent from himself by some ruse, he deserves the wrath and reproach of his master. Allah Most High created the two spouses, created the male and the two testicles, created the sperm in the loins (al-fiqār), prepared for it in the testicles veins and channels, created the womb as a settled place and repository for the sperm, and empowered the demanding agent of desire over each of the male and female. These acts and instruments bear witness with an eloquent tongue in expressing the intent of their Creator, and call out to the people of understanding (arbāb al-albāb) with the definition of what they were prepared for. This is so even if the Creator had not explicitly stated the intent upon the tongue of His Messenger (peace be upon him) where he said: "Marry and multiply (tanāsālū)." How then, when He has explicitly commanded and disclosed the secret? Thus, whoever abstains from marriage is turning away from tilling, wasting the seed, neglecting what Allah created of prepared instruments, and committing an offense against the purpose of nature (fiṭrah) and wisdom understood from the evidences of creation written upon these organs with a divine script — not of letters and sounds — which every possessor of divine insight, penetrating into the subtleties of eternal wisdom, can read. For this reason, the Law magnified the matter of killing children and of burying them alive (waʾd), because it prevents the completion of existence. To this pointed the one who said: "Coitus interruptus (al-ʿazl) is one of the two burials." Thus the married man strives to complete what Allah loves to be completed, while the abstainer neglects and wastes what Allah dislikes to be wasted. And for Allah's love of the preservation of souls, He commanded feeding and urged it, expressing it as the worship of lending, saying: {مَّن ذَا الَّذِي يُقْرِضُ اللَّهَ قَرْضًا حَسَنًا} "Who is it that lends Allah a goodly loan?"

If you say: "Your saying that the preservation of progeny and soul is beloved suggests that their annihilation is disliked by Allah — yet there is a distinction between death and life relative to Allah's will. It is known that all is by Allah's will, and that Allah is independent of the worlds. So how is death distinguished from life, or survival from annihilation, in His regard?" Know that this word is true but intended falsely. For what we have mentioned does not negate the attribution of all existents to Allah's will — their good and evil, their benefit and harm. But love and hatred are mutually opposed, and neither opposes will. Thus there is a willed thing that is hated, and a willed thing that is loved. Acts of disobedience are hated, and they are willed along with hatred; acts of obedience are willed, and being willed, they are loved and approved. As for disbelief and evil, we do not say they are approved and loved, but they are willed. Allah Most High has said: {وَلَا يَرْضَىٰ لِعِبَادِهِ الْكُفْرَ} "And He does not approve for His servants disbelief." So how can annihilation be like survival relative to Allah's love and hatred? For He Most High says: "I did not hesitate in anything as I hesitate in taking the soul of My believing servant: he dislikes death, and I dislike harming him, yet death is inevitable for him." His saying "death is inevitable for him" points to the precedence of will and decree mentioned in His saying: {نَحْنُ قَدَّرْنَا بَيْنَكُمُ الْمَوْتَ} "We have decreed death among you," and in His saying: {الَّذِي خَلَقَ الْمَوْتَ وَالْحَيَاةَ} "Who created death and life." There is no contradiction between His saying "We have decreed death among you" and His saying "I dislike harming him." But clarifying the truth here requires investigating the meaning of will (irādah), love (maḥabbah), and hatred (karāhah), and explaining their realities. For what comes first to minds are matters befitting the will, love, and hatred of creatures — but far be it! For between the attributes of Allah Most High and the attributes of creatures is a distance like that between His exalted essence and their essences. Just as the essences of creatures are substance (jawhar) and accident (ʿaraḍ), and His essence is sanctified from that and does not correspond to what is not substance or accident — so too His attributes do not correspond to the attributes of creatures. These realities fall within the science of unveiling (ʿilm al-mukāshafah) and beyond the secret of destiny (sirr al-qadar) whose disclosure is forbidden. So let us refrain from mentioning it and confine ourselves to what we have pointed out of the difference between proceeding to marriage and abstaining from it. For one of them wastes a progeny whose existence Allah has perpetuated from Adam (peace be upon him), generation after generation, until it reached him. The abstainer from marriage has cut off the perpetuated existence from the time of Adam (peace be upon him) upon himself, dying truncated (abtar) with no successor. Had the motive for marriage been merely the repulsion of desire, Muʿādh would not have said during the plague: "Marry me, lest I meet Allah as an unmarried man."

If you say: "Muʿādh could not expect a child at that time, so what is the point of his desire for it?" I say: The child is obtained through intercourse with the motive of desire, and that is not within choice. What is attached to the servant's choice is only the bringing of the stimulus of desire, and that is expected in every state. Whoever contracts marriage has performed what is upon him and done what is his part; the rest is outside his choice. For this reason, marriage is also recommended (mustaḥabb) for the impotent man (al-ʿanīn), for the surges of desire are hidden and not perceived — even for the one whose testicles are crushed (al-mamsūḥ), from whom no child is expected, the recommendation is not cut off in his case, in the manner that it is recommended for the bald man to pass the razor over his head, following others and imitating the righteous predecessors (al-salaf al-ṣāliḥīn). Likewise, the rapid walk (ramal) and the baring of the shoulder (iḍṭibāʿ) in pilgrimage are recommended now, though their original purpose was to show vigor to the disbelievers; thus imitation of those who showed vigor became a Sunnah for those after them. This recommendation weakens relative to the recommendation for one capable of tilling, and it may weaken further by what opposes it of the dislike of neglecting the woman and wasting her regarding the fulfillment of need — for that is not free of a type of risk. This meaning is what alerts to the severity of their disapproval of abandoning marriage despite the cooling of desire.

The second aspect: striving for the love of the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) and his pleasure by multiplying that by which he boasts, since the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) explicitly stated this. And what indicates the consideration of the matter of offspring in all its aspects is what is narrated from ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him): he married frequently and said: "I marry only for offspring." And the reports censuring the barren woman — for he (peace be upon him) said: "A mat (ḥaṣīr) in the corner of the house is better than a woman who does not bear." And he said: "The best of your women is the fertile, the loving (al-walūd al-wadūd)." And he said: "A black, fertile woman is better than a beautiful one who does not bear." This indicates that seeking offspring is more integral to the merit of marriage than seeking to repel the harm of desire, for the beautiful woman is more suitable for protection, lowering the gaze, and cutting desire.

The third aspect: that there remain after him a righteous child who prays for him, as came in the report that all the deeds of the son of Adam cease except three, and he mentioned the righteous child. And in the report: "Supplications are presented to the dead upon trays of light." The saying of one who says "the child may not be righteous" has no effect, for he is a believer, and righteousness is predominant among the children of the religious — especially if he resolves to raise him and lead him to righteousness. In sum, the supplication of a believer for his parents is beneficial whether the parent is righteous or wicked, for he is rewarded for his supplications and good deeds, as they are of his earning, and he is not held accountable for the parent's sins, for "no bearer of burdens bears the burden of another." For this reason Allah Most High said: {أَلْحَقْنَا بِهِمْ ذُرِّيَّاتِهِمْ وَمَا أَلَتْنَاهُم مِّنْ عَمَلِهِم مِّن شَيْءٍ} "We joined their offspring with them, and We did not diminish their deeds at all" — meaning We did not decrease their works, and We made their children an increase in their beneficence.

The fourth aspect: that the child dies before him, becoming an intercessor for him. It is narrated from the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) that he said: "Indeed the young child drags his parents to Paradise." And in some reports: "He takes hold of his garment, just as I now take hold of your garment." He also said (peace be upon him): "Indeed the newborn is told: 'Enter Paradise,' and he stands at the gate of Paradise, remaining sulking (muḥbanṭiʾ) — that is, filled with grief and anger — and says: 'I will not enter Paradise except with my parents.' Then it is said: 'Enter his parents with him into Paradise.'" In another report: "The children gather at the standing-place (mawqif) on the Day of Resurrection during the presentation of creation for reckoning. It is said to the angels: 'Take these to Paradise.' They stand at the gate of Paradise, and it is said to them: 'Welcome, O offspring of the Muslims! Enter, no reckoning upon you.' They say: 'Then where are our fathers and mothers?' The keepers say: 'Your fathers and mothers are not like you; they had sins and misdeeds, so they are being reckoned and called to account.' He said: 'Then they cry out and clamor at the gates of Paradise with one great cry. Allah Glorified — and He knows them best — says: "What is this clamor?" They say: "Our Lord, the children of the Muslims say: We will not enter Paradise except with our fathers." Then Allah Most High says: "Thread through the gathering and take your fathers by the hand and enter them into Paradise."'" And he said (peace be upon him): "Whoever has two of his children die has been shielded by a fence (ḥiẓār) from the Fire." And he said (peace be upon him): "Whoever has three of his children die before reaching puberty, Allah enters him into Paradise by virtue of His mercy upon them." It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, and two?" He said: "And two."

It is narrated that one of the righteous was offered marriage and refused for a long period of his time. He said: "Then I awoke from my sleep one day and said: 'Marry me, marry me.' So they married him. He was asked about that and said: 'Perhaps Allah will grant me a child and take him, and he will be a vanguard (muqaddimah) for me in the Hereafter.' Then he said: 'I saw in a dream as if the Resurrection had been established, and I was among the creation at the standing-place, with thirst nearly severing my neck, and likewise the creation in severe thirst and distress. While we were thus, young boys threaded through the gathering, upon them handkerchiefs of light, in their hands silver pitchers and golden cups, giving drink one after another, threading through the gathering and passing by most of the people. I extended my hand to one of them and said: "Give me drink, for thirst has exhausted me." He said: "You have no child among us; we only give drink to our fathers." I said: "And who are you?" They said: "We are those who died of the children of the Muslims."'" And one of the meanings mentioned in His saying: {فَأْتُوا حَرْثَكُمْ أَنَّىٰ شِئْتُمْ وَقَدِّمُوا لِأَنفُسِكُمْ} "So come to your tillage however you wish, and send forward for yourselves" — is the sending forward of children to the Hereafter. Thus it has become clear through these four aspects that most of the virtue of marriage is because it is a means to offspring.

The second benefit: self-protection from Satan, breaking the surge (al-tawaqān), repelling the harms of desire, lowering the gaze, and guarding the private parts. To this points his saying (peace be upon him): "Whoever marries has secured half of his religion; so let him fear Allah regarding the other half." And to this points his saying: "Upon you is the ability (bāʾah); whoever cannot, then upon him is fasting, for fasting is a protection (wijāʾ) for him." And most of what we have transmitted of reports and narrations points to this meaning. This meaning is inferior to the first, for desire is appointed to demand the attainment of offspring, and marriage suffices to occupy it, repel its harm, and divert the evil of its assault. The one who answers his Master out of desire to attain His pleasure is not like the one who answers to seek deliverance from the harm of the appointed agent. Desire and offspring are both decreed, and between them is a connection. It is not permissible to say that the purpose is pleasure and the child is incidental to it — as, for example, the relief of need is incidental to eating and not intended in itself. Rather, the child is the purpose by nature (fiṭrah) and wisdom, and desire is a motive upon it. And by my life, in desire there is another wisdom besides driving toward procreation: what is in its fulfillment of pleasure, which no pleasure equals were it to endure. It is a reminder of the pleasures promised in the gardens (jinnān), for urging toward a pleasure one has never tasted is of no use. If one urged the impotent man toward the pleasure of intercourse, or the boy toward the pleasure of kingship and dominion, the urging would not benefit. One of the benefits of worldly pleasures is the desire for their permanence in Paradise, to be a motive for worshipping Allah. So consider the wisdom, then the mercy, then the divine arrangement (al-taʿbiʾah al-ilāhiyyah) — how under a single desire two lives are arranged: an apparent life and a hidden life. The apparent life is a man's life through the survival of his progeny, for that is a kind of continuation of existence. The hidden life is the otherworldly life, for this deficient pleasure, quickly passing, stirs desire for the complete pleasure of permanence, thus urging toward the worship that leads to it. The servant thus gains, through intense desire for it, the facilitation of persisting in what brings him to the bliss of the gardens. There is not a single atom of the atoms of the human body — inner or outer — nay, the atoms of the dominion (malakūt) of the heavens and the earth, beneath which are not subtleties of wisdom and wonders at which minds are bewildered. But this is only unveiled to pure hearts according to their clarity and their turning away from the flower of the world, its delusion, and its harms. Thus marriage, for repelling the harm of desire, is important in religion for everyone not afflicted by incapacity or impotence — and they are the majority of creation. For when desire dominates and the strength of piety does not resist it, it leads to plunging into lewd acts. To this pointed his saying (peace be upon him), relating from Allah Most High: {إِلَّا تَفْعَلُوهُ تَكُن فِتْنَةٌ فِي الْأَرْضِ وَفَسَادٌ كَبِيرٌ} "If you do not do it, there will be tribulation in the earth and great corruption." And even if one is bridled with the bridle of piety, the utmost is that he restrains his limbs from answering desire — lowering the gaze and guarding the private parts. But as for guarding the heart from whisperings (waswās) and thought, that is not within his choice. Rather, the soul continually tugs at him and speaks to him of matters of intercourse, and the whispering Satan does not slacken from him in most times. This may even occur to him during prayer, such that there passes through his mind matters of intercourse which, were he to utter them before the basest of creation, he would be ashamed — while Allah is aware of his heart. The heart in relation to Allah is like the tongue in relation to creation. The head of matters for the seeker (murīd) on the path of the Hereafter is his heart. Persisting in fasting does not cut off the material of whisperings for most people, unless joined to it is weakness of body and corruption of temperament. For this reason Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: "The devotional act of the devotee is not complete except through marriage." This is a general trial (miḥnah) from which few are delivered.

Qatādah said regarding the meaning of His saying: {وَلَا تُحَمِّلْنَا مَا لَا طَاقَةَ

chapters.title_en: The Second Chapter on What is Observed Regarding the Woman's Condition and the Conditions of the Marriage Contract

الأول إذن الولي فإن لم يكن فالسلطان

جامعا بينهما وكل شخصين بينهما قرابة لو كان أحدهما ذكرا والآخرة أنثى لم
يجز بينهما النكاح فلا يجوز أن يجمع بينهما

الخامس عشر أن يكون الناكح قد لاعنها فإنها تحرم عليه أبدا بعد اللعان

النكاح إلا بعد تمام التحلل

الثامن عشر أن تكون يتيمة فلا يصح نكاحها إلا بعد البلوغ
التاسع عشر أن تكون  من أزواج رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم ممن توفى عنها
أو دخل بها فإنهن أمهات المؤمنين وذلك لا يوجد في زماننا فهذه هي الموانع
المحرمة
أما الخصال المطيبة للعيش التي لا بد من مراعاتها في المرأة ليدوم العقد
وتتوفر مقاصده ثمانية الدين والخلق والحسن وخفة المهر والولادة والبكارة
والنسب وأن لا تكون قرابة قريبة
الأولى أن تكون صالحة ذات دين فهذا هو الأصل وبه ينبغي أن يقع الاعتناء
فإنها إن كانت ضعيفة الدين في صيانة نفسها وفرجها أزرت بزوجها وسودت بين
الناس وجهه وشوشت بالغيرة قلبه وتتغص بذلك عيشه فإن سلك سبيل الحمية
والغيرة لم يزل في بلاء ومحنة وإن سلك سبيل التساهل كان متهاونا بدينه
وعرضه ومنسوبا إلى قلة الحمية والأنفة وإذا كانت مع الفساد جميلة كان
بلاؤها أشد إذ يشق على الزوج مفارقتها فلا يصبر عنها ولا يصبر عليها ويكون
كالذي جاء إلى رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم وقال يا رسول الله إن لي امرأة
