chapters.anchors:
- Root: ع-ق-د (ʿAqd)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Binding, knotting, tightening; a firm covenant or compact
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The contractual bond (ʿaqd) as a legal tie effecting permissibility (ḥill) in marriage (nikāḥ)
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) for physical tying; metaphorical (majāz) for legal obligation
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Clause Sequencing (al-Sharṭ wa al-Jawāb) — The four pillars are enumerated with their qualifying conditions (shurūṭ) governing validity and effect
chapters.translation:
I say: As for the marriage contract (al-ʿaqd), its pillars (arkān) and conditions (shurūṭ) for its valid conclusion and its effecting of permissibility (al-ḥill) are four:

**First**: The permission of the guardian (al-walī); if there is none, then the ruler (al-sulṭān).

**Second**: The consent of the woman (riḍā al-marʾah) if she is a previously-married adult (thayyib bālighah), or if she is a virgin adult (bikr bālighah) but is being given in marriage by someone other than her father or grandfather (al-ab wa al-jadd).

**Third**: The presence of two witnesses (shāhidayn) of apparent probity (ʿadālah ẓāhirah); if they are merely of concealed good standing (mustūrayn), we rule the contract valid out of necessity (li-l-ḥājah).

**Fourth**: An offer (ījāb) and acceptance (qabūl) connected to it, expressed by the wording of "giving in marriage" (inkāḥ) or "marrying" (tazwīj), or their specific meanings, in any language, from two legally responsible persons (mukallafayn), neither of whom is a woman—whether they be the husband, the guardian, or their agents.

As for its proprieties (ādāb):

The presentation of the marriage proposal (khiṭbah) with the guardian—not during the woman's waiting period (ʿiddah), but rather after its completion if she is observing one—and not when another has already preceded in proposing, for he (peace and blessings be upon him) forbade proposing over another's proposal. This is the ḥadīth of ʿĀʾishah: "The Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) married me in Shawwāl and consummated with me in Shawwāl." Narrated by Muslim.

As for the woman being married (al-mankūḥah), two categories are considered regarding her: one for permissibility (al-ḥill), and the second for the pleasantness of life (ṭīb al-maʿīshah) and the attainment of objectives (maqāṣid).

**The First Category**: What is considered for permissibility—namely, that she be free of the impediments to marriage (mawāniʿ al-nikāḥ). These impediments are nineteen:

**First**: That she be already married to another.

**Second**: That she be observing a waiting period (ʿiddah) for another—whether it be the ʿiddah of death, divorce, or intercourse under ambiguity (waṭʾ shubhah), or whether she be in the period of ascertaining the womb's purity (istibrāʾ) from intercourse with a slave-woman owned by right of possession (milk yamīn).

**Third**: That she be an apostate (murtaddah) from the religion, due to a word of unbelief (kalimah min kalimāt al-kufr) having passed over her tongue.

**Fourth**: That she be a Magian (majūsiyyah).

**Fifth**: That she be an idolater (wathaniyyah) or a heretic (zindīqiyyah) who does not ascribe to a prophet or a scripture. Among them are those who believe in the doctrine of permissiveness (ibāḥah); marrying them is not lawful. Likewise, every woman who believes a corrupt doctrine whose adherent is judged an unbeliever.

**Sixth**: That she be a Scriptural woman (kitābiyyah) who has adopted their religion after the alteration (tabdīl) or after the mission of the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him), and moreover is not of the lineage of the Children of Israel. If both characteristics are absent, her marriage is not lawful. If only the lineage is absent, there is disagreement (khilāf) concerning it.

**Seventh**: That she be a slave-woman (raqīqah) while the husband is free and able to marry a free woman, or not fearing hardship (al-ʿanat).

**Eighth**: That she be wholly or partially owned by the husband through right of possession (milk yamīn).

**Ninth**: That she be a close relative of the husband—namely, from his ascendants (uṣūl), descendants (fuṣūl), the descendants of his first ascendants, or from the first branch of every ascendant after which there is another ascendant. By "ascendants" I mean mothers and grandmothers; by "descendants" I mean children and grandchildren; by "descendants of his first ascendants" I mean siblings and their children; and by "the first branch of every ascendant after which there is another ascendant" I mean paternal aunts (ʿammāt) and maternal aunts (khālāt), excluding their children.

**Tenth**: That she be forbidden by fosterage (riḍāʿ). What is forbidden by fosterage is what is forbidden by lineage—from ascendants and descendants, as previously mentioned. However, what renders forbidden is five complete breastfeedings (khams raḍaʿāt); less than that does not forbid.

**Eleventh**: The prohibition by affinity (muṣāharah)—namely, that the husband had previously married her daughter or her grandmother, or possessed them by contract or ambiguous contract, or had intercourse with them under ambiguity in a contract; or that he had intercourse with her mother or one of her grandmothers by contract or ambiguous contract. For the mere contract upon a woman forbids her mothers but does not forbid her branches except by intercourse; or that his father or his son had married her before.

**Twelfth**: That the woman being married be a fifth—namely, that the husband already has four wives besides her, either in the marriage itself or in the ʿiddah of revocable divorce (ʿiddat al-rajʿah). If she is in the ʿiddah of irrevocable separation (baynūnah), she does not prevent the fifth.

**Thirteenth**: That under the husband be her sister, her paternal aunt, or her maternal aunt, such that by the marriage he would combine between them. Any two persons between whom there is a kinship such that if one were male and the other female, marriage between them would not be permissible—it is not permissible to combine between them.

**Fourteenth**: That this husband had divorced her three times; she is not lawful for him until a different husband has intercourse with her in a valid marriage (nikāḥ ṣaḥīḥ).

**Fifteenth**: That the husband had engaged in mutual imprecation (liʿān) with her; she is forbidden to him forever after the liʿān.

**Sixteenth**: That she be in a state of iḥrām for pilgrimage (ḥajj) or minor pilgrimage (ʿumrah), or the husband likewise; the marriage does not conclude until after complete release from iḥrām (tamām al-taḥallul).

**Seventeenth**: That she be a previously-married minor (thayyib ṣaghīrah); her marriage is not valid except after puberty (bulūgh).

**Eighteenth**: That she be an orphan (yatīmah); her marriage is not valid except after puberty.

**Nineteenth**: That she be among the wives of the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him)—those from whom he died or with whom he consummated—for they are the Mothers of the Believers (ummahāt al-muʾminīn). This does not exist in our time. These are the prohibiting impediments.

As for the qualities that render life pleasant (al-khiṣāl al-muṭayyibah lil-ʿaysh) which must be observed in the woman for the contract to endure and its objectives to be fulfilled, they are eight: religion (dīn), character (khuluq), beauty (ḥusn), lightness of dowry (khiffat al-mahr), childbearing (wilādah), virginity (bakārah), lineage (nasab), and that she not be a close relative.

**First**: That she be righteous (ṣāliḥah), possessing religion. This is the foundation, and upon it attention should be focused. For if she is weak in religion regarding the safeguarding of herself and her chastity (farj), she disgraces her husband, blackens his face among people, disturbs his heart with jealousy (ghayrah), and his life becomes bitter thereby. If he follows the path of protectiveness and jealousy, he remains in tribulation and trial; if he follows the path of leniency, he is negligent of his religion and his honor, and is attributed to lack of protectiveness and pride. If she is beautiful along with corruption, her affliction is more severe, for it is hard for the husband to part from her—he neither has patience without her nor with her—and he is like the one who came to the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) and said: "O Messenger of Allah, I have a wife who does not repel the hand of any toucher." He said: "Divorce her." He said: "But I love her." He said: "Then keep her." He only commanded him to keep her out of fear for him—that if he divorced her, he would follow her with his soul and be corrupted along with her. He saw that what is in the continuation of his marriage—of repelling corruption from himself—was preferable to the constriction of his heart. If she is corrupt in religion by consuming his wealth or in another way, life remains disturbed with her. If he remains silent and does not denounce it, he is a partner in disobedience, contrary to His saying (Exalted is He): {«Protect yourselves and your families from a Fire»} (Q 66:6). If he denounces and quarrels, his life becomes bitter. For this reason, the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) was emphatic in urging the one possessing religion, saying: "A woman is married for her wealth, her beauty, her lineage, and her religion; so take the one possessing religion—may your hands be dusted." In another ḥadīth: "Whoever marries a woman for her wealth and beauty is deprived of her beauty and her wealth; whoever marries her for her religion, Allah provides him her wealth and her beauty." And he said (peace and blessings be upon him): "Do not marry a woman for her beauty, for perhaps her beauty will ruin her; nor for her wealth, for perhaps her wealth will make her insolent; marry the woman for her religion." The ḥadīth "Do not marry a woman for her beauty, for perhaps her beauty will ruin her" is narrated by Ibn Mājah from the ḥadīth of ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr with a weak chain (sanad ḍaʿīf).

He was emphatic in urging religion because such a woman is an aid upon religion. As for one who is not religious, she distracts from religion and disturbs it.

**Second**: Good character (ḥusn al-khuluq). This is an important foundation in seeking tranquility (farāghah) and seeking aid upon religion. For if she is sharp-tongued (salīṭah), foul of speech (badhiyyat al-lisān), evil in character, ungrateful for blessings (kāfirat al-niʿam), the harm from her is greater than the benefit. Patience with women's tongues is among the trials by which guardians are tested.

Some Arabs said: "Do not marry six types of women: not the anānah, not the manānah, not the ḥanānah, and do not marry the ḥaddāqah, nor the barrāqah, nor the shaddāqah."

The anānah is she who abounds in groaning and complaining, and binds her head every hour. Marriage to the chronically ill, or marriage to the one who feigns illness, has no good in it. The manānah is she who bestows favors upon her husband, saying: "I did such-and-such for your sake." The ḥanānah is she who yearns for another husband or for her child from another husband—this too must be avoided. The ḥaddāqah is she who casts her eye at everything, desiring it, and burdens the husband to buy it. The barrāqah carries two meanings: one, that she spends the whole day polishing and adorning her face so that her face has a shine (barīq) produced by artifice; the second, that she becomes angry at food and eats only alone, deeming her portion of everything too little—this is a Yemeni usage, for they say "barraqat al-marʾah" and "barraqa al-ṣabī al-ṭaʿām" when he becomes angry at it. The shaddāqah is the one who exaggerates in speech (mutashaddiqah), abundant in talk. From this is his saying (peace and blessings be upon him): "Allah (Exalted is He) hates the garrulous and the exaggerators in speech."

It is related that al-Sāʾiḥ al-Azdī met Ilyās (peace be upon him) during his wandering, and he commanded him to marry and forbade him from celibacy (tabattul). Then he said: "Do not marry four: the mukhtaliʿah, the mubāriyah, the ʿāhirah, and the nāshiz." The mukhtaliʿah is she who seeks divorce (khulʿ) every hour without cause. The mubāriyah is she who vies in boasting with others, vaunting the causes of this world. The ʿāhirah is the fornicatress (fāsiqah) who is known by a lover (khalīl) and a secret companion (khidn)—she is the one of whom Allah (Exalted is He) said: {«Nor taking secret companions»} (Q 4:25). The nāshiz is she who rises above her husband in deed and word; al-nashz is the elevated ground.

ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with him) used to say: "The worst qualities of men are the best qualities of women: miserliness (bukhl), pride (zahw), and cowardice (jubn)." For if a woman is miserly, she preserves her wealth and her husband's wealth; if she is proud, she disdains to speak to everyone with soft, suspicious words; if she is cowardly, she fears everything, so she does not leave her house and avoids places of suspicion out of fear of her husband. These narratives guide to the comprehensive qualities sought in marriage.

**Third**: Beauty of face (ḥusn al-wajh). This too is sought, for by it chastity (taḥaṣṣun) is attained, and nature is generally not content with the ugly. How so, when generally good character and good appearance do not separate?

What we have transmitted of urging religion—that a woman is not married for her beauty—is not a deterrent from observing beauty, but rather a deterrent from marriage for the sake of pure beauty along with corruption in religion. For beauty alone, in most cases, inclines one to marriage and makes religion seem insignificant. Evidence for attending to the meaning of beauty is that affection (ulfah) and love (mawaddah) are generally attained by it, and the Law (al-sharʿ) has urged observing the causes of affection. For this reason, he recommended looking, saying: "When Allah casts into the heart of one of you something regarding a woman, let him look at her, for it is more fitting that He create harmony between them"—that is, that He unite them, from the occurrence of "adamah" upon "adamah," which is the inner skin, while "basharah" is the outer skin. He only mentioned this to emphasize union.

And he said (peace and blessings be upon him): "In the eyes of the Anṣār there is something; so when one of you wishes to marry from among them, let him look at them." It was said there was ophthalmia (ʿamash) in their eyes; it was also said smallness. Some of the scrupulous (waraʿah) would not marry their noble women except after looking, as a precaution against deception (ghurūr).

Al-Aʿmash said: "Every marriage that occurs without looking ends in worry and grief." It is known that looking does not reveal character, religion, or wealth; it only reveals beauty from ugliness.

It is related that a man married during the era of ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) and had dyed his hair; his dye became apparent, and the woman's family appealed to ʿUmar against him, saying: "We thought he was young." ʿUmar struck him painfully and said: "You deceived the people."

It is related that Bilāl and Ṣuhayb came to a family of Arabs and proposed to them. It was said to them: "Who are you?" Bilāl said: "I am Bilāl, and this is my brother Ṣuhayb. We were astray, and Allah guided us; we were slaves, and Allah freed us; we were destitute, and Allah enriched us. If you marry us, praise be to Allah; if you reject us, glory be to Allah." They said: "Rather, you both marry—and praise be to Allah." Ṣuhayb said: "If only I had mentioned our battles and our precedence with the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him)." He said: "Be silent—you have spoken truthfully, and truthfulness has married you."

Deception occurs in both beauty and character, so it is recommended to remove deception in beauty by looking, and in character by description and inquiry (al-waṣf wa al-istiṣāf). One should precede this to marriage. One should not inquire about her character and beauty except from one who is perceptive (baṣīr), truthful (ṣādiq), knowledgeable of the outward and inward, who does not incline toward her so as to exaggerate in praise, nor envy her so as to fall short. For natures at the beginnings of marriage and the description of brides incline toward excess and deficiency, and few are truthful and moderate therein. Rather, deception and seduction are more prevalent, and caution therein is important for one who fears for himself the yearning toward other than his wife.

As for one who desires from a wife merely the Sunnah, or offspring, or household management—if he turns away from beauty, he is closer to asceticism (zuhd), for it is, on the whole, a door of this world, even if it may aid religion in the case of some persons.

Abū Sulaymān al-Dārānī said: "Asceticism is in everything, even in the woman—a man marries an old woman, preferring asceticism in this world."

Mālik ibn Dīnār (may Allah have mercy on him) used to say: "One of you leaves off marrying an orphan, being rewarded therein if he feeds and clothes her—she is light of burden, content with little—and marries the daughter of so-and-so and so-and-so, meaning the sons of this world, so she desires luxuries upon him and says: 'Clothe me with such-and-such.'"

Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal chose a one-eyed woman over her sister, though her sister was beautiful. He asked which of them was more intelligent, and it was said: "The one-eyed." He said: "Marry me to her." This is the practice of one who does not intend enjoyment. As for one who does not trust his religion unless he has enjoyment, let him seek beauty, for delight in the permissible is a fortress for religion.

It has been said: If a woman is beautiful, good of character, black of pupil and hair, large of eye, intensely white of complexion, loving her husband, confining her gaze to him—she is in the form of the ḥūr al-ʿayn. For Allah (Exalted is He) described the women of Paradise with this attribute in His saying: {«Good and beautiful»} (Q 55:70)—by "good" meaning good of character—and in His saying: {«Confining their gaze»} (Q 37:48), and in His saying: {«Loving, equal in age»} (Q 56:37). Al-ʿarūb is she who loves her husband and desires intercourse, and by it pleasure is completed. Al-ḥūr is whiteness; al-ḥawrāʾ is she who is intensely white of eye and intensely black of it, in the blackness of hair; al-ʿaynāʾ is the wide-eyed.

And he said (peace and blessings be upon him): "The best of your women is she who, when her husband looks at her, pleases him; when he commands her, obeys him; and when he is absent from her, preserves him in herself and his wealth." He is only pleased by looking at her when she is loving of her husband.

**Fourth**: That she be light of dowry (khafīfat al-mahr).

The Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "The best of women are the most beautiful of them in face and the cheapest of them in dowries." And he forbade exaggeration in the dowry (al-mughālāh fī al-mahr). The Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) married some of his wives for ten dirhams and household furnishings—a hand-mill, a jar, and a leather cushion stuffed with palm fiber. He held a wedding feast (awlamah) for some of his wives with two mudds of barley, and for another with two mudds of dates and two mudds of sawīq. ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) used to forbid exaggeration in the bridal gift (ṣidāq) and say: "The Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) neither married nor gave his daughters in marriage for more than four hundred dirhams." Had exaggeration in women's dowries been an honor, the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) would have preceded to it. Some of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) married for a gold nugget (nawāh) worth five dirhams. Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib married his daughter to Abū Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) for two dirhams, then carried her himself to him at night, entered her himself through the door, then departed. Then he came to her after seven days and greeted her. If one marries for ten dirhams to exit from the disagreement of the scholars, there is no harm.

In the report: "From the blessing of a woman is the swiftness of her marriage, the swiftness of her womb—that is, childbirth—and the ease of her dowry." He also said: "The most blessed of them is the least of them in dowry."

Just as exaggeration in the dowry is disliked from the woman's side, so too is asking about her wealth disliked from the man's side. One should not marry out of greed for wealth. Al-Nūrī said: "When one marries and says, 'What does the woman have?' know that he is a thief." And if he gives gifts to them, he should not give intending to compel them to reciprocate with more. Likewise, if they give to him, the intention of seeking increase is a corrupt intention. As for mutual gift-giving (al-tahādī), it is recommended and is a cause of affection. He said (peace and blessings be upon him): "Give gifts to one another, and you will love one another." As for seeking increase, it falls under His saying (Exalted is He): {«And do not bestow favors seeking more»} (Q 74:6)—that is, giving to seek more—and under His saying (Exalted is He): {«And whatever you give of usury to increase in people's wealth»} (Q 30:39), for usury (ribā) is increase, and this is seeking increase on the whole, even if not in usurious wealth. All of that is disliked and an innovation (bidʿah) in marriage, resembling commerce and gambling, and it corrupts the objectives of marriage.

**Fifth**: That the woman be childbearing (walūd). If she is known to be barren (ʿāqir), one should refrain from marrying her. He said (peace and blessings be upon him): "Take the childbearing, the loving (walūd al-wadūd)." If she has had no husband and her condition is unknown, then one observes her health and youth, for she is generally childbearing with these two attributes.

**Sixth**: That she be a virgin (bikr). He said (peace and blessings be upon him) to Jābir, who had married a previously-married woman: "Why not a virgin, that you might sport with her and she with you?" In virginity there are three benefits:

**One**: That she loves the husband and becomes attached to him, which affects the meaning of affection (wudd). He said (peace and blessings be upon him): "Take the loving (al-wadūd)." Natures are created upon intimacy with the first object of attachment. As for one who has tested men and experienced circumstances, perhaps she will not be content with some attributes that contradict what she has become accustomed to, and she will come to despise the husband.

**Two**: That it is more complete in his love for her, for nature recoils from one whom another than the husband has touched with some recoiling, and that weighs upon nature whenever it is mentioned; some natures are more averse in this.

**Three**: That she does not yearn for the first husband, and the most intense love is what occurs with the first beloved, generally.

**Seventh**: That she be of noble lineage (nasībah)—that is, from a family of religion and righteousness. For she will raise her daughters and sons, and if she is not well-mannered, she will not excel in discipline and upbringing. For this reason he said (peace and blessings be upon him): "Beware of the green one upon dung-heap (khaḍrāʾ al-diman)." It was said: "What is the green one upon the dung-heap?" He said: "The beautiful woman in a bad origin." And he said (peace and blessings be upon him): "Choose for your seed, for the lineage (ʿirq) is a puller."

**Eighth**: That she not be from close kinship (qarābah qarībah), for that diminishes desire. He said (peace and blessings be upon him): "Do not marry close kin, for the child is created thin (ḍāwī)"—that is, emaciated—due to its effect in weakening desire. For desire is only aroused by the strength of sensation through sight and touch, and sensation is only strengthened by the strange and new. As for the familiar, at which one has continuously looked for a long time, it weakens the sense from fully perceiving it and being affected by it, and desire is not aroused by it. These are the qualities desirable in women.

It is also incumbent upon the guardian to observe the qualities of the husband and to look out for his noble one (karīmah), so that he does not marry her to one whose character or appearance is evil, whose religion is weak, who falls short of fulfilling her rights, or who is not her equal (kufʾ) in lineage. He said (peace and blessings be upon him): "Marriage is slavery (riqq); so let each of you see where he places his noble one." Caution on her behalf is more important, for she is a captive by marriage with no way out, while the husband is able to divorce in any case. Whenever one marries his daughter to a wrongdoer (ẓālim), a sinner (fāsiq), an innovator (mubtadiʿ), or a wine-drinker, he has committed an offense against his religion and exposed himself to Allah's wrath, for cutting the tie of kinship (raḥim) and evil choice.

A man said to al-Ḥasan: "Several men have proposed to my daughter; whom shall I marry her to?" He said: "To one who fears Allah—for if he loves her, he honors her, and if he hates her, he does not wrong her."

And he said (peace and blessings be upon him): "Whoever marries his noble one to a sinner has cut her kinship."

chapters.title_en: The Third Book on the Etiquette of Companionship and What Occurs in the Continuance of Marriage

الله عليه وسلم على عبد الرحمن بن عوف رضي الله عنه أثر صفرة فقال {ما هذا}

وأولم رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم على صفية بتمر وسويق (2)

سمعة ومن سمع سمع الله به (3)
ولم يرفعه إلا زياد بن عبد الله وهو غريب
وتستحب تهنئته فيقول من دخل على الزوج بارك الله لك وبارك عليك وجمع
بينكما في خير (4)
وروى أبو هريرة رضي الله عنه أنه صلى الله عليه وسلم أمر بذلك ويستحب
إظهار النكاح
قال صلى الله عليه وسلم فصل ما بين الحلال والحرام الدف والصوت (5)

واضربوا عليه بالدفوف (6)
وعن الربيع بنت معوذ قالت جاء رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم فدخل  غداة
بنى بي فجلس على فراشي وجويريات لنا يضربن بدفهن ويندبن من قتل من آبائي
إلى أن قالت إحداهن وفينا نبي يعلم ما في غد فقال لها اسكتي عن هذه وقولي
الذي كنت تقولين قبلها (7)
الأدب الثاني حسن الخلق معهن واحتمال الأذى منهن ترحما عليهن لقصور عقلهن

الصلاة الصلاة وما ملكت أيمانكم لا تكلفوهم ما لا يطيقون

أعطاه الله من الأجر مثل ما أعطى أيوب على بلائه ومن صبرت على سوء خلق
زوجها أعطاها الله مثل ثواب آسية امرأة فرعون (1) حديث كان أزواجه صلى الله
عليه وسلم يراجعنه الحديث وتهجره الواحدة منهن يوما إلى الليل متفق عليه من

فقالت إن أزواج رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم يراجعنه وهو خير منك (2) حديث

الله عليه وسلم دعيها فنهن يصنعن أكثر من ذلك لم اقف له على أصل (3) حديث
جرى بينه وبين عائشة كلام حتى أدخل بينهما أبا بكر حكماالحديث أخرجه
الطبراني في الأوسط والخطيب في التاريخ من حديث عائشة بسند ضعيف (4) حديث
قالت له عائشة مرة غضبت عنده وأنت الذي تزعم أنك نبي فتبسم رسول الله صلى
الله عليه وسلم أخرجه أبو يعلى في مسنده وأبو الشيخ في كتاب الأمثال من
حديث عائشة وفيه ابن اسحق وقد عنعنه (5) حديث كان يقول لعائشة إني لأعرف
غضبك من رضاك الحديث  متفق عليه سن حديثها (6) حديث أول حب وقع في الإسلام
حب النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم عائشة رواه الشيخان من حديث عمرو بن العاص أنه
قال أي الناس أحب إليك يا رسول الله قال عائشة الحديث وأما كونه أول فرواه
ابن الجوزي في الموضوعات من حديث أنس ولعله أراد بالمدينة كما في الحديث
الآخر أن ابن الزبير أول مولود ولد في الإسلام يريد بالمدينة وإلا فمحبة
النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم لخديجة أمر معروف تشهد له الأحاديث الصحيحة (7)
حديث كان يقول لعائشة كنت لك كأبي زرع لأم زرع غير أني لا أطلقك متفق عليه
من حديث عائشة دون الاستثناء ورواه بهذه الزيادة الزبير بن بكار والخطيب
(8) حديث لا تؤذوني في عائشة فإنه والله ما أنزل علي الوحي وأنا في لحاف
امرأة منكن غيرها رواه البخاري من حديث عائشة (9) حديث أنس كان رسول الله
صلى الله عليه وسلم أرحم الناس بالنساء والصبيان رواه مسلم بلفظ ما رأيت
أحدا كان أرحم بالعيال من رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم زاد علي بن عبد
العزيز والبغوي والصبيان // PageV02P043
الثالث أن يزيد على احتمال الأذى بالمداعبة والمزح والملاعبة فهي التي
تطيب قلوب النساء وقد كان رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم يمزح معهن وينزل
إلى درجات عقولهن في الأعمال والأخلاق حتى روي أنه صلى الله عليه وسلم كان
يسابق عائشة في العدو فسبقته يوما وسبقها في بعض الأيام فقال صلى الله عليه
وسلم هذه بتلك (1)
وفي الخبر أنه كان صلى الله عليه وسلم من أفكه الناس مع نسائه (2)
وقالت عائشة رضي الله عنها سمعت أصوات أناس من الحبشة وغيرهم وهم يلعبون

chapters.anchors:
- Root: و-ل-م (walama)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The wedding feast (walīmah); derived from walm, meaning gathering and union
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A feast of hospitality specifically for marriage, a recommended act (mustaḥabb) of communal joy
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal usage for the marriage banquet; metaphorically extended to any festive meal
- Root: ق-س-م (qasama)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Division, apportioning; fair distribution among co-wives
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The equitable allocation of nights and provisions mandated by justice (ʿadl) in polygyny
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for dividing shares; metaphorical for balancing affection, which lies beyond human capacity
- Root: ن-ش-ز (nashaza)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Rising, elevation; recalcitrance or rebellion of a wife against her husband
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Disobedience (nushūz) as a legal category triggering graduated corrective measures
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for physical rising; metaphorical for moral defiance and discord
- Root: ع-ز-ل (ʿazala)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Separation, withdrawal; coitus interruptus (al-ʿazl)
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A contested practice regarding procreation; its permissibility debated among jurists
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for setting apart; metaphorical for preventing conception, likened to "hidden infanticide" (al-waʾd al-khafī) by some
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Constructions (al-sharṭ wa al-istithnāʾ) — Governing the nuanced legal distinctions between absolute permission, prohibition, and recommendation, as in the graduated discipline of nushūz and the four juridical positions on ʿazl.
chapters.translation:
I say: The third book concerns the etiquette of companionship and what transpires in the continuance of marriage, examining what is incumbent upon the husband and what is incumbent upon the wife.

As for the husband, he must observe moderation and proper conduct in twelve matters: the wedding feast, companionship, jesting, governance, jealousy, expenditure, education, division of nights, discipline in cases of recalcitrance, intercourse, childbirth, and separation through divorce.

**The First Etiquette: The Wedding Feast (al-Walīmah)**

It is recommended (mustaḥabb). Anas, may God be pleased with him, said: The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, saw upon ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf, may God be pleased with him, a trace of yellow fragrance and said: {«What is this?»} He replied: "I have married a woman for the weight of a date-stone in gold." He said: "May God bless you. Hold a wedding feast, even if with a single sheep." (1)

The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, held a wedding feast for Ṣafiyyah with dates and sawīq (roasted barley flour). (2)

He, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: "The food of the first day is a right, the food of the second day is a sunnah, and the food of the third day is for show (sumʿah); whoever seeks to be heard, God will make him heard." (3) This was only raised (marfūʿan) by Ziyād ibn ʿAbd Allāh, and it is anomalous (gharīb).

It is recommended to congratulate him, saying to the husband: "May God bless you, and may He bless upon you, and may He unite you both in goodness." (4) Abū Hurayrah, may God be pleased with him, reported that he, may God bless him and grant him peace, commanded this.

It is recommended to make the marriage public. He, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: "The distinction between the lawful and the unlawful is the drum and the voice." (5) The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: "Proclaim this marriage, hold it in the mosques, and beat drums for it." (6)

Al-Rubayyiʿ bint Muʿawwidh said: The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, came and entered on the morning of my wedding night, and sat upon my bedding. There were young girls of ours beating their drums and lamenting those of my forefathers who had been killed—until one of them said: "And among us is a Prophet who knows what will be tomorrow." He said to her: "Stop this, and say what you were saying before." (7)

**The Second Etiquette: Good Character with Them**

This entails bearing their harm out of compassion for them, due to the deficiency of their intellect. God, exalted is He, said: "And consort with them in kindness" {«وَعَاشِرُوهُنَّ بِالْمَعْرُوفِ»}. And regarding the magnification of their right, He said: "And they have taken from you a solemn covenant" {«وَأَخَذْنَ مِنكُم مِّيثَاقًا غَلِيظًا»}. And He said: "And the companion at your side" {«وَالصَّاحِبِ بِالْجَنبِ»}—it is said this means the wife.

The last thing the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, bequeathed was three matters he kept repeating until his tongue faltered and his speech became faint. He kept saying: "The prayer, the prayer, and what your right hands possess—do not burden them beyond their capacity. God, God! For they are captives (ʿawān) in your hands"—meaning prisoners—"you have taken them as a trust from God, and you have made their private parts lawful to you by the word of God." (8)

He, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: "Whoever endures the ill temper of his wife, God will give him a reward like that which He gave to Job (Ayyūb) for his affliction; and whoever endures the ill temper of her husband, God will give her a reward like that of Āsiyah, the wife of Pharaoh." (1)

The hadith that his wives, may God bless him and grant him peace, would argue with him, and one of them would shun him from day to night, is agreed upon (muttafaq ʿalayh) from the hadith of ʿUmar in the long narration concerning His saying: "If you two turn in repentance to God" {«فَإِن تَظَاهَرَا عَلَيْهِ»}.

ʿUmar's wife, may God be pleased with him, argued with him in speech, and he said: "Do you argue with me, O bald one?" She replied: "The wives of the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, argue with him, and he is better than you." (2)

The hadith that one of them pushed the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, in the chest, and her mother rebuked her, and he said: "Leave her, for they do more than that"—I have not found an original source for it. (3)

The hadith that an exchange occurred between him and ʿĀʾishah until he brought Abū Bakr between them as an arbiter—al-Ṭabarānī narrated it in al-Awsaṭ and al-Khaṭīb in al-Tārīkh from the hadith of ʿĀʾishah with a weak chain. (4)

The hadith that ʿĀʾishah once said to him: "You claim to be a Prophet, yet you get angry"—and the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, smiled. Abū Yaʿlā narrated it in his Musnad and Abū al-Shaykh in Kitāb al-Amthāl from the hadith of ʿĀʾishah, and it contains Ibn Isḥāq who used ʿanʿanah (ambiguous transmission). (5)

The hadith that he would say to ʿĀʾishah: "I know your anger from your pleasure"—agreed upon, from the hadith of her sister. (6)

The hadith that the first love to occur in Islam was the Prophet's love, may God bless him and grant him peace, for ʿĀʾishah—al-Shaykhān narrated it from the hadith of ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ that he said: "Who is most beloved to you, O Messenger of God?" He said: "ʿĀʾishah." As for it being the first, Ibn al-Jawzī narrated it in al-Mawḍūʿāt from the hadith of Anas; perhaps he meant in Medina, as in the other hadith that Ibn al-Zubayr was the first child born in Islam—meaning in Medina. Otherwise, the Prophet's love for Khadījah is a well-known matter attested by authentic hadiths. (7)

The hadith that he would say to ʿĀʾishah: "I am to you like Abū Zarʿ to Umm Zarʿ, except that I will not divorce you"—agreed upon from the hadith of ʿĀʾishah without the exception; al-Zubayr ibn Bakkār and al-Khaṭīb narrated it with this addition. (8)

The hadith: "Do not harm me concerning ʿĀʾishah, for by God, revelation has not descended upon me while I was in the blanket of any woman other than her"—al-Bukhārī narrated it from the hadith of ʿĀʾishah. (9)

The hadith of Anas: The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, was the most merciful of people toward women and children. Muslim narrated it with the wording: "I have not seen anyone more merciful to his family than the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace." ʿAlī ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, al-Baghawī, and others added "and children." (10)

**The Third Etiquette: Adding Jest and Playfulness to Bearing Harm**

This is what delights the hearts of women. The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, would jest with them and descend to the level of their intellects in deeds and character. It is narrated that he, may God bless him and grant him peace, would race ʿĀʾishah on foot; she beat him one day, and he beat her on another day, and he said: "This one for that one." (1)

It is reported that he, may God bless him and grant him peace, was the most jovial of people with his wives. (2)

ʿĀʾishah, may God be pleased with her, said: I heard the voices of some Abyssinians and others playing on the day of ʿĀshūrāʾ. The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said to me: "Would you like to see their play?" I said: "Yes." He sent for them, and they came. The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, stood between the two doors, placed his palm on the door, and extended his hand; I placed my chin on his hand, and they played while I watched. The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, kept saying: "Enough for you?" and I would say: "Be quiet"—two or three times. Then he said: "O ʿĀʾishah, is that enough?" I said: "Yes," so he gestured to them and they departed. (3)

The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: "The most complete of believers in faith is the one with the best character and the most gentle with his family." (4)

He, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: "The best of you is the best to his wives, and I am the best of you to my wives." (5)

ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, despite his harshness, said: "A man should be like a child with his family, but when they seek what he possesses, they find him a man."

Luqmān, may God have mercy on him, said: "The intelligent man should be like a child with his family, but when among the people, he is a man."

Regarding the interpretation of the reported saying that God hates the harsh, haughty man (al-jaʿẓarī al-jawwāẓ) (6): it is said he is the one severe with his family and arrogant in himself. This is one of the interpretations of His saying, exalted is He: "Cruel, moreover, and an illegitimate pretender" {«عُتُلٍّ»}—it is said al-ʿutul is the harsh-tongued, hard-hearted one toward his family.

He, may God bless him and grant him peace, said to Jābir: "Why not a virgin, so you could play with her and she with you?" (7)

A Bedouin woman described her husband after his death, saying: "By God, he was laughing when he entered, silent when he went out, eating what he found, and not asking about what was missing."

**The Fourth Etiquette: Not Overindulging in Jest and Compliance**

One should not overextend in jest, good character, and following her whims to the point of corrupting her nature and entirely losing his awe in her eyes. Rather, he must observe moderation—not abandoning dignity and restraint whenever he sees something objectionable, nor opening the door to assisting in wrongdoings at all. Whenever he sees what contravenes the Sacred Law and manliness, he should show displeasure and indignation.

Al-Ḥasan said: "By God, no man wakes up obeying his wife in her whims except that God casts him into the Fire."

ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, said: "Oppose women, for in opposing them lies blessing." It has been said: "Consult them, then oppose them."

The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: "Wretched is the slave of his wife." (8) He said this only because if a man obeys her in her whims, he is her slave. He is indeed wretched, for God gave him mastery over the woman, yet he gave her mastery over himself—reversing the matter and inverting the case, obeying Satan who said: "And I will command them, so they will change God's creation" {«وَلَآمُرَنَّهُمْ فَلَيُغَيِّرُنَّ خَلْقَ اللَّهِ»}. For the right of a man is to be followed, not to follow. God called men "qawwāmūn" (managers) over women, and called the husband a master (sayyid), saying, exalted is He: "And they found her master at the door" {«وَأَلْفَيَا سَيِّدَهَا لَدَى الْبَابِ»}. When the master becomes subjugated, he has exchanged God's favor for ingratitude.

Your soul is like your own self: if you release its reins a little, it will bolt with you a long way; if you slacken its halter a span, it will drag you an arm's length; but if you bridle it and tighten your grip at the point of firmness, you will master it.

Al-Shāfiʿī, may God be pleased with him, said: "Three people—if you honor them, they dishonor you; if you humiliate them, they honor you: the woman, the servant, and the Nabataean." He meant: if you give pure honor without mixing in your firmness with gentleness and your harshness with kindness.

The Arab women used to teach their daughters to test husbands. A woman would say to her daughter: "Test your husband before advancing and daring against him. Pull out the head of his spear; if he remains silent, cut meat on his shield; if he remains silent, break bones with his sword; if he remains silent, put the packsaddle on his back and ride him—for he is your donkey."

In sum, by justice the heavens and the earth stand. Everything that exceeds its limit inverts into its opposite. One should therefore tread the path of moderation in both opposition and compliance, following the truth in all of this, to be safe from their evil. For their scheming is great, their evil is widespread, and what predominates in them is ill temper and weakness of intellect. This does not become balanced from them except through a kind of gentleness mixed with governance.

He, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: "The likeness of a righteous woman among women is like a white-bellied crow among a hundred crows." (1) Al-aṣʿam means white-bellied.

In the counsel of Luqmān to his son: "O my son, beware the evil woman, for she will age you before your time. Beware the worst of women, for they do not call to good. And be on guard even against the good ones among them."

He, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: "Seek refuge from the three calamities" (2)—and he counted among them the evil woman, for she is the one who ages one before old age. In another wording: "If you enter upon her, she reviles you; if you are absent from her, she betrays you."

He, may God bless him and grant him peace, said regarding the good among women: "You are the companions of Joseph" (3)—meaning: if Abū Bakr's being put forward for the prayer had been diverted by you, it would have been a deviation from truth to whim. God, exalted is He, said when they disclosed the secret of the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace: "If you two turn in repentance to God, your hearts have indeed inclined" {«إِن تَتُوبَا إِلَى اللَّهِ فَقَدْ صَغَتْ قُلُوبُكُمَا»}—that is, they deviated. And He said this concerning the best of his wives. (4)

He, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: "No people will prosper who are ruled by a woman." (5)

The hadith that the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, forbade seeking out the faults of women—al-Ṭabarānī narrated it in al-Awsaṭ from the hadith of Jābir: "He forbade seeking the slips of women." The hadith is in Muslim with the wording: "He forbade a man from returning to his family at night, to betray them or seek their faults." Al-Bukhārī restricted it to mentioning the prohibition of returning at night. In another wording: "to take women by surprise."

When the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, returned from a journey, he said before entering Medina: "Do not return to your women at night." Two men violated this and hurried ahead, and each found in his home what he disliked. (1)

In the famous report: "The woman is like a rib; if you straighten her, you break her. Leave her, and you will enjoy her despite her crookedness." (2) This concerns refining her character.

He, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: "There is a jealousy that God, mighty and majestic, hates—the jealousy of a man over his family without cause for suspicion." (3) For that is from the ill suspicion we have been forbidden, since "some suspicion is sin" {«إِنَّ بَعْضَ الظَّنِّ إِثْمٌ»}.

ʿAlī, may God be pleased with him, said: "Do not be excessively jealous over your family, lest you be accused of evil because of it."

As for jealousy in its proper place, it is indispensable and praiseworthy. The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: "God, exalted is He, is jealous, and the believer is jealous. God's jealousy is that a believing man should commit what God has forbidden him." (4)

He, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: "Do you marvel at Saʿd's jealousy? By God, I am more jealous than him, and God is more jealous than me." (5) For the sake of God's jealousy, He forbade indecencies, both open and hidden. No one loves an excuse more than God, and for that He sent warners and bearers of good tidings. No one loves praise more than God, and for that He promised Paradise.

The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: "On the night of my night journey, I saw in Paradise a palace with a young girl in its courtyard. I said: 'Whose palace is this?' It was said: 'ʿUmar's.' I wanted to look at her, but I remembered your jealousy, O ʿUmar." ʿUmar wept and said: "Shall I be jealous of you, O Messenger of God?" (6)

Al-Ḥasan used to say: "Do you leave your women to jostle with coarse men in the markets? May God disgrace the one who is not jealous."

He, upon him be peace and blessings, said: "There is a jealousy God loves and a jealousy God hates; and there is a pride God loves and a pride God hates. The jealousy God loves is jealousy in the case of suspicion; the jealousy God hates is jealousy without suspicion. The pride God loves is a man's pride in himself at battle and at the clash; the pride God hates is pride in falsehood." (7)

He, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: "I am indeed jealous, and no man who is not jealous has a heart but that it is inverted." (8)

The sufficient way that obviates jealousy is that men should not enter upon her, and she should not go out to the markets.

The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said to his daughter Fāṭimah, peace be upon her: "What is best for a woman?" She said: "That she not see a man, and no man see her." He drew her to him and said: "Offspring, one from another" {«ذُرِّيَّةً بَعْضُهَا مِن بَعْضٍ»} (9)—approving her words.

The companions of the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, used to block the apertures and holes in walls so that women would not look out at men. Muʿādh saw his wife looking through an aperture and struck her; he also saw his wife give a slave-boy an apple she had bitten from, and struck her.

ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, said: "Make women unattractive, and they will stay in their chambers." He said this only because they do not desire to go out in shabby attire.

He said: "Accustom your women to 'no'"—for the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, had permitted women to attend the mosque. (1) The correct view now is to prevent them, except for elderly women. Indeed, this was deemed correct in the time of the companions, so much so that ʿĀʾishah, may God be pleased with her, said: "If the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, had seen what women innovated after him, he would have prevented them from going out." (2)

When Ibn ʿUmar said: "The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: 'Do not prevent the female servants of God from the mosques of God,'" one of his sons said: "Yes, by God, we will prevent them." He struck him and was angry with him, saying: "You hear me saying: 'The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: Do not prevent them,' and you say: 'Yes, we will'?" (3) He only dared to oppose because he knew the times had changed, and he was only angered because of his open utterance of opposition without showing an excuse.

Likewise, the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, had permitted them to go out specifically on the two festivals. (4) But they should not go out except with the consent of their husbands. Going out now is permissible for a chaste woman with her husband's consent, but staying home is safer. She should not go out except for a necessity, for going out for spectacles and non-essential matters detracts from manliness and may lead to corruption. If she does go out, she should lower her gaze from men. We do not say that a man's face is ʿawrah (private) for her, as a woman's face is for him; rather, it is like the face of a beardless youth for a man—forbidden to look at only when there is fear of temptation. If there is no temptation, then it is not forbidden, for men have always throughout time gone out with uncovered faces while women went out veiled. Had men's faces been ʿawrah for women, they would have been commanded to veil, or women would have been prevented from going out except for necessity.

**The Sixth Etiquette: Moderation in Expenditure**

One should not be stingy toward them in spending, nor extravagant, but rather moderate. God, exalted is He, said: "Eat and drink, but do not be extravagant" {«وَكُلُوا وَاشْرَبُوا وَلَا تُسْرِفُوا»}, and He said: "Do not make your hand chained to your neck, nor extend it completely" {«وَلَا تَجْعَلْ يَدَكَ مَغْلُولَةً إِلَى عُنُقِكَ وَلَا تَبْسُطْهَا كُلَّ الْبَسْطِ»}. The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: "The best of you is the best to his family." (5)

He, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: "A dinar you spend in the path of God, a dinar you spend on a slave's emancipation, a dinar you give in charity to a poor person, and a dinar you spend on your family—the greatest in reward is the one you spend on your family." (6)

It is said that ʿAlī, may God be pleased with him, had four wives, and he would buy for each one, every four days, meat for a dirham. Al-Ḥasan, may God be pleased with him, said: "They were fruitful in men and barren in women and clothing."

Ibn Sīrīn said: "It is recommended for a man to prepare for his family every Friday a fālūdhaj (sweet confection)." Sweetness, though not among essentials, its complete abandonment is stinginess in custom.

He should command her to give in charity the leftover food and what would spoil if left. This is the least degree of goodness. The woman may do this by virtue of the situation without explicit permission from the husband.

He should not reserve a fine food for himself and not feed them from it, for that embitters hearts and distances one from kind companionship. If he is determined to do so, let him eat it secretly so his family does not know. He should not describe to them a food he does not intend to feed them. When he eats, all the family should sit at his table. Sufyān, may God be pleased with him, said: "It has reached us that God and His angels send blessings upon a household that eats together."

The most important thing he must observe in spending is to feed her from lawful (ḥalāl) means and not enter evil paths for her sake, for that would be an injury against her, not care for her. We have already presented the reports concerning this when mentioning the harms of marriage.

**The Seventh Etiquette: Learning the Rulings of Menstruation**

The married man should learn from the knowledge of menstruation (ḥayḍ) and its rulings what enables him to observe the obligatory precaution, and he should teach his wife the rulings of prayer—what is made up (qaḍāʾ) during menstruation and what is not. For he has been commanded to protect her from the Fire by His saying, exalted is He: "Protect yourselves and your families from a Fire" {«قُوا أَنفُسَكُمْ وَأَهْلِيكُمْ نَارًا»}. He must therefore instill in her the creed of the People of the Sunnah (Ahl al-Sunnah), remove from her heart every innovation (bidʿah) if she hears one, frighten her regarding God if she is lax in religious matters, and teach her what she needs of the rulings of menstruation and irregular bleeding (istḥāḍah). The knowledge of istḥāḍah is lengthy.

What must necessarily be imparted to women regarding menstruation is the clarification of which prayers she must make up. Whenever her blood ceases shortly before sunset with enough time for one rakʿah, she must make up the ẓuhr and ʿaṣr prayers; and if it ceases before dawn with enough time for one rakʿah, she must make up the maghrib and ʿishāʾ prayers. This is the least that women must observe.

If the man is capable of teaching her, she has no need to go out to ask the scholars. If the man's knowledge is deficient, but he deputizes for her in asking and informs her of the muftī's answer, she has no need to go out. If neither is the case, then she may go out to ask—indeed, it is incumbent upon her, and the man sins by preventing her. Once she has learned what is obligatory upon her, she may not go out to a remembrance gathering or to learn supererogatory knowledge except with his consent. If a woman neglects a ruling of menstruation or istḥāḍah and the man does not teach her, the man bears sin along with her and shares in her guilt.

**The Eighth Etiquette: Justice Among Co-Wives**

If he has multiple wives, he must be just between them and not incline to one over another. If he goes on a journey and wishes to take one with him, he should cast lots among them (1)—for thus did the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, act. If he wrongs a woman by taking her night, he must make it up to her, for making it up is obligatory upon him. At that point, he needs to know the rulings of division (qasm), the mention of which is lengthy.

The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: "Whoever has two wives and inclines to one over the other"—in another wording: "and does not treat them justly—will come on the Day of Resurrection with one side of him leaning." (2)

Justice is required of him in provision and overnight stay. As for love and intercourse, that does not fall under choice. God, exalted is He, said: "You will never be able to be just between women, even if you strive" {«وَلَن تَسْتَطِيعُوا أَن تَعْدِلُوا بَيْنَ النِّسَاءِ وَلَوْ حَرَصْتُمْ»}—that is, justice in the desire of the heart and the inclination of the soul, which entails disparity in intercourse.

The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, was just between them in provision and overnight stays, saying: "O God, this is my effort in what I possess; I have no power over what You possess and I do not own"—meaning love. (3)

ʿĀʾishah, may God be pleased with her, was the most beloved of his wives to him (4), and his other wives knew this. He was carried around during his illness every day and every night, spending the night with each of them, saying: "Where will I be tomorrow?" One of his wives perceived this and said: "He is only asking about ʿĀʾishah's day." They said: "O Messenger of God, we permit you to be in ʿĀʾishah's house, for it is hard on you to be carried every night." He said: "Are you all satisfied with that?" They said: "Yes." He said: "Then move me to ʿĀʾishah's house." (5)

Whenever one wife gifts her night to her co-wife and the husband consents, the right is established for her. The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, used to divide between his wives. When Sawdah bint Zamʿah grew old, he intended to divorce her, so she gifted her night to ʿĀʾishah and asked him to keep her in marriage so she would be gathered in the company of his wives. He kept her, and he would not divide for her, giving ʿĀʾishah two nights and his other wives one night each. (1)

However, due to his justice and strength, when his soul yearned for one of his wives outside her turn and he had intercourse with her, he would circulate among his other wives that day or night. From this is what is narrated from ʿĀʾishah, may God be pleased with her, that the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, circulated among all his wives in a single night. (2) And from Anas, that he, may God bless him and grant him peace, circulated among nine wives in one forenoon. (3)

**The Ninth Etiquette: Concerning Recalcitrance (al-Nushūz)**

Whenever a quarrel occurs between them and their affair does not mend—if it is from both sides, or from the man—the wife has no authority over her husband, and he is not able to reform her. Then two arbiters are necessary: one from his family and one from hers, to look into the matter between them and set it right. "If they both desire reconciliation, God will bring harmony between them" {«إِن يُرِيدَا إِصْلَاحًا يُوَفِّقِ اللَّهُ بَيْنَهُمَا»}. ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, sent an arbiter to a married couple, and he returned without having reconciled them, so ʿUmar struck him with the whip and said: "God, exalted is He, says: 'If they both desire reconciliation, God will bring harmony between them.'" The man returned, improved his intention, and dealt gently with them, and so reconciled between them.

As for when the recalcitrance is specifically from the woman, then "men are managers of women" {«الرِّجَالُ قَوَّامُونَ عَلَى النِّسَاءِ»}, and he may discipline her and compel her to obedience by force. Likewise, if she abandons prayer, he may compel her to pray by force. However, he should proceed gradually in disciplining her: first, he should offer admonition, warning, and intimidation. If that does not work, he turns his back to her in bed or separates from her in the bedding, shunning her while remaining in the house with her, from one night to three nights.

If that does not work in her, he strikes her with a non-violent strike (ḍarb ghayr mubarriḥ)—one that pains her but does not break a bone, does not draw blood, and does not strike the face, for that is prohibited.

It was said to the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace: "What is the right of the woman over the man?" He said: "Feed her when you eat, clothe her when you clothe yourself, do not disfigure the face, do not strike except non-violently, and do not shun her except in the bed." (4)

He may be angry with her and shun her in a matter of religion for ten, twenty

||| القسم الثاني من هذا الباب النظر في حقوق الزوج عليها

والقول الشافي فيه أن النكاح نوع رق فهي رقيقة له فعليها طاعة الزوج
مطلقا في كل ما طلب منها في نفسها مما لا معصية فيه وقد ورد في تعظيم حق
الزوج عليها أخبار كثيرة قال صلى الله عليه وسلم أيما امرأة PageV02P056
ماتت وزوجها عنها راض دخلت الجنة (1)
وكان رجل قد خرج إلى سفر وعهد إلى امرأته أن لا تنزل من العلو إلى السفل
وكان أبوها في الأسفل فمرض فأرسلت المرأة إلى رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
تستأذن في النزول إلى أبيها فقال صلى الله عليه وسلم أطيعي زوجك فمات
فاستأمرته فقال أطيعي زوجك فدفن أبوها فأرسل رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
إليها يخبرها أن الله قد غفر لأبيها بطاعتها لزوجها (2)
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم إذا صلت المرأة خمسها وصامت شهرها وحفظت فرجها
وأطاعت زوجها دخلت جنة ربها (3)
وأضاف طاعة الزوج إلى مباني الإسلام وذكر رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
النساء فقال حاملات والدات مرضعات رحيمات بأولادهن لولا ما يأتين إلى
أزواجهن دخل مصلياتهن الجنة (4)
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم اطلعت في النار فإذا أكثر أهلها النساء فقلن لم
يا رسول الله  قال يكثرن اللعن ويكفرن العشير (5)
يعني الزوج المعاشر
وفي خبر آخر اطلعت في الجنة فإذا أقل أهلها النساء فقلت أين النساء قال
شغلهن الأحمران الذهب والزعفران (6)
يعني الحلي ومصبغات الثياب وقالت عائشة رضي الله عنها أتت فتاة إلى النبي
صلى الله عليه وسلم فقالت يا رسول الله إني فتاة أخطب فأكره التزويج فما حق
الزوج على المرأة قال لو كان من فرقه إلى قدمه صديد فلحسته ما أدت شكره
قالت أفلا أتزوج قال بلى تزوجي فإنه خير (7)
قال ابن عباس أتت امرأة من خثعم إلى رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم فقالت
إني امرأة أيم وأريد أن تزوج فما حق الزوج قال إن من حق الزوج على الزوجة
إذا أرادها فراودها عن نفسها وهي على ظهر بعير لا تمنعه ومن حقه أن لا تعطي
شيئا من بيته إلا بإذنه فإن فعلت ذلك كان الوزر عليها والأجر له ومن حقه أن
لا تصوم تطوعا إلا بإذنه فإن فعلت جاعت وعطشت ولم يتقبل منها وإن خرجت من
بيتها بغير إذنه لعنتها الملائكة حتى ترجع إلى بيته أو تتوب (8)
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم لو أمرت أحدا أن يسجد لأحد لأمرت المرأة أن تسجد
لزوجها من عظم حقه عليها (9)
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم أقرب ما تكون المرأة من وجه ربها إذا كانت في
قعر بيتها وإن صلاتها في صحن دارها أفضل من صلاتها في المسجد وصلاتها في
بيتها أفضل من صلاتها في صحن دارها وصلاتها PageV02P057
في مخدعها أفضل من صلاتها في بيتها (1)
والمخدع بيت في بيت وذلك للستر ولذلك قال صلى الله عليه وسلم والمرأة
عورة فإذا خرجت استشرفها الشيطان (2)
وقال أيضا للمرأة عشر عورات فإذا تزوجت ستر الزوج عورة واحدة فإذا ماتت
ستر القبر العشر عورات (3)
فحقوق الزوج على الزوجة كثيرة وأهمها أمران أحدهما الصيانة والستر
والآخر ترك المطالبة بما وراء الحاجة والتعفف عن كسبه إذا كان حراما
وهكذا كانت عادة النساء في السلف كان الرجل إذا خرج من منزله تقول  له
امرأته أو ابنته إياك وكسب الحرام فإنا نصبر على الجوع والضر ولا نصبر على
النار
وهم رجل من السلف بالسفر فكره جيرانه سفره فقالوا لزوجته لم ترضين بسفره
ولم يدع لك نفقة فقالت زوجي منذ عرفته عرفته أكالا وما عرفته رزاقا ولي رب
رزاق يذهب الأكال ويبقى الرزاق
وخطبت رابعة بنت إسماعيل أحمد بن أبي الحواري فكره ذلك لما كان فيه من
العبادة وقال لها والله مالي همة في النساء لشغلي بحالي فقالت إني لأشغل
بحالي منك ومالي شهوة ولكن ورثت مالا جزيلا من زوجي فأردت أن تنفقه على
إخوانك وأعرف بك الصالحين فيكون لي طريقا إلى الله عز وجل فقال حتى استأذن
أستاذي فرجع إلى أبي سليمان الداراني قال وكان ينهاني عن التزويج ويقول ما
تزوج أحد من أصحابنا إلا تغير فلما سمع كلامها قال تزوج بها فإنها ولية لله
هذا كلام الصديقين قال فتزوجتها فكان في منزلنا كن من جص ففني من غسل أيدي
المستعجلين للخروج بعد الأكل فضلا عمن غسل بالأشنان
قال وتزوجت عليها ثلاث نسوة فكانت تطعمني الطيبات وتطيبني وتقول اذهب
بنشاطك وقوتك إلى أزواجك وكانت رابعة هذه تشبه في أهل الشام برابعة العدوية
بالبصرة
ومن الواجبات عليها أن لا تفرط في ماله بل تحفظه عليه
قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم لا يحل لها أن تطعم من بيته إلا بإذنه
إلا الرطب من الطعام الذي يخاف فساده فإن أطعمت عن رضاه كان لها مثل أجره
وإن أطعمت بغير إذنه كان له الأجر وعليها الوزر (4)
ومن حقها على الوالدين تعليمها حسن المعاشرة وآداب العشرة مع الزوج كما
روي أن أسماء بنت خارجة الفزاري قالت لأبنتها عند التزوج إنك خرجت من العش
الذي فيه درجت فصرت إلى فراش لم تعرفيه وقرين لم تألفيه فكوني له أرضا يكن
لك سماء وكوني له مهادا يكن لك عمادا وكوني له أمة يكن لك
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ر-ق-ق (r-q-q)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Servitude, bondage; the state of being owned (riqq)
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The legal-spiritual condition of subordination entailed by marriage as a form of lawful servitude
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Used here in its literal sense (ḥaqīqah) of legal servitude, not metaphorical
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Clause (al-sharṭ) — "idhā... fa..." constructions governing legal obligations (e.g., "if she prays... and obeys... she enters Paradise")
chapters.translation:
I say: The second division of this chapter is the consideration of the husband's rights over her.

The decisive statement concerning this is that marriage is a type of servitude (riqq); thus she is his bondswoman. Therefore, obedience to the husband is incumbent upon her absolutely, in everything he requests of her concerning herself, provided it involves no disobedience [to God]. Numerous reports have come down regarding the magnification of the husband's right over her. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: «أيما امرأة ماتت وزوجها عنها راض دخلت الجنة» — "Any woman who dies while her husband is pleased with her enters Paradise."

There was a man who had gone out on a journey and had charged his wife not to descend from the upper floor to the lower. Her father was in the lower part, and he fell ill. The woman sent word to the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) seeking permission to descend to her father. He said: "Obey your husband." Then her father died, and she again sought his instruction. He said: "Obey your husband." So her father was buried [without her descending]. Then the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) sent word to her, informing her that Allah had forgiven her father because of her obedience to her husband.

He (peace be upon him) also said: «إذا صلت المرأة خمسها وصامت شهرها وحفظت فرجها وأطاعت زوجها دخلت جنة ربها» — "When a woman prays her five [daily prayers], fasts her month [of Ramadan], guards her chastity, and obeys her husband, she enters the Paradise of her Lord."

He attached obedience to the husband to the foundations of Islam. The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) mentioned women and said: "They are bearers [of children], givers of birth, sucklers, compassionate toward their offspring — were it not for what they do to their husbands, those among them who pray would enter Paradise."

He (peace be upon him) said: "I looked into the Fire and found that most of its inhabitants were women." They said: "Why, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "They curse excessively and are ungrateful to the companion (al-ʿashīr)" — meaning the husband with whom one consorts.

In another report: "I looked into Paradise and found that fewest of its inhabitants were women." I said: "Where are the women?" He said: "The two red things distracted them: gold and saffron" — meaning jewelry and dyed garments.

ʿĀʾishah (may Allah be pleased with her) said: A young woman came to the Prophet (peace be upon him) and said: "O Messenger of Allah, I am a young woman who is sought in marriage, but I dislike marrying. What is the husband's right over the wife?" He said: "Were there pus flowing from his crown to his feet and she licked it up, she would not have fulfilled his due." She said: "Then shall I not marry?" He said: "Yes, marry, for it is good."

Ibn ʿAbbās said: A woman from Khathʿam came to the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) and said: "I am a widow, and I wish to marry. What is the husband's right?" He said: "Among the husband's rights over the wife is that if he desires her and solicits her from herself while she is on the back of a camel, she must not refuse him. And among his rights is that she give nothing from his house except with his permission — for if she does so, the sin is upon her and the reward is his. And among his rights is that she not observe a supererogatory fast except with his permission — for if she does so, she goes hungry and thirsty, and it is not accepted from her. And if she leaves her house without his permission, the angels curse her until she returns to his house or repents."

He (peace be upon him) said: «لو أمرت أحدا أن يسجد لأحد لأمرت المرأة أن تسجد لزوجها من عظم حقه عليها» — "Were I to command anyone to prostrate to anyone, I would have commanded the woman to prostrate to her husband, because of the greatness of his right over her."

He (peace be upon him) said: "The closest a woman comes to the face of her Lord is when she is in the depths of her house. Her prayer in the courtyard of her house is better than her prayer in the mosque; her prayer in her house is better than her prayer in her courtyard; and her prayer in her inner chamber (makhdaʿ) is better than her prayer in her house." The makhdaʿ is a room within a room — this is for the sake of concealment. For this reason he (peace be upon him) said: «والمرأة عورة فإذا خرجت استشرفها الشيطان» — "The woman is an ʿawrah (something to be concealed); when she goes out, Satan gazes at her."

He also said: "The woman has ten ʿawrahs. When she marries, the husband veils one ʿawrah; when she dies, the grave veils all ten."

Thus the husband's rights over the wife are many, and the most important of them are two: first, her protection and concealment (al-ṣiyānah wa al-satr); and second, her refraining from demanding what is beyond need, and her abstaining from his earnings if they are unlawful.

Such was the custom of women among the Salaf: when a man left his home, his wife or daughter would say to him: "Beware of unlawful earning (al-kasb al-ḥarām), for we can endure hunger and hardship, but we cannot endure the Fire."

A man of the Salaf intended to travel, and his neighbors disapproved of his journey. They said to his wife: "Why are you content with his traveling, when he has left you no maintenance?" She said: "Since I have known my husband, I have known him as an eater (akkāl); I have never known him as a provider (razzāq). I have a Lord who is the Provider (Razzāq) — He takes away the eater and remains the Provider."

Rābiʿah bint Ismāʿīl sought to marry Aḥmad ibn Abī al-Ḥawārī, but he disliked this because of his devotion to worship. He said to her: "By Allah, I have no concern for women, for I am occupied with my own state." She said: "I am even more occupied with my own state than you, and I have no desire [for marriage]. But I have inherited abundant wealth from my husband, and I wish to spend it upon your brethren [in faith]. I know you as one of the righteous, so that this may be for me a path to Allah, Mighty and Majestic." He said: "Let me seek permission from my master." He returned to Abū Sulaymān al-Dārānī — and he had been forbidding him from marriage, saying: "None of our companions has married without being changed." But when he heard her words, he said: "Marry her, for she is a friend (waliyyah) of Allah. This is the speech of the ṣiddīqīn (the veracious)." He said: "So I married her. In our house there was a lime cistern (kān min jiṣṣ) which was exhausted by the washing of hands of those hastening to leave after eating — let alone those who washed with ashes (ushnān)."

He said: "I married three other women besides her, and she would feed me delicious foods and perfume me, saying: 'Go with your vigor and strength to your [other] wives.'" This Rābiʿah was compared in Syria to Rābiʿah al-ʿAdawiyyah of Basra.

Among the obligations incumbent upon her is that she not be negligent with his wealth, but rather preserve it for him. The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) said: «لا يحل لها أن تطعم من بيته إلا بإذنه إلا الرطب من الطعام الذي يخاف فساده فإن أطعمت عن رضاه كان لها مثل أجره وإن أطعمت بغير إذنه كان له الأجر وعليها الوزر» — "It is not lawful for her to feed [others] from his house except with his permission, save fresh food that is feared to spoil. If she feeds with his pleasure, she has the like of his reward; if she feeds without his permission, he has the reward and the sin is upon her."

And among her rights upon her parents is that they teach her good companionship and the etiquettes of cohabitation with the husband. It is related that Asmāʾ bint Khārijah al-Fazāriyyah said to her daughter upon her marriage: "You have left the nest in which you grew up, and have come to a bed you do not know and a companion you have not befriended. Be for him a earth, and he will be for you a sky; be for him a resting place (mahād), and he will be for you a pillar (ʿimād); be for him a bondswoman, and he will be for you a slave. Do not cling to him so that he loathes you, nor distance yourself from him so that he forgets you. If he draws near to you, draw near to him; if he withdraws, withdraw from him. Guard his nose, his ear, and his eye — let him not smell from you but fragrance, hear from you but goodness, and see from you but beauty."

A man said to his wife:

"Take the forgiving from me, and you will prolong my affection — and do not speak in my fury when I am angry.
Do not peck at me as you peck the drum once — for you do not know how the unseen will be.
Do not multiply complaints, for they remove desire — and my heart will reject you, for hearts are fickle.
For I have seen that love in the heart, when harm joins it, does not linger — love departs."

The comprehensive statement concerning the etiquettes of the woman, without prolongation, is that she be seated in the depths of her house, devoted to her spindle, not frequently ascending or looking out, sparing in speech with her neighbors, not entering upon them except in a situation that necessitates entry. She preserves her husband in his absence, seeks his pleasure in all her affairs, and does not betray him in herself or his wealth. She does not leave her house except with his permission; if she goes out with his permission, she does so concealed in humble attire, seeking empty places rather than thoroughfares and markets, guarding herself so that no stranger hears her voice or recognizes her person. She does not make herself known to her husband's friend for her needs; rather, she disguises herself from anyone she suspects might know her or whom she knows. Her concern is the rectification of her affairs and the management of her house, devoting herself to her prayer and fasting. If a friend of her husband seeks permission at the door while the husband is absent, she does not inquire [who it is] nor engage him in speech, out of jealousy for herself and her husband. She is content with what Allah has provided her through her husband, and she places his right before her own right and the rights of all her relatives. She is clean in herself, ready in all circumstances for his enjoyment if he so wishes, compassionate toward her children, protective of their concealment, restrained in tongue from cursing the children or answering back the husband.

He (peace be upon him) said: «أنا وامرأة سفعاء الخدين كهاتين في الجنة» — "I and a woman with dark cheeks will be like these two in Paradise" — a woman who was widowed from her husband and confined herself to her daughters until they grew up or died.

He (peace be upon him) said: "Allah has forbidden every human from entering Paradise before me. But I looked to my right, and behold, a woman was hastening before me to the gate of Paradise. I said: 'What is this one hastening before me?' It was said: 'O Muhammad, this is a woman who was beautiful and comely, and she had orphans under her care. She bore them patiently until their affairs reached what they reached, and Allah thanked her for that.'"

Among her etiquettes is that she not boast over her husband of her beauty, nor disdain her husband for his ugliness. It is related that al-Aṣmaʿī said: "I entered the desert, and behold, there was a woman among the most beautiful of people under a man among the ugliest of people. I said to her: 'O woman, are you content for yourself to be under the likes of him?' She said: 'O man, be silent — you have spoken ill. Perhaps he has been excellent in what is between him and his Creator, so He made me his reward; or perhaps I have been remiss in what is between me and my Creator, so He made him my punishment. Shall I not be content with what Allah has willed for me?' And she silenced me."

Al-Aṣmaʿī said: "I saw in the desert a woman wearing a red shirt, dyed with henna, with a prayer-beads (subḥah) in her hand. I said: 'How far is this from that!' She said:

'For Allah there is from me a portion I do not neglect — and for play and idleness there is from me a portion.'

So I knew she was a righteous woman who had a husband for whom she adorned herself."

Among the woman's etiquettes is adherence to righteousness and restraint (al-inqibāḍ) in her husband's absence, and returning to play, expansiveness, and the means of pleasure in her husband's presence. She should not harm her husband in any way. It is related from Muʿādh ibn Jabal that the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) said: «لا تؤذي امرأة زوجها في الدنيا إلا قالت زوجته من الحور العين لا تؤذيه قاتلك الله فإنما هو عندك دخيل يوشك أن يفارقك إلينا» — "No woman harms her husband in this world but that his wife from the ḥūr al-ʿīn says: 'Do not harm him — may Allah curse you! For he is only a guest with you; soon he will part from you to us.'"

Among the rights of marriage incumbent upon her is that if her husband dies, she does not observe mourning (iḥdād) over him for more than four months and ten days, and she avoids perfume and adornment during this period. Zaynab bint Abī Salamah said: "I entered upon Umm Ḥabībah, the wife of the Prophet (peace be upon him), when her father Abū Sufyān ibn Ḥarb had died. She called for perfume containing yellow dye (khalūq) or something else, applied it to a slave-girl, then touched her cheeks with it, and said: 'By Allah, I have no need of perfume, except that I heard the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) say: «لا يحل لامرأة تؤمن بالله واليوم الآخر أن تحد على ميت أكثر من ثلاثة أيام إلا على زوج أربعة أشهر وعشرا» — "It is not lawful for a woman who believes in Allah and the Last Day to mourn over a dead person for more than three days, except over a husband — four months and ten days."'"

She is obliged to remain in the marital home until the end of the ʿiddah (waiting period), and she may not move to her family nor go out except for necessity.

Among her etiquettes is that she undertake every service in the house that she is able to perform. It is related from Asmāʾ bint Abī Bakr al-Ṣiddīq (may Allah be pleased with them both) that she said: "Al-Zubayr married me, and he had no wealth on earth, no slave, and nothing except his horse and his water-camel (nāḍiḥ). I used to feed his horse, suffice him its maintenance, tend it, pound date-stones for his camel, feed it, draw water, stitch its leather bucket (gharb), and knead dough. I used to carry date-stones on my head from a distance of two-thirds of a parasang (farasikh), until Abū Bakr sent me a slave-girl who sufficed me the tending of the horse — and it was as if she had freed me."

She said: "The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) met me one day with his companions, while the date-stones were upon my head. He said: 'Akh, akh' — to make his she-camel kneel so he could carry me behind him. But I felt shy to walk with the men, and I remembered al-Zubayr and his jealousy — and he was the most jealous of men. The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) perceived that I was shy, so he went on. I came to al-Zubayr and told him what had happened. He said: 'By Allah, your carrying the date-stones upon your head is harder upon me than your riding with him.'"

The Book of the Etiquettes of Marriage (Kitāb Ādāb al-Nikāḥ) is completed, by the praise of Allah and His grace. And may Allah send blessings upon every chosen servant.
