وهي أربعة أنواع ثلاثة منها باطلة
الأول شركة المفاوضة وهو أن يقولا تفاوضنا لنشترك في كل مالنا وعلينا
ومالاهما ممتازان فهي باطلة
الثاني شركة الأبدان وهو أن يتشارطا الاشتراك في أجرة العمل فهي باطلة
الثالث شركة الوجوه وهو أن يكون لأحدهما حشمة وقول مقبول فيكون من جهته
التنفيل ومن جهة غيره العمل فهذا أيضا باطل
وإنما الصحيح العقد الرابع المسمى شركة العنان وهو أن يختلط مالاهما بحيث
يتعذر التمييز بينهما إلا بقسمه ويأذن كل منهما لصاحبه في التصرف ثم حكمهما
توزيع الربح والخسران على قدر المالين ولا يجوز أن يغير ذلك بالشرط ثم
بالعزل يمتنع التصرف عن المعزول وبالقسمة ينفصل الملك عن الملك والصحيح أنه
يجوز عقد الشركة على العروض المشتراة ولا يشترط النقد بخلاف القراض
فهذا القدر من علم الفقه يجب تعلمه على كل مكتسب وإلا اقتحم الحرام من
حيث لا يدري
وأما معاملة القصاب والخباز والبقال فلا يستغني عنها المكتسب وغير
المكتسب والخلل فيها من ثلاثة وجوه من إهمال شروط البيع أو إهمال شروط
السلم أو الاقتصار على المعاطاة إذ العادات جارية بكتبه الخطوط على هؤلاء
بحاجات كل يوم ثم المحاسبة في كل مدة ثم التقويم بحسب ما يقع عليه التراضي
وذلك مما نرى القضاء بإباحته للحاجة ويحمل تسليمهم على إباحة التناول مع
انتظار العوض فيحل أكله ولكن يجب الضمان بأكله وتلزم قيمته يوم الإتلاف
فتجتمع في الذمة تلك القيم فإذا وقع التراضي على مقدار ما فينبغي أن يلتمس
منهم الإبراء المطلق لا تبقي عليه عهدة إن تطرق إليه تفاوت في التقويم فهذا
ما تجب القناعة به فإن تكليف وزن الثمن لكل حاجة من الحوائج في كل يوم وكل
ساعة تكليف شطط وكذا تكليف الإيجاب والقبول وتقدير ثمن كل قدر يسير منه فيه
عسر وإذا كثر كل نوع سهل تقويمه والله الموفق
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ش ر ك (sh-r-k)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is mixing or sharing, such that two things become indistinguishable in a joint holding.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal-theological usage, denotes a contractual co-participation in profit and liability, distinct from mere communal ownership.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) for physical mixing of assets; metaphorical (majāz) when extended to shared credit or reputation.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Clause (al-Sharṭ wa al-Jawāb) — The phrase "if they say" governs the ensuing legal apodosis, requiring the protasis to be read as a hypothetical contract-utterance, not a narrative report.
chapters.translation:
I say: The sixth contract is partnership (sharika). It comprises four types, three of which are null.

The first is the partnership of equal delegation (sharikat al-mufāwaḍah), namely that the two parties say, "We have mutually delegated (tafāwaḍnā) to share in all that we possess and all that we owe." Since their two capitals remain distinct, this is null.

The second is the partnership of bodies (sharikat al-abdān), namely that they stipulate mutual sharing in the wages of labor. This is null.

The third is the partnership of credit/faces (sharikat al-wujūh), namely that one of them possesses prestige and an accepted word, so that from his side comes the solicitation of credit (al-tanfīl) and from the other's side comes the work. This too is null.

Only the fourth contract is sound, called the partnership of equal investment (sharikat al-ʿinān), namely that their two capitals become mixed such that distinguishing between them becomes impossible except by division, and each one grants the other permission to dispose (al-taṣarruf). Then their ruling is the distribution of profit and loss in proportion to the two capitals, and it is not permissible to alter that by stipulation. Then, by dismissal (al-ʿazl), disposal is prevented for the dismissed one; and by division, ownership is separated from ownership. The sound position is that the partnership contract is permissible upon purchased commodities (al-ʿurūḍ), and cash (al-naqd) is not a condition, unlike the case of commenda (qirāḍ).

This measure of jurisprudence (fiqh) is obligatory to learn for every earner; otherwise he plunges into the forbidden (ḥarām) without realizing it.

As for dealing with the butcher, the baker, and the grocer, neither the earner nor the non-earner can dispense with it. The defect in it arises from three aspects: neglecting the conditions of sale, neglecting the conditions of salam (advance payment), or restricting oneself to mutual delivery (al-muʿāṭāh). For custom has run to writing down these people's accounts for daily needs, then settling accounts each period, then valuing according to what mutual consent falls upon. This is something for which we see the judges permitting it out of necessity. Their delivery is construed as permission to consume while awaiting the countervalue, so eating it becomes lawful. However, liability (al-ḍamān) is incurred by eating it, and its value on the day of destruction is owed. Those values accumulate in the debtor's liability (al-dhimmah). Then when mutual consent falls upon a certain amount, one should seek from them an absolute acquittal (al-ibrāʾ al-muṭlaq), so that no claim remains against him if any discrepancy in valuation should arise. This is what must be contented with, for obliging the weighing of the price for every need, every day, and every hour is an exorbitant obligation (taklīf shaṭaṭ). Likewise, obliging offer and acceptance (ījāb wa qabūl) and estimating the price of every small amount of it involves hardship. When each type becomes frequent, its valuation becomes easy. And God is the Granter of success.

chapters.title_en: The Third Chapter on Clarifying Justice and Avoiding Injustice in Transactions
chapters.arabic_text:
|| الباب الثالث في بيان العدل واجتناب الظلم في المعاملة

اعلم أن  المعاملة قد تجري على وجه يحكم المفتي بصحتها وانعقادها ولكنها
تشتمل على ظلم يتعرض به المعامل لسخط الله تعالى إذ ليس كل نهي يقتضي فساد
العقد وهذا الظلم يعني به ما استضر به الغير وهو منقسم إلى ما يعم ضرره
وإلى ما يخص المعامل
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ع-د-ل (ʿ-d-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Straightness, equilibrium, and acting with equity; the opposite of deviation (jūr)
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Justice as the mean between excess and deficiency, aligning with divine command in all dealings
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense of physical straightness; metaphorical extension to moral and legal rectitude in transactions
- Root: ظ-ل-م (ẓ-l-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Placing something in other than its proper place; darkness and obscurity
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Transgression against another's right, whether in property, person, or dignity; the cardinal vice opposed to ʿadl
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal meaning of darkness; metaphorical usage for wrongful harm inflicted upon others
- Root: ض-ر-ر (ḍ-r-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Harm, injury, or detriment affecting someone against their will
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Any form of damage, whether physical, financial, or moral, that violates the principle of no-harm (lā ḍarar)
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal physical harm; metaphorical extension to any prejudicial effect in contractual dealings
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Clause with Implied Subject (al-sharṭ bi-fāʾ al-taʿlīq) — The phrase "if a transaction occurs in a manner..." establishes a conditional framework where the ruling (fatwā of validity) is distinguished from the moral judgment (displeasure of God), requiring careful parsing of the apodosis.
chapters.translation: I say: Know that a transaction may occur in a manner such that the jurisconsult (muftī) rules upon its validity and legal soundness (ṣiḥḥah wa-inʿiqād), yet it nonetheless comprises an injustice (ẓulm) through which the transacting party exposes himself to the displeasure (sakhaṭ) of God the Exalted — for not every prohibition necessarily entails the corruption (fasād) of the contract. And this injustice here means that by which harm (ḍarar) is inflicted upon another, and it is divided into that whose harm is general (yaʿummu ḍararuhu) and that which is specific to the transacting party himself.

chapters.title_en: Section 204 — On the First Division of Transgressions of Universal Harm: Hoarding and the Circulation of Counterfeit Coinage
chapters.arabic_text:
||| القسم الأول فيما يعم ضرره وهو أنواع

النوع الأول الاحتكار فبائع الطعام يدخر الطعام ينتظر به غلاء الأسعار
وهو ظلم عام وصاحبه مذموم في الشرع
قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم من احتكر الطعام أربعين يوما ثم تصدق
به لم تكن صدقته كفارة لاحتكاره (1)
وروى ابن عمر عنه صلى الله عليه وسلم أنه قال من احتكر الطعام أربعين
يوما فقد برئ من الله وبرئ الله منه (2)
وقيل فكأنما قتل الناس جميعا وعن علي رضي الله عنه من احتكر الطعام
أربعين يوما PageV02P072
قسا قلبه
وعنه أيضا أنه أحرق طعام محتكر بالنار
وروي في فضل ترك الاحتكار عنه صلى الله عليه وسلم من جلب طعاما فباعه
بسعر يومه فكأنما تصدق به وفي لفظ آخر فكأنما أعتق رقبة (1)
وقيل في قوله تعالى {ومن يرد فيه بإلحاد بظلم نذقه من عذاب أليم} إن
الاحتكار من الظلم وداخل تحته في الوعيد
وعن بعض السلف أنه كان بواسط فجهز سفينة حنطة إلى البصرة وكتب إلى وكيله
بع هذا الطعام يوم يدخل البصرة ولا تؤخره إلى غد فوافق سعة في السعر فقال
له التجار لو أخرته جمعة ربحت فيه أضعافه فأخره جمعة فربح فيه أمثاله وكتب
إلى صاحبه بذلك فكتب إليه صاحب الطعام يا هذا إنا كنا قنعنا بربح يسير مع
سلامة ديننا وإنك قد خالفت وما نحب أن نربح أضعافه بذهاب شيء من الدين فقد
جنيت علينا جناية فإذا أتاك كتابي هذا فخذ المال كله فتصدق به على فقراء
البصرة وليتني أنجو من إثم الاحتكار كفافا لا علي ولا لي
واعلم أن النهي مطلق ويتعلق النظر به في الوقت والجنس أما الجنس فيطرد
النهي في أجناس الأقوات أما ما ليس بقوت  ولا هو معين على القوت كالأدوية
والعقاقير والزعفران وأمثاله فلا يتعدى النهي إليه وإن كان مطعوما
وأما ما يعين على القوت كاللحم والفواكه وما يسد مسدا يغني عن القوت في
بعض الأحوال وأن كان لا يمكن المداومة عليه فهذا في محل النظر فمن العلماء
من طرد التحريم في السمن والعسل والشيرج والجبن والزيت وما يجري مجراه وأما
الوقت فيحتمل أيضا طرد النهي في جميع الأوقات وعليه تدل الحكاية التي ذكرنا
في الطعام الذي صادف بالبصرة سعة في السعر ويحتمل أن يخصص بوقت قلة الأطعمة
وحاجة الناس إليه حتى يكون في تأخير بيعه ضر ما فأما إذا اتسعت الأطعمة
وكثرت واستغنى الناس عنها ولم يرغبوا فيها إلا بقيمة قليلة فانتظر صاحب
الطعام ذلك ولم ينتظر قحطا فليس في هذا إضرار
وإذا كان الزمان زمان قحط كان في ادخار العسل والسمن والشيرج وأمثالها
إضرار فينبغي أن يقضى بتحريمه ويعول في نفي التحريم وإثباته على الضرار
فإنه مفهوم قطعا من تخصيص الطعام وإذا لم يكن ضرار فلا يخلو احتكار الأقوات
عن كراهية فإنه ينتظر مبادئ الضرار وهو ارتفاع الأسعار وانتظار مبادئ
الضرار محذور كانتظار عين الضرار ولكنه دونه وانتظار عين الضرار أيضا هو
دون الإضرار فبقدر درجات الإضرار تتفاوت درجات الكراهية والتحريم
وبالجملة التجارة في الأقوات مما لا يستحب لأنه طلب ربح والأقوات أصول
خلقت قواما والربح من المزايا فينبغي أن يطلب الربح فيما خلق من جملة
المزايا التي لا ضرورة للخلق إليها ولذلك أوصى بعض التابعين رجلا وقال لا
تسلم ولدك في بيعتين ولا في صنعتين بيع الطعام وبيع الأكفان فإنه يتمنى
الغلاء وموت الناس
والصنعتان أن يكون جزارا فإنها صنعة تقسي القلب أو صواغا فإنه يزخرف
الدنيا بالذهب والفضة
النوع الثاني ترويج الزيف من الدراهم في أثناء النقد فهو ظلم إذ يستضر به
المعامل إن لم يعرف وإن عرف فسيروجه على غيره فكذلك الثالث والرابع ولا
يزال يتردد في الأيدي ويعمم الضرر ويتسع الفساد ويكون وزر الكل ووباله
راجعا عليه فإنه  هو الذي فتح هذا الباب قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
من سن سنة سيئة فعمل بها من بعده كان عليه وزرها ومثل وزر من عمل بها لا
ينقص من أوزارهم شيئا (2)
وقال بعضهم إنفاق درهم PageV02P073
زيف أشد من سرقة مائة درهم لأن السرقة معصية واحدة وقد تمت وانقطعت
وإنفاق الزيف بدعة أظهرها في الدين وسنة سيئة يعمل بها من بعده فيكون عليه
وزرها بعد موته إلى مائة سنة أو مائتي سنة إلى أن يفنى ذلك الدرهم ويكون
عليه ما فسد من أموال الناس بسنته وطوبى لمن إذا مات ماتت معه ذنوبه والويل
الطويل لمن يموت وتبقى ذنوبه مائة سنة ومائتي سنة أو أكثر يعذب بها في قبره
ويسئل عنها إلى آخر انقراضها وقال تعالى {ونكتب ما قدموا وآثارهم} أي نكتب
أيضا ما أخروه من آثار أعمالهم كما نكتب ما قدموه وفي مثله قوله تعالى
{ينبأ الإنسان يومئذ بما قدم وأخر} وإنما أخر آثار أعماله من سنة سيئة عمل
بها غيره
وليعلم أن في الزيف خمسة أمور
الأول أنه إذا رد عليه شيء منه فينبغي أن يطرحه في بئر بحيث لا تمتد إليه
اليد وإياه أن يروجه في بيع آخر
وإن أفسده بحيث لا يمكن التعامل به جاز
الثاني أنه يجب على التاجر تعلم النقد لا ليستقصي لنفسه ولكن لئلا يسلم
إلى مسلم زيفا وهو لا يدري فيكون آثما بتقصيره
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ح-ك-ر (ḥ-k-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To withhold, store up, or monopolize goods awaiting scarcity; the act of hoarding (iḥtikār) for price inflation.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A blameworthy act of economic aggression (ẓulm) against the community, tied to Quranic warnings on injustice.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) in its commercial sense; metaphorically (majāz) extended to any act of withholding benefit from creation.
- Root: ز-ي-ف (z-y-f)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Adulteration, falsity, or debasement; a coin (zayf) lacking intrinsic purity.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Moral corruption (fasād) introduced into transactions, akin to falsehood in speech or deed.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for counterfeit currency; metaphorical for any deceptive practice that spreads harm.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Clauses (al-sharṭ wa al-istithnāʾ) — Governing the nuanced legal distinctions (e.g., time, genus, and intent) in the Prophet's prohibitions, parsed through layered conditionals.
chapters.translation:
I say: The first division concerns that whose harm is universal, and it comprises several types.

The first type is hoarding (iḥtikār). Thus, the seller of food stores away grain, awaiting a rise in prices. This is a general injustice (ẓulm ʿāmm), and its perpetrator is blameworthy in the Sacred Law. The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, said: «Whoever hoards food for forty days, then gives it in charity, his charity will not be an expiation for his hoarding.» (1) And Ibn ʿUmar narrated from him, peace and blessings be upon him, that he said: «Whoever hoards food for forty days has indeed severed himself from Allah, and Allah has severed Himself from him.» (2) It was also said: It is as though he has killed all of humanity. And from ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him: Whoever hoards food for forty days, his heart hardens. It is also narrated from him that he burned the food of a hoarder with fire.

Regarding the virtue of abandoning hoarding, it is narrated from him, peace and blessings be upon him: «Whoever brings food and sells it at the price of that very day, it is as though he gave it in charity.» In another wording: «It is as though he freed a slave.» (1) And it was said concerning the saying of Allah the Exalted: {And whoever intends therein a deviation from truth with injustice, We shall cause him to taste a painful punishment} (Q. 22:25) — that hoarding is among the injustices and falls within its scope of threat.

It is narrated from some of the Salaf that he was in Wāsiṭ, and he dispatched a ship of wheat to Baṣrah. He wrote to his agent: "Sell this food on the day it enters Baṣrah, and do not delay it until tomorrow." It coincided with a period of price abundance, and the merchants said to him: "If you delayed it a week, you would profit double." So he delayed it a week and profited twofold, and wrote to his master of that. His master wrote back to him: "O man, we had been content with a small profit alongside the soundness of our religion. You have opposed this, and we do not love to profit double at the cost of any part of our faith. You have indeed inflicted a harm upon us. When this letter of mine reaches you, take all the money and give it in charity to the poor of Baṣrah. And would that I escape the sin of hoarding, even-steven — neither against me nor for me."

Know that the prohibition is absolute, and consideration attaches to it regarding time and genus. As for genus, the prohibition extends to all genera of staple foods (aqwāt). As for what is not a staple, nor an aid to staples — such as medicines, drugs, saffron, and the like — the prohibition does not extend to it, even if it is edible. As for what aids in sustaining life, such as meat, fruits, and what serves as a substitute for staple food in some circumstances, even if one cannot persist on it — this is a matter of consideration. Among the scholars, some extended the prohibition to clarified butter, honey, sesame oil, cheese, olive oil, and what runs their course. As for time, it is also possible to extend the prohibition to all times, as indicated by the story we mentioned concerning the food that coincided with price abundance in Baṣrah. And it is possible to restrict it to times of food scarcity and people's need for it, such that delaying its sale constitutes harm. But when foods are abundant and plentiful, and people are independent of them, not desiring them except at a low price, and the food-owner awaits that (low price) without awaiting famine — there is no harm in this.

And if the time is one of famine, then storing honey, clarified butter, sesame oil, and the like constitutes harm, and it should be judged as prohibited. The criterion in negating or affirming prohibition is harm (ḍarar), for it is understood with certainty from the specification of food. And when there is no harm, hoarding staple foods is not free of disapproval (karāhah), for it awaits the beginnings of harm — namely, the rise of prices. Awaiting the beginnings of harm is forbidden, just as awaiting the harm itself, though it is lesser than it. And awaiting the harm itself is also lesser than inflicting harm. Thus, according to the degrees of harm, the degrees of disapproval and prohibition vary.

In sum, trade in staple foods is not commendable, because it seeks profit, and staple foods are foundations created as sustenance (qiwām). Profit belongs to the superfluities. Thus, profit should be sought in what is created among the superfluities that creation has no necessity for. For this reason, one of the Followers (tābiʿūn) advised a man, saying: "Do not entrust your son to two trades, nor to two crafts: the trade of food and the trade of shrouds — for he would wish for price inflation and the death of people." The two crafts are: being a butcher, for it is a craft that hardens the heart, or being a goldsmith, for he adorns the world with gold and silver.

The second type is the circulation of counterfeit coinage (zayf) during exchange. This is injustice, for the transacting party is harmed if he does not recognize it. And if he does recognize it, he will circulate it to another. Thus, likewise the third and the fourth, and it continues to pass from hand to hand, spreading harm and widening corruption. The burden of all of it and its evil consequence reverts upon the originator, for he is the one who opened this door. The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, said: «Whoever establishes an evil practice (sunnah sayyiʾah), and it is acted upon after him, upon him is its sin and the like of the sins of those who act upon it, without diminishing anything from their sins.» (2)

And some of them said: Spending a single counterfeit dirham is more severe than stealing a hundred dirhams, for theft is a single sin that has been completed and severed, whereas spending counterfeit coinage is an innovation (bidʿah) manifested in religion and an evil practice acted upon after him. Thus, upon him is its sin after his death for a hundred years or two hundred years, until that dirham perishes. And upon him is whatever corruption befell people's wealth through his practice. Blessed is the one who, when he dies, his sins die with him. And woe, long woe, to the one who dies while his sins remain for a hundred years, two hundred years, or more — he is tormented by them in his grave and questioned about them until their final extinction. And Allah the Exalted said: {Indeed, We record what they have put forward and their traces} (Q. 36:12) — meaning, We also record what they have left behind of their deeds' traces, just as We record what they have put forward. And of similar import is His saying: {Man will be informed that Day of what he has put forward and what he has deferred} (Q. 75:13). What he has deferred are the traces of his deeds — namely, an evil practice acted upon by another.

Let it be known that concerning counterfeit coinage there are five matters:

First: If some of it is returned to him, he should cast it into a well where no hand can reach it, and beware of circulating it in another sale. If he corrupts it such that it cannot be transacted with, that is permissible.

Second: It is obligatory upon the merchant to learn the science of coin-testing (naqd) — not to be stringent for himself, but so that he does not hand a Muslim counterfeit coin unknowingly, thereby becoming sinful through his negligence in learning that knowledge. For every knowledge by which the sincere counsel of Muslims is perfected, its acquisition is obligatory. It was for this very purpose that the Salaf learned the signs of coin-testing, out of regard for their religion, not their worldly affairs.

Third: If he hands it over while the transacting party knows it is counterfeit, he does not exit from sin — because the recipient only takes it to circulate it to another without informing him. And were he not resolved upon that, he would not desire to take it at all. Thus, he only extricates himself from the sin of the harm specific to his immediate transacting party.

Fourth: He may take the counterfeit coin intending to act upon his saying, peace and blessings be upon him: «May Allah have mercy on a man who is easy in selling, easy in buying, easy in repaying, and easy in seeking repayment.» (1) He is thus included in the blessing of this supplication if he resolves to cast it into a well. But if he is resolved to circulate it in a transaction, then this is an evil that Satan has adorned for him in the guise of good, and he does not fall under the one who is lenient in seeking repayment.

Fifth: By "counterfeit" (zayf), we mean that which has no intrinsic silver content at all, but is merely plated — or, in the case of dinars, that which has no gold in it. As for that which contains silver, if it is mixed with copper and it is the currency of the land, the scholars have differed concerning transacting with it. The preponderant view in our estimation is permissibility if it is the currency of the land, whether one knows the amount of silver content or not. If it is not the currency of the land, it is not permissible except when one knows the amount of silver content. If one possesses a piece whose silver content is deficient relative to the land's currency, he must inform his transacting party, and must not transact with it except with one who does not deem it lawful to circulate it among the currency by way of deception. As for one who deems that lawful, handing it to him is empowering him toward corruption — like selling grapes to one known to make wine from them. That is prohibited, and it is assistance to evil and participation in it. Traversing the path of truth in such matters in trade is more severe than persisting in supererogatory acts of worship and devoting oneself to them. For this reason, some said: The truthful merchant is more virtuous before Allah than the devoted worshipper. The Salaf were extremely cautious in such matters, to the point that it is narrated from one of the warriors in the path of Allah that he said: "I charged upon my horse to kill a disbeliever, but my horse fell short, so I returned. Then the disbeliever drew near me, and I charged a second time, but my horse fell short, so I returned. Then I charged a third time, and my horse shied from me — and I was not accustomed to that from him. So I returned sorrowful, sitting with bowed head and broken heart, over what had escaped me of the disbeliever and what had appeared to me of the horse's character. I placed my head upon the tent's pole while my horse stood, and I saw in a dream as though the horse was addressing me, saying: 'By Allah, I ask you — did you intend to take the disbeliever three times, while yesterday you bought fodder for me and paid in its price a counterfeit dirham? This shall never be.'" He said: "I awoke in terror, went to the fodder-seller, and exchanged that dirham." This, then, is an example of that whose harm is universal — and let one measure similar cases against it.

chapters.title_en: The Second Division: Matters Pertaining to Harm Against the Transacting Partner
chapters.arabic_text:
|||  القسم الثاني ما يخص  ضرره المعامل

فكل ما يستضر به المعامل فهو ظلم وإنما العدل لا يضر بأخيه المسلم
والضابط الكلي فيه أن لا يحب PageV02P074
لأخيه إلا ما يحب لنفسه فكل ما لو عومل به شق عليه وثقل على قلبه فينبغي
أن لا يعامل غيره به بل ينبغي أن يستوي عنده درهمه ودرهم غيره
قال بعضهم من باع أخاه شيئا بدرهم وليس يصلح له لو اشتراه لنفسه إلا
بخمسة دوانق فإنه قد ترك النصح المأمور به في المعاملة ولم يحب لأخيه ما
يحب لنفسه هذه جملته
فأما تفصيله ففي أربعة أمور
أن لا يثني على السلعة بما ليس فيها وأن لا يكتم من عيوبها وخفايا صفاتها
شيئا أصلا وأن لا يكتم في وزنها ومقدارها شيئا وأن لا يكتم من سعرها ما لو
عرفه المعامل لامتنع عنه
أما الأول فهو ترك الثناء فإن وصفه للسلعة إن كان بما ليس فيها فهو كذب
فإن قبل المشتري ذلك فهو تلبيس وظلم مع كونه كذبا وإن لم يقبل فهو كذب
وإسقاط مروءة إذ الكذب الذي لا يروج قد لا يقدح في ظاهر المروءة وإن أثنى
على السلعة بما فيها فهو هذيان وتكلم بكلام لا يعنيه وهو محاسب على كل كلمة
تصدر منه أنه لم تكلم بها
قال الله تعالى {ما يلفظ من قول إلا لديه رقيب عتيد} إلا أن يثني على
السلعة بما فيها مما لا يعرفه المشتري ما لم يذكره كما يصفه من خفى أخلاق
العبيد والجواري والدواب فلا بأس بذكر القدر الموجود منه من غير مبالغة
وإطناب وليكن قصده منه أن يعرفه أخوه المسلم فيرغب فيه وتنقضي بسببه حاجته
ولا ينبغي أن يحلف عليه البتة فإنه إن كان كاذبا فقد جاء باليمين الغموس
وهي من الكبائر التي تذر الديار بلاقع وإن كان صادقا فقد جعل الله تعالى
عرضة لأيمانه وقد أساء فيه إذ الدنيا أخس من أن يقصد ترويجها بذكر اسم الله
من غير ضرورة وفي الخبر ويل للتاجر من بلى والله ولا والله وويل للصانع  من
غد وبعد (1)
وفي الخبر اليمين الكاذبة منفقة للسلعة ممحقة للبركة (2)
وروى أبو هريرة رضي الله عنه عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم أنه قال ثلاثة
لا ينظر الله إليهم يوم القيامة عتل مستكبر ومنان بعطيته ومنفق سلعته
بيمينه (3)
فإذا كان الثناء على السلعة مع الصدق مكروها من حيث إنه فضول لا يزيد في
الرزق فلا يخفى التغليظ في أمر اليمين وقد روي عن يونس بن عبيد وكان خزازا
أنه طلب منه خز للشراء فأخرج غلامه سقط الخز ونشره ونظر إليه وقال اللهم
ارزقنا الجنة فقال لغلامه رده إلى موضعه ولم يبعه وخاف أن يكون ذلك تعريضا
بالثناء على السلعة فمثل هؤلاء الذين اتجروا في الدنيا ولم يضيعوا دينهم في
تجاراتهم بل علموا أن ربح الآخرة أولى بالطلب من ربح الدنيا
الثاني أن يظهر جميع عيوب المبيع خفيها وجليها ولا يكتم منها شيئا فذلك
واجب فإن أخفاه كان ظالما غاشا والغش حرام وكان تاركا للنصح في المعاملة
والنصح واجب ومهما أظهر أحسن وجهي الثوب وأخفى الثاني كان غاشا وكذلك إذا
عرض الثياب في المواضع المظلمة وكذلك إذا عرض أحسن فردي الخف أو النعل
وأمثاله ويدل على تحريم الغش ما روي أنه مر صلى الله عليه وسلم برجل يبيع
طعاما فأعجبه فأدخل يده فيه فرأى بللا فقال {ما هذا} قال أصابته السماء
فقال فهلا جعلته فوق الطعام حتى يراه الناس من غشنا فليس منا (4)
ويدل على وجوب النصح بإظهار العيوب ما روي أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
لما بايع جريرا على الإسلام ذهب PageV02P075
لينصرف فجذب ثوبه واشترط عليه النصح لكل مسلم (1)
فكان جرير إذا قام إلى السلعة يبيعها بصر عيوبها ثم خيره وقال إن شئت فخذ
وإن شئت فاترك فقيل له إنك إذا فعلت مثل هذا لم ينفذ لك بيع فقال إنا
بايعنا رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم على النصح لكل مسلم
وكان واثلة بن الأسقع واقفا فباع رجل ناقة له بثلثمائة درهم فغفل واثلة
وقد ذهب الرجل بالناقة  فسعى وراءه وجعل يصيح به يا هذا أشتريتها للحم أو
للظهر فقال بل للظهر فقال إن بخفها نقبا قد رأيته وإنها لا تتابع السير
فعاد فردها فنقصها البائع مائة درهم وقال لواثلة رحمك الله أفسدت علي بيعي
فقال إنا بايعنا رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم على النصح لكل مسلم وقال
سمعت رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم يقول لا يحل لأحد يبيع بيعا إلا أن يبين
آفته ولا يحل لمن يعلم ذلك إلا تبيينه (2)
فقد فهموا من النصح أن لا يرضى لأخيه إلا ما يرضاه لنفسه ولم يعتقدوا أن
ذلك من الفضائل وزيادة المقامات بل اعتقدوا أنه من شروط الإسلام الداخلة
تحت بيعتهم وهذا أمر يشق على أكثر الخلق فلذلك يختارون التخلي للعبادة
والاعتزال عن الناس لأن القيام بحقوق الله مع المخالطة والمعاملة مجاهدة لا
يقوم بها إلا الصديقون ولن يتيسر ذلك على العبد إلا بأن يعتقد أمرين
أحدهما أن تلبيسه العيوب وترويجه السلع لا يزيد في رزقه بل يمحقه ويذهب
ببركته وما يجمعه من مفرقات التلبيسات يهلكه الله دفعة واحدة فقد حكي أن
واحدا كان له بقرة يحلبها ويخلط بلبنها الماء ويبيعه فجاء سيل فغرق البقرة
فقال بعض أولاده إن
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ظ-ل-م (ẓ-l-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Placing something in other than its proper place; exceeding the limit; darkness of wrongdoing
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Transgression against another's right; the opposite of justice (ʿadl); a moral violation entailing divine accountability
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal in the sense of wrongful harm; metaphorical when applied to concealment of defects in commerce
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional-Resultative Construction (Shart/Jazāʾ) — governing the "if...then" structures in the prohibitions and obligations
chapters.translation:
I say: The second division concerns that whose harm is specific to the transacting partner.

For everything by which the transacting partner is harmed constitutes wrongdoing (ẓulm), and justice is that one not harm his Muslim brother. The comprehensive governing principle in this matter is that one should not love for his brother anything but what he loves for himself. Thus, everything by which, if one were treated with it, would be grievous to him and heavy upon his heart — he ought not to treat another with it. Rather, his dirham and the dirham of another should be equal in his estimation.

One of the scholars said: Whoever sells his brother something for a dirham, while it would not be suitable for him, had he bought it for himself, except for five dānaqs (i.e., half its value), then he has abandoned the sincere counsel (nuṣḥ) commanded in transactions and has not loved for his brother what he loves for himself. This is the summary of the matter.

As for its detailed exposition, it lies in four matters:
1. That he not praise the commodity for what is not in it.
2. That he not conceal from its defects and hidden qualities anything whatsoever.
3. That he not conceal anything in its weight or measure.
4. That he not conceal from its price anything which, had the transacting partner known it, he would have refrained from it.

As for the first — it is the abandonment of praise. For if his description of the commodity is for what is not in it, it is falsehood (kadhib). If the buyer accepts it, it is deception (talbīs) and wrongdoing along with being falsehood. And if he does not accept it, it is falsehood and a fall in manly virtue (murūʾah), since the falsehood that does not circulate may not impugn the outward appearance of murūʾah. And if he praises the commodity for what is in it, it is idle talk (hadhayān) and speech about what does not concern him — and he is held accountable for every word that issues from him, that he spoke it.

God Most High said: {«مَا يَلْفِظُ مِنْ قَوْلٍ إِلَّا لَدَيْهِ رَقِيبٌ عَتِيدٌ»} ("He utters not a word but that there is with him a watcher, ready") — unless he praises the commodity for what is in it, of that which the buyer would not know had he not mentioned it, such as describing the hidden traits of slaves, slave-girls, and beasts of burden. There is no harm in mentioning the amount that exists therein, without exaggeration or prolixity. And let his intention therein be that his Muslim brother may come to know it, so that he desires it and his need is fulfilled by means of it.

He ought not to swear an oath concerning it at all. For if he is lying, he has brought the false oath that plunges one into the Fire (al-yamīn al-ghamūs), which is among the grave sins (kabāʾir) that leave habitations desolate. And if he is truthful, he has made God Most High an object of his oaths — and he has done ill therein, for this world is too base to seek its circulation by mentioning the name of God without necessity. In the report: "Woe to the merchant from 'By God' and 'No, by God'; and woe to the craftsman from 'tomorrow' and 'after'."

And in the report: "The false oath gives circulation to the commodity but effaces the blessing (barakah)."

And Abū Hurayrah, may God be pleased with him, narrated from the Prophet, peace be upon him, that he said: "Three persons God will not look upon on the Day of Resurrection: the haughty tyrant (ʿutil), the one who reproaches his gift (mannān), and the one who markets his commodity by false oaths."

So if praise of the commodity, even with truthfulness, is disliked (makrūh) insofar as it is superfluous speech that adds nothing to one's provision (rizq), then the severity regarding the matter of oaths is not hidden. It has been related of Yūnus ibn ʿUbayd — who was a silk merchant (khazzāz) — that silk was sought from him for purchase. He brought out his servant with the silk remnants, spread them, and looked at them, then said: "O God, grant us Paradise." Then he said to his servant: "Return it to its place" — and he did not sell it, fearing that this might be an indirect praise of the commodity. Such are those who traded in this world and did not squander their religion in their trades, but rather knew that the profit of the Hereafter is more worthy of pursuit than the profit of this world.

The second: that he make manifest all the defects of the sold item — its hidden and its apparent — and conceal nothing of it. For that is obligatory (wājib). If he conceals it, he is a wrongdoer and a deceiver (ghāshsh) — and deception (ghishsh) is forbidden (ḥarām) — and he has abandoned the sincere counsel in the transaction, while sincere counsel is obligatory. Whenever he shows the better face of the garment and conceals the second, he is a deceiver. Likewise, when he displays garments in dark places, and likewise when he shows the better of the two sandals or shoes and the like.

That the prohibition of deception is established is shown by what is related: that he, peace be upon him, passed by a man selling food, and it pleased him, so he inserted his hand into it and found dampness. He said: {«مَا هَذَا»} ("What is this?") The man said: "The sky (rain) afflicted it." He said: "Then why did you not place it on top of the food so that people could see it? Whoever deceives us is not of us."

And that the obligation of sincere counsel by manifesting defects is established is shown by what is related: that when the Prophet, peace be upon him, took the pledge of allegiance (bayʿah) from Jarīr for Islam, Jarīr went to depart, so he pulled his garment and stipulated upon him sincere counsel for every Muslim. Thus Jarīr, when he stood over a commodity to sell it, would point out its defects, then give him the choice, saying: "If you wish, take it; and if you wish, leave it." It was said to him: "If you do such a thing, your sale will not go through." He said: "We pledged to the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, sincere counsel for every Muslim."

And Wāthilah ibn al-Asqaʿ was standing by when a man sold his she-camel for three hundred dirhams. Wāthilah was heedless, and the man had gone off with the she-camel. So he ran after him, shouting at him: "O this man! Did you buy her for meat or for riding?" He said: "Rather, for riding." He said: "Indeed, in her hoof there is a crack that I have seen, and she does not keep up with the pace of travel." So he returned and gave her back. The seller reduced the price by a hundred dirhams and said to Wāthilah: "May God have mercy on you — you have spoiled my sale!" He said: "We pledged to the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, sincere counsel for every Muslim." And he said: "I heard the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, say: 'It is not lawful for anyone to sell a sale unless he makes manifest its defect; and it is not lawful for one who knows that except to make it manifest.'"

Thus they understood from sincere counsel that one should not be content for his brother except with what he is content with for himself. And they did not believe that this was among the supererogatory virtues (faḍāʾil) and elevations of stations, but rather believed it to be among the conditions of Islam entering under their pledge. And this matter is grievous for most creatures — therefore they choose to devote themselves to worship and to withdraw from people, because fulfilling the rights of God amidst social mixing and transactions is a striving (mujāhadah) that none can uphold except the veracious (ṣiddīqūn). And this will not be facilitated for the servant except by his believing two matters:

One of them: that his concealing defects and marketing commodities does not increase his provision, but rather effaces it and takes away its blessing; and what he gathers from scattered deceptions, God destroys at once. It has been related that a certain man had a cow which he milked, mixing water with its milk, and sold it. Then a flood came and drowned the cow. One of his sons said: "Those scattered waters which we poured into the milk gathered together at once and took the cow."

How [could he doubt this] when he, peace be upon him, said: "The two transacting parties, if they are truthful and sincere, are blessed in their sale; and if they conceal and lie, the blessing of their sale is removed."

And in the ḥadīth: "The hand of God is over the two partners as long as they do not betray each other; and when they betray each other, He lifts His hand from them."

So since wealth is not increased by treachery, just as it is not decreased by charity — whoever does not know increase and decrease except by the scale has not believed in this ḥadīth. And whoever knows that a single dirham may be blessed such that it becomes a cause of happiness for a man in this world, in religion, and in the Hereafter, while thousands upon thousands may have God remove the blessing from them such that they become a cause of destruction for their owner — to the point that he wishes for bankruptcy from them and sees it as more fitting for him in some of his states — then he knows the meaning of our saying: "Treachery does not increase wealth, and charity does not decrease it."

The second meaning which must be believed for sincere counsel to be perfected and facilitated for him: that he know that the profit of the Hereafter and its riches are better than the profit of this world, and that the benefits of worldly wealth come to an end with the end of one's lifespan, while its injustices and burdens remain. So how can the intelligent man deem it permissible to exchange that which is lower for that which is better — and all good lies in the soundness of religion? The Messenger of God, peace be upon him, said: "The declaration 'There is no god but God' (lā ilāha illā Allāh) will not cease to ward off God's wrath from creation as long as they do not prefer the bargain of this world over their Hereafter." And in another wording: "As long as they do not care what diminishes from their worldly life for the soundness of their religion. And when they do that and say 'There is no god but God,' God Most High says: 'You have lied; you are not truthful in it.'" And in another ḥadīth: "Whoever says 'There is no god but God' sincerely enters Paradise." It was said: "And what is its sincerity?" He said: "That it restrain him from what God has forbidden."

And he also said: "He has not believed in the Qurʾān who deems lawful its prohibitions." And whoever knows that these matters are defects in his faith, and that his faith is his capital for the Hereafter, will not squander his capital — prepared for a life with no end — for the sake of a profit enjoyed for a few numbered days.

It is related of one of the Followers (tābiʿīn) that he said: "If I entered the mosque while it was crowded with its people and it was said to me: 'Who is the best of these?' I would say: 'The most sincerely counseled of them for them.' And if they said: 'This one,' I would say: 'He is the best of them.' And if it were said to me: 'Who is the worst of them?' I would say: 'The most deceitful of them toward them.' And if it were said: 'This one,' I would say: 'He is the worst of them.'"

Deception (ghishsh) is forbidden in all sales and crafts alike. The craftsman ought not to be negligent in his work in a manner that, were another to treat him with it, he would not approve it for himself. Rather, he should perfect the craft and execute it soundly, then make manifest its defect if there is a defect in it — for by that he is delivered.

A man asked Ḥaddāʾ ibn Sālim: "How can I be safe in selling sandals?" He said: "Make the two faces equal, and do not prefer the right over the left; perfect the stuffing, let it be one complete thing; and bring the stitching close together, and do not overlay one sandal upon the other."

From this art is what Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal, may God have mercy on him, was asked about — the darning (rafw) of a garment such that it is not discernible. He said: "It is not permissible for the one who sells it to conceal it; rather, it is only lawful for the darner if he knows that he will make it apparent, or that he does not intend it for sale."

If you say: "Then the transaction cannot be completed whenever it is incumbent upon a man to mention the defects of the sold item" — I say: It is not so. For the condition of the merchant is that he not buy for resale except the good which he would approve for himself were he to keep it. Then let him be content in its sale with a small profit — and God will bless him in it, and he will have no need for deception. This has only become difficult because they are not content with small profit, and much is not obtained except through deception. Whoever accustoms himself to this will not buy defective goods; and if a defective item falls into his hand rarely, let him mention it and be content with its value.

Ibn Sīrīn sold a sheep and said to the buyer: "I declare myself innocent to you of a defect in her: that she turns over the fodder with her leg."

And al-Ḥasan ibn Ṣāliḥ sold a slave-girl and said to the buyer: "She once spat blood in our presence." Thus was the way (sīrah) of the people of religion. Whoever cannot bear this, let him abandon transactions — or let him accustom himself to the chastisement of the Hereafter.

The third: that he conceal nothing in the measure — and that is by adjusting the scale and being cautious in it and in the measure (kayl). He should measure as he is measured to. God Most High said: {«وَيْلٌ لِلْمُطَفِّفِينَ الَّذِينَ إِذَا اكْتَالُوا عَلَى النَّاسِ يَسْتَوْفُونَ وَإِذَا كَالُوهُمْ أَوْ وَزَنُوهُمْ يُخْسِرُونَ»} ("Woe to the defrauders — those who, when they take measure from people, take in full; and when they measure for them or weigh for them, they give less"). And one is not delivered from this except by giving extra when giving and giving less when taking — for true justice is rarely conceived. So let him seek protection by manifesting increase and decrease, for whoever exacts his full right completely is likely to transgress beyond it.

One of them used to say: "I will not buy 'Woe' from God for a grain." So when he took, he would decrease half a grain, and when he gave, he would increase a grain. And he would say: "Woe to him who sells, for a grain, a Garden whose breadth is the heavens and the earth. How lost is he who sells Ṭūbā for 'Woe'!"

They were extreme in guarding against this and its like only because these are injustices (maẓālim) from which repentance is not possible — for the owners of the grains are not known, so that one might gather them and render their rights. For this reason, when the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, bought something, he said to the weigher, when he was weighing its price: "Weigh, and add extra."

Fuḍayl looked at his son while he was washing a dīnār, intending to exchange it and remove its tarnish and clean it, so that its weight would not increase thereby. He said: "O my son, this act of yours is better than twenty-two ʿumrahs."

One of the Salaf said: "I marvel at the merchant and the seller — how he is saved: he weighs and swears by day, and sleeps by night."

And Solomon, peace be upon him, said to his son: "O my son, just as the grain enters between the two stones, so does the sin enter between the two transacting parties."

One of the righteous prayed over an effeminate man (mukhannath). It was said to him: "He was a sinner." He was silent. Then it was repeated to him, and he said: "It is as though you said to me: 'He was a man of two scales — giving with one and taking with the other.'" He indicated thereby that his sin was an injustice between him and God Most High — and this is among the injustices against servants, where leniency and pardon are more remote. The severity regarding the matter of the scale is great, and deliverance from it is attained by a grain and half a grain.

In the reading of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd, may God be pleased with him: "Do not transgress in the scale, and establish the weight with the tongue, and do not diminish the scale" — that is, the tongue of the scale, for the decrease and increase appear by its inclination. In sum, whoever exacts justice for himself from another, even in a single word, and does not render justice to the like of what he exacts — he falls under the saying of God Most High: {«وَيْلٌ لِلْمُطَفِّفِينَ الَّذِينَ إِذَا اكْتَالُوا عَلَى النَّاسِ يَسْتَوْفُونَ»} ("Woe to the defrauders — those who, when they take measure from people, take in full") — the verses. For the prohibition of that in the measured item is not because it is measured, but because it is a matter in which justice and equity are intended — so it applies to all works. The man of the scale is in the danger of "Woe," and every accountable person (mukallaf) is a man of scales in his acts, his words, and his passing thoughts. So "Woe" to him if he deviates from justice and inclines from uprightness. Were it not for the difficulty and impossibility of this, the saying of God Most High would not have come: {«وَإِنْ مِنْكُمْ إِلَّا وَارِدُهَا كَانَ عَلَى رَبِّكَ حَتْمًا مَقْضِيًّا»} ("And there is none of you but will pass over it — it is upon your Lord a decree determined"). No servant who is not infallible is free from inclining from uprightness — except that the degrees of inclination differ greatly. Therefore the durations of their stay in the Fire differ, up to the time of deliverance — so that some remain only for the duration of an oath's expiation, while others remain for thousands upon thousands of years. So we ask God Most High to bring us near to uprightness and justice — for firmness upon the straight path without inclining from it is not to be hoped for, for it is finer than a hair and sharper than a sword. Were it not for it, the one who is upright upon it would not be able to cross the bridge (ṣirāṭ) stretched over the Fire, whose description is that it is finer than a hair and sharper than a sword. And by the measure of one's uprightness upon this straight path, the servant is lightened on the Day of Resurrection upon the ṣirāṭ.

Whoever mixes dust or anything else with food, then measures it — he is among the defrauders in measure. And every butcher who weighs a bone with the meat, of a kind not customary — he is among the defrauders in weight. And measure all other estimations by this analogy — even in the measuring (dhirāʿ) practiced by the cloth merchant: for when he buys, he lets the cloth run loose at the time of measuring and does not stretch it; and when he sells, he stretches it in measuring, to make a difference appear in the amount. All of that is from the defrauding (tatfīf) that exposes its practitioner to "Woe."

The fourth: that he be truthful in the price of the time (siʿr al-waqt) and conceal nothing of it. For the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, prohibited meeting the caravans (talqī al-rukbān), and prohibited najash (artificial price inflation).

As for meeting the caravans — it is that one go out to meet the traveling party, intercept the merchandise, and lie about the price in the town. For he, peace be upon him, said: "Do not meet the caravans; and whoever meets them, the owner of the commodity has the option (khiyār) after he arrives at the market." This purchase is concluded, but if his lie becomes apparent, the seller has the option established; and if he was truthful, there is disagreement concerning the option, due to the conflict between the generality of the report and the removal of deception.

He also prohibited that a townsman sell for a Bedouin (ḥāḍir li-bādin) — which is that the Bedouin arrives in town with provisions (qūt) which he wishes to sell quickly, and the townsman says to him: "Leave it with me until I inflate its price and wait for its rise." This is forbidden in provisions, and in other commodities there is disagreement — the more apparent view is its prohibition, due to the generality of the prohibition, and because it is a delay causing hardship to people in general, without benefit to the meddling one who causes hardship.

And the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, prohibited najash — which is that one step forward to the seller in the presence of the desiring buyer and demand the commodity at an increase, while not desiring it himself, but only seeking to stir the buyer's desire for it. If there is no prior collusion with the seller, it is a forbidden act on the part of its doer, and the sale is concluded. And if there is collusion, there is disagreement concerning the establishment of the option — and the preferable view is to establish the option, because it is a deception by an act analogous to the deception in the case of the milk-impregnated animal (muṣarrāh) and meeting the caravans.

These prohibitions indicate that it is not permissible to deceive the seller or the buyer regarding the price of the time, nor to conceal from him a matter which, had he known it, he would not have proceeded with the contract. For doing this is from the forbidden deception (ghishsh) that opposes the obligatory sincere counsel.

It has been related of a man among the Followers that he was in Basra, and he had a slave in Sūs who would send him sugar. His slave wrote to him: "The sugarcane has been afflicted by a blight this year — so buy sugar." He said: "So I bought much sugar. When its time came, I profited thirty thousand in it. Then I returned to my home and reflected that night, saying: 'I have profited thirty thousand and lost the sincere counsel of a Muslim man.' When morning came, he went to the sugar seller and gave him the thirty thousand, saying: 'May God bless you in it.' He said: 'And from where did this come to me?' He said: 'I concealed from you the true state of affairs — and the sugar had risen in price at that time.' He said: 'May God have mercy on you — you have informed me now, and I have made it lawful for you.' He said: 'So I returned with it to my home and reflected, staying awake the night, and said: "I have not counseled him sincerely — perhaps he was too ashamed before me and left it for me." So I went early to him the next day and said: "May God heal you — take your wealth back, for it is more wholesome for my heart." So he took the thirty thousand from him.'"

These reports concerning the prohibitions and the narratives indicate that one may not seize an opportunity and exploit the heedlessness of the owner of the merchandise, concealing from the seller the rise in price or from the buyer the fall in prices. For if he does that, he is a wrongdoer, abandoning justice and sincere counsel toward the Muslims.

And whenever he sells on the basis of declared cost (murābaḥah) — saying: "I sold it to you for what it cost me" or "for what I bought it" — he must be truthful. Then he must inform of whatever occurred after the contract of defect or diminution. And if he bought on credit (ilā ajal), he must mention it. And if he bought through leniency from a friend or his son, he must mention it — because the transacting partner relies upon his custom of exactness, that he does not leave off looking out for himself. So when he leaves it off for some reason, he must be informed, for the reliance therein is upon his trustworthiness.

chapters.title_en: The Fourth Book on Excellence (Iḥsān) in Commercial Dealings
chapters.arabic_text:
|| الباب الرابع في الإحسان في المعاملة

وقد أمر الله تعالى بالعدل والإحسان جميعا والعدل سبب النجاة فقط وهو
يجري من التجارة مجرى رأس المال
والإحسان سبب الفوز ونيل السعادة وهو يجري من التجارة مجرى الربح ولا يعد
من الغفلاء من قنع في معاملات الدنيا برأس ماله فكذا في معاملات الآخرة فلا
ينبغي للمتدين أن يقتصر على العدل واجتناب الظلم ويدع أبواب الإحسان وقد
قال الله وأحسن كما أحسن الله إليك وقال عز وجل إن الله يأمر بالعدل
والإحسان وقال سبحانه إن رحمت  الله قريب من المحسنين ونعني بالإحسان فعل ما
ينتفع به المعامل وهو غير واجب عليه ولكنه تفضل منه فإن الواجب يدخل في باب
العدل وترك الظلم وقد ذكرناه وتنال رتبة الإحسان بواحد من ستة أمور
الأول في المغابنة فينبغي أن لا يغبن صاحبه بما لا يتغابن به في العادة
فأما أصل المغابنة فمأذون فيه لأن البيع للربح ولا يمكن ذلك إلا بغبن ما
ولكن يراعي فيه التقريب فإن بذل المشتري زيادة على الربح المعتاد إما لشدة
رغبته أو لشدة حاجته في الحال إليه فينبغي أن يمتنع من قبوله فذلك من
الإحسان
ومهما لم يكن تلبيس لم يكن أخذ الزيادة ظلما وقد ذهب بعض العلماء إلى أن
الغبن بما يزيد على الثلث يوجب الخيار ولسنا نرى ذلك ولكن من الإحسان أن
يحط ذلك الغبن
يروى أنه كان عند يونس بن عبيد حلل مختلفة الأثمان ضرب قيمة كل حلة منها
أربعمائة وضرب كل حلة قيمتها مائتان فمر إلى الصلاة وخلف ابن أخيه في
الدكان فجاء أعرابي وطلب حلة بأربعمائة فعرض عليه من حلل المائتين
فاستحسنها ورضيها فاشتراها فمضى بها وهي على يديه فاستقبله يونس فعرف حلته
فقال للأعرابي بكم اشتريت فقال بأربعمائة فقال لا تساوي أكثر من مائتين
فارجع حتى تردها فقال هذه تساوي في بلدنا خمسمائة وأنا أرتضيها فقال له
يونس انصرف فإن النصح في الدين خير من الدنيا بما فيها ثم رده إلى الدكان
ورد عليه مائتي درهم وخاصم ابن أخيه في ذلك وقاتله وقال أما استحييت أما
اتقيت الله تربح مثل الثمن وتترك النصح للمسلمين فقال والله ما أخذها إلا
وهو راض بها
قال فهلا رضيت له بما ترضاه لنفسك وهذا إن كان فيه إخفاء سعر وتلبيس فهو
من
PageV02P079
باب الظلم وقد سبق وفي الحديث غبن المسترسل حرام (1)
وكان الزبير بن عدي يقول أدركت ثمانية عشر من الصحابة ما منهم أحد يحسن
يشتري لحما بدرهم فغبن مثل هؤلاء المسترسلين ظلم إن كان من غير تلبيس فهو
من ترك الإحسان  وقلما يتم هذا إلا بنوع تلبيس وإخفاء سعر الوقت
وإنما الإحسان المحض ما نقل عن السري السقطي أنه اشترى كر لوز بستين
دينارا وكتب في روزنامجه ثلاثة دنانير ربحه وكأنه رأى أن يربح على العشرة
نصف دينار فصار اللوز بتسعين فأتاه الدلال وطلب اللوز فقال خذه قال بكم
فقال
بثلاثة وستين فقال الدلال وكان من الصالحين فقد صار اللوز بتسعين فقال
السري قد عقدت عقدا لا أحله لست أبيعه إلا بثلاثة وستين فقال الدلال وأنا
عقدت بيني وبين الله أن لا أغش مسلما لست آخذ منك إلا بتسعين
قال فلا الدلال اشترى منه ولا السري باعه فهذا محض الإحسان من الجانبين
فإنه مع العلم بحقيقة الحال
وروي عن محمد بن المنكدر أنه كان له شقق بعضها بخمسة وبعضها بعشرة فباع
غلامه في غيبته شقة من الخمسيات بعشرة فلما عرف لم يزل يطلب ذلك الأعرابي
المشتري طول النهار حتى وجده فقال له إن الغلام قد غلط فباعك ما يساوي خمسة
بعشرة فقال يا هذا قد رضيت فقال وإن رضيت فإنا لا نرضى لك إلا ما نرضاه
لأنفسنا فاختر إحدى ثلاث خصال إما أن تأخذ شقة من العشريات بدراهمك وإما أن
نرد عليك خمسة وإما أن ترد شقتنا وتأخذ دراهمك فقال أعطني خمسة فرد عليه
خمسة وانصرف الأعرابي يسأل ويقول من هذا الشيخ فقيل له هذا محمد بن المنكدر
فقال لا إله إلا الله هذا الذي نستسقي به في البوادي إذا قحطنا
فهذا إحسان في أن لا يربح على العشرة إلا نصفا أو واحد على ما جرت به
العادة في مثل ذلك المتاع في ذلك المكان ومن قنع بربح قليل كثرت معاملاته
واستفاد من تكررها ربحا كثيرا وبه تظهر البركة
كان علي رضي الله عنه يدور في سوق الكوفة بالدرة ويقول معاشر التجار خذوا
الحق تسلموا لا تردوا قليل الربح فتحرموا كثيره
قيل لعبد الرحمن بن عوف رضي الله عنه ما سبب يسارك قال ثلاث ما رددت ربحا
قط ولا طلب مني  حيوان فأخرت بيعه ولا بعت بنسيئة
ويقال إنه باع ألف ناقة فما ربح إلا عقلها باع كل عقال بدرهم فربح فيها
ألفا وربح من نفقته عليها ليومه ألفا
الثاني في احتمال الغبن والمشتري إن اشترى طعاما من ضعيف أو شيئا من فقير
فلا بأس أن يحتمل الغبن ويتساهل ويكون به محسنا وداخلا في قوله صلى الله
عليه وسلم رحم الله امرءا سهل البيع سهل الشراء فأما إذا اشترى من غني تاجر
يطلب الربح زيادة على حاجته فاحتمال الغبن منه ليس محمودا بل هو تضييع مال
من غير أجر ولا حمد فقد ورد في حديث من طريق أهل البيت المغبون في الشراء
لا محمود ولا
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ح-س-ن (Ḥ-S-N)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Beauty, goodness, excellence; doing what is good and beneficial beyond obligation
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Iḥsān as the highest rank of virtue—acting with beneficence toward others without being bound by duty, contrasted with ʿadl (justice) which is obligatory
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense is "doing good"; here used in its ḥaqīqah sense as voluntary beneficence, distinct from justice (ʿadl) which is the mere fulfillment of obligation
- Root: ع-د-ل (ʿ-D-L)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Equity, justice, straightness; giving what is due and taking no more than what is owed
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): ʿAdl as the mean between excess and deficiency; the obligatory minimum in all transactions
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense of balance and evenness; metaphorically applied to moral rectitude in dealings
- Root: غ-ب-ن (Gh-B-N)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To cheat, defraud, or overcharge in a sale; the act of deceiving in price
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The permissible margin of profit versus the blameworthy deception that exceeds customary practice
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense is "to be deceived in a bargain"; the term carries both a permissible sense (ordinary profit) and a blameworthy sense (excessive overcharging)
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Constructions (al-sharṭ wa al-istithnāʾ) — The text employs complex conditional sentences (e.g., "if he does not deceive, then taking extra is not injustice") and exceptive clauses (e.g., "except with a type of deception") that require careful parsing to preserve the logical structure of legal distinctions.
chapters.translation:
I say: God—exalted be He—has commanded both justice (ʿadl) and excellence (iḥsān) together. Justice is a cause of salvation only, and it stands in relation to commerce as capital stands in relation to trade. Excellence is a cause of victory and the attainment of felicity, and it stands in relation to commerce as profit stands in relation to trade. None among the heedless would be content in his worldly dealings with merely his capital; so likewise in the dealings of the Hereafter, it befits not the religious man to confine himself to justice and the avoidance of injustice while abandoning the gates of excellence. God—exalted be He—has said: {«وَأَحْسِنْ كَمَا أَحْسَنَ اللَّهُ إِلَيْكَ»} ("And do good as God has done good to you") [Al-Qaṣaṣ 28:77], and He—mighty and majestic—said: {«إِنَّ اللَّهَ يَأْمُرُ بِالْعَدْلِ وَالْإِحْسَانِ»} ("Indeed, God commands justice and excellence") [Al-Naḥl 16:90], and He—glorified be He—said: {«إِنَّ رَحْمَتَ اللَّهِ قَرِيبٌ مِنَ الْمُحْسِنِينَ»} ("Indeed, the mercy of God is near to those who do good") [Al-Aʿrāf 7:56].

By excellence (iḥsān) I mean the doing of that which benefits one's counterpart in a transaction, which is not obligatory upon him, but is rather a voluntary favor from him. For the obligatory falls under the category of justice and the avoidance of injustice, which we have already mentioned. The rank of excellence is attained through one of six matters:

**The First: Concerning Overcharging (al-ghabānah).** One ought not to overcharge his counterpart beyond what is customary in such transactions. As for the principle of overcharging itself, it is permitted, because selling is for profit, and that cannot be achieved except through some measure of overcharge. However, one must observe moderation therein. If the buyer offers an increase beyond the customary profit—whether due to intense desire or intense need at that moment—then one ought to refrain from accepting it, for that is of excellence.

Whenever there is no deception (talbīs), the taking of the increase is not injustice. Some scholars have held that overcharging beyond one-third of the value gives the buyer the option of rescission, but we do not hold that view. Nevertheless, it is of excellence to remit such overcharge.

It is related that Yūnus ibn ʿUbayd had garments of varying prices; he set the value of each garment at four hundred, and set the value of other garments at two hundred. He went off to prayer, leaving his nephew in the shop. A Bedouin came and requested a garment for four hundred. He showed him one of the two-hundred garments, which he admired and approved, so he bought it and departed with it in his hands. Yūnus met him, recognized his garment, and said to the Bedouin: "For how much did you buy it?" He said: "For four hundred." He said: "It is worth no more than two hundred. Return so that you may give it back." He said: "It is worth five hundred in our land, and I am satisfied with it." Yūnus said to him: "Go your way, for sincerity in religion is better than the world and all that is in it." Then he returned it to the shop and gave him back two hundred dirhams, and he rebuked his nephew over that and contended with him, saying: "Were you not ashamed? Did you not fear God—to profit the like of the price and abandon sincerity toward the Muslims?" He said: "By God, he took it only while being satisfied with it." He said: "Then why were you not satisfied for him with what you would be satisfied with for yourself?" If this involves concealing the market price and deception, it falls under the category of injustice, which has already been discussed. In the ḥadīth: "Overcharging the unsuspecting (al-mustarsil) is forbidden." (1)

Al-Zubayr ibn ʿAdī used to say: "I reached eighteen of the Companions, and not one of them knew how to buy meat for a dirham." So overcharging such unsuspecting persons is injustice; if it is without deception, then it is the abandonment of excellence. And rarely does this occur except with some type of deception and concealment of the current market price.

Pure excellence (al-iḥsān al-maḥḍ) is what is transmitted from al-Sarī al-Saqaṭī: he bought a kurr of almonds for sixty dīnārs and wrote in his ledger three dīnārs as his profit—as if he deemed it right to profit half a dīnār per ten. Then almonds rose to ninety. The broker came and requested the almonds. He said: "Take them." He said: "For how much?" He said: "For sixty-three." The broker—who was among the righteous—said: "The almonds have reached ninety." Al-Sarī said: "I have concluded a contract which I will not dissolve; I will not sell them except for sixty-three." The broker said: "And I have concluded between myself and God a covenant that I will not deceive a Muslim; I will not take them from you except for ninety." He said: "So neither did the broker buy from him, nor did al-Sarī sell to him." This is pure excellence from both sides, for it was with knowledge of the true state of affairs.

It is related of Muḥammad ibn al-Munkadir that he had garments, some for five and some for ten. His slave, in his absence, sold one of the five-value garments for ten. When he learned of it, he kept seeking that Bedouin buyer the whole day until he found him. He said to him: "The slave has erred; he sold you what is worth five for ten." He said: "O man, I am satisfied." He said: "Even if you are satisfied, we are not satisfied for you except with what we are satisfied for ourselves. Choose one of three things: either take a garment from the ten-value ones for your dirhams, or we return five to you, or you return our garment and take your dirhams." He said: "Give me five." So he returned five to him, and the Bedouin departed asking: "Who is this shaykh?" It was said to him: "This is Muḥammad ibn al-Munkadir." He said: "There is no god but God—this is the one through whom we seek rain in the deserts when we suffer drought."

This is excellence in not profiting more than half per ten, or one per ten, according to what is customary for such merchandise in such a place. Whoever is content with little profit, his transactions multiply, and he gains much profit through their repetition, and through that blessing (barakah) appears.

ʿAlī—may God be pleased with him—used to circulate in the market of Kūfah with a whip, saying: "O company of merchants, take the right and be safe; do not reject little profit, lest you be deprived of much."

It was said to ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf—may God be pleased with him: "What is the cause of your wealth?" He said: "Three things: I never rejected a profit, no animal was ever requested of me and I delayed its sale, and I never sold on credit." It is said that he sold a thousand camels and profited only their halters—he sold each halter for a dirham, profiting a thousand thereby, and profited a thousand from his expenditure upon them for that day.

**The Second: Concerning Bearing Overcharge (iḥtimāl al-ghabn).** If a buyer purchases food from a weak person, or something from a poor person, there is no harm in his bearing the overcharge and being lenient, and thereby he is one who does good, entering under his saying—peace and blessings be upon him: "May God have mercy on a man who is lenient in selling, lenient in buying." (1) But if he buys from a wealthy merchant who seeks profit beyond his need, then bearing overcharge from him is not praiseworthy; rather, it is squandering wealth without reward or praise. For it has come in a ḥadīth transmitted through the People of the House (Ahl al-Bayt): "The one overcharged in a purchase is neither praised nor rewarded." (2)

Iyās ibn Muʿāwiyah ibn Qurrah, the judge of Baṣrah, who was among the intelligent Followers (tābiʿūn), used to say: "I am not a deceiver, and the deceiver cannot overcharge me; nor can he overcharge Ibn Sīrīn. But he can overcharge al-Ḥasan, and he can overcharge my father"—meaning Muʿāwiyah ibn Qurrah. Perfection is in neither overcharging nor being overcharged, as some described ʿUmar—may God be pleased with him—saying: "He was too noble to be deceived, and too intelligent to be deceived."

Al-Ḥasan, al-Ḥusayn, and others among the best of the Salaf used to be exacting in their purchases, then would give away abundant wealth. It was said to one of them: "You are exacting in your purchase over a trifle, then you give away much and do not care." He said: "The giver gives of his surplus, while the overcharged one is overcharged of his intellect." Another of them said: "I only overcharge my intellect and my sight, so I do not give the overcharger access to them; and when I give, I give for God, and I do not count anything from Him as great."

**The Third: Concerning Collecting the Price and Other Debts.** Excellence therein is sometimes by leniency and remitting part, sometimes by granting respite and delay, and sometimes by being easy in demanding good coin. All of this is recommended and urged upon. The Prophet—peace and blessings be upon him—said: "May God have mercy on a man who is lenient in selling, lenient in buying, lenient in collecting." (1) So let one seize the Prophet's supplication—peace and blessings be upon him. And he said—peace and blessings be upon him: "Be generous, and you will be treated generously." (2)

And he said—peace and blessings be upon him: "Whoever grants respite to a debtor in difficulty, or forgives him, God will reckon with him with an easy reckoning." In another wording: "God will shade him under the shade of His Throne on the day when there is no shade but His shade." (3)

The Messenger of God—peace and blessings be upon him—mentioned a man who had been extravagant against himself; he was reckoned and no good deed was found for him. It was said to him: "Have you done any good at all?" He said: "No, except that I was a man who lent to people, and I would say to my young servants: 'Be lenient with the affluent, and grant respite to the one in difficulty.'" (4) In another wording: "And overlook the one in difficulty." So God—exalted be He—said: "We are more worthy of that than him." So God overlooked his sins and forgave him.

And he said—peace and blessings be upon him: "Whoever lends a dīnār until a fixed term, he has for every day a charity until its term; and when the term falls due, if he grants him respite after that, he has for every day the like of that debt as charity." (5) Some of the Salaf, because of this report, did not like that their debtor should repay the debt, so that they might be like one who gives it all in charity every day.

And he said—peace and blessings be upon him: "I saw written at the gate of Paradise: 'Charity is rewarded tenfold, and the loan eighteenfold.'" (6) It was said concerning its meaning: charity falls into the hand of the needy and the non-needy alike, whereas none bears the humiliation of seeking a loan except the needy.

The Prophet—peace and blessings be upon him—looked at a man who was pressing another man for a debt, and gestured to the creditor with his hand to remit half. He did so. Then he said to the debtor: "Arise and pay him." (7)

Whoever sells something and leaves its price for the time being, without pressing hard in demanding it, is in the meaning of one who lends.

It is related that al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī sold a mule of his for four hundred dirhams. When the money became due, the buyer said to him: "Be generous, O Abū Saʿīd." He said: "I have remitted one hundred of it." He said to him: "Then do good, O Abū Saʿīd." He said: "I have gifted you another hundred." So he collected two hundred dirhams of his due. It was said to him: "O Abū Saʿīd, this is half the price." He said: "Thus is excellence; otherwise it is not." And in the report: "Take your right in sufficiency and chastity, whether it is full or not; God will reckon with you with an easy reckoning." (8)

**The Fourth: Concerning Fulfilling the Debt (tawfiyat al-dayn).** Part of excellence therein is good repayment—namely, that one walks to the one who holds the right and does not burden him to walk to demand it. For he said—peace and blessings be upon him: "The best of you is the best of you in repayment." (1) Whenever one is able to repay the debt, let him hasten to it, even before its term, and let him deliver what is better and more excellent than what was stipulated upon him. And if he is unable, let him intend to repay it whenever he is able.

He said—peace and blessings be upon him: "Whoever incurs a debt intending to repay it, God entrusts angels to him who guard him and supplicate for him until he repays it." (2) A group of the Salaf used to borrow without need, because of this report.

Whenever the holder of the right speaks to him with harsh words, let him bear it and respond with gentleness, following the example of the Messenger of God—peace and blessings be upon him—when the creditor came to him at the fall of the term, and his repayment had not yet been arranged. The man began to speak harshly to the Messenger of God—peace and blessings be upon him—and his Companions intended to rebuke him. He said: "Leave him, for the holder of a right has a claim to speak." (3)

Whenever discourse passes between the borrower and the lender, excellence is that the greater inclination of the mediators should be toward the one upon whom the debt lies, for the lender lends from wealth while the borrower borrows from need. Likewise, assistance to the buyer should be greater, for the seller is desirous of parting with the merchandise, seeking to circulate it, while the buyer is in need of it. This is the most excellent—unless the one upon whom the debt lies transgresses his bounds; at that point, aiding him is in preventing his transgression and assisting his counterpart, for he said—peace and blessings be upon him: "Aid your brother whether he is the wrongdoer or the wronged." It was said: "How do we aid him when he is the wrongdoer?" He said: "Your preventing him from wrongdoing is your aid to him." (4)

**The Fifth: To Grant Rescission (iqālah) to Whoever Seeks It.** For none seeks rescission except one who regrets and is harmed by the sale; and one ought not to be satisfied for himself to be the cause of harm to his brother. He said—peace and blessings be upon him: "Whoever grants rescission to a regretful one of his transaction, God will grant rescission of his slip on the Day of Resurrection" (5)—or as he said.

**The Sixth: To Intend in His Dealings a Group of the Poor with Credit (nasīʾah),** while being resolved at the time not to demand payment from them if no ease appears for them. For among the righteous of the Salaf there was one who had two ledgers for accounts: one of them, whose heading was "Unknown," contained the names of those he did not know among the weak and poor. That was because the poor man would see food or fruit and desire it, and say: "I need five raṭls, for example, of this, and I have no price for it." He would say: "Take it, and pay its price when ease comes." And he did not count this among the best; rather, he counted among the best the one who did not record his name in the ledger at all, nor make it a debt, but would say: "Take what you wish; if ease comes to you, pay; otherwise, you are absolved of it and in abundance." These are the ways of the commerce of the Salaf, and they have become obliterated; the one who upholds them is a reviver of this Sunnah.

In sum, commerce is the touchstone of men, and by it a man's religion and scrupulousness (waraʿ) are tested. Therefore it was said:

"Let not the patched shirt of a man deceive you,
Nor a waist-wrapper raised above the ankle of his leg,
Nor a forehead upon which appears the mark of prostration—
But at the dirham, look at his error or his piety."

Therefore it was said: When a man's neighbors in the town, his companions in travel, and his business partners in the markets all praise him, then do not doubt his righteousness.

A witness testified before ʿUmar—may God be pleased with him—and he said: "Bring me one who knows you." So he brought a man who praised him well. ʿUmar said: "Are you his nearest neighbor, who knows his coming in and going out?" He said: "No." He said: "Were you his companion in travel, by which noble character is discerned?" He said: "No." He said: "Did you deal with him in dīnār and dirham, by which a man's scrupulousness is made evident?" He said: "No." He said: "I think you saw him standing in the mosque, murmuring the Qurʾān, lowering his head at times and raising it at others." He said: "Yes." He said: "Go, for you do not know him." And he said to the man: "Go, and bring me one who knows you."

chapters.title_en: The Fifth Chapter on the Merchant's Compassion for His Religion in What Concerns His Own Affairs and His Afterlife
chapters.arabic_text:
|| الباب الخامس في شفقة التاجر على دينه فيما يخصه ويعم آخرته

ولا ينبغي للتاجر أن يشغله معاشه عن معاده فيكون عمره ضائعا وصفقته خاسرة
وما يفوته من الربح في الآخرة لا يفي به ما ينال في الدنيا فيكون اشترى
الحياة الدنيا بالآخرة بل العاقل ينبغي أن يشفق على نفسه وشفقته على نفسه
يحفظ رأس ماله ورأس ماله دينه وتجارته فيه
قال بعض السلف أولي الأشياء بالعاقل أحوجه إليه في العاجل وأحوج شيء إليه
في العاجل أحمده عاقبة في الآجل
وقال معاذ بن جبل رضي الله عنه في وصيته إنه لا بد لك من نصيبك في الدنيا
وأنت إلى نصيبك من الآخرة أحوج فابدأ بنصيبك من الآخرة فخذه فإنك ستمر على
نصيبك من الدنيا فتنظمه
قال الله تعالى ولا تنس نصيبك من الدنيا أي لا تنس في الدنيا نصيبك منها
للآخرة فإنها مزرعة الآخرة وفيها تكتسب الحسنات
وإنما تتم شفقة التاجر على دينه بمراعاة سبعة أمور
الأول حسن النية والعقيدة في ابتداء  التجارة فلينو بها الاستعفاف عن
السؤال وكف الطمع عن الناس استغناء بالحلال عنهم واستعانة بما يكسبه على
الدين وقياما بكفاية العيال ليكون من جملة المجاهدين به ولينو النصح
للمسلمين وأن يحب لسائر الخلق ما يحب لنفسه ولينو اتباع طريق العدل
والإحسان في معاملته كما ذكرناه ولينو الأمر بالمعروف والنهي عن المنكر في
كل ما يراه في السوق فإذا أضمر هذه العقائد والنيات كان عاملا في طريق
الآخرة فإن استفاد مالا فهو مزيد وإن خسر في الدنيا ربح في الآخرة
الثاني أن يقصد القيام في صنعته أو تجارته بفرض من فروض الكفايات فإن
الصناعات والتجارات لو تركت بطلت المعايش وهلك أكثر الخلق
فانتظام أمر الكل بتعاون الكل وتكفل كل فريق بعمل ولو أقبل كلهم على صنعة
واحدة لتعطلت البواقي وهلكوا وعلى هذا حمل بعض الناس قوله صلى الله عليه
وسلم اختلاف أمتي رحمة (1)
أي اختلاف همهم في الصناعات والحرف
ومن الصناعات ما هي مهمة ومنها ما يستغنى عنها لرجوعها إلى طلب النعم
والتزين في الدنيا فليشتغل بصناعة مهمة ليكون في قيامه بها كافيا عن
المسلمين مهما في الدين وليجتنب صناعة النقش والصياغة وتشييد البنيان بالجص
وجميع ما تزخرف به الدنيا فكل ذلك كرهه ذوو الدين فأما عمل الملاهي والآلات
التي يحرم استعمالها فاجتناب ذلك من قبيل ترك الظلم ومن جملة ذلك خياطة
الخياط القباء من الإبر يسم للرجال وصياغة الصائغ مراكب الذهب أو خواتيم
الذهب للرجال فكل ذلك من المعاصي والأجرة المأخوذة عليه حرام ولذلك أوجبنا
الزكاة فيها وإن كنا لا نوجب الزكاة في الحلي لأنها إذا قصدت للرجال فهي
محرمة وكونها مهيأة للنساء لا يلحقها بالحلي المباح ما لم يقصد ذلك بها
فيكتسب حكمها من القصد
وقد ذكرنا أن بيع الطعام وبيع الأكفان مكروه لأنه يوجب انتظار موت الناس
وحاجتهم بغلاء السعر PageV02P083
ويكره أن يكون جزارا لما فيه من قساوة القلب وأن يكون حجاما أو كناسا لما
فيه من مخامرة النجاسة وكذا الدباغ وما في معناه وكره ابن سيرين الدلالة
وكره قتادة أجرة الدلال ولعل السبب فيه قلة استغناء الدلال عن الكذب
والإفراط في الثناء على السلعة لترويجها ولأن العمل فيه لا يتقدر فقد يقل
وقد يكثر ولا ينظر في مقدار الأجرة إلى عمله بل إلى قدر قيمة الثوب هذا هو
العادة وهو ظلم بل ينبغي أن ينظر إلى قدر التعب وكرهوا شراء الحيوان
للتجارة لأن المشتري يكره قضاء الله فيه وهو الموت الذي بصدده لا محالة
وحلوله
وقيل بع الحيوان واشتر الموتان وكرهوا الصرف لأن الاحتراز فيه عن دقائق
الربا عسير ولأنه طلب لدقائق الصفات فيما لا يقصد أعيانها وإنما يقصد
رواجها وقلما يتم للصيرفي ربح إلا باعتماد جهالة معامله بدقائق النقد فقلما
يسلم الصيرفي وإن احتاط ويكره للصيرفي وغيره كسر الصحيح والدنانير إلا عند
الشك في جودته أو عند ضرورة
قال أحمد بن حنبل رحمة الله ورد نهي عن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم (1)
وعن أصحابه في الصياغة من الصحاح وأنا أكره الكسر وقال يشتري بالدنانير
دراهم ثم يشتري بالدرهم ذهبا ويصوغه واستحبوا تجارة البز
قال سعيد بن المسيب ما من تجارة أحب إلي من البز ما لم يكن فيها أيمان
وقد روي خير تجارتكم البز وخير صنائعكم الخرز (2)
وفي حديث آخر لو اتجر أهل الجنة لاتجروا في البز ولو اتجر أهل النار
لاتجروا في الصرف (3)
وقد كان غالب أعمال الأخيار من السلف عشر صنائع الخرز والتجارة والحمل
والخياطة والحذو والقصارة وعمل الخفاف وعمل الحديد وعمل المغازل ومعالجة
صيد البر والبحر والوراقة قال عبد الوهاب الوراق
قال لي أحمد بن حنبل ما صنعتك قلت الوراقة قال كسب طيب ولو كنت صانعا
بيدي لصنعت صنعتك ثم قال لي لا تكتب إلا مواسطة واستبق الحواشي وظهور
الأجزاء
وأربعة من الصناع موسومون عند الناس بضعف الرأي الحاكة والقطانون
والمغازليون والمعلمون
ولعل ذلك لأن أكثر مخالطتهم مع النساء والصبيان ومخالطة ضعفاء العقول
