chapters.anchors:
- Root: ش-ف-ق (shafaqa)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning of tenderness, compassion, and solicitude—an anxious care that impels one to protect what is beloved from harm.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, shafaqah denotes the believer's vigilant guardianship over his faith (dīn) as his most precious capital, entailing both fear of loss and active preservation.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Used here in its literal sense (ḥaqīqah) of genuine protective compassion, not metaphorical pity; it is an active, governing disposition.
- Root: ر-ب-ح (ribḥ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Profit, gain, increase in capital through trade.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Metaphorically extended to the afterlife—true profit (ribḥ al-ākhirah) is the increase of one's standing before God through righteous works; worldly loss may be celestial gain.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): The literal commercial sense is retained but transposed to the spiritual economy; the metaphor (majāz) of trade as the soul's transaction with God is operative throughout.
- Root: خ-س-ر (khasira)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To lose, to perish, to suffer diminution of one's capital.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In Quranic usage, khusrān is the ultimate loss of the self and one's eternal portion—the opposite of falāḥ (success).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal commercial loss is the vehicle for the metaphorical ruin of the afterlife; the contrast between the two markets (sūq al-dunyā vs. sūq al-ākhirah) structures the entire chapter.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and imperative constructions (sharṭ wa-jazāʾ) governing the merchant's obligations; also the use of the imperative (amr) with lām of command to establish normative duties (e.g., "fal-yanwi," "fal-yajtanib").
chapters.translation:
I say: The fifth chapter on the merchant's compassion for his religion in what concerns his own affairs and his afterlife.

It behooves not the merchant that his livelihood occupy him from his return to God, such that his life becomes wasted and his transaction a loss. Whatever profit he misses in the afterlife is not compensated by what he attains in this world, for he would have purchased the life of this world with the afterlife. Rather, the intelligent man ought to have compassion for his soul, and his compassion for his soul preserves his capital—and his capital is his religion, and his trade is therein.

One of the Salaf said: "The worthiest thing for the intelligent man is that which he most needs in the immediate term, and the thing he most needs in the immediate term is that whose consequence is most praiseworthy in the hereafter."

Muʿādh ibn Jabal, may God be pleased with him, said in his testament: "You must have your share of this world, but you are more in need of your share of the afterlife. So begin with your share of the afterlife and take it, for you will pass by your share of this world and will set it in order."

God Most High said: {وَلَا تَنسَ نَصِيبَكَ مِنَ الدُّنْيَا} ("And do not forget your share of this world")—that is, do not forget, in this world, your share of it for the afterlife, for this world is the sowing-field of the afterlife, and in it are good deeds acquired.

The merchant's compassion for his religion is only completed by observing seven matters:

**The First:** Good intention and sound creed at the commencement of trade. Let him intend thereby: abstaining from begging, restraining covetousness from people, being independent of them through what is lawful, seeking aid through his earnings for his religion, and undertaking the sufficiency of his dependents—so that he may be among the mujāhidūn (strivers) thereby. Let him intend sincerity (nuṣḥ) toward the Muslims, and that he love for all creation what he loves for himself. Let him intend following the path of justice (ʿadl) and excellence (iḥsān) in his dealings, as we have mentioned. Let him intend commanding the good and forbidding the evil in everything he sees in the market. When he conceals these creeds and intentions, he is a worker on the path of the afterlife. If he gains wealth, it is an increase; if he loses in this world, he profits in the afterlife.

**The Second:** That he intend, in his craft or trade, the fulfillment of a communal obligation (farḍ kifāyah). For if crafts and trades were abandoned, livelihoods would be ruined and most of creation would perish. The order of all things is maintained by the mutual cooperation of all, with each group undertaking a work. If all turned to a single craft, the rest would be disrupted and they would perish. Upon this, some people interpreted the saying of God's Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him: "The differing of my community is a mercy"—that is, the differing of their concerns in crafts and trades.

Among crafts, some are essential and some are dispensable, as they revert to seeking luxuries and adornment in this world. Let him occupy himself with an essential craft, so that in his pursuit of it he suffices the Muslims in what pertains to religion. Let him avoid the craft of engraving, goldsmithing, erecting buildings with plaster, and all that adorns this world—for all such things were disapproved by people of religion. As for making instruments of amusement and devices whose use is forbidden, avoiding that falls under refraining from injustice. Among that is the tailor's sewing of a cloak with silk brocade for men, and the goldsmith's fashioning of gold vessels or gold rings for men—all of that is disobedience, and the wage taken for it is unlawful. For this reason we have made zakāh obligatory upon it, though we do not make zakāh obligatory upon jewelry—because when it is intended for men, it is forbidden, and its being prepared for women does not attach it to permissible jewelry unless that is intended by it; thus it acquires its ruling from the intention.

We have mentioned that selling food and selling shrouds is disliked, because it entails awaiting people's death and their need through high prices. It is disliked to be a butcher, due to the hardness of heart it involves; and to be a cupper or a sweeper, due to the contamination with filth; likewise tanning and what is in its meaning. Ibn Sīrīn disliked brokerage, and Qatādah disliked the broker's wage. Perhaps the reason is the broker's scant freedom from lying and excess in praising the commodity to promote it, and because the work therein is not delimited—it may be little or much, and the wage is not measured by the effort but by the value of the garment; this is the custom, and it is injustice. Rather, one should look to the measure of exertion. They also disliked buying animals for trade, because the buyer dislikes God's decree concerning it—namely, death, which inevitably approaches and befalls it. It was said: "Sell the animal and buy the dead." They disliked money-changing (ṣarf), because guarding against the subtleties of usury (ribā) therein is difficult, and because it is a pursuit of subtle qualities in things whose essences are not intended but only their circulation. Rarely does the money-changer profit except by relying on his counterpart's ignorance of the subtleties of coinage; thus the money-changer seldom escapes, even if he is cautious. It is disliked for the money-changer and others to break sound dinars, except when doubting their quality or in necessity.

Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal, may God have mercy on him, said: "A prohibition was reported from the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, and from his Companions, regarding fashioning from sound coins, and I dislike the breaking." He said: "One buys with dinars dirhams, then buys with the dirham gold and fashions it." They recommended the cloth trade. Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib said: "No trade is more beloved to me than cloth, as long as there are no oaths in it." It has been related: "The best of your trades is cloth, and the best of your crafts is leather-working." In another hadith: "If the people of Paradise traded, they would trade in cloth; and if the people of the Fire traded, they would trade in money-changing."

The predominant occupations of the righteous among the Salaf were ten crafts: leather-working, trade, porterage, tailoring, shoemaking, laundering, making socks, iron-working, making spindles, and the pursuit of hunting on land and sea, and book-copying. ʿAbd al-Wahhāb al-Warrāq said: "Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal said to me: 'What is your craft?' I said: 'Book-copying.' He said: 'A good earning. Were I a craftsman with my hand, I would practice your craft.' Then he said to me: 'Write only the middle portions, and preserve the margins and the backs of the fascicles.'"

Four of the craftsmen are marked among people as weak in judgment: weavers, cotton-carders, spinners, and teachers. Perhaps that is because most of their mixing is with women and boys, and mixing with the weak-minded weakens the intellect, just as mixing with the intelligent increases the intellect. It is related from Mujāhid that Mary, peace be upon her, while seeking Jesus, peace be upon him, passed by weavers and asked for the road; they directed her to the wrong road. She said: "O God, remove blessing from their earnings, and make them die poor, and make them contemptible in people's eyes." Her supplication was answered.

The Salaf disliked taking wages for everything that falls under acts of worship and communal obligations—such as washing the dead and burying them, likewise the call to prayer (adhān) and the tarāwīḥ prayer, even if hiring for it is ruled valid; likewise teaching the Qurʾān and teaching the science of the Sacred Law. For these are works whose right is that one trade in them for the afterlife, and taking wages for them is exchanging the afterlife for this world; that is not recommended.

**The Third:** That the market of this world not prevent him from the market of the afterlife—and the markets of the afterlife are the mosques. God Most High said: {رِجَالٌ لَّا تُلْهِيهِمْ تِجَارَةٌ وَلَا بَيْعٌ عَن ذِكْرِ اللَّهِ وَإِقَامِ الصَّلَاةِ وَإِيتَاءِ الزَّكَاةِ} ("Men whom neither trade nor sale distracts from the remembrance of God, the establishment of prayer, and the giving of zakāh"). And God Most High said: {فِي بُيُوتٍ أَذِنَ اللَّهُ أَن تُرْفَعَ وَيُذْكَرَ فِيهَا اسْمُهُ} ("In houses God has permitted to be raised, and His name to be mentioned therein").

Thus he should make the beginning of the day, up to the time of entering the market, for his afterlife—keeping to the mosque and persevering in his litanies (awrād). ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, used to say to the merchants: "Make the beginning of your day for your afterlife, and what follows it for your worldly affairs." The righteous among the Salaf made the beginning and end of the day for the afterlife, and the middle for trade. None sold porridge and heads in the early morning except boys and the people of the covenant (ahl al-dhimmah), because they were in the mosques afterward.

In the report: "When the angels ascend with the servant's scroll, and in it, at the beginning of the day and its end, is remembrance of God and goodness, God forgives him whatever evil deeds lie between them." In the report: "The angels of night and day meet at the dawn's rising and at the ʿaṣr prayer. God says—and He knows best about them—'How did you leave My servants?' They say: 'We left them praying, and we came to them praying.' God, glorified and exalted, says: 'I make you witnesses that I have forgiven them.'"

Then, whenever he hears the call to prayer in the middle of the day for the noon (ẓuhr) and the afternoon (ʿaṣr) prayers, he should not turn aside to any occupation, but should be stirred from his place and abandon whatever he was engaged in. For what he misses of the virtue of the first takbīrah with the imam at the beginning of the time is not equaled by this world and all it contains. And if he does not attend the congregation, he has disobeyed, according to some scholars.

The Salaf used to hasten at the call to prayer and leave the markets to boys and the people of the covenant. They would hire, for small coins (qarārīṭ), guardians for the shops at prayer times, and that was a livelihood for them.

It has come in the interpretation of God's saying {لَا تُلْهِيهِمْ تِجَارَةٌ وَلَا بَيْعٌ عَن ذِكْرِ اللَّهِ} ("Neither trade nor sale distracts them from the remembrance of God") that they were blacksmiths and leather-workers. One of them, when he raised the hammer or inserted the awl and heard the call to prayer, would not withdraw the awl from the hole nor strike the hammer—he would throw it down and rise to prayer.

**The Fourth:** That he not be content with this, but rather persevere in the remembrance of God, glorified be He, in the market, occupying himself with tahlīl (saying "there is no god but God") and tasbīḥ (glorification). For the remembrance of God in the market among the heedless is more excellent. The Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "The one who remembers God among the heedless is like the fighter behind the fleeing, and like the living among the dead." In another wording: "Like the green tree among dry brushwood." And he said, peace and blessings be upon him: "Whoever enters the market and says: 'There is no god but God alone, with no partner; His is the dominion and His is the praise; He gives life and causes death, and He is Living and does not die; in His hand is all good, and He is powerful over all things'—God writes for him a thousand thousand good deeds."

Ibn ʿUmar, Sālim ibn ʿAbd Allāh, Muḥammad ibn Wāsiʿ, and others used to enter the market intending to attain the virtue of this remembrance. Al-Ḥasan said: "The one who remembers God in the market will come on the Day of Resurrection with a light like the light of the moon and a proof like the proof of the sun. And whoever seeks God's forgiveness in the market, God forgives him to the number of its people."

ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, when he entered the market, said: "O God, I seek refuge in You from disbelief and wickedness, and from the evil of what the market encompasses. O God, I seek refuge in You from a false oath and a losing transaction."

Abū Jaʿfar al-Farghānī said: "One day we were with al-Junayd, and mention was made of people who sit in the mosques, imitating the Sufis, falling short of what is incumbent upon them of the right of sitting, and censuring those who enter the market. Al-Junayd said: 'How many are there in the market whose ruling is that they should enter the mosque, take permission from some of those in it, bring him out, and sit in his place! And I know a man who enters the market with his daily litany of three hundred rakʿahs and thirty-three thousand glorifications.'" He said: "It sprang to my mind that he meant himself."

Thus was the trade of those who trade for sufficiency, not for luxury in this world. For whoever seeks this world as an aid toward the afterlife—how could he abandon the profit of the afterlife? The market, the mosque, and the house have for him one ruling; salvation is only through piety (taqwā). The Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Fear God wherever you are." The duty of piety is not cut off from those devoted to religion, however their circumstances turn; and by it is their life and their livelihood, for in it they see their trade and their profit. It has been said: "Whoever loves the afterlife lives; whoever loves this world is scattered; the fool goes morning and evening in nothingness; and the intelligent one searches out his own faults."

**The Fifth:** That he not be intensely eager for the market and trade—namely, by being the first to enter and the last to leave, and by taking to the sea for trade; both are disliked. It is said: "Whoever rides the sea has been extreme in seeking provision." In the report: "None rides the sea except for pilgrimage (ḥajj), ʿumrah, or raiding (ghazw)." ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ, may God be pleased with them both, used to say: "Do not be the first to enter the market nor the last to leave it, for in it the devil has laid his eggs and hatched his young."

It is related from Muʿādh ibn Jabal and ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar that Iblīs says to his offspring: "O Zalanbūr, march with your battalions and come to the people of the markets; adorn for them lying, oath-taking, deceit, cunning, and treachery, and be with the first to enter and the last to leave them." In the report: "The worst of places are the markets, and the worst of their people are the first to enter and the last to leave."

The completion of this caution is that he watch the time of his sufficiency. When he has obtained the sufficiency of his time, he departs and occupies himself with the trade of the afterlife. Thus were the righteous among the Salaf. Among them was one who, when he profited a small coin (dāniq), departed, content with it. Ḥammād ibn Salamah used to sell silk in a basket before him; when he profited two grains, he would lift his basket and depart.

Ibrāhīm ibn Bashshār said: "I said to Ibrāhīm ibn Adham, may God have mercy on him: 'Today I am commanded to work in clay.' He said: 'O ibn Bashshār, you are a seeker and one sought. One seeks you whom you cannot escape, and you seek what has already been guaranteed to you. Have you not seen a greedy one deprived, and a weak one provided for?' I said: 'I have a dāniq owed to me by the grocer.' He said: 'It is grievous to me that you possess a dāniq and yet seek work.'" Among them were those who departed after the noon prayer, some after the afternoon prayer, and some who worked only one or two days a week, contenting themselves with that.

**The Sixth:** That he not be content with avoiding the forbidden, but rather guard against ambiguous matters (shubuhāt) and places of suspicion, and not look to legal opinions (fatāwā) but rather consult his heart. When he finds in it a twinge of unease, he avoids it. When a commodity is brought to him and its matter troubles him, he asks about it until he knows—otherwise he consumes the ambiguous. Milk was brought to the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, and he said: "Where did you get this?" They said: "From the sheep." He said: "And where did you get this sheep?" It was said: "From such-and-such a place." Then he drank from it and said: "We, the company of prophets, have been commanded not to eat except what is good (ṭayyib), and not to work except what is righteous." And he said: "God Most High commanded the believers with what He commanded the messengers, saying: {يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا كُلُوا مِن طَيِّبَاتِ مَا رَزَقْنَاكُمْ} ('O you who believe, eat of the good things We have provided you')." Muslim transmitted it from the hadith of Abū Hurayrah—the hadith that he did not ask about everything brought to him. Aḥmad transmitted from the hadith of Jābir that the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, and his Companions passed by a woman who slaughtered a sheep for them—the hadith—and the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, took a morsel but could not swallow it, and said: "This is a sheep slaughtered without the permission of its owners"—the hadith. And from his hadith of Abū Hurayrah: "When food was brought to him from other than his own family, he asked about it"—the hadith. Their chains are sound. In this is that he did not ask about what was brought from his own family. And God knows best.

What is obligatory is that the merchant look to whom he deals with. Anyone attributed to injustice, treachery, theft, or usury—he should not deal with him. Likewise, the soldiers and the oppressors—he should not deal with them at all, nor with their companions and helpers, because he thereby aids in injustice.

It is related of a man that he undertook the building of a wall for one of the frontier outposts. He said: "Something fell into my heart about that, even though that work was among good deeds—nay, among the obligations of Islam—but the commander who undertook it in his district was among the oppressors." He said: "I asked Sufyān, may God be pleased with him, and he said: 'Do not be a helper to them in little or much.' I said: 'This is a wall in the path of God for the Muslims.' He said: 'Yes, but the least that enters upon you is that you love their continued existence so that they pay you your wage—and thus you have loved the continued existence of one who disobeys God.'"

It has come in the report: "Whoever prays for the continued existence of an oppressor has loved that God be disobeyed in His earth." In the hadith: "God is angered when a wicked person is praised." In another hadith: "Whoever honors a wicked person has aided in the demolition of Islam." Sufyān entered upon al-Mahdī, who had in his hand a white scroll, and he said: "O Sufyān, give me the inkwell so I may write." He said: "Tell me what you will write. If it is right, I will give it to you." Some commanders sought from one of the imprisoned scholars with him that he hand him clay to seal a letter with it. He said: "Hand me the letter first, so I may see what is in it." Thus were they cautious about aiding the oppressors. Dealing with them is the severest kind of aid, and people of religion should avoid it as long as they find a way to do so.

In sum, people should be divided for him into those he deals with and those he does not. Let those he deals with be fewer than those he does not, in this age. One of them said: "There came upon people a time when a man would enter the market and say: 'Whom do you see that I should deal with among the people?' It would be said: 'Deal with whomever you wish.' Then came another time when they would say: 'Deal with whomever you wish, except so-and-so and so-and-so.' Then came another time when it was said: 'Do not deal with anyone except so-and-so and so-and-so.' And I fear that a time will come when this too will pass away." As if what he feared had already come to be—"Truly we belong to God, and to Him we return."

**The Seventh:** He should watch over all the channels of his dealings with each one of those he deals with, for he is watched and held to account. Let him prepare the answer for the Day of Reckoning and Punishment for every deed and every word: "Why did I embark upon it, and for what purpose?" For it is said that the merchant will be stopped on the Day of Resurrection with every man to whom he sold something, a stopping, and he will be held to account for each one—so he is accountable to the number of those he dealt with.

One of them said: "I saw one of the merchants in a dream and said: 'What did God do with you?' He said: 'He spread out for me fifty thousand scrolls.' I said: 'Are all these sins?' He said: 'These are the dealings with people—for every person I dealt with in this world, a separate scroll of what was between me and him, from the beginning of the dealing to its end.'"

This is what is incumbent upon the earner in his work of justice, excellence, and compassion for religion. If he confines himself to justice, he is among the righteous (ṣāliḥūn); if he adds excellence to it, he is among the near ones (muqarrabūn); and if he observes, along with that, the duties of religion as mentioned in the fifth chapter, he is among the veracious (ṣiddīqūn). And God knows best what is correct.

The Book of Earning and Livelihood is completed, by the praise of God and His grace.

بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم
الحمد لله الذي خلق الإنسان من طين لازب وصلصال ثم ركب صورته في أحسن
تقويم وأتم اعتدال ثم غذاه في أول نشوه بلبن استصفاه من بين فرث ودم سائغا
كالماء الزلال ثم حماه بما آتاه من طيبات الرزق عن دواعي الضعف والانحلال
ثم قيد شهوته المعادية له عن السطوة والصيال وقهرها بما افترضه عليه من طلب
القوت الحلال وهزم بكسرها جند الشيطان المتشمر للإضلال ولقد كان يجري من
ابن آدم مجرى الدم السيال فضيق عليه عزة الحلال المجرى والمجال إذ كان لا
يبذرقه إلى أعماق العروق إلا الشهوة الماثلة إلى الغلبة والاسترسال فبقي
لما زمت بزمام الحلال خائبا خاسرا ما له من ناصر ولا وال
والصلاة على محمد الهادي من الضلال وعلى آله خير آل وسلم تسليما كثيرا
أما بعد فقد قال صلى الله عليه وسلم طلب الحلال فريضة على كل مسلم (1)
رواه ابن مسعود رضي الله عنه وهذه الفريضة من بين سائر الفرائض أعصاها
على العقول فهما وأثقلها على الجوارح فعلا ولذلك اندرس بالكلية علما وعملا
وصار غموض علمه سببا لاندراس عمله إذ ظن الجهال أن الحلال مفقود وأن السبيل
دون الوصول إليه مسدود وانه لم يبق من الطيبات إلا الماء الفرات والحشيش
النابت في الموات وما عداه فقد أخبثته الأيدي العادية وأفسدته المعاملات
الفاسدة وإذا تعذرت القناعة بالحشيش من النبات لم يبق وجه سوى الاتساع في
المحرمات فرفضوا هذا القطب من الدين أصلا ولم يدركوا بين الأموال فرقا
وفصلا وهيهات هيهات فالحلال بين والحرام بين وبينهما أمور مشتبهات ولا تزال
هذه الثلاثة مقترنات كيفما تقلبت الحالات
ولما كانت هذه بدعة عم في الدين ضررها واستطار في الخلق شررها وجب كشف
الغطاء عن فسادها بالإرشاد إلى مدرك الفرق بين الحلال والحرام والشبهة على
وجه التحقيق والبيان ولا يخرجه التضييق عن حيز الإمكان
ونحن  نوضح ذلك في سبعة أبواب
الباب الأول في فضيلة طلب الحلال ومذمة الحرام ودرجات الحلال والحرام
الباب الثاني في مراتب الشبهات ومثاراتها وتمييزها عن الحلال والحرام
الباب الثالث في البحث والسؤال والهجوم والإهمال ومظانها في الحلال
والحرام

chapters.anchors:
- Root: ح-ل-ل (ḥ-l-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To untie, unbind, become permissible; the opposite of prohibition (taḥrīm); also denotes settling in a place (ḥill).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The lawful (ḥalāl) is that which the divine law (sharʿ) permits without restriction, contrasted with the forbidden (ḥarām) and the ambiguous (shubhah); it carries a moral weight as a commanded pursuit.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense is "unbinding" (ḥall) — used metaphorically for what releases the soul from culpability; the phrase "seeking the lawful" (ṭalab al-ḥalāl) is a metonymy for earning through permissible means.
- Root: ح-ر-م (ḥ-r-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To forbid, make sacred, or deprive; the sacred precinct (ḥaram) and the forbidden (ḥarām) share the notion of being set apart.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The unlawful is what God has sealed off from human action, entailing punishment for transgression; its opposite is the ḥalāl, and between them lies the shubhah (ambiguous).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: "to be barred" (manʿ); metaphorical: the "forbidden" as that which the soul must treat as a boundary (ḥudūd) not to be crossed.
- Root: ش-ب-ه (sh-b-h)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Resemblance, ambiguity, confusion between two things; the plural shubuhāt denotes doubtful matters.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The ambiguous (shubhah) is that whose legal status is unclear to the believer, requiring discernment (taʿabbud) to avoid falling into the unlawful.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: similarity (tashābuh); metaphorical: the "gray zone" between ḥalāl and ḥarām, as in the prophetic hadith on "ambiguous matters" (umūr mushtabihāt).
- Sībawayh Rule: ʿAṭf al-Bayān (Appositional Clarification) — In the opening doxology, phrases like "from clay clinging and dried clay" (ṭīn lāzib wa-ṣalṣāl) and "between dung and blood" (bayna farth wa-dam) are coordinated via apposition to specify successive stages of creation, requiring the translator to preserve the sequential, causal flow of the Arabic periodic sentence.
chapters.translation:
In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

Praise be to God, who created man from clinging clay and dried clay, then fashioned his form in the most excellent proportion and most complete balance. Then He nourished him in his earliest growth with milk, which He extracted from between dung and blood — palatable, like pure water. Then He protected him, through the wholesome provisions He granted him, from the impulses of weakness and decay. Then He restrained his appetitive soul — which is his enemy — from violence and assault, and subdued it by making obligatory upon him the pursuit of lawful sustenance (ṭalab al-ḥalāl). By breaking that appetite, He routed the hosts of Satan, who is girded for misguidance. For Satan indeed used to course through the son of Adam like flowing blood; so the might of the lawful narrowed his course and his field, since nothing could penetrate to the depths of the veins except that appetite which inclines toward domination and unchecked release. Thus, when it was bridled with the rein of the lawful, Satan remained frustrated and defeated, having no helper or protector.

And blessings be upon Muhammad, the guide from error, and upon his family — the best of families — with abundant peace.

To proceed: The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: «Seeking the lawful is an obligation upon every Muslim» — narrated by Ibn Masʿūd, may God be pleased with him. This obligation, among all other obligations, is the most difficult for minds to comprehend and the heaviest for bodily members to enact. For this reason, it has become entirely effaced — both in knowledge and in practice. The obscurity of its science became the cause of the effacement of its practice, since the ignorant assumed that the lawful is nonexistent, that the path to reaching it is blocked, and that nothing remains of the wholesome things except fresh water and the herbage growing in dead land — and that everything besides these has been corrupted by tyrannical hands and spoiled by corrupt transactions. And when contentment with the herbage of plants proved impossible, no course remained save plunging into the forbidden. So they abandoned this pivot of religion altogether, and they did not perceive any distinction or difference among wealth. Far from it! Far from it! For the lawful is clear, and the unlawful is clear, and between them are ambiguous matters. And these three remain ever conjoined, however circumstances may turn.

And since this innovation — whose harm spread throughout religion and whose sparks flew among creation — had arisen, it became incumbent to unveil its corruption by guiding toward the source of distinction between the lawful, the unlawful, and the ambiguous, in a manner of verification and clarification. Nor does the constriction [of the matter] remove it from the realm of possibility.

We shall now elucidate this in seven chapters:

Chapter One: On the virtue of seeking the lawful, the blameworthiness of the unlawful, and the degrees of the lawful and the unlawful.

Chapter Two: On the ranks of ambiguities, their sources, and distinguishing them from the lawful and the unlawful.

Chapter Three: On inquiry, questioning, intrusion, and negligence, and their loci in relation to the lawful and the unlawful.

Chapter Four: On how the penitent exits from financial injustices.

Chapter Five: On the stipends of rulers and their gifts — what is permissible therein and what is forbidden.

Chapter Six: On entering upon rulers and mixing with them.

Chapter Seven: On miscellaneous questions. [Page V02P088]

chapters.anchors:
- Root: ح-ل-ل (ḥ-l-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To untie, loosen, or render permissible; the opposite of binding (ʿaqd) or prohibition (taḥrīm). In legal-theological usage, it denotes what is licit by divine decree.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The lawful (ḥalāl) is that which the divine law (sharʿ) permits without restriction, carrying no punitive or eschatological consequence; its opposite is the unlawful (ḥarām), which entails divine censure.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) sense is the untying of a knot or the dissolution of a restriction; metaphorically (majāz), it applies to the removal of legal prohibition, as in «أَحَلَّ اللَّهُ الْبَيْعَ» (God has made trade lawful).
- Root: و-ر-ع (w-r-ʿ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To withdraw, abstain, or keep away from something out of caution; the root also conveys a mountain's steepness, implying a rigorous ascent toward piety.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Scrupulous abstinence (waraʿ) is the soul's restraint from what is doubtful (shubhah) and from the unlawful, as a protective measure for religious integrity; it is a station above mere lawfulness.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense is avoidance or retreat; metaphorically, it denotes the heart's flight from anything that might taint one's standing before God, even if technically permissible.
- Root: ذ-م-م (dh-m-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Blame, censure, or reproach; the opposite of praise (madḥ). It implies a deficiency or defect that invites disapproval.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Blameworthiness (dhamm) is the attribute of an act or state that incurs divine or human reproach, often linked to transgression of limits (ḥudūd).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense is the utterance of censure; metaphorically, it describes the intrinsic moral repugnance of the unlawful, which merits condemnation in this world and the next.
- Sībawayh Rule: The Construct Phrase (al-iḍāfah) — The title employs a series of genitive constructions (e.g., fī faḍīlat al-ḥalāl, madhammat al-ḥarām) where the first noun is indefinite and the second is definite, establishing a specific, hierarchical classification. The repetition of "aṣnāf" (categories) and "darajāt" (degrees) with the conjunction "wa" (and) creates a balanced, enumerative structure, requiring the translator to preserve the parallel syntactic rhythm.
chapters.translation: I say: The first chapter concerns the virtue of the lawful (faḍīlat al-ḥalāl), the blameworthiness of the unlawful (madhammat al-ḥarām), and the exposition of the categories of the lawful with its degrees, the categories of the unlawful with its degrees, and the degrees of scrupulous abstinence (waraʿ) therein.

||| فضيلة الحلال ومذمة الحرام

قال الله تعالى كلوا من الطيبات واعملوا صالحا أمر بالأكل من الطيبات قبل
العمل
وقيل إن المراد به الحلال
وقال تعالى ولا تأكلوا أموالكم بينكم بالباطل وقال تعالى إن الذين يأكلون
أموال اليتامى ظلما الآية
وقال تعالى يا أيها الذين آمنوا اتقوا الله وذروا ما بقي من الربا إن
كنتم مؤمنين {ثم قال} فإن لم تفعلوا فأذنوا بحرب من الله ورسوله {ثم قال}
وإن تبتم فلكم رءوس أموالكم {ثم قال} ومن عاد فأولئك أصحاب النار هم فيها
خالدون جعل آكل الربا أول الأمر مؤذنا بمحاربة الله وفي آخره متعرضا للنار
والآيات الواردة في الحلال والحرام لا تحصى
وروى ابن مسعود رضي الله عنه عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم أنه قال طلب
الحلال فريضة على كل مسلم ولما قال صلى الله عليه وسلم طلب العلم فريضة على
كل مسلم (1)
قال بعض العلماء أراد به طلب علم الحلال والحرام وجعل المراد بالحديثين
واحدا
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم من سعى على عياله من حله فهو كالمجاهد في سبيل
الله ومن طلب الدنيا حلالا في عفاف كان في درجة الشهداء (2)
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم من أكل الحلال أربعين يوما نور الله قلبه وأجرى
ينابيع الحكمة من قلبه على لسانه (3)
وفي رواية زهده الله في الدنيا وروي أن سعدا سأل رسول الله صلى الله عليه
وسلم أن يسأل الله تعالى أن يجعله مجاب  الدعوة فقال له أطب طعمتك تستجب
دعوتك (4)
ولما ذكر صلى الله عليه وسلم الحريص على الدنيا قال رب أشعث أغبر مشرد في
الأسفار مطعمه حرام وملبسه حرام وغذي بالحرام يرفع يديه فيقول يا رب يا رب
فأنى يستجاب لذلك (5)
وفي حديث ابن عباس عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم إن لله ملكا على بيت
المقدس ينادي كل ليلة من أكل حراما لم يقبل منه صرف ولا عدل (6)
فقيل الصرف النافلة والعدل الفريضة
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم من اشترى ثوبا PageV02P089
بعشرة دراهم وفي ثمنه درهم حرام لم يقبل الله صلاته ما دام عليه منه شيء
(1)
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم كل لحم نبت من حرام فالنار أولى به (2)
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم من لم يبال من أين اكتسب المال لم يبال الله من
أين أدخله النار (3)
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم العبادة عشرة أجزاء تسعة منها في طلب الحلال (4)
روي هذا مرفوعا وموقوفا على بعض الصحابة أيضا
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم من أمسى وانيا من طلب الحلال بات مغفورا له
وأصبح والله عنه راض (5)
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم من أصاب مالا من مأثم فوصل به رحما أو تصدق به
أو أنفقه في سبيل الله جمع الله ذلك جميعا ثم قذفه في النار (6)
وقال عليه السلام خير دينكم الورع (7)
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم من لقي الله ورعا أعطاه الله ثواب الإسلام كله
(8)
ويروى أن الله تعالى قال في بعض كتبه وأما الورعون فأنا أستحي أن أحاسبهم
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم درهم من ربا أشد عند الله من ثلاثين زنية في
الإسلام (9)
وفي حديث أبي هريرة رضي الله عنه المعدة حوض البدن والعروق إليها واردة
فإذا صحت المعدة صدرت العروق بالصحة وإذا سقمت صدرت بالسقم (10)
ومثل الطعمة من الدين مثل الأساس من البنيان فإذا ثبت الأساس وقوي استقام
البنيان وارتفع وإذا ضعف الأساس واعوج انهار البنيان ووقع
وقال الله عز وجل أفمن أسس بنيانه على تقوى من  الله الآية
وفي الحديث من اكتسب مالا من حرام فإن تصدق به لم يقبل منه وإن تركه
وراءه كان زاده إلى النار (11)
وقد ذكرنا جملة من الأخبار في كتاب آداب الكسب تكشف عن فضيلة الكسب
الحلال
وأما الآثار فقد ورد أن الصديق رضي الله عنه شرب لبنا من كسب عبده ثم سأل
عبده فقال تكهنت لقوم فأعطوني فأدخل أصابعه في فيه وجعل يقيء حتى ظننت أن
نفسه ستخرج ثم قال اللهم إني أعتذر إليك مما حملت العروق وخالط الأمعاء
(12)
وفي بعض الأخبار أنه صلى الله عليه وسلم أخبر بذلك فقال أو علمتم
أن الصديق PageV02P090
لا يدخل جوفه إلا طيبا وكذلك شرب عمر رضي الله عنه من لبن إبل الصدقة
غلطا فأدخل إصبعه وتقيأ وقالت عائشة رضي الله عنها إنكم لتغفلون عن أفضل
العبادة هو الورع وقال عبد الله بن عمر رضي الله عنه لو صليتم حتى تكونوا
كالحنايا وصمتم حتى تكونوا كالأوتار لم يقبل ذلك منكم إلا بورع حاجز
وقال إبراهيم بن أدهم رحمه الله ما أدرك من أدرك إلا من كان يعقل ما يدخل
جوفه
وقال الفضيل من عرف ما يدخل جوفه كتبه الله صديقا فانظر عند من تفطر يا
مسكين وقيل لإبراهيم بن أدهم رحمه الله لم لا تشرب من ماء زمزم فقال لو كان
لي دلو شربت منه
وقال سفيان الثوري رضي الله عنه من أنفق من الحرام في طاعة الله كان كمن
طهر الثوب النجس بالبول والثوب النجس لا يطهره إلا الماء والذنب لا يكفره
إلا الحلال
وقال يحيى بن معاذ الطاعة خزانة من خزائن الله إلا أن مفتاحها الدعاء
وأسنانه لقم الحلال
وقال ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما لا يقبل الله صلاة امرىء في جوفه حرام وقال
سهل التستري لا يبلغ العبد حقيقة الإيم
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ح-ل-ل (ḥ-l-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To untie, loosen, dissolve; that which is permissible, unbound by prohibition
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The licit (ḥalāl) as that which divine law (Sharʿ) has released from constraint, contrasted with the sacred (ḥarām) which is bound and forbidden
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense of untying a knot; metaphorically, the removal of legal restriction
- Root: ح-ر-م (ḥ-r-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To forbid, make sacred, render inviolable; the sanctum (ḥaram) of Mecca
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The unlawful as that which God has sealed off from human action, carrying punitive consequence
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: enclosure/protection; metaphorical: divine interdiction with threat of punishment
- Root: ك-س-ب (k-s-b)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To acquire, earn, gain through effort and striving
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Acquisition (kasb) as the human act of earning, central to Ashʿarī theology of human agency
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: gathering profit; metaphorical: the moral quality of one's livelihood
- Root: و-ر-ع (w-r-ʿ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To be cautious, abstinent, refrain from what is doubtful
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Scrupulous piety (waraʿ) as the highest form of God-consciousness in matters of sustenance
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: retreating from danger; metaphorical: abstaining from the dubious (shubhāt)
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Construction (al-Sharṭ wa al-Jawāb) — The frequent "whoever does X, then Y" (man... fa...) pattern establishes causal nexus between human action and divine recompense, requiring the apodosis to be grammatically bound to the protasis.
chapters.translation:
I say — Know that the virtue of the lawful (ḥalāl) and the blameworthiness of the unlawful (ḥarām) is established by the Book of God, the Sunnah of His Messenger ﷺ, and the consensus of the scholars.

God Most High has said: {«كُلُوا مِنَ الطَّيِّبَاتِ وَاعْمَلُوا صَالِحًا»} "Eat of the good things and do righteous deeds" (Q 23:51). He commanded eating from the good things before [commanding] righteous action. And it is said that what is meant by this is the lawful (ḥalāl).

And He Most High said: {«وَلَا تَأْكُلُوا أَمْوَالَكُم بَيْنَكُم بِالْبَاطِلِ»} "And do not consume your wealth among yourselves in falsehood" (Q 2:188). And He Most High said: {«إِنَّ الَّذِينَ يَأْكُلُونَ أَمْوَالَ الْيَتَامَىٰ ظُلْمًا»} "Indeed, those who consume the wealth of orphans unjustly..." (Q 4:10) — the verse [continues with the threat of fire].

And He Most High said: {«يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا اتَّقُوا اللَّهَ وَذَرُوا مَا بَقِيَ مِنَ الرِّبَا إِن كُنتُم مُّؤْمِنِينَ»} "O you who believe, fear God and give up what remains of usury (ribā), if you are believers" (Q 2:278). Then He said: {«فَإِن لَّمْ تَفْعَلُوا فَأْذَنُوا بِحَرْبٍ مِّنَ اللَّهِ وَرَسُولِهِ»} "But if you do not, then be warned of war from God and His Messenger" (Q 2:279). Then He said: {«وَإِن تُبْتُمْ فَلَكُمْ رُءُوسُ أَمْوَالِكُمْ»} "And if you repent, then you shall have your principal sums" (Q 2:279). Then He said: {«وَمَنْ عَادَ فَأُولَٰئِكَ أَصْحَابُ النَّارِ هُمْ فِيهَا خَالِدُونَ»} "And whoever returns [to usury], those are the companions of the Fire; they shall abide therein eternally" (Q 2:275). Thus He made the consumer of usury, at the outset of the matter, one who is given notice of war against God, and at its end, one who exposes himself to the Fire. The verses concerning the lawful and the unlawful are beyond enumeration.

Ibn Masʿūd, may God be pleased with him, narrated from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "Seeking the lawful is an obligation (farīḍah) upon every Muslim." And when the Prophet ﷺ said: "Seeking knowledge is an obligation upon every Muslim," some scholars said: "What is meant by this is seeking the knowledge of the lawful and the unlawful," making the meaning of the two hadiths one.

And he ﷺ said: "Whoever strives for his family from what is lawful, he is like the warrior (mujāhid) in the path of God. And whoever seeks the world lawfully, in chastity, he will be in the rank of the martyrs."

And he ﷺ said: "Whoever eats the lawful for forty days, God illuminates his heart and causes springs of wisdom to flow from his heart upon his tongue." In another narration: "God makes him abstinent (zāhid) in this world."

It is narrated that Saʿd asked the Messenger of God ﷺ to ask God Most High to make his supplication answered. He ﷺ said to him: "Purify your morsel (ṭuʿmah), and your supplication will be answered."

And when the Prophet ﷺ mentioned the one eager for this world, he said: "Perhaps a disheveled, dusty man, driven about in journeys, whose food is unlawful, whose clothing is unlawful, nourished with the unlawful, raises his hands saying: 'O Lord, O Lord!' — so how could that be answered for him?"

In the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās from the Prophet ﷺ: "Indeed, God has an angel at the Holy House (Bayt al-Maqdis) who calls out every night: 'Whoever eats the unlawful, neither supererogatory (ṣarf) nor obligatory (ʿadl) deed is accepted from him.'" It was said: al-ṣarf is the supererogatory act, and al-ʿadl is the obligatory act.

And he ﷺ said: "Whoever buys a garment for ten dirhams, and in its price there is one unlawful dirham, God will not accept his prayer as long as any of it remains upon him."

And he ﷺ said: "Every flesh that has grown from the unlawful, the Fire is more deserving of it."

And he ﷺ said: "Whoever does not care from where he earns wealth, God does not care from which gate of the Fire He enters him."

And he ﷺ said: "Worship consists of ten parts; nine of them are in seeking the lawful." This is narrated as raised (marfūʿ) [to the Prophet] and also as stopped (mawqūf) upon some of the Companions.

And he ﷺ said: "Whoever reaches the evening weary from seeking the lawful, he passes the night forgiven, and wakes with God pleased with him."

And he ﷺ said: "Whoever obtains wealth from a sinful source (maʾtham), and thereby joins ties of kinship, or gives charity, or spends it in the path of God — God will gather all of that together, then cast it into the Fire."

And he, peace be upon him, said: "The best of your religion is scrupulous piety (waraʿ)."

And he ﷺ said: "Whoever meets God as one possessing waraʿ, God will give him the reward of all of Islam."

It is narrated that God Most High said in some of His books: "As for the scrupulous (waraʿūn), I am ashamed to call them to account."

And he ﷺ said: "A dirham from usury (ribā) is more severe before God than thirty acts of fornication in Islam."

In the hadith of Abū Hurayrah, may God be pleased with him: "The stomach is the basin (ḥawḍ) of the body, and the veins flow into it. When the stomach is sound, the veins issue forth with soundness; and when it is diseased, they issue forth with disease."

The similitude of one's food (ṭuʿmah) in religion is like the similitude of the foundation in a building: when the foundation is firm and strong, the building stands upright and rises high; and when the foundation is weak and crooked, the building collapses and falls. God, Mighty and Majestic, said: {«أَفَمَنْ أَسَّسَ بُنْيَانَهُ عَلَىٰ تَقْوَىٰ مِنَ اللَّهِ»} "Is he who founded his building upon piety from God..." (Q 9:109) — the verse.

And in the hadith: "Whoever earns wealth from the unlawful, then gives it in charity, it is not accepted from him; and if he leaves it behind him, it is his provision (zād) to the Fire."

We have already mentioned a collection of reports in the Book of the Etiquettes of Earning (Kitāb Ādāb al-Kasb) which reveal the virtue of lawful earning.

As for the traditions of the Salaf: It is narrated that al-Ṣiddīq [Abū Bakr], may God be pleased with him, drank milk from the earnings of his slave. Then he asked his slave [about it], and he said: "I practiced divination (takahhanat) for a people, and they gave me [this]." So he put his fingers into his mouth and began to vomit, until I thought his soul would depart. Then he said: "O God, I seek Your pardon for what the veins have carried and what has mixed with the intestines."

In some reports, it is mentioned that the Prophet ﷺ was informed of this and said: "Did you not know that al-Ṣiddīq does not let anything enter his belly except what is pure (ṭayyib)?"

Likewise, ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, drank from the milk of the charity camels (ibil al-ṣadaqah) by mistake, so he inserted his finger and vomited.

And ʿĀʾishah, may God be pleased with her, said: "You are indeed heedless of the most excellent act of worship — it is waraʿ."

And ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, said: "If you prayed until you became like bows (ḥanāyā), and fasted until you became like arrow-strings (awtār), none of that would be accepted from you except with a waraʿ that restrains [you from the unlawful]."

Ibrāhīm ibn Adham, may God have mercy on him, said: "Those who attained [the truth] only attained it by being mindful of what enters their bellies."

Al-Fuḍayl [ibn ʿIyāḍ] said: "Whoever knows what enters his belly, God writes him as a ṣiddīq (truthful one). So consider, O wretched one, with whom you break your fast."

It was said to Ibrāhīm ibn Adham, may God have mercy on him: "Why do you not drink from the water of Zamzam?" He said: "If I had a bucket, I would drink from it."

Sufyān al-Thawrī, may God be pleased with him, said: "Whoever spends from the unlawful in obedience to God is like one who purifies a filthy garment with urine — and a filthy garment is only purified by water. Likewise, a sin is only expiated by the lawful."

Yaḥyā ibn Muʿādh said: "Obedience is a treasure from the treasures of God, except that its key is supplication (duʿāʾ), and its teeth are lawful morsels (luqam al-ḥalāl)."

Ibn ʿAbbās, may God be pleased with them both, said: "God does not accept the prayer of a man in whose belly there is the unlawful."

Sahl al-Tustarī said: "A servant does not attain the reality of faith (ḥaqīqat al-īmān) until four qualities are in him: performing the obligatory acts according to the Sunnah; eating the lawful with waraʿ; avoiding what is prohibited, both outwardly and inwardly; and patience upon that until death."

And he said: "Whoever loves to be unveiled with the signs of the ṣiddīqīn, let him eat nothing but the lawful, and do nothing but in accordance with the Sunnah or necessity."

It is said: "Whoever eats the dubious (shubhah) for forty days, his heart is darkened." This is the interpretation of God's saying: {«كَلَّا بَلْ رَانَ عَلَىٰ قُلُوبِهِم مَّا كَانُوا يَكْسِبُونَ»} "Nay, but that which they earned has covered their hearts with rust" (Q 83:14).

Ibn al-Mubārak said: "To return a dirham of dubious origin is more beloved to me than to give in charity one hundred thousand dirhams, and one hundred thousand, and one hundred thousand" — until he reached six hundred thousand.

Some of the Salaf said: "A servant eats a morsel, and his heart turns over and becomes corrupted (yanghal) just as leather becomes corrupted, and it never returns to its former state."

Sahl, may God be pleased with him, said: "Whoever eats the unlawful, his limbs disobey [God] whether he wills or not, whether he knows or does not know. And whoever's food is lawful, his limbs obey him and are guided to good deeds."

Some of the Salaf said: "Indeed, the first morsel a servant eats from the lawful causes forgiveness of his past sins. And whoever places himself in a station of humility in seeking the lawful, his sins fall away from him like the falling of leaves from a tree."

It is narrated in the traditions of the Salaf that the preacher (wāʿiẓ), when he sat before the people, would say: "The scholars — examine three things in him. If he holds a heretical belief (bidʿah), do not sit with him, for he speaks with the tongue of Satan. If his food is evil, he speaks from caprice (hawā). And if he is not firm in intellect, he corrupts by his speech more than he rectifies — so do not sit with him."

In the well-known reports from ʿAlī, peace be upon him, and others: "This world — its lawful brings account (ḥisāb), its unlawful brings punishment (ʿadhāb)." Others added: "And its dubious brings reproach (ʿitāb)."

It is narrated that one of the righteous gave food to one of the Abdāl (substitutes), and he did not eat. He asked him about that, and he said: "We eat nothing but the lawful — therefore our hearts remain upright, our state endures, we are unveiled to the Kingdom (malakūt), and we witness the Hereafter. If we ate what you eat for three days, we would not return to anything of the knowledge of certainty (ʿilm al-yaqīn), and fear and witnessing would depart from our hearts." The man said to him: "But I fast perpetually and complete the Qurʾān thirty times every month." The Badal said to him: "This drink which you saw me drink at night is more beloved to me than thirty completions of the Qurʾān in three hundred units of prayer from your deeds." And his drink was from the milk of a wild gazelle.

There was a long companionship between Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal and Yaḥyā ibn Maʿīn. Aḥmad then abandoned him when he heard him say: "I do not ask anyone for anything — even if Satan gave me something, I would eat it." Yaḥyā apologized, saying: "I was joking." He [Aḥmad] said: "Do you joke about religion? Do you not know that eating is part of religion — God Most High placed it before righteous action, saying: {«كُلُوا مِنَ الطَّيِّبَاتِ وَاعْمَلُوا صَالِحًا»} 'Eat of the good things and do righteous deeds' (Q 23:51)."

And in the report: It is written in the Torah: "Whoever does not care from where his food comes, God does not care from which of the gates of the Fires He enters him."

And it is narrated from ʿAlī, may God be pleased with him, that after ʿUthmān was killed and the house was plundered, he did not eat any food except what was sealed, out of caution against the dubious (shubhah).

Al-Fuḍayl ibn ʿIyāḍ, Ibn ʿUyaynah, and Ibn al-Mubārak gathered at the house of Wahīb ibn al-Ward in Mecca, and they mentioned fresh dates (ruṭab). Wahīb said: "It is among the most beloved of foods to me, except that I do not eat it because of the mixing of Mecca's dates with the orchards of Zubaydah and others." Ibn al-Mubārak said to him: "If you look into such matters, bread would become straitened upon you." He said: "And what is its cause?" He said: "The origins of the estates have become mixed with the conquered lands (ṣawāfī)." Wahīb then fainted. Sufyān said: "You have killed the man." Ibn al-Mubārak said: "I only intended to make it light upon him." When he regained consciousness, he said: "God has upon me [an oath] that I will never eat bread again until I meet Him." He then drank milk. His mother brought him milk, and he asked her about it. She said: "It is from the sheep of so-and-so's family." He asked about its price and from where they had obtained it, and she mentioned [the details]. When he brought it near his mouth, he said: "It remains [to know] from where it was grazing." She was silent, so he did not drink, because it had grazed in a place in which there was a right of the Muslims. His mother said: "Drink, for God will forgive you." He said: "I would not love that God forgive me while I have drunk it, attaining His forgiveness through disobedience to Him."

Bishr al-Ḥāfī, may God have mercy on him, was among the scrupulous (waraʿūn). It was said to him: "From where do you eat?" He said: "From where you eat — but the one who eats while weeping is not like the one who eats while laughing." And he said: "A hand is shorter than a hand, and a morsel is smaller than a morsel." Thus were they — guarding themselves against the dubious (shubhāt).

chapters.title_en: The Categories of Lawful Sustenance and Its Entrances
chapters.arabic_text:
||| أصناف الحلال ومداخله

اعلم أن تفصيل الحلال والحرام إنما يتولى بيانه كتب الفقه ويستغني المريد
عن تطويله بأن يكون له طعمة معينة يعرف بالفتوى حلها لا يأكل من غيرها فأما
من يتوسع في الأكل من وجوه متفرقة فيفتقر إلى علم الحلال والحرام كله كما
فصلناه في  كتب الفقه
ونحن الآن نشير إلى مجامعه في سياق تقسيم وهو أن المال إنما يحرم إما
لمعنى في عينه أو لخلل في جهة اكتسابه
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ط ع م (ṭ-ʿ-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Sustenance, food, and that which is consumed for nourishment; also denotes tasting and the act of eating.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, ṭuʿmah refers to the lawful provision (rizq) that sustains the body, tied to divine decree and ethical acquisition.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) for physical food; metaphorical (majāz) for any means of benefit or livelihood.
- Root: ك س ب (k-s-b)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Acquisition, earning, and the act of seeking gain through effort or trade.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Kasb denotes the voluntary human act of acquiring wealth, distinct from divine provision (rizq), and is central to moral accountability.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for material gain; metaphorical for the spiritual earning of reward or sin.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Causal Clauses (al-Sharṭ wa al-Jazāʾ) — The phrase "إنما يحرم إما... أو..." employs a bipartite causal structure, where the prohibition is conditioned on either an intrinsic defect or an extrinsic flaw in acquisition, requiring precise parsing of the disjunctive (إمّا) and its correlative (أو).
chapters.translation:
I say: Know that the detailed exposition of the lawful and the unlawful is undertaken solely by the books of jurisprudence (fiqh), and the seeker (murīd) is spared its prolixity by having a specific sustenance whose permissibility he ascertains through legal opinion (fatwā), partaking of nothing beyond it. As for one who expands his eating across diverse sources, he stands in need of the entire science of the lawful and the unlawful, as we have detailed in the books of jurisprudence.

Now, we shall indicate its comprehensive principles in the form of a division: wealth is rendered unlawful either due to a meaning inherent in its very essence (ʿayn), or due to a defect in the manner of its acquisition (kasb).

chapters.title_en: The First Division: What Is Unlawful by Virtue of an Intrinsic Attribute (al-ḥarām li-ṣifatin fī ʿaynihi)
chapters.arabic_text:
|||| القسم الأول الحرام لصفة في عينه كالخمر والخنزير وغيرهما

وتفصيله أن الأعيان المأكولة على وجه الأرض لا تعدو ثلاثة أقسام فإنها
إما أن تكون من المعادن كالملح والطين وغيرهما أو من النبات أو من
الحيوانات
أما المعادن فهي أجزاء الأرض وجميع ما يخرج منها فلا يحرم أكله إلا من
حيث أنه يضر بالآكل وفي بعضها ما يجري مجرى السم والخبز لو كان مضرا لحرم
أكله والطين الذي يعتاد أكله لا يحرم إلا من حيث الضرر
وفائدة قولنا إنه لا يحرم مع أنه لا يؤكل أنه لو وقع شيء منها في مرقة أو
طعام مائع لم يصر به محرما
وأما النبات فلا يحرم منه إلا ما يزيل العقل أو يزيل الحياة أو الصحة
فمزيل العقل البنج والخمر وسائر المسكرات ومزيل الحياة السموم ومزيل الصحة
الأدوية في غير وقتها وكأن مجموع هذا يرجع إلى الضرر إلا الخمر والمسكرات
فإن الذي لا يسكر منها أيضا حرام مع قلته لعينه ولصفته وهي الشدة المطربة
وأما السم فإذا خرج عن كونه مضرا لقلته أو لعجنه بغيره فلا يحرم
وأما الحيوانات فتنقسم إلى ما يؤكل وإلى ما لا يؤكل وتفصيله في كتاب
الأطعمة والنظر يطول في تفصيله لا سيما في الطيور الغريبة وحيوانات البر
والبحر وما يحل أكله منها فإنما يحل إذا ذبح ذبحا شرعيا روعي فيه شروط
الذابح والآلة والذبح وذلك مذكور في
كتاب الصيد والذبائح وما لم يذبح ذبحا شرعيا أو مات فهو حرام ولا يحل
إلا ميتتان السمك والجراد وفي معناهما ما يستحيل من الأطعمة كدود التفاح
والخل والجبن فإن الاحتراز منهما غير ممكن فأما إذا أفردت وأكلت فحكمها حكم
الذباب والخنفساء والعقرب وكل ما ليس له نفس سائلة لا سبب في تحريمها إلا
الاستقذار ولو لم يكن لكان لا يكره فإن وجد شخص لا يستقذره لم يلتفت إلى
خصوص طبعه فإنه التحق بالخبائث لعموم الاستقذار فيكره أكله كما لو جمع
المخاط وشربه كره
PageV02P092
ذلك وليست الكراهة لنجاستها فإن الصحيح أنها لا تنجس بالموت إذ أمر رسول
الله صلى الله عليه وسلم بأن يمقل الذباب في الطعام إذا وقع فيه (1)
وربما يكون حارا ويكون ذلك سبب موته ولم تهرت نملة أو ذبابة في قدر لم
يجب إراقتها إذ المستقذر هو جرمه إذا بقي له جرم ولم ينجس حتى يحرم
بالنجاسة وهذا يدل على أن تحريمه للاستقذار ولذلك نقول لو وقع جزء من آدمي
ميت في قدر ولو وزن دانق حرم الكل لا لنجاسته فإن الصحيح أن الآدمي لا ينجس
بالموت ولكن لأن أكله محرم احتراما لا استقذارا
وأما الحيوانات المأكولة إذا ذبحت بشرط الشرع فلا تحل جميع أجزائها بل
يحرم منها الدم والفرث وكل ما يقضى بنجاسته منها بل تناول النجاسة مطلقا
محرم ولكن ليس في الأعيان شيء محرم نجس إلا من الحيوانات
وأما من النبات فالمسكرات فقط دون ما يزيل العقل ولا يسكر كالبنج فإن
نجاسة المسكر تغليظ للذجر عنه لكونه في مظنة التشوف ومهما وقعت قطرة من
النجاسة أو جزء من نجاسة جامدة في مرقة أو طعام أو دهن حرم أكل جميعه ولا
يحرم الانتفاع به لغير الأكل فيجوز الاستصباح بالدهن النجس وكذا طلاء السفن
والحيوانات وغيرها فهذه مجامع ما يحرم لصفة في ذاته
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ح-ر-م (ḥ-r-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning of prohibition and sacred inviolability; what is withheld or made forbidden.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Technical legal-theological sense of that which the Lawgiver (al-Shāriʿ) has rendered absolutely unlawful, whether in essence (ʿayn) or by attribute (ṣifah).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Used here in the literal (ḥaqīqah) sense of legal prohibition, not metaphorical sanctity.
- Root: ع-ي-ن (ʿ-y-n)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The physical substance or entity itself, as opposed to its accidental qualities.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The concrete particular (al-jawhar al-shakhṣī) as the locus of legal ruling.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal designation of the thing's own essence, contrasted with attribute-based rulings.
- Root: ض-ر-ر (ḍ-r-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Harm, injury, or detriment to body or health.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The operative rationale (ʿillah) for prohibition in non-intrinsically-unlawful substances.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal physical harm, not metaphorical or moral harm.
- Root: ن-ج-س (n-j-s)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Ritual impurity; filth in the legal sense.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Legal impurity (najāsah) that attaches to specific substances and transmits by contact.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal legal impurity, distinguished from mere disgust (istiqdhār).
- Root: ق-ذ-ر (q-dh-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Disgust, abhorrence, or revulsion of the soul.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The basis for prohibition of creatures lacking flowing blood — not impurity, but universal repugnance.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sensory disgust, as opposed to legal impurity.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Constructions (al-sharṭ wa al-istithnāʾ) — The text employs intricate conditional clauses (in/idhā) and exceptions (illā) to delineate legal categories; parsing requires identifying the protasis, apodosis, and the scope of the exceptive particle to preserve the precise juridical distinctions.
chapters.translation:
I say: The first division is that which is unlawful by virtue of an attribute residing in its very essence (al-ḥarām li-ṣifatin fī ʿaynihi), such as wine (al-khamr), the pig (al-khinzīr), and others like them.

The detailed exposition is that the edible substances (al-aʿyān al-maʾkūlah) upon the face of the earth do not exceed three categories: for they are either from minerals (al-maʿādin), such as salt, clay, and the like; or from plants (al-nabāt); or from animals (al-ḥayawānāt).

As for minerals, they are parts of the earth and everything that issues forth from it. Nothing of them is unlawful to eat except by virtue of the fact that it harms the eater. Among them there are things that run the course of poison. Even bread, if it were harmful, would become unlawful to eat. And the clay that people habitually eat is not unlawful except from the aspect of harm.

The benefit of our saying that it is not unlawful — even though it is not eaten — is that if some of it were to fall into a broth or a liquid food, it would not thereby render the whole unlawful.

As for plants, nothing is unlawful from them except that which removes the intellect (al-ʿaql), or removes life, or removes health. That which removes the intellect is henbane (al-banj), wine, and all other intoxicants (al-muskirāt). That which removes life is the poisons (al-sumūm). That which removes health is medicines taken at other than their proper time. It is as though the totality of this reverts to harm — except for wine and the intoxicants, for even that which does not intoxicate from them is also unlawful, however little it may be, by virtue of its essence and by virtue of its attribute, namely, the exhilarating potency (al-shiddah al-muṭribah).

As for poison, when it departs from being harmful — due to its small quantity or due to its being mixed with something else — it is not unlawful.

As for animals, they divide into what is eaten and what is not eaten. Its detailed exposition belongs to the Book of Foods (Kitāb al-Aṭʿimah). The inquiry would grow long in detailing it, especially concerning strange birds, beasts of the land and the sea, and which of them is lawful to eat. For it is only lawful when slaughtered with a legal slaughter (dhabḥ sharʿī) in which the conditions of the slaughterer, the instrument, and the act of slaughter are observed. That is mentioned in the Book of Hunting and Slaughtered Animals (Kitāb al-Ṣayd wa al-Dhabāʾiḥ). Whatever is not slaughtered in the legal manner, or dies [of itself], is unlawful. Nothing is lawful from carrion (maytah) except two: fish and locust. And in their meaning are included what transforms from foods, such as the worms of apples, vinegar, and cheese — for guarding against them is not possible. But if they are isolated and eaten [deliberately], their ruling is the ruling of the fly, the beetle, and the scorpion. And everything that has no flowing blood (nafs sāʾilah) has no cause for its prohibition except disgust (al-istiqdhār). Were it not for that, it would not be disliked. If a person is found who does not find it disgusting, no attention is paid to his particular temperament, for it has joined the category of abominations (al-khabāʾith) due to the universality of disgust. Thus eating it is disliked, just as if one were to gather mucus and drink it — that would be disliked.

PageV02P092

That [dislike] is not due to its impurity (najāsah), for the correct position is that it does not become impure by death, since the Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded that the fly be dipped into the food when it falls into it. And perhaps it may be hot, and that would be the cause of its death. Nor has an ant or a fly that fell into a cooking pot necessitated the throwing away of [the pot's contents]. For the disgusting thing is its body when its body remains; it does not become impure so as to render [the food] unlawful by impurity. This indicates that its prohibition is for disgust. For this reason, we say: if a part of a dead human being were to fall into a pot — even if it weighed a dāniq — the whole would become unlawful, not due to its impurity, for the correct position is that the human being does not become impure by death, but because eating him is prohibited out of reverence (iḥtirām), not out of disgust.

As for edible animals, when they are slaughtered according to the condition of the Law, not all their parts become lawful. Rather, unlawful from them are the blood, the excrement (al-farth), and everything of them that is judged to be impure. Indeed, consuming impurity absolutely is unlawful. But there is nothing among the [edible] substances that is both unlawful and impure except from animals.

As for plants, only the intoxicants are [unlawful and impure], not that which removes the intellect without intoxicating, like henbane. For the impurity of the intoxicant is an intensification of the deterrent against it, because it stands in the position of being eagerly desired. And whenever a drop of impurity, or a part of solid impurity, falls into a broth, a food, or an oil, eating all of it becomes unlawful. But using it for other than eating is not unlawful, so it is permissible to burn impure oil in lamps, and likewise to coat ships, animals, and other things with it. These, then, are the comprehensive principles of what is unlawful by virtue of an attribute in its very essence.
